en: Having prostrated with devotion before the primordial deity Vāsudeva, who is the true nature of all phenomena and the dissolution of all effects,
this compendium of all Smṛtis is [composed] under the guise of the Gautamīya.
Today, this commentary is composed by me, the son of Vāmana.
What, then, is its connection? This is stated: there are fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*).
As it is said: "The limbs [of the Veda], the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive Nyāya, the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstra—these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge."

The connection [of the text] is that this *Dharmaśāstra* is now commenced as one counted among them. Alternatively: *Saṃsāra* is the continuous cycle of birth, old age, and death, consisting of the conjunction and disjunction of the body, senses, and objects for the sake of a person’s experience of pleasure and pain. And that [cycle] has merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) as its cause, not any other cause. Since those two, merit and demerit, are the causes of the experience of desired and undesired [results], they are to be respectively adopted and avoided. Since both of these are not possible without full knowledge, Gautama composed this treatise for the purpose of awakening an understanding of the true nature of merit and demerit. This is also its specific purpose, because the adoption and avoidance of merit and demerit constitute the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). The subject matter (*abhidheya*) consists of the *Aṣṭakā* rites and so forth; just as the *Agniṣṭoma* and other sacrifices prescribed by the Vedas are necessarily to be performed, so too are the *Aṣṭakā* rites and others.
In this regard, since it is observed that all effects proceed from causes, [the author] first states the following in order to establish the specific nature of the cause:
"The Veda is the root of Dharma" (1.1).

Now, since a treatise consists of injunctions and prohibitions, one might object that only such statements as “the initiation of a Brahmin should take place in the eighth year” ought to be stated; however, statements such as “the Veda is the root of Dharma” should not be, because they are merely restatements (anuvāda) and thus lack purpose. Furthermore, the authority of the Veda is not established by this [statement], for its authority is self-evident (*svataḥ-siddha*). Otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), wherein the authority of that which establishes the authority [of the Veda] would require another, and that yet another.

It is said: This restatement (*anuvāda*) that the Veda is the root of Dharma is for the purpose of establishing that Smṛti and conduct (*śīla*) are also rooted in Dharma by means of it. If one asks how so, it is said: That cognition which arises without doubt regarding a specific meaning from the uttered words of the Veda for those who know the meaning of its terms—and which does not undergo subversion at another time, in another place, in another person, or in another state—is the root of Dharma. And since a cognition that arises as certain and non-erroneous can be determined to possess validity (*prāmāṇya*), and since there is no falsity in the conviction produced by the Veda caused by defects in the cause—because an author is not admitted—since it is a defect residing in an author that brings about the falsity of a cognition produced by sound; thus, the restatement serves the subsequent purpose.

Now the Sūtra is being explained: therein, the Veda is a collection of texts known as Mantra and Brāhmaṇa. The root *vid* means "to know"; it is called the Veda because by means of it the nature of Dharma and other matters is known. Although this definition applies equally to the Smṛtis and other such works, there is no fault here because the term is used in its conventional sense (*rūḍha*), like the word "parivrājaka" (wandering ascetic). Thus, another Smṛti states: "The Śruti is to be understood as the Veda, while the Dharmaśāstra is indeed the Smṛti" (MDh 2.10).

And that [Veda] is divided according to the distinctions of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth; the singular number is used with reference to its generic class (*jāti*). "Dharma" means action, conduct, or else that which is termed the "unseen potency" (*apūrva*). "Root" means cause, indicator, or authority (*pramāṇa*). Now, if it is argued that only the Veda consisting of injunctions (*vidhi*) and prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) functions as the means of cognizing Dharma and the like, and not that which takes the form of mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), we reply: since even the explanatory passages and the rest are auxiliary by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with an injunction, their status as the root of Dharma through an indirect lineage (*pāraṃparya*) is not contradictory. To begin with, the explanatory passage attains the nature of an injunction or prohibition by way of praise or censure; the mantra, however, serves this purpose by reminding one of the enjoined matter at the time of performance. Therefore, the Veda in every form is the root of Dharma.

Some maintain that the basis for dharma is solely the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) within the mantras; for instance, regarding the mantra "Thou art like a water-shed in the desert" (*dhanvann iva prapā asi*, RV 10.4.1), they conclude that a water-shed must be constructed, and so forth.
Others, however, say that the accomplishment of dharma arises from the mere study [of the Veda] itself. As it is said:
"He indeed performs the highest austerity even unto his fingertips."
"He who, even though wearing a garland, is a twice-born man who studies his own Veda daily according to his ability" [Manu Smṛti 2.168].
Therefore, the recitation itself is the root of Dharma.

This is incorrect, because it would result in the scriptural statements regarding the fruits of ritual actions being rendered meaningless, and because the fruit of study has been refuted by the Mīmāṃsakas. Alternatively, the word "Veda" refers to the action expressed by the Veda; that [action] is the root of Dharma.

If it is argued that this does not apply to acts such as the Śyena sacrifice, it is replied: even there, dharma certainly exists by way of protecting one's life, wealth, children, wife, and so forth, from the killing of enemies. From this, it is understood: "Whatever is seen here, such as children, cattle, and villages, and whatever is unseen, such as [rebirth in] heaven and so on—all that has dharma as its cause."

Dharma is of five kinds: the dharma of caste (*varṇadharma*), the dharma of life-stage (*āśramadharma*), the dharma of quality (*guṇadharma*), the dharma of both caste and life-stage (*varṇāśramadharma*), and the dharma of occasion (*nimittadharma*). The dharma of caste consists of study and so forth; the dharma of life-stage consists of the placing of fuel on the sacred fire and so forth; the dharma of quality consists of the protection and other duties of one endowed with qualities such as consecration (*abhiṣeka*); the dharma of both caste and life-stage consists of the palāśa staff for a Brāhmaṇa and so forth; and the dharma of occasion consists of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth. The "root" (*mūla*) means the cause. Thus it has been said: "For Dharma shone forth from the Veda" (MDh 2.10). Furthermore, the purpose of commencing this treatise is to show that just as the Veda is the root of Dharma, so too are the Smṛti and established conduct (*śīla*).
But the Veda alone is not the sole root of Dharma; rather—[the root of Dharma is] also the tradition (smṛti) and conduct (śīla) of those who know it. 1.2.

And for those who know the Vedas, both *smṛti* and *śīla* are also rooted in *dharma*. These two are also non-contradictory to the Vedas, because the text begins with the phrase "for those who know them" (*tadvidām*). Furthermore, the word *mūla* (root), being connected with two [terms], should be understood as having a dual ending. By the pronoun *tat* (that), the Veda with its six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is indicated. *Smṛti* is a formal composition created by Manu, Yama, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, Bhāradvāja, Gautama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Vyāsa, Śātātapa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Hārīta, Bodhāyana, Yājñavalkya, Pracetas, and others. *Śīla* is uncodified customary practice, such as auspicious rites for weddings and so forth; it is "uncodified" because it is manifold and varies according to region. The particle *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. As Manu said:

"The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛti and the conduct of those who know it, the practice of the virtuous, and also self-satisfaction" (MDh 2.6). At the time of concluding the twilight devotions, the performance of three circumambulations and so forth constitutes the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). Self-satisfaction is that knowledge which arises from those who know the Veda and are devoted to the performance of all [prescribed] duties, being free from fault. As he will state: "And that which the self-possessed elders... (GDh 9.62), and so forth.

Some describe it as follows: like the *aṣṭakā* and other such rites, there is no formal injunction for these [practices] such as festive auspiciousness (*kautuka-maṅgala*), because there is no sin in their non-performance. Furthermore, both "customary practice" (*ācāra*) and "self-satisfaction" (*ātmatuṣṭi*) are included within "virtue" (*śīla*) itself, and thus are not mentioned separately. The particle "and" (*ca*) also serves merely to collect what has already been stated. (1.2)
Now, he sets forth the prima facie argument: the conduct of those who know the Vedas is not the root of Dharma;
for, "A transgression of Dharma is observed. (1.3)

The ellipsis is "it does not attain the status of being rooted in Dharma. For example: Prajāpati’s lustful desire for his own daughter; Indra’s illicit approach to Ahalyā and so forth; and the failure of Vyāsa, Bhīṣma, and others to abide within the stages of life (āśrama). 1.3.
Moreover: "The daring of the great. 1.4.

The implication here is that even in this case, the status of being rooted in *dharma* is not attained, as indicated by the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*). By the word *sahas*, strength (*bala*) is meant; as Nārada says: "In this world, *sahas* is said to be strength" (NSm 14.1). Therefore, that which is done without regard for the scriptures and worldly convention is *sāhasa* (violence/transgression). This refers to the deeds of those renowned in the world, such as Rāma’s slaying of women like Tāṭakā, Paraśurāma’s cutting off of his mother’s head, and Vasiṣṭha’s entering the water, and so forth. Consequently, it is improper to claim that good character (*śīla*) is rooted in *dharma*.

Furthermore, what is the distinction between transgression of dharma (*dharmavyatikrama*) and rashness (*sāhasa*)? That which is performed improperly out of desire for sense objects is a transgression of dharma; that which is done under the sway of anger and the like is rashness. (1.4)
To this he replies:
"But not so when the object is perceived, because of the weakness of non-existence. (1.5)

The word *tu* serves to set aside the previous position. "Having a visible purpose" (*dṛṣṭārtha*) means having a perceptible motive; in such a case of a visible motive, virtuous conduct (*śīla*) is not the root of Dharma. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Dharma is that whose cause is not perceived" (VaDh 1.7). This is not the intended meaning here, for the context concerns transgression of Dharma and violence committed for a visible purpose. If that were the case, since the term *pragṛhya* would apply by the rule "īd udet" (Pāṇini 1.1.11) and so forth, the reading would have to be "dṛṣṭārthe ’varadaurbalyāt. Regarding "due to the weakness of the inferior" (*avaradaurbalyāt*): "inferior" (*avara*) means not excellent (*na vara*), i.e., base, overcome by hatred and other passions, and lacking knowledge of the ultimate truth—this is the meaning. "Due to his weakness" means due to his incapacity to discern between Dharma and Adharma. By this, it is made known that even great persons who possess such knowledge may sometimes be overcome, because for one who possesses a body, pleasure and pain are inevitable. Therefore, as long as these individuals are overcome by defects such as passion, their conduct should not be accepted as authoritative. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "But the cultured person (*śiṣṭa*) is one whose soul is free from desire" (VaDh 1.6). Alternatively, by the word *avara*, people of the present Kali age are meant; "due to their weakness" means due to their lack of capability. (1.5)

Having thus stated the authority of recollection (smṛti), he now says [the following] regarding what should be done when there is a mutual contradiction between sentences that apply to the same subject matter:
"In the case of a contradiction between those of equal strength, there is an option" (1.6).

An object established by an equal means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) possesses equal force. When there is a mutual contradiction between two such objects, an option (*vikalpa*) is to be understood, in the sense of "either this or that. There is no abandonment of both, because both have been established by valid cognition. Nor is there the acceptance of only one, for if one were accepted, it would follow that the second would be rendered purposeless. What is an example? First, in the Śruti: "The oblation should be offered after sunrise; the oblation should be offered before sunrise," and so forth. Also in the Smṛti, Gautama says: "Food into which hair or insects have fallen is always unfit to be eaten" (GDh 17.8–9).
"Food that has been pecked at by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon,
sneezed upon, or defiled by hair or insects, is purified by the scattering of earth," so says Manu (MDh 5.125).

But surely, since an option (*vikalpa*) is established here by implication alone, this sūtra is redundant; for a conjunction (*samuccaya*) is simply not possible here. Indeed, having offered after sunrise, one cannot offer again at sunrise, because it is improper for the principal act—the oblation—to be repeated on account of its subordinate element—time. For subordinate elements (*guṇa*) must follow the principal (*pradhāna*), but the principal does not follow the subordinate. Furthermore, it is impossible to perform the oblation at both times without repetition. Thus, even in the case of the Smṛti rules regarding purification and abandonment, a conjunction is likewise impossible due to their mutual contradiction. Nor is the abandonment of both reasonable, as has already been stated. Therefore, since only an option results here, this [sūtra] serves no purpose.

In that case, this is a restatement of what is established by logic for the sake of specifying a particular point. What is the distinction? It is that there is an option (*vikalpa*) only when two things of equal strength conflict; however, when they are of unequal strength, there is simply sublation (*bādha*). Therefore, when there is a conflict between *Śruti* (Vedic revelation) and *Smṛti* (tradition), the *Smṛti* alone is sublated. For in the case of *Śruti*, the word is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), whereas in the case of *Smṛti*, it is inferential (*ānumānika*). And an inference does not become a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when it contradicts direct perception. Likewise, in the case of a conflict between *Smṛti* and custom (*ācāra*), customs such as marrying the daughter of one’s maternal uncle are sublated; for in those cases, the *Smṛti* is inferred from the custom. This is because of the statement regarding an option in the case of conflict; but in the absence of conflict, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the rules of those who are equally authoritative, as in the case of ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) and so forth during Vedic rites.

Now, if it is argued that the inequality of strength between *smṛti* and *śruti* is established only by accepting that *smṛti* originates from the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the Veda, then those indicative marks found in mantra and *arthavāda* passages—which, though intended for another purpose, serve as the basis for *smārta* duties, such as "the boys like arrows" (RV 6.75.27) and so forth—would necessarily be weak when they contradict an explicit Vedic statement, because their inferential capacity would be blocked by that contradictory statement. On the other hand, if it is accepted that *smṛti* is preceded by lost Vedic recensions—as Āpastamba says: "The injunctions are stated in the Brāhmaṇas; their readings, having been lost, are inferred from usage" (ĀpDh 1.12.10)—then, since both are Vedic in origin, they would necessarily possess equal strength. For there is no distinction in strength between an inferred Vedic sentence and a perceived one, just as there is none between fire determined through perception and fire determined through inference. It might be argued: "In cases where a *smṛti* statement contradicts the Veda, it does not at all lead to the inference of a Vedic sentence; rather, it arises solely from error and the like."

And that is not tenable, because if one were to accept that the author of the *Dharmaśāstra* is untrustworthy, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of a general lack of confidence [in all authorities]. Even when the *Smṛti* is accepted as having come down through an uninterrupted tradition like the Veda, its status as being of equal strength is still not established; for that reason, even in that case, it is not tenable. As for the practice of marrying the daughter of a maternal uncle and so forth which was put forward, since it is a corrupt practice occurring only when one is overcome by desire and the like, it cannot be considered the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). However, that which is practiced by the learned according to the aforementioned characteristics without contradiction must indeed have equal strength with the *Smṛti*, because there is no difference in their being rooted in the Veda. Furthermore, a different purpose has been taught regarding the presence or absence of a formal textual basis (*nibandhana*). Nor can the relative strength or weakness of a practice—which takes the form of a *Smṛti* statement interposed between [the practice and the Veda]—be established based on its proximity to the inference of a Vedic statement.

To this it is replied: First of all, the inequality of strength between the Vedas and the others is understood precisely from the very capacity for the composition of the Sūtra. For if these were of equal strength, then in the event of conflict, an option (*vikalpa*) would already be established by that very capacity; what, then, would be the purpose of this Sūtra? Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "equal strength" would be redundant. On this view, the fact that the Smṛti is weaker than the Veda becomes logically consistent. It has already been stated that in that case, its origin from an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is established. Therefore, this very position is the correct one. As for the independent position that was mentioned, since the rule "and the tradition and conduct of those who know that" (GDh 1.2) exists, that position is indeed difficult to maintain. Consequently, the view that the Smṛtis originate from Vedic indicative marks is the most faultless.

But even so, this is not tenable, because in some cases we observe that *smṛti* sublates *śruti*. For example, while the qualification for Vedic rites applies generally, it is restricted by *smṛti* to specific individuals such as those who have undergone initiation (*upanīta*). Likewise, when there is a connection with a quality of the self through even a portion of the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), a specific fruit is declared. Similarly, although the killing of a cow is enjoined by the *śruti* in the injunction "one should sacrifice a cow," it is not performed because the prohibition found in *smṛti* is more powerful. Likewise, even though rites such as the *agnihotra*—which are conditioned by one's livelihood and require material substances—are enjoined, they are not performed by acquiring the necessary materials through means prohibited by *smṛti*, such as theft. Therefore, it is incorrect to say that "the *smṛti* is sublated by the *śruti*."

It is said: An investigation into the relative strength and weakness of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is appropriate only when there is a contradiction; however, where no contradiction exists, even that which is weak is not sublated at all. First of all, the eligibility for ritual action (*karmādhikāra*) of one who has been initiated is not contradicted by direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), because initiation is for the purpose of acquiring the Vedas, and that [acquisition] is for the purpose of ritual action; furthermore, the accomplishment of the primary act does not occur without a connection to a transcendental result (*apūrva*). As for what was stated—that "the killing of a cow, though enjoined by *śruti*, is nevertheless not performed"—that too is not based on *smṛti* alone, but also from the wording of a mantra: "Do not cause the cows to perish, cause the horses to perish," and so forth. Therefore, *śruti* is never sublated by *smṛti*.
Some say that the Smṛti is preceded by [Vedic] branches that have been lost.

That is incorrect. In this regard, it is investigated: did the lost branches perish even before the recollection, or at a later time? If they perished first, then recollection would not be possible, because they have already ceased to exist, and because memory is similar to a prior cognition. If they perished later, then it is not logical to say that they were preceded by lost branches, since they are perceived at that time. This is also the intended meaning of what Āpastamba stated: "They are lost in certain places, but not everywhere. Thus, an explanation must also be provided for the passage: "The readings of those [branches] which are lost are inferred from usage" (ĀpDh 1.12.10). 1.6.
Thus, this definition of the means of knowing dharma has been stated. Now, he speaks for the purpose of designating that which is known through memory:
"The initiation of a Brāhmaṇa is in the eighth [year]. (1.7)

*Upanayana* is the leading near (*upanayana*) to the Veda, to the fire, to the teacher, or to the restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*). This occurs in the eighth year, because of the capacity for counting years at that time. This is the obligatory (*nitya*) time for *upanayana*, since the optional (*kāmya*) and emergency (*āpatkalpa*) times are mentioned later. Because the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya are mentioned later, and because the Śūdra possesses only one caste (*ekajāti*), the mention of the Brāhmaṇa—though its meaning was already established—is undertaken here to establish that it is based on caste. Furthermore, being a Brāhmaṇa is not something produced like being twice-born (*dvijatva*). Thus, for a Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor, rules such as "They should pour hot [liquor] upon the Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor" (GDh 23.1), which are prescribed with reference to a Brāhmaṇa, apply even to one who has not been initiated. Alternatively, without the mention of the Brāhmaṇa, this [obligatory initiation] would apply to all three [castes]; however, the optional [initiation] would occur for the Brāhmaṇa in the ninth or fifth year (GDh 1.8), while for the other two, it would occur in the eleventh or twelfth years (GDh 1.13), because they are mentioned immediately after the optional [time]. Even in the absence of prior sacraments (*saṃskāra*), one is entitled [to Vedic study] through *upanayana*, but not by means of subsequent rites without this. Therefore, without mentioning the *garbhādhāna* and other rites, the *upanayana* alone is commenced here. (1.7)
The optional [rite] is performed on the ninth or the fifth day. || 1.8 ||

*Kāmya* means beneficial for a desired object—that which is capable of producing it. Although one might have said "in the fifth or the ninth," the deviation from the sequence is intended to include the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya between these two for the sake of adopting the time for optional rites (*kāmya*). Thus says Manu: "For a king desiring power, in the sixth; for a Vaiśya desiring wealth, in the eighth" [MDh 2.37]. The irregular compound is for the purpose of indicating the distinction between the optional rites. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "In the ninth for one desiring long life, and in the fifth for one desiring Vedic luster. The word *vā* (or) signifies an option; it should be understood according to one's own wish. 1.8.
The number of years begins from conception. 1.9.

The ten months accompanied by the embryo are called "the womb" (*garbha*). From that point onward, the calculation of years should be made, not starting from birth. Consequently, in such passages as "The initiation (*upanayana*) of a Brāhmaṇa," the phrase "in the eighth year from conception" (*garbhāṣṭame*) and so forth should be applied. 1.9.
That is the second birth. 1.10

That initiation is the second birth; the meaning is that one becomes a twice-born (dvija) when consecrated by it. The designation "twice-born" is established for the sake of conventional usage in such passages as, "The study of the Vedas is for the twice-born" (GDh 10.1). The inclusion of the term "that" (tat) is intended to encompass both the obligatory and optional initiations. 1.10.
Therefore, because he is the teacher. 1.11.

The inclusion of the word "that" (tad-) is for the purpose of including both the obligatory and optional initiations (*upanayana*). The designation is made for the sake of conventional usage in such passages as, "The teacher (*ācārya*) is the best among gurus" (GDh 2.57). || 1.11 ||
And because of the study of the Vedas. 1.1.12.

"Vedānuvacanaṃ" means the recitation of the entire Veda. It is for the sake of an unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*) that the teacher [is so called] by virtue of teaching even a single portion. And thus Manu says:
"One should know him here as a *guru* who, by that service of imparting sacred learning, benefits another with either little or much of what has been heard" (MDh 3.22).

If the purpose is visible, he is an *upādhyāya*. Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "But he who [teaches] one part is an *upādhyāya*" (VaDh 3.22). Because of the word "and" (*ca*), one who explains the ancillary sciences (*aṅga*) is also included. Likewise, Yāska says: "An *ācārya* gathers (*ācinoti*) proper conducts, gathers meanings, or [gathers] the intellect" (Nirukta 1.4).
Some explain the word "and" as having the sense of a conjunction with the preceding sūtra; thus, one becomes an *ācārya* precisely by performing both functions. And so Manu says:
"That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda..."
"One who possesses the ritual manuals (kalpa) and the secret doctrines (rahasya) is declared to be an Ācārya.
[MDh 2.140] Thus [ends the section]. 1.12.
The eleventh and twelfth [days] are for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, respectively. || 1.13 ||
This time is obligatory (nitya), because it is prescribed after the optional (kāmya) and the subsidiary (āpatkalpa) rites. 1.13.
But when there should be an omission of either the obligatory or the optional rites due to some cause such as famine, he then states the rule for times of distress:
"The *sāvitrī* of a Brāhmaṇa does not lapse until the sixteenth year. (1.14)

The prefix *ā-* here has the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*), meaning "together with the sixteenth year," as indicated by the mark [of the rule] "of more than two" (GDh 1.16) and because another Smṛti text is seen stating, "at the sixteenth, [one may perform] all desires. "Not fallen" means not having lost [caste]. By the word *sāvitrī*, that which effects it—initiation (*upanayana*)—is expressed. The meaning is that he becomes eligible for initiation. The mention of "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of ensuring that the birth-status (*jāti*) of even one who has not been initiated is not destroyed. And thus, even if the father and others have not been initiated, one becomes eligible for initiation through penance. Accordingly, Āpastamba says: "He whose father, grandfather, and great-grandfather... (ĀpDh 1.1.32), and so forth. 1.14.
For a Rājanya, there are two parts. 1.15.

Here too, the prefix *āṅ* continues [from the previous rule], along with the requirement of being accompanied by the word *varṣa*. The employment of the term *rājanya* is for the purpose of establishing the status of a king; for it is only one who has been initiated (*upanīta*) that possesses the qualification for kingship. || 1.15 ||
For a Vaiśya, [the fine is] two more than that. || 1.16 ||

That which is twenty-two together with two additional [units] is "dvyadhikā," meaning "of twenty-four. Although one should have said "caturviṃśateḥ" (of twenty-four), this specific expression is used in order to indicate that the prefix *aṅ* [in the previous rule] has an inclusive sense (*abhividhi*). || 1.16 ||
The time for initiation has been stated. Now, with the intention of explaining its requirements, he says:
"The girdles are made of muñja grass, a bowstring, or hempen thread, respectively. (1.17)

*Mauñjī* is a product of *muñja* grass. *Mūrvā* is well known; a product of that is *maurvī*. The term *jyāmaurvī* is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*), meaning "the bowstring which is made of *mūrvā*. Consequently, it should be taken after removing it from the bow. *Sūtra* refers to hemp-thread. The *maurvī* consists of a single strand, while the other two are triple-stranded. As Manu says:
"A girdle for a Brāhmaṇa should be made of *muñja*, triple-stranded, even, and smooth.
For a Kṣatriya, however, it is a bowstring of *mūrvā*; for a Vaiśya, it is made of hemp or flax. (MDh 2.42)
The mention of "in order" (*krama*) is for the purpose of excluding the duality of the bowstring and the sinew.
Some describe it as being optional in the absence [of the primary materials]. Thus says Manu:
"In the absence of *muñja* grass, however, [the girdle] should be made of *kuśa*, *aśmantaka*, or *balbaja*."
"By means of a threefold knot, or with one, three, or five [knots].
[MDh 2.43] This is because the sequence is established by logic, and the mention of "sequence" serves another purpose. || 1.17 ||
The skins of the black antelope, the spotted deer, and the goat. || 1.18 ||

The word *ajina* (deerskin) is connected with each [term]. *Kṛṣṇa* is the black antelope; *ruru* is the spotted deer; *basta* is well known [as the goat]. These are, respectively, the upper garments. And so it is stated in another Smṛti: "They should wear deerskin as their upper garment. 1.18.
The garments of hemp, linen, bark, and blankets are for all [classes]. 1.19.

*Śāṇa* is a product of hemp (*śaṇa*). *Kṣauma* is a product of *kṣumā*, which is flax (*atasī*). *Cīra* is [cloth] produced from *darbha* grass and similar materials. *Kutapa* is produced from the wool of mountain-dwelling goats. These are the lower garments. Since it is established that all [of these] possess an odd number [of strands], the mention of "all" (*sarveṣām*) in this context—despite the fact that another Smṛti states, "The garment of a Brāhmaṇa shall be of hemp or linen"—is intended either to preclude any specific sequential correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) or to serve as a general heading (*adhikāra*). (1.19)
And cotton that has not been processed. 1.20.

The word "of all" (sarveṣām) and "garment" (vāsaḥ) carry over [from the previous rule]. "Unaltered" (avikṛtam) means not connected with color [dye]; the meaning is that it is naturally white. The word "and" (ca) is for the purpose of indicating that the same applies to the preceding [garments] as well, insofar as they are unaltered. || 1.20 ||
Some [say] even the saffron robe [is not a cause for offense]. 1.21.

Some also maintain that there is a connection with passion (*rāga*); the word "also" (*api*) is used for the sake of censure. Therefore, this should be understood as applying in the absence of the aforementioned [causes].
Now, for the sake of establishing a rule regarding the side of the ochre robe, he says:
"The tree-bark [garment] is for the Brāhmaṇa. (1.22)
Or it may be made of tree bark processed with the decoction of *vṛṣaka*; that indeed is the garment of a Brāhmaṇa. 1.22.
Māñjiṣṭha and hāridra [are the colors] for the other two. || 1.23 ||
That which is dyed with madder is *māñjiṣṭha*, for a Kṣatriya; that which is dyed with turmeric is for a Vaiśya. 1.23.
The staffs of a Brāhmaṇa are made of *bailva* or *pālāśa* wood. || 1.24 ||

The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Bilva or Palāśa wood. Although they are mentioned here in a dual compound, nevertheless, because of the singular designation in the rule "or one fit for sacrifice for all" (GDh 1.26), and because of the observation in another Smṛti text that "having taken the desired staff" (MDh 2.48), it is proper that only a single staff be carried. 1.24.
The *āśvattha* and *pailava* [woods] are used for the remaining [vessels]. 1.25.

The *aśvattha* is well known; the *pīlu* is the *kalki*; regarding the remaining cases, those pertaining to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas: therein, for the Kṣatriya it is the *aśvattha*, and for the Vaiśya it is the *pailava*. (1.25)
Or rather, [the guest] is worthy of sacrifice for everyone. 1.26.

"Or he may be fit for sacrifice" means a specific type of tree, excluding the *vibhītaka*, *bilvaka*, *yāvaka*, and so forth. The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative in the absence [of the previous options]; thus, it applies when the preceding ones are unavailable. Otherwise, the word "or" would be redundant. The inclusion of the term "all" is intended to ensure that it does not apply only to the two immediately preceding cases. (1.26)
Now he states the qualities of the staff:
"Unworn, curved like a sacrificial post, and with its bark. (1.27)

"Unoppressed" (apīḍitāḥ) means not damaged by things such as vines, insects that wrap around them, or fire. "Bent like a sacrificial post" (yūpavakrāḥ) means having tips curved like a sacrificial post (yūpa). "With their bark" (saśalkāḥ) means possessing their outer skin. Because they are mentioned individually, all [of these qualities] apply to each tree, and not according to the respective order [of the list]. Thus Manu says: "They should all be straight, free from wounds, pleasant to behold, not causing distress to men, with their bark intact, and undamaged by fire. (MDh 2.47) || 1.27 ||
They are measured by the head, the forehead, and the tip of the nose. || 1.28 ||

The word *pramāṇa* (measure) is connected with each [term]. The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be measured to the top of the head; that of a Kṣatriya, to the forehead; and that of a Vaiśya, to the tip of the nose. And so says Manu: "The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made according to measure reaching to the hair-line; for a king (Kṣatriya), it should reach the forehead, but for a Vaiśya, it should reach the nose" (MDh 2.46). || 1.28 ||
Now he describes the dress of the religious student (brahmacārin):
"Those with shaven heads, those with matted hair, and those with topknots of matted hair. (1.29)

"Muṇḍa" means one whose head is shaved. "Jaṭila" means one who has hair. "Śikhājaṭa" refers to one for whom the tuft itself constitutes the matted locks. Thus, by the word *muṇḍa*, complete shaving is expressed. The particle *vā* (or) has the sense of "either... or" and is connected to each term—meaning "either a muṇḍa, or a jaṭila, or a śikhājaṭa. The plural number is used with reference to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. The word "or" (*vā*) was not stated for the purpose of excluding a sequential order. And so Manu says: "He may be a muṇḍa, or a jaṭila, or he may be a śikhājaṭa" (MDh 2.219). || 1.29 ||
Now, since one who possesses purity has the right to study, the purification of objects is first described for the sake of that purity:
"If one is impure while holding an object in the hand, he should set it down and perform ācamana. (1.30)

When one who has begun the feeding of Brahmins or similar rites, holding an object in hand, becomes impure due to contact with something defiled (ucchiṣṭa) for some reason—though previously he was not defiled—he should then place that object on the ground and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). Thus says Vasiṣṭha:
"If, while engaged in serving food, he should touch something defiled, he should place that object on the ground, sip water, and proceed again. [VaDh 3.43]

If the intention were to prescribe purification for the person, the mention of "taking hold of the object with the hand" would be redundant; therefore, purification of the object occurs merely by setting it down, while the person is purified by sipping water (ācamana). As for the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of an object mentioned in another Smṛti—"An object is purified by being set on the ground and then sprinkled"—that should be understood as referring specifically to edible cooked substances.
But how is a distinction to be understood from a sūtra composed of equal [syllables], such that purification follows from setting it down and sipping water, and not otherwise when it is not set down?

It is replied: If it were intended that one should sip water (ācamana) without setting down [the object], then only this much would need to be stated: "One who has something in hand and has become impure (ucchiṣṭa) should sip water. Why, then, would the act of setting it down be mentioned? Therefore, because it exceeds the requirements of the rule, it is understood that the position of setting it down is indeed what is intended. As for that which was stated by Manu: "But if one who has something in hand is somehow touched by someone who is impure, he shall attain purity by sipping water even without setting that object down" (MDh 5.143).

Thus, this [rule] should be understood as referring to substances that are not intended for consumption. Accordingly, non-edible items such as unripe plantains and the like are purified by mere setting aside; edible items, once cooked, are purified by being placed on the ground and sprinkled with water; and non-edible items such as clothing are purified by not setting them aside and simply rinsing the mouth. Now he states the purification of objects: "1.31.
The purification of metallic, earthen, wooden, and woven-cloth vessels is by wiping, burning, scraping, and washing, respectively."

The purification of metallic and other substances is achieved through scrubbing and so forth, in due order. Once their status as substances is established, the specific mention of them as "substances" (*dravya*) is for the purpose of indicating their capacity to perform their own functions. Consequently, there is no purification required for broken vessels and the like. Those things which are made by means of fire (*tejas*) as the instrumental cause are "metallic" (*taijasa*), such as gold and the like. Regarding those metallic objects defiled by food remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*): why is this so? Because for those defiled by urine and the like, other methods of purification are prescribed in another Smṛti. Thus says the *Auśanasa*: "For metallic objects defiled by urine, feces, semen, or a corpse, there shall be heating (*āvartana*), scraping (*ullekhana*), and scrubbing twenty-one times with ashes. For non-metallic objects in such a state, there shall be discarding. Likewise, regarding an object defiled by the bodily impurities of others, the statement of Kaṇva begins: "For those defiled by phlegm and the like, purification comes from twenty-one scrubings. Similarly, the statement of Uśanas concerning those defiled by the remnants of untouchables begins appropriately: "For those defiled by a Śūdra of the same caste (anuloma), a dog, or a crow, there is scraping; for those defiled by touchable persons among the inverse castes (*pratiloma*), there are twenty-one scrubings; for those defiled by untouchables, there is heating. Likewise, the statement of Śaṅkha concerning those defiled by meat or blood begins: "Clay, brick, the paste of *iṅguda*, *bilva*, and mustard seeds, cow's urine, cow dung, and so forth, are the materials for purification. Likewise, the statement of Paiṭhīnasi is: "For those defiled by a menstruating woman, one should place them in the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for one day, and purification comes from twenty-one scrubings. Thus, other methods of purification are ordained in other Smṛtis for metallic objects defiled by various other impurities. Therefore, it is logical to apply these [rules] specifically to those defiled by food remnants. For those defiled by food remnants, "scrubbing" means rubbing all around with ashes. Regarding earthenware (*mārttika*)—that is, those made of clay—defiled by untouchables: why? Because a specific rule is seen in another Smṛti. Thus says Uśanas: "For earthenware defiled by food remnants, there is wiping away; for those touched by food remnants, there is sprinkling. Likewise is the statement of Vasiṣṭha.
Earthenware that has come into contact with liquor, urine, feces, phlegm, pus, tears, or blood cannot be purified by re-firing. [VaDh 3.59]

Thus, the abandonment of items defiled by liquor and the like has been stated. Therefore, in this context, it is logical to prescribe purification only for those things defiled by *caṇḍālas* and others. "Burning" (*pradāha*) means thorough burning, that is, the restoration of the original nature. For wooden objects such as seats and beds defiled by impure substances (*amedhya*) and the like, there is "planing," which is the thinning away of the surface to the extent that it was defiled. For those touched by the untouchable (*aspṛśya*), there is sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). Why? Because of the statement of Manu: "Sprinkling is for solid masses" (MDh 5.115). For those things capable of being washed, there is washing. This applies to woven goods (*tāntava*), i.e., items made of threads such as cotton and its derivatives, when defiled by the untouchable. Regarding defilement by filth (*mala*), another Smṛti text should be consulted: "Washing, cutting out that portion, or discarding. This refers to the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: "Of clothes and the like defiled by filth and so forth. Likewise, one should refer to the rules stated by Manu, such as "of woolen cloths (*aṃśupaṭṭa*) with bilva fruits" (MDh 5.120). For many garments defiled by the untouchable, there is sprinkling, because Manu prescribes purification by sprinkling alone for "many grains and garments" (MDh 5.118). Therefore, for a small number of items defiled by the untouchable, there is cleansing (*nirṇejana*). 1.31.
As in the case of fire, [the color] of stones, gems, conch-shells, and mother-of-pearl [is perceived]. 1.32.

The purification of stones and the like is like that of metallic objects. This extension [of the rule] is intended to refer to the purifications mentioned in other Smṛtis. Regarding stones and gems, it is heard in scripture:
"A golden vessel free from stains is purified by water alone;
so too one made of stone, and likewise a silver vessel that has not been [chemically] treated" (MDh 5.112).
And for conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and gems, [purification is performed] with cow urine or water.
Thus says the word of Manu: "With milk [one purifies] conch shells and mother-of-pearl," so says the word of Paiṭhīnasi. 1.32.
The bones and the earth are like wood. 1.33.

"Bones" refers to substances fit for common use, such as ivory and the like. By stating that "land, houses, and so forth are like wood," he indicates an extension (*atideśa*) by means of the material substance; this makes known that whatever purification is prescribed for a product (*vikāra*), that same purification applies to its constituent material (*prakṛtidravya*). Otherwise, it would have had to be stated simply as "like wood. This extension regarding bones and land serves the purpose of referring to what is taught in other Smṛtis. And thus says another Smṛti: "The purification of land and bones touched by those who are untouchable is by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*)," according to the statement of Kaṇva. (1.33)
And the sowing of the ground. 1.34.

The mention of "ground" (*bhūmi*) is for the purpose of excluding bones. By the word "and" (*ca*), those things mentioned in other *smṛtis* should also be understood. Thus it has been stated by Vasiṣṭha:
"By digging, by burning, by scraping, and also by being trodden upon by cows—by these four means the ground is purified, and fifthly by smearing. [VaDh 3.57]
And so Manu says:
"By sweeping, by sprinkling, by burning, by scraping, and by the dwelling of cows—the earth is purified by these five means. (MDh 5.124)
Purification should be performed according to the nature of the stain, either by means of individual options or by their combination. 1.34.
[The same applies] to cloth, rope, split bamboo, and leather. || 1.35 ||

A rope is made of *darbha* grass and the like; a wicker-work (*vidala*) is made of bamboo, peacock feathers, and so forth; and leather is tiger-skin and the like. The purification of these when touched by the untouchable is like that of cloth—that is, like that of a garment. By the word "leather" (*carman*), the inclusion of its derivatives is intended through the inclusion of the raw material itself. This extension [of the rule] is for the purpose of including even sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) for ropes and the like; therefore, sprinkling must also be performed for those touched by the untouchable. And thus Paiṭhīnasi says: "The purification of ropes, wicker-work, and leather when touched by the untouchable is by means of sprinkling. (1.35)
Or there is the discarding of those that are utterly corrupted. 1.36.

Or there may be the abandonment of ropes and such. This is an alternative based on specific circumstances; therefore, those that are utterly ruined are to be abandoned, while for others, purification is required. 1.36.

Now, since it has been stated that "one who has something in hand or is impure from eating should set it down and perform ācamana," he speaks with the intention of prescribing that rite of sipping water:
"One should begin the purification facing either the east or the north. (1.37)

"Facing east or north" is an option according to one's preference. Now, an objection might be raised: "The mention of 'purity' (śauca) is redundant, because it will be stated later that 'one should sip water' (ācāmet), and by that alone the purpose is already accomplished. To this it is replied: This is intended to show that other ancillaries of purity as well should be performed while facing these very directions. And thus, even acts such as washing the feet should be performed while facing those same directions. The word "should begin" (ārabheta) is for the sake of concentration; therefore, until the completion of the sipping of water, one should remain with an undistracted mind. (1.37)

Seated in a clean place, having placed his right arm between his knees, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, having washed his hands up to the wrists, and remaining silent, he should sip water three or four times so that it touches his heart. 1.38.

"In a clean place, in a spot that is not defiled. By this, it is established that even the washing of the feet must be performed there; otherwise, because of contact with the impure feet, the place itself might become impure. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "Having washed both feet and the hands up to the wrists" (VaDh 3.26). "Seated indeed," meaning not in any other posture. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "One should not sip water while walking, standing, lying down, or bowing" (VaDh 3.30). "Placing the right arm between the knees. Regarding the term *yajñopavītī*: even if one happens to be sitting without the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), one must nevertheless necessarily be wearing the sacred thread during the sipping of water. And so says Āpastamba: "In the service of teachers, elders, and guests; at the fire-oblation (*homa*); in the rite of silent recitation (*japa*); at a meal; when sipping water; and in private Vedic study—one should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder" (ĀpDh 1.15.1). This is either as an ancillary part of the sipping of water, or for the purpose of producing another sacred thread [if the previous one was improperly worn]. And so says Vasiṣṭha.

"For those who have completed their Vedic studies (snātakas), there should always be an inner garment as well as an upper garment, two sacred threads, a staff, and a water-pot with water. [VaDh 12.14]

The wrist-joint (*maṇibandha*) is that region where a jewel is bound; therefore, having washed the hands up to the wrist-joint, one should—remaining silent and with speech controlled—touch the heart with water reaching the heart. This is for the purpose of defining the quantity of water: they should be just enough to submerge a bean (*māṣa*). Thus Uśanas says: "They should reach the heart, being just enough to submerge a bean. The option between "three times" or "four times" here is fixed: when one sips water after reciting the mantra beginning with "May the waters purify," then it is four times; otherwise, it is three times. The mention of "water" (*ap*) is for the purpose of excluding cow-urine and the like, so that they might not be included due to their commonality as causes of purification. Or, it is for the purpose of avoiding hot water, bubbles, foam, astringent extracts, and so forth. While one could simply say "he should drink" (*pibet*), the use of the longer term "he should sip" (*ācāmet*) in the aphorism is for the sake of including other injunctions. Regarding this, Uśanas says: "Having formed the palm of the right hand in the shape of a cow's ear, he should drink silently through the *brāhma* tīrtha, meditating upon the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. (1.38)
One should wipe it twice. 1.39.

The lips are part of the *prakṛti* (the primary source), because they are not explicitly mentioned here and because it is seen in other scriptural traditions; [therefore, one should touch them] with the *brāhma* *tīrtha* alone. The prefix *pari-* is used for the purpose of including other injunctions. Regarding this, Kaṇva has stated: "While meditating upon the Atharvaveda, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas, one should wipe the hairy region of the lips with the *brāhma* *tīrtha*. (1.39)
And he should sprinkle his feet with water.

By the use of the word "ca" (and), the mouth is also included. The prefix *abhi-* is intended to include other alternative rules. Regarding this, Bhārgava says: "One should wipe the lips, then wipe the mouth while meditating on the fires; then one should sprinkle the feet while meditating on Viṣṇu. (1.40)
And he should touch the cavities of the head. 1.41.
The apertures in the head are the eyes, the nose, and the ears; by the word "and" (*ca*), the heart is also included. And so Manu says:
"One should first sip water three times, then wipe the mouth twice;
one should touch the apertures with water, as well as the self, the heart, and the head. (MDh 2.60)

The prefix *upa-* is intended to include other alternative methods. In this regard, Uśanas says: "Having meditated on the sun and moon as the two eyes while touching them with the thumb and the ring finger; then, having meditated on the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) as the cavities of the nose while touching them with the index finger and the thumb; then, having meditated on the quarters of space as the two ears while touching them with the little finger and the thumb; then, one should touch the heart with the thumb alone, meditating upon the Self. (1.41)
And one should place it upon the head. || 1.42 ||

Although it would have been sufficient to say "on the head" (*mūrdhani*), the inclusion of the word "should give" (*dadyāt*) is for the purpose of including all the fingers. Thus, another *smṛti* states: "Having meditated on Śrī with all the fingers, one should cast [the water] upon the head. By the use of the particle "and" (*ca*), it is also implied that [water] should be given to the left hand. Accordingly, Vasiṣṭha says: "And one should give [water] on the head and to the left hand" (VaDh 3.29). Since no specific distinction is mentioned for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, this same method of sipping applies to them as well. Furthermore, because another *smṛti* states, "Women and Śūdras [sip] once each" (MDh 5.139), it should be understood that for women and Śūdras, purification is achieved by drinking once and touching the lips once, even though this is not explicitly stated here. (1.42)
Rinsing the mouth is not required only upon touching what has been left over from eating; he now states other occasions for rinsing the mouth:
"After sleeping, after eating, and after sneezing, again. (1.43)

The repetition of the word "again" is for the purpose of indicating that one should perform the sipping of water (ācamana) both at the beginning and at the end; the particle *ca* implies also after bathing and after weeping. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Having slept, eaten, sneezed, bathed, drunk, or wept, one who has already sipped water should sip again" [VaDh 3.38]. If it is argued that because sneezing occurs at an indefinite time, it is impossible to perform the sipping at the very beginning, even in that case the undertaking is for the sake of constant purity. As Āpastamba says: "Even for a moment, as long as he is able, he should not remain impure" [ĀpDh 1.15.8]. Therefore, since the sipping is prescribed even for one who was already pure immediately after sleeping and so forth—by the force of the initial injunction—one should perform the sipping both at the beginning and at the end.

Regarding that, some desire a double sipping of water (ācamana) even at the beginning of a meal. Thus says Āpastamba: “One who is about to eat, being pure, should sip water twice” [ĀpDh 1.16.9]. Others, however, desire a double sipping only at the end of sleeping and so forth, as Uśanas says: “Having slept, eaten, sneezed, bathed, drunk, or wept, one who has already sipped water should sip twice again. And thus, there is a double sipping at the beginning and the end of a meal; for sleeping and the like, there is a single sipping at the beginning and a double sipping at the end. Since sneezing is not fixed [in timing], the established conclusion is that there is a double sipping only at the end. 1.43.
Now, since impurity would result from contact with food remnants, he says:
"Regarding particles stuck between the teeth, they are treated like the teeth themselves, except when touched by the tongue. (1.44)
The meaning is that when the parts of food—whether solid or soft—are caught between the teeth, one does not become impure by leavings, provided they are not touched by the tongue. 1.44.
In this case as well, some say: "prior to falling away" (prāk cyuteḥ). 1.45.
Some maintain that even if there is contact with the tongue, one remains pure as long as [the food] has not fallen from its place. 1.45.
One should know that when [food] has fallen [to the ground], it is like a leak; one remains pure by simply swallowing it. 1.46.

One should understand that the water which falls into the mouth is like saliva; swallowing it, one remains pure. The meaning is that there is no requirement for sipping water (ācamana). Thus, even by swallowing saliva, one remains pure. Why? Because, whereas it would have been sufficient to state simply that "one is pure by swallowing what has fallen," the author begins by saying, "one should know it is like saliva. Gautama, however, maintains that one becomes impure when food stuck between the teeth is touched by the tongue. Another opinion holds that this applies only before such falling [from the teeth]. This is a settled option (*vyavasthitavikalpa*): for one authorized to perform ritual acts (*karmānuṣṭhāna*), there must be sipping of water, but not for anyone else. 1.46.

Just as a remnant of food that has fallen outside renders one impure, so too it might be thought that a drop of saliva would do the same; therefore, he says: "Droplets do not make one impure by their very nature, provided they do not fall upon the body. (1.47)

"Oral" (*mukhya*) means those things pertaining to the mouth; "droplets" (*vipruṣaḥ*) refers to the particles of saliva. These, when emitted by one who is reciting a mantra, do not cause a loss of ritual purity (*aprāyatya*) provided they do not fall upon a limb such as the breast or the belly. The word "ni-" signifies certainty. Therefore, it is certain that only if they fall upon a limb do they immediately render one impure; this does not happen through mere suspicion. Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that while a particle of saliva falling anywhere else causes impurity, a droplet of saliva [only causes impurity] when it falls upon a limb. 1.47.
Now, for the sake of all forms of purification, this is stated: "Purification consists in the removal of stains and odors from that which is smeared with impurities. (1.48)

When the removal of stains and odors has been performed, that which was smeared with impurity—that is, connected with impurity—attains purity. By the word "impurity" (*amedhya*), the twelve types of bodily excretions are meant. As Manu says:
"Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nasal mucus, phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat—these are the twelve impurities of human beings. (Manusmṛti 5.135)

The mention of "smearing" (*lepa*) is because phlegm and other such substances, whose odors are not manifest, are seen merely as smears. The mention of "odor" (*gandha*) is because urine and other such substances do not have smears perceived, but their odor alone is perceived. Furthermore, the repetition of the word "purification" (*śauca*) in the section on purification is for the purpose of indicating that even metallic objects and the like are purified only by the removal of both smears and odors. 1.48.
To the question "By what means should that be done?", he says: "That [should be done] first with water and with clay. (1.49)

That purification is first with water, then with earth; by the use of the word "then" (*ca*), it is implied that it is subsequently done with both. The mention of "that" (*tat*) is for the purpose of removing even food-stains with powder and the like. Although one could simply say "with water and earth," the inclusion of the word "first" (*pūrva*) is for the sake of indicating that where no significant stain is perceived, purification is to be performed with water alone. As Manu says:
"A gold vessel free from stains is purified by water alone, as are those made of lotus-material, stone, and silver, provided they are not tarnished. (MDh 5.112)

Alternatively, this is for the purpose of establishing that wherever purification is prescribed, purification with water alone must first be performed there. Just as [water] is combined with clay according to the rule "with clay and water," the use of a non-compound (visamāsa) here is likewise for the sake of including other materials such as ashes. Since substances like *taijasa* (metallic) and others have already been mentioned, this purification should be understood to apply to a part of the body smeared with impure substances.
And in the conjunctions of urinating, defecating, discharging semen, eating, and sexual intercourse. || 1.50 ||

The word *ca* (and) serves to draw in the requirement for sipping water (*ācamana*). "Dropping" (*visraṃsana*) means casting out; this is connected individually with urine, feces, and oily substances (*sneha*). "Contact with food" (*abhyavahārasaṃyoga*) is the consumption of edible substances. This statement is made for the purpose of removing stains and odors because of their impurity (*amedhya*), since the sipping of water is already established by the rule "having slept and having eaten," and the removal of stains and odors should be performed by washing with earth and water. Thus, in the passage "that [removal] first with water," what was stated regarding the removal of food-stains by means of powder and so forth should be understood as referring to cases where this [washing with earth and water] is impossible.

Alternatively, even the mention of the connection with eating is intended solely for the purpose of *ācamana* (ritual rinsing). That which is already established by the phrase "having slept and having eaten" is restated for the sake of establishing the proper sequence. How so? By the mention of "that" (*tat*), the removal of food-smeared particles is indicated; the meaning is that one should rinse after first performing that removal. Otherwise, there would be doubt. Thus says Āpastamba: "Having voided urine or feces, having washed away the smears of urine and feces, the smears of food, the smears of food-leavings, and those smears of semen, and having washed his feet and performed *ācamana*, he becomes pure" [ĀpDh 1.15.23]. "Urine" and "feces" are well known. "Sneha" refers to semen. The mention of urine and the others is for the purpose of *ācamana*, since the removal of smears and odors is already established by the rule: "Purity consists in the removal of smears and odors. (1.50)
And where the sacred tradition (Āmnāya) may enjoin [a practice]. 1.51.

In this context, the remainder of the sentence is "that very thing [remains]. The *āmnāya* is the Veda; where, in the domain of sacrifice, it prescribes purification by the mere washing of the wooden sword (*sphya*) and other implements, there that very thing [applies], and not [purification] such as carving based on the commonality of being wood. If it is argued that this is established simply because their strengths are unequal, [we reply: this statement is made for the purpose of preventing what is declared in the Veda from entering into worldly affairs. For example, since the Veda has stated that in the context of sacrifice purification occurs through the washing of a ladle (*darvī*), when that same ladle is employed in a worldly activity, one should not assume purification based on the commonality of being a ladle; rather, this statement is made so that one should perform only what is prescribed by *smṛti*.

Alternatively—the word *āmnāya* refers to Manu. Wherever he prescribes purification, that alone should be followed, as in the passage beginning, “But for ascetics, fourfold” (MDh 5.137). If it is argued that there is no doubt precisely because it has been stated by him, we reply: in a matter where nothing at all is stated, that which is stated in another Smṛti applies. However, in a case where something such as the removal of stains and odor is mentioned, a suspicion arises that there may be an option (*vikalpa*) with another Smṛti; therefore, to dispel that, it is said, “and wherever the *āmnāya* prescribes. And thus, even when the removal of stains and odor has been performed, one must still resort to rules such as, “Twofold for a student” (MDh 5.137). || 1.51 ||
Now, he describes the rule for approaching the teacher for the purpose of study by the student who has performed his purification:
"Having grasped the left hand [of the teacher] except for the thumb, he should address the teacher, saying: 'Recite, sir! (1.52).

Having grasped with his right hand the left hand—excluding the thumb, that is, omitting the thumb—he should request the teacher, the instructor, saying, "Recite, sir! The mention of the "hand" is for the purpose of excluding the feet. Since the context concerns the hand, it is understood that he grasps the left *hand* as well. It is understood that the grasping occurs at the region of the fingers, because it was stated "excluding the thumb.
Furthermore: therein, the eye and the mind. 1.53.
The meaning is that one should fix one's eyes and mind upon the guru therein. || 1.53 ||
Furthermore: the touching of the vital breaths with *darbha* grasses. 1.54.

The word "should be done" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Since it is impossible to touch the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) directly, the term "vital breaths" refers here to the sense organs located in the head, such as the eyes and so forth. One should touch them with *darbha* grass, following the sequence prescribed for the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). 1.54.
Furthermore: "The three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) consist of fifteen measures (mātrās). [1.55]

The word "should be performed" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. *Prāṇāyāma* is the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is remaining in a state of suspended breathing; these three [postures] should be performed. Each consists of fifteen *mātrās*. A *mātrā* is what is commonly known in the world by the term "the snap of the middle finger and thumb. (1.55)
Furthermore:
"And the seat is upon grasses with their tips pointing eastward. (1.56)

"On blades of *darbha* grass with their tips pointing eastward"—this follows from the context; "seating" means sitting down; "should be performed" is the ellipsis. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that he should also have *darbha* strainers in his hands. 1.56.
Furthermore: "The five vyāhṛtis preceded by Oṃ and ending with Satya. (1.57)

The word "should be cited" is the ellipsis. Each [of these worlds] is preceded by the *praṇava* (OM), beginning with *bhūr*, followed by *bhuvaḥ*, and so on, up to *puruṣaḥ* and ending with *satyam*. Thus it is well known in the *Jābāli-śruti*. (1.57)
Furthermore: the clasping of the teacher's feet in the morning. 1.58.

The word "kāryam" (it should be done) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Although "upasaṃgrahaṇam" (clasping the feet) should have been stated, the use of the term "pāda" (feet) is for the purpose of including the rules taught in other Smṛtis. As Manu says:
"The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands;
the left foot should be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand. [MDh 2.72]
Rising day after day at dawn, he should perform the touching of the vital breaths before the teacher, lest the teacher should perceive his own [impurity]. (1.58)
Furthermore:
And at the beginning and end of the recitation of the Brahman, [the word "svasti" is uttered]. 1.59.
"At the beginning and end of the Veda-recitation" means at its commencement and conclusion. The word "and" (ca) serves to include the clasping of the teacher's feet. || 1.59 ||
Furthermore: Having been permitted, the disciple should sit to the south, facing either east or north. 1.60.

Instructed by the teacher, he should sit to the south of him, facing either east or north; the option depends on what is possible. The meaning is that he should sit facing either east or north in such a way that he is directly opposite the seated teacher. How so? Because it has been stated: "There, his eye and mind [should be fixed on the teacher]" (GDh 1.53). The mention of the "disciple" is for the purpose of making known that this same rule applies to anyone else who has approached for instruction. Furthermore, the phrase "permitted, to the south" is a restrictive rule, meaning that one should not sit down without permission, nor should one sit anywhere other than to the south. 1.60.
Moreover:
"And the Sāvitrī is the recitation at the beginning when undertaking the Veda. (1.61)
The *sāvitrī* is that beginning with "tat savituḥ" and so forth; by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the syllable *oṃ* are also included. Thus says Manu:
"The three imperishable great *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, and the three-footed *gāyatrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman. [MDh 2.81]
The recitation is to be studied. "At the taking up of the Brahman" means at the commencement of the Veda; that is to say, at the time of beginning the study. From the beginning, first. 1.61.
Furthermore: "The syllable Oṃ occurs elsewhere as well. (1.62)

Immediately after the recitation, the syllable *oṃ* should also be uttered; this applies elsewhere as well. Here is the sequence: having risen in the morning, one should perform the clasping of the teacher’s feet; then, being summoned by him, one should sit upon *darbha* grass. Then, touching the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with *darbha* blades, and having performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and recited the five Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), one should address the teacher with joined palms, saying, “Recite, sir! Having then uttered the *Vyāhṛtis* preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and the *Sāvitrī*, one should study, beginning with the *Praṇava*. This rule applies only to the first study. Why? Because, although it would have been sufficient to say, “And the *Sāvitrī*, then he should study,” the text begins with the words, “From the very beginning, the taking up of the Veda. On every subsequent day, one should utter only the syllable *oṃ*. Why? Because it was stated, “The syllable *oṃ* elsewhere. “Elsewhere” means other than the first study. The word “also” (*api*) is intended to include the *Praṇava* even in the first study. Some, by the phrase “elsewhere also,” maintain that the *Praṇava* should be used at the beginning of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and so forth. (1.62)
But in the case of an intermediate approach, there must be a renewed initiation. 1.63.

If someone should pass between them while they are studying, then for the sake of expiation, one must again perform the entire procedure beginning with the clasping of the feet and ending with the utterance of the *praṇava*. Although this occurs outside of the formal context (*aprakaraṇe*), the expiation is performed so that the study may be resumed immediately. This applies to the passage of humans; for others, it is mentioned later. Since no mention of a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) is heard here, one should study immediately after the expiation. The term "again" (*punar*) refers to the first commencement of study, because there is no formal sitting down (*upasadana*) elsewhere. Therefore, in other cases, the sitting down must be performed solely for the purpose of expiation, and study should be undertaken immediately thereafter. Thus says Āpastamba: "Having said, 'Recite, sir,' one should either study or teach" (ĀpDh 1.10.15–16). || 1.63 ||
Furthermore: for dogs, mongooses, snakes, frogs, and cats, there shall be a three-day fast and a period of staying away from home. 1.64.

These [animals] are well known. For dogs and the others, if one passes between them individually, the penance is the abandonment of food for three days; "separation from the Guru" (*vipravāsaḥ*) means staying in the absence of the Guru for one day. And thus, by the very instruction regarding separation from the Guru, the establishment of non-study (*anadhyāya*) for one day is achieved. If it is asked why it is understood to be one day, it is because of the lack of a compound. Otherwise, he would have said, "three days of fasting and separation. Therefore, the non-study lasts for exactly one day. And so says Manu: "In the case of cattle, frogs, cats, dogs, snakes, and mongooses..."
"One should know that there is no study during the interval while traveling, day and night. [MDh 4.126]

Thus, here too, the mention of the dog is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for four-footed domestic animals, since the cat is included under the category of "four-footed" creatures. Its separate mention, however, is for the purpose of imposing a heavier penance (*prāyaścitta*). As Uśanas says: "Upon the approach of a cat, one should consume clarified butter and fast for three days. The particle *ca* serves to draw in the requirement of sitting nearby (*upasadana*). Therefore, having performed that [penance] during the time of study, one should then proceed with the recitation. Some say that the "fasting" implies the abandonment of study; whether this is correct or not must be deliberated upon. Furthermore:
For others, there shall be breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the consumption of clarified butter (ghṛtaprāśana).

For others, such as crows and the like, there are three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), because of the hearing of the plural number. The consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*) is merely a bathing of the body. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to draw in the act of sitting near (*upasadana*). Therefore, having performed three breath-restraints, consumed clarified butter, and performed the sitting near, one may study, since no prohibition of study (*anadhyāya*) is heard [in this case]. 1.65.
And likewise regarding study near a cremation ground, and likewise regarding study near a cremation ground. 1.66.

Āpastamba has stated: “One should not study within the range of a *śamyā*-throw from any direction” (ĀpDh 1.9.6). Therefore, studying in its vicinity constitutes “studying at a cremation ground. The prefix *abhi-* is intended to indicate that the act was intentional. Consequently, for an unintentional act, another expiation that is lighter should be understood. Thus Uśanas says: “If one studies at a cremation ground unintentionally, one should study after saying, ‘Recite, sir! By the word *ca* (“and”), there is the application of everything mentioned immediately prior, such as the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and so forth; however, by the word *evam* (“thus”), the application is restricted specifically to the *upasadana* (approaching the teacher) mentioned immediately before. If it is argued that only the word *evam* should have been used, we say no; this meaning is obtained only when both are present. How so? When either the word *evam* or the word *ca* would have sufficed, it is proper to assume a different purpose for the reading of both, rather than for just one alone. Therefore, the *upasadana* itself must be performed. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: “Having studied near a cremation ground, one should restrain the breaths, perform the ritual touching of the breaths (*prāṇopasparśana*), perform salutation (*abhivādana*), and recite the Sāvitrī,” and so forth. The repetition [of the concluding phrase] is for the purpose of marking the end of the chapter. All this aforementioned expiation applies only to the student, because the study and related acts are for his sake. Furthermore, in all cases, the expiation consists precisely of the *upasadana*; and since *upasadana* involves salutation and the like, and such salutation is not possible toward the teacher himself, [the rule refers to the student’s conduct]. 1.66.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Maskarīya Gautama-bhāṣya.
The second chapter:

Initiation (*upanayana*) has been described for the twice-born. Since it is maintained that they possess authority regarding certain duties of their social class (*varṇadharma*) even prior to initiation, he says the following for that purpose:
"Before initiation, there is freedom of action, speech, and eating" (2.1).
But surely this should have been stated even before the initiation ceremony; in that case, the phrase "prior to the initiation" would not need to be mentioned.

It is said: This is true; however, the purpose for mentioning the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) at the beginning has already been stated. It is not enjoined by this [sūtra], because it is already established by the sense of the matter (*arthaprāptatva*). Nor is it restricted (*niyamyate*), because there is no necessity for its performance, given that it will be stated later that "the initiation and so forth constitute the rule" (GDh 2.10), and because there is an absence of optionality (*pākṣikatva*). Nor is it an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), because there is nothing to be excluded; for the state of acting without desire and so forth has not been previously established for this [act]. Therefore, this sūtra is a restatement (*anuvādaka*) intended to make known the absence of penance (*prāyaścitta*) and royal punishment (*rājadaṇḍa*), since those two have been taught in a general manner.

But surely, royal punishments and penances are prescribed for the non-performance of what is enjoined or the practice of what is prohibited; yet this person has no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to either injunctions or prohibitions, nor is any injunction or prohibition heard regarding him. It might be argued that his status as one who has not offered the *āhuti* and so forth will be either enjoined or prohibited, such that both [punishment and penance] would apply upon its transgression, because of the instruction concerning fathers and others. Therefore, this sūtra is useless.

To this it is replied: whatever expiation has been prescribed for the non-performance of what is enjoined or the practice of what is forbidden, or whatever royal punishment [is ordained], both of these certainly apply to him as well. Even though no specific injunction or prohibition is heard with reference to him alone, nevertheless, that which is stated in general terms—such as "non-violence, truthfulness, and non-stealing" (MDh 10.63)—applies to him too because it constitutes the duty of his social class (*varṇadharma*). Upon its transgression, both royal punishment and expiation occur. Therefore, the aphorism is commenced in the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of precluding that [transgression].

Regarding the sūtra, “The rule begins with the initiation ceremony” (GDh 2.10), since it will be stated that expiation applies only to the transgression of that injunction which is prescribed starting from the initiation ceremony, and not to the transgression of anything else, it can be understood from that very source that there is no expiation for the transgression of the duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*), nor even a royal punishment. Nevertheless, this sūtra has been commenced for the following purposes: to introduce half of the expiation for one who, having passed the fixed time for initiation, possesses a distinct consciousness and is capable, when he is between eleven and sixteen years of age; to introduce the full expiation for his father and others when he is between five and eleven years of age; and to indicate the absence of any offense when he is younger than that. Thus says the Bhārgavīya:
A child who is less than sixteen years old, as well as one who is eighty years of age,
women, and those who are afflicted by disease, deserve only half of the prescribed penance.
For one who is less than eleven years of age and more than five years old,
a friend and the teacher alike should perform the penance for the sake of purification.
"Therefore, there is no offense whatsoever for one who is even more ignorant [than that];
consequently, neither royal punishment nor penance is prescribed for him.

Thus, although it has been stated in general that prior to initiation (*upanayana*) one may act according to one's desires, nevertheless, absolute freedom of action applies only until the age of five; thereafter, the child must be directed toward the duties of his social class (*varṇadharma*) by his father and others, since scriptural authority is heard regarding penance for the parents and others when such a child deviates from those duties. Enough of this digression.

Now the Sūtra is being explained: prior to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), there is freedom of action (*kāmacāra*), meaning he may act according to his own will. Therefore, regarding the touching of a *caṇḍāla* and similar acts, the author will state that mere sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) suffices, as in the rule: "until the sprinklings" (GDh 2.6).
