That too is said to apply only before the age of five years. After that, upon touching a *caṇḍāla* or others, he must be bathed. From the age of eleven onwards, he should bathe by himself. This applies everywhere. "Freedom of speech" (*kāmavāda*) means he speaks even vulgarities and the like. "Freedom of eating" (*kāmabhakṣa*) means he eats even stale food and the like. After the age of five, he should be made to perform those duties that do not conflict with the specific laws of his caste (*varṇadharma*). The phrase "prior to initiation" includes the initiation performed in times of distress (*āpadkalpa*). Why? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "a student of sacred knowledge" (*brahmacārī*). Since it is already established that a lapse in celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is impossible before the regular time for initiation, an instruction on the protection of celibacy would be redundant. He himself will give an example of freedom of action: "He voids urine and excrement wherever he happens to be" (GDh 2.4). Therefore, even in the state of extreme childhood, he must be diligently prevented from committing such acts as killing a Brahmin. Even in the state of extreme childhood, he must be diligently prevented from false accusations and the like under the heading of "freedom of speech," and from drinking liquor and the like under "freedom of eating," because these two—speech and eating—are mentioned again despite being already covered by the term "freedom of action. The inclusion of the word "prior" (*prāk*) when one could have simply said "from initiation" (*upanayanāt*) is for the sake of restriction, implying that freedom of action exists only prior to initiation. If this restriction were absent, then by the rule "and for the subsequent stages, this is not contradictory" (GDh 3.10), practices such as eating the remnants of oblations (*hutaśiṣṭa*) and so forth would apply even to ascetics (*yatis*). 2.1.
Now he states an exception regarding the eating of food obtained through begging:
"The student (brahmacārī) [may eat] from what has not been offered in sacrifice. 2.2.

The term *hutam* refers to what has been offered in sacrifice, such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*, and not the remnants of the *vaiśvadeva* offering, because that is intended for all purposes. Thus says Āpastamba: "One should make all [deities] sharers in the *vaiśvadeva*" [ĀpDh 2.9.5]. The phrase "from what is not offered" (*ahutāt*) implies that it should be performed from the remainder. This prohibition of what is naturally expected is an instruction specifically for the ancestors and others, since a child lacks discernment; it is stated that after the eleventh year, the rule applies to him alone. (2.2)
A celibate student. || 2.3 ||
One must practice the preservation of celibacy. 2.3.
Now he states an illustration of acting according to one's own will: "He passes urine and excrement wherever it may happen. (2.4)

The meaning is that just as urine and feces are produced even when one has covered one's head while plowing and so forth, or while standing, one should do [the evacuation] in that very same place. 2.4.
Moreover: "For him, no rule for sipping water exists. (2.5)

From the age of five years until before the eleventh year, the ritual rule for sipping water (*ācamana*)—the procedure for sipping—is not prescribed. Because of this prohibition of the *kalpa*, it is understood that there is merely the act of sipping itself. In this regard, since another Smṛti states, "For he is equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born through the Veda" (MDh 2.172cd), and because his duties are heard to be the same as those of a Śūdra, his sipping of water should be regarded as being like that of a Śūdra. Why is it said "of one less than eleven years"? Because of the commencement with the word "of him" (*asya*), because the absence of fault is heard prior to the fifth year, and because from the eleventh year onwards he is entitled to the duties of his caste (*varṇadharma*). It is thus understood that even the ritual rule for sipping water exists for him after the eleventh year. (2.5)
Now, regarding the very young child, [the rule] says:
except for wiping, rubbing, and sprinkling. (2.6)

The phrase "is not found for him" carries over [from the previous rule]. The meaning is that for this child under five years of age, no method of purification other than wiping (*apamārjana*) and so forth exists. Wiping is the removal of food remnants from the mouth with the hand moistened with water. Washing (*pradhāvana*) refers to cleansing after urination, defecation, and the like. Sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*) is the sprinkling [of water] upon contact with a *caṇḍāla* or similar persons. If it is argued that since there is no possibility of its application, the two prohibitions—"no ritual for sipping water (*ācamana*) exists for him, except for wiping, washing, and sprinkling"—would never even begin, this is not a fault. By the statement "no ritual for sipping water exists for him," the ritual for sipping water is prescribed for one under sixteen years of age by means of a prohibition for those under eleven. Furthermore, by the statement "except for wiping, washing, and sprinkling," wiping and the others are prescribed for one under five years of age by means of a prohibition against other methods of purification. (2.6)
Furthermore: "There is no impurity resulting from touching that [corpse]. (2.7)

By the mention of "that," one who has not yet performed purification is meant. Because of touching one who has not performed purification, or because of being touched by him, impurity does not occur; this refers specifically to the case of very young children.

In that case, the prescription for its purification would be purposeless. Why? Because only two purposes for the prescription of purification are observed: to make it fit for contact with others, and for the sake of ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). However, this [purification] does not serve to make it fit for contact with others, because even one who has not performed purification is fit for contact, according to the rule: "There is no impurity from touching it. Nor does it serve for the sake of ritual performance, because there is no performance of this [purification].

It is not purposeless, because the prescription for purification is for the sake of protection. And so says another Smṛti: "One should perform purification for the sake of protection until the child reaches five years of age. The use of the prefix *upa-* is intended to indicate the absence of fault upon touching this very person when he has not yet performed purification. Thus, when touching others who have been rendered impure by contact with food-leavings, urine, or feces, one must perform sipping of water (*ācamana*). There is no fault in touching them, as they are included in the list [of those] enumerated in the Sūtra on touching a corpse. Likewise, another Smṛti states: "He who touches an impure person is indeed defiled alone."
"Having touched that, another shall not become defiled; this is the rule regarding all substances.

Regarding the touch of a *caṇḍāla*, however, he will state in the sūtra concerning the touch of a corpse [GDh 14.22]: "One should touch water. Although it could have been stated simply as "there is no impurity from touching that," the author composed the heavy sūtra "there is no impurity from touching that" in order to override even the restriction found in the rule "prior to initiation" (GDh 2.1). Consequently, even after initiation, one must perform *ācamana* upon touching those things rendered impure by food remnants, or urine and feces. 2.7.
Moreover:
"But one should certainly not employ him for the Agnihotra oblation or for the receiving of sacrificial offerings. 2.8.

The word *enam* (him) is used for the purpose of including everyone who has not yet been initiated (*anupanīta*). That which is performed in the fire, such as the *agnihotra* oblation and so forth, is called *agnihavana*. The *baliharaṇa* is the offering made to the deities of the directions at the time following the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. The particle *tu* expresses a distinction: one should not employ him even for tasks such as washing the feet of Brahmins at the *aṣṭakā* rites and others, let alone for the specific acts of *agnihavana* and *baliharaṇa*. Because of his status as one who acts according to his own will, if he were to study a mantra somewhere and proceed on his own accord in the *agnihotra* or other rites, then even the one who permitted it would not be considered a consenter; it is for this very reason that the word *eva* (only/alone) is used. This statement is intended to enjoin the employment of the initiated boy (*upanīta*), since there is no possibility of such employment occurring elsewhere, and thus it serves as a prohibition [of others]. Furthermore, although the injunction "the learned man should offer the *agnihotra*" implies through the Vedic text that only one of extensive learning is qualified, nevertheless, in the absence of such a person, one should employ even a boy of little knowledge who has been initiated. And so says Manu:

“Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool, nor one who is afflicted, nor likewise one who is uninitiated, shall be the *hotṛ* priest for the *agnihotra*. [MDh 11.36] Since the prohibition of one with little learning already establishes the prohibition [of the uninitiated], the specific prohibition “nor one who is uninitiated” is explained as being intended to permit even one of little learning provided he is initiated, in the absence of another who is learned. As for what was stated beginning with “prior to initiation” [GDh 2.1], that should be understood to apply to women also until their marriage. Why?
The marriage rite is declared to be the initiation ceremony for women. [MDh 2.67]

This is because of the observation of another *smṛti* text. In this way, the prohibition of *niyoga* for a maiden—even when performing the *agnihotra* and *baliharaṇa*—is established. Therefore, *niyoga* is to be performed after marriage. In that regard, since it is prohibited for a woman to offer oblations in the *agnihotra* by the Vedic injunction, "A woman shall not sacrifice," it should be understood as applying to the *aupāsana* fire and other such rites. And so says another *smṛti*: "The wife shall offer oblations in the *aupāsana* fire and perform the *vaiśvadeva*," and so forth. Furthermore, the prohibition "not a young woman" (*na yuvatiḥ*) is not a fault, as it refers specifically to the wives of others (*paradāra*). (2.8)
Furthermore:
"One should not utter the word 'Brahman' except when pouring the *svadhā* offering.

The word "thus" (*evam*) is understood to carry over. By the word *brahman*, the Vedas are meant. Therefore, one should not teach him [the Veda]. Since the prohibition for one who has not been initiated is already established by the injunction for Vedic study—namely, "after initiation and the formal commencement of study (*upākaraṇa*), he should study the *chandas*"—the repeated prohibition of the Veda is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*): that the Veda alone must not be taught. Consequently, there is no fault in teaching the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*). Because of the principle of acting according to one's own will, one should not even utter a mantra acquired by any other means. Why? Because the verb "should cause to teach" (*adhyāpayet*) is used without a specific context, whereas "should utter" (*abhivyāhārayet*) is used with a specific context. "Except for the offering of the *svadhā*," meaning excluding the offering of the *svadhā*. The "offering of the *svadhā*" refers to what is given to the deceased, such as the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) and water, after saying, "Svadhā to so-and-so. This also serves as an indication for the entire ritual for the deceased. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Except for the water-rites connected with the *svadhā* and the ancestors" (VaDh 2.7). And thus, even when a son has not been initiated, the funeral rites for the deceased should not be performed by the *sapiṇḍas* and others, lest the injunction of the scripture be rendered meaningless. 2.9.
Having stated [the rules] for one who has not been initiated, he now speaks regarding one who has been initiated: "The rule begins with the initiation ceremony. (2.10)

The rule that has been declared beginning from the initiation (upanayana) is designated as "observance" (niyama). Thus, in the case of its non-performance, there is an expiation (prāyaścitta), but not for the preceding [period]. Or rather, starting from this point, the observance—the maintenance of vows (vratadhāraṇa) which will be described, such as the kindling of the fire and so forth—is the niyama; it must be performed beginning from the initiation. 2.10.
Furthermore, the practice of celibacy has been explained. 2.11.

The inclusion of the word "stated" [in the verse] indicates that this restriction applies even prior to initiation (*upanayana*). Consequently, in the event of a lapse in that regard, it should be understood that even for one who has not been initiated, eligibility for the rite is established solely through the penance for a *avakīrṇin*. To this effect, another *smṛti* states: "One who has become defiled should be purified by the vow of an *avakīrṇin* and initiated before reaching the age of seventeen; beyond that, he is purified by both the *vrātya* and *avakīrṇin* vows. If it is argued that for a religious student (*brahmacārin*), this is already established by implication due to the prohibition against looking at women and so forth, we say no, because such an act is possible even with animals and the like.
Furthermore:
[The refutation of] fire and fuel, and the practice of begging for alms. (2.12)

The kindling of the fire, the fuel, and the oblation—these are as well known as the rest. These two are to be performed every day. Their mention together is for the purpose of ensuring their immediate performance one after the other. Thus says Manu:
"Having taken up the prescribed staff and having worshipped the sun, and having circumambulated the fire from left to right, he should go about for alms according to the rule. (MDh 2.48)

In that regard, it has been stated that the offering of fuel (samiddhoma) is prescribed by the rule: "having circumambulated the fire clockwise. Since the twice-daily meal is enjoined by the text: "One should eat food offered with respect in the evening and in the morning, without disparaging it" (GDh 9.59), it should be understood that the kindling of the fire also occurs twice—in the evening and in the morning. Accordingly, another Smṛti states:
"Having brought fuel from afar, one should place it in the open air;
one should offer oblations into the fire with those sticks, unwearied, in the evening and in the morning" (MDh 2.186).
Some desire the offering into the kindled fire to take place only at evening. 2.12.
Furthermore:
Truthful speech. 2.13.

The phrase "must be performed" (*kartavyā*) is to be supplied everywhere. The explicit mention of the word "speech" (*vacana*) is for the sake of removing doubt; otherwise, there might be the doubt that "the touching of water" (*apām upasparśanam*) alone constitutes the truth. The separate mention [of speech] is for the purpose of ensuring its performance even by one who is ill. Consequently, that [rule] does not apply to the two preceding cases. And so Manu says:
"Without having gone for alms and without having kindled the fire, one who is not ill shall perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin* for seven nights. (MDh 2.187)
Thus [ends verse] 2.13.
Moreover: touching water. 2.14.
The mention of "ashes" (ab) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for ashes and the other [means of purification]. Thus says Bhṛgu:
"Five meritorious baths have been proclaimed by the great seers:
the fiery (*āgneya*), the watery (*vāruṇa*), the brahmic (*brāhma*), the windy (*vāyavya*), and the celestial (*divya*)."

Bathing with ashes is said to be of Agni; immersion in water is that of Varuṇa; the rite performed with the hymn "āpo hi ṣṭhā" is that of Brahmā; and bathing in the dust raised by cows is remembered as that of Vāyu.
"That which is the divine rain accompanied by heat is called the 'divine bath' (divya-snāna).
One who is unable to perform the Varuṇa bath should instead perform the Āgneya or other [substitutes]. Thus it is said.

Although one should have simply said "bathing" (*snānam*), this specific expression is used for the purpose of including the rules for bathing mentioned in other *smṛtis*. Thus, what is stated in other *smṛtis* should be understood here as well. The prefix *upa-* is intended to exclude water that is not clearly known [to be pure]. The separate mention of kindling the fire and begging for alms is for the purpose of prohibiting the daily bath after a meal, but not the occasional (*naimittika*) bath; therefore, the occasional bath must be performed. The separate mention of speaking the truth is for the purpose of prohibiting even the occasional bath for one who is ill. Some say that the prefix *upa-* is intended to prohibit bathing at midnight. Whatever has been stated here has all been stated by Manu as well.
"One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight,
nor with one's clothes on, nor constantly, nor in an unknown body of water.
[MDh 4.129] Thus [ends verse 2.14].
Some [say it consists of] the gift of a cow and so forth. 2.15.

The *godāna* is the second vow (*vrata*) for the *chandoga*s; it must also be observed by others in the sixteenth year. Some desire that even for them the *godāna* be performed in the sixteenth year. From that point onward, some desire the ritual bath (*snāna*). Before the *godāna*, one should not perform the daily bath (*nityasnāna*); only the occasional bath (*naimittika*) should be performed. After that, however, some teachers desire that the daily bath also be performed. Because of the use of the word "some," Gautama does not hold this view. (2.15)
And [it possesses] the state of being external to the junctions. 2.16.

The word "and" (ca) is used for the purpose of following the opinion of some [teachers]. Some desire that the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) be performed outside the village; but Gautama does not [hold this]. This is what is meant: the view of some is that the twilight worship must be performed only outside the village; the view of Gautama is that it should be performed anywhere—in either a place outside or inside [the village]—provided it is a pure location. 2.16.

Now, as an incidental matter, [the author] states how and when that twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) should be performed: "One should stand during the morning [twilight] and sit during the evening [twilight], while the light is still visible, or until the stars appear, remaining restrained in speech. (2.17)

The term "vāgyataḥ" (with speech restrained) is connected to each of the two acts, standing and sitting. That time at which the sun rises is the morning twilight (*pūrvā saṃdhyā*). The word *saṃdhyā* is carried over from the preceding fragment of the sūtra. That time at which the sun sets is the later twilight (*uttarā saṃdhyā*). Standing and sitting are here subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), while the act of worship (*upāsana*) is the primary action (*pradhāna*). Therefore, although it is said that "he should stand," it should nevertheless be understood as "he should worship while standing" and "he should worship while sitting. And so says Manu: "Reciting [the Gāyatrī] while standing during the morning twilight, one removes the sin of the night."
"Seated facing the west, however, one destroys the impurity committed during the day" (MDh 2.101).

"Sajyotis" refers to the time when light is present: in the east, this is the light of the stars; that period of time which exists together with the light of the stars is "sajyotis. The commencement [of the rite] must be made during that sajyotis time. In the other direction [the west], it is likewise the light of the sun. Therefore, "until the appearance of the light"—meaning until the sun is seen in the east or until the stars are seen in the west. Although it should have been said "until the light," the inclusion of the term "appearance" (darśana) is for the sake of completeness. And so says Manu:

"One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the appearance of the sun; but one should sit during the evening twilight until the stars are clearly visible. (MDh 2.102) The meaning is that the recitation should be concluded at that point. Here, the prefix *ā* signifies inclusion (*abhividhi*), because the state of "prolonged twilight" (*dīrghasaṃdhyatva*) is intended. And so says Manu:
"By virtue of the long *saṃdhyā* rites, the sages attained long life, as well as wisdom, fame, renown, and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*)" (MDh 4.94).

Now, one might object: "By the rule 'and for those to the north, this is not inconsistent' (GDh 3.10), this does not apply to a *snātaka* who maintains the sacred fires, because his time is already occupied by the fire-oblation."

It is said: First, regarding the *smārta* (tradition-based) evening and morning *homa*, there is no contradiction at all due to the difference in time. How so? By the word "evening" (*sāyam*), night is meant, and by the word "morning" (*prātaḥ*), day is meant. Since there is no such [specific] rule here as in the scriptural injunctions concerning the *udita-homa* (offering after sunrise) and so forth, the *homa* must be performed immediately following the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). Furthermore, even for those for whom the *homa* is prescribed specifically during the twilight period, because a "long twilight" (*dīrghasaṃdhyā*) is desired, there is still room for the twilight worship to occur even after the *homa*. Thus, even regarding the Vedic (*śrauta*) matters of the *udita-homa* and so forth, there is indeed no contradiction.

Although it should have been stated simply as, "One should perform the morning twilight devotion standing and the evening twilight devotion seated," the phrasing used here is for the purpose of including the injunctions mentioned in other Smṛtis. Thus says Uśanas:

Having gone to water in the evening and in the morning, having become pure and having sprinkled himself with a purifier (*pavitra*), he should recite the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, as well as those without specific marks (*abliṅga*) and the *vāmadevya* hymn. Then, seated on *darbha* grass in a clean place, holding *darbha* blades, facing west, with speech restrained, and meditating upon the Self, he should perform three breath-control exercises (*prāṇāyāma*) consisting of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*). Following this, preceded by meditation on the seers (*ṛṣi*), meters (*chandas*), and deities (*devatā*), he should repeat the *Sāvitrī* beginning with *bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ* one thousand times, or one hundred times, or at least ten times. Then, rising and bowing toward the west, south, and north to Agni, Yama, and Brahmā, and having circumambulated three times clockwise, he should again bow toward the western direction. In the same manner in the morning, standing and facing east, he should bow to Mitra and the other deities.
Thus [ends verse] 2.17.
One should not look at the sun. 2.18.

If this prohibition applied only to the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*), then a single sūtra would have been composed as follows: "One should stand during the former twilight and sit during the latter, remaining silent until the stars appear or until the light [of the sun] is seen; one should not look at the sun. If it were intended to apply at all times, then [the author] would have mentioned looking at the sun even in the context of the rule "one should avoid honey and meat" (GDh 2.19) and so forth. Since he has not done so in either case, it can be understood that this was stated with another intention in mind. That intention should be seen as expressed in other Smṛtis. As Uśanas says: "One should not look at the sun when it has reached the twilight, when it is at midday, when it is eclipsed by Rāhu, or when it is reflected in water."

One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, collyrium, ointments, vehicles, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, speaking, playing musical instruments, bathing, brushing the teeth, exhilaration, dancing, singing, slander, and fear. 2.19.

The word "one should avoid" (*varjayet*) is connected to each [item]. "Honey" (*madhu*) refers to honey produced by bees. There is no fault in consuming it unintentionally, as another *smṛti* states: "In the *Vājasaneyaka*, honey that has come about unintentionally does not cause impurity" (VaDh 23.13). Regarding "meat" (*māṃsa*), although it is not prohibited for a householder, there is likewise no fault in consuming meat that is the leavings of one's guru for the sake of medicine when one is ill, as another *smṛti* states: "If he should fall ill, he may at will eat all the leavings of his guru for the purpose of medicine" (VaDh 23.9). Thus, even in the case of a *śrāddha* feast, it must be avoided by one who is not ill. And so says Manu:
At a rite for the gods, he may eat like one observing a vow; at a rite for the ancestors, he may eat like a seer (ṛṣi).
If invited, he may eat at his pleasure; his vow is not thereby violated. [MDh 2.189]

And so forth. "Fragrance" refers to sandalwood and the like. This prohibition applies even to that which is for the sake of pleasure, but not to that which is consecrated by a deity, because another *smṛti* text is seen stating: "A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should accept only that which is consecrated by a deity. The same applies to garlands. "Sleeping by day" means indulging in sleep during the daytime; this too is not a fault for one who is ill. "Collyrium" refers to [application] to the eyes. Here too, the prohibition is for the sake of enjoyment, not for medicinal purposes. "Anointing" is the rubbing of the limbs with oil. Some say this is a prohibition against scented oil; in that view, there is no fault regarding other types. If it is argued that this prohibition is already established by the prohibition of fragrance itself, we say no; because it is specifically well-known in common usage, it does not refer to fragrance in general. "Vehicles" refer to palanquins and the like; these also apply only to one who is not ill. "Shoes and umbrellas" are well known. There is no fault regarding those made of peacock feathers. "Lust" is the desire for enjoyment directed toward women. "Anger" is the thinking of harm toward another. "Greed" is the seizing of another's property and so forth through unjust means. "Delusion" is ignorance. "Disputation" is excessive prattle. "Playing musical instruments" refers to beating drums and the like. "Bathing" refers to bathing the head and so forth, provided it is for the sake of enjoyment; as for other [prescribed] bathing, it is permitted because it is ordained. "Cleaning the teeth" is well known. That should not be done even with a betel leaf, because another *smṛti* text is seen stating: "The observer of the vow should have his teeth like mud (unclean). "Joy" is delight. And thus, the prohibition of witnessing plays and the like—which are the causes of that joy—is also established, since it is impossible to prevent the arising of delight upon seeing them. "Dancing" is the movement of the limbs. "Singing" is the utterance of words related to music (*gāndharva*). "Slander" is the proclaiming of another's faults. "Fear" is the terrifying of another; as for other [natural] fear, it cannot be avoided.
Furthermore:
In the presence of one's guru, one should avoid covering the neck, using a cloth wrapped around the thighs as a seat, leaning against a support, and stretching out the feet. 2.20.

"Guru" refers to the teacher (*ācārya*) and others. Why? If only the *ācārya* were intended, then one should have said "seeing the *ācārya*" (*ācāryadarśane*). The mention of "guru" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes all those who occupy the position of a guru. Accordingly, another *smṛti* states: "One should stand with contracted limbs in the presence of all those worthy of honor. "Covering the neck" (*kaṇṭhaprāvaraṇa*) means throwing a cloth around the neck. "The *avasakthikā*" is the binding of a cloth around the thighs over the knees. The rest is well known. Since these actions are performed under the influence of others, they are prohibited [when one sees a guru]. (2.20)
Furthermore:
spitting, laughing, yawning, and cracking the knuckles. 2.21.

The separate mention [of these acts] is for the purpose of avoiding them both in the presence of the guru and in the presence of others. Spitting is well known. Laughter, even when under the control of another, must be avoided with effort; and thus Āpastamba says: “One should not smile; if one should smile, one should smile by covering [the mouth], according to the Brāhmaṇa” (ĀpDh 2.7.6–7). Yawning is well known. Cracking the joints is the forceful release of a joint with sound. 2.21.
Furthermore:
looking at or touching a woman when there is a suspicion of sexual intercourse [is a minor offense]. 2.22.

The word "should avoid" (*varjayet*) carries over from the previous verse. "Beholding" (*prekṣaṇa*) means looking intently, that is, the examination of individual parts; it does not mean merely seeing the form, because it is impossible to prevent that even while blinking. "Touching" (*ālambana*) means physical contact. Although one could have said simply "touching" (*sparśana*), this specific term is used for the purpose of excluding intentional touching. Thus, there is no fault if it occurs through negligence. However, if done intentionally, one must not touch her even in darkness and similar circumstances. One should not perform either of these two acts with a woman—only with one regarding whom others might suspect sexual intercourse, and not with any other. (2.22)
Gambling, service to the base, taking what is not given, and violence. || 2.23 ||

One should avoid these very things: gambling with dice and the like; service to the lowly, such as cleaning away urine and excrement; and likewise, one should not perform even for a guru any service that is unsuitable. Taking what is not given means seizing even discarded things without permission. Violence means the killing or harming of living beings. One should neither cause others to engage in these nor even give them approval. (2.23)
Furthermore: [One should avoid] the names of the teacher, his son, women, and initiated persons. (2.24)
"One should avoid" is the topic under discussion. One should not utter the names of one's teacher, his son, his wife, or one who has been initiated, as given by the father or others. (2.24)
Furthermore: "Acid words. (2.25)
One should avoid all speech that is harsh, cruel, and causes distress to others. 2.25.
A Brāhmaṇa must always avoid intoxicants. || 2.26 ||

"One should avoid" is the subject under discussion. A Brāhmaṇa should always avoid liquor—whether it be that made from molasses, honey, or flour, or any other intoxicant—even prior to his initiation (*upanayana*). In the case of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, there is no prohibition against *surā* (liquor) other than that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*) both before initiation and after, until the period of studenthood (*brahmacarya*), as seen in other Smṛtis. As Manu says: "Liquor is to be known as threefold: that made from molasses, that made from honey, and that made from flour.
Just as one is so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born. (MDh 11.94)
Thus [ends verse] 2.26.
Now, for the purpose of explaining what ought to be done, he says:
"Sleeping on a low bed or seat, rising before [others], and retiring last. (2.27)

In the presence of the guru, one should occupy a lower bed and seat; one should rise before him and go to rest after him. As Manu says: "In the presence of the guru, his bed and seat must always be lower;
he should rise before him and be the last to lie down" (MDh 2.198).
Thus [ends verse] 2.27.
Furthermore:
"Restrained in speech, arms, and belly. (2.28)

The word "should be" (syāt) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Restrained in speech" means one who has desisted from idle chatter. "Restrained in arm" means one who avoids crushing clods of earth and similar acts. "Restrained in belly" means one who eats what is wholesome and in moderation. Some read the text as "restrained in the actions of speech, arms, and belly"; however, since this is already established by the state of being restrained in arm, it must be considered whether that reading is appropriate or not. (2.28)
Furthermore:
One should mention the name and lineage of the teacher with respect. 2.29.

The mention of the *guru* is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the teacher (*ācārya*) and others. "From the equal" means properly bowed down, i.e., humble; the meaning is that having meditated upon him, one should perform a salutation. And thus, in that same context, the mention of the "teacher and his son" [GDh 2.24] is also an elliptical indication for the *guru* and others, because the utterance of their names is likewise prohibited. Accordingly, another *Smṛti* states:
"The teacher and his son, his wife, the initiated person, the *guru*, the father and paternal uncle, as well as the mother and maternal uncle."
A learned man should not mention by name his father-in-law, his husband, or his mother’s sister, even if they are well-wishers and wise.
But if he should speak, one should meditate upon him, pay homage, and then address him. (2.29)
And thus, when the superior one has been honored. || 2.30 ||

"Venerable" (arcita) means one who is worthy of honor and learned; "superior" (śreyān) should be understood as one who desires one's welfare and is advanced in age. Since this [meaning] is already established by the word "and" (ca), the word "thus" (evaṃ) serves to extend [the rules] to the whole [set]. Consequently, whatever [rites] such as salutation (abhivādana) and so forth are prescribed upon seeing a guru, those should be observed here as well. || 2.30 ||
Having abandoned one's bed, seat, and place, there is the act of responding [to a summons]. || 2.31 ||

When the guru gives an order, then—having abandoned and left behind his bed (such as a couch), his seat (such as a wooden plank), and his place (where he is standing)—he should give a response; this is the meaning. || 2.31 ||
Approaching [the teacher] is [required] because of the verbal instruction, even if [the teacher] is not seen. 2.32.
The meaning is that when an instruction is being given by an invisible teacher, one should perform an *abhikramaṇa*, which is to say, go toward him. 2.32.
One should rise upon seeing one's teacher when he is situated below, seated, or moving horizontally, as well as when one is in the presence of wind. || 2.33 ||

When the teacher stands or sits below or at a lower level, or when he is engaged in the service of crosswinds or the voiding of urine and excrement, the student, upon seeing the teacher there, should stand up; the word "and" (ca) implies that he should also turn his face away. Likewise, another Smṛti states: "Upon seeing the teacher standing in a well or likewise on the bank of a pond, the disciple and the servant should likewise stand with their faces turned away."

Alternatively—the word "and" (ca) indicates departure. Thus, the meaning of the sūtra should be understood at that time as follows: "In the case of [the wind] staying below, sitting, or moving horizontally, one should rise and depart respectively. In this regard, the sequence is: seeing [the wind] staying below or sitting, one should rise; in the case of its moving horizontally, one should depart. (2.33)
One should follow him as he walks. || 2.34 ||

"Having seen him going, one should follow after him. The word "and" (*ca*) carries over from the previous rule; by it, even what is not explicitly stated is included: "having seen him sitting, one should stand up; having seen him lying down, one should sit. And so says another *Smṛti*: "One should follow him as he goes, stand up when he is sitting, and while sitting, attend upon him when he is lying down" (VaDh 7.12). || 2.34 ||
Karma is that which is designated as "making known. 2.35.

Having informed the teacher, "I shall perform whatever task is to be done by him," and having performed it, he should stand while announcing, "It is done. Because the sentence is incomplete, the word "having performed" (*kṛtvā*) must be supplied after "having informed" (*vijñāpya*), and the verb "he should stand" (*tiṣṭhet*) must also be supplied after "having announced" (*ākhyāya*), just as in the example: "Enter, [eat] the rice-ball" (*praviśa piṇḍīm*). (2.35)
One who studies when summoned. 2.36.
Only when he is summoned by the teacher should he study; the meaning is that he should not prompt him [to teach]. 2.36.
One who is disciplined is devoted to what is pleasant and beneficial. || 2.37 ||

The word "should be" (*syāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. He is "devoted to that" (*tatparaḥ*). This refers to the conjunction of what is pleasant (*priya*) and what is beneficial (*hita*). Since that which is beneficial but unpleasant cannot be performed, the meaning is: one should do only that which is both pleasant and conducive to the future; that is, pleasant in the sense of being gratifying, and beneficial in the sense of being sustainable for the long term. (2.37)
And the same applies to his wife’s sons. (2.38)

He should also be intent upon the welfare and benefit of his wife and son who are of the same caste (*savarṇa*) and similar to him; by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), even [the protection of] those covered by a cloak and so forth is included. If it is asked why only those of the same caste are mentioned, it is because the plural number is used for the sake of honor. (2.38)
Now he states the exception to that:
"There shall be no eating of leftovers, bathing, adorning, washing of the feet, massaging, or clasping [the feet]. (2.39)

One should not perform these for his wife or son; since they are naturally expected to act out of affection and for their own welfare, this is prohibited. Because these acts are specifically forbidden for these two, they must indeed be performed for the teacher (*guru*). Thus says Āpastamba: “When away from home, he should eat alms-food after having offered it into the fire; alms-food is praised as being equivalent to a sacrificial oblation (*havis*). In that regard, the teacher serves the purpose of a deity and the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire; having fed him, whatever remains as leavings he eats—that is truly the leavings of the sacrificial oblation” (ĀpDh 1.3.42–1.4.2), and so forth. Likewise, Vasiṣṭha also says: “The leavings of one who is not a teacher are not to be eaten” (VaDh 14.20), and so forth. *Prasādhana* means adornment. The rest is well known. 2.39.
Now he states the exception to the rule regarding salutation:
"Upon returning from a journey, one should salute the wives of one's gurus. (2.40)
One who has returned from a journey abroad must perform the salutation by clasping the feet of his teacher’s wives; not at any other time, nor toward any other women. 2.40.
But even there, it is not [permitted] for many young women who have entered into worldly affairs. 2.41.

The meaning is: by one who is capable of legal transactions and has reached the full age of sixteen years. Some maintain that one should not have dealings with young women even when traveling abroad, but Gautama does not hold this view; [this rule] is to be understood in consideration of whether the women are suspected or unsuspected of misconduct. (2.41)

It has been stated: "The fire, fuel, and begging for alms" (GDh 2.12). Among these, since the fire and fuel are obtained individually from the householders alone, he now states the rule for begging for alms:
"Begging for alms is to be done among all castes, with the exception of those accused of crimes and those who have fallen from their status.

For what purpose is this sūtra commenced? First of all, the practice of wandering for alms is not enjoined by this [sūtra], because it has already been enjoined by the rule: “In fire-tending, fuel-gathering, and wandering for alms” (GDh 2.12). Furthermore, the avoidance of those accused of crimes has already been stated by the rule: “Of those who are praiseworthy in their own duties” (GDh 17.1). Regarding this, some say: this commencement is for the purpose of including the Śūdra, because [the status of the Śūdra] was not covered by the rule “of those who are praiseworthy in their own duties.”

And this is not tenable; for by the rule, "If there is no subsistence without a Śūdra woman" (GDh 17.5), the permission to take a Śūdra wife is established for times of distress (*āpad*). Nor is it proper to assume from this that a student (*brahmacārin*) is permitted to have a Śūdra wife even when not in distress, because in another Smṛti it is absolutely prohibited:
"He whose limbs are nourished by the essence of a Śūdra's food, even though he constantly studies, offers oblations, or recites prayers, does not attain the higher goal" (VaDh 6.28).

Therefore, this undertaking is intended solely for the purpose of providing [food] to unworthy members of the twice-born (*dvijāti*) by a religious student (*brahmacārin*), even when no emergency exists. Since there would otherwise be an unrestricted application to all unworthy persons, the prohibition—"excluding those accused of grave sins and outcasts"—is appropriate. Otherwise, if the provision were restricted to *śūdras*, a prohibition against those accused of grave sins and others would be illogical, as they would not have been included in the first place. Furthermore, one cannot argue that this exception applies exclusively to the case of *śūdras*; for where members of the twice-born who are worthy are authorized, the *śūdra* is likewise worthy, and thus there is no possibility of the other [unworthy person] being involved at all.

Therefore, it is established that for one in the first stage of life, the practice of begging for alms should be from those who are commendable; in their absence, from those who are not commendable; in their absence, from the teacher and others; and in the absence of all these, in times of distress, even from a Śūdra.

It is called *sārvavarṇika* because it is fit for all classes (*sarvavarṇa*); the meaning is that it belongs to all. The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is intended to include the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas; otherwise, since only a Brāhmaṇa has the right to accept gifts, it would belong to him alone. The inclusion of the word "class" (*varṇa*) is intended to include the Śūdra as well; for if the word "class" were not used, the term "all" would apply only to those two (the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya). Therefore, the word "class" is employed to extend the rule to the Śūdra who was not previously included. Consequently, there is no fault in a Śūdra who lacks a livelihood wandering for alms. *Bhaikṣa* is a collection of alms; therefore, it should be gathered from many houses. An "accused person" (*abhiśasta*) is understood to be one accused of a minor offense (*upapātaka*), because one accused of a major sin (*pātaka*) is already covered by the mention of the "outcast" (*patita*). Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a crime causing loss of caste (*patanīya*) or one not causing loss of caste (*upapatanīya*)" [VaDh 23.39].

Some provide the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) as *sārvavarṇika*, meaning "belonging to all castes" (*sarveṣu varṇeṣu bhavam*). For them, we do not see the purpose of the word "all" (*sarva*). If it is for the sake of including those of inferior twice-born status, that cannot be so, because that very purpose is already served by the commencement of the Sūtra itself. Even if it were for the sake of including Śūdras, the same refutation applies. Therefore, this matter should be investigated by the Brahmins (*bhūsura*). (2.42)
The word "existence" (bhava) should be employed at the beginning, middle, and end [of each section], according to the sequence of the syllables. 2.43.

Regarding the two-footed [request], when the word "give alms" (*bhikṣāṃ dehi*) is used in a request, the word *bhavat* (sir) must be employed at the beginning by a Brāhmaṇa, in the middle by a Kṣatriya, and at the end by a Vaiśya, as this is obtained through the inherent power (*sāmarthya*) of the word *dehi* itself. Since *bhavat* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and cannot be used in isolation, it must be used in the vocative case-ending in the presence of women, such as: "O Lady, give alms" (*bhavati bhikṣāṃ dehi*). In the presence of men, it is: "O Sir, give alms" (*bhavan bhikṣāṃ dehi*). Regarding the prefix *pra*, one should also observe what is stated in another Smṛti: "The letters *kṣa* and *h* should not be pronounced loudly. As the Gṛhya-smṛti says:

A Brāhmaṇa should beg, saying, "Lady, give alms"; a Rājanya, using the word *bhavat* in the middle, saying, "Lady, give alms"; and a Vaiśya, using the word *bhavat* at the end, saying, "Give alms, lady. Furthermore, one should not lengthen the syllables *kṣāṃ* and *hiṃ*. Thus it is said.

The mention of the *varṇa* (caste) is for the purpose of providing the mantra to the Śūdra; consequently, one of the mantras belonging to the three [higher] castes alone should be seen as applicable, or else another specific composition should be made. This is because of the observation in another Smṛti that "the livelihood of a Śūdra is like that of a Vaiśya," and thus the [mantra] mentioned for the Vaiśya should be seen as applicable. The mantra was not stated explicitly in order to indicate that his livelihood is unrestricted. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "And his livelihood is unrestricted, and his hair and dress are unrestricted," and so forth. The mention of the sequence is so that there may be no option regarding only one [mantra]. (2.43)
In the absence [of these], it may be done with one's teacher, kinsmen, elders, or relatives; otherwise, with someone else. 2.44.

The Teacher has said: "kinsman" refers to a sapinda; "teacher" refers to a maternal uncle and others; "one's own" means one's own property. If [food] is not obtained elsewhere, alms should be requested from these; the sequence, however, has already been established. (2.44)
In this case as well:
one should avoid each preceding one among them. (2.45)

Whichever among them is mentioned first in each respective case, that one he should avoid. However, if [the food] cannot be obtained elsewhere, even after avoiding those mentioned earlier, he should continue to seek alms from those very same persons; it is for the purpose of establishing this rule that they are specifically mentioned, so that it should be understood that if nothing can be found anywhere else, he may indeed go to the house of his preceptor (*upādhyāya*). Thus, another *Smṛti* states: "If it is not obtained elsewhere, even from the house of the preceptor. (2.45)
Having offered it to the teacher and being permitted by him, he should eat. 2.46.

Having announced to the teacher, "This is the alms-food," he should eat it only after being permitted by him with the words, "Eat. This announcement is for the purpose of consecrating the alms-food, as indicated by the expression "being permitted. If the teacher should take [the food], then another portion must be brought. (2.46)
In his absence, [the debt shall be paid] by his wife, son, fellow student, or a virtuous person.

In the absence of the teacher, an announcement should be made to his wife and others as far as possible. The mention of "his" (tad-) is for the purpose of indicating that the wife and son must belong to the same caste. A *sabrahmacārī* is one who studies the same Vedic branch; "good" (*san*) means virtuous, possessing excellent qualities. (2.47)
To the question "How, then, should he eat?", he says:
"Restraining his speech, satisfied, and not being greedy, having placed water nearby. (2.48)

"Restrained in speech" means silently; "being satisfied" means practicing contentment—the sense being that even if one was previously dissatisfied, one should rejoice at the mere sight of food. And so another Smṛti says:

"Upon seeing [the food], he should rejoice, become serene, and welcome it in every way" (MDh 2.54). "Not being greedy" means avoiding excessive eating by abandoning specific cravings; and so another Smṛti says:
"Excessive eating is detrimental to longevity, detrimental to health, and detrimental to strength;
it is meritless and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it. (MDh 2.57).

Alternatively, the meaning is "without abandoning the rules for eating. Accordingly, the rules for eating should be observed according to another *smṛti*: "having properly set down water and having sipped [it]"—this is the meaning. The prefix *sam-* is intended to include the procedure mentioned in other *smṛtis*. Thus Uśanas says: "One should sprinkle water with [the mantra] beginning 'Truth, do not deceive,' and cause [the food] to be sipped with [the mantra] beginning 'The underlayer of nectar.'"

Alternatively, "water" (udaka) refers to a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). Having placed that nearby, it follows that the religious student (brahmacārin) must also carry a water-pot. Likewise, Manu also indicates the carrying of a water-pot by the religious student, because it is prescribed as a rite of acquisition along with the girdle and other items:
"Having thrown away the girdle, the skin, the staff, the sacrificial thread, and the water-pot when they are worn out, one should take others according to the mantras. (MDh 2.64)

And in this manner, the sipping of water (ācamana) must be performed from that very source, by virtue of the force of the scriptural statement. There is no fault in touching what has been defiled by food remnants. Or else, one should observe what is stated in another Smṛti. As Vasiṣṭha says:
"Fire is considered pure when placed upon water, on the hand, or on wood;
therefore, one should wipe the water-pot with both hands and water. [VaDh 12.15]
Some justify this meaning based on the prefix *sam* alone. 2.48.
Now, if a religious student (brahmacārī) should not abide properly in the discipline of the teacher, what then should be done? To this he says:
"The correction of the pupil is by means of non-corporeal punishment" (2.49).

"Disciplining the pupil" (*śiṣyāśiṣṭiḥ*) means the instruction of the pupil; the meaning is that it should be carried out by means of censure and so forth, excluding "killing," that is, killing excepted. Although this is already established from the context, the mention of the "pupil" is for the purpose of making known that this same rule of conduct applies to others who are to be disciplined as well, such as a wife, a son, and so on. (2.49)
If one is unable [to do so], [one may strike] with thin strips of rope or bamboo. || 2.50 ||

If he cannot be corrected by means of reprimand and so forth, he should be punished with a rope or a split bamboo cane; since these two, when prescribed together, serve the same purpose, there is an option between them. Even with that, he should be punished only mildly. (2.50)
One who kills with another [weapon] is to be punished by the king. || 2.51 ||
One who strikes with anything other than the hand or foot out of anger should be punished by the king; the mention of the "king" is for the sake of showing respect. 2.51.
Now, he states for how long a time one should conduct oneself in this manner:
"One should practice the student's life (brahmacarya) for twelve years regarding a single Veda. (2.52)

One who is about to study a single Veda should practice—that is, observe—the student’s discipline (*brahmacarya*) for twelve years in the manner previously described. By the word *brahmacarya*, the entire collection of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) is meant, because it is for the sake of Brahman. 2.52.
Or twelve times each. 2.53.
Or he should observe the vow of celibacy for twelve years for each Veda. || 2.53 ||
Or, in all cases, [the rule applies] up to the point of grasping. 2.54.

One should observe the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*) for exactly as long as it takes to complete the study of all the Vedas, because that is the purpose of it. The inclusion of the word "all" is for the sake of indicating whether one studies one, two, or all of them. And thus says Manu:

"Having studied the Vedas, or two Vedas, or even one Veda, in due order... [MDh 3.2]. This [rule] is an exception regarding the previously mentioned limit, whether it be exceeded or fallen short; the statement regarding the rule is that "what is studied according to the rule becomes powerful. (2.54)
At the conclusion of his studies, the teacher is to be invited with a gift of wealth. || 2.55 ||

Upon the completion of his studies, but not necessarily upon the conclusion of his vows, the student should invite the teacher—the *ācārya*—for a purpose or need, asking: "What may I do for the sake of my teacher? (2.55)
Then, having performed the bath, or [the bath] permitted [by the teacher]. 2.56.

"Having performed" means having given; that is, the purpose instructed by the teacher. Or else, for one who has been permitted [to depart] with the words, "Enough with the teacher's fee," the ritual bath is the *samāvartana*. 2.56.
Now, since there may be many gurus such as one's father and others present together, [the author] states who is to be honored first:
"The teacher is the most excellent among gurus. (2.57)

The teacher (ācārya) is defined by the characteristics already stated; he is the most excellent and the foremost among other gurus, such as one's father and so forth. Consequently, in the rule "In the case of a conflict, [the word] 'another' [refers to him]" (GDh 6.4), it is this very person who is denoted by the word "another" (para). || 2.57 ||
"Mother," say some; "mother," say others. 2.58.

Some consider the mother to be superior; others [consider] the father, because of the use of the particle *iti* [to indicate a different opinion]; otherwise, the form *mātā ekaḥ* would have sufficed. The teacher is more important than the father alone. And so says Manu:
"That which the mother and father produce from each other out of desire, one should know that to be his mere physical birth (*saṃbhūti*), which occurs when he is born from the womb."
"But that birth which the teacher, having mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to rule by means of the Sāvitrī—that is true, that is free from old age and death" (MDh 2.147–48).
If the father himself is the teacher, then the father is distinguished; yet the mother is the most excellent of all. And so Vasiṣṭha says:
"Ten times more venerable than the preceptor (upādhyāya) is the teacher (ācārya); a hundred times more venerable than the teacher is the father;
but a thousand times more venerable than the father is the mother. [VaDh 13.48].
Here, by the word "father," only that father who is also the teacher (ācārya) is intended. 2.58.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Maskarīya-gautama-bhāṣya.
Chapter Three:
Some authorities state that for one who has thus established his observances and acquired knowledge, there is an option regarding the stages of life (āśrama). 3.1.
Of him whose brahmacarya has remained unbroken. And so Manu says:
"Having studied the Vedas—either all of them, two of them, or even one—in due order, one who has not violated his brahmacarya shall enter the stage of the householder" (MDh 3.2).

And thus, for one who has fallen away in this manner, the penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) should be observed. Alternatively, the mention of "him" (*tad-grahaṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding the Śūdra, so that the description of the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*) does not apply to him as well. Or else, the phrase "of each and each" (*tasya tasya*) is used in the sense of repetition, meaning "of the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya. If it is argued that even without that mention, this is established simply by virtue of the general qualification [of the subject], we say no; for its purpose is to eliminate the suspicion that this might be a mere semblance of another Smṛti. For another Smṛti appears in this way: "This fourfold dharma of the Brāhmaṇa has been declared to you... (MDh 6.97).

Thus, one might suspect that this fourfold dharma belongs exclusively to the Brāhmaṇa, while for the other two [castes] it is of only one kind. If it is asked, "How then is that so?", the mention of the Brāhmaṇa there is for the sake of illustration. If it is asked, "How is that understood?"—it is because of the observation of another Smṛti which states: "The four stages of life (āśramas) belong to the three castes alone. And likewise Āpastamba says: "For all [castes], residence in the teacher's family begins from the initiation ceremony (upanayana). For all, there is no relinquishing until the completion of learning. Having understood the duties, one may undertake whatever one desires" [ĀpDh 2.21.3–5].

Some say: “Because the fruit is the same, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the stages of life (*āśrama*). For the fruit is twofold—consisting of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and consisting of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)—and it is obtained by either one [of these paths]. And thus says the Śruti: “There are three branches of dharma: sacrifice, study, and charity—this is the first; austerity alone is the second; and dwelling in the teacher’s family is the third. Having ascended these, one goes to the world of Brahman; established in Brahman, one attains immortality” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1). The meaning is as follows: there are three bases of dharma. “Sacrifice, study, and charity” is the designation for the householder; “torture alone” is the dharma of the forest-dweller and the wandering mendicant; and “dwelling in the teacher’s family” is that of the student. “Having ascended these” means having properly entered the stage of the student, the stage of the householder, the stage of the forest-dweller, or the stage of the wandering mendicant. “He who among them is established in Brahman”—that is, the knower intent on Brahman—“attains immortality,” i.e., he goes to liberation. Thus, because the attainment of the world of Brahman is taught for all of them, the equality of their fruits has been stated. Similarly, in the Jābāla Śruti, the equality of the fruits is heard: “Having completed the student life, one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce. Or otherwise, one may renounce directly from the student life, or from the house, or from the forest; he goes to the world of Brahman” (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4). Manu also says:
“All these, when practiced in succession according to the scriptures, lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal” (MDh 6.88).

Here, by the force of the word *api* (“even”), it should be understood that even a single one [of them leads there]. Āpastamba also says: “There are four stages of life (*āśrama*): the householder’s stage, dwelling in the teacher’s family, the stage of silence [the student], and forest-dwelling. One who conducts himself without distraction in all of these according to the instruction attains security” (ĀpDh 2.21.1–2). Therefore, because they yield an equal result, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between them.

But surely, if they were equal, then since both kinds of fruits would be attained through celibacy alone, there would follow the contingency that the injunctions for the other stages of life are purposeless.

It is said: the injunction for other stages of life (*āśrama*) is intended for one who is capable of practicing a particular stage, so that he may enter that specific stage; or else, it is for the purpose of entering a desired stage through the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from previous births. Scripture also states: "Knowledge and action take hold of him, as does his prior wisdom" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). Furthermore, the scriptural injunction regarding "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) should be understood as applying to a householder who possesses the requisite capacity and desire. When this is accepted, the scriptural passage concerning renunciation (*vyutthāna*) also becomes consistent: "Having known this very Self, they rise above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, and then lead the life of a mendicant" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1); otherwise, the instruction to "lead the life of a mendicant" would not be tenable as a teaching on renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). Moreover, by the verse beginning with "being born," the necessity of performing sacrifices and other duties for the householder is established, but not for the mere fact of being born, because the connection to the three debts (*ṛṇa*) is absolutely impossible for one who has not entered the householder stage, and because such an interpretation would contradict the scripture: "One should renounce even from the stage of studentship" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4). This is further supported by Smṛti texts which are not contradictory, such as: "From that very stage of studentship he renounces" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.21.8) and "He may dwell in whichever [stage] he desires" (Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra 7.3), as well as the fact that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are subordinate to the actual injunctions. Therefore, the meaning of the words should be understood as follows: "The householder" refers to one who, being born, has entered the state of householdership due to past impressions. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya as well. He becomes bound by three debts: he becomes indebted to the gods by sacrifice, therefore sacrifice must be performed; to the ancestors by progeny, therefore the procreation of offspring must be performed; to the sages by studentship (*brahmacarya*), therefore the observance of celibacy on sacred days and at other times must be maintained. When understood in this way, there is no contradiction between the Śruti and Smṛti anywhere. Regarding the use of the word "some" (*eke*), it is not Gautama who is meant, for his view is that all stages are to be combined. How is this known? From the statement: "But the teachers [hold] to a single stage of life" (Gautama Dharmasūtra 3.36), where the position of a single stage is presented as the opinion of others (*paramata*) for the sake of refutation; and from the indicative mark: "There are three stages of life before the last one" (Gautama Dharmasūtra 28.49), since the triad cannot exist before the final stage. Gautama, however, holds the view of option (*vikalpa*) in this manner.
Through sacrifice one attains the gods; through austerity, the Vairāja realm;
through renunciation, the station of Brahman; and through dispassion, dissolution into Prakṛti.

Because they are taught as having distinct results; because even in the *Jābāla-śruti*, instead of saying "having ascended any one [of them]," it says "having ascended these," thus expressing the intention of their combination (*samuccaya*); because the attainment of the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) is also taught as the result of their combination; because in the *Jābāla-śruti* as well, the position of combination is stated first as the primary view; because in the verse of Manu, "All [stages] also in succession" (MDh 6.88), the word "also" (*api*) has the sense of combination; because in the statement of Āpastamba, "In all of those" (ĀpDh 2.21.2), the plural number is used with the intention that one does not abide in only one, but rather in all of them; because the scriptural teaching of the three debts (*ṛṇatraya*) is also logically consistent only in this way; because the scriptural passage "and former knowledge" (*pūrvaprajñā ca*) is also consistent when understood as referring to knowledge (*vidyā*); because even the scriptural rule for lifelong performance (*yāvajjīva-śruti*) shows its non-permanence in the *Jābāla-śruti* passage: "If a householder enters the forest, and if he should desire the household state alone, then he should offer the *agnihotra* as long as he lives"; because in this view, the scriptural teaching on renunciation (*vyutthāna-śruti*) is all the more easily justified; and because by the verse "The fourth part of his life" (MDh 4.1), Manu also speaks while relying precisely on the position of combination. Therefore, the positions of option (*vikalpa*) and sublation (*bādha*) are presented merely as the views of others. Thus, it should be understood that statements such as "He may dwell in whichever he desires" (VaDh 7.3) were spoken from the perspective of teachers who advocate option. The mention of the position of option—even though it is established by implication—is made with the intention that one who is incapable of performing the combined practice due to defects such as blindness or lameness, or due to poverty and so forth, should resort to the position of option. This is the meaning.

Alternatively, he who possesses knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātmajñānin*) should resort to the path of mental construction (*vikalpapakṣa*), while the other should follow the path of combination (*samuccayapakṣa*). Why? Because the purpose of religious practice (*anuṣṭhāna*) is the arising of realization (*vijñānotpatti*). Once that has arisen, the goal of human existence (*puruṣārtha*) is accomplished for a person regardless of which stage of life (*āśrama*) they occupy. The mention of "stages of life" is for the sake of conventional usage, as in such passages as "the castes and the stages of life" (GDh 11.9). 3.1.
What, then, are those stages of life (āśrama)? To this he says: the student (brahmacārī), the householder (gṛhastha), the mendicant (bhikṣu), and the hermit (vaikhānasa). 3.2.

One who practices *brahmacarya* (celibacy), or one who moves about without desire for the domain of *Brahman* itself, is a *brahmacārī*. A *gṛha* is a wife; because of union with her, one is a *gṛhastha* (householder). Because of the habit of begging for alms, one is a *bhikṣu* (mendicant). The scripture taught by Vikhanas is the *Vaikhānasa*; one who conducts himself according to its rules is a *vaikhānasa*. This non-compound form (*avisamāsa*) is intended to indicate their distinctness. As Uśanas says: "There are two types of *brahmacārīs*: the *upakurvāṇa* and the *naiṣṭhika*; two types of *vaikhānasas*: those with a wife and those without a wife; two types of renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*): the *bhikṣu-saṃnyāsī* and the *veda-saṃnyāsī*; and the householder is of many kinds through distinctions such as the *śālīna*, the *yāyāvara*, and so forth. And so on.

But surely, in another Smṛti, after mentioning the *vaikhānasa*, the term *bhikṣu* is used. For what reason is there a difference in sequence here? It is said: the difference in sequence is for the purpose of excluding the *vaikhānasa* in the rule, "The first three are those belonging to the stages of life" (GDh 28.49). If it is argued that this is already established because of the prohibition against his entering a village, we say no; for it is possible that seekers might go to the forest as well. And so says another Smṛti:
"One learned in the four Vedas, one who knows the alternatives, an etymologist, and a reciter of Dharma..."
"The student, the householder, and the mendicant—this assembly consists of at least ten members.
However, some say:
"Having performed the Prajāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee..."
Having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brahmin should go forth from his home.

Relying on this other Smṛti text, some explain that the "difference in sequence" means that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) must be performed from the state of the householder alone; whether this has already been established by the preceding sūtra or not is for the learned Brahmins to investigate. 3.2.
Among them, the householder is the source of the others, because they do not produce offspring on their own. 3.3.

The householder is the cause for all four stages of life (*āśrama*), because the others—the student (*brahmacārin*) and so forth—lack progeny. The mention of the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*) is for the sake of providing a reason; for the student is already established [in his duty] simply by the preservation of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) is likewise enjoined to be one whose semen is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*). Thus, even in the case of the forest-dweller who maintains a wife, the preservation of celibacy must be observed. Although their eligibility is already established by the context, the explicit mention of them is for the purpose of showing that their entitlement to these duties belongs only to those who have been born from a householder. And so says Śātātapa:
"Cāṇḍālas, those who have fallen from their caste, wandering mendicants, and ascetics—the offspring born of them should be made to dwell together with the Cāṇḍālas. Thus it is said.

When it is stated, “For them, the householder stage alone is the source,” the use of the restrictive particle *eva* (alone) already establishes that others must observe celibacy; nevertheless, this specific formulation is intended so that there may be no turning back for these [ascetics]. If they were to turn back toward the householder state, then they become outcasts (*caṇḍāla*). Why? Because of the cited statement of Śātātapa. In that regard: “They become outcasts. This refers to those wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) and ascetics (*tāpasa*), as well as lifelong students (*naiṣṭhika*) and forest-dwellers (*vaikhānasa*) who have fallen away or turned back. Therefore, the meaning is that the king or the village headman should cause their offspring to dwell together with outcasts. 3.3.

Now, since the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma) must be explained in their proper sequence, and because they are common to all stages, the author—having already described those pertaining to the student (upakurvāṇa)—states what pertains to the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) as it follows in order:
"In that regard, [the duties] of the religious student have been stated" (3.4).

In this regard, the extension (*atideśa*) is that whatever has been prescribed concerning the kindling of the sacred fires and so forth by way of the *upanayana* ceremony applies to him as well. Now, one might ask: how is it known that this pertains only to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) and not to the temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*)? It is said: because [the duties] have already been stated for the temporary student; because the householder, the mendicant, and the forest-dweller will be described later; and therefore, it belongs only to the lifelong student.

If it is asked, "Then for what purpose is the mention of the *brahmacārin*?"—it is for this purpose: that only he who has performed the *upakurvāṇa* vow has the qualification for being a *naiṣṭhika*. 3.4.

Having stated that the vow of the *upakurvāṇa* (the student who returns home) must indeed be performed by the *naiṣṭhika* (the lifelong student) as well because of its extension [to him], he now states the specific rule for this [latter]:
"Dependence upon the teacher until the end. (3.5)
Dependence upon the teacher—that is, following his will—must be maintained until death. (3.5)
Furthermore: he should mutter [the mantra] with the remainder of the teacher's ritual duties. 3.6.

During times other than those spent in service to the guru, one should perform *japa*. Thus, *japa* alone is his distinguished means for accomplishing dharma. Although "teacher" (*ācārya*) was the subject under discussion, the use of the term "guru" here is intended to include the service of both mother and father as well. Accordingly, Manu states:
"Service to these three is called the highest austerity;
without being authorized by them, one should not practice any other dharma" (MDh 2.229).
Thus [ends the section]. 3.6.
In the absence of the guru, one's conduct [toward him] is the same toward his offspring. 3.7.

"In the absence of the guru, service to his offspring; in the absence of the teacher, service to his offspring"—this is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). The mention of "guru" is intended to include offspring of the same caste (*samānajātīya*). The mention of "offspring" is intended to exclude the wife (*bhāryā*).
In the absence of these, [the gift should be made] to an elder fellow-student or into the fire. || 3.8 ||

In the absence of that [the teacher], [one should serve] the son of the teacher; in the absence of him, one who is advanced in knowledge and so forth; in the absence of him, a fellow-student (*sabrahmacārin*) who practices the same discipline (*caraṇa*); in the absence of him, the fire. Service to the fire means meditation upon the fire in its form as light. 3.8.
What, then, is the fruit of this stage of life? To this he says: "One who conducts himself thus, having conquered his senses, attains the world of Brahman. (3.9)

Thus, acting according to the instruction, one attains the world of Brahmā, the abode of Brahmā, provided that he has conquered his senses. Since the organ of generation was mentioned in the instruction regarding the protection of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), this [conquest of the senses] should be understood as referring to the objects of the eyes and the other senses. As Manu said:
“That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled, neither rejoices nor desponds—he should be known as one who has conquered his senses. (MDh 2.98)
The injunction at the conclusion of the fruit is for the purpose of showing that this very [practice] is the primary one even for those who follow the higher paths. 3.9.
Now he states the common characteristic of the others as well:
"And this is not incompatible with those that follow" (3.10).

Whatever has been prescribed for the student (*brahmacārin*) applies also to those who follow him, provided it is not contradictory—such as the avoidance of gambling and similar activities. That which is contradictory is excluded; for example, the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) is excluded for the wandering mendicant (*pravrajita*), living in the teacher’s house for the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*), and the observance of celibacy for the householder. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that whatever will be stated hereafter also applies to the preceding stages if it is not contradictory, such as: "One should not converse with barbarians, the impure, or the unrighteous" (GDh 9.17), and so forth. 3.10.
A monk is one who has no accumulation. 3.11

Now, it might be asked: "Since the duties of the householder come next in order, why are they being bypassed and the duties of the mendicant being explained instead? To this it is replied: The householder has much to be said about him. Some of his duties, being non-conflicting, are stated here so that they may be known by those who came before; for that purpose, they are mentioned out of sequence. If it is then asked, "In that case, the duties of the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*) should be stated," there is no fault, because they have already been mentioned according to the order of their introduction.

Therefore, it is said first regarding the monk: by the word "non-accumulation" (*anicaya*), the relinquishing of material objects that are subject to increase is meant, not the relinquishing of permanent objects such as the topknot (*śikhā*) or the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
But is it not rather the relinquishing of the permanent alone that is appropriate? By the word "sacred thread" (*upavīta*), a specific mode of wearing is designated—as it is said:
"When the right hand is raised, one is called 'invested with the sacred thread' (*upavītī*) by the wise" (Manu Dharmaśāstra 2.63).
The *upavīta* is for the sake of sacrifice; it is called the *yajñopavīta* because he lacks the qualification for performing sacrifices.
"He who has no attachment to a water-pot, nor to water, nor to clothing, nor to the three *puṣkaras*, nor to a house, nor to a seat, nor to food—he is indeed a knower of liberation" (VaDh 10.23).

[The opponent argues: "Because there is an instruction for the renunciation of the water-pot (*kuṇḍī*) and other items; and because in the *Jābāla-śruti* it is also said, 'Having clipped his nails, having cast off the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*)', there is an instruction for the renunciation of the sacrificial thread.

To this, it is replied: First, regarding what was stated—that there is no entitlement to sacrifice (*yajña*)—the word "sacrifice" (*yāga*) also applies to the worship of the gods and similar acts. And for him, the worship of the gods certainly exists in the form of the worship of the Supreme Self through meditation. Why? Because he is one who dwells constantly in the forest and has conquered his senses.
For one who turns away from all worldly pleasures,
whose mind is intent on contemplation of the inner self, and who remains in equanimity, there is indeed certain non-return [to rebirth]. [VaDh 10.17]

This is because of the observation of another *smṛti* text, as the qualification for this very sacrifice of the self (*ātmayāga*) is established there. And so it is heard in the *Śruti*: “Dharma and adharma are the oblation; the mind is the dipping-spoon (*sruva*); the vital breath is the *adhvaryu* priest; the senses are the *udgātṛ* singers; sound and the other objects of sense are the *hotṛ* priests. With these officiating priests and with that spoon, the ascetic (*yati*) must daily offer that oblation into the fire of the Supreme Self. Therefore, since the qualification for this sacrifice exists, there is no fault. As for what was said: “There is no attachment to the water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), nor to water” (VaDh 10.23), even there, the abandonment of attachment alone is intended for the sake of avoiding the diversity [of worldly concerns] regarding the water-pot and such things, not the abandonment of the water-pot itself. Why? Because it will be stated in that very same context: “Wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavītin*), with a water-pot in his hand” (VaDh 10.31). If it is argued: “Since it is said, ‘The most righteous practice among all stages of life’ (VaDh 10.30), and because this applies to all stages of life (*āśrama*) by virtue of being a general rule, it is set aside by the specific rule,” we say: No, provided that the qualification for all stages of life is indeed intended there. In that context, for the purpose of constructing the meaning of the sentence and its utterance, the author would have used the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) to express the state of “wearing the sacred thread and having a water-pot in hand.
