Having first stated, “The avoidance of backbiting, envy, pride, egoism, dishonesty, self-praise, reviling others, hypocrisy, greed, anger, and delusion is the most righteous practice for all stages of life” (VaDh 10.30), the subsequent mention using the negative suffix (*abhāvapratyaya*) with the specific reference, “Wearing the sacred thread, with a water-pot in hand” (VaDh 10.31), can be understood as intended to exclude the qualification of all stages of life. Therefore, since there is no qualification for all stages of life in that instance, one can certainly understand that the statement “No attachment to the water-pot, nor to water” (VaDh 10.23) intends the abandonment of attachment alone, so that no contradiction between the preceding and following passages may arise. For that very reason, the word “attachment” (*saṅga*) is employed. Consequently, by that [text] also, there is no abandonment of the water-pot and such items. And as for what was said: “Having clipped his nails and discarded the sacred thread,” even there, at the time of first entering the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), only the discarding of the old sacred thread is performed; there is no prohibition against the one being taken up at that time. Why? Because another *smṛti* states: “Having clipped his nails, and having discarded his old garment, sacred thread, and water-pot, he should enter the stage of life after taking up new ones. Therefore, the abandonment refers to those items belonging to the previous stage.

Furthermore, if one were to abandon the permanent wearing of the substance (the sacred thread), it would follow that a mendicant lacks the means for ritual sipping (*ācamana*), because the rule begins with, "One should sip water while wearing the sacrificial thread" (ĀpDh 1.15.1); in its absence, even the act of sipping water would become impossible.

If you argue that—just as in the case of the rule "He may be shaven-headed or wear a topknot" (GDh 3.22)—you accept that sipping water is permissible even when the topknot, which is an ancillary part of the rite, is absent, we too maintain the same position.

No; in that case there is no fault because of a specific scriptural statement: "He may be shaven-headed or wear a topknot" (GDh 3.22). For you, however, there is indeed a fault because there is no such statement that the sacred thread must be discarded.

Although it should have been stated as "a monk is one without accumulation," the mention of "dharma" at the beginning is for the purpose of renouncing even those things considered permanent, such as the *agnihotra* fire and one's wife. Thus, he who goes forth from the state of a householder must renounce both the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires, along with the expansion of a wife, sons, sacrifices, and so forth. Likewise, he who goes forth from the state of a forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*)—even in that case, if he belongs to the category of one accompanied by a wife—must renounce his wife, as well as the prescribed five great sacrifices and the *śrāmaṇaka* fire.
Some explain that the mention at the beginning is for the purpose of enjoining the state of non-accumulation even for the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong student).

That is incorrect, because recitation (*japa*) alone is taught as the primary duty in the rule, "He should recite with the remainder of his duties to the teacher" [GDh 3.6]; by that very fact, the absence of the maintenance of the sacred fires and so forth can certainly be understood. 3.11.
One whose vital energy is drawn upward. || 3.12 ||

By the rule, "And this is not inconsistent with the subsequent [stages]" (GDh 3.10), since the preservation of celibacy already established for the *brahmacārin* applies here as well, the mention of *ūrdhvaretas* (one whose semen is drawn upward) is for the purpose of indicating that one should employ such means as ensure that the semen does not diminish. And the means consists of consuming very little food and so forth. As the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva has said:
"The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food;
even the taste for them turns away when he has seen the Supreme. (BhG 2.59).

Likewise, with the intention of restricting the consumption of food, it is stated in another Smṛti: "The sage’s meal consists of eight morsels," and so forth. Thus, there is no fault in a student (brahmacārin) eating a full meal. Accordingly, another Smṛti states:
"The ox, the student, and the one who has established the sacred fires—these three achieve their purpose only while eating; for them, there is no success through fasting. (VaDh 6.21)
Thus [ends the section]. 3.12.
He should remain steadfast in his conduct during the rainy season.

Because of the plural form in the word *varṣāsu* ("during the rains"), the meaning is that one should not travel from one village to another during the four months of the rainy season. The mention of "conduct" (*śīla*) implies that even while staying in one place, one should avoid the exertion of wandering about. By this very rule, his state of having no fixed abode (*aniketana*) is established. And so says another Smṛti: "At the edge of a village, in a temple, in an empty house, or at the foot of a tree" (VaDh 10.13). Furthermore, by using the term "conduct," he makes it known that this is not necessarily an absolute requirement; therefore, in cases such as famine or the collapse of a kingdom, one may indeed travel. (3.13)
One seeking alms should go to the village. 3.14.

"Bhikṣā" refers to food because it is begged for, as well as clothing, a water-pot, and so forth; for the sake of these, he should go to a village. By implication, it is established that during the remaining time, he should stay in the forest, in a temple, or similar places. || 3.14 ||
When the time for alms has arrived, the student says:
"One should wander at the end [of the village] without turning back. (3.15)
"Jaghanya" means after the act of eating; that is the meaning. And so Manu says:

"When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle is laid aside, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal, and when the removal of the dishes has been completed, the ascetic should always go for alms. (MDh 6.56)

The meaning is that he should not enter again on that same day the house in which food was refused to him without being turned away. The word "should practice" (*caret*) is intended to include other Smṛti texts; as Vasiṣṭha says: "When the smoke has ceased and the pestle is at rest, wearing a single garment or an antelope skin... (VaDh 10.8). || 3.15 ||
One whose desires have ceased. || 3.16 ||

The meaning is that he does not offer blessings in response to alms-giving, salutations, and the like. If it is argued that this is already understood from the rule, "He does not undertake acts of injury or favor" (GDh 3.25), we say no; for while favor (*anugraha*) consists of an action, a blessing (*āśis*) consists of speech. 3.16.
Restrained in speech, sight, and action. || 3.17 ||

In the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*), although the requirement is already established by the rule, “Restrained in speech, arms, and belly” (GDh 2.28), this is stated again for the sake of emphasizing excellence. Therefore, restraint of speech is silence (*mauna*), except for Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), recitation (*japa*), asking the way while traveling, and inquiries regarding dharma and yoga.
For one who asks the way, for dharma and yoga, and likewise for Vedic study, even the begging for alms and speaking the word “give” do not constitute a fault for the ascetic.

This is because of the statement in another Smṛti: "Restraint of the eyes" means that one must not even look at one's own disease. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "One who is indifferent toward all beings" (VaDh 10.29). "Restraint of action" means performing only what is prescribed; it implies that there should be no engagement in actions for the sake of desired rewards (kāmya). (3.17)
Now, by the rule "the monk is without accumulation" (GDh 3.11), once all accumulated property has been renounced, an exception is made:
he may wear a garment for the purpose of covering his private parts. 3.18.

"Kaupīna" refers to nakedness; one should wear only such clothing as serves to cover that [nakedness]. And thus, there is no fault in accepting only that much from praiseworthy members of the twice-born. Furthermore: "He who, having granted safety to all beings, turns back from his vow, and he who always accepts gifts—[he] slays both those born and those unborn."
Thus, the enumeration of faults found in another Smṛti should be understood as referring to cases other than this one. (3.18)
Some say it is abandoned after having been washed. 3.19.

Some think that, for the sake of avoiding the fault of accepting gifts, one should wash and then wear what has been discarded on the road or elsewhere after it has been cast away; [the term] "having washed" (*nirṇijya*) is used for the purpose of attaining personal purification. (3.19)
One should not take a limb from medicinal plants or trees that has not been separated [from the parent].

Plants end with the ripening of their fruit. Those that bear fruit without flowers are called *vanaspati*. By the inclusion of both terms, all stationary beings (*sthāvara*) are also included. One should not take from them anything inseparable or inherent, such as branches or leaves. If it is argued that this is already established by the rule, "One who does not undertake acts of injury or favor" (GDh 3.25), [the answer is: some say that in that context, "injury" refers only to the killing of mobile beings (*jaṅgama*). Since [the present rule] is stated with that intention, there is no fault. Because of the prefix *upa*, even the one who causes another to act [should not engage in such acts]. 3.20.
Since it has been taught that his conduct must be constant, and because one might otherwise act according to whim outside of the rainy season, he says:
"He shall not stay in a village for a second night during the non-rainy season. (3.21)

By the word *ṛtu* (season), only the rainy season (*varṣā*) is intended. When the season has passed, he should not stay in a village for a second night; the meaning is that he should not stay in a single village for two days. Because of the mention of "village," there is no fault in staying in the forest. Because of the mention of "when the season has passed" (*apartu*), there is no fault even if he stays for a second [night] during the rains. By the word *varṣā*, the winter and summer seasons are also implied. Consequently, it is established by implication that during that time of the rains, he may stay in one place alone and should not stay elsewhere. (3.21)
He may be either shaven-headed or wear a topknot.
This undertaking is for the purpose of prohibiting the matted-hair ascetic; there is an option according to one's wish. 3.2.22.
One should avoid the destruction of seeds. 3.23.
One should not perform the destruction of seeds, such as rice and other grains, by means of threshing and similar processes. || 3.23 ||
He is equal toward all beings. 3.24.
The meaning is that one should remain impartial toward all living beings, avoiding the distinction between one's own side and the side of others. 3.24.
One who does not undertake acts of injury or favor. 3.25.

Since this is already established by the rule "violence" (hiṃsām) [GDh 2.23] within the section on the religious student (brahmacārin), this repetition is for the sake of emphasizing the gravity of the matter. Consequently, even when the killing of a living being occurs unintentionally, an expiation must be performed day after day to avoid that [sin]. Thus Uśanas says: "For the purification of an unintentional killing, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) during the night and during the day. By the word "favor" (anugraha), affection (sneha) is meant; the sense is that he should not even show such affection [toward those who have committed violence]. 3.25.
Having spoken concerning the monk, he now describes the dharma of the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*):
"The forest-dweller lives in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, and is devoted to austerity. (3.26)

The term *vaikhānasa* has already been etymologically explained. He, dwelling in the forest, should be one whose habit is eating roots and the like; the meaning is that he should not eat prepared food. He should be devoted to austerity, having the habit of withering the body. And thus, even of roots, fruits, and so forth, he should eat only a very small amount. This is because another Smṛti text is seen which states, "For the forest-dweller, sixteen [mouthfuls]" (VaDh 6.20). || 3.26 ||
Having established the sacred fire according to the Śrāmaṇaka rite. 3.27.

The *śrāmaṇaka* is the treatise of the *vaikhānasas*. By means of it, having established the sacred fires, one should perform the evening and morning oblations; this is the remainder [of the sense]. 3.27.
He shall not eat vulgar food. 3.28.
One should not eat even wild roots and fruits that have been cultivated in a village. || 3.28 ||
He is a worshiper of the gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, and sages. || 3.29 ||

The five great sacrifices (*pañca mahāyajñāḥ*) of the householder are accomplished by means of village food. This section is commenced so that there might not be an abandonment of them due to the prohibition against non-village (wild) food for him. And thus says Manu:
"With various kinds of pure wild plants, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits, he should perform these very great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule. (MDh 6.5) || 3.29 ||
He should be a host to all guests, with the exception of those who are prohibited. 3.30.

Everything that goes to his hermitage is indeed his guest. The meaning is that there is no restriction regarding caste, such as "a non-Brāhmaṇa is not a guest of a Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 5.43), nor is there any restriction regarding number; however, this excludes those who are prohibited, such as thieves and others, as well as those born of inverse unions (pratiloma). 3.30.
One may also consume [the meat] of a porcupine. 3.31.

The meat of an animal killed by wild beasts such as tigers is called *vaiṣka*. One may consume that. The word "api" (even/also) is used here in a sense of censure; therefore, one should consume it only in times of distress. 3.31.
He should not stand upon ground that has been ploughed by a plow. 3.32.

The meaning is that even in the forest, one should not step upon a ploughed area, nor should one make a dwelling there. Although the word *ākrāmet* (should step upon) would have sufficed, the use of the word *adhitiṣṭhet* (should occupy/stand upon) is intended to indicate the absence of fault when one steps upon such ground unintentionally. Although the word *kṛṣṭam* (ploughed) would have sufficed, the inclusion of the word *phāla* (plough) is for the purpose of prohibiting residence in the immediate vicinity of a field. (3.32)
And he should not enter a village. 3.33.
One should not enter a human habitation even by a path not ploughed by a plow; because of the word "and" (ca), this applies to entering another village as well. 3.33.
With matted hair, he was clothed in rags and skins. || 3.34 ||

*Jaṭilaḥ* means one with matted hair (*keśī*). This rule is established for the purpose of restriction, so that he must indeed be one with matted hair. *Cīra* is made from *darbha* grass and other materials; this is to be understood as his lower garment. *Ajina* is a skin; this is his upper garment. And so it is stated in another *smṛti*: "Clad in rags and having a skin as an upper garment. (3.34)
One should not eat [the meat of an animal] less than one year old. 3.35.

One should not consume even roots and fruits that are more than a year old. Thus says Manu: "In the month of Āśvayuja, one should discard [the store]," and so forth. In this way, the rule of storing for only a single year is established. (3.35)
Having spoken regarding the Vaikhānasa, he now says, desiring to state the position that the stages of life (āśramas) are mutually exclusive according to the view of certain teachers:
"But the teachers [maintain] a single stage of life, because of the direct injunction of the householder's life. (3.36)

*Aikāśramya* means "belonging to a single stage of life" (*ekāśrama*). The word *tu* is used for emphasis. The genitive case in *gārhasthyasya* denotes the object of the action; thus, the teachers maintain that only the householder’s stage (*gārhasthya*) is intended. Why? Because of its direct injunction; the meaning is that it is because an injunction is found in the revealed scripture (*śruti*). Even though it is not explicitly enjoined in the form "one should be a householder," nevertheless, since the performance of rites such as the *agnihotra*—which are to be accomplished by a householder—is enjoined, the injunction must be understood to apply to that very stage. (3.36)
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Maskarīya-gautama-bhāṣya*.
Regarding the fourth chapter:
the duties (*dharma*) of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) and others have been stated; now, the duties of the householder (*gṛhastha*) must be explained, and for this reason he says:
A householder should take a wife who is of equal status, not previously married to another, and younger than himself.

The designation "householder" is used here as a future title, intended for the student (*snātaka*) to enter the duties of a householder—which are not yet contradictory to his current state—until he takes a wife. A "suitable" woman is one who is equal in caste (*jāti*), but not necessarily in lineage (*kula*). Learning, once lost, can be regained;
but upon the loss of caste, there is total ruin in this world.
Since she is to be honored according to the reputation of her family,
one should therefore marry a woman of noble birth.

Thus, because it is heard in another Smṛti that realization [of dharma] belongs only to those of an eminent family; "a wife" means one who is endowed with auspicious marks and is to be supported; "should obtain" means he should solicit her; "one who has had no other [husband before]" means she who has not been given away even by word of mouth to another; "younger" means of lower age than himself. (4.1)
The exception to this is: marriage with those who do not share the same *pravara*. 4.2.

"Samānapravaratva" means having the same ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya*); the absence of that is "asamānapravaratva. Marriage should be performed with those who possess this lack of common ancestry. Although one could have simply said "those with different lineages" (*asamānapravarān*), the expression used here is intended to make known that there is no fault even if she belongs to the same *gotra* on the mother's side. Thus, the prohibition against a *sagotra* marriage applies only from the father's side. And so says Manu: "She who is not a *sapinda* of the mother and she who is not of the same *gotra* as the father," and so forth (MDh 3.5). 4.2.
Beyond the seventh generation from the paternal relatives. 4.3.

The paternal kinsmen (pitṛbandhu) are the father’s maternal uncles, sisters, and so forth; marriage [is permitted] beyond the seventh degree from them. The meaning is that marriage should be performed starting from the eighth degree. || 4.3 ||
And [the same applies] to one who possesses the seed. 4.4.120.

The word "ca" (and) serves to draw forward [the phrase] "beyond the seventh. Regarding the seed that has been sown in another's field, [the prohibition applies] from the very moment it is born. This is a prohibition intended for a case where [marriage) would otherwise be permitted due to the absence of a common *pravara*. (4.4)
From the maternal relatives, up to the fifth degree. || 4.5 ||

The phrase "one should find [a bride] above" carries over. "Maternal kinsmen" refers to the maternal uncle, the mother's sister, and so forth. In that regard, marriage should be performed with one who is beyond the fifth degree. 4.5.
Now he describes the rules for marriage:
"In the *brāhma* rite, one should give [the daughter], having clothed and adorned her, to a man endowed with learning, good conduct, kinship, and virtuous character. (4.6)

"Brahma" is the designation for this form of marriage. "Vidyā" refers to the triple Veda (*trayī*). "Cāritra" is the performance of enjoined duties. "Bandhu" is a noble lineage. "Śīla" is the very orientation toward righteousness (*dharma*). The word "endowed with" (*saṃpanna*) is to be connected with each [of these]. Having clothed the bridegroom with a pair of garments and having adorned her with ornaments and the like, he should give her away preceded by the pouring of water. The phrases "having clothed" and "having adorned" are to be understood as applying to the three subsequent forms of marriage as well. (4.6)
The mantra for the formal union in the Prājāpatya rite is: "Let dharma be practiced together. (4.7)

*Prājāpatya* is the designation for this form of marriage. In that *prājāpatya* marriage, the mantra intended for the purpose of union is the "union-mantra"; having recited it at the time of giving her away, he should give her. What is that mantra? "Let dharma be practiced together. (4.7)
In the r̥ṣi-rite, he should give a pair of cattle to the one who provides the maiden.
"Ārṣa" is the designation for this form of marriage. In that rite, after the groom has first given a pair of cattle, he should afterwards give the bride, having clothed and adorned her.
The giving of a gift to a priest within the sacrificial altar-ground is the divine [form of marriage]. 4.9.

The term *antarvedi* is used for the purpose of referring to the sacrifice that has commenced. This is because, as seen in such rules as "the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the father-in-law" (GDh 5.28), the designation *ṛtvij* is applied even after the ritual action has concluded. The mention of "giving" (*dāna*) is intended to indicate that this exceeds the regular sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The term *daiva* is a technical name for the marriage rite. 4.9.
When a man unites with a woman who desires him after she has adorned herself, that is the Gāndharva form of marriage.

Having adorned herself by her own hand, she will say: "Having cast off the ornaments of my father" (GDh 18.21); this refers to that case. Desiring [him], she should unite with the groom of her own accord; that is the Gāndharva marriage. 4.10.
The Āsura [form] is the bending down of those who possess wealth by means of riches. || 4.11 ||

That marriage in which the bending down [of the bridegroom] is performed by the giving of wealth to the bride's kinsmen is called the Āsura form. Although it should have been stated as "to the bride's kinsmen" (*kanyāvatām*), the inclusion of the word "women" (*strī*) is for the purpose of precluding the fruit that results from the gift of a maiden. (4.11)
The Rākṣasa [form of marriage] results from taking [the bride] by force. 4.12.
Where there is taking by force, that is the Rākṣasa [form]. || 4.12 ||
Because it is performed without the woman's consent, that is the Paiśāca rite. 4.13.

When one approaches a maiden who is unknown to him—whether she is asleep, intoxicated, or distracted, or engaged in another activity—that is the marriage called *paiśāca*. The term "approaching" (*upagamana*) should be understood here in the sense of embracing and so forth, because for one whose virginity has been violated, the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) are absent. And thus Manu says: "The mantras pertaining to the taking of the hand are established only for maidens" (MDh 8.226). 4.13.
The first four are lawful. 4.14.

Only the first four [stages] are not devoid of the Dharma. Although one could simply say "the first," the term "initial" (*prathama*) is used for the purpose of indicating that whatever is first is what is praised. Consequently, each subsequent stage should be understood as existing only in the absence of its respective predecessor.
"Some say there are six. 4.15.

Some, however, consider even the Gāndharva and Āsura forms to be lawful; thus Vasiṣṭha says: "There are six types of marriage: Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Gāndharva, Kṣatra, and Mānuṣa" (VaDh 1.28). In this way, the Rākṣasa and Paiśāca forms, though extremely base, should be understood as permissible by virtue of scriptural injunction when the preceding forms are not possible. (4.15)
Now, for the sake of specifying those sons born of them, he says:

"Those born in the direct order from women one degree, two degrees, or three degrees lower are of the same caste [as the father], as well as the Ambaṣṭha, Ugra, Niṣāda, Dauṣyanta, and Pāraśava. (4.16)

The *anuloma* [progeny] are those born according to the sequence of the castes (*varṇa*). For a Brāhmaṇa, the immediate [caste] is the Kṣatriya; the one-removed is the Vaiśya; the two-removed is the Śūdra. For a Kṣatriya, the immediate is the Vaiśya; the one-removed is the Śūdra; for him, there is no two-removed. For a Vaiśya, the immediate is the Śūdra; for him, there is no one-removed. And thus, one born from a Brāhmaṇa by an immediate [woman] is of the same caste (*savarṇa*). One born from a Kṣatriya by an immediate [woman] is an Ambaṣṭha. One born from a Vaiśya by an immediate [woman] is an Ugra. One born from a Brāhmaṇa by a one-removed [woman] is a Niṣāda. One born from a Kṣatriya by a one-removed [woman] is a Dauṣyanta. One born from a Brāhmaṇa by a two-removed [woman] is a Pāraśava. (4.16)
The inverse [castes] are the Sūta, Māgadha, Āyogava, Kṣattṛ, Vaidehaka, and Caṇḍāla. || 4.17 ||

Those born in the reverse order (*prātilomyena*) are *pratiloma*. Among these [wives], they are born only from those who are immediate, one degree removed, or two degrees removed. For a Kṣatriya, the immediate [wife] is a Brāhmaṇī; for a Vaiśya, the immediate is a Kṣatriyā; for a Śūdra, the immediate is a Vaiśyā. For a Vaiśya, the one-degree-removed [wife] is a Brāhmaṇī; for a Śūdra, it is a Kṣatriyā. For a Śūdra, the two-degree-removed [wife] is a Brāhmaṇī. One born to a Kṣatriya by an immediate [wife] is a Sūta; one born to a Vaiśya by an immediate [wife] is a Māgadha; one born to a Śūdra by an immediate [wife] is an Āyogava. One born to a Vaiśya by a one-degree-removed [wife] is a Kṣattṛ; one born to a Śūdra by a one-degree-removed [wife] is a Vaidehaka. One born to a Śūdra by a two-degree-removed [wife] is a Caṇḍāla. Such, then, is the opinion of Gautama (4.17).
Now, he states the difference in terminology according to the opinion of others:
"The Brāhmaṇī bore sons from the [other] castes in successive order: the Brāhmaṇa, the Sūta, the Māgadha, and the Caṇḍāla. (4.18)

The Brahmin woman gave birth [to children] from the social classes beginning with the Brahmin in their respective order: from the Brahmin a Brahmin, from the Kṣatriya a Sūta, from the Vaiśya a Māgadha, and from the Śūdra a Caṇḍāla. The use of the past tense "gave birth" (ajījanat) is for the purpose of demonstrating the beginninglessness of saṃsāra. (4.18)
From those very [castes], the Kṣatriyas [beget] the Mūrdhāvasikta, the Kṣatriyadhīvara, and the Pulkasa.

The phrase "she gave birth in due order" also applies here. From those very same [classes], beginning with the Brāhmaṇa and so forth, she gave birth—in regular succession—to Kṣatriyas. From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother was born the Mūrdhāvasikta; from a Kṣatriya father and a Kṣatriya mother was born a Kṣatriya; from a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother was born a Dhīvara; and from a Śūdra father and a Kṣatriya mother was born a Pulkasa. (4.19)
From those very same [Kṣatriyas], Vaiśyas give birth to the Bhṛjjakaṇṭha, Māhiṣya, Vaiśya, and Vaidehaka.

The phrase "he procreated in due order" continues [from the previous verse]. Thus, one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Vaiśya mother is a Bhṛjjakaṇṭha; one born from a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother is a Māhiṣya; one born from a Vaiśya father and a Vaiśya mother is a Vaiśya; and one born from a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother is a Vaidehaka. (4.20)
Some say that a Śūdra woman [may bear] Pāraśava, Yavana, Karaṇa, and Śūdra sons. 4.21.

She produced [these children] from these very men in successive order: one born of a Brāhmaṇa from a Śūdra woman is a Pāraśava; one born of a Kṣatriya from a Śūdra woman is a Yavana; one born of a Vaiśya from a Śūdra woman is a Karaṇa; and one born of a Śūdra from a Śūdra woman is simply called a Śūdra. Some teachers explain this through these various designations. And the statement of these different designations according to the opinion of some is for the purpose of showing that even if these names are found in other regions, one should not consider them to be distinct castes. (4.21)
And for these as well,
there is entry into another caste through the seventh [generation] by means of either elevation or degradation.

By the word *varṇa*, the generative seed (*utpādakabīja*) is meant; the meaning is that one should become of the same *varṇa* as the generative seed. By the seventh revolution of the generations (*yugaparivartana*). By the word *antara*, the field (*kṣetra*) is meant. And from this, the sequence is to be understood: through excellence (*utkarṣa*), the state of having the quality of the generative seed, and through deficiency (*apakarṣa*), the state of having the quality of the field. From that, excellence is to be considered in relation to the female, and deficiency in relation to the male. For example: when a Brāhmaṇa [begets] a Kṣatriya woman, a Mūrdhāvasiktā is born. That Mūrdhāvasiktā, possessing the superior quality of the seed, begets a daughter with the superior quality of the seed by a Brāhmaṇa himself, and she likewise [begets one] by a Brāhmaṇa; thus, in the seventh generation, she becomes a Brāhmaṇī—this is excellence. Likewise, when a Brāhmaṇa [begets] a Kṣatriya woman, a Mūrdhāvasikta is born. When he unites with a Kṣatriya woman, as before, he becomes a Kṣatriya himself—this is deficiency. In this manner, it is to be observed everywhere, even in the case of the offspring of a Śūdra woman and so forth. And so says Manu: *mūrdhāvasiktas tu kṣatriyāyām viśaḥ kṣattāryāyām ambaṣṭhaḥ | śūdryām niṣādo māhiṣyo ’rthe rājanyāt* || (Manu 10.8) *brāhmaṇād vaiśyakanyāyām śūdrāyām ca nigadyate | vaiśyān māgadhavaidehau rājadārān tathaiva ca* || (Manu 10.9) *śūdrād āyogavaḥ kṣattā caṇḍālaś cādhamo nṛṇām | vaiśyarājanyaviprāsu jāyante varṇasaṅkarāḥ* || (Manu 10.12) *strīṣv anantarajātāsu dvijair utpāditān sutān | sadṛśān eva tān āhur* || (Manu 10.5) *anantarāsu jātās tu tāḥ savarṇāḥ smṛtāḥ striyaḥ | ekāntare tv ānulomyād ambaṣṭhograu yathākramam* || (Manu 10.6) *vyatyaye karmaṇām sāmyam* || (Manu 10.41) And likewise Manu: *savarṇābhyo vidhau dharme jāyante hi sajātayaḥ | aninditaiḥ strīvivāhair anindyā bhavati prajā* || (Manu 3.12) *viparyayeṇa tu kṣetre bījāny uptāni na prarohanti* || (Manu 10.70) *naiva tasmāt prajāyante dvijātibhyaḥ kṣetrajāḥ kvacit* || (Manu 10.71) Thus, the excellence of the seed overcomes the field, while the deficiency of the field results in the offspring following the status of the mother. This is the principle governing the mixed castes (*saṅkara*).
If one born of a Śūdra woman from a Brāhmaṇa father procreates with someone of superior status,
he attains the higher caste of his superior within seven generations.
"A Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa goes to the state of a Śūdra;
one should know that it is likewise for those born from a Kṣatriya and similarly from a Vaiśya" (MDh 10.64–65).
Thus ends section 4.22.
By the fifth [sūtra], the teachers [are established]. 4.23.
Some teachers explain that the transition to another caste occurs precisely through five cycles of the age; this too should be understood with reference to the conduct [of the individual]. (4.23)
And [the same applies] to those born in other creations. 4.24.

"Creation" refers to the four castes (*varṇas*). Following that are those such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others. Those born from them are "born from another creation. The phrase "transition to another caste" occurs through both elevation and degradation; the word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the teachers' view that this occurs by means of the seventh and the fifth [generations]. Consequently, even in those cases, one should understand the transition between the castes of the progenitor and the offspring by postulating both direct (*anuloma*) and inverse (*pratiloma*) orders. (4.24)
But from the reverse order, one is devoid of dharma. || 4.25 ||

The word *tu* (but) serves to indicate a distinction: even among those born from inverse unions (*pratiloma*), such as the *sūta* and others, there is a lack of *dharma*; however, one born from an inverse union within that [specific] interval is especially devoid of it. By the term *dharma*, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is to be understood. Thus, the initiation of those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) is established. Regarding the study of the Vedas, however, a prohibition is to be observed. Why? Because of the observation of other Smṛtis stating: "For those born in the natural order, there is initiation alone; there is no study of the Vedas, no performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*), no maintenance of the domestic fire (*aupāsana*), no *agnihotra*, no ritual with fuel-sticks (*samitkārya*), and no twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*); even the initiation is performed silently (*tūṣṇīm*)," and so forth.

Some do not read the word *ca* (and). For them, the word *ca* must be supplied from the subsequent sūtra, "And in the case of a Śūdra woman" [GDh 4.26], and joined to this sūtra, "Of those born from other unions" [GDh 4.24].
Others explain that this is actually a single sūtra: "Of those born from other unions, but from the reverse order, he is devoid of dharma.
In every case, the interpretation remains essentially the same. 4.25.
And [the same applies] in the case of a Śūdra woman. 4.26.

One born from a Śūdra woman through men of the same or higher castes is likewise excluded from the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and other rites. Among those of equal caste, however, initiation is prescribed for the Ambaṣṭha and Niṣāda. Thus, another Smṛti states: "Having initiated a Savarṇa, one should teach him the Veda; having initiated an Ambaṣṭha, the science of medicine; having initiated a Niṣāda, the training in elephant-lore; for others, there is no initiation. Some explain that for one born to an Ambaṣṭha woman from a man of equal caste, one should initiate him and teach him dancing. The Ugra and others are to be understood by their specific occupations: the Ugra is a slayer of wild beasts and the like; the Dauṣyanta is a fisherman; the Pāraśava is a worshipper of Bhadrakālī; the Sūta is a trainer of horses; the Māgadha is one who follows the trade of commerce; the Āyogava is a maker of mats; the Kṣattṛ is a wheelwright (or a charioteer), and he is also a seller of salt; the Vaidehaka is a keeper of goats, and so forth. (4.26)
And from a Śūdra woman who is not of equal status, one follows the livelihood of an outcast. || 4.27 ||
The meaning is that one born from a Śūdra woman to a man of a higher caste is like an outcast (patita) and must be avoided in matters such as physical contact, receiving gifts, and so forth. (4.27)
The last is the most wicked. 4.28.

One born of a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is most sinful; therefore, he must be strictly avoided. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "One should go [beyond] a Caṇḍāla, a dog, or a cow-tail fan," and so forth.

In this regard, because the rule for taking a wife applies only to those born in the direct order (*anuloma*), one born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) is unfit for it; thus, although the injunction "one should marry a wife of equal status" (GDh 4.1) prescribes marriage only among those of the same caste, it nevertheless indicates that for one who has already married first, there is marriage in sequence even with women of lower castes. Accordingly, Vasiṣṭha states: "A Brāhmaṇa may have three wives according to the order of the castes, a Kṣatriya two, and a Vaiśya and a Śūdra each one" (VaDh 1.24). Furthermore, while it would have been sufficient to say "one born from a woman of the inverse order or a Śūdra is devoid of *dharma*," the fact that the Sūtra is composed separately as "and also from a Śūdra woman" (GDh 4.26) shows that marriage with a Śūdra woman possesses some degree of eligibility. Consequently, for a lustful man who has previously fathered sons with women of higher castes, marriage to a Śūdra woman—even though it excludes the recitation of mantras—should be understood as permissible. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Some [allow] even a Śūdra woman, excluding the mantras" (VaDh 1.25). Here, the word "even" (*api*) implies censure, and the meaning therein is "for one who has already fathered sons. By the statement "but from the inverse order, one is devoid of *dharma*" (GDh 4.25), he shows the absence of marriage with a higher caste for one of lower status. And so says Vasiṣṭha.

"But whatever [sons] are born of secret [unions], they are to be known by their actions due to the lapse in their qualities and conduct, as they rely on the qualities of the inverse order (*prātilomya*).
[VaDh 18.7], and so forth. The meaning therein is that, because they are born of secret [unions], there is an absence of marriage in the inverse order (*prātilomya*). 4.28.
Having explained the ritual of marriage and the procreation of sons, he now speaks for the purpose of praising marriage: "Virtuous sons purify. (4.29)
The meaning is that they purify and protect one from suffering. And so Vyāsa says:
"The word *pud* is a name for hell, and they know hell to be suffering;
because he protects (*trāṇa*) one from that which is *pud*, therefore they desire a son both in this world and in the next."

The virtuous are born only through lawful marriage; therefore, one should not procreate a son through a paramour, by means of a woman of a lower caste, or in a contrary manner. Sons should be educated. Why? Because of the Vedic revelation: "Therefore, they say that a son who has been instructed is conducive to the world" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.17).
The *tripuruṣa* [metre] is derived from the *ārṣī* [metre]. 4.30.
The meaning is that one born of a woman wedded by the *ārṣa* rite rescues three generations of ancestors, beginning with the father, from hell. (4.30)
Ten [years] from fate. 4.31.
One born from a Daiva marriage [purifies] ten generations of ancestors. || 4.31 ||
From the Prājāpatya, exactly ten. 4.32.

Lest there be confusion regarding the number ten in both cases, the word "also" (*ca*) was not stated [after *prājāpatyāt*] as would have been appropriate; rather, the particle *eva* is used for the sake of clarity.
A son of Brahmā saves ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself; such is a son of Brahmā. || 4.33 ||

A son born of the *brāhma* marriage is called a *brāhma* son; he purifies ten ancestors of the past and ten descendants of the future. Although the sequence of enumeration has been set aside in favor of stating the results out of order, this is for the purpose of showing that the reward for the giver of the girl is even greater: as the *Jābāla-śruti* states, "He who gives his daughter to one who is accomplished obtains the fruit of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice"; likewise, the *Kauṣītaki-brāhmaṇa* says, "His sons inherit his property, his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds. (4.33)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Paurāṇika* [section] of Maskari’s *Gautama-bhāṣya*.
The fifth chapter:
The marriage of a wife for the purpose of procreating offspring and for the performance of ritual acts has been described. In this regard, he first states the rule for procreating offspring.
He should approach his wife during her season. 5.1.
The *ṛtu* is a period of sixteen days and nights, characterized by the woman’s capacity for conception. Thus says Manu:
"The natural *ṛtu* of women is recorded as sixteen nights, together with four other days which are censured by the virtuous" (MDh 3.46).
He should approach—that is, go toward—his wife as she is naturally present, gladdening her, but not like an animal, because of the association with the prefix *upa*.

This is not an injunction (*vidhi*), because the matter is already established by one's own desire. Nor is it a restrictive rule (*niyama*). What is this restrictive rule? A restrictive rule is a restatement of that which is already optionally obtained; it is an engagement based on desire. Since both approaching and not approaching during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) are already possible, the rule "one must certainly approach during the fertile period" serves as a restriction. If this position is accepted, then regarding non-fertile periods, there is neither an injunction nor a prohibition, and thus activity occurs just as in the case of *marīca* and similar substances. It is nowhere heard in the *Dharmaśāstra* that "one should eat *marīca*, or one should not eat it. Nevertheless, the learned (*śiṣṭas*) do eat it; likewise, in this case too, activity would simply occur, and the rule "or in all cases" (GDh 5.2) would become redundant, as would the penance for non-approach.

But surely both cases are accepted, since it is heard that one who acts out of desire falls into hell: "But where there is activity arising from the perception of pleasure, there the scripture does not apply; he who follows such [impulse] prepares himself for hell. Because of this statement regarding the fall into hell when acting out of desire, the rule "or in all cases" (GDh 5.2) was initiated for the purpose of preventing that. Furthermore, in another Smṛti, an expiation is heard for non-approach:
"He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present near him, is joined with the terrible sin of killing an embryo; of this there is no doubt. (BDh 4.1.18).

This is not so. First, the meaning of the passage beginning with “But where there is activity due to the perception of pleasure” (*yatra tu prītyupalabdhitaḥ pravṛttiḥ*) is as follows: “where,” that is, in whatever performance there is activity due to the perception of pleasure—meaning activity out of a desire for that pleasure after having recognized it as a fruit; the meaning is that such activity is undertaken with a view toward a result (*phalābhisaṃdhinā*). Regarding such activity, there is no scriptural authority (*śāstram*), meaning it does not bear fruit at all. One who follows that, performing the performance with a view toward a result, “prepares for hell” (*rādhyati*), which means he goes to hell. This statement is intended for the purpose of performing rites such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) by abandoning the view toward a result. And thus the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva said: “Do not let the fruit of action be your motive” (*mā karmaphalahetur bhūḥ*, BhG 2.47), and so forth. If there were a prohibition against activity motivated by pleasure in every case, then scripture would have to be prescribed even for Marīci and others [who engage in sexual intercourse], on the grounds that falling into hell occurs without scripture. Therefore, even the rule “or in all cases” (*sarvatra vā*, GDh 5.2) need not be stated for the sake of being favored by scripture. As for what was said regarding “he who [approaches] his wife who has bathed after her menses” (*ṛtusnātāṃ tu yo bhāryām*, BDh 4.1.18), etc., that too is a statement for the purpose of the husband seeing himself [reflected] in his wife who has bathed after her menses. Why? Because of the observation of the Jābāli-Śruti. For it is heard there: “A wife who has bathed after her menses gives birth to a son resembling the one whom she first sees. Therefore, the husband himself should first show himself in her presence. Consequently, since there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for approaching her [at that time], the absence of fault follows as a matter of necessity (*niyamena*). For those whose position is that a restatement of what is already established constitutes a restrictive rule (*niyama*), even the suspicion of a restrictive rule is not applicable here, because there is no prior establishment of approaching only during the fertile period (*ṛtu*); rather, activity occurs everywhere according to one's own desire.

Therefore, this Sūtra is for the purpose of restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*). What is this restrictive enumeration? It is a statement made when there is a possibility of application both in that case and elsewhere. Since sexual intercourse might proceed according to one's desire—whether during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) or outside of it—the rule establishes that one must engage in intercourse only during the fertile period. If it is argued that this [rule] is also redundant because of the commencement of the rule "or at all times" (*sarvatra vā*), we say no; for its purpose is to establish a fixed alternative (*vyavasthitavikalpa*). The restriction should be understood as follows: if the engagement is solely for the sake of obtaining a son, then one should approach [the wife] only during the fertile period. But if it is for the sake of pleasure (*rati*), then "or at all times. If it is argued that the taking of a wife is for the purpose of procreating a son and fulfilling the duty enjoined by the Vedic texts on the three debts (*ṛṇatraya*), and not for the sake of pleasure, we say no; for another Smṛti states: "A woman has pleasure and sons as her fruits" (*ratiputraphalā nārī*). Furthermore, the view of Vasiṣṭha is seen: "That pleasure which occurs without transgression is based on Dharma" (*yā syād anaticāreṇa ratiḥ sā dharmasaṃśritā*, VaDh 12.23). The view of Uśanas is seen: "One should be content with one's own wife" (*svadāratuṣṭa eva bhavet*). The Vājasaneyaka Śruti is seen: "Even women who are about to give birth should sleep with their husbands" (*api nāryo vijaniṣyamāṇāḥ patibhiḥ saha śayīran*). And another Smṛti is seen: "The detached man should become a mendicant (*bhikṣu*); the other should enter the householder stage" (*virakto bhikṣur bhaved itaro gārhasthyaṃ praviśet*).
But for those who act out of desire, these following [penances] shall apply in order as inferior [alternatives]. [MDh 3.12]

Because of this teaching of Manu, and because even the scriptural mention of the three debts (*ṛṇatraya*) implies that the option of remaining a student (*ācāryapakṣa*) is taught for the period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) outside the fertile season (*anṛtu*), whereas under the view of their combination (*samuccayapakṣa*), the phrase "by means of sacrifice and offspring" would serve as a supporting illustration; furthermore, so that there may be no conflict with the Smṛti injunction regarding the householder's life, it follows that for one who has not lost his passion, the taking of a wife exists indeed even for the sake of sexual pleasure (*raty-artha*). Consequently, if both husband and wife become dispassionate (*virakta*), and their approach is solely for the sake of a son, then they should approach only during the fertile season. For those who are still passionate, the rule "or at all times" (*sarvatra vā*) is appropriate. If it is argued that, in that case, it would follow that there is no fault for one who does not approach during the fertile season, and if you say that this is a fault, we reply: No, for even we desire precisely the absence of fault. If it is further argued that even so, a penance (*prāyaścitta*) would apply to one seeking a son who approaches outside the fertile season, and if you say that this is a fault, we reply: No, because that very [penance] is the result of an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*). Even for those who hold that a restatement of what is already established by scripture constitutes an exclusion, this is consistent. For example: "One who has fathered a son should establish the sacred fires," and from the Śruti, "One is born burdened with three debts," and from the Smṛti, "Virtuous sons purify. Since approaching only during the fertile season is already established by the capacity for conception required for the purpose of producing a son, this restatement regarding one who has not yet produced a son is understood to be intended for the prohibition of approaching outside the fertile season. Therefore, this is indeed an exclusion: "If he should approach, only during the fertile season."
Now, if the journey is for the sake of obtaining a son, then it would not apply to one who has already fathered a son.
To this it is replied: because having many sons is desired. As Śaṅkha says:
"For one who is established in sons and grandsons, who has many offspring, and who is living..."

And so on. Likewise, the Śruti says: "Place ten sons in her; make the husband the eleventh. Therefore, it is established that this Sūtra is for the purpose of restrictive enumeration (parisaṃkhyā). 5.1.1.
Or, in all cases, except for what is prohibited. 5.2.
Festive days (*parvan*) and so forth are prohibited. As Manu has said:
"A twice-born *snātaka* shall always remain celibate on the new moon day, the eighth day, the full moon day, and the fourteenth day—even during the fertile period (*ṛtu*). [MDh 4.128]
The word *vā* (or) signifies an optional alternative (*vyavasthitavikalpa*).

Others, however, explain: "By the rule ‘one should approach her during the season’ [GDh 5.1], approaching only once during the season is enjoined; by the rule ‘or at all times,’ approaching only once at any time is enjoined. That is incorrect, because of the observation of the Vedic revelation: “One should approach her during the season twice or once, or at will outside the season. (5.2)
He is a worshiper of the gods, ancestors, humans, sages, and spirits. || 5.3 ||

These are the five great sacrifices (*pañca mahāyajñāḥ*). Among them, by the term "worshiper of the gods" (*devapūjaka*), the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice is meant. By "worshiper of the ancestors" (*pitṛpūjaka*), it is meant that one should daily feed a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of the ancestors. And so Manu says: "One should feed even a single Brāhmaṇa for the sake of the ancestors during the fivefold sacrifice; however, one should not feed anyone there specifically for the *vaiśvadeva*. (MDh 3.83)
In the absence of food, one should give milk; in its absence, roots; in their absence, fruit; and when all these are unavailable, water. Thus Manu says:
"One should offer the Śrāddha daily with food, or with water, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing satisfaction to the ancestors" (MDh 3.82).

In that regard as well, if all these are unavailable, one should understand that water is required. "One who honors humans" refers to the honoring of guests. Even there, if food is unavailable, one should give grass for a seat; if that is unavailable, ground for lying down; fire for warding off the cold; water for removing mud; and sweet speech. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Grass, ground, fire, water, pleasant speech, truthfulness, and freedom from envy—these are never lacking in the houses of the virtuous" (VaDh 13.61). He himself will also speak of the honoring of guests later on; the remainder of that topic is to be understood as stated by Vasiṣṭha. "One who honors beings" refers to the offering of bali-oblations to the deities of the directions following the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. "One who honors sages" refers to the daily private recitation of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*). These are mentioned before the mention of maintaining the sacred fires so that they may apply even to one who does not maintain the fires, using the common (*laukika*) fire. Consequently, this should be understood to apply to a Śūdra even in the case of a *pākayajña* sacrifice, using the common fire; the same applies to the *avakīrṇi-homa* sacrifice. (5.3)
Constant private recitation of the Veda. 5.4.

The "daily recitation" (*nityasvādhyāya*) is designated as the "sacrifice to Brahman" (*brahmayajña*). This has already been indicated previously by the term "worshipper of the sages" (*ṛṣipūjaka*); even when one is unable to perform the other [five] sacrifices, this [Brahma-sacrifice] must be performed daily, though perhaps deficient in its details. Although it should have been called the "sacrifice to the sages" (*ṛṣiyajña*) according to the manner previously stated, it is expressed in this way in order to incorporate the injunction found in another Smṛti. Thus Uśanas says: "Now, in the Brahma-sacrifice, sitting upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* blades, facing either east or north, one should recite a portion of the Vedas preceded by the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī*; or the beginning of the Vedas; or one verse from the Ṛg, Yajur, or Sāma Vedas three times; or the *praṇava*; or a verse from the Itihāsas—remaining composed," and so forth. (5.4)
And the offering of water for the ancestors. 5.5.

By the use of the word "and" (ca), [the offering is extended] to the deities and the sages (*ṛṣis*). Although the term "water" (*udaka*) would have sufficed, the inclusion of the word "giving" (*dāna*) is for the purpose of making known that this must be preceded by the *tarpaṇa* (libation). Thus, another *smṛti* states:
"Having offered libations to the deities and the sages with a concentrated mind, one should afterwards give to the ancestors, preceded by the word *svadhā* and accompanied by sesame seeds."

By the very injunction for the daily offering of water to the ancestors (*pitṛs*), bathing every day is also established by implication, since the offering of water is preceded by that [bathing]. And so says Manu:
"Having bathed daily, being pure, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods, the sages, and the ancestors" (MDh 2.176).
The offering of water is of two kinds: that which is offered into the water and that which is offered into the air.

But is it not the case that [the offering] is enjoined on the ground alone, and not in water, as Bhṛgu says: "That water which is not offered on the ground does not reach [the ancestors], whether it is in liquid form, in vessels, offered while angry, or with only one hand"?
Likewise, Bṛhaspati also says:
"One should never offer water for libation to the ancestors while standing in water;
rather, having stepped out onto a clean place, one should perform the water-libation (udakatarpaṇa)."
This is not so, because it contradicts other Smṛti texts and because it describes a specific distinction of objects. As Uśanas has said:
"All the hosts of gods are water, and the hosts of ancestors are remembered as water;
therefore, water should be given in water, for what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible."
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the distinction of the domains:
"One should offer handfuls of water for the gods and the ancestors in the water; for those who have died without having received the sacraments, one should offer handfuls of water on dry land."

The procedure from the libation (*tarpaṇa*) up to the offering of water should be performed with both hands. Regarding the offering of water, there is no fault, because of the scriptural statement, "a handful of water" (*udakāñjali*). However, this does not apply to the *tarpaṇa* rite, because one hears a contradictory injunction: "not with a single hand. Thus says Bhṛgu: "A twice-born man who offers water for libation with both hands goes to the Kālasūtra hell, head downwards, as a fool."
This is not a fault, because of the hearing of the statement regarding the division [of duties]. Thus said Bṛhaspati:
"If it is the time for pouring [water] during a śrāddha, one should cause [the performer] to give with one hand;
but in the case of libation (tarpaṇa), one should use both hands—this is the eternal law."
Therefore, one [offering] is prescribed specifically in water; that which is prescribed in space is the other. As Bhṛgu said:
"Standing in water reaching up to the navel, with his mind directed upwards and reflecting, [he should say]:
'May my ancestors come; may they accept this handful of water.'"

The wise man, restraining his speech and facing south, should cast water three times each into the air with joined palms, saying [the mantra] loudly and increasingly higher as he speaks it again and again.
"Space is the abode of the ancestors, as is the southern direction;
therefore, whatever is given to the ancestors in that manner shall be inexhaustible for them.
Thus it is said. Whatever is offered to the ancestors should be understood as being accompanied by sesame seeds and *darbha* grass, as Bhṛgu has stated:
"Whatever water mixed with sesame and *darbha* grass is offered with the utterance of *svadhā*, all that becomes nectar and becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors.
Therefore, the offering of water to the ancestors must be performed. (5.5)
The rest according to one's enthusiasm. 5.6.

Whatever remains after the *brahmayajña* and the offering of water—namely, that which constitutes the duties of a householder—one should perform that according to one's ability, because of the statement regarding enthusiasm (*utsāha*). Consequently, when the primary means are unavailable, the duty must still be performed by secondary means; as it has been cited: "Or even with milk, roots, and fruits" (MDh 3.82), and so forth. 5.6.
The fire [is represented by] the wife and so forth, or the inheritance and so forth. 5.7.

By the word *bhāryā* (wife), the marriage is understood; by the word *agni* (fire), the *aupāsana* fire is meant. The meaning is that one should maintain the nuptial fire in the form of the *aupāsana*.
Some explain it thus: this is a designation for the very fire of birth (*jātakāgni*) transmitted through tradition, intended for maintenance in the form of the *aupāsana* after the time of marriage.

That is incorrect, because of the Gṛhya-smṛti: "Performing the marriage, having established the worldly fire (*laukika-agni*). If the birth-fire (*jātakāgni*) itself were to arrive [at that time], then one would not employ the term "worldly" in that context. Therefore, due to its impurity, the birth-fire must indeed be abandoned. Alternatively, one may take possession of the fire at the time of partition with his brothers or father; even after the marriage, there is an option depending on one's wealth, since rituals are accomplished by means of material resources. For he who possesses wealth should take possession of it at the time of marriage, while one who is destitute should do so at the time of inheritance.

Some explain that one may take possession of the inheritance and the sacred fire even before marriage; however, this is incorrect, because another Smṛti states: "A man who has lost his wife and remarried should again take up the fire, since there is no fire for one who is without a wife. How is it understood that this refers only to the maintenance of the Smārta fires and not the Śrauta fires? Because of the Vedic injunction, "One who has fathered a son should establish the fires," and because the plural number is used there in the word *agnīn* (fires). 5.7.
In that [fire], the domestic rites are performed. 5.8.

One should perform the domestic rites, such as the *puṃsavana* and others, in that very same *aupāsana* fire. This applies to the case where [the fire] has been formally taken; if it has not been taken, they are to be understood as being performed in the ordinary (*laukika*) fire. 5.8.
The sacrifices to the gods, the ancestors, and humans, as well as the private recitation of the Vedas. || 5.9 ||

The sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*) is the *vaiśvadeva* offering. The feeding of Brahmins for the sake of the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*) is the sacrifice to the ancestors. The feeding of guests (*atithipūjana*) is the sacrifice to men (*manuṣyayajña*). Although a connection with fire is well-known for the *vaiśvadeva*, for the sacrifice to the ancestors it is the cooking intended for their meal, and for the sacrifice to men it is the cooking intended for the guest’s meal. By the word *svādhyāya* (Vedic study), the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*) is meant. According to the opinion of some, that [sacrifice to Brahman] also has a connection with fire; thus there is a non-compound construction (*visamāsa*). And so Uśanas says, beginning with “Now the sacrifice to Brahman near water,” and having described the sacrifice to Brahman, he states: “Near the fire, according to some. If it is argued that this is already established because these are rites prescribed in the *Gṛhyasūtras*, we say no; for the repetition is for the purpose of removing a doubt. What is the doubt? It might be that since the sacrifice to the gods and the others were previously enjoined in the ordinary (*laukika*) fire, they belong only to that [fire] and not to the domestic (*aupāsana*) fire. Furthermore, one might have the doubt that by the rule “In that [fire] are the *gṛhya* rites” [GDh 5.8], only those *gṛhya* rites are included that exclude those [five sacrifices], because they were previously mentioned separately. Thus, [the author shows] that they belong to both fires. Consequently, there is no fault even if the fire is used from the ordinary fire. And thus is the *sūtra* of Bādarāyaṇa: “Even from the ordinary fire, the five sacrifices are prohibited for one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) by virtue of the scriptural statement. (5.9)
The rite for the return [of the deceased]. 5.10.

By this, the *bhūtayajña* (offering to beings) is described. Its explicit mention is for the purpose of removing any doubt [regarding its necessity]. The word "and" (*ca*) is carried over from the preceding sūtra; its purpose is to draw that [preceding rule] into this context. It is performed immediately after the *vaiśvadeva* and not as a separate act; it is for this reason that it is treated separately once again. Thus says the author of the *Gṛhya-sūtra*: "Having first offered to the gods, one should afterwards offer the *bali*. While it could have been stated simply as "the *bhūtayajña* as before," the phrasing used here is intended to indicate that the sacrificial food (*havis*) is distinct from that of the *vaiśvadeva*. Consequently, one should take a portion of the prepared food for the sake of both the *vaiśvadeva* and the *bhūtayajña*. Thus says Jaimini: "Having increased the *bali* of the food. The dual number indicates that it is to be performed both evening and morning. The inclusion of the term "rite" (*karman*) implies that the *vaiśvadeva* itself is also to be performed evening and morning. Accordingly, the *Gṛhya-smṛti* states: "The *vaiśvadeva* and the offering of the *bali* [are to be done] evening and morning," and "Then, evening and morning, one should offer of the prepared sacrificial food," and so forth. (5.10)
Now he describes the Vaiśvadeva offering for the sake of including even those whose Gṛhya-sūtras have not been mentioned:
"Agni in Agni, Dhanvantari, the Viśvedevas, Prajāpati, and Sviṣṭakṛt"—these are the oblations. (5.11)

Although fire is already implied by the mention of *homa* (oblation), the phrase "in a well-kindled fire" is stated again for the purpose of specifying the fire used for the oblation. The plural form "oblations" (*homāḥ*) is intended to exclude the offering of a single oblation. The mention of *homa* is also for the purpose of indicating the utterance of *svāhā*. The particle *iti* is for the purpose of including the dative case ending. The separation of the compound is for the sake of establishing the presence of other mantras. Thus: *agnaye svāhā*, *dhanvantaraye svāhā*, *viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ svāhā*, *prajāpataye svāhā*. The word *sviṣṭakṛt*, having *agni* as its prefix and ending in the dative case, should be understood as *agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā*. This much constitutes the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. 5.11.
Now he states the rule for the sacrifice to the beings:
"And to the deities of the directions, each according to their own [quarter]. (5.12)

One should offer the bali-oblation to the deities of the directions in the east: to Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna, proceeding clockwise from the east; to Viṣṇu above, and to Ananta below. In this context, the mantra "Obeisance to Indra" (indrāya namaḥ) is to be understood [as the model]. Because of the word "and" (ca), it should also be understood as "Obeisance to Indra’s attendants" (indrasya puruṣebhyo namaḥ), and so forth. "According to their respective [deities]" means according to their respective positions. (5.12)
To the Maruts at the doors. || 5.13 ||

Because of the plural number, [the formula] "Obeisance to the Maruts" (marudbhyo namaḥ) is to be understood as applying to all [of them]. In this case, there is no injunction for a *tatpuruṣa* compound, because of the absence of the particle *ca*. 5.13.
Having entered for the household deities. || 5.14 ||

Because of the statement "having entered," it should first be observed outside the house. Then, having prepared a circular mark (*maṇḍala*) with cow dung in one place outside the house and having offered the oblation (*bali*) to the deities of the directions, and then having offered the oblation at the outer and inner doors, one should enter the interior itself and offer the oblation to the deities of the house. These are Śrī and the others, as Uśanas has said:

One should offer [oblations] saying "Salutation to Śrī" at the head-end of the bed; "Salutation to Bhadrakālī" at the foot-end; "Salutation to Dhanapati" in the storehouse; "Salutation to Rudra" in the dwelling of the pillars; "Salutation to Mitra" in the cow-pen; "Salutation to Varuṇa" at the mortar and pestle; "Salutation to Ahi Budhnya" at the well; and at the grinding stone and near the fire, one should offer [oblations] saying "Salutation to these deities. Thus [ends the section]. 5.14.
To Brahmā, in the center. || 5.15 ||
In the middle of the house, one should offer [the seat] with the words, "Salutation to Brahmā. || 5.15 ||
From water, into a water-pot. || 5.16 ||
He should offer [water] into the water-jar with the words, "Adoration to the waters! (adbhyo namaḥ). || 5.16 ||
"To the space," [he offers] into the intermediate region. || 5.17 ||

With the words "Salutation to Ākāśa," one should offer [the oblation] in the intermediate space (antarikṣa), that is, in the courtyard area. The word "iti" indicates a manner or type. Consequently, it should be understood that with the words "Salutation to Mṛtyu," one offers it in the kitchen, and with the words "Salutation to Aja Ekapād," one offers it upon the threshing floors. 5.17.
And [he should offer it] in the evening to those who roam at night. 5.18.

If [the offering] is in the evening, one should give [the food] into the air after the presentation of the fruit-oblation, saying, "Obeisance to the night-walkers (*naktañcarāḥ*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the previous [procedure]; otherwise, [the offering] would apply only to the night-walkers. (5.18)
Having pronounced a blessing, the giving of alms is not preceded by [the formal ritual]. 5.19.

Having caused the mendicant to say "Svasti," the householder should then give him alms, preceded by the offering of water. Since a woman has the authority to give alms and it is she who is requested [for them], the householder should have her perform that very act. Some explain that because this rule is prescribed immediately after the Vaiśvadeva, it applies only to the "first alms" (agrabhaikṣa) and not to ordinary alms; according to their view, it should be understood that the recitation of "Svasti" must be performed by the man himself. (5.19)
And likewise in the case of righteous acts of giving. 5.20.

By the word *dadāti* (gives), the giving of gold and so forth is meant. Because of the inclusion of the term *dharmya* (righteous), the giving to friends and others for a visible purpose is not intended. In this very manner, one should give preceded by water. Although the word "thus" (*evam*) is already established by the particle "and" (*ca*), it is used here to ensure that the entire [preceding] procedure is applied. Consequently, just as the giving of alms performed by a woman is valid when done with the husband's permission, so too is the giving of gold and other such items valid. And thus says Nārada: "They declare that transactions performed by a woman are invalid except in times of distress; especially so are gifts of houses, fields, and religious endowments, as well as sales."
"These very means of proof [are valid] if the husband permits," and so forth. Even the giving of alms must not be performed without the husband's permission. And thus says Manu:
"By a woman—whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an old woman..."
"Nothing whatsoever should be done independently, even within one's own home. (MDh 5.147) [5.20]
The fruits [of giving] to non-Brahmins, Brahmins, learned Śrotriyas, and those who have mastered the Vedas are respectively equal, double, a thousandfold, and infinite. || 5.21 ||

This undertaking is for the purpose of demonstrating that the excellence of the fruit depends upon the excellence of the recipient (*pātra*). "Equal" means having a slight fruit; this refers to gold and so forth, or even alms-food (*bhikṣā*), given to one who is not a Brahmin. By the word "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), one who has merely undergone initiation (*upanayana*) is meant. Thus Uśanas says: "He by whom the Vedas have not been studied and whose vows have not been observed—he is indeed a non-Brahmin. It was a Brahmin himself who employed the term "non-Brahmin" [in this context]. "Twofold is what is given to a Brahmin": by the word "Brahmin," one who has performed the Vedic vows but has not studied the Vedas is meant. As Vasiṣṭha says:
An elephant made of wood, a deer made of leather, and a Brahmin who has not studied the Veda—these three are bearers of names only. [VaDh 3.11]

What is given to a *śrotriya* becomes multiplied a thousandfold. By the term *śrotriya*, one who has studied a single *śākhā* is meant. As Baudhāyana says: “Having studied one *śākhā*, one becomes a *śrotriya*” [ĀpDh 2.6.4]. What is given to one who has mastered the Veda (*vedapāraga*) is infinite. By the term *vedapāraga*, one who has studied the Veda together with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-veda*) is meant. As Kaṇva says: “He by whom the Veda with its limbs has been studied becomes a *vedapāraga*. Since the fruits for these [recipients] have been stated previously, it should be understood in the same way regarding specific castes as well. As Prajāpati says:
A gift given to a Śūdra yields an equal reward; to a Vaiśya, it becomes twofold;
they say it is threefold for a Kṣatriya, and it becomes immeasurable when given to a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus [ends verse] 5.21.
Having thus explained the fruit of giving with respect to its specific results, he now describes another mode of giving in connection therewith:

"The distribution of wealth to those who have come for the sake of their teacher, for marriage, for medicine, for the sake of livelihood, those whose means are exhausted, those about to sacrifice, students, travelers, and those seeking universal victory."
Outside the sacrificial altar. || 5.22 ||

The mention of the "guru" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for one's mother, father, and dependents. As Manu has said: "One who seeks offspring, one about to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given away all his possessions, one who provides for a guru, one who provides for parents or dependents, one seeking to study the Veda, and one who is afflicted by illness [should be fed]. (MDh 11.1)

And so forth. Furthermore, for the purpose of providing a dwelling: even after having requested in this manner, a house must be provided. This also should be understood as applying to the view that these items are to be combined. Regarding the mention of "wealth" (*artha*) when the context was already the taking of wealth for the sake of medicinal herbs, the repetition of the word "wealth" is intended to indicate the relative weight or lightness of the wealth according to the specific nature of the knowledge [of the recipient], or rather, to show that it must be given only to those who are destitute (*niḥsva*). As Manu says:
"Gifts should be given to these [worthy persons] who are destitute, according to the excellence of their learning. (MDh 11.2)

And so forth. "One whose livelihood is exhausted" means one who has fallen into distress. "One about to sacrifice" refers to this statement for the sake of obligatory (*nitya*) sacrifices; consequently, other *smṛti* passages such as, "Enough for Soma; one who has not sacrificed with Soma is not [qualified], he is worthy to drink the Soma," are to be understood as applying to optional (*kāmya*) sacrifices. Even by begging, one is considered "about to sacrifice" because of the obligatory nature of the sacrifice. "For the sake of study" means for the purpose of Vedic study. "On a journey" means being on a road; "exhausted" is included because of the mention of "connection" (*saṃyoga*), which implies being on a journey for the purpose of obtaining food. "The performer of the Viśvajit" is one who has sacrificed with the Viśvajit. To these, a distribution must be made, even of gold and other things, because of the mention of "substance" (*dravya*). It must be done as a rule (*niyamena*), because of the use of the prefix *sam*. Since begging is prohibited for the performer of the Viśvajit for up to a year, it should be given only to one who does not ask. To others, one may give whether they ask or do not ask. Furthermore, the distribution of wealth must be done in such a way that no calamity befalls one's own family, because of the use of the prefix *vi*. Therefore, the meaning is that only a portion should be given. Because of the mention of "outside the sacrificial altar" (*bahirvedi*), it may be given to others even within the altar (*antarvedi*). And since it must be done as a rule, for one who does not do so, there is not merely an absence of fruit; rather, there is sin (*pratyavāya*). If it is argued that even for one who does perform it, the only purpose is the absence of that sin and not the attainment of fruit, we say no; the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "according to the distinction of knowledge" indicates that there is a distinction of fruit based on the distinction of the recipient (*pātra*). Thus Vyāsa says:
O Bhārata, for the sake of a teacher’s household or medicine, for the purpose of Vedic study,
or likewise for one set out on a journey, and also for the sake of a sacrifice;
O King, even one who has performed the Vaiśvajit sacrifice, if his livelihood is exhausted,
is honored in the heavenly world by giving [to such a person] through the excellence of his knowledge.

And so forth. Therefore, this should be understood as being like the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). Just as for one who does not perform the twilight worship there is transgression, while for one who performs it there is the absence of transgression and the attainment of the fruit. || 5.22 ||
When others are begging for cooked food, [one should give it]. 5.23.
One should give prepared food to those who beg when they are distinct from those already mentioned. Some read "to others" (*itarebhyaḥ*), and for them, too, this is the very same meaning.
Now, one might object that since this is already established by the rule, "The giving of alms occurs after the *svasti* has been pronounced" (GDh 5.19), this need not be stated.

It is said: that [rule] refers merely to the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*). This one, however, is for the purpose of ensuring that alms must be given as a matter of rule. If this is so, then this too should be regarded as being like the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and other such duties, because it is stated without distinction. And the giving may take place both outside the sacrificial altar (*bahirvedi*) and inside the altar (*antarvedi*). Since cooked food (*kṛtānna*) is specified, there is no restriction regarding rice grains (*taṇḍula*) and the like. Although it would have been sufficient to say "alms from others" (*bhaikṣam itareṣu*), the use of the phrase "while they are begging" (*bhikṣamāṇeṣu*) indicates that the rule applies only when they are actually requesting with such mantras as "Sir, please give alms. Alternatively, this rule applies specifically to those who are worthy of receiving alms. As Vasiṣṭha has said:
"For that village where twice-born men wander for alms while being vow-less and unlearned, the king should punish; for it provides sustenance for thieves. (VaDh 3.4).
In that regard, when giving alms, water must also be offered into the hand of the ascetic. As Bhṛgu says:
One should give water into the hand of the ascetic, then offer alms, and again give water;
for such alms may be as vast as a mountain, and that water is like the ocean.
Thus [ends the verse]. 2.23.
The censure of giving is now stated: even after having made a promise, one should not give if it is joined with unrighteousness. 5.24.

One should not give even what has been promised to one who, being joined with unrighteousness, makes a request for the sake of his teacher or others but does not carry it out; by the use of the word "even," it is implied that one should not give even what has already been prepared. 5.24.
One should not accept that something is connected with unrighteousness merely because of anyone’s word; thus he says:
"The words of one who is angry, joyful, afraid, afflicted, greedy, childish, aged, deluded, intoxicated, or insane, even if false, do not constitute a sin. (5.25)

One should not determine the unreliability of the speech of those possessed by anger, joy, fear, disease, or greed, nor of children and the like, on the basis of their words alone, because their speech lacks authority. The mention of "speech" (*vākya*) is intended to establish that their words are unauthoritative even in other contexts. (5.25)
Having spoken of the incidental matter, he now states the subject at hand:
"One should first feed the guest, the youth, the sick, the pregnant woman, the woman in her courses, the elderly, and those of lower status. (5.26)

He should feed these first before himself: the guest (to be described below), the youth, the child, the sick person, those afflicted by disease, the women in their courses, daughters, the elderly, the attendants, and—by virtue of the word "and"—the poor, the helpless, and others are included. The irregular order of the compound is intended to establish a specific sequence; therefore, he should feed them according to their relative need for favor. 5.26.
But for one's teacher, father, and friends, one should carry out their instructions after having informed them.

For if at that time anyone—such as a teacher or another—should come to the house, then having offered the prepared food to him, one must carry out whatever words he speaks; the meaning is that one should do exactly what they say. The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of restriction, implying that one should do only that and never act independently. Since it has been stated that this refers to the performance of their words, if they do not say anything at all, then one may act independently. 5.27.
The honey-mixture (madhuparka) is offered upon the arrival of the officiating priest, the teacher, the father-in-law, the paternal uncle, and the maternal uncle. 5.28.
