But when officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others arrive at one's house, worship with the *madhuparka* offering must first be performed; because of the mention of "approaching" (*upasthāna*), it is not required for a second visit and so forth. The procedure for the *madhuparka* is to be found in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*. (5.28)
Again, after a year. || 5.29 ||
If they, having been honored, should return after a year, then the madhuparka should be offered again; not before that. 5.29.
Before [the completion of] a sacrifice or a marriage. 5.30.

Even within a year, the madhuparka should be offered to those who have arrived at a sacrifice or a wedding; since the offering of the madhuparka to officiating priests at a sacrifice is already established by the sacred tradition (Śruti), this rule is commenced for the sake of fathers-in-law and others. 5.30.
And [the same applies] to a king who is a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya). || 5.31 ||

And at the reception of a king, the honey-mixture (madhuparka) should be offered if he is a Śrotriya; because of the separate mention [of the king], this applies even before a year has passed. By the use of the word "and" (ca), clothing is also included. 5.31.
One should not offer a seat or water to one who is not learned in the Vedas. 5.32.
If the king is not learned in the Vedas (aśrotriya), he should be honored merely with a seat and water. || 5.32 ||
But for a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya), one should provide water for the feet, the guest-offering (arghya), and various kinds of food. || 5.33 ||

[The guest] of a Brāhmaṇa who is a learned scholar (śrotriya). Why is this so? Because of the repeated mention of the term "learned scholar. If it were intended for a Vaiśya, it would not be so, because another Smṛti is seen to state: "A Vaiśya is not to be honored with the madhuparka; therefore, one should simply feed him. The word *tu* (but/however) is for the sake of specification. If he is endowed with good conduct (*vṛttasaṃpanna*), then upon his arrival, water should be given for the purpose of washing his feet and for the purpose of worship. [The terms] *pādya* and *arghya* are used as separate compounds; and *madhuparka* refers to specific kinds of food distinguished by varieties such as boiled rice with lentils (*mudga*) and so forth. By the use of the word *ca* (and), specific side dishes (*upadaṃśa*) and the like are also included. [The madhuparka] should contain an abundance of ghee due to the prefix *pra-*. And thus says the Śruti: "For a Brāhmaṇa who has arrived as a guest, he cooks food rich in ghee. (5.33)
But when there is incapacity, [the mind is] either constant or distinguished by mental formations. 5.34.
Whatever food is always available in his house, that alone—distinguished by abundant side dishes—is superior to that which is common [to all]. 5.34.
The gift of food to one who is of good conduct but not a learned scholar is of middling merit. || 5.35 ||

But when a Brāhmaṇa who is not a *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas) is present—one who is of virtuous conduct and possesses good character—food accompanied by the middle refinement (*saṃskāra*) should be given to him. The mention of "food" (*anna*) is for the purpose of restriction; only food is to be given, not water for the feet and so forth. The mention of "giving" is for this purpose: that he should not be deprived of the refinement simply because he is not a *śrotriya*. (5.35)
But in the opposite case, it consists of grass, water, and earth. 5.36.

By the word "tu" (but), the case opposite to both is indicated. Consequently, if even a learned man is of improper conduct, for him also it should be understood thus: "Or he is always distinguished by his refinement" (GDh 5.34). Not merely grass, water, and ground are to be given. 5.36.
Welcome at last! || 5.37 ||

"Welcome" means kind and truthful speech. "At the very least" means that in times of distress, when even the giving of grass and water is impossible, one should at least utter kind and truthful words. || 5.37 ||
And there is also the desire for honor and fame. || 5.38 ||

After speaking pleasant and truthful words, one should offer honor; indeed, the very act of not showing contempt is honor. Therefore, the meaning is that one must not show contempt. Furthermore, "not being overly eager" means that one should not eat even a single mouthful if one has not first fed [the guest], and ultimately, one should not eat oneself even in times of distress. (5.38)
Providing a bed, a seat, a dwelling, following after, and attending upon are the same for both an equal and a superior. 5.39.

For a guest who is one’s equal or superior, bedding and other such items should be provided that are equal to one’s own. "Bedding" refers to couches and the like; "seats" refer to wooden planks and the like; "lodgings" refer to inner rooms and the like; "following" means walking behind; and "attending" means offering salutations and so forth. Since it is impossible for following and attending to be exactly equal to oneself, this instruction is intended to mean that one should follow and attend upon a guest who is one’s equal or superior. However, the bedding, seats, and other such items should be provided with equality relative to one's own. This equality is relative to oneself and not between the two guests, because the superior guest deserves greater honor. As he will state later: "In the case of equals and unequals, there is inequality based on the degree of honor; and [the guest] who is unhonored... (GDh 17.18–19). Therefore, it should be understood that for a guest who is similar or superior, these items are equal when compared to oneself, but unequal when compared to each other, since the superior guest is to be treated with greater distinction. 5.39.
Even to a small extent, [one should not give] to an inferior person. || 5.40 ||
Even when slightly deficient, they should be made equal. 5.40.
He states the definition of a guest [atithi]:
"A guest is one from a different village, staying for only one night, who waits under a tree until the sun has risen. (5.41)

A guest who has come from another village, whose habit it is to stay for only one night, and who presents himself after midday, should be understood as a *atithi*. To such a person, a gift must be given according to this rule; and in failing to give, there is sin. Even if he lacks a single characteristic due to an irregularity, he does not cease to be one. By the expression "the sun behind the trees," the evening time is indicated. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "One should not neglect a guest who arrives in the evening" (VaDh 8.4). 5.41.
Furthermore, as to what should be said to a guest, he says:
"The final inquiry for a Śūdra concerns his welfare, his well-being, and his health. (5.42)

The guest should be questioned in due order: a Brahmin is asked about his *kuśala* (well-being), a Kṣatriya about his *anāmaya* (freedom from illness), and a Śūdra about his *ārogya* (health). Regarding the Vaiśya, that which is stated in another Smṛti should be observed. Thus Manu says:
"One should ask a Brāhmaṇa about his *kuśala*, a Kṣatriya relative about his *anāmaya*, and upon meeting a Vaiśya about his *kṣema*, and a Śūdra about his *ārogya*. [MDh 2.127]
Thus [ends verse] 5.42.
A non-Brahmin who is not invited is not a guest for a Brahmin, provided he is not present at a sacrifice. 5.43.

Even if a Kṣatriya or others possess the aforementioned characteristics, they are not guests for a Brāhmaṇa; therefore, one must not give to them as a rule. "In non-sacrifice" means other than at a sacrifice; however, at a sacrifice, it certainly occurs. If that Brāhmaṇa is well-conducted but poor, [the gift] occurs even outside of a sacrifice when there is abundant food. Because of the mention of "a Brāhmaṇa," it certainly occurs for a Kṣatriya and so forth. Since there is a prohibition against a Brāhmaṇa giving to a non-Brāhmaṇa, it certainly occurs for a Brāhmaṇa to give to a Brāhmaṇa. (5.43)
But the meal for the Kṣatriya is after that of the Brāhmaṇas. || 5.44 ||
The word "tu" (but) is intended to indicate an alternative view: according to the view of the guests, one should feed the Kṣatriya after the Brāhmaṇas have eaten. 5.44.
Others, together with their servants, for the sake of compassion—for the sake of compassion. || 5.45 ||

If he has the means, he should feed others, such as Vaiśyas and so forth, together with his servants—namely, slaves, attendants, laborers, and the like—even if they are not guests; for even though they are not guests, it is for the sake of non-cruelty and compassion, since in the world there would be cruelty in rejecting them. (5.45)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Maskarīya-gautama-bhāṣya*.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
In this context of honoring guests (*atithi-pūjana*), he describes another mode of worship for others as well.
In a gathering, one should daily perform the clasping of the feet.

The clasping of the feet must be performed according to the procedure taught in other Smṛtis due to the employment of two prefixes. As Manu says: "The grasping [of the feet] should be done with crossed hands," and so forth. "In meeting" means in a gathering. "Daily" means every day; the word "must be performed" is to be supplied. It should be understood that this applies to the meeting with those who will be mentioned hereafter. 6.1.
But having approached [a guest] after he has been away for a long time. || 6.2 ||

Having returned from a distant foreign land, he should go to that house facing him directly; the word "tu" (but/however) is for the purpose of emphasizing respect. Consequently, he should not wait for a chance encounter. 6.2.
To whom, then, should this be performed? To this he says:
"Of one's mother, father, their relatives, ancestors, teachers of knowledge, and their teachers. (6.3)

The mother and father are well known. Their kinsmen include the maternal uncle, the maternal grandfather, the paternal uncle, the paternal grandfather, and so forth. "Elder kin" refers to one's own elder brothers. "Teachers of learning" (vidyā-guru) are those who teach the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), since the teacher of the Vedas was mentioned previously. "Their teachers" are those who are the teachers of learning for the fathers and others. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), friends of the teacher and others are also included. When these [categories] are gathered together, one should visit them daily; and when one has been away from home, one should visit them upon returning. The non-compounding of the term "elder kin" and the rest is intended to include the father-in-law and other such elders. (6.3)
In the presence of another. 6.4.

When many people are gathered in one place, then that which belongs to the most eminent among them should be performed first. And he has been described [as such] by the passage beginning with: “The teacher is the best of gurus” (GDh 2.57). || 6.4 ||
In an assembly of learned men, one should offer salutation by pronouncing one's own name, saying, "I am so-and-so. (6.5)

One’s own name is that given by one’s father and others. Having pronounced that with excellence, and immediately thereafter having uttered the word *aham* (“I”), there is the direct instruction *ayam* (“this one”). For its purpose, the word *asmin* (“in this”) should be employed. The word *iti* expresses a manner. At the end, the word *bhoḥ* is used because it occupies the place of the teacher’s name, as that is the subject under discussion. Thus, one should employ the formula: “I am the one named Devadatta, sir. This is the salutation at the time of the formal greeting (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*). The meaning is that it must be uttered while facing [the teacher]. “In the presence of those who know” means in the presence of those who know the rule for returning a salutation (*pratyabhivādana*). And the rule for returning a salutation is to be found in another Smṛti. As Manu says: *yo na vetty abhivādasya vipraḥ pratyabhivādanam | nābhivādyaḥ sa viduṣā yathā śūdras tathaiva saḥ ||* “A Brahmin who does not know how to return a salutation should not be saluted by one who knows; he is just like a Śūdra. *yo ‘vetty abhivādasya vipraḥ pratyabhivādanam | āyuṣmān bhava saumyeti vācyo vipro ‘bhivādane ||* “The Brahmin who knows how to return a salutation should be addressed with ‘May you be long-lived, O gentle one’ when being saluted. *akāraś cāsya nāmno ‘nte vācyaḥ pūrvākṣaraḥ plutaḥ | āmantrite tu plutasya sarvatraiva svaritoditaḥ ||* “And the vowel *a* at the end of his name should be pronounced with the preceding syllable as *pluta* (protracted). But in the case of an address (*āmantrita*), the *pluta* is always said to have the *svarita* accent. *yo na vetti svaro ‘py asya vidvān api hi kilbiṣī | na cet saṃnihito jñātir yasya syād abhivāditā || sa tena śūdreṇa tulyo bhavet ||* “Even if he is learned, he who does not know the accent of this [name] is indeed a sinner. If no relative is present to whom the salutation was addressed, he becomes equal to that Śūdra. *abhivāde kṛte yastu na karoti tathottaram | āśīrvādaṃ sa vijñeyo vācyo nābhivādanam ||* “When a salutation has been performed, he who does not likewise offer a reply is to be known as one who does not deserve a blessing; the salutation itself should not be addressed to him. *yo vai sam̐nihito jñātiḥ sa tena śūdreṇa tulyo bhavet ||* “If a relative is present, he [who ignores him] becomes equal to that Śūdra. *āyuṣmān bhava saumyeti vācyo vipro ‘bhivādane | akāraś cāsya nāmno ‘nte vācyaḥ pūrvākṣaraḥ plutaḥ ||* “‘May you be long-lived, O gentle one’—thus should a Brahmin be addressed when saluting. And the vowel *a* at the end of his name should be pronounced with the preceding syllable as *pluta*. *yo na vetty abhivādasya vipraḥ pratyabhivādanam | nābhivādyaḥ sa viduṣā yathā śūdras tathaiva saḥ ||* “A Brahmin who does not know how to return a salutation should not be saluted by one who knows; he is just like a Śūdra. *yo ‘vetty abhivādasya vipraḥ pratyabhivādanam | āyuṣmān bhava saumyeti vācyo vipro ‘bhivādane ||* “The Brahmin who knows how to return a salutation should be addressed with ‘May you be long-lived, O gentle one’ when being saluted. *akāraś cāsya nāmno ‘nte vācyaḥ pūrvākṣaraḥ plutaḥ | āmantrite tu plutasya sarvatraiva svaritoditaḥ ||* “And the vowel *a* at the end of his name should be pronounced with the preceding syllable as *pluta*. But in the case of an address, the *pluta* is always said to have the *svarita* accent. *yo na vetti svaro ‘py asya vidvān api hi kilbiṣī | na cet saṃnihito jñātir yasya syād abhivāditā | sa tena śūdreṇa tulyo bhavet ||* “Even if he is learned, he who does not know the accent of this [name] is indeed a sinner. If no relative is present to whom the salutation was addressed, he becomes equal to that Śūdra. *abhivāde kṛte yastu na karoti tathottaram | āśīrvādaṃ sa vijñeyo vācyo nābhivādanam ||* “When a salutation has been performed, he who does not likewise offer a reply is to be known as one who does not deserve a blessing; the salutation itself should not be addressed to him. *yo vai sam̐nihito jñātiḥ sa tena śūdreṇa tulyo bhavet ||* “If a relative is present, he [who ignores him] becomes equal to that Śūdra. *āyuṣmān bhava saumyeti vācyo vipro ‘bhivādane | akāraś cāsya nāmno ‘nte vācyaḥ pūrvākṣaraḥ plutaḥ ||* “‘May you be long-lived, O gentle one’—thus should a Brahmin be addressed when saluting. And the vowel *a* at the end of his name should be pronounced with the preceding syllable as *pluta*. *yo na vetty abhivādasya vipraḥ pratyabhivādanam | nābhivādyaḥ sa viduṣā yathā śūdras tathaiva saḥ ||* “A Brahmin who does not know how to return a salutation should not be saluted by one who knows; he is just like a Śūdra. *yo ‘vetty abhivādasya vipraḥ pratyabhivādanam | āyuṣmān bhava saumyeti vācyo vipro ‘bhivādane ||* “The Brahmin who knows how to return a salutation should be addressed with ‘May you be long-lived, O gentle one’ when being saluted. *akāraś cāsya nāmno ‘nte vācyaḥ pūrvākṣaraḥ plutaḥ | āmantrite tu plutasya sarvatraiva svaritoditaḥ ||* “And the vowel *a* at the end of his name should be pronounced with the preceding syllable as *pluta*. But in the case of an address, the *pluta* is always said to have the *svarita* accent. *yo na vetti svaro ‘py asya vidvān api hi kilbiṣī | na cet saṃnihito jñātir yasya syād abhivāditā | sa tena śūdreṇa tulyo bhavet ||* “Even if he is learned, he who does not know the accent of this [name] is indeed a sinner. If no relative is present to whom the salutation was addressed, he becomes equal to that Śūdra. *abhivāde kṛte yastu na karoti tathottaram | āśīrvādaṃ sa vijñeyo vācyo nābhivādanam ||* “When a salutation has been performed, he who does not likewise offer a reply is to be known as one who does not deserve a blessing; the salutation itself
"A Brahmin should be addressed with the words 'May you be long-lived, O gentle one' during a salutation;
and at the end of his name, the vowel 'a' preceded by the preceding syllable should be pronounced as protracted (pluta). [MDh 2.125]

And likewise Vasiṣṭha says: “When addressed, the final vowel undergoes prolation (*pluta*), as do diphthongs that are not *pragṛhya*, and they undergo the substitution of *āy* and *āv*; the same applies to the vocative particle *bhoḥ*” [VaDh 13.46]. Examples such as “May you be long-lived, gentle Viṣṇumitra! (*āyuṣmān bhava saumya viṣṇumitrā*) and “May you be long-lived, gentle son of Daśaratha! (*āyuṣmān bhava saumya dāśarathāya*) are to be seen in the rule for returning a greeting. However, when one is among ignorant people, one should not perform the clasping of the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*). The same applies to the formal salutation (*abhivādana*). If it is asked what should be done in that case—it should be said simply, “I salute you” (*abhivādaye*). One should perform only the salutation itself, as Āpastamba says: “A Brāhmaṇa should salute, extending his right arm level with his ear; a Kṣatriya level with his chest; a Vaiśya level with his waist; and a Śūdra low, with palms joined and the prolation of the vowel” [ĀpDh 1.5.16–17], and so forth. Thus, it should be understood that the rule for clasping the feet, beginning with “with crossed hands” [MDh 2.72], is the procedure for clasping the feet, whereas the rule stated by Āpastamba is the procedure for the formal salutation (*abhivādana*). || 6.5 ||
Some say that in the case of greeting upon meeting a woman or a man, there is no fixed rule. 6.6.1.198.

Regarding the matter of husband and wife, the meaning is that when the wife has arrived at the point where she ought to perform a salutation to her husband, even though the husband may be one who knows how to return a salutation (*pratyabhivādana*), some authorities maintain that there is no fixed rule. They hold that there is no restriction such as "I am so-and-so," and that it may be performed in any manner whatsoever. Gautama, however, maintains that it must indeed be performed according to the fixed rule of "I am so-and-so" and so forth. This option depends upon the presence of wit or discernment. (6.6)
One should not kiss women other than one's mother, paternal uncle’s wife, or sister after returning from a journey abroad.

One should not perform the salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) of women when away from home. "Mother" is well known. "The wife of the paternal uncle" is the wife of the father’s younger brother. "Sister" refers to a co-uterine sister who is older. Having excluded these [other women], one must perform the salutation of them daily. And so it is stated in another *Smṛti*:
"One should perform the salutation of the mother and likewise the sister, as well as the wife of the paternal uncle; indeed, having approached them, he should do so every day."

Upon returning from a journey, one must perform either a salutation (*abhivādana*) or a formal grasping of the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) for other women who occupy the position of a guru. In this regard, it should be understood that for those who stand in the position of an absolute guru, such as the wives of maternal uncles and others, the formal grasping of the feet is required, whereas for others, a simple salutation suffices. (6.7)
One must not engage in sexual intercourse with the wives of one's brothers or with one's mother-in-law. 6.8.

Even for one who has returned from abroad, [the greeting] obtained through a person standing in the position of an absolute guru is prohibited; consequently, the act of salutation (*abhivādana*) is established [as the proper form]. The use of the compound *visama* (unequal) is for the purpose of including the clasping of friends (*sakhi*). And the word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including the clasping of the wife of one's father-in-law’s friend. (6.8)
But one must rise for officiating priests, fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles who are younger; they are not to be saluted by bowing down. 6.9.

When officiating priests and others who are younger than oneself are present, honor should be rendered by merely rising from one's seat. Since they are not persons to be saluted (*anabhivādya*), they are therefore also not to be clasped by the feet (*nopasaṃgrāhya*). The word "but" (*tu*) expresses a distinction: those of equal age are not to be saluted, and especially so those who are younger. (6.9)
Likewise, another who is an elder of at least eighty years, even if he is a Śūdra, [is honored] as an equal to one's own offspring.

Just as these [others] are not to be saluted and must be stood up for, so too is this other person who is older by age than the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others; he is a fellow citizen (*paura*), a resident of the same locality, and at least eighty years old—the meaning being that he is firmly established at eighty years of age. And from that point on, even a *śūdra* should be regarded [in this manner]; by the use of the word "even" (*api*), Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas are also included. Even if one is of a different caste, one is to be treated like a son by a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya. One might have the suspicion that, despite the presence of the word "other" (*anya*), the term "equal to a son" (*apatyasama*) refers only to those of the same caste; therefore, [the text clarifies this]. (6.10)
Even a lower noble may [be saluted] by a Śūdra. 6.11.

Even one who is lower—that is, even one of extremely inferior age—a noble twice-born man (dvija) must rise to meet a Śūdra. The mention of the Śūdra is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for Vaiśyas and others as well; therefore, it should be understood that a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya must rise to meet a Śūdra, a Brāhmaṇa or Kṣatriya must rise to meet a Vaiśya, and a Brāhmaṇa must rise to meet a Kṣatriya. The word "even" (api) serves to include the act of salutation. (6.11)
And he should avoid uttering his name. 6.12.

The repetition of the word *asya* is for the sake of distributive emphasis (*vīpsā*), meaning "of this one and that one"; [it implies] that a low-born person should not utter the name of each and every high-born person. The term "without qualification" (*nirupapada*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Because of the word *ca* ("and"), it also includes derision. Consequently, a high-born person may take the names of low-born persons. 6.12.
And the king’s messenger shall not be subject to the ajapa fine. || 6.13 ||

A Brahmin who serves as a messenger and carries out errands for a king should avoid addressing him by name. This prohibition applies because such behavior would result from his low status; it refers to one who does not recite [the Veda], that is to say, one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*). By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), this also applies to a Vaiśya. However, there is no fault in the case of a Śūdra. (6.13)
"Bho bhavan" is used for a friend born on the same day. 6.14.

One should address him as "bho bhavān. The words *bho* and *bhavān* are to be employed with reference to the specific action at hand; this much constitutes the mark of respect. As for the companion or friend (*vayasya*), his characteristic is that he was born on the same day (*samāne ’hani jātaḥ*). Here, the word *ahaḥ* is a synonym for *saṃvatsara* (year), because in the *Naighaṇṭuka* lexicon one finds it listed among synonyms for the year: "abdaḥ, saṃvatsaram, ahar, jalam. Consequently, [the definition] means "born in the same year. In common worldly usage as well, those born in the same year are well known to be of equal age. Therefore, after a year has passed, he becomes older. (6.14)
A citizen who is ten years older [is to be honored]. || 6.15 ||

The term "bho bhavan" (O sir) continues [from the previous rule]. The meaning is that one should address [a fellow citizen] as "bho bhavan," just as one would a friend. Even if he is ten years older, he is a fellow citizen (*paura*) living in the same place. 6.15.
With five [parts], it is Kalābhara. || 6.16 ||

Even one who dwells in the same place as oneself, if he lives by means of artistic skills—such as music, painting, leaf-cutting, and other arts and sciences—he may be addressed like a peer, even if he is five years older. (6.16)
A learned Śrotriya who is also a wandering minstrel (Cāraṇa) is purified by three [days and nights].
A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* portions [of the Veda]. A *cāraṇa* is one who shares the same conduct;
some describe him as being habituated to dance, song, and so forth, but that is incorrect, as such a person is already included under the term *kalābhara*. (6.17)
One who performs the duties of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya but is devoid of learning [is a Śūdra]. 6.18.

Whether one subsists by the occupation of a Kṣatriya or the occupation of a Vaiśya, even if that person’s own work is superior, as long as they remain engaged in that [lower] work, they are not yet fully matured until that work has ceased. And he who is devoid of learning remains inferior even to one whose learning is superior. (6.18)
And one who has been initiated [remains so] until the purchase [of the Soma]. 6.19.

Even one who is associated with the status of a *vayas* (a youth or peer) becomes a *dīkṣita* (initiated); he is a *vayas* only prior to the sale of the *soma*. After that, he is to be honored—this is the purpose of the instruction. By virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), it should be understood by implication that even one residing in a higher stage of life (*uttamāśrama*) is [honored] only prior to the consumption of the *trivṛt* [oblation]. Thus said Uśanas: "He by whom the *trivṛt* has been consumed becomes the teacher of all. (6.19)
Wealth, kinship, occupation, birth, knowledge, and age are grounds for respect. 6.20.

Since it is impossible for wealth and the other qualities to be honored directly, it should be understood that those who possess them are what are honored. One who possesses wealth is one rich in riches; one who possesses kin is one with many distinguished brothers and so forth; one who possesses action is one who performs as prescribed; one who possesses birth is one endowed with noble lineage; one who possesses learning is one who has studied the Vedas and the Shastras; and one who possesses age is one of advanced years. (6.20)
The stronger [force] prevails over the others. 6.21.

Whatever is subsequent should be understood as more venerable than each preceding one. Consequently, one who possesses wealth is more honorable than one who possesses kinsmen; one who possesses merit is more honorable than both, and so forth—this principle should be applied accordingly. *Māna* refers to salutation and other such marks of respect. 6.21.
But learning is weightier than all [these]. 6.22.

"Śruta" means the thorough comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas. But surely this should have been taught at the end of the previous sūtra; since that would be established by the very fact of its superior strength, a separate instruction here is redundant. It is said in reply: This separate undertaking is for the sake of specification. What is intended here by "śruta" is a specific kind of learning, namely the thorough comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas. Previously, it was merely the recitation of the Veda itself. The word "tu" (but) also serves to express this distinction. Consequently, this [learning] is to be honored by all. (6.22)
Why? Because dharma has that as its root. 6.23.
That which one who has heard the Veda practices is also established as a root of Dharma, as previously explained: "And the tradition and conduct of those who know it" (GDh 1.2). Likewise, Manu says:
"The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as well as the tradition and conduct of those who know it, the practice of the virtuous, and also self-satisfaction" (MDh 2.6).
Alternatively, because Smṛti is preceded by a thorough understanding of the meaning of the Veda—as Manu has said:
"The sages perceive the Śruti; they likewise remember the Smṛti. (6.23)
And because of scripture. 6.24.
He alone is more authoritative than even the *Śruti*. As for the *Śruti*, one should look to the *Śaiśava-brāhmaṇa* mentioned by Manu:
"The wise child Aṅgiras taught his ancestors;
having encompassed them with knowledge, he said to them, 'O little sons! (MDh 2.151).
And so forth. The citation of scriptural passages is for the purpose of making known the superior authority of that which has been heard when there is excellence in its study. 6.24.
Way must be yielded to a wheel-turning monarch, one who stands at the tenth stage, a bridegroom, a bride, a student who has completed his studies, and a king. 6.25.

One should assist others on the road by giving way to those who do not possess the aforementioned qualities, such as those with wheeled vehicles and so forth. A "wheeled vehicle" (cakra) refers to a cart; one who possesses such a vehicle is a "cart-owner" (cakrī). One "standing in the tenth stage" (daśamīstha) is one existing in the tenth state, meaning one who is extremely aged. One "to be favored" (anugrāhya) is one afflicted by disease. A "bride" (vadhū) refers to a pregnant woman and the like. A "graduate" (snātaka) is one who has completed his studies and vows. A "king" (rājā) is one who has been consecrated. (6.25)
Regarding the meeting of a king and a Brāhmaṇa: [the king should honor] a Śrotriya with [gifts] for a Śrotriya. 6.26.

The word "tu" (but) serves to indicate a distinction. If the king is of lesser [merit] and the Śrotriya is more highly endowed with excellence—provided he is indeed a Snātaka—then the path must be yielded to him by the king. Likewise, in other cases, it must be yielded to the king alone. Regarding the preceding [categories] as well, the application should be understood according to the relative superiority when they are in proximity to one another. (6.26)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Gautama-bhāṣya* by Maskari. Regarding the seventh chapter:

"But sacred learning (*śruta*) is weightier than all [other duties]" (GDh 6.22); thus, the preeminence of knowledge has been stated. And its acquisition must be obtained from a Brāhmaṇa, because he alone has the authority for teaching. But when there is an absence of a Brāhmaṇa capable of teaching, then how should one proceed? To this, he says:
In times of distress, it is permissible for a Brahmin to acquire knowledge from one who is not a Brahmin. 7.1.

The heading "the rule for times of distress" (*āpatkalpa*) is maintained until the end of this chapter. "Distress" (*āpad*) refers to the absence of Brāhmaṇas capable of expounding the sacred tradition; the "rule" (*kalpa*) applicable therein is the "rule for times of distress. Even in times of distress, the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is intended to ensure that Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas acquire knowledge only from a Brāhmaṇa. Non-Brāhmaṇas here refer to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, because others lack the qualification to study. Furthermore, it should be understood that among them, one should first learn from a Kṣatriya and then from a Vaiśya, as indicated by the observation: "In the absence of that, the occupation of a Vaiśya" (GDh 7.7). Knowledge consists of fourteen branches. Thus says another Smṛti.
"The limbs [of the Veda] are four: Mīmāṃsā, Nyāyavistara, Purāṇa, and Dharmaśāstra; these are the fourteen sciences (*vidyā*).

Here, "utility" (*upayoga*) means acceptance, because the root *yuj* denotes a connection. By this very principle of "otherwise inexplicability," the teaching of the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas is inferred. That too has only an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose.
"Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood: officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts from pure persons. [MDh 10.76]

Because Manu has prohibited [it] by stating that "only for a Brāhmaṇa is the purpose visible, not for the other two," one might think that since it should have been stated simply as "studying from a non-Brāhmaṇa," the present formulation—"the application of knowledge"—is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) meaning that in times of distress, one must study only from a non-Brāhmaṇa. Consequently, even in cases such as the expiation for killing a Brāhmaṇa where there is an injunction to give away all one's possessions, if no Brāhmaṇa capable of receiving the gift is available, it should not be given to a Kṣatriya or others. (7.1)
Now, since the fulfillment of all forms of service is obtained through the gateway of study, he says:
"Following [the teacher] is service. (7.2)

Service consists merely in following behind him as he walks; no other duties, such as salutation and so forth, need be performed. This is stated for a time other than that of formal study, because those [other duties] are already implied during that period. (7.2)
When it is completed, the Brāhmaṇa is the teacher. || 7.3 ||

When the study is completed, not even the mere act of following [the teacher] should be performed. That [following] must be performed by the Brāhmaṇa alone with that teacher; for although it should have been stated that "following consists of service until completion," the expression "the Brāhmaṇa is the guru" is used [to indicate this]. (7.3)
Now another rule for times of distress is stated:
sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts are permitted for all [twice-born]. (7.4)

By the term "all" (*sarva*), only the three [higher] castes are understood as being unpraiseworthy, because the prescribed rules for those who are praiseworthy apply except in times of distress; furthermore, the rule for a Śūdra begins with, "If there is no livelihood other than from a Śūdra" (GDh 17.5). If it is argued that the word "all" should be taken in the ablative case (*sarvasmāt*), there is no fault, as the word "from" (*sakāśāt*) is supplied as an ellipsis. The plural number in "of all" (*sarveṣām*) is intended to include those born in the direct order (*anuloma*). This is stated specifically regarding the Brāhmaṇa, due to his eligibility (*adhikāra*) and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating, "In the absence of that, the occupation of a Kṣatriya. Consequently, in this state, there is no fault in performing censurable acts such as officiating at sacrifices, owing to the force of the scriptural injunction. Thus says Manu:

"Neither from teaching, nor from officiating at sacrifices, nor from accepting gifts—even from those that are censured—does a fault accrue to Brahmins, for they are like fire and water. A Brahmin who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone. [MDh 10.102–103]
And so on. Likewise, the Śruti says: "Therefore, by whatever means possible, one should obtain abundant food" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.10.1). || 7.4 ||
Each preceding one is more venerable than the following. || 7.5 ||

Among these activities, such as officiating at sacrifices and so forth, whichever has been mentioned earlier is to be understood as more weighty than the one following it. Consequently, the mention of the "former" is intended to establish the sequence that, when it becomes impossible to subsist by each subsequent means, one should live by each preceding one. A penance should be observed for violating this order, since the word "weightier" (*guru*) was used instead of saying "each preceding one is better" (*pūrvaḥ pūrvaḥ san*). (7.5)
In the absence of that, the occupation of a Kṣatriya [is permitted]. || 7.6 ||

The word "syāt" (it may be) is to be understood as the ellipsis. In the event that the previously mentioned mode of livelihood for a Brāhmaṇa cannot be obtained, the mode of livelihood of a Kṣatriya consists of subsisting through the performance of sacrifices and so forth, or by means of protection and the like. The mention of this is for the purpose of making it known that even a Brāhmaṇa’s mode of livelihood, though entirely devoid of merit, is better. And thus says Manu:
"One's own duty, though deficient, is better than the duty of another well-performed;
for one who lives by the duty of another falls immediately from his caste" (MDh 10.97).

When it is said, “or likewise the occupation of a Kṣatriya,” since the word *vā* (or) implies an option, one might understand that the Kṣatriya occupation is permitted only in the absence of the Brāhmaṇa occupation. However, the inclusion of the term *alābhe* (in the absence [of livelihood]) indicates that even for one living by the Kṣatriya occupation, when the Brāhmaṇa occupation alone becomes sufficient for subsistence, he should abandon the Kṣatriya occupation and resort solely to the Brāhmaṇa occupation. Thus says Nārada: “Once a Brāhmaṇa has crossed over a time of distress and his people have been supported by the Kṣatriya occupation, he should abandon that Kṣatriya occupation after performing a purification for himself. (NSm 1.55)
In the absence of that, he may follow the occupation of a Vaiśya. || 7.7 ||

The mention of "non-acceptance" (alābha) is so that there may be no confusion of livelihoods (*vṛttisaṃkara*). And thus, even in the case of such confusion, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is to be observed. The explanation of that [term] has already been stated. However, in this case, because there is an absence of a specific injunction, there is no possibility at all of resorting to a higher mode of life (*uttamavṛtti*). As Vasiṣṭha says: "But never [should one resort to] a higher [mode]" (VaDh 2.23). 7.7.
That is his merchandise. 7.8.

That acceptance [of gifts] applies only to a Brāhmaṇa, not to a Kṣatriya who is established in the livelihood of a Vaiśya. And thus, for a Vaiśya, the fact that selling is established by implication is prohibited; having abandoned it, he may take what is prohibited or what is not prohibited after giving [in exchange]. In the absence of that, even what is not normally for sale may be sold. (7.8)
What is that which is not for sale? To this he says:
"Perfumes, liquids, prepared food, sesame, hemp, linen, and skins. (7.9)

Fragrance and unguents; liquids such as oil and the like; prepared foods such as sweetmeats (*modaka*) and the like; sesame seeds, which are well known; *śāṇa*, a product of hemp; *kṣauma*, a product of *kṣumā* or flax (*atasī*); since the prohibition applies to the derivative product, it does not apply to the raw material; and *ajina*, meaning skin. 7.9.
Two garments dyed red. || 7.10 ||
"Red" means dyed with lac or similar substances; "washed" means cleansed. || 7.10 ||
Milk and its derivatives. 7.11.

"Milk" (*kṣīram*) refers to *payaḥ* (the liquid) together with its derivatives (*vikāraiḥ*), such as curd (*dadhi*) and so forth. Here, because of the inclusion of the term "derivatives," it is understood that there is no prohibition regarding the derivatives of sesame. Alternatively, the inclusion of "derivatives" is for the purpose of indicating that wherever there is a mention of milk alone, it includes its derivatives as well. Regarding the former position, it must be stated that the mention of the derivatives of hemp and linen is intended to prohibit their primary substances (*prakṛti*). (7.11)
Roots, fruits, flowers, medicinal herbs, honey, meat, grass, water, and unwholesome things [are not to be accepted]. 7.12.

Roots include turmeric and the like; fruits include betel nut and the like; flowers include *damanaka* and the like; medicinal herbs include lentils and the like; honey includes that of bees and the like. Although the prohibition of honey is already established by the mention of "flavors" (*rasa*), it is stated again for the purpose of prohibiting it even under the alternative view that "in case of incapacity, one may subsist on anything" (GDh 7.22). Meat and water are well known. Grass is well known. Unwholesome food refers to poison. (7.12)
And [the same applies] to animals when they are connected with violence. 7.13.

Domestic animals, such as cows and the like, must not be sold when associated with violence (*hiṃsā*). Although the word "yoga" (association) would have sufficed, the prefix (*upasarga*) is employed to indicate that they must not be sold even when held in the hand of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). If it is argued that there is no association with violence because there is no fault in the act of killing in that context, that is true; however, that [absence of fault] applies only to the sacrificer and not to anyone else. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), peacocks and other such creatures are also included. (7.13)
And [the meat] of a man-servant, a maiden, and a cow-calf is always [permissible]. 7.14.

“Puruṣa” means a human being; the inclusion of that term also covers women because it denotes the genus (*jāti*). Thus says the Śruti: “He places the head of a man [on the altar], not that of a woman. *Vaśā* is a barren cow. *Kumārī* is also a cow; since a human girl is female, she is already included by the mention of “man” (*puruṣa*). *Vehat* is a cow that destroys its own fetus; she too is a cow, according to the same reasoning as stated before. The word “and” (*ca*) is for the purpose of including the “barren crow” (*kākavañdhya*) and others. Some say that the word “always” (*nityam*) implies that this applies even in cases other than those involving injury (*hiṃsā-saṃyoga*). That is incorrect, because in the case of injury, the prohibition is already established by the fact that they are animals (*paśu*); the force of the repeated commencement [of the rule] allows us to understand that it applies elsewhere as well. Others qualify the substance with the word “always,” meaning “these are always of such a nature. That too is incorrect, for humans and the like might never be of such a nature [as cows]. Therefore, the word “always” is intended to indicate the non-constant nature of others, such as sesame seeds. Consequently, it should be understood that sesame seeds and the like produced by one’s own cultivation may be sold, whereas those produced otherwise must not be sold. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: “Or, at will, they may sell sesame seeds produced by their own cultivation” (VaDh 2.31). The sense there is: “If they may even sell sesame seeds, how much more so other things? (7.14)
According to some, [the term "cattle" (paśu) refers to] land, rice, barley, goats, sheep, horses, bulls, milch-cows, and oxen. 7.15.

"Land" (*bhūmi*) means "house" (*gṛha*), for in the *Naighaṇṭuka* lexicon we hear "house" as a synonym for land in such passages as "the house, the dwelling, the home, the abode. "Rice" (*vrīhi*) is well known, as is "barley" (*yava*); the mention of these two serves as an illustration for all grains. "Goat" (*aja*) means a he-goat; "sheep" (*avi*) is well known; "horse" (*aśva*) means a steed; "bull" (*ṛṣabha*) means a male ox; "milch cow" (*dhenu*) means a cow that gives milk; "ox" (*anaḍvān*) means a draft-ox capable of pulling a cart. These are not to be sold. Some teachers maintain that this prohibition applies even in cases other than those involving injury, but Gautama does not hold this view. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include the camel, as Uśanas says: "Camels, bulls, and horses are not to be sold. Others say it is intended to draw in [the requirement of] permanence [of ownership].
But as for the exchange: 7.16.

The word "should be performed" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. *Nimaya* is the exchange of two prohibited substances. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a qualification: an exchange may be performed whether the items are equal or inferior. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "An exchange may be made with something equal or even with something inferior. (7.16)
With the juices of juices. || 7.17 ||

The commencement of this sūtra is for the purpose of establishing a rule: that when an exchange is to be made between liquids such as oils and liquids such as molasses and the like, the exchange must be made only with liquids. 7.17.
And [the same applies] to animals. 7.18.

The word "ca" (and) is intended to bring forward the word "paśūn" from the third case [of the previous verse], as in "paśūnām paśubhiḥ. This should be understood as referring to animals whose sale is prohibited; for the sale of those not prohibited is already established by the very fact that they are not forbidden. (7.18)
Not [the word *lavaṇa*] with *anna*. 7.19.

Salt must not be bartered for another flavor. This prohibition, which follows from the rule that "flavors may be exchanged for flavors," precludes what would otherwise be obtained. Cooked food, however, may be exchanged for any other substance whatsoever, as there is no such restrictive rule regarding it. (7.19)
And of sesame seeds. 7.20.

The word "and" (ca) serves to carry forward the prohibition of exchange. The meaning is that there is no exchange of sesame seeds for anything whatsoever. Their separate mention is intended to permit exchange with an equal amount of grain in times of distress. Thus Manu says: "Sesame seeds may be exchanged for grain of equal value" (MDh 10.94). 7.20.
Now, for the purpose of providing an exception regarding cooked food, he says:
"But with equal raw grain, [one may eat] cooked [food] when there is immediate need. (7.21)

An exchange occurs with something equal, similar, or identical; in the sense of "at that very time," it means if cooked food is consumed at that same moment. The word *tu* expresses a specific qualification of equality, and therefore it should be understood as "with rice.
Some say that the word *tu* serves a restrictive purpose, meaning that the exchange must be made in that very manner and not otherwise.

That is incorrect, because the restriction is established by the very force of the commencement of the Sūtra itself. If the exchange were permitted with just anything, then, since it would already be established by the general rule "But [there shall be] an exchange," the present Sūtra would not have been commenced at all. Consequently, those substances which are *rasa* (flavors) and so forth must be exchanged only for specific substances; as for the remaining three [categories], it should be understood that they may be exchanged for anything. The meaning is that an exchange of cooked food must be made with rice measured in *prastha*s and so on, using only those same measures. Furthermore, this indicates that in the phrase "perfumes, flavors, and prepared food" (*gandharasakṛtānna*), the word "prepared food" (*kṛtānna*) applies to rice as well. Otherwise, since there would be no prohibition against selling it, the commencement of the rule regarding exchange would not apply—because the commencement of exchange pertains only to those things that are prohibited from being sold. (7.21)
In every way, however, one who is unable [to follow the prescribed duties] may subsist by means other than those of a Śūdra. 7.22.

He may also live by selling forbidden items, by bartering, by engaging in the occupations of other castes, or by combining these means. In the event of incapacity during an extreme emergency, he may even adopt the livelihood of a Śūdra, provided it does not involve serving Śūdras; however, he must avoid eating the remnants of others' food, practicing crafts for hire, and similar activities. The word "tu" (but/however) is used to indicate that there is some degree of sin associated with what is prescribed for times of distress. As another Smṛti text has illustrated: "Having purified himself. (7.22)
Some say that even this [is permissible] when there is a danger to life. 7.23.
Some maintain that even the work of a Śūdra is permissible when the risk of death has arisen, because life must necessarily be preserved. Thus Vyāsa says:
"Life is the foundation for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; by killing it, what is not destroyed? By protecting it, what is not protected?"

By the mention of "life" (*prāṇa*), there is also the inclusion of one's wife, children, and so forth, whose livelihoods depend upon it, based on the scriptural insight: "For these [dependents] are the life-breaths moving outside [the body]. The use of the word "some" (*eke*) indicates that this is not the view of Gautama, because even in this state, such an act is censurable according to him. Here, by the mention of "danger to life," it is understood that there are other types of calamities as well. Consequently, the state in which the aforementioned alternative rule is taught should be understood as characterized by a lack of capacity to perform obligatory (*nitya*) duties. As Manu says: "He who [does not feed] the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself..."
"He who does not offer oblations for these five is not truly alive" (MDh 3.72).
Thus ends section 7.23.
But there is a restriction regarding the mixing of castes and the consumption of forbidden food. || 7.24 ||

By the term "tad" (that), the Śūdra is meant. "Saṃkara" (mixture) refers to sitting together on the same seat and so forth. "Abhakṣya" (unfit food) refers to his leavings and the like, or garlic and such which are unfit for him; "niyama" (restriction) means the avoidance of these two. The word "tu" (but/and) expresses a distinction: that in this particular state, it applies specifically to the Brāhmaṇa. (7.24)
Even a Brahmin may take up arms when his life is in danger. (7.25)

By the mention of "life-breaths" (prāṇa), sons, wives, gold, and so forth are also included, based on the scriptural insight that "these external things are indeed the life-breaths. By the word "also" (api), Vaiśyas and Śūdras are likewise included; for the Kṣatriya’s duty is already established by his engagement in protection and other such tasks. Or rather, [the rule applies] even to the Kṣatriya. 7.25.
The duty of a Rājanya is indeed the duty of a Vaiśya; the duty of a Vaiśya is indeed the duty of a Vaiśya. 7.26.

Even a Kṣatriya, being unable to subsist by his own duty, may adopt the mode of life of a Vaiśya; it has been stated that for him, too, there is no prohibition against selling forbidden goods. The commencement of this Sūtra is intended to make known that one should not conceive the notion that, just as a Brāhmaṇa may follow the occupation of a Kṣatriya and a Kṣatriya the occupation of a Vaiśya, so too a Vaiśya may follow the occupation of a Śūdra, or that just as a Brāhmaṇa may follow the occupation of a Vaiśya, so a Kṣatriya may follow the occupation of a Śūdra. Why? If it were intended for others as it was for a Brāhmaṇa, then [the author] would have said that all [castes] may adopt the occupation of the one immediately following or the one separated by one degree. Since he did not say that, but instead began with "The Rājanya [may perform] the work of a Vaiśya," he makes it known that the occupation prescribed for a Kṣatriya in times of distress belongs only to the Kṣatriya, and not to the Vaiśya or the Śūdra; furthermore, even for a Kṣatriya, there is no occupation of a Śūdra. Therefore, a Kṣatriya may also adopt the occupation of a Vaiśya in times of distress. And so says Manu:
"A Kṣatriya who has fallen into misfortune may live by all of this," [Manu Dharmaśāstra 10.95].
Thus [ends verse 7.26].
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Maskarīya-Gautama-bhāṣya*.
The Eighth Chapter:

Now, if someone should become involved in an action prescribed for times of distress (*āpad*) out of ignorance of its faults or out of greed, by whom should he be restrained? By the king and the Brahmin, through instruction and punishment respectively; for it is they alone who—
In this world, two are firm in their vows: the king and the learned brahmin.

The word *dvau* (two) expresses excellence (*prakarṣa*) rather than being a mere numerical designation, because duality is already established by the use of the dual number itself. There are indeed instances where a numerical designation serves to indicate excellence, such as: "In this village, there are only two Brāhmaṇas. In that case, it is understood that although there are other Brāhmaṇas, these two alone are devoted to the performance of religious duties (*anuṣṭhāna*). Here too, the purpose is to show that the King and the Brāhmaṇa possess vows with particular excellence, not to exclude others. The inclusion of the word *loka* (world) is for the sake of distributive repetition (*vipsā*); the meaning is "in every world," that is, in every kingdom. Otherwise, since all activities fall within the domain of the world, this [mention] would be redundant. Thus, it is understood that just as one must be a king in every kingdom, so too must one be deeply learned (*bahuśruta*). "Dhṛtavratau" means the two who uphold (*dhārayitārau*) vows—that is, ritual acts. A "king" (*rājā*) is a Kṣatriya endowed with qualities such as consecration (*abhiṣeka*), according to the statement of Śaṅkha: "He becomes a king when consecrated on the head. A "Brāhmaṇa" is one who is deeply learned. Although the Brāhmaṇa holds primary importance, the mention of the King first is intended to qualify the Brāhmaṇa as being deeply learned. The particle *ca* (and) serves to draw the quality of deep learning over to the King as well. Consequently, it should be understood that while the Brāhmaṇa must especially be deeply learned, the King must also be so. "Deeply learned" (*bahuśruta*) means one by whom much has been heard. While one might have said "the King and Brāhmaṇa are deeply learned," the use of a non-compound expression (*visamāsa*) is intended to show that the King also possesses qualities such as valor with particular excellence. Therefore, the ellipsis to be supplied is: "those two shall be upholders of their vows" (*tau dhṛtavratau syātām*). (8.1)
For this reason: "The life of those two, of the fourfold species of humans, and of the internally conscious beings—those that move, fall, and crawl—is dependent upon them. (8.2)

Because these two are mentioned together with a common designation; "of the fourfold human race" means of the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*). "Those with internal consciousness" refers to those born in the natural (*anuloma*) and inverse (*pratiloma*) orders, and by the word "and" (*ca*), gods as well—according to the Vedic revelation: "For from this [human] offering, the gods subsist. "The moving" are the stationary, such as trees and so forth; "the flying" are the birds; "the crawling" are the insects and so forth. Their life—the maintenance of the vital breaths—is dependent upon these [Brāhmaṇas]. How so? Those belonging to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramin*), when favored by the Brāhmaṇa, engage in activities for visible and invisible purposes; thus, through the mediation of rain and other such means, they exist for the benefit of the world, and in that sense, they are dependent on the Brāhmaṇa. And so says Manu: [Insert Manu verse here] Thus ends the section.
"A libation duly cast into the fire reaches the sun," and so forth (Manu Dharmaśāstra 3.76).
Furthermore, the king is a direct cause of livelihood by means of suppressing highway robbers and by means of restraining violence. 8.2.
And their livelihood alone is not dependent on them; rather—procreation, protection, and non-confusion [of castes] are their duty (dharma). 8.3.

Procreation is growth, and that [growth] is dependent upon him; for through his instruction on the wielding of punishment against kings and Brahmins, they act as prescribed, and through rain and other means, there is an absence of calamities such as disease, whereby growth occurs. Furthermore, protection from thieves and the like results from the suppression of criminals, which follows from his wielding of punishment and his instruction on expiatory rites; and the absence of social confusion results from his instruction on restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*). Since he wields punishment for the non-performance of what is enjoined and the practice of what is forbidden, even *dharma* itself is dependent upon him alone. (8.3)
Now, by how much learning does one become "one who has heard much"? To this he says: "He is such a one as becomes a bahuśruta. (8.4)

“This is he” is an instruction that combines the indirect and the direct. Regarding the statement, “But what has been heard is weightier than all [other things]” (GDh 6.22), it is precisely this kind [of learning] that is intended there as well. The meaning of the phrase “he becomes one who has heard much” (*bahuśruta*) is that he attains such a state. Furthermore, the inclusion of the verb *bhavati* (“becomes”) is for the purpose of indicating that even if one possesses only a slight understanding of these [subjects] such as the worlds and so forth, or if one has heard something else besides these, one still indeed “becomes” a learned person; otherwise, since the status of being a *bahuśruta* would already be established by the mere fact of having heard much, the inclusion of *bhavati* would be redundant. (8.4)
One who knows the worlds, the Vedas, and the Vedāṅgas. || 8.5 ||

By the word *loka*, worldly conventions such as village boundaries and the like are denoted. By the first word *veda*, the *upavedas*—such as Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and so forth—are denoted. By the second word *veda*, the four Vedas are denoted. By the word *aṅga*, grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), phonetics (*śikṣā*), prosody (*chandas*), ritual manuals (*kalpasūtra*), astronomy (*jyotiṣa*), and etymology (*nirukta*) are denoted. The word *vi-* is connected with each [of these]. By the phrase "one who knows the Vedas" (*vedavit*), the recitation of the Vedas (*vedapāṭha*) is also to be understood, because another Smṛti prohibits other sciences for one who has not studied the Veda. As Manu says:
"The twice-born who, without having studied the Vedas, exerts himself in other pursuits,
quickly falls to the status of a Śūdra while still alive, along with his lineage.
(MDh 2.168) Thus [ends verse 8.5].
He was skilled in dialogues, discourses, histories, and ancient lore.
"Vākovākya" means a treatise on logic (*tarka-śāstra*) consisting of dialogues in the form of questions and answers. Thus says Manu:
"He who investigates by means of reasoning knows the Dharma, and no other" (MDh 12.106).

*Itihāsa* refers to the *Mahābhārata* and the *Rāmāyaṇa*. *Purāṇa*—that in which the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the universe] are described—is the *Brahmāṇḍa* and other such texts. He should be proficient (*nipuṇa*) in these as well, but only in their meanings, not in both the text and the meaning as in the case of the Vedas, because he begins with different verbs. And thus, not only the Veda but also its auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) must be studied. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "The Veda with its auxiliaries (*sāṅga*) should be studied. (8.6)
Dependent on that, it functions therein. || 8.7 ||

Dependent on that [the Vedas], he is one whose habit is the recitation of the meanings well-known from the Vedas; his livelihood consists in being devoted to the performance of the rites prescribed therein. 8.7.
It is conditioned by forty formative forces. || 8.8 ||

And those [rites] are the ones to be described hereafter, beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception); he is "endowed" (*upeta*) with them. Since this is already established by the fact that they will be described, the specific mention of their number is intended to prevent the sense of mere conjunction (*samuccaya*). Because the plural is employed, the requirement is fulfilled by three or more. If it is argued that even in the passage, “But for whom even a single part (*ekadeśa*) of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)... (GDh 8.25), the word “even” (*api*) implies conjunction, we say no; for the word “part” (*ekadeśa*) would then be redundant, as it could already signify a portion of the rites. Therefore, since conjunction is explicitly stated here, it follows that in other cases where the term “part” is used, it serves to include only a few of the purificatory rites. 8.8.
One who delights in the three types of action. || 8.9 ||

These—characterized by study together with its ancillaries (sāṅga), giving, and sacrifice—are those mentioned here in the rule: "Study for the twice-born" (GDh 10.1). "Devoted to these" means one whose habit is their constant performance. Since the performance is already established by the rule "subsisting by that" (GDh 8.7), this is commenced again for the sake of specification. The specification consists either in the practice of them with excellence, or in making known that they have an unseen (transcendental) purpose. 8.9.
Or in six [fingers]. 8.10.

Together with officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts, there are six [occupations]. This [re]commencement is for the purpose of making known that even these have an invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose. 8.10.
He is thoroughly trained in the rules of customary conduct. || 8.11 ||

The Smārta rites are those recorded in the scriptures; the Ācārika rites are those practiced by the learned and are not recorded in texts. He is thoroughly trained in both these types of rituals, and having understood them, he is devoted to their performance. (8.11)
Such is the Brahmin:
he is one who must be avoided by the king, yet he is not to be killed, nor bound, nor punished with a fine, nor banished, nor censured, nor excluded. (8.12)

Even when an offense occurs unintentionally that would otherwise merit execution or similar punishment, he must avoid these six things—because there is no possibility of such acts occurring intentionally, as they pertain to intentional conduct. The inclusion of the number "six" implies that this applies even when multiple offenses are combined. "Execution" (*vadha*) means repeated beating; since that is not applicable here, it is excluded. "Imprisonment" (*bandha*) is the binding with shackles and the like. "Fine" (*daṇḍa*) is the confiscation of wealth. "Exile" (*bahiṣkaraṇa*) is banishment from the village and so forth. "Censure" (*parivāda*) is the public proclamation of one's faults. "Abandonment" (*parihāra*) is the act of forsaking him. The word "and" (*ca*) has the purpose of indicating that one should not be his approver or instigator. The particle "iti" denotes a manner; consequently, one should not engage in conversation with him or similar interactions. (8.12)

It has been stated, “by means of forty sacraments” (GDh 8.8). To explain what these are, he says: conception, the rite for a male child, parting the hair, birth-rite, naming, the first feeding of solid food, tonsure, and initiation. 8.13.

The rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception) are prescribed in the *Pratigṛhya* texts. Their mention here, however, is for the purpose of making known their nature as *saṃskāras* (purificatory rites). Manu also has stated their status as *saṃskāras*: “From conception (*niṣeka*) until the end at the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*),” and so forth. *Garbhādhāna* occurs only during the fertile period; it should be understood from the *Pratigṛhya* texts that one performs the oblation at the time of cohabitation (*saṃveśane hutvā*), and so on. *Puṃsavana* is enjoined in the third month, specifically in the first pregnancy and not otherwise, provided the embryo is manifest; some authorities maintain it should be performed for every pregnancy, while others say only once. The same applies to *sīmantonnayana*. That rite is enjoined in the fourth, sixth, or eighth month. *Jātakarma* (birth-rite) should be understood as taking place before the infant begins to suckle, eat solid food, or have its navel cord cut. *Nāmakaraṇa* (naming) occurs on the tenth or twelfth day, or under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). *Annaprāśana* (first feeding of solid food) takes place in the sixth month or after one year. As Śaṅkha says: “*Annaprāśana* is performed after one year or in the sixth month. *Caula* (tonsure) is performed in the first year or the third. *Upanayana* (initiation) has already been discussed. *Upaniṣkramaṇa* (the first outing) is not mentioned here because it is included within *annaprāśana*; this was stated by Manu.
"In the fourth month, the infant's first exit from the house should be performed.
Furthermore: there are four Vedic vows. 8.14.
The separate instruction is for the purpose of grasping the Veda; the mention of "Veda" is for the sake of indicating that four [verses] are to be learned from each Veda. 8.14.
Furthermore: bathing, union with the wife who shares in the dharma, and the performance of the five sacrifices—namely, those for the gods, the ancestors, humans, beings, and Brahman. (8.15)

Bathing refers to the completion of Vedic studies (*samāvartana*). Marriage is the union with a partner in the practice of Dharma (*sahadharmacāriṇī-saṃyoga*). The use of the term *visamāsa* (separation) is intended to indicate that marriage does not necessarily follow immediately after bathing. While "marriage" alone would have sufficed, the inclusion of the term *sahadharmacāriṇī* is intended to indicate that the taking of a wife is for the purpose of performing ritual acts. Consequently, there is no fault in the case of one who has not taken a wife or one who is widowed, provided they are unable to perform the five sacrifices and so forth. The performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) refers to the carrying out of the five sacrifices, beginning with the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*). The use of the genitive case (*pañcānām yajñānām*) is for the purpose of connecting them with the act of performance. The inclusion of the word "performance" is not to imply that these occur only occasionally, like the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice; rather, it means "day by day. Although the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) are indeed the sacrifices to the gods and so on, the explicit mention of "gods" and the others is for the purpose of indicating that there are five distinct sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*); otherwise, there might be the suspicion that the performance of the five sacrifices constitutes only a single sacrament. The deities and others have already been explained. The particle *ca* ("and") in the phrase "of these" (*eteṣāṃ ca*) serves to aggregate the qualities of the self. Thus, it is established that the five sacrifices, when accompanied by the qualities of the self, lead to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and not when they exist in isolation. The term "of these" (*eteṣām*) is an elliptical reference (*upalakṣaṇa*) to those things yet to be mentioned, and does not refer solely to the five sacrifices already stated. Why? Because if it were intended that only the five sacrifices are to be accompanied by the qualities of the self, then he would have said, "the performance of the five sacrifices together with their qualities. Therefore, it should be understood that even the things yet to be mentioned lead to union with Brahman only when accompanied by the qualities of the self. (8.15)
The Aṣṭakā, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, the Śrāvaṇī, the Āgrahāyaṇī, the Caitrī, and the Āśvayujī—these are the seven forms of the Pākayajña sacrifices. (8.16)

“The three dark fortnights following the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī—on each of these, one [rite] occurs; these are called the Aṣṭakās. The *pārvaṇa* (is the *sthālīpāka*) because it occurs on a *parvan* (lunar change). The *śrāddha* is called the *māsi-śrāddha*. By the word *śrāvaṇī*, the *upākaraṇa* is meant, because it is joined with the full moon of Śrāvaṇa. By the word *āgrahāyaṇī*, the *āgrahāyaṇa* is meant. By the word *caitrī*, the *śūlagava* is meant. By *āśvayujī*, the *indradhvaja-homa* is meant. The mention of “seven” is for the purpose of counting each one individually. The mention of “cooked food” (*pāka*) is for the purpose of connecting them with the *sthālīpāka*. The mention of “sacrifices” (*yajña*) is for the purpose of connecting them with the sacred fires (*agni*). “The *saṃsthās*” means they are properly established; the meaning is that they have been fully explained in the *Gṛhyasūtra* itself. (8.16)

The establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the fire-oblation (agnihotra), the new- and full-moon sacrifices (darśapaurṇamāsa), the first-fruits sacrifice (āgrayaṇa), the four-monthly sacrifices (cāturmāsya), the independent animal sacrifice (nirūḍhapaśubandha), and the Sautrāmaṇī—these are the seven forms of the havis-sacrifices. 8.17.

This is a restatement of rites well-known from the Śruti for the purpose of establishing their nature as purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*). Here, by the word *āgrayaṇa*, the *Āgrayaṇeṣṭi* sacrifice is meant, because the other [sacrifice of that name] has already been mentioned previously. By *agnyādheya*, the *Ādhāna* (the laying of the fires) is meant. The *Agnihotra* is a well-known *Haviryajña* (oblation sacrifice) in the Śruti. The *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, however, is counted as only one among the purificatory acts. The others are well known. The purpose of mentioning the number "seven" has already been stated; the same applies to the remainder. 8.17.
The Agniṣṭoma, the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśī, the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma—these are the seven forms of the Soma sacrifice. || 8.18 ||
The Sūtra is to be explained by the very same reasoning already stated. The separate mention of the *pākayajña* and other rites is for the purpose of making known that they have distinct results.
Thus, these are the forty formative forces (saṃskāra). || 8.19 ||

"Thus these"—this is the conclusion of what has been stated. "Forty" is for the purpose of restriction, meaning that there are exactly this many purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*). Consequently, one becomes endowed with the complete accomplishment of all Smārta and Śrauta rituals. 8.20.
Now, there are eight qualities of the self (ātman). 8.20.

The word "will be stated" (*vakṣyanti*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The word *atha* signifies "immediately following"; thus, the meaning is that the qualities of the self (*ātmaguṇāḥ*) will be stated immediately after the [eight] purificatory rites (*saṃskārāḥ*). Some maintain that the mention of "eight" is for the purpose of indicating that all these [qualities] are to be combined with the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*), and not taken according to their availability. That is incorrect, because it would result in the redundancy of the mention of "eight" in the passage: "But he who possesses even a portion of these purificatory rites, namely the eight qualities of the self... Therefore, the statement is for the sake of a technical designation (*saṃjñā*); its purpose is so that wherever the "eight qualities of the self" are mentioned, they may be understood as referring specifically to compassion (*dayā*) and the rest. The creation of this heavy technical term is for the purpose of ensuring that only when they are combined are they included. (8.20)
Compassion toward all beings, patience, freedom from envy, purity, lack of exertion, auspiciousness, lack of miserliness, and non-attachment. 8.21.

Compassion (*dayā*) is the thought of the welfare [of others]. Thus it is stated in the Purāṇa: "He who always conducts himself joyfully toward all beings as toward himself, for their auspiciousness and welfare—this indeed is remembered as complete compassion."
Because of the inclusion of the word "all," this applies even to stationary beings (*sthāvara*). Patience (*kṣānti*) is the endurance of external and internal dualities. As Vyāsa said:
"Whether reviled or even struck, one should not revile in return nor strike back;
being free from malice through speech, mind, and body—that is remembered as *titikṣā*, which is forbearance (*kṣamā*)."
Anasūyā is the absence of malice toward those who possess virtues. As it is said:
"The wise person should never feel hatred toward one who attains dharma, artha, kāma, or even mokṣa; this is remembered as anasūyā."
Purity (*śauca*) refers to the purity of objects and so forth. As Vyāsa has said:
"The seers who perceive reality have declared that purity is fourfold: purity of objects, purity of mind, purity of speech, and likewise purity of body."

Absence of exertion (*anāyāsa*) means not undertaking that which causes pain to oneself. As Vyāsa said: "If an action, though consistent with dharma, should cause constant and extreme pain to oneself, one should avoid it; that is called absence of exertion."
Auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is indeed that which is praiseworthy. As Vyāsa has said:
"The constant practice of what is praiseworthy and the avoidance of what is not praiseworthy—this is declared to be auspiciousness by the sages who perceive reality. Thus it is said.
Lack of meanness, lack of dejection even in adversity, and a delight in sharing—just as Vyāsa has said: "Even in the midst of terrible adversity, one should not become dejected toward anyone;
one should have a delight in sharing—that is called 'lack of meanness'."
Aspṛhā is contentment with objects that are not craved and the absence of longing for the property of others. As Vyāsa has said:
"A person should always avoid attachment to sense-objects and longing for the property of others; this is called *aspṛhā* by the wise. Thus it is stated.

The particle *iti* serves the purpose of indicating completion, signifying that "this much is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) to be performed for a person. The use of the non-compound form (*visamāsa*) is intended to indicate the distinctness of the results. As Vyāsa has said: "The patient man conquers the earth; the compassionate man enjoys happiness;
the man free from envy attains heaven; and through purity, he attains the supreme self (*adhyātma*)."
He is to be honored even more than auspiciousness in this world and the next;
through lack of effort and lack of meanness, he attains equality with the gods and absorption into primordial nature.

"One who is free from longing always obtains infinite happiness, as well as the station of Brahman through all the purificatory rites. Thus, even when nothing at all is obtained, one should accept whatever may be obtained, because the scripture declares that there is a distinct fruit for doing so. (8.21)
He who possesses these forty refinements but lacks the eight qualities of the self does not attain union with Brahman nor residence in the same world as Brahman. 8.22.

But for that person for whom these [qualities] exist—this reference to the *saṃskāras* (refinements) is for the sake of honoring the virtues. "Forty" is intended to indicate that even when combined, they lack the capacity [to lead to liberation]. Nor are there only eight personal virtues; because of the word "and" (*ca*), they are both taken collectively and individually. This too is a praise of the virtues. He does not attain union with or residence in the same world as Brahman. "Brahman" refers to a particular deity. "Union" (*sāyujya*) means oneness of self; "residence in the same world" (*sālokya*) means dwelling in the same abode. And this censure is solely for the purpose of praising the virtues. Because of its preeminence, union is taught first. (8.22)

But he for whom even a single portion of these conditioned factors consists of the eight qualities of the self, indeed attains union with Brahman and residence in the same world as Brahman; he attains it. 8.23.

The word *tu* expresses a distinction, meaning that by the mention of a single part, only the *upanayana* (initiation) is intended. The particle *khalu* is used for emphasis, meaning "he alone goes. From the word *api*, it is understood that all [the stages] go as well. From the word *atha*, it is understood that he goes immediately following [the initiation]. It should be observed that through connection with a single part one attains *sālokya* (residing in the same world), while through connection with all parts one attains *sāyujya* (union). This too is a praise of the qualities [of the rite]. 8.23
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Maskarīya-gautama-bhāṣya*.
The ninth chapter:

The observance of vows (*vratadhāraṇa*) has been described as being especially incumbent upon kings and Brahmins. Now, for the purpose of explaining the nature of these vows and for determining their duration, he says:

Having bathed according to the prescribed rule and having taken a wife, the Snātaka, while practicing the duties of a householder as they have been described, should observe these following vows. (9.1)

The word "he" (saḥ) is used for the purpose of referring individually to both the king and the Brahmin. "According to rule" (vidhipūrvam) means by the scriptural injunction; because of the inclusion of the word "preceded" (pūrva), this refers to [being endowed] with knowledge, with the vow, or with both. Otherwise, one would have to say simply "according to rule" (vidhivat). The mention of "having bathed" (snātvā), although already implied by the statement regarding the taking of a wife, is stated for the purpose of making it known that the "bath" (snāna) occurs only upon entering the householder stage of life (gṛhasthāśrama), and not upon entering any other stage of life. "Having taken a wife" (bhāryām adhigamya) means having performed the formal acquisition of a spouse.

Regarding this, some explain that after bathing, one must take a wife, because of the use of the suffix *ktvā* (indicating sequence), and because it is improper for one to remain without belonging to an āśrama.

That is incorrect, because immediate succession (ānantarya) is impossible; for the acquisition of a maiden depends on others, and because other Smṛtis prescribe a fixed time for marriage. As Uśanas says: "A man of thirty years should marry a maiden. Even in that case, since the matter is already established by the very injunction regarding the time for the ritual bath (snāna), it need not be stated; this is also evident from established practice. Indeed, no one is observed to perform a penance after the bath without having performed the marriage, nor is such a person censured by the learned (śiṣṭas). Furthermore, there are instructions to wait for the northern solstice (udagayana), the waxing fortnight, and an auspicious day (puṇyāha); and in the Code of Manu, the instruction to remain [in celibacy] applies to one who has not yet married, as in the verse: "One who seeks offspring, one who intends to sacrifice... (MDh 11.1). Moreover, in that same context, the phrase "for the sake of the teacher" (GDh 5.22) implies that [marriage] has already been mentioned. Grammarians maintain that the suffix -ktvā merely indicates priority in time. Even the mention of immediate succession is intended to prohibit the state of a householder for one who has not taken the bath; thus, marriage must be performed immediately after the bath.

As for what was said—that it is improper for one who does not belong to an āśrama to remain [without one]—to that it is replied: he is certainly not a non-āśramin. How so?
