Having completed his student life (brahmacarya) and bathed with the permission of his teacher, for as long a time as he acquires a wife through effort, during that period he is one who has undertaken the vows of a snātaka and whose student life remains unviolated; thus, he is indeed included within the householder stage itself. For this very reason, in the rule "The householder [takes] a suitable [wife]" (GDh 4.1), the term "householder" is employed even when the marriage has not yet been performed.

Nor is this state of residence for an indefinite period, because in another *Smṛti* there is a prescription for entering the stages of life (*āśrama*) within the division of the lifespan. As Manu says: "The fourth part of the lifespan," and so forth (MDh 4.1). And according to the example of the statement of Uśanas: "One who has completed forty years shall be a householder"; the statement of Vyāghra: "A *snātaka* should not remain [without marrying] for three years"; and the statement of Kaṇva: "[He should not remain] for three years. Since the division of the lifespan is difficult to ascertain, the fourth part of a hundred-year lifespan is taken [as the standard]. That too applies to one who studies a single Veda. As for what was said, "forty years," that refers to one who studies the three Vedas, provided he has already completed his learning. If he has not completed his learning, then for as long as it takes to complete it and perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*), after that time he should not remain without having taken a wife; thus, the residence is indeed for a fixed period. Therefore, this person is included within the stage of the householder. And consequently, [the verse continues:]

"A twice-born man should not remain without an āśrama even for a single day"—this statement by Dakṣa should be understood as referring to one who is not widowed (*vidhura*). In that context, the phrase "even for a single day" implies "if it is possible," because the acquisition of a maiden depends on others. Alternatively, [the rule] "one should not remain without an āśrama even for a single day" [applies generally].

The phrase "without making an effort" is to be understood as the ellipsis. In that regard, in the former position, there is fault for one who does not act when it is possible; in the absence of possibility, there is no fault. In the latter position, there is fault for one who does not make an effort.

One who practices the duties of a householder as they have been described should observe these vows as well. Although this is already established because they are mentioned in that very same context, their instruction here is for the purpose of including them within the *snātaka* vows, even though they were previously mentioned in the rule, "A householder [should marry] a suitable [woman]" (GDh 4.1). Therefore, even in the event of a transgression of these, one should observe the penance for the violation of *snātaka* vows prescribed in other Smṛtis. As Manu says:
"In this world, however, the penance for violating a *snātaka* vow is fasting" (MDh 11.203).

The inclusion of the phrase "as stated" (*yathokta*) is for the purpose of removing the doubt that some might think there are duties of the householder not mentioned here. Since those duties of the student (*brahmacārin*) which are governed by the rule, "And this applies to the subsequent ones provided it is not inconsistent with them" (GDh 3.10), would already be established by the mere inclusion of the word "stated," the inclusion of the phrase "as stated" is intended to include them as well, so that even in the case of their transgression, there may be the expiation for the breach of a *snātaka*’s vow.

But surely it should be stated, "having obtained a wife, one who practices the duties as they have been described," because it is only after the acquisition of a wife that one is authorized by the duties of a householder.

It is said: the mention of the "householder" (*gṛhastha*) is for the purpose of making known the distinctness between the duties of the householder and those of the *snātaka*. The duties of the householder have already been stated; the *snātaka* duties, which are about to be described, are distinct from them. Furthermore, this is for the purpose of establishing that the observance of the *snātaka* vows and the penance for their transgression apply as a rule only to kings and Brahmins, whereas for others, there is spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*) in performing them, but no sin (*pratyavāya*) or penance in failing to do so. Thus says another Smṛti: [The text continues with the citation of the Smṛti.]
"But when there is a lapse in the *snātaka* vows, an expiation is prescribed;
however, this applies only to kings and Brahmins, never to others.
Here too, the intended meaning is precisely this, because of the specific mention of "two who uphold the vows in the world" (GDh 8.1).

One should carry out these vows that are about to be described for as long as one lives; one should perform them as obligatory duties and not for the sake of rewards. The mention of "vows" (*vrata*) is for this purpose. Furthermore, the teaching regarding the reward—that "the *snātaka* never falls from the worlds of Brahman"—should be regarded as being like the teaching of rewards in the injunction, "One desiring heaven should conquer by means of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. The inclusion of the word "these" (*imāni*) is intended to dispel the doubt that the vows to be described are merely a subset of vows rather than distinct vows themselves. Once their performance as vows is established, the phrase "one should carry out" (*anukarṣet*) serves to indicate they must be performed throughout one's life. The inclusion of the term "*snātaka*" is for the sake of defining a technical designation: a householder who performs the vows about to be described is called a *snātaka*. Otherwise, since this would already be established by the rule, "Having bathed according to the prescribed rite," it need not have been stated here. (9.1)
What, then, are these? To this he says: "Always pure, having the habit of bathing with fragrant substances. (9.2)

The word "should be" (*syāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. "Constantly pure" means pure through ritual sipping (*ācamana*) and so forth; because of the inclusion of the word "constant," this applies even during a state of illness. "One whose habit is bathing with fragrant substances" refers to one whose nature it is to bathe with fragrant items such as *āmalaka* and the like. This is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to what was prohibited in the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*) in the rule: "Bathing and cleaning the teeth" (GDh 2.19). Because of the inclusion of the word "habit" (*śīla*), there is no fault if, due to impossibility, he bathes with water alone. The compound is irregular (*visamāsa*), intended to include those items which a *snātaka* must always wear. As Vasiṣṭha has said:

"For those who have completed their Vedic studies (snātakas), however, there are these obligatory items: an inner garment as well as an upper garment, two sacred threads, a staff, and a water-pot with water.

[VaDh 12.14] Because of the inclusion of the word "well" (*su*) in the phrase "one whose habit is bathing with fragrant substances," it follows that anointing with ointments must also be performed after bathing. 9.2.
If wealth were available, he would not be one whose clothes are like worn-out rags. || 9.3 ||
If another is available, one should not wear worn-out clothing, like soiled garments. (9.3)
One should not wear clothing that is dyed red, gaudy, or worn by another. 9.4.

"Red" means dyed with safflower and the like. "Excessive" means over-saturated; "not red" refers to that which has been worn by others, provided it is not the property of a teacher, since his leftovers are permitted [for use]. Because of the force of the separate commencement [of the compound], one should not wear it even in times of distress. The use of the non-compound (visamāsa) is for the purpose of excluding each [term] individually. 9.4.
Nor [should he wear] a garland or sandals. 9.5.

The garland (*sraj*) is distinguished by the previously mentioned qualifications; the sandals (*upānaha*) are dyed with lac and the like, but not with a decoction (*kaṣāya*). The commencement of two rules is for the purpose of precluding their application according to numerical order. || 9.5 ||
If [the husband] is incapable, she shall be released after being cleansed. || 9.6 ||
But in the absence of others, he should wear clothing and so forth that have been purified; "absence of others" refers to incapacity. (9.6)
One whose beard has grown should not [enter] suddenly. 9.7.

The mention of the beard (*śmaśru*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the nails and other parts as well. Because of the use of the term "grown" (*rūḍha*), there is no shaving; rather, it refers merely to arranging them so they are even. Thus Manu says: "With his hair, nails, and beard trimmed" (MDh 6.52). In that context, the trimming of the hair consists of removing impurities and making it smooth. As Uśanas says: "A *snātaka* should maintain his hair and so forth to be clean, smooth, and exceedingly fragrant. (9.7)
One should not carry fire and water at the same time. || 9.8 ||

“Simultaneously” means at one and the same time. The irregular compound (*visamāsa*) is for the purpose of connecting with the subsequent sūtra. The particle *ca* (and) serves to include food. As Vyāghra has said: “A Snātaka and likewise his wife should never carry water, fire, and food simultaneously. (9.8)
One should not drink from one's cupped hands. 9.9.

Water, because it is the subject under discussion. *Añjali* is the joining of two hands; therefore, there is no fault in using one hand. However, there is no prohibition regarding milk and the like. Some say that since there is no specific distinction made, one should not drink anything at all; for them, the purpose of the preceding sūtra’s composition must be sought. 9.9.
Nor while standing. 9.10.

And one should not drink while standing. Although the prohibition "while standing" was already established, this further prohibition is for the purpose of including milk and other such liquids as well. (9.10)
One should sip water from which the surface has been drawn up. 9.11.
The word *uddhṛtodaka* means "that by which water has been drawn up"; by this term, a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) is denoted, and with it one should sip water (*ācāmet*). 9.11.
Nor with food offered by a Śūdra, nor that which is impure, nor that which is offered with only one hand. || 9.12 ||

One should not sip water with a person of the Śūdra caste; nor even with one who is not of the Śūdra caste if he is impure; nor even with one who is pure and not of the Śūdra caste if he uses only one hand. By this prohibition of what would otherwise be permissible, [the author] indicates that there is no absolute rule for the preceding Sūtra. Consequently, an option is to be understood: one may sip water from a *kamaṇḍalu*, or from [the hands of] one who is not a Śūdra and is pure, or from [the hands of] one who has discarded both hands. And thus, since there is no rule that sipping must be done exclusively from a *kamaṇḍalu*, it indicates that the carrying of it is also not mandatory, because the carrying of it is solely for the purpose of sipping water. (9.12)
Nor should he discard urine, feces, or other impurities while facing the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, deities, or cows. (9.13)

One should not discharge urine and so forth while facing the wind and other such directions; nor should one do so even when not facing them, provided one is looking at them. By the word "deities," their images in the form of paintings and the like are meant. Although the mention of "deities" alone would suffice to include the wind and others, their explicit inclusion is for the sake of further specification. Consequently, there is no fault in seeing the moon, eclipses, constellations, and so on. From the word "ca" (and), it follows that one should not perform these acts even while recollecting them. Because urine and feces are impure, the term "impure" is repeated for the purpose of specifying particular types of impurity. From this, it should be understood that one must also not discharge semen and similar substances. 9.13.
One should not stretch out one's feet toward these deities. || 9.14 ||

The mention of "deity" again is for the purpose of indicating that cows and Brahmins are deities. Regarding the dual number in the word "pādau" (feet), it is not intended to be significant; one should not extend even a single foot, much less both. 9.14.
One should not remove urine or feces with leaves, clods of earth, or stones. 9.15.
By the word "loṣṭa," clay is meant; from that, one should effect its removal by other means. 9.15.
One should not stand upon ashes, hair, chaff, potsherds, or impure things. 9.16.
One should not step upon ashes and the like; [specifically] human hair, fragments of broken vessels such as skulls, and impure substances such as urine. (9.16)
One should not converse with barbarians, the impure, or those who are unrighteous. 9.17.

"Mlecchas" refers to the Persians and others; "impure ones" refers even to Aryans [who are so]; and "unrighteous ones" refers to those who have fallen from their status and the like. One should not deliberate with them. Although the state of being together is already established by the use of the third case ending itself, the word "saha" (with) is employed for the sake of emphasis. Consequently, one should not converse with such a person after having entered into a common purpose with him; however, there is no fault in asking for directions on the road and similar matters. 9.17.
Having conversed with those who have performed meritorious deeds, one should meditate upon them in the mind.

But if, out of ignorance or due to necessity, he should converse with them, then he should mentally contemplate many virtuous doers of good deeds—many being indicated by the use of the plural number. The mention of "mind" is for the purpose of recollection through the visualization of their individual features. 9.18.
Or he may converse with a Brāhmaṇa. 9.19.

Only one who has performed meritorious deeds is a Brāhmaṇa. Because of the inclusion of the word "together," it is understood that if a Brāhmaṇa should speak [thus], it is for the purpose of immediate performance; or else, this prescription of penance outside of the specific context is for the sake of brevity. (9.19)
One should say of a non-cow, "She is a cow that will become one. || 9.20 ||

A "non-cow" is a barren cow; one might designate her as "one who is to become a cow" (*dhenubhavyā*). The particle *iti* is used for the purpose of excluding other such forms, so that there may not be the designation of others of this kind. This is precisely the purpose of all instances of *iti*, even those to be mentioned hereafter. (9.20)
"An inauspicious thing as auspicious. || 9.21 ||
"Unfortunate" means not to be approached because of its lack of splendor or its inauspiciousness; one would call that "fortunate," just as one might call the unfortunate "fortunate. 9.21.
"A skull is a *bhagāla*. || 9.22 ||
One should call a skull (kapāla) a fragment of a broken vessel (bhinnabhāṇḍāvayava), that is, a skull-bone (bhagāla). || 9.22 ||
The "jewel-bow" (maṇidhanus) refers to the rainbow. || 9.23 ||
One should call it either "Indra’s bow" or "the jeweled bow. By virtue of the authority of the scriptural statement, these alone are its designations. 9.23.
One should not point out to another a cow that is suckling. 9.24.
One should not point out to another a cow that is suckling; because of the mention of "another," one may point out one's own. 9.24.
And one should not prevent her. || 9.25 ||
The word "enām" (her) refers specifically to another's wife; by the use of the particle "ca," it is also understood to include women who are under confinement and so forth. 9.25.
Having engaged in sexual union, he should not delay regarding purification. 9.26.

Having united with a woman and enjoyed her, one should not delay regarding purification; the meaning is that one should perform purification immediately. Because of the prefix *vi-*, one may even delay for as long as the pleasure does not cease. The delay in purification does not apply only to the matter of sexual intercourse; rather, the inclusion of the word *prati* is for the purpose of indicating that no delay should be made even regarding urine, feces, and so forth. But is this not already established by the rule, "He is always pure" (GDh 9.2)?

To this it is replied: here, by the word *śauca* (purity), the mere removal of impurities is meant; the purpose of the commencement of the Sūtra is that when water suitable for sipping (*ācamana*) is unavailable, the removal of its stains must be performed by whatever means possible. And thus, the meaning of the rule "he shall be constantly pure" (GDh 9.2) is obtained as "he shall be constantly pure whenever possible. Consequently, there is no fault in being impure when such [means] are unavailable. || 9.20 ||
And one should not recite the Veda on that bed. 9.27.

One should not study the Veda from the acquisition of its recitation on that bed upon which sexual intercourse has been practiced; and because of the word "ca" (and), one should not seat those worthy of honor there either. 9.27.
And having studied during the latter part of the night, he should not go back to sleep again. 9.28.

Having studied during the latter part of the night, he should not sleep again. By the inclusion of the word "again," there is no prohibition against sleeping before that time. By the mention of the "latter part of the night," there is no fault in sleeping during the first part of the night. And just as he previously lay down for the purpose of study, so he should not lie down again even for the sake of rest; such is the meaning of the repetition. (9.28)
One should not take pleasure in an unvirtuous woman. || 9.29 ||

One should not take pleasure with a woman who is unwell, whose body is unadorned, or who is indisposed; for the word *abhī* signifies approaching [her]. Therefore, there is no prohibition against play intended for diversion. 9.29.
Nor one who is menstruating. || 9.30 ||
And one should not approach a woman in her courses.
Now, it might be argued that the prohibition is already established by the injunction of penance, namely: "For approaching a woman in her courses, there is a three-night [penance]" (GDh 23.35).

It is replied: because another Smṛti text states, "A menstruating woman remains impure for three nights," the penance mentioned refers to intercourse occurring within those three nights. Here, however, the prohibition applies after [the first three days], while the menstrual flow has not yet ceased.

Others, however, say that a woman is *rajasvalā* (menstruating) when blood appears at an improper time. That is incorrect, because the term *rajas* applies only to blood appearing at the proper time, and because only that [blood] causes impurity. Thus, another Smṛti states: "The wise say that whatever blood occurs for women at an improper time..."
"But that [blood] which occurs at the proper time is declared to be *rajas*; therefore, she is impure only during that [period]. Likewise, there is also the statement of Bhārgava:
"One should designate as pure that which occurs for women outside of the [menstrual] period."
"One should know that to be impure which occurs month after month.
Likewise, Vasiṣṭha says:
"Women are an incomparable purifier; they are never defiled."

"For indeed, their monthly flow carries away their sins" (VaDh 28.4). And likewise the Śruti says: "This very sin of killing an embryo manifests itself month after month. Therefore, the prohibition applies from after the three nights. Thus, even beyond the three nights, as long as the menstrual flow has not ceased, she remains impure. And so Manu says:
"When her menses have ceased, a menstruating woman becomes pure by bathing" (MDh 5.65).

In that case, after three nights have passed, she remains fit for touch even if her flow has not yet ceased; for the injunction to bathe on the fourth day—"the menstruating woman shall bathe"—is intended for the purpose of touching. Although the rule regarding the menstruating woman is already established [by the previous verse], this separate commencement is for the sake of what follows. (9.30)
And he should not embrace her. 9.31.

The phrase "this woman" (*enām*) is intended to include a woman who has become menstruating within the three-night period. This is precisely the purpose of the separate injunction, "not one who is menstruating" (GDh 9.30). Thus, even if the embracing continues after the three nights have passed, there is no fault.

Now, one might object: since touching is prohibited by the rule beginning with "an outcaste, a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or a corpse" (GDh 14.29), the prohibition of embracing is established by implication as well.

To this it is replied: the undertaking [of the ritual] is for the purpose of entering into the penance for the violation of the *snātaka* vows once the embrace has been performed. The word "and" (*ca*) serves the purpose of conjunction, meaning "her and that which is unchaste. (9.31)
Not a maiden. || 9.32 ||

One should not embrace a maiden who has not been married, even if she was obtained with the pouring of water (*udakapūrva*). Although this is already established by the term "maiden" (*kanyā*), the separate formulation of this rule is for the purpose of indicating that there is no fault in embracing her with pure intent (*aduṣṭabhāvena*). Thus, the defilement of a maiden occurs solely through an embrace performed with corrupt intent (*duṣṭabhāvena*). Accordingly, it is logical that in the *paiśāca* form of marriage, what is expressed by the word "union" (*saṃgamana*) is precisely such an embrace. In this regard, is he subject to the penance for defiling a maiden, or rather to the penance for the transgression of a *snātaka*’s vow?

To this it is replied: the qualification for the rite is obtained solely through the expiation for the breach of a *snātaka* vow, not through the expiation for sexual intercourse with a maiden, because another *smṛti* begins with the words "the emission of semen. As Manu says:
"The emission of semen among one's own female relatives, among virgins, and among women of the lowest castes...
Blowing on fire with the mouth, engaging in contentious speech, wearing external perfumes and garlands, scraping oneself with a vile object, eating together with one's wife,
looking at collyrium, entering by a side door, and sitting on a wooden stool while washing one's feet.
One should avoid swimming across many rivers, climbing or descending trees that are difficult to traverse, and exerting oneself to the point of risking one's life. 9.33.

Blowing on fire with the mouth means fanning the fire by means of the mouth. Quarreling means a worldly verbal dispute; since the form of idle chatter (*jalpa*) has already been established in the section concerning the religious student (*brahmacārin*), it is not repeated here. Wearing perfumes and garlands outdoors means wearing scentless garlands; likewise, another *smṛti* states: "One should not wear a fragranceless garland, except for one made of gold. Scratching with something inferior means scratching the head or other parts of the body with wood or other impure substances. Eating together with one's wife means consuming food from the same vessel as her. Since the prohibition is applicable because of the scriptural statement—"The wife is indeed half of one's own self"—this rule serves as a restriction rather than a permission to eat with someone other than one's wife, as other *smṛtis* prohibit eating the remnants of women and *śūdras* in general. Looking at the application of ointments means looking at one's wife while using substances such as oil for anointing the body. Entering through a side door means entering a house or similar place through an unestablished or improper entrance. Washing one foot with the other means scrubbing one foot with the other. Eating while seated on a chair means consuming food placed upon a support such as a stool or bench. Crossing a river by swimming means crossing to the other side by means of one's arms; the mention of "river" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes ponds and other bodies of water. Climbing a tree and descending into a pit or other uneven places means going down into them. Exertion involving the vital breaths means obstructing the breath through jumping and similar activities. One should avoid these. (9.33)
One should not board a boat that is doubtful of its safety. 9.34.

One should not board a boat that is unsteady because it is afflicted by the fault of excessive loading for the purpose of crossing to the other side; nor, due to the force of the prefix *adhi*, should one even step upon it, as it serves no purpose. 9.34.
Having stated several dharmas that serve as means for protecting the body, [the author] now says: "One should protect oneself from all sides. (9.35)

One should protect the body from all calamities—for instance, as in: "One should not set out on a journey alone" (MDh 4.60), "Nor with a woman as a companion," and so forth. By the use of the word "all," this includes even those things prohibited by rule. By the use of the word "even" (*eva*), it includes [protection] through the pacification of planetary influences (*graha-śānti*) and other such means. By the word "self" (*ātman*), the body is meant; the meaning is that one must act so as to protect it so that it does not perish. Although time alone is the destroyer, the intention is that because the duration of life is difficult to discern, one should not be devoid of human effort. Likewise, there is the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*).
"Knowledge of lifespan, knowledge of age, and the characteristics of pregnant women—even the sages are bewildered by these, how much more so those with only the eye of flesh?

Some explain it otherwise: "By all means one should protect the Supreme Self; one should strive for victory," because verbal roots have multiple meanings. And thus says the Śruti: "The Self is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).

Others, however, say that by the word "self" (ātman), four types are expressed: the Supreme Self (paramātman), the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the individual self (jīvātman), and the elemental self (bhūtātman). As Manu says:
"That which causes this self to act is called the Knower of the Field;
but that which performs actions is called the elemental self by the wise."
The inner self known as the *jīva* is innate to all embodied beings;
it is by means of this that one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout births.
[MDh 12.12–13] It is the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtle.
"One should know that supreme Person, who has the luster of gold and is accessible through the intellect in a state of dream" (MDh 12.122).
Thus ends verse 9.35.
One should not wander about during the day with one's head covered.

Having covered his head with a cloth or similar garment, he should not walk about on all sides during the day; he may even go through a narrow space, because of the use of the word "pari" (all around). In that case, there is no fault for the purpose of avoiding a headache, since it has been stated: "One should protect oneself from everything" [GDh 9.35]. || 9.36 ||
But having covered [it] at night. || 9.37 ||

This undertaking is for the sake of a restriction, even though the meaning is already established: one should go only after having covered oneself, even if it provides little room [for the garment]. || 9.37 ||
And also in the case of urine and excrement. 9.38.
The word "should do" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Because of the word "and" (ca), it means specifically "having covered [the head]. 9.38.
Furthermore: during the day, he should perform [the rite] facing north. (9.39)

If he performs it during the day, he should face north. This indicates that the rule is not universally mandatory in certain circumstances, because of the prohibition against facing the wind, fire, Brahmins, the sun, water, deities, or cows (GDh 9.13). For if this were an absolute injunction, then facing the sun would never be possible. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "In shade or in darkness, and when there is danger to life, one may perform it facing whichever direction is comfortable; such is the settled law."

It should be understood that the sūtra beginning with "not toward wind or fire" (GDh 9.13) was composed with the intention that even when facing shadows and the like, one must avoid facing the sun and other such objects. 9.39.
And during the two twilights. 9.40.
The word "ca" (and) is used for the purpose of drawing in [the requirement] of facing north. || 9.40 ||
But at night, however, he should face the south. || 9.41 ||
The word *tu* has the sense of the word *ca*; it also serves to carry over the verb "he should do" (*kuryāt*). (9.41)
Not without having vanished from the ground. || 9.42 ||

With grass unfit for sacrifice. And so another Smṛti states: "Having covered the ground with grass that is not a constituent part of a sacrifice, one should void urine and excrement. Because of the mention of "ground," there is no fault in using bricks and the like. 9.42.
Nor while standing. || 9.43 ||
And while standing, one should not discharge urine or feces. 9.43.
And from a human habitation. 9.44.
One should not do it near a house; because of the word "and" (ca), [it also means] not near a temple, an assembly hall, or the like. 9.44.
Nor [should one study] in places covered with ashes or cow-dung, in ploughed fields, or on paths frequented by travelers. 9.45.

One should not perform [the voiding of urine or excrement] even upon ashes and the like that are distant from one's home. "Shadow" refers to a shadow that provides sustenance. "Karīṣa" means cow-dung. "Kāmya" refers to a desirable place, such as a marketplace and the like. The use of the plural in "kāmyeṣu" is for the purpose of including other locations taught in other Smṛtis. As Vasiṣṭha says: "One should not urinate in a river, nor on a path, nor in ashes; nor in cow-dung, nor in a ploughed field, nor in a sown field, nor in grassy areas or in shadows that provide sustenance. (VaDh 6.12)
Thus [ends verse] 9.45.
One should avoid a seat made of palāśa wood, as well as sandals and a tooth-stick made of the same.

One should not make a seat or the like out of *pālāśa* wood. By the use of the particle "iti," other items of this same nature, such as a chariot and so forth, are included; and because of the non-compound construction (*visamāsa*), a bed is also excluded. From the word "ca" (and), household implements such as a ladle and the like are understood. Thus, another *smṛti* states: "One should avoid a seat, a bed, a vehicle, and household implements made of *pālāśa*; likewise, one should avoid sandals and a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa*."
Thus [ends the verse] 9.46.
And wearing shoes, one should avoid eating, sitting, saluting, or bowing down. 9.47.
One should avoid eating, sitting, saluting, or prostrating before deities while wearing shoes; by the word "and" (ca), it is also implied that one should not do so while standing on sandals. 9.47.
One should not let the forenoon, midday, or afternoon pass fruitlessly; according to one's ability, one should devote them to dharma, artha, and kāma. 9.48.

One should not fail to occupy oneself with dharma and the other [ends] during the divisions of the day, such as the forenoon and so forth, according to one's capacity and in their respective order. Although it would have been sufficient to say "one should act according to one's ability," the inclusion of the term *yathā* (according to) is intended to indicate that these may be practiced even in combination. Furthermore, because of the use of the dative case (*dharmādibhyaḥ*), it should be understood that one acts "with" dharma and the others. In this regard, one should perform recitation (*japa*) and the like in the forenoon as far as possible; in the midday, the means for acquiring wealth; and in the afternoon, the enjoyment of perfumes, garlands, and so forth. 9.48.
But among them, Dharmottara would be the most excellent. || 9.49 ||

Among these—dharma, artha, and kāma—one should make dharma the primary concern. The intention is that even when the pursuit of the other two is impossible, dharma must be practiced as a rule. The word "tu" (but/however) implies that one should perform all three duties while remaining bound to dharma. 9.49
One should not engage in the restlessness of the genitals, the stomach, the hands, the feet, the speech, or the eyes. 9.50.

The term *cāpala* (restlessness) is connected with each [of the following]. Restlessness of the genitals is the desire for sexual intercourse at an improper time. Restlessness of the belly is the longing for various flavors. Restlessness of the hands is the longing to learn artistic crafts. Restlessness of the feet is wandering about aimlessly. Restlessness of speech is speaking of dharma and other matters when unasked, or when asked improperly. Thus says Manu: "One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks improperly" [MDh 2.110].
Restlessness of the eyes is an insatiable desire to see.
But is this not a partial redundancy with the rule, "Restrained in speech, arms, and belly" (GDh 2.28)?

This is not so; for in that context, being restrained in speech refers to the absence of incoherent chatter, being restrained in arms refers to the absence of actions such as clod-battering, and being restrained in belly refers to the absence of eating in excess or unwholesome food. || 9.50 ||
One should not, without cause, perform cutting, splitting, scratching, rubbing, or tearing. 9.51.

Cutting grass and the like; breaking [clay] pots and the like; scratching walls, the ground, and so forth with the nails and such; crushing clods of earth and the like by rubbing them together; and cracking the joints of fingers and the like—these one should not perform without a specific reason. Since it is already established in the section on the student (*brahmacārin*) that his arms must be restrained, this is for the purpose of permitting these actions when there is a valid cause. 9.51.
One should not pass over a rope to which a calf is tied. 9.52.
The rope with which a calf is tied is called the *vatsatantrī*. One should not pass over it by stepping upon it. The word "calf" (*vatsa*) is an elliptical expression for the bovine species. (9.52)
He would not be one who goes from family to family. || 9.53 ||

The meaning is that he should not go from house to house; or rather, he should not go from one house to another without a specific reason. Or, he is "kulamkula" because he belongs to one family [only]; the meaning is that even though he has the authority to practice dharma, he should not remain within his paternal family alone. (9.53)
One who has not been invited should not go to a sacrifice. || 9.54 ||
One should not go to a sacrifice unless invited. 9.54.
But for the sake of seeing him, however, [I shall go]. 9.55.

"Kāmam" means "not necessarily"; even so, for one who goes [to see her], lightness of heart (lāghava) is inevitable. The word "tu" (but/however) is for the purpose of restriction, indicating that it is solely for the purpose of seeing her and not even for the purpose of eating. 9.55.
One should not eat food from one's lap. 9.56.
Edibles such as *pṛthuka* (flattened rice) and others—those which one is habituated to eating while holding in the lap—one should not eat after placing them upon the lap. 9.56.
Nor [should he eat] what has been brought by a servant at night. 9.57.

One should not eat anything brought at night by a servant, such as a Śūdra or others. Why is this so? Because, while the subject under discussion is "foods" (bhakṣān), there is a singular indication [of the agent]. There is no prohibition, however, regarding what is brought during the day. 9.57.
One should not eat oil-cakes from which the oil has been extracted, molasses, oil-cakes, buttermilk, and the like, once their potency has been removed. 9.58.

Curdled milk (*dadhi*) and the like from which the cream has been removed and the surface-scum (*maṇḍa*) taken off; *vilayana* is that produced from clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and the like; oil-cake (*piṇyāka*) from which the essence has been extracted, because there is no fault in the other kind. And thus says the explanatory scripture (*arthavāda*): "On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, they should give oil-cake from which the essence has not been extracted. Churned buttermilk (*mathita-takra*), that too from which the butter has been removed, because there is no fault in the other kind. And thus says the *Gṛhya-smṛti*: "Having churned curd, one should eat it before the butter has been extracted. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), items such as *kīlāṭa* and *kucaka* are included. The particle *ca* is for the purpose of drawing in the [prohibition of] night [meals]. One should not eat these at night.

Alternatively—the term *uddhṛtasneha* (from which the oil has been extracted) is connected with each [item]. That is, one should not eat that which has had its oil extracted: namely, melted butter (*vilayana*), oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), and those things beginning with churned milk (*mathita*). By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*prabhṛti*), curd and milk are meant. Their state of having had the oil extracted consists in having the surface-scum (*maṇḍa*) removed. Although the rule "one should not eat things from which the oil has been extracted" would already suffice, the specific mention of melted butter and the others is for the purpose of permitting other items from which the oil has been extracted, such as mango fruits, molasses, and so forth. These one should not eat at night; there is no fault in eating them during the day.

"Having taken their strength" (*āttavīryāṇi*): by the word "strength" (*vīrya*), the essential sap is meant. That in which this has been taken is called "having taken its strength," such as the skin of the plantain fruit and so forth. It is mentioned separately because it is commenced [as a rule] even for the daytime. Now, one might object: "Should this not have been stated in the very section concerning the eating of forbidden food? To this it is replied: [It is mentioned here] so that in the event of such a transgression, there would be the expiation for the violation of a *snātaka*'s vow, and not the expiation for eating forbidden food. Furthermore, the separate commencement [of this rule] regarding "even those brought by one who is not sent" and "not at night" applies specifically to substances like alkaline salts (*vilayana*) and the like. (9.58)
In the evening and in the morning, however, he should eat food that has been honored, without finding fault with it.
This undertaking is for the purpose of prohibiting eating in between [the two prescribed meals], since it is already established by implication. And so Manu says:
"For the twice-born, eating in the evening and in the morning is enjoined by the Śruti;
one should not eat in between. This rule is equal to the Agnihotra."

The word *tu* expresses a distinction; it indicates that the prohibition applies to specific types of food, and not to sweetmeats (*modaka*) and the like. "Honored" means accompanied by a salutation. By the use of the prefix *abhi*, he shows that it must be performed with a mantra. Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "One should honor the meals with the words 'It is pleasing' in the evening and in the morning" [VaDh 3.69]. One should eat without disparaging, that is, without censuring it for defects such as being poor quality food. 9.59.
One should never sleep naked at night. 9.60.

[The rule] may apply even at times other than [the night]. The mention of "night" (*rātri*) is for the purpose of restriction, meaning "only at night. If daytime were also intended, then by saying "one should never sleep naked," everything would be established; consequently, there would be no fault during the day. Furthermore, by this [mention of night], he also makes known that there is no prohibition against sleeping during the day for him. Otherwise, if it were said "one should never sleep naked" even then, since sleeping during the day would be obtained by implication through the very prohibition of daytime sleep, the mention of "night" would be redundant on account of the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). Thus, [it applies] only at night. (9.60)
Or he may bathe. 9.61.

Because it is begun separately, this applies even during the day; by the word "or" (vā), descending into water is also included. And so says another Smṛti: "One should not enter the water naked. 9.61.
Now, because conduct is infinite and impossible to describe in its entirety, he speaks concisely:
"And whatever those who possess self-control, the elders, the well-disciplined, those free from hypocrisy, greed, and delusion, and the knowers of the Vedas declare—that one should practice. (9.62)

The word *ca* (and) has the sense of the word *tu* (but); that too expresses a distinction, namely, "with reference to what is unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). "Possessed of self" (*ātmavantaḥ*) means those who are devoted to the combination of knowledge and action. "Elderly" (*vṛddhāḥ*) means those whose knowledge of reality is established in the Vedas. "Well-disciplined" (*samyagvinītāḥ*) means those whose conduct has been well-trained by their teachers. "Hypocrisy" (*dambha*) is the practice of dharma for the sake of pleasing the world. "Greed" (*lobha*) is the desire to obtain another's property through unjust means. "Delusion" (*moha*) is knowledge contrary to worldly consensus; they are "free from these," meaning unpermeated by them. "Knowers of the Veda" (*vedavidaḥ*) are those who have studied the entirety of the Vedas. That which they declare with reference to an unseen purpose—for example, "Give fodder to my cows"—is [unseen]. An "seen purpose" (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) is, for example, "Having given fodder to my cows, take an *āḍhaka* measure [in return]. All of that, he should perform "without guile" (*amāyayā*). Since the relationship between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat* is constant, the mention of the word *tat* is established simply by the inclusion of the word *yat*; nevertheless, the reference is made again by the word *tat*. He should "practice" (*ācaret*), i.e., perform it, having become composed, as indicated by the use of the prefix *sam-*. The irregular compound implies that even in the absence of the possession of all qualities, it must be performed when there is a possession of two or three qualities. One should not consider his purpose fulfilled merely by enjoining one person, but rather only by enjoining many; thus the plural number is used. If such a person enjoins this himself, then that alone should be done, and not the enjoining of another person. Regarding what should have been said as "they say" (*vadanti*), the use of the term "they declare" (*ācakṣate*)—due to the formation of a heavy aphorism—implies that it must be performed repeatedly until death. Regarding what should have been said as "it should be done" (*kartavyam*), the use of the verb "he should practice" (*ācaret*) indicates the beginning. Whether combined or separate, whether concerning a single object or various objects, whatever injunction is to be performed, that entire thing must indeed be performed. This is because, instead of saying "the word of those possessed of self, elderly, well-disciplined, free from hypocrisy, greed, and delusion, and knowers of the Veda should be followed," it is expressed in this specific manner. 9.62
One should approach the Lord for the sake of security and well-being. 9.63.

Yoga is the acquisition of what has not been obtained; kṣema is the preservation of what has been acquired. The word *artha* denotes purpose; thus, it means "the purpose of yoga and kṣema. By the word *īśvara*, the king is meant. One should go to him, and not out of wretchedness, because of the use of the prefix *adhi*. (9.63)
Except for gods, teachers, and those who follow the Dharma. || 9.64 ||

Another is incapable of performing both. By beginning with the prohibition of those who have not previously approached [the king], he makes it known that one must seek out someone other than the king who is capable of performing both. "With the exception of others" refers to deities, images, teachers, parents and the like, and righteous persons—those whose nature is the practice of the combination of knowledge and action—because approaching them serves a transcendental purpose (adṛṣṭārtha).

One should strive to dwell in a residence that has abundant firewood, water, fodder, kusha grass, and garlands; one from which people may easily exit, where noble persons abound, which is free from laziness and well-provided for, and which is presided over by righteous people.

One should make a supreme effort to resort to a place that has abundant wood, water, grass, *darbha* grass, and flowers, and is pleasant for going out; one where the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas are numerous; one crowded with people whose nature is devoted to religious practice (*anuṣṭhāna*); and one protected by a king who conducts himself according to justice. The use of the non-compound form implies that even if all these qualities are not present together, one may dwell wherever such qualities are found as they occur. For in such a place alone will there be what is sufficient for both dharma and delight. (9.65)
One should circumambulate clockwise such places as those praised by the virtuous, auspicious objects, temples, and crossroads. || 9.66 ||

One should pass by keeping to the right those things that are praiseworthy, such as cows, Brahmins, well-known trees, and so forth; auspicious objects, such as curds, clarified butter, and full jars; a temple, which is the abode of a deity; and a crossroads, which is well known. One should go around these keeping them to the right (pradakṣiṇa), not to the left (apasavya), so that as one passes, they are traversed with the right side toward them. Since the text begins with the word "āvarteta" (one should turn around) rather than saying "kuryāt" (one should do), it implies that one should perform a circumambulation for each individual object, rather than merely passing by them. (9.66)
Or, as an alternative for times of distress, he may observe that entire code of conduct mentally.
If, however, due to haste one does not perform the circumambulation, then some explain that one should accomplish it by means of mental visualization alone.

That is incorrect, because [the meaning] is already obtained by the phrase "or one should protect it with the mind" alone. Therefore, [the interpretation is as follows]: from the inclusion of the word *tat* ("that"), the word *yat* ("which") must be supplied; that which was stated as the collection of practices beginning with "always pure"—all of that in its entirety. The inclusion of the word *samagra* ("entirety") is so that it may not be restricted to what immediately precedes it. The mention of "practice" (*ācāra*) is so that the duties of a householder (*gṛhasthadharma*) might not also be included—[in this context] "one should protect" means "one should contemplate. *Āpatkalpa* is the rule for times of distress. Distress (*āpad*) is so called because, due to urgency, the performance of the [usual] ritual action is impossible.

If it is argued that this meaning is already obtained by the word "vā" (or) itself in the sense of an alternative when something is absent, and thus the mention of the "emergency rule" (*āpatkalpa*) is redundant, we say no. The mention of the emergency rule is for the purpose of showing that from the performance of duties prescribed for emergencies there arises merely the absence of the fault of non-performance, and not spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*) as well. Its inclusion here, rather than at the end of the chapter, is for the sake of excluding what will be mentioned later, such as "one whose nature is truth and who acts like an Ārya" (GDh 9.68). 9.67.
One whose conduct is noble and whose nature is truth and righteousness. || 9.68 ||

He is one whose conduct is both true and noble; thus he is "one of true dharma and noble conduct" (*satyadharmāryavṛtta*). He is "of true dharma" (*satyadharman*) because he is faithful to his word; the meaning is that he does exactly what he says or intends. He is "of noble conduct" (*āryavṛtta*) because his conduct—consisting of pleasant speech and the like—is such that he becomes dear to the noble ones (*ārya*), that is, to the virtuous. (9.68)
He should be a teacher of the cultured, purified by cleanliness, and devoted to the sacred revelation.

A teacher of the learned is one who instructs the virtuous, but not the unworthy; he is purified by water and other means and is devoted to that. Although it is established by the rule, "He is always pure; having engaged in sexual intercourse, he should not delay in purification" (GDh 9.2, 26), the rule "or mentally" (GDh 9.67) is taught again as a reiteration of purification so that there may be no entry into the provisions for times of distress. He is intent on the Śruti, meaning he is devoted to the study of the Vedas. The mention of *Śruti* is for the purpose of excluding Manu and others. 9.69.
Always non-violent, gentle, firm in action, and characterized by self-control and generosity.

Because of the inclusion of the word "constant" (*nitya*), he is non-violent (*ahiṃsra*) even when a cause for harm exists, being by nature one who avoids injuring living beings. He is gentle (*mṛdu*), meaning he is disposed toward reconciliation even in the face of offenses. He is firm in action (*dṛḍhakārī*), meaning he is one who completes what has been begun, or one who undertakes actions only after due reflection. He is self-controlled (*damaśīla*), meaning he is one who restrains his senses from excessive attachment to their respective objects. He is generous (*dānaśīla*), meaning he delights in sharing even when his wealth is meager. The use of the irregular compound (visamāsa) is intended to indicate that one achieves the goal even through the performance of these virtues according to one's capacity, should they all not be possible. (9.70)
A Snātaka who conducts himself in this manner, seeking to liberate his parents and his ancestors and descendants from misfortunes, never falls from the worlds of Brahman; he never falls. 9.71.

"One who has such conduct and such actions is a *snātaka*": this is the connection with the word supplied from earlier. The repetition of what has already been introduced is for the purpose of making known that this is the fruit of the *snātaka*-vows. If it is argued that the term "parents" (*mātāpitarau*) should result in a *ekaśeṣa* compound (meaning "the father together with the mother"), we say no; for both are his parents, and they are intended to be grasped here—namely, the teacher and the progenitor. "Former relations" refers to paternal grandfathers and so on; "latter relations" refers to maternal grandfathers and so on. Desiring to liberate these from sins, he indeed liberates them, and he himself does not depart from the worlds of Brahman. The mention of "conduct" (*ācāra*) is for the sake of including the fruits of all the duties of a *snātaka*, lest it be thought that [only] the rule "he should always be pure" and so forth were meant. The inclusion of the word "constantly" (*śaśvat*) is for the purpose of excluding a merely relative permanence. The double statement is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter. (9.71)
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Maskarīya-gautama-bhāṣya*.
The tenth chapter:
For the twice-born, study, sacrifice, and giving. 10.1.

*Adhyayana* (study) consists of the acquisition, retention, practice, and recitation (*japa*) of the Veda. *Ijyā* (sacrifice) is the performance of ritual offerings (*yāga*) and the worship of gods and ancestors. *Dāna* (charity) is the distribution of wealth to those who ask according to one’s capacity. The use of separate words (*asamāsa*) is for the purpose of indicating a conjunction (*samuccaya*), so that they might not be understood as applying to the twice-born (*dvijāti*) classes respectively. If it is argued that this is already understood from the inclusion of the word "moreover" (*adhika*), there is no fault; rather, it is intended to make known the predominance of each specific duty for each individual. For example: study is the primary duty of the Brāhmaṇa, as Manu has said.

"A Brāhmaṇa shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter" (MDh 2.87), and so forth. For the Kṣatriya, sacrifice is prescribed; thus it is said: "The king shall sacrifice with rituals" (MDh 7.79). For the Vaiśya, giving is prescribed; and thus it is said:
"And he should diligently give food even to all living beings" (MDh 9.333).
The use of the non-compound form (visamāsa) is also intended to indicate that each preceding [act] is more powerful than the one following it. As Uśanas said:
"Sacrifice is a hundred times more effective than giving; recitation is a hundred times more effective than sacrifice.
Likewise, Manu also demonstrated the superiority of recitation over sacrifice.
"The four *pākayajñas*, together with the *vidhiyajñas*—all these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*). [MDh 2.86].

Here, since for the twice-born, study, sacrifice, and giving are prescribed only after the initiation (*upanayana*), it should be understood that any gift given by one who is uninitiated is ineffective. 10.1.
For the Brāhmaṇa, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts are additional [duties].

The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate that, because the entitlement belongs to the twice-born (dvijāti), superiority arises only when there are those who precede him. But one might object: since the author will later state, "more for the Vaiśya" (GDh 10.48) and "more for the King" (GDh 10.7), this [penance] must belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone; therefore, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" should not have been made.

It is said: as before, this is not for the purpose of indicating that these are duties of the *āśramas*, but rather to make it known that they are duties of the *varṇas*. Consequently, even one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) has the entitlement to receive gifts; however, officiating at sacrifices and teaching do not apply because they are impossible [for such a person]. Although it would have been sufficient to say "for a Brāhmaṇa, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts," the inclusion of the word "additional" (*adhika*) is for the purpose of making it known that these also serve as means of livelihood (*vṛtti*). As in the previous sūtra, a compound was not formed so that they might be performed as a collective whole, lest there be an option (*vikalpa*) since they serve a single purpose. "Teaching" (*pravacana*) means reciting after [the teacher] (*anuvacana*). The rest is explained by its very mention (*nigadavyākhyāna*). 10.2.
But there is a restriction regarding the former ones. 10.3.

Regarding the first [duties], such as study and the like, there is a necessity to perform them; consequently, there is fault (*doṣa*) in their non-performance and spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*) in their performance. Regarding teaching and the others, there is no such necessity; therefore, while there is merit in performing them, there is an absence of transgression (*pratyavāya*) in not performing them. The word "but" (*tu*) expresses a distinction: that for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya as well, there is a rule regarding these [first duties], whereas for the Brāhmaṇa, it is especially so. For this very reason, the aphorism was not formulated as: "For the twice-born, study, sacrifice, and giving are mandatory," lest the requirement of a rule (*niyamādhikāra*) should also follow for the subsequent [duties]. (10.3)
The gift of the Veda may be made to a teacher, a kinsman, a friend, a guru, one who has provided wealth, or one who has mastered the rules, except in cases as previously stated. 10.4.

The teacher (*ācārya*) is defined by the previously stated characteristics. A kinsman (*jñāti*) is one related through the mother or father. A dear friend (*priya*) is a companion. A preceptor (*guru*) includes the father, an elder brother, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), and so forth. The "regulation of wealth" (*dhananiyama*) refers to the exchange of wealth. The "regulation of knowledge" (*vidyāniyama*) refers to the exchange of one branch of learning for another. The mention of the *brahma* (the Veda) implies the purpose of the Vedic meaning; consequently, there is no such regulation regarding the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and the like. "Bestowing" (*saṃpradāna*) means teaching; the word "should be performed" is to be understood as the ellipsis. This applies except in cases other than the service already described, beginning with "having been permitted, he should sit down," and so on. Although it would have been sufficient to say "except what has been stated," the use of the phrase "as stated" (*yathāgrahaṇa*) indicates that this exception applies only to the specific rule concerning the manner of study that was previously mentioned, and not to the rule "one who teaches disciplined students" (*śiṣṭādhyāpaka*). Therefore, even by the regulation of wealth or knowledge, one must not give [instruction] to an unworthy person. 10.4.
And agriculture and trade, provided they are not performed by oneself. || 10.5 ||

Agriculture and trade are well known; these may be performed by a Brāhmaṇa through others as his primary occupations. From the word "and" (ca), it follows that cattle-rearing likewise must not be performed by him himself. (10.5)
And laziness. 10.6.

Usury is the investment of wealth for the purpose of accumulation; that is indeed not performed by oneself, because of the use of the word "and" (ca). Its separate mention is for the purpose of permitting even what is done by oneself. And so he will state later: "Interest on usury is lawful" (GDh 12.26). 10.6.
The king’s duty is the superior protection of all living beings. 10.7

The protection and preservation of all beings—that is, all living creatures—is the duty of a consecrated Kṣatriya king. Because of the use of the word "all," this includes even stationary things; thus, his livelihood is established through that means, which is why the term "all" is employed. (10.7)
Furthermore, as to how that should be carried out, he says:
"The state of administering just punishment. (10.8)

The wielding of punishment must not contradict worldly norms; it is not, however, the arbitrary infliction of punishment according to one's own will out of pride in one's sovereign power. And the author will say: "They say that 'daṇḍa' is so called because of 'damana' (taming); therefore, one should tame those who are untamed" [GDh 11.30]. By the restraint of the untamed, the protection of others is accomplished. || 10.8 ||
Furthermore:
He should support Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas. 10.9.

"Brahmins" refers to those endowed with the qualities of Brahman, learned in the Vedas, and possessing scriptural knowledge; by implication, those residing in their own territory. "Supporting" means providing food and other necessities. 10.9.
And those non-Brahmins who are devoid of energy. || 10.10 ||

Lack of energy (*nirutsāhatva*) means the incapacity to perform actions for the sake of one's livelihood. "Non-Brāhmaṇas" refers to Kṣatriyas and others. Here, because of the mention of "non-Brāhmaṇas," the mention of "Brāhmaṇas"—though already obtained from the preceding sūtra—is repeated so that there may be support even for those Brāhmaṇas who are not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) but are incapable of maintaining themselves. By the word "and" (*ca*), the poor and the helpless are also included. (10.10)
And those who do not perform services, as well as those who provide assistance. || 10.11 ||

Those who have gone forth [into homelessness] without [proper] characteristics are indeed not Brāhmaṇas, because it is they alone who possess the entitlement [to such gifts]. However, those who have gone forth as Brāhmaṇas are not mentioned [here], precisely because they lack the entitlement to accept gifts. One should support them by providing means of subsistence and so forth; the word "and" (ca) implies those afflicted by disease, fear, and the like. Those who are "beneficial" (*upakurvāṇāḥ*) are physicians and others who benefit the world; some say they are one's own personal attendants, but that is incorrect, as their status is already established by the context. By the word "and," those who know the proper times are also included. (10.11)
And there is yoga in victory. 10.12.

When victory is to be achieved, effort (*yoga*) must be exerted. *Yoga* is the acquisition of what has not yet been obtained. The meaning is that one should diligently collect taxes from forest-dwellers (*āṭavika*) and others who have not paid them due to favoritism or other reasons. By the word "and" (*ca*), the protection of what has already been acquired is also implied; the meaning is that one must act so that thieves and others do not seize it. Thus, it should be understood that after first securing both *yoga* and *kṣema*, one should subsequently apply effort toward the defeat of the enemy. (10.12)
Especially in times of fear. || 10.13 ||
In that particular case, there is fear of being overcome by others; therefore, one must especially and with extreme effort attend to its security and well-being. || 10.13 ||
And the practice is by means of the chariot and the bow. || 10.14 ||

“Wandering” (*caryā*) means roaming everywhere throughout the kingdom. The mention of the chariot is an illustration for vehicles such as elephants and horses; the mention of the bow is an illustration for swords and other weapons. By the word “and” (*ca*), staying in one place is also included. The distinction between wandering and staying should be understood according to the requirements of the task at hand. (10.14)
In battle, his standing firm and not retreating [constitute the perfection of power]. || 10.15 ||

In battle—that is, in war—*saṃsthāna* is the fearless standing firm, and *anivṛtti* is the renunciation of life right there; by the word "and" (*ca*), fighting itself is also included. Due to the lack of a compound, it also implies having a secure refuge. (10.15)
Now he states an exception to the rule "one should always be non-violent":
"There is no fault in killing in battle" (10.16).

*Āhava* means battle. The repetition of what has already been mentioned is for the sake of specification: there is no fault only in that situation where men proceed by challenging one another, and not in any other state. (10.16)

Except in the case of those who are without horses, charioteers, or weapons; those with joined palms; those with disheveled hair; those with their backs turned; those who are seated; those on the ground; those mounted on trees; messengers; cows; Brahmins; and those engaged in debate. (10.17)

Such is the fault for one who strikes [these]. The word *vi-* is connected with three terms: *vyaśvaḥ* (one whose horse has fled), *visārathiḥ* (one whose charioteer has fled), and *vyāyudhaḥ* (one whose weapons have fallen away). With palms joined (*kṛtāñjaliḥ*) means with hands folded in reverence. With disheveled hair (*prakīrṇakeśaḥ*) means with hair loose and untied. With face turned away (*parāṅmukhaḥ*) means facing another direction. Seated (*upaviṣṭaḥ*) means sitting down. Mounted on high ground (*sthalārūḍhaḥ*) means mounted on a mountain. Mounted on a tree (*vṛkṣārūḍhaḥ*) is well known. And for one who says, "I am a messenger" or "I am a Brāhmaṇa," and for one who makes the sound of a cow—apart from these, there is no fault. (10.17)
The duty of a Kṣatriya endowed with the qualities of consecration has been stated. Now he speaks of another [type]:
"If another [person] should live by that [profession], being a Kṣatriya, he may do so by that livelihood. (10.18)

There is another connection based on mere birth; one may subsist upon that king by means of his service, according to the rule beginning with, "And [his] conduct [is defined] by the chariot and the bow" (GDh 10.14). 10.18.
The victor shall obtain the wealth of the battle. || 10.19 ||
If one, commissioned by the king, conquers an enemy and acquires wealth, he shall receive that as booty from battle. 10.19.
He states an exception to this: "But [the theft of] a king's vehicle [is not an offense]. (10.20)

"Vāhana" refers to elephants and so forth. The word "tu" (but/however) expresses a distinction. Even highly valuable items such as jewels belong to the king alone, let alone vehicles; therefore, regarding vehicles, even the slightest [item] should be understood [as belonging to the king]. || 10.20 ||
And there is extraction when there is no separate victory. 10.21.

Victory is not distinct from the king; victory belongs to the king. In this context, "extraction" refers to the king's essential resources. The word "and" (ca) is used for the purpose of including the collection of mounts.
But the king shall distribute the remainder as is appropriate. || 10.22 ||

One should give to the warriors in consideration of their bravery and other qualities. The mention of the "king" is intended to show that by acting in this way, he becomes a king through the affection [of his subjects]. Or rather, it means that he himself should perform the distribution, and not others. (10.22)
Now he describes his livelihood for the purpose of protection:
"The farmers shall pay to the king a tenth, an eighth, or a sixth part as a tribute. (10.23)

The mention of "the king" implies that [the tax] is to be given to one appointed [for the purpose]. The mention of "tribute" (*bali*) implies that it is to be given every year. The remainder [of the sense] is that "giving" must be performed. "By cultivators" refers to as many as live by agriculture, and not by the Vaiśya alone. The option between the tenth, eighth, or sixth [part] is to be understood as being established according to the sequence of inferior, middling, and superior land portions. (10.23)
Some [teachers] maintain that for cattle and gold as well, the share is one-fiftieth.

From one who lives by tending cattle, he shall take a fiftieth part of the livestock; from a moneylender, gold. He who, having taken wealth at its ordinary price, gives it back at a high price, is indeed called a usurer and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda. (VaDh 2.41)

If it is argued that the non-existence of this [type of usurer] follows simply from the prohibition of usury, this is not a fault; for Vasiṣṭha has permitted it by another means, stating: "One may give to a most sinful person whose duties have been utterly abandoned" (VaDh 2.43). Because of the mention of "some" (eke), Gautama does not [include all]; thus, one should understand that among those for whom there is no counter-exception, one should not accept [gifts], whereas among those for whom there is no prohibition at all—such that they would otherwise be considered usurers—one may accept them. 10.24.
A twentieth part of the merchandise shall be the duty. 10.25.

"Merchandise" (*paṇya*) refers to that which is to be sold, such as asafoetida and other goods sold by merchants; from these, he should take a twentieth part. The mention of "toll" (*śulka*) is for the sake of technical designation (*saṃjñā*), and consequently, terms such as "surety-money, merchant-toll, and so forth" [GDh 12.38] are established in legal usage. 10.25.
There are six types of theft regarding roots, fruits, flowers, medicinal herbs, honey, meat, grass, and fuel. 10.26.

The roots are turmeric and so forth; the fruits are black pepper and so forth; the flowers are safflower and so forth; the medicinal herbs are chebulic myrobalan and so forth; the grasses are whatever is such as *kaṭa* and the like. The remaining items are well known. 10.26.
But why, then, should this be given to the king? He says: because it is his duty to protect it. 10.27.

The protection of those who pay taxes is "tadrakṣaṇa"; that itself is his duty, and he is one whose duty is that protection (*tadrakṣaṇadharmī*). The state of being such is *tadrakṣaṇadharmitva*; therefore, "because of that state of having the duty of protecting them" means because of his habit of doing so. The statement of the reason regarding a matter understood from the words is for the purpose of taking a smaller portion even than the previously mentioned measure, depending on the place and time; otherwise, if it were simply said that the king protects everything, this reason would become a common one [applicable to anyone]. Thus Uśanas says: "He should determine taxes in accordance with the place, time, and profit. (10.27)
But one should be constantly devoted to them. 10.28.

Regarding those offerings of oblations and so forth, even when one is always preoccupied with other duties, one should remain devoted to them; the word "tu" (but/however) expresses a distinction, meaning that one should likewise remain devoted to other means of acquiring wealth that are not contrary to dharma, but especially in this case. 10.28.
There is no application [of the rule] when there is an excess. 10.29.

The word "syāt" (should be) is to be understood as the ellipsis. The meaning is that he should not take from that treasury—namely, that which exceeds what is required for maintaining his family and has entered into the form of a treasury—for the purpose of maintaining his family, except in times of distress; he should not seize from it at any other time. And so Vyāghra says: "He should constantly maintain his family and increase the treasury;
except in times of calamity, he should never seize the treasury."

Some explain: "One's livelihood might come through the means of protection provided by one's superior. In that regard, it must be examined whether or not there is the consequence of redundancy with the phrase "the king’s superior [share]. 10.29
Artisans shall perform one day's work each month.
Artisans, such as blacksmiths and others, shall perform one day’s work for the king each month according to their own capacity; that alone shall be their tax, and nothing else. (10.30)
By this, those who subsist upon the self are explained. || 10.31 ||

Actors, dancers, and others who subsist by their own labor—these too should perform work for the king for one day. Although they could have been included under the category of "those who subsist by their own labor" (*ātmopajīvinaḥ*), they are mentioned separately because those who subsist by their own labor provide only minor assistance, and [this separate mention] is for the purpose of indicating that their obligation is not permanent. Nor was it formulated simply as "and those who subsist by their own labor," so that it might include everything else that has been stated regarding artisans in other legal codes (*smṛti*). As Uśanas says: "It is ordained that artisans shall perform one day's work every month; in the absence of such work, they shall pay a *kārṣāpaṇa*. (10.31)
And they have no wheels on their feet. || 10.32 ||

A *cakra* is a cart; those who subsist by means of boat-wheels are included. Because of the plural number, carpenters, barbers, and others are meant. By the word "and" (*ca*), hunters of wild animals and the like are included. They are mentioned separately so that, as in the previous case, they may not be considered merely temporary [outcastes]. 10.32.
One should give food to them. 10.33.
One should give food and wages as a fee to those artisans and others; the mention of "that" [the fee] is intended so that it may not apply only to those immediately following. (10.33)
Merchandise should be delivered by merchants at a reduced price. 10.34.

The phrase "one each month" is understood to carry over. This is in addition to the toll (*śulka*). "Depreciation of value" (*arghāpacaya*) refers to a price lower than the market rate. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"He shall pay the toll, and then one [coin] per month for the merchandise itself;
those merchants shall pay separately according to a price that is half the market rate."
Having found lost property that has no owner, they shall announce it to the king.

"Lost" means gone away from its owner, ownerless, with its owner unknown—whereas if the owner were known, one should inform the owner himself. Having found or recovered it, they should report it to the king or to the ministers and others; by the use of the prefix *pra-*, they should report it without guile, saying: "This was obtained in such a manner in this place; let it be investigated as to whose it is. Because of the use of the plural number, it follows that the neighbors and others must also speak. (10.35)
Thus it was said:
having made it known, it must be protected by the king for one year. 10.36.

Having made it known by means of a drum and having proclaimed it: "An object of such-and-such a kind has been found; let its owner come forward himself," it shall be guarded and protected for one year without disturbance. If the owner arrives before the end of the year, it must be returned to him, since the protection depends upon him and he possesses the authority [to claim it]. The mention of the title "King" (*rāja*), even though it has already been acquired, is intended to indicate that highly trustworthy persons should be appointed to guard it. Thus Uśanas says: "One should appoint elders, endowed with learning and noble birth, whose integrity has been observed previously, to the guarding of treasure. (10.36)
For one who has attained the higher [stages], the remainder belongs to the fourth king. || 10.37 ||

After one year, the fourth part belongs to him by whom the thief was identified; the remainder belongs to the king. Having given the fourth part to the informant, he should take the remainder himself. [The phrase] "the remainder belongs to the king" is stated to remove any doubt that might arise as to whether the remainder should instead be given to the appointed official (niyukta). 10.37.

Now, as for how it is understood that he who says "this is mine" before the lapse of a year is the owner, the author says: "The owner [is established] by means of inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, and finding. (MDH 10.38)

When these grounds have been established and understood, he shall be the owner. "Inheritance" (riktha) is that which has come from the father. "Purchase" (kraya) is that which has been bought for a price. "Partition" (saṃvibhāga) is that which was previously lost and is obtained as a legacy in its original form. "Appropriation" (parigraha) is the property of a wife. Some say it refers to the taking possession of something not previously owned by another, such as trees and the like in rivers and so forth; in this regard, it must be considered whether this is redundant because it is already included under "finding" (adhigama), or if it is not. "Finding" (adhigama) is that which is acquired from mines and the like, such as gems and the like. (10.38)
These, first of all, are common to all social classes; for a Brāhmaṇa, however, there is an additional [means of livelihood] consisting of what is obtained. 10.39.

That which is acquired through receiving gifts [is impure], because that is its inherent nature. What is meant is this: it should be understood that even what is acquired through officiating at sacrifices or teaching must be regarded in the same way.
The conquest belongs to the Kṣatriya. 10.40.
That which is conquered by means of weapons after being subdued is the specific prerogative of a Kṣatriya.
It has indeed been entered [into the system] for the Vaiśyas and Śūdras. || 10.41 ||
"Consumed" means acquired through one's own labor—by a Vaiśya through agriculture and the like, and by a Śūdra through service and the like. The word "excessive" carries over from the previous verse.
It is said that the fourth [type of property] belongs to the finder of what was lost; he specifies this: "the discovery of a hidden treasure is the king's wealth. (10.42)

The discovery of a previously buried treasure is a "gain" (lābha) that belongs to the king alone; it does not belong to the fourth part for the discoverer. And thus, it should be understood that any other property besides the treasure [found] likewise belongs to the fourth part of that same [discovery].

Now, one might object: since the property other than the treasure belongs to the king, how can there be its acquisition? For it has been stated that the act of discovery is common [to all], and therefore it must be taken by whoever discovers it first.

To this it is replied: one should report to the king that in which signs of previous experience are seen, while one should take the other oneself; for there is a fault for one who takes after stealing items with signs of previous experience. As Lokākṣi says: "For one who takes after stealing items with signs of previous experience, the punishment is the first *sāhasa* fine, and the king shall seize twice the value of that property. If the seizure of wealth were not mentioned, then since it was stated that "the discovery of a treasure belongs to the king," one might also suspect a prohibition against anyone other than the king. (10.42)
Not for a handsome Brahmin. 10.43.

He should be handsome and devoted to the six duties. Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "If a Brāhmaṇa should obtain [property], while remaining engaged in the six duties, the king shall not take it away," because he is the means for performing those duties. (10.43)
Some say that even one who is not a Brahmin may obtain the sixth [share] if he is an expounder [of the law]. 10.44.

A non-Brāhmaṇa refers to a Kṣatriya or others. An "announcer" is one who previously made it known. Some maintain that he should receive a sixth part, for that is the fruit of his labor and hardship; however, because of the word "some," this is not Gautama’s view, since treasures are of unlimited value. Therefore, whatever may be given to him is appropriate, but it is not necessarily a sixth part alone. By the use of the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that even a Brāhmaṇa who is unattractive [is included]. (10.44)
The property of a minor must be protected until he reaches legal majority, that is, until he enters upon business or completes his studies. || 10.45 ||

A "child" (*bāla*) is one who has not reached the age of sixteen. The mention of him is an indicative term (*upalakṣaṇa*) for others as well who are incapable of protecting their own property. One should protect that wealth from kinsmen; however, protection from others is already established by the rule, "the protection of all beings" (GDh 10.7). This protection lasts until he reaches legal capacity—that is, until the capacity to protect arises—or until his initiation (*samāvartana*), even though the characteristic of capacity may have appeared.
