The alternative options are to be explained with regard to his application to Vedic study and other duties. (10.45)
Having recovered what was stolen by thieves, he shall restore it to its proper place. || 10.46 ||

Having recovered what has been stolen by thieves and others, he shall restore it to the owner alone; however, he must not live off anything under the pretext of suppressing criminals, on the basis of the rule: "The victor shall take the booty of war" (GDh 10.19). Although one should have said "having recovered" (*ācchidya*), the use of the word "having won back" (*apajitya*) implies that even one who recovers it by other means must cause it to be given to the owner. Although one should have said "he shall give it to the owner," the introduction of the phrase "he shall restore it to its proper place" implies that even in the absence of the owner, he shall restore it to the owner's dependents as is appropriate. The mention of "thieves" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for forceful seizure and other such acts. (10.46)
Or he may give from the treasury. || 10.47 ||

In a case where there is no possibility of recovery, because the property has been taken to inaccessible regions and the like, one should cause [the offender] to pay from his own wealth exactly as much as was stolen. It is not stated "or from the treasury," so that the suspicion might not arise: "He should cause it to go to its proper place, or he should cause it to come from the treasury. (10.47)
For a Vaiśya, agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and money-lending are additional duties. 10.48.
Agriculture and so forth are well known. "Kṛṣiśca vaṇikca" (agriculture and trade) is a copulative compound treated as a singular. By the term "vaṇik," the activity of commerce is meant.
The Śūdra is the fourth caste. 10.49.

The designation *śūdra* is derived from the Vedic text because he "runs away" (*dravati*). The term *varṇa* is intended to establish the designation of *varṇa* for the three beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. Consequently, the designation *varṇa* applies only to these four, not to those born of intermediate unions (*antaraja*). Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "There are four *varṇas*: the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra" (VaDh 2.1). || 10.49 ||
Of a single birth. || 10.50 ||

A second birth does not exist for him, because even "initiation" (*upanayana*)—which is called "the second birth"—is designated as a "birth. Thus, there is a prohibition of initiation for him. And since that alone is prohibited, it should be understood that the performance of the rites preceding it, which are without mantras, must take place at their proper times. Accordingly, the author of the *Gṛhya-sūtra* states: "For a Śūdra also, the rites of conception (*niṣeka*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), the naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first outing (*upaniṣkramaṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), and the tonsure (*caula*) are prescribed to be performed at their proper times without mantras. As for the subsequent rites, however, the prohibition is established precisely because they have initiation as their basis. (10.50)
For him as well, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and purity [are required]. 10.51.

"Of that Śūdra"—by the word "also" (*api*), those of higher castes and intermediate sub-castes (*avāntarajāḥ*) are included. This restatement (*anuvāda*) is for the purpose of establishing these as duties of caste (*varṇadharma*), even though they have already been mentioned in the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*) and among the duties of the *snātaka* for the twice-born; it is so that those who are uninitiated (*anupanīta*) may also be included. Truthfulness (*satyam*) is speaking of things as they actually are. Absence of anger (*akrodhaḥ*) is the state of mind that does not seek to harm others. Purity (*śaucam*) is by means of clay and other such substances. The use of a non-compound (*visamāsa*) is for the purpose of including non-stealing, restraint of the senses, and so forth. And thus Manu says: "Non-violence, truthfulness, absence of anger, purity, and restraint of the senses."
"These are the duties in brief.
Thus [it is said]. And likewise Vasiṣṭha also states: "For all [castes], truthfulness, freedom from anger, charity, non-violence, and procreation. (VaDh 4.4) || 10.51 ||
Some say that for the purpose of sipping water (ācamana), one should merely wash the hands and feet. 10.52.

Some maintain that for the purpose of sipping water (*ācamana*) or bathing, one should perform merely the washing of hands and feet; however, Gautama holds that a bath must indeed be performed even without mantras. This alternative should be understood as referring to a *sacchūdra* (a virtuous Śūdra). Thus Uśanas says: "A *sacchūdra* should bathe; an *asacchūdra* should wash his hands and feet. This rule applies to the obligatory daily bath (*nityasnāna*); however, regarding the occasional bath (*naimittika*), since there is no other option, the full bath itself must be performed.

Alternatively, it is simply the *ācamana* (sipping water) that is being discussed. Regarding this, some authorities maintain that only the washing of the hands and feet is required, but Gautama does not hold this view. His intention is that after washing the hands and feet, one must also perform the sipping once. And so says Manu: "But for a woman and a Śūdra, [the sipping] is done once each" (MDh 5.137). The alternative view, however, should be explained as before. 10.52.
The rite of ancestral offerings (śrāddha). || 10.53 ||
"He will state [later], 'Now, the śrāddha' (GDh 15.1). The mention of the word *karman* (rite) is for the purpose of including all types of śrāddhas. As Kaṇva has said:
'The obligatory, the occasional, the optional, the prosperity-śrāddha, and furthermore the pārvaṇa—thus the śrāddha is traditionally known to be fivefold.'"

Some say that since [the performance of rites] is already understood by the mention of *śrāddha* alone, the mention of "rites" (*karman*) is for the purpose of including all ritual injunctions. Others, however, argue that this is so that, through the prohibition of mantras, there might not also follow a prohibition of the injunctions to be accomplished by them. (10.53)
The maintenance of dependents. 10.54.

The maintenance of servants, wife, and so forth—this is stated even though it follows from the acquisition of wealth, lest one become destitute of dependents due to the rule regarding the eating of leftovers. 10.54.
One should confine one's conduct to one’s own wife. 10.55.

Since all subsequent rites are rooted in the *upanayana* (initiation), a prohibition would otherwise apply to them all; therefore, an exception (*pratiprasava*) is made for the mere taking of a wife. By the use of the word "own" (*sva*), it is indicated that his wife must be of the same caste and not of a lower one. Consequently, the taking of wives from different castes is established for Brāhmaṇas and the others. Thus says Manu: "A Śūdra woman alone is the wife of a Śūdra; she and her own [woman] are prescribed for a Vaiśya; she and her own for a Kṣatriya; and they and her own for one of the highest birth. [MDh 3.13]

Although the meaning "one's own wife" is already established, the inclusion of the word *vṛtti* (conduct/livelihood) is for the purpose of prohibiting commission by a brother-in-law (*devara*) and others; that is, one’s conduct must be toward one’s own wife alone, not toward another’s wife. The absence of a compound is for the purpose of including the giving of gifts for the sake of elders and so forth. The separate formulation of this rule indicates that for him, the householder stage (*gārhasthya*) alone is the *āśrama*, and not the others. || 10.55 ||
And service toward those who are superior. 10.56.

Service, attendance, and obedience are the duties for the three higher castes; by the word "and" (ca), agriculture and so forth are also included. Some hold that service is for the virtuous Śūdra (*sacchūdra*), while agriculture and so forth are for the other [Śūdra]. Gautama’s intention, however, is this: he who is a virtuous Śūdra should perform both [service and agriculture] without conflict, whereas the other should perform only agriculture and so forth. Although the term "for the others" (*itareṣām*) would have sufficed, the inclusion of the word "higher" (*uttara*) is intended to indicate that as one moves to each successive [caste], the fruit [of the duty] becomes greater. And thus Āpastamba says: "In each preceding caste, the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) is greater. (10.56)
Now, as to how he who is to be served should conduct himself, he says: "He should seek his livelihood from them. (10.57)

One should desire to obtain one's livelihood from those very persons whom one serves. Thus it is established that service is for one who seeks a means of subsistence, and not necessarily for everyone. 10.57.
What, then, should one request from them, and what should they give to him? To this he says:
"Worn-out sandals, umbrellas, garments, brooms, and so forth. (10.58)
"Worn out" means used up; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), other things of little value are also included. As Manu says:
"Remnants of food should be given, as well as worn-out garments, the dregs of grain, and worn-out household utensils. (MDh 10.125)
The mention of "holding a parasol" is an elliptical expression that includes those made of peacock feathers as well; the rest is well known. 10.58.
Eating the remnants of others' meals and subsisting by a craft. 10.59.

There is no restriction regarding water, because the word "food" (*aśana*) is specifically mentioned. "Leftover" (*ucchiṣṭa*) means what remains after eating. That too applies only to one who has not yet married, because for the other [the married man], there is no application [of this rule] due to his entitlement to perform *pākayajña* sacrifices. Why is this so? Because of the lack of a compound construction [in the text] and because of another *smṛti*: as Vyāghra says, "Food that is leftover should be given to a Śūdra who is not a householder;
however, food that is not leftover should be given day by day to a householder."

The "occupation of crafts" (*śilpavṛtti*) refers to subsisting on the work of carpenters, blacksmiths, and the like; by the word "and" (*ca*), the work of artisans is included. The use of the compound *visamāsa* (irregular compound) is intended to indicate an alternative course of action in times of distress (*āpadkalpa*). Thus says Manu: "But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born, having reached a state where his wife and children are in peril, may live by the work of artisans" (MDh 8.250).

If he is unable to perform service, he may subsist by the profession of a craftsman (*śilpa*). If even by that he cannot maintain himself, it should be understood that he may resort to the profession of an artisan (*kāru*). The distinction between *śilpa* and *kārukarma* is to be understood from common usage: the work of artisans includes barbers, washermen, painters, and so forth; because these are occupations of the inverse order (*pratiloma*), they are censured compared to the occupations of the direct order (*anuloma*). The crafts (*śilpa*), however, such as carpentry and blacksmithing, are superior to the work of artisans because they belong to the direct order. (10.59)
And whoever one may rely upon as a noble protector, by him one should be supported, even if he himself is destitute.

Whichever Brahmin or other [member of the higher castes] he should rely upon and serve, he must be supported by him. By the word "and" (ca), it is implied that even a non-Aryan of one's own caste [must be supported], because the instruction for service is given specifically regarding the Āryas, provided they are engaged in other [proper] activities. While it would have been sufficient to say "whomsoever he should rely upon," the inclusion of the term "Ārya" is intended to indicate the distinction of the virtuous even among those of the same caste. The phrase "by him" (tena) is intended to indicate that this duty is obligatory. "Even when exhausted" means even when afflicted by disease, old age, or similar conditions. (10.60)
And by him, Uttara [was won]. 10.61.

And that Śūdra upon whom the Ārya might depend; this indicates that even for one whose means of livelihood have failed, recourse to a Śūdra is permitted. This "recourse" consists merely in making oneself visible to him. As Jātūkarṇi says: "If a noble man should take refuge with a low-born person, he should always show himself [as a servant];
considering himself as a slave, the low-born person should likewise behave toward him."

By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that even one who is not dependent [on another] is considered destitute (*avasanna*). Thus says Jātūkarṇi: "A poor Brāhmaṇa who is self-controlled and has mastered the Vedas—even if he is not dependent on others, he must always be supported even by a Śūdra."

Since it could have been stated simply as "the other," the inclusion of the word *uttara* (the latter) is for the purpose of making known that a Brāhmaṇa must necessarily be supported, whereas the other is not so restricted. And thus says Jātūkarṇi:
"A wise man should always support a Brāhmaṇa with every effort;
and even a Śūdra, if he possesses wealth, should always support another out of compassion."
Thus [ends verse] 10.61.
His accumulation [of wealth] would be for that purpose. || 10.62 ||

"For that purpose"—meaning for the sake of maintaining [the family]—there shall be "an accumulation" (nicaya), that is, a store of goods, for this Śūdra. The word "because" (yasmāt) is to be supplied. In this way, his possession of wealth for any other purpose is prohibited. Furthermore, the statement of the reason—as before—is that maintenance is not to be carried out with worthless goods, but rather by giving away all one's possessions without detriment to one's own family.
The mantra for his salutation is authorized. || 10.63 ||
The learned authorize this for a virtuous Śūdra who has heard the scriptures, but not for one who is wicked. The mantra known as the *namaskāra* is as follows:
"Salutation to the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis; salutation to Svadhā and Svāhā, indeed eternally. Thus it is said.

Its application is in the rite for the ancestors (pitṛkārya). As the author of the Gṛhyasūtra says: "Having seated the Brāhmaṇas, one should mutter the mantra beginning with the deities. The mention of the word "mantra" is intended so that there may be no apprehension that only a salutation (namaskāra) is permitted here. 10.63.
Some say that he should himself perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices. 10.64.

The *pākayajñas* are sacrifices accomplished by means of cooked food, such as the *aṣṭakā* and others; with these, he should sacrifice himself and not appoint another. In this way, the appointment of another is established for other [sacrifices]. Because of the mention of "some" (*eke*), however, Gautama does not hold this view. This option is to be explained as referring to the case of a virtuous Śūdra and an unvirtuous Śūdra. 10.64.
Not only the Śūdra alone should act in this manner; rather, all [the lower castes] should serve each successive higher one. 10.65.

All those who are inferior should serve those of superior caste. Now, one might object: since the Śūdra has already been mentioned and there is no subsequent [category] for the Brāhmaṇa, this undertaking must refer to the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya; therefore, the use of the plural "all" (*sarve*) in the phrase "they should all serve" is inappropriate. It is replied: the plural is used because even a person of the same caste, if he is of lower quality, should serve one of higher quality. Furthermore, by the word "all," those born in the direct order (*anuloma*) are also included; otherwise, since the context concerns castes (*varṇa*), they would not be included. The particle "and" (*ca*) serves the purpose of including the Śūdra as well, so that he too may serve one of his own caste who possesses superior qualities. (10.65)
In the case of the interchange between the noble and the ignoble, there is equality of action. 10.66.

In the case of a confusion or interchange—meaning a mutual reversal—between the noble person of superior birth and the non-noble person of inferior birth, the equality or parity of their respective actions and conduct must be understood. Even a noble person, such as a Brahmin and so forth, if he performs the work of a non-noble person, should not be served by a Śūdra; likewise, even a non-noble Śūdra who acts according to what has been prescribed is to be relied upon. And thus Manu, referring to Śūdras, says:
"But those who desire dharma, who know dharma, and who follow the conduct of the virtuous..."

"Except for the recitation of mantras, they do not incur sin and even receive praise. [MDh 12.127] Thus, by this, equality of caste is not stated; rather, one should not perform what is contemptible by relying on the strength of one's caste. Likewise, the other [the inferior person] should not show disrespect by thinking, "I am lowly. If there is a reversal—namely, the non-performance of what is enjoined and the practice of what is prohibited—one should look to the expiation that will be stated later. 10.66.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Maskarīya-gautamasūtrabhāṣya*.
The eleventh chapter:
It has been stated that when there is an intermingling of the noble and the ignoble, the king shall prevent it; now he declares the duties thereof.
The king has authority over all, with the exception of the Brāhmaṇas. 11.1.

It has been stated previously that the king is the master of all people residing within his realm in matters of restraint and favor, conduct and the administration of enjoyments: in the restraint of offenders, in the favoring of those deserving of favor, in conduct—that is, in the maintenance of boundaries—and in the administration of enjoyments, namely the collection of taxes; and in the appointment of men for the performance of duties. The exception to this is "with the exception of Brāhmaṇas," meaning excluding Brāhmaṇas. Even when they have committed a transgression, he should establish them in their own duty through conciliation first, and not by means of restraint as in the case of other castes; so it should be understood. The purpose of this initial statement is to declare his independence in all actions. And thus says Nārada:
"All subjects are dependent; the lord of the earth is independent. (NSm 1.29) || 11.1 ||
Even while possessing lordship, he should be a doer of good and a speaker of good. 11.2.

A "doer of good" (*sādhukārī*) is one whose character is to act in accordance with what is prescribed in the scriptures. A "speaker of good" (*sādhuvādī*) is one who, at the time of presiding over legal proceedings, speaks without partiality. Although his sovereignty over all has been stated, nevertheless he must not transgress the boundaries prescribed by the scriptures; the meaning is that he should not engage in such acts as seizing the property of others or gambling with another’s wealth. Therefore, his independence pertains only to matters that do not contradict the scriptures, and not without qualification. (11.2)
Furthermore:
"He is well-trained in the three Vedas and in the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī). (11.3)

The *trayī* consists of the characteristics of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas. *Ānvīkṣikī* is the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*) and the science of the self (*ātmavidyā*). He is well-trained—that is, proficient—in these two; and by the use of the non-compound form, he is also proficient in *daṇḍanīti* (the science of government). By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that he is also proficient in *vārtā* (the science of economics). And so Manu says: "From those learned in the three Vedas, let him learn the triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*), and from experts the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*);
from those who know logic (*ānvīkṣikī*) and the science of the self (*ātmavidyā*), and the undertaking of economic activities (*vārtārambha*) from the people. (MDh 7.43)
Thus [ends the section]. 11.3.
Pure, with senses conquered, and endowed with virtuous assistants and skillful means. || 11.4 ||

Pure and free from greed; having conquered his senses and being devoid of vices such as hunting; possessing virtuous assistants—meaning he is endowed with ministers, feudal lords, envoys, and others who are possessed of virtues such as learning and good conduct; and skilled in means—meaning he is equipped with the expedients of conciliation and so forth, applied in consideration of place, time, and circumstances. Although it would have been sufficient to say "possessing virtuous assistants and [skillful] means," the inclusion of the term *saṃpanna* (endowed/perfected) is for the purpose of including the quality of not leaking one's secret counsel. 11.4.
He should be impartial toward all subjects. || 11.5 ||
In worldly affairs, one should maintain an equal disposition toward both the disliked and the beloved. || 11.5 ||
And one should do what is beneficial for them. 11.6.

The meaning is that he should establish for them, in every village, beneficial works such as the digging of tanks, the building of embankments, and the planting of groves; and by the word "and" (ca), it is implied that he should prohibit harmful activities such as gambling and the consumption of intoxicants. 11.6.
Others, other than the Brahmins, should sit below him as he sits above. 11.7.

Kṣatriyas and others should attend upon that king, who is endowed with such qualities, while standing below and close by him as he stands above. Although it would have been sufficient to say "non-Brāhmaṇas" (*abrāhmaṇāḥ*), the expression "others than Brāhmaṇas" (*anye brāhmaṇebhyaḥ*) is used for the purpose of including those Brāhmaṇas who possess [excellent] qualities, and not merely those of the [inferior] caste. Since it was already established that they should sit below him, the specific mention of "above" (*upari*) is intended to indicate that they should remain in a superior position even during festivals and similar occasions. (11.7)
They too would think thus of him. || 11.8 ||

Even those virtuous Brahmins would consider him, standing below, as their superior and would honor him with blessings and the like, regarding him as a portion of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). As Manu says: "Since this king was fashioned from portions of the lords of the gods," and so forth. By the use of the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that even Brahmins who stand lower and lack such virtues [would do so]. (11.8)
He shall protect the social classes and the stages of life according to the law. || 11.9 ||

The *varṇas* are those such as Brāhmaṇas and others who have not yet undergone initiation (*upaneyas*). The *āśramas* pertain to the subsequent period of life. "In accordance with justice" means by a path that is not opposed to worldly custom or the scriptures; the meaning is that he should protect them in such a way that there is no interference with their performance of duties prescribed by the scriptures, nor any disruption of the social order. The prefix *abhi-* in *abhigrahaṇam* signifies directness; therefore, having investigated the matter himself, he should provide protection. The compound is analyzed as a non-coordinative (visamāsa) for the sake of protecting even those who possess neither the status of a *varṇa* nor an *āśrama*, namely those born in the inverse order (*pratilomas*). The inclusion of the term *āśrama* is intended to include those born in the natural order (*anulomas*) who possess the status of an *āśrama* but not that of a *varṇa*. For regarding them, the status of a *varṇa* is excluded in the passage: "The Śūdra is the fourth *varṇa*" (GDh 10.49). Furthermore, since the injunction for initiation is given in the passage: "But one born in the inverse order is devoid of dharma" (GDh 4.25), they do not lose the status of a *varṇa* even while possessing the status of an *āśrama*; thus, they are already included by the mention of *varṇa*. By the word "and" (*ca*), images of deities are also included. Thus says Vyāghra:

“The king should protect with diligence the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those born of intermediate castes, as well as the images of the deities. Since it has already been stated that “the protection of all beings” (GDh 10.7) consists of guarding them from thieves and the like, the instruction given here is for the purpose of ensuring that they do not intermingle with one another. 11.9.
And he should establish those who have strayed in their own duty. || 11.10 ||

The meaning is that if those previously mentioned [duties] are not performed due to laziness or other such causes, one should restrain them and compel them to perform their own specific duty; the word "and" (ca) implies this also applies when they engage in prohibited acts. 11.10.
Why does he act in this way? He says:
"For it is understood that one becomes a sharer in a portion of the Dharma. (11.11)

The word *hi* signifies a reason (*hetu*). Since a sixth part of dharma accrues to the king from protection, it follows by implication that a sixth part of adharma accrues from non-protection. "A part" means a sixth portion. And so Manu says:
"A sixth part of dharma accrues to the king from protecting all; likewise, a sixth part of even adharma accrues to him for failing to protect. (MDh 8.304)

Since it is impossible for an immaterial *dharma* to be divided, one should understand that whatever measure of *dharma* arises from the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), a sixth part of that measure arises for the king as well from the performance of his prescribed duties. The particle "iti" (thus) is intended to indicate a conclusion: "since this is so, therefore he should protect and establish [it]. The phrase "it is known" (*vijñāyate*) is used to point to the Veda (*śruti*); this too is for the purpose of generating a sense of gravity regarding protection, because all *dharmas* have the Veda as their root.
And he should appoint a Brāhmaṇa as his domestic priest. || 11.12 ||
One should place a Brahmin at the forefront in all undertakings; by the word "and" (ca), it is implied that one should also appoint a commander of the army. 11.12.
Endowed with learning, noble lineage, eloquence, beauty, youth, and virtuous conduct. || 11.13 ||

By the word "learning" (vidyā), the Atharvaveda is meant; for that alone is capable of rites such as pacification (śānti) and so forth. "Noble birth" (abhijana) refers to good character (cāritra); one endowed with that engages in the task. "Endowed with speech" (vāk-saṃpanna) means he delights everyone by virtue of being a speaker of refined Sanskrit. "Endowed with beauty" (rūpa-saṃpanna) means that because he is pleasant to behold, his words become trustworthy. "Endowed with age" (vayas-saṃpanna) means neither too young nor too old; only such a person is fit for great tasks. "Endowed with virtue" (śīla-saṃpanna) means being possessed of forbearance (kṣamā); for him, nothing is impossible. (11.13)
And what more?
[He was] an ascetic who lived according to the right way. || 11.14 ||

One who acts according to justice and is endowed with conduct not contrary to worldly custom does not abandon the king even in times of distress; this means that an ascetic (tapasvin) is one whose inclination is to approach [his wife] only during her season, and such a person is fit for entry into the inner quarters and similar duties. The grammatical analysis (*yogavibhāga*) indicates that other assistants as well must be of this same character. The compound is used for the purpose of including those who are skilled in the treatises on Dharma. || 11.14 ||
Impelled by that [knowledge], one should perform actions. || 11.15 ||

The word "that" (tat) is intended to include all [the aforementioned] assistants. "Permitted" (prasūtaḥ) means authorized by them; the meaning is that one should perform actions for visible and invisible purposes after they have deliberated. || 11.15 ||
Moreover, it is known from scripture: "For the kṣatriya power, when born from Brahman, prospers and does not falter. || 11.16 ||

The word *hi* has the sense of "because. Because [an action] undertaken as a kṣatriya duty with the permission of Brāhmaṇas succeeds—that is, it is necessarily joined with its fruit—this is the meaning. Since it is performed according to the rule (*vidhi*), there is no defect such as that of an unworthy recipient; thus it does not fail, meaning it does not turn out otherwise. The two particles *iti* and *ca* are for the purpose of indicating two scriptural citations (*śruti*). The word *vijñāyata* is for the purpose of indicating a scriptural citation. The presentation of the scripture is for the purpose of showing that these [duties] must indeed be performed after due deliberation. 11.16.
Furthermore,
he should pay heed to whatever those who contemplate divine portents might proclaim.

Those who contemplate fate are experts in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). Those who contemplate portents are knowers of omens and signs. They should "declare," that is, they should speak with certainty; by the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that teachers (*guru*) are also included. One should respect them—that is, one should have faith in them—and act in accordance with their advice; this is the meaning. (11.17)
Why?
Because some indeed declare that even one's acquisition (yoga) and preservation (kṣema) are dependent upon Him. 11.18.

The attainment of the fruits of action depends either on destiny (*daiva*) or on human effort (*puruṣakāra*). By the word "destiny," the karma acquired in previous births is meant; by the word "human effort," the karma performed in this life is meant. Thus says Kaṇva: "Karma performed in a previous birth is designated as 'destiny,' while that which is performed in this birth is called 'human effort' here."

In this regard, because even those devoid of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), such as the lame and others, are seen to obtain treasures and the like, while even those who perform excellent deeds do not see the results, they believe that the fruit depends solely on fate (*daiva*) and not on human effort; thus, they assert that it is "dependent on that" (*tadadhīna*). By the word "that" (*tat*), the speech of those who contemplate fate and portents is meant, for by that alone is the knowledge of unseen fruits (*adṛṣṭa-phala*) obtained. Security and well-being (*yogakṣema*) are dependent on that: acquisition (*yoga*) is the gaining of what has not been gained, and security (*kṣema*) is the protection of what has been gained. Acquisition is indeed dependent on that, because when there is knowledge of the gain or non-gain of something through a sign (*nimitta*), one either exerts effort or does not exert effort accordingly. Security is also [dependent on that], because when there is knowledge of a calamity through a sign, it is possible to remove it by means of pacification and so forth. They "assert" means they make a formal proposition (*pratijñā*). The word "also" (*api*) is intended to indicate another underlying intention.

Others also speak thus: since the connection with food and other necessities is untenable without human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and because it is observed that even for those who have exerted themselves, results are sometimes fruitless, yet there is never an absence of deviation [from effort], they consider [the result] to be dependent solely on human effort; whereas, because the speech regarding the occurrence of fate (*daiva*) is sometimes seen to be non-deviant, they hold it not to be dependent on that.

Gautama maintains that [the result arises] from both, because of the mention of "either one. Neither destiny (*daiva*) nor human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is exclusively predominant. What then? Sometimes destiny depends upon human effort, and likewise human effort depends upon destiny. Just as in agriculture and similar activities, human effort depends on destiny—for without rain and other such factors, there is no accomplishment of the fruit through human effort alone—so too, in the acquisition of food and other things, destiny depends on human effort, since its connection [to the result] is impossible without it. This is Gautama’s intention: regarding destiny, one should heed the words of those who observe portents; regarding human effort, however, one should heed the words of the authoritative (*āpta*). (11.18)

One should perform in the domestic fire (śālāgni) those rites associated with peace, auspicious days, prosperity, longevity, and blessings—namely, the *ābhyudayika* ceremonies—as well as those involving incantations for causing enmity, subjugation, malevolent sorcery, and the ruin of enemies. || 11.19 ||

The word "connected" (*saṃyukta*) is to be applied to each [term]. That which is performed for the sake of averting misfortune indicated by divine portents, such as rites for the pacification of the planets (*grahaśāntyādi*), is "connected with peace" (*śāntisaṃyukta*). That which is performed at weddings and other occasions for the purpose of destroying defects of the day, so that through the destruction of those defects the rite becomes auspicious, is "connected with merit" (*puṇyāhasaṃyukta*). That which is performed during journeys and similar circumstances is "connected with well-being" (*svastyayanasaṃyukta*). Thus Vyāsa says: "In a journey, one should meditate on Vāsava; likewise, Nārasiṃha in battle; and Vāsudeva in fear. These three are remembered as 'well-being' (*svastyayana*)."

That which is performed on one's birth-star (*janmanakṣatra*) for the sake of increasing longevity is "connected with longevity" (*āyuṣyasaṃyukta*). That which is performed for the sake of wealth and so forth, such as the *śrī-homa* and others, is "connected with auspiciousness" (*maṅgalasaṃyukta*). These alone are called "prosperity-rites" (*abhyudayika*), because they are the causes of prosperity (*abhyudaya*). If it is argued that this [definition] need not be stated because they are themselves the causes of prosperity, we reply: there is no fault, because it indicates the absence of defect for the performer of those acts. Furthermore, it makes known that for the subsequent rites, there is some expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the performer. And thus says Paiṭhīnasi: "The best of the twice-born who performs a prosperity-rite for a king..."
Having spoken that which causes pain to others, he is not smeared by sin.

"Having committed an act that causes suffering to others, purification is declared by the wise to result from what is prescribed by the Brahmins, or from an expiation, or even with the permission of the King. Thus it is said.

The subsequent rites are mentioned separately because they cause harm to others. That which is joined with *vidveṣaṇa* (sowing dissension) is that by which another person becomes hostile toward his own subjects. That which is joined with *saṃvanana* (subjugation) is that by which an enemy bows down before him. That which is joined with *abhicāra* (malevolent magic) is that by which an enemy dies. *Vyṛddhi* means the loss of prosperity; *dviṣad-vyṛddhi* is the loss of prosperity belonging to an enemy. That which is joined with this is that by which another person is deprived of power, such as *uccāṭana* (driving away), and so forth. Because of the mention of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) above, these [rites] should be performed by the domestic priest (*purohita*) in the hall-fire (*śālāgni*). By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that they may also be performed in the common fire (*laukika-agni*). In this regard, it should be understood that the previously mentioned rites are performed in the common fire, while the others are performed in the hall-fire. (11.19)
As it has been said: "The other [sacrificial fees] belong to the officiating priests. (11.20)

The officiating priests (ṛtvij) shall perform other rites, such as the Putrakāmeṣṭi, as prescribed; the phrase "as prescribed" is used so that the king may not be greedy for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 11.20 ||
And its conventional expression consists of the Veda, the Dharmaśāstras, the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), the Upavedas, and the Purāṇa. || 11.21 ||

"Vyavahāra" (legal procedure) is so called because one transacts by means of it. These are the instruments for establishing legal order for that king who is authorized to protect his subjects. The Vedas and the rest are well known: in the Veda, because we see legal procedures such as "Like a pitfall for the winning of riches" (RV 1.124.7); in the Dharmaśāstra, because of the exposition of the castes, stages of life, and so forth; in the Aṅgas, because of the exposition of the rules governing words and other elements; in the Upavedas, because of the exposition of legal procedures regarding weaponry and the like; and in the Purāṇas, because of the knowledge of the world's maintenance. The lack of compound (in the list) is intended to indicate that each preceding member is more authoritative than the following. Consequently, in case of conflict between earlier and later authorities, one should act according to what was stated earlier. In the observation of the true nature of legal procedure, the Vedas and the rest are called "vyavahāra" in the sense that they serve as its constituent parts (*aṅga*). The meaning is that, having reflected upon these, he should establish legal proceedings. (11.21)
Furthermore:
"The customs of regions, castes, and families, when not in conflict with the sacred traditions (āmnāya), are authoritative.

The *deśadharma* (local custom) consists of festive rites, auspicious ceremonies, and the like. The *jātidharma* (caste duty) consists of such things as the absence of red dye on the teeth among Ābhīras and others. The *kuladharma* (family duty) is exemplified by such rules as "the topknot is on the right side for the Vasiṣṭhas. By the use of the plural, these are understood to include the aforementioned *āmnāyas*—the Vedas, the Dharmaśāstras, and so forth. When they are not in conflict and are not sublated, they are authoritative. The particle *ca* (and) is intended to indicate that even the duties of those to be mentioned later, such as farmers and others, are authoritative provided they do not contradict the *āmnāyas*. Having properly understood even the local customs and the rest, one should adopt them in accordance with the *āmnāyas*; if there is a contradiction, one should abandon them. This is the purpose of the instruction. (11.22)
Farmers, merchants, cattle-herders, usurers, and artisans [should be assigned] to their respective classes.

The term "authority" (*pramāṇam*) carries over from the previous context. This instruction is intended to mean that when it is impossible to consult the king, one should consult only those within one's own group. "Farmers" (*karṣakāḥ*) are those who live by agriculture. "Merchants" (*vaṇijaḥ*) are well known. "Cattle-herders" (*paśupālāḥ*) are cowherds. "Moneylenders" (*kusīdinaḥ*) are usurers. "Artisans" (*kāravaḥ*) are metal-workers and the like. Although it would have been sufficient to say "one's own group," the use of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) indicates that not only farmers and the others are authorities within their own groups, but Brahmins and others as well. Even in that case, by the force of other *smṛtis*, at least three must be consulted, based on the statement of Prajāpati: "In their own group, at least three shall declare the laws. Since it has been stated that "what is not contradicted by the sacred traditions (*āmnāya*) is authoritative" (GDh 11.22), if they should speak in contradiction to those traditions, then everyone must go before the Brahmins; for they alone have the capacity to speak in accordance with non-contradiction, as it is stated: "His legal proceeding" (GDh 11.21). It should be understood that if there is still dissatisfaction even then, one must go before the king, because he too must speak in accordance with the sacred traditions, and since a single person lacks the capacity to ascertain such non-contradiction, it follows by implication that one should speak together with Brahmins who know those traditions. And so says Manu: [Manu 8.39] "If the members of the court, being asked about the law, deliberate falsely through greed, fear, or affection, they shall incur the sin of the crime and be fined one thousand [paṇas]. [Manu 8.40] "But if, being asked, they declare the law correctly, they, being pure and versed in the Veda, shall obtain great merit leading to heaven. [Manu 8.41] "One who knows the law should examine the witnesses in cases concerning debts and the like, in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, according to the rule. [Manu 8.60] "When a witness, having been summoned in a lawsuit, does not speak, though he knows [the truth], he shall be cast into hell for six months, feeding upon his own excrement. [Manu 8.73] "A man who, knowing the facts, speaks falsely in a judicial proceeding, shall dwell for a hundred years in hell, surrounded by worms. [Manu 8.105] "When a witness speaks the truth in his testimony, he obtains great merit; but when he speaks a falsehood, he incurs sin. [Manu 8.106] "Truth liberates a witness from all sins; therefore, a witness should always speak the truth in his testimony. [Manu 8.108] "When a witness gives false testimony regarding small cattle, he falls for five years into the hell called Tāmisra, enveloped in darkness. [Manu 8.109] "For false testimony regarding large cattle, he dwells for ten years in the hell Andhatāmisra, which is filled with blind darkness. [Manu 8.110] "For false testimony regarding humans, he sinks for eleven years into the hell Mahātāmisra, which is full of great darkness. [Manu 8.111] "For false testimony regarding gold, he falls into the hell Kālasūtra for twelve years, where he is tormented by hunger and thirst. [Manu 8.112] "For false testimony regarding land, he is born in a foul-smelling womb, such as that of a dog, a donkey, a pig, or a camel. [Manu 8.113] "A witness who gives false testimony concerning water, women, or land, destroys the merits of both this world and the next; therefore, he should not give false testimony. [Manu 8.114] "Falsehood regarding small cattle is equal to falsehood regarding water; falsehood regarding large cattle is equal to falsehood regarding women; falsehood regarding land is equal to falsehood regarding gold. [Manu 8.115] "One who gives false testimony regarding grain incurs the same sin as one who gives false testimony regarding land; one who gives false testimony regarding silver incurs the same sin as one who gives false testimony regarding gold. [Manu 8.116] "The gods, the ancestors, and the sages do not accept the offerings of a man who gives false testimony, just as they do not accept the offering of a Śūdra. [Manu 8.117] "He who, having entered the assembly, speaks what is contrary to the law, or he who, being asked, remains silent, becomes a partaker in the guilt of the litigants. [Manu 8.118] "The gods, the ancestors, and the sages do not accept the offerings of a man who is ignorant of the law, nor of one who speaks falsely. [Manu 8.119] "The gods, the ancestors, and the sages do not eat the food of a man who is ignorant of the law, nor of one who speaks falsely. [Manu 8.120] "The gods, the ancestors, and the sages do not eat the food of a man who is ignorant of the law, nor of one who speaks falsely. [Manu 8.121] "The gods, the ancestors, and the sages do not eat the food of a man who is ignorant of the law, nor of one who speaks falsely. [Manu 8.122] "The gods, the ancestors, and the sages do not eat the food of a man who is ignorant of the law, nor of one who speaks falsely. [Manu 8.123] "The gods, the ancestors, and the sages do not eat the food of a man who is ignorant of the law, nor of one who speaks falsely. [Manu 8.124] "The gods, the ancestors, and the sages do not eat the food of a man who is ignorant of the law, nor of one who speaks falsely. "But the king, desiring to oversee legal proceedings, [should sit] together with Brahmins," and so forth. (MDh 8.1) ... 11.23.
Now, if farmers and others were to approach the king himself, how would the king decide their cases? To this he says:
"Having brought back the matters from them according to their respective jurisdictions, there is the establishment of justice. (11.24)

"From them"—that is, from the cultivators and others—"according to their respective jurisdictions," meaning that whoever is authorized in a particular matter should stand for each respective category. "Having brought forth the matters"—meaning the rules of conduct (*ācāra*)—having personally and correctly deliberated upon them individually; this is the meaning. Why is this so? Because while one might simply say "having brought forth" (*avahṛtya*), the author begins by saying "having brought forth again" (*pratyavahṛtya*). Therefore, the ellipsis is that "the settlement of the law (*dharma-vyavasthā*) must be made. The intention is that the determination of the true state of affairs (*tattva-pariccheda*) must be performed. While one might simply say "he should speak" (*brūyāt*), the inclusion of the term "settlement" (*vyavasthā*) is intended to prevent the reversal of what has already been decided by the king. Furthermore, this indicates that even if a matter is already established elsewhere, there may be a need to deliberate upon it again and again if dissatisfaction arises. The mention of "law" (*dharma*) implies that he should settle the case solely with the intent of justice (*dharma-buddhi*), and not out of a desire for material gain (*artha-āśaya*). (11.24)
Reasoning is the means for attaining right understanding. 11.25.
In the comprehension and ascertainment of that which is consistent with logic, *tarka* (reasoning) is the means of inference; that is, it is the primary means. Thus said Nārada:
"Just as a hunter tracks the path of a deer by drops of blood, so should a king track the path of *dharma* through inference. [MDh 8.44]
Thus [ends the verse]. 11.25.
Having inferred this, he should cause it to go to its proper place. || 11.26 ||
One should infer by means of that inference, as Manu has said:
"By outward forms, by gestures, by gait, by activity, and by speech, as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the internal mind is grasped. [MDh 8.26]
One should cause [the disciple] to go to, that is, to reach, their proper place according to reality. || 11.26 ||
In the event of doubt, he should resolve it by consulting those who are aged and learned in the three Vedas. || 11.27 ||

"Contradiction" (*vipratipatti*) refers to the inability of a single person to determine [the truth] through reasoning alone, due to the extreme subtlety of the matter and because signs (*liṅga*) are observed in both ways. Regarding that [contradiction], "those aged in the three Vedas" (*traividyavṛddhāḥ*) are those who have mastered all three Vedas; having "withdrawn from them"—that is, having understood from them—[one should act]. This means: having investigated such things as "this is the sign for this," "this is the determiner of this," "previously this was the sign for this, but now there is another sign," and "what does this determine? and thus having known the reality (*tattva*). These very assistants who were mentioned for the purpose of making known the lack of contradiction with the *Āmnāya* (Scripture) and so forth, are here reiterated for the purpose of establishing the definition of those "versed in the three Vedas. As Manu said: [Manu 12.105–106] "One should not, by one's own will, initiate a judicial investigation; nor should one, even if questioned, declare the law to an unworthy person. But when asked in a court of justice, or even unasked, one should declare the law to those who seek it, being pure and composed. One should speak the truth when asked in a court of justice; for by speaking the truth, one attains both this world and the next."
"Trained by ministers who are experts in counsel, he should enter the assembly hall. [MDh 8.1]

If it is argued that this should be stated in that very same place, there is no such fault; for the purpose of this instruction here is to show that they do not merely conduct an investigation in accordance with the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), but also when there is doubt regarding the indicative marks (*liṅga*). When there is no doubt regarding the marks and no contradiction, the king alone should be seen as the decider, because the assembly exists for both those purposes. However, when there is doubt regarding the marks, he should have the matter brought forward by those aged in the three Vedas (*traividyavṛddha*) and not decide it himself; for although this was already established by the general rule "he should cause [the litigant] to go to his proper place," the phrase "he should cause him to reach a final conclusion" is introduced again as a specific injunction. (11.27)
He asks what happens for one who acts in this way, and says: "In that manner, his supreme good (niḥśreyasa) comes to be. || 11.28 ||

For one who makes this determination, there is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) consisting in victory over both worlds: by the attainment of merit (*dharma*) in the next world, and by the affection of the people in this world as well. The word "iti" has the sense of a reason, meaning "because it is thus. (11.28)
Thus it occurs to the king: "What happens to those who are elders learned in the three Vedas, standing in the capacity of his companions? To this, the scripture provides a corresponding illustration:
"It is known that Brahman, when conjoined with Kṣatra, sustains the gods, the ancestors, and human beings. (11.29)

The Brahman, characterized by the three Vedas, when joined with—that is, united with—the Kṣatriya king, meaning performing the discernment of dharma together with the king, sustains the gods and the ancestors through the performance of unimpeded rites, according to the principle that "the gods subsist on what is offered from here," by means of oblations and the like; and it sustains human beings through the production of food. Therefore, it must be said that the discernment of questions regarding dharma belongs to kings. 11.29.
But if, even while such a rule is being established, they do not desist from immorality, then:
"Punishment is so called because it subdues"; therefore, one should subdue those who are unsubdued. (11.30)

It subdues those who are unsubdued, or it is that in which they are subdued; thus it is called *daṇḍa*. And because it is joined with the act of subduing (*damana*), it is termed *daṇḍa*; so say Manu and others. As Manu has said:
"Even the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, birds, and serpents—they too exist for the sake of enjoyment only when constrained by the rod alone" (MDh 7.23).
Therefore, by whatever means one is to be disciplined—whether by speech or by wealth and so forth—as Manu has said:

"One should first apply the punishment of censure (dhig-daṇḍa), then the punishment of speech (vāk-daṇḍa); thirdly, the punishment of wealth (dhanadaṇḍa), and after that, the punishment of corporal death (vadha-daṇḍa). [MDh 8.129]
In this manner, one should deal with those who persist in improper conduct, such as immorality and the like.
Having thus established the subjects, he explains how they proceed:

"The castes and stages of life, being devoted to their own duties, after death experience the fruit of their actions; then, by the remainder [of that karma], they obtain a birth distinguished by place, caste, family, form, lifespan, sacred learning, conduct, wealth, happiness, and intelligence. (11.31)

The *varṇas* are the Brāhmaṇas and so forth who have not yet been initiated; the *āśramas* are the students (*brahmacārins*) and so forth. Devoted to their own duties—that is, intent on the performance of their respective duties—they, after death in the other world, having experienced and enjoyed the fruit of their actions, obtain in this world a birth characterized by a connection with a distinguished place and so forth, as a remainder of that enjoyment of the fruits. The word "distinguished" (*viśiṣṭa*) is connected with each [term]: a distinguished place such as Āryāvarta; a distinguished caste such as Brāhmaṇa; a distinguished family endowed with Vedic study and the like; a distinguished form, meaning a pleasing appearance; a distinguished lifespan, such as a full hundred years; distinguished learning, accompanied by the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas; distinguished conduct, meaning excellent character; distinguished wealth, characterized by cattle, horses, and so forth; distinguished happiness, the successful attainment of the experience of desired objects without obstacle; by the word "intellect" (*medhas*), health is meant—distinguished health being the absence of disease even when eating desired foods. By speaking thus, it is established that the performer of obligatory duties and the enjoyer of their fruits is a Self (*ātman*) distinct from the body. And so says the Śruti:

"This very one is the great unborn Self (ātman), which consists of consciousness, the agent, the enjoyer; it is indeed the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), composed of immortality, established in the vital breath. Thus [says the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22]. And likewise Manu:
"For that which causes the self to act, they call the Knower of the Field."
But he who performs actions is called the "elemental self" (bhūtātman) by the wise. [MDh 12.12]

And so forth. When that eternal being, upon the exhaustion of its karma, falls from the body initiated by that [karma], it experiences the fruit of that karma—such as heaven and so on—by means of a body initiated by that very karma and rendered fit for the enjoyment of its fruits, accompanied by ego, senses, power, mind, and vital breath. Having become composed of food (*annamaya*) through the medium of medicinal herbs and the like, and having been transformed into the form of semen, it is drawn in by the wind residing therein—which had previously entered the mother’s womb—and, joined with the mother’s blood, it is called "birth" (*janman*), which is the material cause of the body sustained by the residual karma of previous experiences.

The meaning of the Sūtra being thus established, the following objections are raised: The mention of *āśrama* (stages of life) is redundant, because the stages are prescribed only for those belonging to the social classes (*varṇa*), and even when they are in a stage of life, their status as belonging to a class does not cease. Furthermore, the mention of *sva* (one’s own) is redundant, since one's ownership [of the results] is already established by the very fact of performance. The mention of *karman* (action) is also redundant, because its purpose is already fulfilled by the phrase "having experienced the fruit of action" (*karmaphalam anubhūya*). The mention of *niṣṭhā* (completion) is likewise redundant, because it is impossible to perform an action without prior intention. The word *pretya* (having departed/dead) need not be used either, as its meaning is already established by the phrase "they obtain another birth" (*janma pratipadyante*). When it should have been said "having experienced the fruit," the inclusion of *karman* is superfluous, since the fruit is necessarily produced by action. The word *tataḥ* (from that) is also redundant, as the reference to the action is already established by the context (*adhikāra*). Moreover, the notion of a "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is untenable, because the entire action is exhausted by the enjoyment of its fruit. It is not possible for a portion of an action that is ready to yield its fruit to remain over; just as milk does not begin to produce curds by means of only a part of itself. Nor can a "remainder" denoted by the word *śeṣa* refer to a residue of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), because actions, being formless, cannot have a residue of impressions. Nor can an action performed in the afterlife be called a "remainder" here, because there is no further eligibility (*adhikāra*) for it there, and because it is impossible for anything other than what has been utilized to remain. It is not logical to determine that the interruption of the enjoyment of the fruit is itself the "remainder," for that would entail abandoning what is stated in scripture and imagining what is not stated; for the scripture speaks of the fruit of the action, not of the interruption of the fruit. Furthermore, an interruption of enjoyment is impossible while the action remains unexhausted, since such interruption depends upon the action—just as a lamp, which depends on oil, is extinguished only by the exhaustion of the oil. Moreover, while there may be a remainder of things like moths [consuming the flame], there is no remainder of the fruit of an action. Therefore, the interruption of the fruit cannot be denoted by the word "remainder. Nor can one divide the fruit of an action itself, thinking, "By this portion I shall experience happiness in the afterlife, and by this I shall obtain a connection with a specific place and so forth," because the fruit is already accomplished. Indeed, division is heard of regarding things that are not yet accomplished—such as "this is the field for rice, this is for barley"—but one does not say that already accomplished rice or barley is being divided. If those who have reached the completion of their own actions still obtain a birth here through a remainder of the enjoyment of fruits in the afterlife, then the consequence of the non-existence of liberation (*mokṣa*) arises, which contradicts scriptural passages such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1) and "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8). If birth characterized by the attainment of specific places and so forth occurs due to a remainder of action, then the impossibility of the world's diversity (*jagadvaicitrya*) follows, yet that diversity is clearly observed. Furthermore, if it is admitted that an action already obtained [its result] yields fruit, then human effort (*puruṣakāra*) would also be rendered useless. Therefore, because there is no object denoted by the word "remainder," and because the intended meaning of the Sūtra is untenable even in its entirety, this Sūtra is inconsistent.

In this regard, the compound should be analyzed as follows: first, both categories must be included because there is a distinction between the duties (*dharma*) of the social classes (*varṇa*) and those of the stages of life (*āśrama*). Before initiation (*upanayana*), one belongs to the *varṇas*; after it, one belongs to the *āśramas*. Furthermore, even for those who have not been initiated, there is eligibility for certain duties of the *varṇas*. The lack of a compound (*asamāsa*) is intended to ensure the inclusion of the *dvandva* (copulative) sense, so that there be no suspicion of it being a *sāmānādhikaraṇya* (appositional) compound. For in the case of a *dvandva*, since both members are primary, the inclusion of both is established. And the word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of including the *sṛṣṭis* (created beings) and *yantras* (mechanical devices), for they too attain excellence through the performance of their own respective duties. Thus says Manu:

"Renouncing the body for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow, and for the protection of women and children—even if unadorned (or without expectation of reward)—is the cause of success for those of the outer castes. [MDh 10.62] The inclusion of the word "own" (*sva*) is intended to encompass the primary alternative course of action. If it is argued that this is already established because penances are prescribed specifically for acts performed during times of distress (*āpad*), we say no; for the prescription of penance applies only to the performance of the duties of another caste, not to one's own duty when it is merely deficient. Thus, it has been stated in the words of Nārada:
Having crossed over the calamity when people have died, a Brāhmaṇa who has subsisted by the occupation of a Kṣatriya should abandon that Kṣatriya occupation after performing purification for himself.

And so forth. Therefore, the mention of "one's own" (*sva*) is for the purpose of negating the fruit of a defective rite. And thus it should be understood that a defective rite is neither a means to a fruit—because there is no injunction for expiation (*prāyaścitta*)—nor is it a cause of sin. The mention of "completion" (*niṣṭhā*) is for the sake of continuity; for only he who performs the rite until the fall of the body is connected with this fruit. The mention of "after death" (*pretya*) is for the purpose of making known that the fruit is inevitable; just as success is achieved here through visible fruits, so too there, it is achieved through invisible fruits. It does not mean, however, that a performed rite becomes fruitless. The mention of "rite" (*karman*), moreover, is to show that the connection with this fruit belongs only to the rite performed, and not to one who practices the combination of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*); such a person is indeed liberated. By this very point, the objection regarding the consequence of the non-existence of liberation (*mokṣa*) should also be seen as refuted. The word "from that" (*tataḥ*) is also for the purpose of demonstrating the diversity of rites: by the remainder or excess of each respective rite. And thus, since the variety of fruits arises from the gradations of rites, the diversity of the world is logically established. The gradation of rites is due to differences in place, time, purity, materials, faith, the recipient (*pātra*), and practice; and the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) should be understood with reference to the aggregate of rites. How so? A rite whose fruit is heaven yields its fruit right there; but a rite whose fruit is worldly yields a birth connected with a specific place and so forth, and that is the "remainder" of that aggregate. Alternatively, the rite that is subsidiary (*aṅga*) to a principal rite (*pradhāna-karman*), such as the *agnihotra*, is denoted by the word "remainder. For example: "One desiring cattle should fetch water in a *godohana* vessel" (ĀpŚr 1.16.2), "One desiring vigor should make a sacrificial post of *khadira* wood" (ṢaḍviṃBr 4.4), and so forth. In that case, the fruit of the principal rite is enjoyed in the next world, while the fruit of the subsidiary is experienced here. Or this should be viewed like a tree: a tree is produced with many roots; when its principal roots are mostly severed, it falls because it cannot support the weight due to having only small, sapless roots. Similarly, when a rite in its principal form is exhausted through enjoyment, it is unable to keep the agent in that state, and thus it yields a fruit connected with a specific place and so forth. Or it should be viewed like a jar of ghee: just as even when a jar of ghee has been used up, it burns when joined with fire due to the residue of the oily impression (*vāsanā*), so too the performer of the rite will experience a specific place and so forth solely due to the residue of the impression. And because a rite possesses parts (*sāvayavatva*), an impression is indeed possible; and its possession of parts is also due to its being an effect (*kāryatva*).

As for what was said—that human effort (puruṣakāra) is purposeless—it is replied here: only that which is endowed with human effort has a connection with the fruit; for one devoid of it, there is not even a connection with food and such. Therefore, since the previously mentioned cause is the bestowing of the fruit, and human effort is the cause of the connection, human effort is not purposeless; thus, this entire sūtra is indeed logically consistent. 11.31
Moving in all directions, they perish, turned upside down. || 11.32 ||

Furthermore, those who do not perform their own duties (*svakarma*) and are not established by the king are "wandering" (*viśvañcaḥ*); they perish as beings in the animal realm (*tiryaggati*), due to the absence of connection with distinguished places and so forth. Those who are the opposite are "devoted to their own duties" (*svakarmaniṣṭha*). By speaking thus, it is shown that those devoted to their own duties attain the highest state (*uttamagati*), those who are established by the king in their own duty attain the middling state (*madhyamagati*), and those who are neither devoted to their own duties nor established by the king attain the lowest state (*adhamagati*). Thus it is said in the *Purāṇa*:
Through auspicious deeds one becomes a deity; through mixed deeds, a human birth;
and through inauspicious deeds, a person attains a lower rebirth. (11.32)
The teacher’s instruction and punishment protect them. || 11.33 ||

The instruction of the teacher protects those members of the castes and stages of life who are perishing through the non-performance of prescribed duties and the practice of forbidden ones; for others, however, there is punishment. (11.33)
Therefore, the king and the teacher are beyond reproach; they themselves are blameless. || 11.34 ||

And because they serve as the cause of protection, even when harshness and the like are present, they must be spoken of [as such]. Therefore, both the teacher who instructs even what is harsh and the king who maintains even what is fierce are beyond reproach, owing to their being extremely beneficial. 11.34.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Maskarīya-Gautama-bhāṣya*.
The twelfth chapter begins:

"They say that punishment (*daṇḍa*) is so called because of its capacity to subdue (*damana*); therefore, one should subdue those who are unsubdued. This has been stated in general terms. Now, it must be explained what the specific punishment is for which particular offense; thus he says:
A Śūdra who, having deceived or struck the twice-born with verbal or physical violence, shall have that very limb by which he committed the offense cut off. 12.1.

The Śūdra is mentioned. He, having "deceived" (*atisaṃdhāya*)—that is, having intentionally transgressed against—the twice-born, namely the Brāhmaṇas and others who have been initiated (*upanīta*), and not merely through jesting or the like; and having "assaulted" (*abhihatya*)—the prefix *abhi-* being for the purpose of indicating intentional knowledge; having struck them, either sequentially by means of verbal and physical cruelty. In this regard, the sequence should be understood as: having deceived by means of verbal cruelty, and having assaulted by means of physical cruelty. Transgression by means of verbal cruelty consists of speaking harsh words and the like after having transgressed. The word *paruṣa* is a synonym for "fierce. The meaning is: having transgressed with fierce speech and having assaulted with a fierce blow. Consequently, there is no fault [if the injury is caused] by a stone or similar object. An "extremity" (*aṅga*) is a limb of the body; it is "to be cut off" (*mocya*) or severed—that hand or other limb by which he might strike or cause pain. And thus, he makes known that physical cruelty (*daṇḍapāruṣya*) occurs even without an actual weapon. In the case of verbal cruelty, the tongue is to be cut off; in the case of physical cruelty with the hand or other limbs, that specific limb is to be cut off—so it should be understood. From the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it follows that when both offenses are committed, both punishments are to be inflicted. (12.1)
For violating an Arya woman, there shall be the excision of the organ and the confiscation of one's property.

If a woman of noble conduct belongs to Āryas such as Brāhmaṇas and others, [the following applies]. Why is this so? Because although one should have said "sexual intercourse with a woman" (*stry-abhigamana*), the text begins by saying "sexual intercourse with an Ārya woman" (*ārya-strī-abhigamana*). Consequently, if she is present in the form of a prostitute, there is no punishment. Since the term "approaching" (*abhigamana*) is well-established in relation to a woman, the word "woman" (*strī*) was included even though "approaching an Ārya" (*ārya-gamana*) would have sufficed; its purpose is to indicate that this applies even to a Śūdra woman who has been taken into the household of an Ārya. The prefix *abhi-* in "approaching" (*abhigamane*) signifies that the act was intentional. Therefore, in cases where it is done unintentionally—such as during sleep—a lighter punishment is to be understood. "Extraction of the organ" means its removal, and "confiscation of all property" must be carried out. Although one might have said "extraction of that organ and [confiscation] of wealth," the expression "and confiscation of his own [property]" (*sva-haraṇam ca*) is used. The particle *ca* serves to join them together; the lack of a compound (using *ca*) is intended to prevent the implication of an option between the two. In the case of approaching a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman, each respective penalty applies according to the order; however, for a Brāhmaṇa, both penalties apply. (12.2)
If he is the protector, the punishment is death. 12.3.
If he is their protector, then upon having sexual intercourse with them, he must carry out both the previously mentioned acts and, because of his superior status, inflict a capital punishment. 12.3.

Now, for one who eavesdrops upon his Veda, there shall be the filling of the ears with molten tin and lac; for reciting it, the cutting off of the tongue; and for memorizing it, the splitting asunder of the body. 12.4.
This [refers to one] above five years of age, because of the employment of the word *atha*; and likewise another Smṛti states:
"But having heard the Veda, a Śūdra who is five years old becomes liable to punishment;
one who has not reached five years of age does not deserve punishment anywhere."

The word *ha* is for the purpose of indicating that [the act] was intentional (*buddhipūrva*). This word is employed so that it does not apply only to the protector (*goptṛ*). "Veda" means the Veda together with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*). Why? Because of the observation in the Gṛhya-smṛti: "The Veda, along with its auxiliaries, must not be studied in the presence of women or Śūdras. By the prefix *upa*, which signifies proximity, he shows that the fault lies only in the hearing of the syllables (*akṣara*). And therefore, there is no fault in merely hearing the sound (*dhvani*). Since the punishment is prescribed only for intentional acts by the word *ha*, it should be understood that there is an absence of fault even if syllables are heard occasionally through negligence. It should be understood as "with tin and lac," meaning with tin and with lac; and it should be understood as "with [them] heated," because of the force of the instruction regarding filling [the ears]. The prefix *prati* is for the purpose of including both ears. In the case of reciting (*udāharaṇa*), the tongue should be cut off by the twice-born along with [the offender]; in the case of memorizing (*dhāraṇa*), the meaning is that one should cut off one's own tongue. With an axe (*paraśu*), the body should be split. (12.4)
One who seeks to obtain [another's] seat, bed, speech, or path shall be fined.

Desiring equality with the noble ones in matters such as seating according to his own wish—equality regarding qualities such as the height of seats meaning verbal parity and simultaneous utterance; equality on the road meaning traveling together rather than following behind; the punishment should be understood as being less than one hundred [paṇas], depending on the circumstances such as the location. (12.5)
A Kṣatriya [should pay] one hundred [paṇas] for insulting a Brāhmaṇa. || 12.6 ||

The word "committed" (*kṛta*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Regarding verbal abuse (*ākrośa*), that is, harshness of speech; however, in the case of physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*), double the fine should be prescribed, according to the force of other legal codes (*smṛti*). And so says Bṛhaspati: "When verbal abuse has been committed against someone for which a certain punishment is ordained, one should cause double that punishment to be inflicted, except in the case of death."

And thus Uśanas said: "In the case of threatening, the penalty is equal to that for verbal abuse; in the case of striking, it is double that; in the case of drawing blood, it is triple," and so forth. A Kṣatriya should be fined one hundred kārṣāpaṇas for insulting a Brāhmaṇa. (12.6)
A Vaiśya [should give] one and a half [times]. || 12.7 ||

The phrase "insulting a Brahmin" continues [from the previous rule]. That which is one hundred increased by half is "one hundred and fifty"; for insulting a Brahmin, a Vaiśya shall be fined that amount.
But a Brāhmaṇa [should pay] fifty [paṇas] for a Kṣatriya. 12.8.

The phrase "when reviled" (ākruṣṭe) continues to apply here. When a Brāhmaṇa reviles a Kṣatriya, the Brāhmaṇa shall be fined fifty [paṇas] if he is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*). Why? Because of the inclusion of the word "but" (*tu*). Among those of equal caste, the fine is twelve; in cases where [the reviler] should not be addressed, double that amount should be prescribed. And so says Manu:
"For among the twice-born of equal caste, when there is an offense, the fine is exactly twelve. In disputes where one should not be addressed, that same fine shall be doubled. [MDh 8.269]
Half of that [is the period] for a Vaiśya. || 12.9 ||
If a Vaiśya is abused, a Brāhmaṇa should be fined twenty-five [paṇas]. || 12.9 ||
For a Śūdra, there is nothing [to be done]. || 12.10 ||

When reviled, a Brāhmaṇa is not to be fined at all. If it is argued that this is established simply by his remaining silent, we say no; for the purpose [of the rule] is to impose a fine upon the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. Thus, a fine should be prescribed in their case: twenty-four paṇas for a Kṣatriya and thirty-six for a Vaiśya. Accordingly, Uśanas says: "Having reviled a Śūdra, a Kṣatriya shall incur a fine of twenty-four [paṇas], and a Vaiśya thirty-six," and so forth. (12.10)
The Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya are like the Brāhmaṇa and the Rājanya.

What has been stated regarding mutual verbal abuse between a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya should also be understood to apply to a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya—the fine being one hundred for the Kṣatriya and fifty for the Vaiśya. The same should be understood to apply to those born of intermediate castes as well. Thus says Jamadagni: "For those born in the natural order (anuloma), the status is equal to that of the mother; for those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), it is equal to that of the father. (12.11)
Having stated the punishment for violence, he now speaks regarding theft:
"The guilt of theft for a Śūdra is eightfold. (12.12)

That property which has been acquired through theft for the sake of unrighteousness is called by the word *kilbiṣa*; the meaning is that it is "the sin of theft" or "stolen wealth. An eightfold fine is the punishment for this. Regarding the rule "one who seeks to recover [stolen goods] shall be fined" (GDh 12.5), the word *daṇḍya* (to be fined) is here transformed into *daṇḍa* (fine) in accordance with the genitive case, following the analogy of the flow of a river. Alternatively, the word *kilbiṣa* denotes the punishment itself; thus, *steyakilbiṣa* means "the punishment for theft. That [fine] should be taken as eightfold. In this context, however, one must exclude gold belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, because since its theft is taught among the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), the severity of the punishment for it is greater. (12.12)
For the other castes, the [distances] double at each successive stage.

For the others—namely the Vaiśya, the Kṣatriya, and the Brāhmaṇa—the fines are double for each successive caste in reverse order (*prātilomya*), as indicated by the phrase "for each caste" at the beginning; that is, each subsequent fine is double the preceding one. Thus, for a Vaiśya it is sixteenfold, for a Kṣatriya thirty-twofold, and for a Brāhmaṇa sixty-fourfold. In all cases, the restoration of the wealth to the owner must be understood, because it has been stated: "Having recovered what was stolen by thieves, he should restore it to its proper place" (GDh 10.46). 12.13.
In the case of an offense committed against a learned man, the punishment shall be more severe. || 12.14 ||

Just as there is an increase in punishment based on the excellence of caste, so too it should be understood that there is an increase in punishment due to the excellence of knowledge, because another Smṛti text states: "That [punishment] for a learned man should be known to be one and a half times that prescribed for his own caste. And this is logical, since it says, "He transgresses after having known [the law]. Once it is established that there is a greater punishment for the learned, the mention of "transgression" is for the sake of restriction; this applies only to the case of theft, not to the case of violence (*sāhasa*), nor even to the case of penance (*prāyaścitta*). By speaking thus, it is demonstrated that from the prescription of punishment, there is also a determination of the relative gravity or lightness of the penance. And what was stated in the section on violence—"half the punishment for a *Śrotriya*"—is likewise justified. (12.14)
He states an exception to this:
"In the case of taking fruit, green vegetables, grain, or potherbs, [the fine is] five *kṛṣṇalas* when the amount is small. (12.15)

In the case of stealing fruits such as mangoes, green grain such as rice and the like—meaning while they are unripe—and vegetables such as radishes and the like, the fine is one *māṣa*. Why? Because another Smṛti text states: "A *māṣa* consists of five *kṛṣṇalas*" (MDh 8.134). This applies when the amount is small, merely enough to fill the stomach; for a larger quantity or other types of goods, this very rule of "eightfold" (GDh 12.12) should be understood to apply. || 12.15 ||
When cattle are harmed, the fault lies with the owner. 12.16.
When crops and other produce are damaged by cattle, the punishment for the owner of those cattle will be stated hereafter. || 12.16 ||
But when that [body] is joined with a protector (pāla), || 12.17 ||

The meaning is that when the act is accompanied by a keeper, the keeper alone bears the penalty. The word *tu* (but) is intended to indicate that the penalty is greater when the act was caused by the keeper. This greater degree is indeed twofold, as seen in another Smṛti text: "When caused by a keeper, the penalty is double. (12.17)
On a path or in an uncultivated field, [the responsibility for damage falls] on both the herdsman and the owner of the field. || 12.18 ||
The meaning is that because the guardian acts without effort and the other likewise fails to perform his duty, they both shall pay half and half. 12.18.
Now he states the specific fines with respect to specific animals:
"Five māṣas for a cow. (12.19)
A *māṣa* is one-twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*. Thus says Uśanas:
"A *māṣa* should be known as one-twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*;
a *kākaṇī*, moreover, is proclaimed to be one-fourth part of a *māṣa*."
