For these five offenses, he shall be punished with the five products of the cow.
Six [mātrās] for a camel or a donkey. || 12.20 ||
For an offense against a camel and for an offense against a donkey, the fine shall be six māṣas in each case. || 12.20 ||
Ten [times] for a horse and a buffalo. 12.21.
In this case as well, the fine for each individual shall be ten māṣas. || 12.21 ||
In goats and sheep, there are two each.

The plural number is used for the purpose of excluding calves; that [plural] should also be understood in the preceding case. Two māṣas each is the fine. The statement of repetition at the end is for the sake of applying it to the preceding cases as well; otherwise, there would be doubt. (12.22)
There is a fine for total destruction. || 12.23 ||

If there is the capacity for regrowth despite total destruction, the owner of the field shall be given a share of the fruit proportionate to the extent of what was destroyed, after considering the yield; and the king shall impose a corresponding fine. (12.23)
If he fails to perform his prescribed duties and engages in forbidden practices, he shall, after three years, forfeit his right to the rag-robe and must provide for himself.

If one constantly fails to perform what is prescribed for the virtuous (*śiṣṭa*), that is, constantly neglects what is enjoined—not merely once—and if one habitually indulges in what is forbidden, such as eating forbidden food (*abhakṣya*) and so forth—not out of negligence—then a seizure of property must be carried out, except for a mere lump of alms-food and clothing sufficient for food and shelter. However, food and clothing must be released to him until there is an acquisition of other property; even after that, if he exceeds [the limit], his own property must again be seized from him. When this is done, through fear of punishment, he will engage only in his own proper work. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that he must also be made to perform penance (*prāyaścitta*). (12.24)

Now he states an exception to the prohibition against taking what is not given, which was mentioned in the section on the student (brahmacārin): "For the sake of cows or for the sake of fire, one may take grass, fuel, and the flowers of herbs and trees as if they were one's own; and likewise fruits from those that are unenclosed. (12.25)

Grass for the sake of cattle; by the mention of "fire," both the Vedic (*śrauta*) and the Smārta fires are included, but not the worldly fire; for their sake, fuel-wood (*edhas*); and the flowers of shrubs (*vīrudh*), such as the *karavīra* and others—the word "forest-tree" (*vanaspati*) here is a synonym for "tree," because flowers do not directly grow on [the category of] forest-trees. As Manu says: "Those which bear fruit but have no flowers are known as forest-trees" (MDh 1.47).

Flowers are for the purpose of worshipping the gods, not for one's own enjoyment, because of their association with cows and fire. By the use of the word "ca" (and), it is implied that leaves are for the purpose of feeding Brāhmaṇas. While it could have been stated as "the flowers of herbs and trees," the use of the compound *oṣadhārtham* (for the sake of herbs) and the lack of a compound in *mūlāder api brāhmaṇārtham* (even roots, etc., for the sake of Brāhmaṇas) indicates that even roots and so forth are intended for Brāhmaṇas. The term *svavat* means that they should be taken in such a way that no injury is caused to them. As Vyāsa has said: "One should pluck what is ripe again and again, but one should avoid cutting the root; like a gardener in a grove, not like a charcoal-maker."

"Fruits" refers to mangoes and the like; they are mentioned separately for the purpose of indicating times of distress (*āpad*). By the word "and" (*ca*), vegetables are also included. "Of those not enclosed" means those that have not been made into a monastery garden (*ārāma*); this qualifies both [fruits and vegetables]. Thus, it is established that even grass and such are prohibited within a monastery garden. (12.25)

Now, since taking the property of another even by means of legal right constitutes theft, this [rule] is commenced for the purpose of avoiding that: "Interest on a loan is lawful at the rate of five *māṣas* per month for every twenty [units of principal]. (MDh 8.142)

Lending capital is *kusīda*. In that context, "interest" (*vṛddhi*) means accumulation; "lawful" (*dharmyā*) means not departing from the law. When twenty *kārṣāpaṇas* are lent for one month, then its interest per month is of the measure of five *māṣas*; the meaning is that the interest per month is the measure of half a *guñjā* of a *niṣka*. By the word *māṣa*, an object measured by a grain of rice is denoted. And thus, the taking of exactly the eightieth part as stated by Manu is accomplished. As Manu said:

"One should grant the interest prescribed by Vasiṣṭha, which increases wealth; a moneylender may take an eightieth part of a hundred per month" (MDh 8.140). Regarding that which was prescribed by Vasiṣṭha: "Or one may give at will to a more wicked person who has failed in his duties" (VaDh 2.43). In the case of gold and kārṣāpaṇas, it becomes a sixty-fourth part: "Sixteen of those [kārṣāpaṇas] make one suvarṇa" (YDh 1.358). || 12.26 ||
Some say that it should not exceed one year. 12.27.

Some maintain that interest accruing beyond a month—that is, annual interest—should not be accepted. This is what is meant: one should not think, "I shall collect everything that ought to be collected month by month all at once when the year is complete," and thus accept it only once every year. Because of this prohibition against annual collection, monthly and six-monthly collection is permitted. Therefore, the opinion of some is that interest should be collected month by month or every six months, but not annually. And this should be understood to apply specifically to the acceptance of monthly interest. Gautama holds that as long as there is financial transaction with the debtor, interest must indeed be accepted; however, upon the cessation of that relationship, the established rule "not exceeding the annual amount" (NS 3.51) should be observed. (MDh 8.152)
In a long-term loan, there is a doubling of the principal.

When interest has been outstanding for a long time and remains uncollected, it ceases to increase beyond the point at which the principal becomes double by means of that interest; after that, it does not grow further. The inclusion of the term "loan" (prayoga) is intended to prevent the doubling limit from being exceeded in the case of a different transaction. As Manu says:
"Interest on a loan, when stipulated once, does not exceed the doubling [of the principal]" (MDh 8.151).

The mention of "place" (*sthāna*) is for the purpose of making known that the doubling limit applies specifically to gold; grains and other items continue to increase even beyond double. Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "Gold [may be increased] twofold, grain threefold; liquids are explained by [the rule for] grain, as are flowers, roots, and fruits; and what is weighed on a scale [is increased] eightfold" (VaDh 2.44–47). By speaking in this way, it is shown that the interest which is declared to be lawful for usury is universal; otherwise, since the case of gold would already be established by the context, the mention of "place" for its sake would be useless. Consequently, one should understand that the one-eighth part applies everywhere. The inclusion of the word "long" (*cira*) indicates that it does not increase even over thousands of years. (12.28)
A pledge that has been used does not increase [in value]. || 12.29 ||
In that case, enjoyment itself becomes the increase. || 12.29 ||
Furthermore: "And for one who desires to give, and for one who is obstructed. (12.30)

When a creditor who wishes to give [the loan] does not accept it under some pretext out of greed for interest, then [the debt] ceases to increase even from that point. He who wishes to give must establish a formal agreement (*saṃsthā*) with witnesses, because of the potential failure of mental discernment due to ignorance. And "one who is thus obstructed" means one who has become destitute and gone to another country; the word "and" (*ca*) is used so that there may be no doubt regarding the preceding qualification. It should be understood as starting from that very day. Some say it refers to imprisonment by the king or others; in this matter, the Brahmins (*bhūmideva*) are the authority. (12.30)
Now, in times of distress, the various forms of interest contracted by oneself are permitted: compound interest (cakravṛddhi) and periodical interest (kālavṛddhi). 12.31.
The word *vṛddhi* (interest) is connected with each term individually. *Cakravṛddhi*: that application of capital in which interest itself increases further is *cakravṛddhi*. As Nārada says:
"Interest upon interest is declared to be *cakravṛddhi*" [NSm 1.89].

*Āravṛddhi* (interest based on time): Having made an agreement such as, "This must be paid to me either before this time by simple interest alone, or by the stipulated interest; if you do not pay it, then after that time, threefold or fourfold [the principal] must be paid," that interest which is taken to be large is *kālavṛddhi*. Even though the stipulated interest has already been obtained, the taking of further interest is permitted; this arrangement applies only to what was agreed upon by oneself, and not to that which is limited to five *māṣas*. The mention together [with the stipulated interest] implies that if one means of livelihood is impossible, there is no fault in living by both.

But is it not the case that this should have been stated right there [in GDh 12.26]: “The lawful interest on a loan is twenty [paṇas] per month, consisting of five māṣas”? Since it is taught separately here, its purpose is understood to be for times of distress (*āpad*). Furthermore, by the maxim that “the understanding of a specific distinction arises from the commentary,” it can be known through the commentary alone that the rule “not exceeding one year” (GDh 12.27) refers specifically to interest measured at five *māṣas*.

To this it is replied: In the case of a lazy person, whether in times of distress or non-distress, and in the case of one who does not perform the work himself in times of non-distress, he should accept only five māṣas; however, in times of distress, even when the work is not performed by himself, he should not accept interest such as that of the water-wheel (cakravṛddhi) and the like. The instruction is given with this intention. Furthermore, the instruction following the rule “not for more than a year” (GDh 12.27) is also for the purpose of clarifying that point. || 12.31 ||
And [the fruits] consisting of activity, body, crest-ornament, and mastery. || 12.32 ||

*Kāritā* interest is that which is made by the debtor himself, independent of the creditor’s instruction, such as the agreement that "one-quarter, one-half, or some other portion of a *niṣka* shall be paid every year. *Kāyikā* interest is that which, in addition to the agreed-upon interest, is taken day by day, month by month, or year by year; it is so called because it is "bodily" (*kāyikā*) attached to the person. And thus says Nārada:
"That which does not conflict with the body, being constant, and consisting of an additional quarter of a *paṇa* or similar amount. (NSm 1.88)

The *śikhā* is the interest on grain, such as the fifth [unit] out of four *prasthas*, and so forth. *Adhibhoga* refers to that for the sake of which clarified butter and the like are taken day after day for the purpose of interest; this is *adhibhogavṛddhi*. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to draw in the term "interest" (*vṛddhi*). It is mentioned separately for the purpose of showing its distinct nature. (12.32)
One should not lend [money] at interest exceeding five percent on cattle, wool, fields, and debtors who have fled. || 12.33 ||

Although the term *kusīda* (loan) has already been introduced, its mention here again is made for the purpose of indicating that this form of transaction is of a different nature. The intention is that regarding livestock products such as ghee and the like, it is stipulated that after purchasing them, "the price must be paid at such-and-such a time; if it is not paid then, it shall increase. The use of the prefix *upa-* in the word *upajā* is intended to exclude the calf itself from being included. *Loman* refers to wool and the like. It should be understood that by the mention of the raw material (*prakṛti*), its derivatives are also included. This applies specifically when even the price for those items is not paid. Regarding land (*kṣetra*): when a field is used for a fixed amount of grain, the fee for it increases if it is not paid at that time. Regarding transport (*vāhya*): for the purpose of conveying goods, as when someone causes grain to be brought by means of oxen and so forth, the fee for it increases if it is not paid at that time. The meaning is that among these, whatever loan was advanced is to be returned with interest later; that does not exceed fivefold. Although the mention of "livestock products" (*paśūpaja*) already establishes the inclusion of wool, its separate mention is for the sake of including items made from peacock feathers, as seen in the Vedic text: "O Agni, speak for me regarding the wings and the feathers of birds, as I have heard. If it is argued that this should have been stated right where it says, "In a long-term loan, the principal becomes double" (GDh 12.28), there is no fault in this; the instruction here is for the purpose of making known that these cases lack the application of compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*). Since the fivefold limit is already established by the phrase "fivefold," the use of the word *ati* (exceeding) is to indicate that this limit may be exceeded in other forms of transactions. (12.33)

Now another legal proceeding is stated: Property belonging to one who is neither an idiot nor a minor, if it has been enjoyed by others for ten years in the presence of the owner, belongs to the enjoyer. (12.34)

A *jaḍa* is one whose mind is deluded and thus unfit for worldly transactions; a *pogaṇḍa* is one who has not yet attained legal capacity. Excluding these two, if the property of another is enjoyed by others who are unrelated to him—in the presence of the owner (meaning while the owner is residing in the same village)—that property belongs to the enjoyer alone after ten years. The underlying intention is that such long-term neglect would not be possible if ownership still existed. However, the property of a *jaḍa* or a minor is not to be confiscated. The mention of these two is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for deposits and other such items. As Nārada says: [text follows].
“A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property, and the property of a Vedic scholar do not become lost through adverse possession.

[NSm 1.73] If it is argued that the property of one who is not mentally incompetent (*ajaḍa*) was not included here, it is so that even after twenty years, such property shall not suffer loss through adverse possession. As Nārada has said:

"And due to direct enjoyment by the owner, [the property] is lost after twenty years; even mortgages and the like may be forfeited, except for the property of a woman or a king. [NSm 1.74] And thus, the property of a minor is indeed lost after twenty years. By the word "in the presence of" (*saṃnidhau*) alone, the point is already established for others; therefore, the inclusion of the word "other" (*para-*) is for the purpose of making known that there is no transgression when the relative himself enjoys the property. Because of the mention of "presence," there is no fault in the case of one residing in another village. (12.34)
He states an exception to this rule by means of a specific type of enjoyer.
Nor with Vedic scholars, renunciants, or royal officials. || 12.35 ||

Even when being used by a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) and others, it is not taken away, because a reason for indifference is present: the learned scholar and the renunciant (*pravrajita*) are overlooked due to a thirst for dharma, while the king’s officer is [overlooked] out of fear. If it is asked how this applies to the renunciant, it is said in response: it is indeed possible, because of the instruction on the impression (*vāsanā*) of living in an empty house, as in the case of a renunciant who remains in an empty house. 12.35.
Now he states an exception based on the specific nature of the object being used: "In the case of cattle, land, and women, there is no offense for moderate use. (12.36)

By the word *paśu* (livestock), all four-footed animals fit for sacrifice are understood, based on the Vedic revelation: "Four-footed animals are indeed those fit for sacrifice. *Bhūmi* (land) refers to fields, gardens, and the like, but not houses, according to the statement of Auśanas: "Land does not belong to the occupant after ten years from the house. *Striyaḥ* (women) refers to female attendants. The meaning of "non-excessive enjoyment" (*anatibhoga*) of these is that ownership does not arise through enjoyment for ten years. And so says Nārada: "But that which has been enjoyed without legal title, even for hundreds of years... [NSm 1.75].
This statement as well has been explained as referring to the domain of cattle, the earth, and women. || 12.36 ||
Those who inherit the estate shall discharge the debt.

The meaning is that those who enjoy and take possession of his wealth shall pay that debt, and not merely by virtue of being an heir. The plural number is used to include those who take the son or the wife as well. Thus says Nārada: "Among the taker of wealth, the taker of the wife, and the son, he who takes the wealth shall bear the debt;
the son [bears it] when the wife and the owner of the wealth are absent; the taker of the wife [bears it] when the son and the wealth are absent. [NSm 1.20]

Thus, whether or not there is a son, the debt must necessarily be paid by the one who takes the woman's property and by those others who are heirs to the estate; however, it should be understood that among sons, only those who possess the status of heirs to the estate shall pay the debt, and not every son merely by virtue of being a son. (12.37)
Now he states an exception regarding the son:
"Surety-money, trade-duties, fines for liquor, gambling, and judicial penalties shall not devolve upon sons. (MDh 6.38)
There are three types of sureties. As Vyāghra has stated:
"The witness of the foot, the trustworthy one, and the provider of funds are thus proclaimed.
Here, with the exception of the surety for payment, the other two are intended. Why?
When the master of the gift has died, he should cause even the heirs to give it. [MDh 8.161]

This is because of the statement of Manu: "The debt contracted on account of a surety (*prātibhāvya*) is that which is caused by a guarantor; likewise, the debt of a merchant is that which is caused by trade. The meaning is as follows: if someone, having agreed, "I will pay the price," takes goods from another's possession and goes to another country for the purpose of trading, but dies, and that [debt] remains unpaid, then the intention is that this debt does not fall upon the son. Regarding the *śulka* (bride-price): if, after promising a bride-price in an *āsura* or other form of marriage and having performed the wedding, the person dies, that bride-price does not fall upon the son. Regarding *madya* (liquor): since liquor is forbidden for a Brāhmaṇa, this should be understood as referring to Kṣatriyas and others. If, after saying, "I will give the money," he drinks liquor and dies without giving the money, that [debt] also does not belong to the son. Likewise, there is the debt caused by gambling, and likewise the debt caused by fines resulting from losing a legal suit. "These shall not extend to the sons" means they do not fall upon the sons; this is to be understood provided the son is an heir (*rikthabhāk*). (12.38)
Deposits, pledges, borrowed goods, purchases, and trusts that have been lost—all these are not to be blamed when there has been no fault on the part of the person.

A *nidhi* is a deposit; a *nikṣepa* is a sealed deposit; an *anvādhi* is a pledge for use; an *upanidhi* is a deposit placed in the hand of another; a *yācita* is an ornament or similar item brought by request for festivals and other occasions; an *avakrīta* is something borrowed without payment or with only half-payment; an *ādhi* refers to a pledge for custody, such as a bronze vessel or the like. If these items are lost through theft, fire, or other such causes, they do not fall upon the sons alone. What then? They fall upon those in whose presence the deposits and other items were made, as indicated by the use of the word "all" (*sarva*). This means those who are blameless and have acted with care. Provided they are lost without fault on the part of the person (the keeper). "Fault of the person" (*puruṣāparādha*) means negligence or laziness on the part of the person. Thus, if they are lost through the fault of those who are blameworthy and negligent, they must indeed be restored. (12.39)

If no one among these—sons and the rest—were to discharge the debt owed to the father, he would become a thief; since the punishment for such theft has been ordained by the rule, "The guilt of theft is eightfold" (GDh 12.12), it is in this very context that the punishment for a stealer of gold is also stated:
"A thief, with disheveled hair and carrying a club, shall go to the king confessing his deed.

A thief is one who steals gold; however, for those who steal other types of property, it has been stated that they undergo "the eightfold downfall," and this is also seen from other Smṛti texts. A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king, should confess his own deed and say: "May Your Majesty punish me. (MDh 11.99)
In the section on punishments, the instruction regarding going forth is for the purpose of expiation. And so says Manu:
"But men who have committed sins, having been punished by kings, go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed meritorious deeds. (MDh 8.318)

When theft has been committed, one becomes a thief. Theft is the taking away of another's property; this [penalty] applies only to cases where there is intentional agency, for unintentional theft is not possible. However, this should be understood to apply when a great amount has been stolen, since no specific distinction is made. With disheveled hair—that is, with loose hair—regarding himself as equal to a corpse, carrying a club in his hand as the means of his own execution, he should go to the king, declaring his deed: "I am a thief. (12.40)
Then he was thus established, purified by both death and liberation. 12.41.

"He becomes purified and cleansed. This refers to either execution or killing, or alternatively, to liberation from it. "Execution" (*vadha*) means beating; and that too should be done only once, as seen in another Smṛti text: "Having seized the mace, the king himself shall strike him only once" (MDh 11.100). In this regard, it should be understood that even if he does not die after being struck by the king without hesitation, he nevertheless becomes purified. Furthermore, this beating applies to non-Brāhmaṇas, because it will be stated later: "There is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 12.43). And so says Manu:
"A thief is purified by execution, or a Brāhmaṇa by austerity alone. (MDh 11.100)

In this very context, the Commentator has explained the restrictive particle *eva* as meaning "the Brāhmaṇa [is freed] by penance alone. Consequently, it should be understood that for a non-Brāhmaṇa there is beating, while for a Brāhmaṇa there is release (*mokṣa*). Nevertheless, in the case where a Brāhmaṇa goes of his own accord, there is release; however, for one who is brought by force, both release and penance should be understood. Likewise, in all cases, when one goes of one's own accord, both punishment and expiation (*prāyaścitta*) should be understood. As for penance, in the case of stealing gold from a Brāhmaṇa who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), the *sāntapana* penance should be observed. Thus says Manu: [Manu 11.100] "For stealing gold from a Brāhmaṇa who is not learned in the Vedas, the king shall prescribe the *sāntapana* penance. Thus it is said.
"He shall perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance for the sake of his own purification. (MDh 11.124)

It should be understood that "returns" (niryātya) follows as the remainder of all thefts. Regarding the *śrotriya*, that which was stated by Āpastamba should be consulted: "Having committed theft, drunk liquor, or violated the teacher's wife, but not having committed the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), they should eat limited food at every fourth mealtime," and so forth. If one asks how there is greater gravity regarding a *śrotriya*, it is because it has been stated: "In the case of an offense against a learned man, the punishment is more severe" (GDh 12.14). However, in the case of stealing gold from a *śrotriya* Brāhmaṇa, this same [penance] for a non-*śrotriya* should be seen as lasting six years for a *śrotriya*. As Uśanas said: "One who steals gold should perform the vow for six years, even if he is a Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, when a penance is combined even for a Kṣatriya, then in the case of stealing gold from a non-*śrotriya*, the penance prescribed by Bhṛgu for a *śrotriya* should be observed.
"He who would take the property of a Brāhmaṇa should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances.

Regarding the taking of the property of one who is not a Śrotriya, the previously mentioned rule of Auśanasa is to be observed. However, for the theft of the property of a Śrotriya, this very same penance is doubled, according to the statement of Kaṇva: "In the case of stealing the property of a Śrotriya, the penance is double. For a Vaiśya as well, the rule should be understood to be like that for a Kṣatriya, based on the statement of Auśanasa: "The punishment for a thief from a Vaiśya is the same as for a Kṣatriya. Regarding the theft of the property of a Śrotriya, [the text continues]:
"But he who desires to remove the impurity born of stealing gold by means of austerity..."

Or it should be understood as stated by Manu: "A twice-born man, clothed in bark, shall perform the vow for the slayer of a Brahmin in the forest" (MDh 11.101). Regarding the expiation for a Śūdra, in all cases, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "Alternatively, having smeared himself with clarified butter, he should burn himself from the feet upward with a fire of cow-dung, remaining naked" (VaDh 20.42). Furthermore, the gravity or lightness of the expiation must be determined according to the value of the stolen property. Why? Because, in the same way, for measurable things, there is death for stealing more than one hundred.

This is because of the indicative mark [in the text]. Punishment by the king applies only when the value exceeds one *kārṣāpaṇa*; in all other cases, however, only release should be understood. Entry into the entirety of the penance occurs only when the value exceeds one *kārṣāpaṇa*. And it should be understood that "half [the penance] for half [the value], and a quarter for a quarter. For a Śūdra, the penance should be determined as for a Vaiśya, according to the statement of Śaṅkha: "In the absence of any reduction, the penance for a Śūdra should be determined as for a Vaiśya. (12.41)
A king who does not strike is a sinner. 12.42.

By failing to execute [the offender] out of compassion and other such motives, the king becomes a sinner; the meaning is that he incurs as much sin as the thief possesses. And so says another Smṛti: "He incurs the guilt of the thief" (NSm 19.56). Just as there is a fault in not killing one who deserves to be killed, so too should a fault be seen in not releasing one who deserves to be released. And thus Vasiṣṭha says: "The guilt reaches the king who releases the offender along with his crime" (VaDh 19.46). || 12.42 ||
There shall be no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa. || 12.43 ||
Even for one who has appeared before him voluntarily, that corporal punishment which is execution does not exist for a Brāhmaṇa; therefore, it must not be carried out. [Objection:
But surely, even by means of other punishments such as the deprivation of rights and so forth, the cessation of the body's [function] occurs.
[Reply: It is true. However, this introduction is for the purpose of prohibiting corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa in cases of other offenses. (12.43)
If that is so, how is he to be disciplined? To this he says:
"Exile, public proclamation of his crime, banishment, and branding. (12.44)

The meaning is that one must act in such a way that the person does not commit that same deed again. "Proclamation" (*vikhyāpana*) means causing the person to wander everywhere with the mark of theft. "Banishment" (*vivāsana*) means depriving them of their territory. "Branding" (*aṅkana*) means making a mark upon the body. As Manu says: "For violating the Guru’s bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a liquor-jar; for theft, the foot of a dog should be made; but for the slayer of a Brahmin, a headless male figure. [MDh 9.237]
The appropriate punishment for these should be determined in consideration of their repetition. 12.44.
If he does not return, he must perform penance. || 12.45 ||

When this has been done, that king becomes liable for penance (*prāyaścitta*). However, the specific penance is to be determined from another Smṛti text. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Upon the release of one who deserves punishment, the king shall fast for one night, and the domestic priest for three nights; in the case of punishing one who does not deserve punishment, the domestic priest shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance and the king for three nights" (VaDh 19.40–43). || 12.45 ||
A minister who acts with deliberate intent is equal to a thief. 12.46.
A minister or associate of a thief who intentionally provides food and other necessities should be punished like a thief; however, there is no fault in such an act if it was unintentional. 12.46.
The recipient as well [is not purified] when [the gift] is joined with unrighteousness. || 12.47 ||

The phrase "intentionally" (*matipūrva*) carries over [from the previous verse]. Although the recipient is also included because the thief is the subject under discussion, the explicit mention of "one associated with unrighteousness" (*adharmasaṃyukta*) is intended to show that for whatever sin a person commits, the recipient who accepts it intentionally incurs the same penance as the perpetrator—for instance, the penance for one who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), and so forth. However, if the act is unintentional (*abuddhipūrva*), a lighter penance should be prescribed. (12.47)
The application of punishment follows from the knowledge of the continuity of the offender's personal capacity and transgression.

The meaning is: having ascertained birth and so forth from the testimony of the person. *Śakti* refers to weakness and the like; *aparādha* refers to acts such as speaking with insolence. As Vasiṣṭha says: “A thief is not considered guilty merely by entering [the house]; however, one who carries a weapon, one who was caught in the act (*sahoḍha*), or one who has wounds—these are [guilty], according to some. *Anubandha* refers to the intent or resolve. Having taken these factors into account, the infliction of punishment must be carried out. (12.48)
Or there is permission [to eat it] because of the statement of an assembly of those who know the Vedas, because of the statement of an assembly of those who know the Vedas. 12.49.
Alternatively, liberation may be achieved through the word of the assembly (*saṅgha*) of those who know the Vedas. An assembly is a gathering of four or three. As Manu has said:
"Whether they be four or even three who have mastered the Vedas, what they declare should be known as Dharma; not that of thousands of others."
Or [it may be done] with the permission of the assembly of at least ten members to be mentioned later. And in this way, the fault in performing it oneself should be observed. 12.49.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Maskarīya-gautama-bhāṣya*.
Regarding the thirteenth chapter:
the punishment for verbal abuse when there is agreement has been stated; however, as to what happens when they disagree, he says the following:
In the case of a dispute, the determination of truth is based on witnesses. 13.1.

"Vipratipatti" refers to various types of conflicting claims by the plaintiff and the defendant. When such a conflict exists, a determination of the truth—establishing the facts—must be made based on witnesses. There are five kinds of witnesses, as Nārada has stated:
"The written witness, the reminded witness, the voluntary witness, the cognizant witness, and the secret witness; these are recorded as the five kinds of witnesses. (NSm 1.130)

The meaning is that the realization of the truth comes from deliberating upon them. Although it should have been stated simply that "truth is based on witnesses," the inclusion of the term "decision" (*vyavasthā*) is for the purpose of indicating that when witnesses disagree, the testimony of the majority is authoritative; and even in case of doubt regarding that, it is for the purpose of establishing that the matter must be determined by those very witnesses after they have taken an oath. 13.1.
Furthermore, as to how many they should be and what their characteristics are, he says:
"They should be many, blameless in their own duties, and trustworthy to the kings.
The meaning is that there should be many, at least three; as Manu says:
"There should be at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and the Brahmins" (MDh 8.61).

The inclusion of the word "syuḥ" (should be) is for the purpose of removing doubt. "Aninditāḥ" means those who perform their own duties by carrying out what is prescribed. The inclusion of the word "sva" (own) implies even wealth, sons, and so forth; as Manu says: "Householders, having sons, and being honorable," and so on. The plural number in "karmasu" (in duties) is for the purpose of including even those duties prescribed for times of distress. "Prātyayikāḥ" refers to those who act with confidence toward kings; they are those who have been tested in many tasks by kings and are determined to be entirely vigilant in all matters. By virtue of the plural number, this includes the members of the assembly and others appointed by the king. (13.2)
And in one [of these two], there is freedom from both delight and distress. (13.3)

"Free from affection and free from aversion" means they have neither formed attachments nor enmities; by the word "and" (ca), it is implied that they are neither interested parties (*arthasaṃbandhin*) nor relatives (*āpta*). Thus Manu says: "Neither interested parties, nor relatives, nor allies, nor enemies...
[MDh 8.64], and so forth. "In one of the two" means either in the plaintiff (*arthin*) or in the defendant (*pratyarthin*). || 13.3 ||
Even Śūdras. 13.4.
Such are even the Śūdras; how much more so the twice-born (dvijātayaḥ)! Thus, it should be understood that such Śūdras are also [eligible] only in the absence of virtuous twice-born and others. 13.4.
But a Brahmin, if he is not bound by the word of a non-Brahmin, is not to be detained. 13.5.

A non-Brāhmaṇa is one such as a Kṣatriya and so forth. Although the term "non-Brāhmaṇa" alone would have sufficed, the inclusion of the word "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of selecting those who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*). The meaning is that others are indeed acceptable, but specifically Brāhmaṇas are not to be accepted. Because of the mention of "non-Brāhmaṇa," one who is not to be excluded is not to be accepted; the sense is that if a non-Brāhmaṇa says, "This Brāhmaṇa is the witness to this matter," he must not be accepted as a witness by the king. Furthermore, if a Brāhmaṇa is "unregistered," meaning if he has not been entered upon a formal document, [he is not to be accepted]; the intention is that if he has been registered, he certainly is. (13.5)
Those who are not members of the assembly shall not speak unless they have been questioned. 13.6.

However many witnesses may have assembled together, even if they are gathered in one place, they shall not speak unless questioned by the king or the judge. The inclusion of the word "pra" (in *prabrūyuḥ*) implies that until the questioning begins, they should remain silent regarding their involvement in the matter. 13.6.
Furthermore: "And they would be at fault if they did not speak. (13.7)
Even at the time of questioning, by the force of the word "and" (*ca*), those who fail to speak or speak otherwise shall be guilty and subject to punishment. Thus says Manu:
"One should either not enter the court, or one should speak the truth; for a man who remains silent or speaks falsely becomes a sinner. (MDh 8.13)
Therefore, the intention is that only the truth should be spoken. || 13.7 ||
It is not merely that there is an absence of punishment for truthful speech; rather, in the opposite case, there is indeed the liability to punishment. What then?
Heaven results from truthful speech, and hell from its opposite. (13.8)

From the dharma caused by truthful speech, heaven is attained; conversely, from the adharma caused by untruthful speech, hell is attained. This result belongs to the witnesses because of their speaking, and not to the king, who is the cause of the legal settlement.
Now, as to how it should be in a case where even the five kinds of witnesses are not available, he says: "It may also be stated by those who are not [formally] enrolled. (13.9)

"Nibaddhāḥ" means definitely bound; that is to say, they are recorded as being of five kinds. Those who are not recorded as being of five kinds are "anibaddhāḥ," meaning those who know of their activities [the witnesses'] in some way or another and reside in their village. They too must speak. The word "api" (also/even) is intended to indicate the absence of the "nibaddha" category. Although it was said "even the anibaddhas," since this occurs in the section on witnesses (*sākṣin*), it follows by implication that they would be witnesses; thus, even though the full sense is already obtained through the force of the context, the inclusion of the word "vaktavyam" (must speak) serves to specify: even among them, one should accept the testimony only of those whose speech has been designated as authoritative, and not the speech of mere interested parties. Consequently, the testimony must be given only by those who are free from defects such as having a personal interest in the matter.
There is no binding [of the mind] for the sake of causing pain. || 13.10 ||

In this context, by the word *bandha* (bond), a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) is expressed. *Nibandha* means a settled determination; [the phrase] "there is no *bandha*" means there is no restriction or prohibition regarding acts such as violence committed for the sake of causing pain. The intended meaning is that [the act] must indeed be spoken of even through the five types of other [grounds], including those involving defects such as connection with a purpose (*arthasaṃbandha*). And thus Uśanas says: "In cases of violence, all [parties] become [liable]. (13.10)
Likewise: "And [the word of] one who speaks while intoxicated. (13.11)

"Negligent" (*pramatta*) means ignorant or deceived, as indicated by the inclusion of the prefix *pra*. When witnesses are kept secret and, through various means, cause a person to fall into a state of concealment, then those standing in that position—though possessed of defects such as a connection to the matter at hand—become witnesses. "Spoken by one who is negligent" means having been addressed while under such influence. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), this also applies to the act of sexual intercourse with women. Thus Vyāghra says: "In cases of theft, violence, association [with outcasts], and likewise with women, and in the administration of poisons and the like, no fault is recorded regarding the witnesses."
In the opposite case, hell is said to occur; that [result] is not for them alone. 13.11.
What then?
"In the case of injury to the administration of justice, guilt lies with the witnesses, the members of the court, and the king.

Where an injury to the administration of justice (*dharma*) is committed through the failure to examine legal proceedings correctly, there the perpetrator is tainted by the fault in exactly the same way as the witnesses and others.
Now, it may be asked: since the fault of witnesses has already been stated, for what purpose is it mentioned again here?

It is said: if the mention of "witnesses" (*sākṣin*) were not made here, then it would follow that the fault stated applies only to legal proceedings lacking witnesses, and not even to those with witnesses. However, one should understand that whatever fault attaches to the perpetrator, an equal measure of that same fault accrues to the members of the court (*sabhyas*) and others individually due to their own negligence, and not merely in part. By the word *tatra* ("therein"), worldly legal procedure is meant; and thus the mention [of witnesses] is for the purpose of showing that harm to them must not be inflicted. (13.12)
Some perform their duty through an oath. 13.13.

But when there is a disappearance of other means of proof such as witnesses and the like, then some maintain that one should establish the truth through an ordeal (*satyakarman*), such as an oath or the *kośa* (water-ordeal). And an oath is employed because the other party has already determined [the matter]. Although one should simply say "truth" (*satyam*), the inclusion of the word "act" (*karman*) is for the purpose of allowing the introduction of oaths even outside of legal proceedings, in cases of doubt regarding ordinary worldly transactions. Thus says the Śruti: "If I am a sorcerer, may another woman... and so forth. Gautama, however, maintains that it is by reasoning alone. In this regard, it should be understood that an oath is used when there is a slight trace of evidence, whereas when there is none, it is by reasoning alone. (13.13)
That [consecration] should take place in the assembly of Brahmins and the king of the gods for those who are not Brahmins.

And that oath [is to be taken] in an assembly of gods (*devasaṃsadi*), in the presence of the gods (*devasannidhau*). By the word "gods" (*deva*), either images of deities or [deities such as] the Ādityas and others are meant. "King" refers to the judge who oversees legal proceedings (*vyavahāradarśin*). "Brāhmaṇas" refers to the members of the court (*sabhyas*) and so forth. The mention of these [specific persons] is for the purpose of excluding ordinary worldly transactions (*laukikavyavahāra*). Thus, it should be understood that [the oath applies] in a legal proceeding when in the presence of deities and the like, but in a worldly matter anywhere at all. A legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) is caused by a dispute over property (*arthāntara*), whereas a worldly matter (*laukika*) is caused by an offense (*aparādha*). "Non-Brāhmaṇas" refers to Kṣatriyas and others. The inclusion of the word "or" (*syāt*) is for the purpose of precluding a fixed sequence. In that regard, if a deity is available, [the oath is taken] in an assembly of Brāhmaṇas; if not, it should be understood that it is taken in an assembly of the King. And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
The king should cause non-Brāhmaṇas to undergo the ordeal properly in the presence of the gods;
and in the absence of that, he should cause them to undergo it in the presence of a Brāhmaṇa.

"In the absence of that, the Blessed Kāśyapa said [to take an oath] before the king. This "absence" should be understood as referring to being preoccupied with other duties. Although one should have said "of those who are not Brahmins," the use of the term *guru* (teacher) in the sūtra is intended to include even a non-learned (*aśrotriya*) Brahmin for the purpose of entering the presence of the deity. And thus, it should be understood that for a learned (*śrotriya*) Brahmin, an oath occurs through the mere utterance of the word "truth.
Some say that the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of incorporating other Smṛtis, as Manu says:
"One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by truth, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons, a Vaiśya by his cattle, grain, and gold, and a Śūdra by all mortal sins" (MDh 8.113).

Although it could have been stated simply "in the presence of the deity, the king, and the Brāhmaṇa," the inclusion of the term *saṃsad* (assembly) is intended to include a place where the deity is present and an assembly that is free from defects such as deceit. As Nārada has said:
That is no assembly where there are no elders;
they are not elders who do not speak the Dharma;
that is not the Dharma where truth is not found.
"That which is permeated by deceit is not truth.
[NSm Mātṛkā 3.17] Thus [ends the section]. 13.14.
The general defect of witnesses has been stated; now he speaks for the sake of specific cases:
"In the case of a lie regarding small cattle, a witness destroys ten. (13.15)

Small animals are goats, sheep, and the like. Regarding false testimony concerning them, it destroys ten men. Since no distinction is made, it is understood that he destroys his own kinsmen; the meaning is that he incurs as much sin as would result from the destruction of ten of his own kinsmen. This applies everywhere. Consequently, the determination of punishment and penance should be made in accordance with that. The mention of "witnesses" is intended to include members of the court and others as well. (13.15)
In the case of cows, horses, humans, and land, [the fines] increase tenfold for each subsequent one. || 13.16 ||
Each subsequent [falsehood] becomes ten times [more serious] than the preceding one. In the case of cattle, it is a hundredfold; in the case of horses, a thousandfold, and so forth.
"In the case of falsehood regarding five animals, one destroys [the merit of] five; in the case of falsehood regarding cattle, one destroys ten;
in the case of falsehood regarding horses, one destroys a hundred; in the case of falsehood regarding humans, one destroys a thousand" (Manu Dharma Śāstra 8.98).
Whatever has been stated in other Smṛtis beginning with these words is to be understood as being contingent upon specific types of acceptance or upon specific purposes.
Or everything on the ground. || 13.17 ||
Regarding the subject of the earth, one hundred thousand [units] or the entire human race should be understood as a conceptual distinction based on the division of cultivated and uncultivated fields.
In the case of stealing [it], there is hell. || 13.18 ||
"The transformation of the earth" occurs without distinction until the end of the kalpa; this was stated in connection with the discussion of defects.
Now he states the subject at hand:
"And [the same applies] to sexual intercourse in water. (13.19)

"In waters" means in reservoirs such as wells and the like; "in sexual union" means in acts such as approaching another's wife. By the inclusion of the term "union," it is implied that [the same applies] even in cases such as the abduction of a maiden. The particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of ensuring that the mention of "waters" does not become a qualification of "sexual union. And thus, hell should be understood to result even from the act of abduction. (13.19)
As with animals, so it is with honey and clarified butter. || 13.20 ||
In the case of honey and ghee, the fault is equal to that of lying for the sake of small livestock. || 13.20 ||
As in the case of a cow, so it is with clothing, gold, grain, and Brahmins. || 13.21 ||
In matters concerning clothing and the like, lying incurs the same fault as lying about a cow; this applies whether one speaks falsely regarding a Brahmin who has studied the Veda or one who has not.
Like horses in vehicles. || 13.22 ||

In the case of a falsehood regarding vehicles such as elephants, the fault is equal to that of a falsehood regarding horses. The plural number in the word *yāneṣu* (vehicles) is intended to include inanimate objects such as palanquins and the like. Some explain it otherwise: beginning with "like [theft of] cattle, [so is the fault] for honey and clarified butter," they say that in the taking of honey and clarified butter, the fault is like that of stealing cattle; in the taking of clothing and other such items, the fault is like that of stealing a cow. In this context, by the word *brahman*, they mean the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*), as well as written books. And in the taking of vehicles, the fault is equal to a falsehood regarding horses. (13.22)
But if, even when such a fault has been pointed out, the witness still speaks a falsehood, then that witness is to be censured and punished for his false testimony. (13.23)

When a false statement has been made, the witness is to be censured and reproached in the presence of all people for the purpose of terminating legal transactions. Furthermore, he shall be punished according to the value of the matter, based on an assessment of the person's capacity and other factors. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include both the collective and individual considerations, namely the purpose of the transaction and the specific nature of the property involved. Although this follows from the general context, the explicit mention of the "witness" (*sākṣin*) indicates that it is the witness alone who is to be censured and punished; the members of the court (*sabhyas*) and others are to be punished only. (13.23)
He states an exception to this: "There is no fault in speaking untruth if one's livelihood depends upon it. (13.24)

When the life of another would necessarily be cut short because of a truthful statement, then even a falsehood must be spoken by the witness; when that is spoken, the previously mentioned fault does not apply. (13.24)
But not the life of one who is more wicked. || 13.25 ||

The word *tu* (but) has the sense of a qualification; it makes known this: although there is certainly a fault in speaking untruth, nevertheless, compared to truth that would cause death, untruth alone is superior because its fault is much smaller. And so Manu says:

"In cases where the execution of a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of a stated purpose would occur, an untruth must be spoken; for that [untruth] is distinguished as superior in such a case. [MDh 8.104]

Thus, one might think: "Even while living, this person is devoted solely to evil deeds and performs only acts such as theft"; in that case, the intention is that one must speak the truth. The term *pāpīyasaḥ* indicates the superlative degree (*ātiśāyanika*). Truth must be spoken even if it causes suffering to others; it does not refer merely to the non-performance of what is enjoined, nor merely to the performance of what is prohibited. (13.25)
The witnesses have been described; now, as to by whom they are to be questioned, he says:
"The king, or the judge, or a Brahmin learned in the scriptures. (13.26)

One who asks is a *prāṭ*. One who discerns what has been asked is a *vivāka*. Or, he is a *prāḍvivāka* because he examines what has been said by the litigants or the witnesses; that is, he deliberates upon it. He should be the king himself; when the king is exhausted or engaged in other duties, it may be a Brahmin who knows the scriptures—that is, one who is deeply learned—this is the meaning. And so Manu says: "When the king does not personally conduct the investigation of legal cases, then he should appoint a learned Brahmin to investigate the cases" (MDh 8.9).
Thus [ends the verse]. 13.26.
One should approach the judge who possesses the characteristics thus described. 13.27.

“*Adhyābhavet*” means he should go above him; this also applies to the case of a Brāhmaṇa. However, in the case of a king, since it has been stated: “They should wait upon him as he sits above, from below” (GDh 11.7), the rule is established as *tam adhyābhavet*. The specific mention of the *prāḍvivāka* (judge) is for the purpose of a restriction: one should approach only that person seated above, not even an assistant. The inclusion of the prefix *ā-* indicates that he should merely decide the case of the plaintiff and should not reopen it. And so Manu says: “He should not himself initiate a legal matter” (MDh 8.43), and so forth. 13.27.
If there is no immediate realization, one should wait for a year.

When the defendant, the plaintiff, or the witnesses lack presence of mind—that is, when they are unable to respond—then one should wait for them for one year. After a year has passed, one should decide the case according to their capacity; this is the meaning.
The exception to this is:
"And [the killing of] a cow, a bull, or a female animal engaged in procreation is [punishable with death] immediately. (13.29)

In a legal transaction involving a milch cow (*dhenu*) or similar items, one should not wait for a full year; for if time is delayed, the period for the enjoyment of the milch cow and other such items will have passed. A *dhenu* is a cow that yields milk. An *anaḍvān* is a draft ox; he too becomes worn out through use over the course of a year. And in the case of a marriage connected with procreation (*strī-prajanana*), the term "connected" (*saṃyukta*) applies to each [item] individually. Marriage (*strī-prajanana*) refers to the wedding of a maiden; if one were to wait for a year, there would also be a lapse of the proper time for that. If it is argued that one should simply say "marriage," we reply no, because the purpose is to include those who are capable of procreation. Thus, there is no fault even in waiting for a year in the case of an incapable woman. The mention of "woman" (*strī*) is intended to include women of the same caste (*savarṇa*); from this, it indicates that in the case of a woman of a different caste, one must wait [for the proper age]. The particle "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of indicating that [the rule] applies to each item individually—such as "connected with a milch cow" or "connected with a draft ox"—so that it does not apply only to the collection of all items together. The prompt inclusion [of the term "woman"] is for the purpose of including women of the same caste. (13.29)
And in cases of urgency. 13.30.

The meaning is that one should reach a decision quickly. "Urgent matters" (*atyayakarma*) refers, for example, to cases where one who was traveling together with another departs alone, or when one of them is in a state of dying, or when a village is under attack, and so forth. Because of such urgency, these must be investigated even before those involving cows and the like; hence they are treated separately. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include theft, violence, assault, and other such matters. Accordingly, another *smṛti* states: "In cases of violence, theft, assault, false accusations regarding cattle, urgent matters, and women..."
"One should institute a lawsuit immediately; in other cases, the time is said to depend on one's wish.
[YDh 2.12] Thus [ends verse 13.30].
Truthfulness in speech before the judge is weightier than all other dharmas; truthfulness in speech, truthfulness in speech! 13.31.

The meaning is that, among all duties taught in the Śruti and Smṛti which serve as means for accomplishing dharma, the most important is the judge’s—i.e., the observer of legal proceedings—seeing the matter exactly as it is; or rather, when the judge is present, it is the truthful speech of witnesses and others. 13.31.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Maskarīya-Gautama-bhāṣya*.
The fourteenth chapter:

Punishment and penance have been declared for the non-performance of prescribed duties. To address the question of at what time these two are not desired for one who fails to perform what has been prescribed, he says:
The impurity due to death lasts ten nights for the sapinda relatives, except for those who are officiating priests, those consecrated for a sacrifice, and religious students. 14.1.

The state of impurity caused by a corpse lasts for ten days and nights. For whom? For those who are *sapiṇḍas*. Its specific nature will be explained [later]. This applies to those excluding the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others. Here, "officiating priest" refers to one who is currently engaged in the ritual act, because of his association with the term "initiated" (*dīkṣita*). If the status of having previously been such were accepted here—as in the case of "the father-in-law is an officiating priest"—then the same would apply to the initiated and the student (*brahmacārin*). Consequently, since everyone has at some point been a student, the separate mention of the "officiating priest" and the "initiated" would be redundant. Therefore, all those currently engaged in the performance of the rite are included. The "initiated" is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). The "student" remains so as long as he observes the vow of studentship. Since [the rules] regarding Kṣatriyas and others are taught later, this refers specifically to Brāhmaṇas. Since the impurity of birth (*sūtaka*) will be mentioned later, the statement "impurity lasts ten nights" already establishes the rule for that caused by a corpse; however, the specific mention of "corpse" (*śāva*) is for the purpose of indicating that the counting of days should begin from the moment the corpse appears.

But is it not the case that in another Smṛti, regarding the rites performed prior [to cremation], it is heard from the point of the post-mortem consecration (*saṃskāra*) onwards: "In the forest, having abandoned [the body] like a log, one should let it remain for three days" (MDh 5.69)? Likewise: "If one who has maintained the sacred fires dies while away from home, after performing the consecration again, purification is to be carried out as if for a corpse" (VaDh 4.37). Therefore, this [present rule] is contradictory.

To this it is replied: there is no contradiction because of the distinction of subject matter (*viṣaya-vibhāga*). Thus, in the *Vyāghra-dharma*, a statement intended to establish the distinction of subject matter is heard: "The funeral rite (*saṃyoga*) must be performed for one who has no connection with the sacred fires;
the cremation (*dahana*) must be performed for one for whom the Vedic ritual (*vaitānika-vidhi*) is prescribed. Thus it is said.

By the rule, "One who has touched an outcaste, a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or a corpse" (GDh 14.29), since the state of impurity is already established by the prescription of bathing upon touching a corpse, the explicit mention of "impurity" (*āśauca*) is for the purpose of prohibiting study and other such activities. Thus says Manu: "In both cases, for ten days the food of the family is not to be eaten;
giving, receiving, sacrifice, and Vedic study are suspended."

Although it should have been stated as *śāvāśaucam* (impurity due to a corpse), the use of the non-compound form *śāvam āśaucam* is for the purpose of making known that the state of impurity regarding mutual contact lasts only until the collection (*saṃcayana*) of the bones which constitute the limbs of the corpse. And so says Saṃvarta: "After the collection of the bones, the touching of the limbs is prescribed.
The nature of the collection of bones is to be understood from another Smṛti; and thus Vyāghra says:
"On the first, second, third, and fourth days, the collection of bones should be performed by the relatives who desire what is beneficial.

In this context, it should be understood that for those entitled to immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*), it occurs on the first day; for those related by a one-day period, on the second day; for those related by a three-day period, on the third day; and for those related by a four-day period or a ten-day period, on the fourth day. Likewise, another statement is heard in that very same source:

"On the fourth, the fifth, the seventh, and likewise the tenth day, one should perform the collection of the bones (asthisaṃcayana) for the social classes in their respective order. In this regard, it should be understood that for a Brāhmaṇa it is on the fourth day, for a Kṣatriya on the fifth, for a Vaiśya on the seventh, and for a Śūdra on the tenth. It has been stated for the Brāhmaṇa; in the same way, for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya as well, it should be determined according to the principle that "for those with shorter periods of impurity, the period is shorter," taking into account their conduct and Vedic study. The mention of the *brahmacārin* is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) including the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) and others. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"For lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika), forest-dwellers, ascetics, and students, no impurity is declared during birth-impurity (sūtaka), nor likewise during death-impurity (śāva).
The mention of "initiated persons" (dīkṣita) is for the purpose of including those who have begun the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such penances. And so says Vasiṣṭha:

“There is no fault of sin for kings, nor likewise for those observing vows or performing sacrificial sessions; for they, seated in the station of Indra, are always purified by Brahman. [VaDh 19.48] And because of the indicative marks of the texts, “after the tenth day” [GDh 14.24] and “for a Kṣatriya, eleven nights” [GDh 14.2], it is possible to understand that the period is ten nights. The mention of ten nights serves as a restrictive rule (niyama) to show that even for a Kṣatriya and others, the period of impurity (āśauca) is exactly ten nights when it concerns a Brāhmaṇa. And so says another Smṛti:

"Those who are the heirs of a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra, but are relatives of a Brāhmaṇa—for them, during a period of impurity, the Brāhmaṇa's *sūtaka* shall last for ten days. Thus, the meaning therein is that when impurity affects a Brāhmaṇa, it lasts for those [relatives] for exactly ten days. Manu also says:

"All [members] of the higher castes, however, should respectfully observe the period of impurity according to the rules prescribed for their own caste; but they should perform their own purification among those of their own birth. Thus, since a ten-day period of impurity is prescribed for them during the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, one must look to what is stated in other Smṛtis regarding a Brāhmaṇa's impurity when they themselves are in a state of impurity. As Lokākṣi says:
Impurity on account of death lasts ten days among those of one's own caste;
for births and deaths among the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, it is declared to be six, three, and one day respectively.
Thus [ends the section]. 14.1.
For a Kṣatriya, it is eleven nights. || 14.2 ||
The impurity on account of a birth or death pertains to sapinda relatives, with the exception of the officiating priest, the initiated sacrificer, and the student. 14.2.
For a Vaiśya, it is twelve nights. || 14.3 ||
It continues as before. || 14.3 ||
Some [say] for half a month. 14.4.

"Others say fifteen days. This option should be understood as being dependent upon one's conduct (*vṛtta*) and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). And thus it is understood that for Brahmins and others as well, there is a dependence on conduct and Vedic study. Accordingly, Parāśara says:
"A Brahmin who is endowed with the sacred fires and the Vedas is purified in one day; one who possesses only the Vedas in three days; but one devoid of virtues is purified in ten days. [PārSm 3.5]
And so Manu also says:
"Impurity on account of a death is ordained for ten days among sapindas;
it may be until the collection of the bones, or for three days, or even for one day. (MDh 5.59)

In this context, the phrase "prior to the collection of the bones" (*arvāk saṃcayanāt*) is an elliptical expression for a period of four days. When there is the presence of one quality, purification occurs in four days; when two qualities are present, in three days; but when all qualities are present, in one day. The Commentator has explained that when all qualities are present, there is even a restriction on one's livelihood, and in that case, purification is immediate (*sadyaḥśauca*). Likewise, a set of four statements is also commenced for the Kṣatriya: Gautama says, "by eleven nights" (GDh 14.2); Vasiṣṭha says, "by fifteen nights" (VaDh 4.28); Yājñavalkya says, "by twelve nights" (YDh 3.22); and Parāśara says, "by ten nights. Just as ten nights is fixed for a Brāhmaṇa, fifteen days is likewise fixed for a Kṣatriya. Among these, when one quality is present, it is twelve nights; when two qualities are present, eleven nights; when all qualities are present, ten days; and for one devoid of qualities, fifteen days. Similarly for the Vaiśya: when one quality is present, "some say half a month," which is half a month; when two qualities are present, "twelve nights for a Vaiśya," which is twelve days; when all qualities are present, the eleven nights mentioned by Parāśara; and for one devoid of qualities, twenty nights as stated by Vasiṣṭha. This should be understood as the conceptual framework, with that [latter period] being the standard rule (*nitya*). 14.4.
For a Śūdra, [the penance lasts] one month. || 14.5 ||

Because this person lacks initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the like, the rule applies specifically to "those who share the funeral rice-ball" (*sapiṇḍas*). And because he lacks [proper] conduct and so forth, this very same rule applies. This refers to the case of an unworthy Śūdra, according to the statement of Auśanasa: "For worthy Śūdras, [the period is] half a month. (14.5)
If that [offense] occurs again within [the same period], they shall be purified by the remainder of the penance. || 14.6 ||

That very same [period] should be understood as death upon the occurrence of a death of the same kind, and birth upon the occurrence of a birth, because of the inclusion of the word "that" (*tat*). The word "again" (*punar*) means "once more," or even "repeatedly. It would "occur" (*āpated*), meaning it would arrive. Consequently, purification would take place by the very time remaining from the previous period of impurity; the meaning is that one need not wait for the arrival of the subsequent period. The inclusion of the word "within" (*antar-*) is for the sake of clarity, since the intermediate case can be understood from these very rules: "They shall be purified by the remainder" (GDh 6.7), and "If a night remains, by two [days]; at dawn, by three" (GDh 18.8).

Others, however, say that since this is already established by the extended application (*atideśa*) in the rule, "The same applies even to birth" (GDh 14.14), the explicit mention of that [birth] refers to cases where [the two impurities] are of equal duration—for example, when one period of impurity lasting ten nights occurs during another period of impurity lasting ten nights. They hold that if a longer period of impurity arrives while a shorter one is still current, the former shall not be superseded by the latter. Thus states the *Paiṅgi-gṛhya-smṛti*: "In the case of an increase in impurity (*aghavṛddhi*), one should conclude with the latter. By the expression "in the case of an increase in impurity," it should be understood that if a small amount of impurity is occurring, one must indeed observe it. 14.6.
During the remainder of the night, [he should recite] two [verses]. || 14.7 ||

If another impurity should occur when only one night remains of a previous impurity, then purification does not come through that first [period] alone; rather, it comes after two nights. In this way, the three-night period becomes fully encompassed. (14.7)
At dawn, with three [verses]. || 14.8 ||

"At dawn" means before the *saṅgava* period; this is because we see an explanatory passage stating, "Having bathed at the *saṅgava*, those who have incurred sin should enter the village. If [the impurity] should occur then, purification is not achieved by the remainder of that night; rather, it is by three nights. (14.8)
For those killed by cows or Brahmins, [the purification is] immediate.

For those killed for the sake of cows or for the sake of Brahmins, the period of impurity lasts only until they are seen; that is to say, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). Thus says Manu: "In the case of [death] for the sake of cows or Brahmins, and also for whomsoever the king desires [to be purified immediately]" (MDh 5.95). This was stated under the heading of immediate purification: "for those killed by cows or Brahmins, or those caused to be killed by either of them. Likewise, Uśanas states: "There is immediate purification for those killed by cows and those killed by Brahmins. (14.9)
And also from the king's anger, even without fighting. 14.10.

The term *anvakṣam* (immediately) carries over. The word *ca* has the sense of *api* (even/also), and its position is displaced. This means "even in the absence of battle due to the king’s wrath"; by the force of the word *api*, it also includes "even in the case of battle. And so Manu says: "But for one slain according to the duty of a Kṣatriya with weapons raised in combat, the sacrifice is immediately completed; such is the rule regarding that impurity. [MDh 5.98]

The word *ca* (and) has the sense of conjunction. Consequently, some explain it thus: immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) applies to one whom a king causes to be killed out of anger in a situation other than battle, as well as to one who is killed in battle even without the king’s anger.
Others explain it as referring to those killed through the king’s wrath, as well as those killed in battle due to disturbances such as civil unrest. And so Manu says:
"And for those killed in a riotous fray, by lightning, or by the sovereign... [MDh 5.95].

Others, however, state that this refers to the time of marriage: there is immediate purification for those killed due to a king’s wrath in battle, and there is immediate purification at the time of marriage. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"In times of distress, at marriage, at a sacrifice, in battle, during a national calamity, and even in the face of dire adversity, immediate purification is ordained."
Thus [ends the verse]. 14.10.
And for those who desire [liberation] through fasting, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling [from a precipice]. || 14.11 ||

The term "immediately" (*anvakṣam*) carries over from the previous context. For those who intentionally bring about their own death by means of fasting and the like, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). "Fasting" (*prāyaḥ*) refers to the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*); since this may occur even against one’s will due to fear of the king or other causes, the word "intentionally" (*icchatām*) is specified. "Fasting until death" (*anāśaka*) is the abstention from food; this too may occur even against one’s will during times of famine and so forth. "A weapon" (*śastra*) refers to a sword and the like; even in that case, death may occur through negligence. "Hanging" (*udbandhana*) is by means of a rope and the like; here too, it may occur even against one’s will through joking or similar circumstances. "Falling" (*prapatana*) is from a mountain or a tree; even in that case, it may occur by chance even without prior intention. Thus, it should be understood that for those who die by these means unintentionally, the rules are exactly as they apply in each case. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it should be understood that this also applies to other such causes of self-destruction. (14.11)
Now he states the nature of sapinda-relationship:
"The cessation of the offering of rice-balls occurs at the seventh or the fifth [generation]. (14.12)

Having passed beyond six persons, when the seventh is reached, the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) is made to three ancestors beginning with the father. While those [three] are living, the son gives to the very same ones to whom his father gives; thus, to three others, making six persons who are connected by the rice-ball offering. When, for one whose father is living, it is accepted that "one does not offer beyond a living person," and so the father gives to the grandfather and the great-grandfather, then the cessation occurs at the fifth. This is the same for women; or rather, on the paternal side, the cessation is at the seventh, while on the maternal side, it is at the fifth. (14.12)
The same applies even to the act of procreation. || 14.13 ||

The period of ten days alone is extended [to the mother]. Otherwise, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) would apply even to the mother, which contradicts established practice and the *Gṛhya-smṛti*: “For ten nights, both husband and wife remain impure due to birth. Therefore, it should be understood that whatever period of ten days is prescribed for impurity due to death (*śāva*) applies to all *sapiṇḍa* relatives. And so says Manu: “Whether a child has teethed, has not yet teathed, or has had its tonsure (*caula*) performed, when it dies, all its kinsmen remain impure; the same is declared regarding birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). [MDh 5.58]
Likewise, [it is stated] regarding a tiger:

"In the case of birth-impurity (sūtaka), the impurity for sapinda relatives—or for the parents, or specifically for the mother—shall last ten nights; for those who offer water, it shall last three days. Thus [it is said].

In that case as well, the avoidance of those who have undergone initiation (dīkṣita) and others should be observed; this is indicated by the word "api" (also), referring to such rules as "If that [impurity] should occur again within [the period]" (GDh 14.6). 14.13.
That [belongs] to the mother and father. || 14.14 ||

"Or the birth-impurity of the mother and father. The word "or" (*vā*) from above should be supplied here as well; and thus Vasiṣṭha also stated the word "or" in this very context: "Or [it applies] to the mother and father, because it is caused by them" (VaDh 4.21–22). 14.14.
Or from the mother. 14.15.

The meaning is that [the impurity belongs] to the mother of that very child who was born, not to the co-wife. Here, a restricted option (*vyavasthitavikalpa*) is to be understood: if all [members of the family] are devoid of good conduct (*vṛtta*), then there shall be birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for all; if all possess good conduct but the father is devoid of good conduct, then [it applies] to both parents; when the father possesses good conduct but follows a restricted livelihood (*saṅkocavṛtti*), then it applies to the mother alone; however, if the father is a maintainer of the *agnihotra* fire and does not follow a restricted livelihood, then, having touched water and offered the *agnihotra*, he should again observe the period of impurity. (14.15)
The nights equal in number to the months of gestation [are spent] when the embryo is miscarried. || 14.16 ||

In the case of a miscarriage, however, there are as many days and nights as the number of months the fetus has been in the womb. One should understand that miscarriage occurs up to the fifth month, whereas beyond that it is a fall of the fetus. Why? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the Brāhmaṇa: "Therefore, in the fifth month, fetuses are transformed. Consequently, the meaning is that for as many months as the fetus has miscarried, there are an equal number of days and nights [of impurity]. (14.16)
Or for three days. || 14.17 ||

In the case of a miscarriage occurring at two or three months of gestation, the impurity lasts for three days; beyond that, the rule should be understood to be equal to the number of months elapsed. Even in the case of a full-term birth (patana), the impurity should be understood to last for a period equal to the months [of pregnancy], based on the statement in the *Paiṅgi-gṛhya*: "In the case of a fetus, the day of impurity is equal to the number of months. This impurity belongs to the mother alone, because she is the one authorized [in the ritual context]. Accordingly, the *Devagṛhya* states: "When the fetus dies while still in the womb, the impurity shall belong to the mother alone. By the same logic applied to the duration of the months, it is established that even for one who dies after the time of birth, the impurity lasts ten nights. From the use of the restrictive particle (*eva*) in the phrase "to the mother alone" when the fetus dies, it is understood that after the time of birth, the impurity pertains to both parents. And so says Vyāghra:
"When an infant dies, immediate purification is ordained for the sapinda relatives;
likewise, for the husband and wife, and for uterine brothers, it is by ten days alone."

The mention of the ten-day period for siblings should be understood as applying only after the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). Thus says the *Paiṅgi-Gṛhya-Smṛti*: "If the fetus dies, the impurity shall belong to the mother alone; if born, to both; and when the name has been given, to the siblings as well. Some say this applies even before the name is given. When teeth have appeared and the tonsure (*cūḍā*) has been performed, [the impurity lasts ten days] for all. This should be understood to mean that when teeth have appeared and the tonsure has been performed, the ten-day period applies to all twelve types of sons. Although the rule "for a miscarriage, the nights are equal to the months" (GDh 14.16) already establishes this, the explicit mention of the "fetus" (*garbha*) is for the purpose of restriction, indicating that this impurity belongs specifically to the mother who is closely connected to the fetus. (14.17)
And having heard [the news], after the tenth day, one should observe the *pakṣiṇī* fast.

The mention of the tenth day is for the purpose of indicating all periods of impurity (*āśauca*). A *pakṣiṇī* is a night situated between two days, or a day situated between two nights. Upon hearing of the birth or death of a *sapiṇḍa*, there is *pakṣiṇī* impurity. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), and because it has been stated that "for those whose tonsure (*caula*) has not been performed, [impurity lasts] three nights," this [rule of *pakṣiṇī*] should be understood to apply to those for whom the tonsure has been performed. Even among them, this should be understood to apply to those related by a four-day period. However, for those related by a three-day period, one should follow what was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "If one hears of a deceased person who was in another country after ten days have passed, the impurity lasts for one night. For those related by a one-day period, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) according to the rule: "In the case of a child in another country... For those related by a ten-day period, however, [the following applies]:

Regarding the statement by Manu, "But when ten days have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights" (MDh 5.76), this period of three days (*tryaha*) is to be understood as applying to all cases. Furthermore, after a year has elapsed, there is only bathing; for it is said:
"But when a year has passed, one becomes pure merely by touching water" (MDh 5.76).
