Thus, from the statement of Manu. 14.18.
In the case of a kinsman not related by sapinda-relationship, a relative by birth, or a fellow student. || 14.19 ||

One who is not a *sapiṇḍa* but a *samānodaka* (a distant relative) is one for whom, upon his death, the impurity for the *samānodakas* lasts for a "bird-night" (*pakṣiṇī*). This also applies to those related by four days of kinship; however, for those related by one day of kinship, the impurity lasts until the same time the next day (*sadyaḥśauca*). By the rule "in the case of a child or one residing in another country," a three-day period is prescribed for a non-relative, while for one day's kin, a single day is to be understood. For those related by ten days of kinship, it should be seen that the period is exactly three days, according to the rule: "But after three days, [the impurity ceases] for those who offer water" (MDh 5.64). Regarding those related by birth (*yonisaṃbandhin*), such as a maternal uncle, a mother’s sister’s son, and a father’s sister’s son: when they have died, the impurity lasts for a "bird-night. The same applies to a fellow student (*sahādhyāyin*). A fellow student is one who has the same teacher. From the word "and" (*ca*) in the verse, it is understood that this also applies to a friend (*suhṛd*). (14.19)
For one day [of impurity] in the case of a fellow religious student (sabrahmacārin). || 14.20 ||

A fellow religious student (*sabrahmacārī*) is one who practices the same observances; the meaning is that upon his death, one should observe impurity for one day and night, because the word "should observe" (*gṛhṇīyāt*) is to be supplied in every case. (14.20)
And also when a learned Brahmin (śrotriya) has arrived. || 14.21 ||

"One night" is understood [from the previous rule]. "To a *śrotriya*" means one who has studied the Veda with its six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), who is "endowed" (*upasaṃpanna*)—that is, possessed of the perfection of knowledge and practice—even if he is not a fellow student (*asabrahmacārī*). Or, "endowed" may mean one who has taken refuge for some reason or is a neighbor-student. From the word "and" (*ca*), it is also [to be given] to a king. (14.21)
Upon touching a corpse, there is impurity for ten nights, provided that one did so intentionally.

“Touching a *preta* (a deceased person)” means carrying out the corpse; this is because of the use of the prefix *upa*, which indicates that it does not refer to mere touching. The impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for ten nights, provided that one touches the body intentionally—that is, having seen it and accepted the act—not merely out of duty, for the sake of wealth, or by chance. Here, the impurity refers only to contact, and not to the rules to be mentioned later, such as “they should sleep and sit on the ground” (GDh 2.27), because the term “impurity” is used again within this section on impurity itself. In this very context, the distinction of the subject matter should be understood: among the *sapiṇḍas*, there is no specific difference for whoever carries the body or performs the funeral rites, as there is no statement to that effect. However, for those who are *samānodakas* (distant kinsmen), the impurity lasts for ten nights.

"By one day and night, and by three periods of three nights, those who touch a corpse are purified; but those who offer water [for the deceased] are purified after three days" (Manu Smṛti 5.64). According to this statement of Manu, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has explained that for those *samānodaka* kinsmen who carry out the removal of the corpse or perform the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*), there is impurity (*āśauca*) for ten nights, while for others it is three nights. Furthermore, regarding those who are other than the *samānodaka* kinsmen, the rule stated by Manu should also be observed.
Having carried out the corpse of a deceased twice-born man who is not a sapinda, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights, as does one who carries out the maternal relatives of his mother.
"If one eats the food of those [who have died], he becomes pure after ten days; but if he does not eat their food, he is purified in a single day and should not dwell in that house. [MDh 5.101–102]

In this case, if one performs the removal of the corpse or the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*), and also prepares the funeral mat (*kaṭakaraṇa*), and eats that food, the impurity lasts for ten days. If he performs only the preparation of the funeral mat and does not eat that food, it lasts for three days. If he neither prepares the funeral mat nor dwells in that house, it lasts for a day and a night. And if he does not enter the village, it lasts for the duration of the day alone; because of the word "alone" (*eva*), it becomes "with the light" (*sajyotis*). This *sūtra* is to be understood as applying to one who carries [the corpse] out of a sense of duty, whether the person is a *sapiṇḍa* or a non-*sapiṇḍa*. This applies specifically to a Brāhmaṇa touching a Brāhmaṇa, since separate rules are initiated for the Vaiśya and Śūdra. For a Kṣatriya as well, when touching a Kṣatriya, his own specific rule applies; for when the beginning and end are specified, the middle is understood by implication. (14.22)
The [rules] for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra have been stated. || 14.23 ||
The meaning is that upon touching a deceased person of the same caste, the impurity belonging to oneself alone—which has been acquired as a constant rule—comes into effect. 14.23.
Or [the verses] relating to the menstrual period. 14.24.

Alternatively, the period of impurity for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra lasts for as many nights as there are seasons. Although it would have been sufficient to say "six," the mention of the menstrual period (*ārtava*) is intended to indicate that there are five seasons. In this regard, it should be understood that for a Śūdra it is six [nights], and for a Vaiśya it is five. Among these, for a Vaiśya who possesses the proper conduct (*vṛtta*), it is five; for one who lacks such conduct, it is his own [standard] period. Regarding the Śūdra as well, for a virtuous Śūdra (*sacchūdra*) who possesses proper conduct, it is six; for another, it is half a month; and for an unworthy Śūdra (*asacchūdra*) who lacks proper conduct, it should be understood that it is indeed a full month. (14.24)
And [the same applies] to the two preceding ones. 14.25.

For the two previously mentioned [castes], the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya, it is either the Ārtvī or that which was stated before. The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of drawing in the alternative options. 14.25.
Or for three days. 14.26.

The phrase "of the two former" carries over [from the previous rule]. In that regard, for a Brāhmaṇa who has not completed his studies, the period is ten nights; for one who has completed them, it is five; for one who has established the sacred fires, it is three days; and the same should be understood to apply to a Kṣatriya as well. 14.26.
The same applies toward the teacher, his son, a wife, one for whom one performs sacrifices, and a pupil. || 14.27 ||

When the teacher, his son, or his wife has died; when the person for whom one performs sacrifices (the patron) or a pupil has died; and by the word "and" (ca), when the teacher’s teacher has died—as indicated by the word "thus" (evam)—only a three-day period is extended [to these cases], because of the observation of the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti which states: "And when the teacher has died, there is a three-night [period of impurity]" (VaDh 13.39).

The case regarding those of the same caste has been explained previously. However, regarding those of different castes: if a person of lower caste touches one of higher caste, or if one of higher caste touches one of lower caste, the period of impurity in that instance is as prescribed for a corpse. (14.28)

The *avara* (lower) is the *kṣatriya* and so forth. The mention of "caste" (*varṇa*) serves to indicate that in the case of *pratiloma* (inverse-order) unions, there is not merely impurity (*āśauca*), but rather that there is also a penance (*prāyaścitta*). Although those born in the *anuloma* (direct-order) unions are also not denoted by the word "caste," nevertheless, because of the rule "But those born in the inverse order are devoid of *dharma*" [GDh 4.25], which establishes that only *pratiloma* offspring lack *dharma*, it should be inferred that for *anuloma* offspring, the mother's status prevails. He should touch or carry the elder caste, such as the Brāhmaṇa; this is due to the use of the prefix *upa-* [in the verb *upasparśet*]. Or, he may carry the younger caste, such as the Kṣatriya, when the elder carries the younger. In that case, whatever impurity has been declared regarding the carrying of corpses applies here as well. Thus, for a Kṣatriya touching a Brāhmaṇa corpse, the impurity lasts ten nights; likewise, for a Brāhmaṇa touching a Kṣatriya corpse, it lasts fifteen days. This applies everywhere. Since the section is already under the heading of impurity, the repetition of the term "impurity" is intended to mean that the rules apply specifically to the state of impurity itself, and not merely to the suspension of Vedic study and other activities. While one could have simply said "impurity regarding a corpse" (*śāvāśauca*), the inclusion of the word "said" (*ukta*) is for the purpose of including that impurity even during activities such as eating. Furthermore, regarding the penance heard in other Smṛtis, such as "In the case of a *pāraśava* within ten days" [VaDh 4.32], that should be understood as applying after the period of impurity has passed. Here, while one could have said "the aforementioned impurity," the use of the word "corpse" (*śava*) is intended to include everything caused by a corpse. Therefore, having accepted the visible purpose [of the rule], the penance stated in other Smṛtis regarding mutual carrying should be observed. Thus says Vyāghra: [The text continues with Vyāghra’s verse.]
"If a lower person carries a superior caste, or if a superior person carries a lower one, he shall observe impurity like a corpse; if it concerns a visible purpose, it shall be double.
Thus it is also for an invisible purpose.
Those twice-born who carry a deceased brahmin who is without a protector obtain,
step by step, the fruit of a sacrifice in successive order.

And so forth. Although it should have been stated simply that "the impurity is as declared for the corpse," the inclusion of the word *tatra* (in that case) is intended to prevent the application of the impurity prescribed for one's conduct and Vedic study. And thus, just as the ten-day period is mandatory for a Brāhmaṇa, so too should the fifteen-day period and others be understood to apply to Kṣatriyas and the rest. Whatever impurity has been stated regarding the carrying [of the corpse], that same impurity is to be understood to apply to the preparer of the funeral rites as well. Why? Because of the identical instruction in the text of Uśanas: "Both the preparer and the carrier are purified after three nights. (14.28)
The impurity resulting from carrying a corpse has been declared for those of the same caste as well as for those of a different caste. Now he speaks regarding touching it intentionally:

"Upon touching an outcaste (patita), a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or a corpse, or upon touching someone who has touched them, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on. (14.29)

An outcast (*patita*) is one who has killed a Brahmin and so forth. A *caṇḍāla* is as previously defined. A woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*) is one whose period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) has not yet ended. A menstruating woman (*udakyā*) is one who has her menses. By the mention of "the corpse" (*śava*), everything caused by it is expressed: namely, the corpse itself, those who are subject to the impurity on its account, those who prepare the funeral pyre, those who carry it, and those who perform the cremation, and so forth. The term "touching" (*upasparśana*) is connected with each [of these]. Thus, "touching an outcast, a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or a corpse" refers to touching them directly, touching one who has touched them, or touching one who has touched that person. The word "directly" (*spṛṣṭī*) refers to one who touches the outcast and others face-to-face; "one who has touched them" (*tatspṛṣṭī*) refers to one who touches someone who has already touched the outcast and others. The prefix *upa-* signifies intentional action. Touching a corpse intentionally is for the purpose of decoration and the like, or out of mere whim. Whether it be a corpse of one's own caste or a corpse of a different caste makes no difference, as there is no distinction made. However, in the case of unintentional contact, the rule stated by Manu should be observed. As he says:
Having touched one for whom the *divākīrtya* hymns are recited, a woman in her courses, an outcaste, a woman who has recently given birth,
a corpse, or one who has touched a corpse, one becomes pure by bathing.

Thus, the impurity for two [classes] has been prescribed; however, Gautama states it applies even to three. "With his clothes on" means with his garment; "from the touching of water" (*udakopasparśanāt*). If it is argued that one should have said "from bathing" (*snānāt*), there is no such fault: the phrase "from the touching of water" is stated for the purpose of indicating that after first plunging like a staff, one should bathe again properly. Although it could have been stated as "one should touch water with one's clothes on," the use of the term "touching of water" is intended to include the libation (*tarpaṇa*) within this occasional bath (*naimittika-snāna*). And so says the *Bhārgavīya*:
"Bathing is said to be of three kinds: daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and for the sake of desire (kāmya).
Prajāpati has declared that the libation (tarpaṇa) belongs to all three. (14.29)
And [the same applies] to dogs. || 14.30 ||

Regarding "purification through touching water while clothed": the phrase "he shall be purified" is understood to carry over from the previous context. The separate mention of the dog is for the purpose of excluding those who have touched such a person or been touched by them. The mention of the "dog" (śva) is intended as an illustration to include jackals and similar animals. By the word "and" (ca), bone is also included, provided it is still moist. As Manu has said:
"Having touched a human bone that is still moist, a Brahmin is purified by bathing;
but having touched one that is dry, he is purified merely by sipping water (ācamana), or by touching a cow, or by looking at the sun. [MDh 5.87]

This, however, refers to touching [the bone] unintentionally. But regarding intentional contact, Vasiṣṭha says: "Having touched a moist human bone, there is impurity for three nights; but if it is not moist, for a day and a night" (VaDh 23.24). By the use of the word *ca* ("and"), blood and so forth are also included. Some say this refers to following a corpse; in that case, bathing with one's clothes on and consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*) should also be observed. Thus Manu says: "If one intentionally follows a deceased person, whether a relative or a stranger..."
"Having bathed with one's clothes on, touched fire, and consumed clarified butter, one becomes purified. [MDh 5.103]

This rule applies only to those of one's own caste (*sajāti*). However, regarding the following of a *kṣatriya* or a *vaiśya*, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed. Thus he says: "But in the case of following one who is not a relative, or in the case of following a corpse, it is for a day and a night" (*VaDh* 23.25). In that context, the extension (*atideśa*) of the three-night and one-night periods applies to the following of a corpse. Consequently, one should observe that the penance for following a *kṣatriya* is one night, for following a *vaiśya* it is a *pakṣiṇī* (two nights with the intervening day), and for following a *śūdra* it is three nights. Likewise, Aṅgiras says: "A Brāhmaṇa weak in knowledge who follows a *śūdra* who has become a corpse..."
One who follows a corpse being carried away shall remain impure for three nights.

"But when three nights have passed, having gone to a river that flows into the ocean and performed a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), he becomes pure after consuming clarified butter. This rule for a Kṣatriya following a Vaiśya, and for a Vaiśya following a Śūdra, should be understood as being the same as for a Brāhmaṇa. For a Kṣatriya approaching a Śūdra woman, one hundred breath-restraints accompanied by one night [of fasting] should be observed. (14.30)
Some say that one should destroy it. 14.31.

Some, however, maintain that one should perform a washing only of that very limb which a dog touches. This is an alternative view: it should be understood that bathing is required when there is contact with the upper part of the body, whereas washing is sufficient for contact with the lower part of the body. The same applies to contact with birds. Likewise, Jātūkarṇi states: "If a bird touches any limb above the navel, excluding the hands, bathing must be performed; in all other cases, one becomes pure by washing [the affected part]."
And in this same way, it should be understood that even in the case of a dog, [the rule] applies with the exception of the hand. || 14.31 ||
The offering of water is performed by the sapindas for one who has grown matted hair.

By virtue of the context, water should be offered for the deceased by the *sapiṇḍas* once the hair has been matted (*jaṭa*) or the tonsure (*caula*) has been performed; it is not to be done by all who are impure. Impurity (*āśauca*) is also to be understood from the injunction regarding the water-rite (*udakakriyā*), because Vasiṣṭha mentions them together: "The water-rite and impurity" (VaDh 4.9). The purpose of that joint mention is that whoever performs the water-rite must also undergo impurity. Similarly, a period of three nights (*trirātra*) is to be observed based on another *smṛti* text. Thus Manu says:
"But for those whose hair has been shorn, purification is held to occur after three nights" (MDh 5.66).

This is exactly the same for Kṣatriyas and the other castes as well, because there is no distinction. And thus, those various options for impurity (āśauca) heard of—such as three days and so forth—which depend on the stage of life, should be understood as applying equally to all, precisely because there is no distinction. Likewise, those periods such as fifteen days which are prescribed depending on one's conduct (*vṛtta*) and other factors, are to be understood as applicable when the deceased has already undergone the initiation (*upanayana*). The same applies to impurity due to being in another country (*deśāntara*). And so Vyāghra says: "For all [castes], it is equal regarding age, and likewise when that [period] has elapsed."
"But when he has been initiated, that [impurity] becomes irregular, arising from the lapse of time in that very case.

This means that what is heard prior to the completion of the period of impurity already mentioned—namely, "whatever remains of the ten nights," and so forth—should be understood as applying even before initiation. Furthermore, the cremation of one who has grown matted hair (*jaṭā*) should also be observed according to another *smṛti*. Thus says Lokākṣi:
"One should offer water silently, and likewise the fire silently."
"For all those who have had their tonsure performed, there are two [rites] even elsewhere, according to one's wish.

Thus, it should be understood that for one whose hair has been matted (*jaṭā*), the cremation with fire (*agnisaṃskāra*) and the offering of water (*udakadāna*) are mandatory, whereas for one whose tonsure (*caula*) has not yet been performed, they are not mandatory. And so says Manu:
"The offering of water should not be performed by relatives for one who is under three years of age."
"Or they may perform it for one whose teeth have appeared, or even when the naming ceremony has been completed.
And that [is the rule] for women as well. 14.33.

That offering of water is accompanied by the cremation with fire, because that is what is understood from the mention [of the rite]. And it must be performed for women as well. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include the pulling out of matted hair (*jaṭā*). It is mentioned separately for the purpose of lightening the period of impurity (*āśauca*); this is to be understood from another Smṛti text. In that regard: "In the case of an immature girl, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is prescribed.
Thus, before the performance of the tonsure (*caula*), there is immediate purification. By the word "immature" (*prauḍhā*), the performance of the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*) is meant.

"But for unmarried girls and young children, purification takes one day" (YDh 3.24). Thus, from the time of the tonsure ceremony until the time of marriage, purification is one day. However, "for women who have not undergone sacramental rites, the kinsmen are purified after three days" (MDh 5.72ab).

By this [rule], it is meant that for one who has not been given away [in marriage], the period is three nights after the time of the gift. Regarding the statement, "But those of the same lineage (sanābhayaḥ) are purified by the very rule already mentioned" (MDh 5.72cd), by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (daṇḍāpūpikayā), it should be understood that in the case of women, the period for the parents is ten days. Even regarding the *sapiṇḍas*, the period should be understood as extending to three generations (*tripūruṣa*), according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "But for unmarried women, it extends to three generations" (VaDh 4.18). 14.33.
Some [say it belongs] to those who have been given away. 14.34.

Some maintain that even for those given away with water and speech, the rites must be performed by the bridegroom's party alone. Gautama, however, says: "If the groom should die before [the marriage is completed], a girl who has been given by water and word should be given to another according to the rule; such is the case with a maiden."

Thus, because of the extension [of rules] by the phrase "as in the case of a maiden," it should be given by the father and others themselves; in that regard, it should be understood that in the absence of the father's side, it must be performed by the bridegroom's side. (14.34)
Now, as to how they should conduct themselves during the period of impurity (āśauca), he says: "All shall sleep and sit on the ground and remain celibate. (14.35)

They should sleep and sit only on the ground and avoid sexual intercourse for as long as the period of impurity lasts. The inclusion of the word "all" is intended to indicate that this applies to the Samānodaka relations as well. 14.35.
They should not wipe [the feet]. || 14.36 ||
The meaning is that they should not wear brightly colored garments; or rather, they should avoid removing the dirt from their bodies. 14.36.
They shall not eat meat until the offering has been made. 14.37.
They should not consume meat even at the risk of their lives until the performance of the *śrāddha* ceremony. (14.37)
The water-rites are performed on the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth days.

It should be understood that on the first and subsequent days, the rite is to be performed by the sapinda relatives, whereas on each day thereafter, it is to be performed by the sons. The inclusion of the term "rite" (kriyā) is for the purpose of including the procedure for the offering of water as prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, such as: "The sons pour out water once for the deceased," and so forth.
And there is the discarding of garments. 14.39.

There is the discarding of the garments worn at the time of the water-offering; the meaning is that other [garments] are to be worn. By the word "and" (ca), hair and so forth are also included. And likewise, another Smṛti states:
"On the second day, the rite of shaving should be performed with care;
or on the third, the fifth, or even the seventh, until the [final] offering. (14.39)
But for the last [of the last], it is before. || 14.40 ||

"At the end of the ninth [day], for the last-born [castes], the discarding of clothes" is the rule that carries over. The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of specification. The offering of water must be performed on the first day and so forth; however, the discarding of clothes occurs only at the very end. The plural number in the term "last-born" (antyānām) indicates that this same rule applies even to those born in the direct order (anuloma) who are eligible for social intercourse. 14.40.
The appearance of teeth and so forth [are determined] by the mother and father. || 14.41 ||

From the time of the eruption of the teeth onwards, the mother and father must invariably perform the offering of water; thus it should be understood that for them as well, there was previously no fixed rule. || 14.41 ||
For children, those living in a foreign land, renunciants, and those who are not sapinda relatives, there is immediate purification.

An infant (*bāla*) is one prior to the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). Therefore, from the time of the naming ceremony until the eruption of teeth, the period of impurity should be understood as one day, as stated in another *Smṛti*: "For men who have not yet undergone the tonsure (*caula*), impurity is declared to last for one night" (MDh 5.67). From the eruption of teeth until the performance of the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*), the period lasts for three days.
"Having abandoned him like a log in the forest, they should observe impurity for only three days.

[MDh 5.69] One who has died in another country and whose death is not heard of at that very time is one "dwelling in a foreign land. An ascetic includes the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). Upon his death, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) for those who are not *sapindas*. A non-*sapinda* is one who shares the same water-libation (*samānodaka*); the scope regarding such a person has already been stated. (14.42)
And because of the obstruction of the kings' business. || 14.43 ||

The term "immediate purification" (sadyaḥśauca) carries over from the previous context. The plural number in "of kings" (rājñām) is intended to include ministers who resemble kings; this is also indicated by the word "and" (ca), which implies "whomsoever the king desires. Thus says Manu: "And whomsoever the king desires" (MDh 5.95). Regarding "the impossibility of his duty," such as protection and so forth, it means there would be an obstruction or an impossibility [in performing them]. 14.43.
And for the sake of not interrupting the Brahmin's private Vedic recitation—for the sake of not interrupting his private Vedic recitation. || 14.44 ||

The statement of the reason is for the purpose of making it known that impurity occurs in relation to Vedic study already performed. By the word "and" (ca), the aforementioned subjects are established for the purpose of allowing even Kṣatriyas and others to enter [the rite] on account of their own Vedic study. The double repetition is for the purpose of concluding the chapter.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Maskarīya Gautama-bhāṣya.
The fifteenth chapter: Now, one should offer the Śrāddha to the ancestors on the new moon day. 15.1.
The *śrāddha* is fivefold, as Vyāghra has stated:
"The *nitya*, the *naimittika*, the *kāmya*, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, and likewise another;
it should be known that *śrāddha* is traditionally remembered as being fivefold, including the *pārvaṇa*."
Among these, that which is performed day after day is the *nitya* (obligatory) rite, as Manu has said:
"One should offer the *śrāddha* to the ancestors every day with food and water, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing them satisfaction" (MDh 3.82).
Likewise, it is stated in that very same work:

"For the sake of the ancestors in the fivefold sacrifice (*pāñcayajñika*), one should feed even a single Brahmin; but for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva* offering, one should not feed any twice-born (*dvija*) at all. [MDh 3.83]
And so also another *smṛti* states:

"Except for the period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*), the daily *śrāddha* is not [interrupted]. As for what was said regarding the occasional *ekoddiṣṭa*—it is called *ekoddiṣṭa* because it is performed with reference to only one person—as Kātyāyana says: "Now, the *ekoddiṣṭa*: there is one twice-born man, one vessel, one purifier (*pavitra*), even one *arghya* offering, one *piṇḍa*; there is no invocation (*āvāhana*) and no offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*). This should be performed starting immediately after the period of impurity (*āśauca*) and prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, as Laugākṣi says:
"The *ekoddiṣṭa* should be performed every month for a year, and likewise once a year; the first [of these] is on the eleventh day. Likewise, Vyāghra also says:

"On the eleventh day it should be performed, and likewise on the three fortnights; one should diligently perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite also at the six-month mark. Thereafter, when the year is complete, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must be performed. And so says Jātūkarṇi:

"Therefore, when a year has passed, or likewise after three fortnights, one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony; it may take place even earlier if there is an occasion for a festive rite (*vṛddhi*). The phrase "three fortnights" refers to the case of one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). Why? Because of the statement of Bṛhaspati. He says as follows:
If the new moon occurs immediately after the tenth night,
the son who maintains the sacred fires must perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on that very day.
"In the absence of that [the first anniversary], the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is prescribed after three fortnights.

Thus it is heard in the *Jābāla-śruti*: "The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* occurs at the end of three fortnights. After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, on occasions such as the *saṃkrānti*, a *śrāddha* must be performed by offering three *piṇḍas*. On the anniversary of the death each year, an *ekoddiṣṭa* should be performed. As Uśanas said:
"On the *saṃkrānti*, during an eclipse, on a festival day (*parvan*), at the solstice (*ayana*), and during the *mahālaya*..."
"In that case, one should offer three morsels; however, if the day is spoiled, one should offer only one."

Every year, after the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī, the Aṣṭakā rites must be performed. Thus says the author of the Gṛhyasūtra: “After the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī, there are three dark fortnights; in each of these, there is one Aṣṭakā: the Śākāṣṭakā, the Māṃsāṣṭakā, and the Apūpāṣṭakā,” and so forth. Among these, that which is performed out of desire is *kāmya*, such as “one desiring a son [should sacrifice] on the eleventh day,” and so on. The *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is the *nāndīmukha*. That which is called *pārvaṇa* is the monthly *śrāddha*. Alternatively, whatever is performed by means of the offering of the three *piṇḍas*—such as the Aṣṭakā and others—all the remainder is *naimittika* (occasional).

While this fivefold [classification] stands—[regarding the statement]: "Then one should offer the *śrāddha* to the ancestors on the new moon day" (*amāvāsyā*)—the word "then" (*atha*) means immediately after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Why? Because the text begins with "One should offer the *śrāddha* to the ancestors on the new moon day," and it is possible to understand this as the monthly *śrāddha* (*māsi-śrāddha*). Furthermore, other *smṛtis* prohibit the monthly *śrāddha* prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. As Bṛhaspati says:
"But he who performs the *pārvaṇa* [rite] before the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* becomes a worm and sinks into the excrement of dogs along with his ancestors."

If it is argued that, in that case, only those *śrāddha* rites performed prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be mentioned, [the answer is] that this is for the purpose of indicating the absence of such rites for some; immediately thereafter, only the *pārvaṇa* rite is to be performed. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"For ascetics and for those who have died [as such], no other ritual act is seen;
when the eleventh day arrives, the *pārvaṇa* is prescribed."
"For those who have taken lifelong vows (naiṣṭhika), for forest-dwellers (vanastha), and likewise for the liberated (mukta),
neither the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa nor the Ekoddiṣṭa is prescribed."

*Śrāddha* is the name of a ritual act, so called because it is accomplished through extraordinary faith (*śraddhā*). Indeed, only one who possesses faith undertakes it, as seen from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "By means of the food offered by their sons, the ancestors, wherever they may be, dwell in happiness through its enjoyment. On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), when the sun and moon are at their closest approach, [the offering] is made for the ancestors; because of the plural number, it should be given for the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather as well. (15.1)
Or, beginning from the fifth day of the latter fortnight, according to one's faith. (15.2)

Or one should offer [the śrāddha] beginning from the fifth day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa). The meaning is that it should be performed according to the śrāddha and according as faith exists. The intention is that the aṣṭakā-śrāddha should be offered starting from the fifth day. The mention of the "latter fortnight" (aparapakṣa) is so that it may not occur during the former fortnight (pūrvapakṣa), because of the context concerning the new moon (amāvāsyā). 15.2.
Or in all [cases]. || 15.3 ||

The meaning is that one should perform [the rite] either during the entire dark fortnight or beginning from the first day (pratipad). This is to be understood as applying to one who possesses abundant wealth.
Or [it may be performed] when there is the presence of the substance, the place, and a Brāhmaṇa. || 15.4 ||
"Of the substance," such as silver and so forth. And likewise Vyāghra says:
"Silver, black śāka-vegetables, rhinoceros meat, fish, meat, honey, and all kinds of food fit for sages (munyanna) are prescribed for the sake of infinite [merit]."

Regarding the location, such as Puṣkara and others; as Vyāghra has said: "At Puṣkara, the Śrāddha is inexhaustible, and likewise at Kurukṣetra, at a river, at the ocean, at a lake, in a cow-pen, and likewise on a mountain."

Regarding Brāhmaṇas and ascetics who purify the company (*paṅktipāvana*), as Vyāsa has stated: "The *svadhā* offering, a silver vessel, a daughter's son, a *kutapa* blanket, sesame seeds, clothing, and a triple-staffed ascetic (*tridaṇḍī yati*)— these are the purifiers."
The intention is that one should perform [the rite] either when [the materials] are at hand, upon rebirth, or according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa). || 15.4 ||
The restriction of time is according to one's capacity. || 15.5 ||

When there is an absolute impossibility for him to obtain the requisite materials and so forth, then the previously stated restriction of time—namely, that it must be performed after the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī—is no longer applicable. The intention is that the rite should be performed in whichever month those materials are absolutely available. The point is that just as there is no specific restriction regarding the fortnight when materials are unavailable, likewise there is no restriction regarding the specific month. By this same logic, the absence of any restriction regarding the lunar day (*tithi*) is also established. (15.5)
And at all times during a funeral rite,
he should enhance the qualities and preparations of the food.

One should "exert" (prakarṣet), meaning one should perform with excellence: the qualities of the food, such as its specific types like vegetables or cakes; the preparations, such as being well-cooked or fragrant; and the ritual rules, such as using *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, and wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). || 15.6 ||
He should feed at least nine persons. || 15.7 ||
This is so when there is capacity. 15.7.
Or with uneven numbers, or according to one's enthusiasm. || 15.8 ||

"Odd-numbered [guests], according to one's enthusiasm and according to one's capacity, fewer than nine; because of the mention of 'fewer' (*avara*) in the preceding [rule], and because there is no possibility of [reaching] more than nine.

Now, one might object: "It should simply have been stated as 'or odd-numbered' (*ayujo vā*). Since [the number] beyond nine has not been prescribed [by that rule], this [new] undertaking would serve only to prescribe a lower number. Consequently, the option would be established solely by the incapacity [to feed more], and thus the phrase 'according to one's enthusiasm' (*yathotsāham*) would be redundant.
It is replied: Even when there is enthusiasm, one should feed [the guests] without contradicting [the requirements of] hospitality and so forth. As Vasiṣṭha says: [text follows].
One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one for each of the two; even if very wealthy, one should not be overly attached to a large company.
"Hospitality, the proper place and time, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should avoid it. (VaDh 11.27–28).
The "gods" are the Viśvedevas, who constitute a part of that rite. As Vyāsa said:
The virtuous daughter of Dakṣa was celebrated by the name Viśvā;
her sons were the high-souled and exceedingly powerful Viśvedevas.
Kratu, Dakṣa, Vasu, Satya, Kāla, Kāmya, Śuci, Ruci,
Purūravas, and Ādruvas— these are to be known as the ten immortals.
In the *iṣṭi-śrāddha*, Kratu and Dakṣa; in the *aṣṭakā*, Kāla and Kāmyaka;
in the *nāndīmukha*, Vasu and Satya; and in the optional (*kāmya*) rite, Śuci and Ruci.
Purūravas and Āyus are indeed proclaimed [as the ancestors] for the Pārvaṇa rite.
"One should address them by name according to their respective assignments.
Likewise, another Smṛti states:
"The Śrāddha should begin and end with the gods; it should not begin and end with the ancestors."
"If it should end with the father and so forth, the *rakṣasas* indeed consume it.
Likewise, there is also a verse by Bhārgava:
"When there is only one Brahmin and no second is available..."
"The portion for the ancestors (pitṛs) should be assigned to the Brāhmaṇa, and the portion for the gods (daiva) should be assigned to the hand.
Likewise, Bṛhaspati says:
"One should seat two Atharvan Brāhmaṇas facing east for the rite of the gods (daiva)."
And likewise, for the ancestral rite (pitrya), three twice-born men who recite the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, facing north.
Thus [ends the verse]. 15.8.
He states what kind of brahmins one should feed:
those learned in the Vedas who are endowed with eloquence, beauty, youth, and good character. (15.9)

One should feed such Brahmins as are learned in the Vedas, who have studied the meters; who are endowed with eloquence, speaking in refined Sanskrit; who are endowed with beauty, possessing pleasing forms; who are endowed with age, being advanced in years; and who are endowed with character, having tranquil minds. (15.9)
He states an exception regarding the excellence of age:
"The gift to the young comes first. (15.10)
That which is the first *ekoddiṣṭa* should be given to those who are young.
Some [behave] like fathers. || 15.11 ||

Some maintain that one should offer [the oblation] at the very same ages at which the father and others passed away. This rule should be understood as referring specifically to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite performed during the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Indeed, the *ekoddiṣṭa* is explicitly prescribed for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* in another Smṛti; as Yama says:
"When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is reached, one should likewise perform two *śrāddhas*;
at the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should feed the Brahmins according to the *pārvaṇa* rite."
"And he should prepare food separately according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.

Alternatively, "as for the father" means that one should feed the young [relative] with the father in mind, the elder with the grandfather in mind, and the very old with the great-grandfather in mind. (15.11)
And one should not perform the duties of a friend with him. 15.12.
That faithful person should not engage in mutual affairs with friends; by the use of the word "and," [it is implied that] one should also avoid forming alliances with enemies. 15.12.
In the absence of a son, the sapindas, the mother’s sapindas, and the pupils shall offer [the funeral oblation].

This is first of all the primary rule: that sons perform the *śrāddha*. In their absence, however, the *sapiṇḍas* are mentioned. In their absence, the mother’s *sapiṇḍas*, such as maternal uncles (*mātula*) and others. In their absence, the disciples; because they are designated by a term denoting a relationship, [the rule applies] to the teacher (*ācārya*), and by the word "and" (*ca*), also to the sacrificer (*yājya*) and the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). And this refers specifically to the subject of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, because the mother’s *sapiṇḍas*, the disciple, and the sacrificer are taught as the givers [of the offering]. For indeed, one person’s mother’s *sapiṇḍa* does not necessarily become the mother’s *sapiṇḍa* of that person’s father. The same applies to the disciple and the sacrificer. Thus, in the case of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and other rites, a different order is to be observed. As Uśanas says: "In the absence of sons, the *sapiṇḍas*, the *samānodakas*, the *sagotras*, and those of the same *ṛṣi*-lineage," and so forth. The compound is analyzed as meaning that the *ekoddiṣṭa* should be performed by any single one of them, and not by all of them together as is the case with impurity (*āśauca*).
In their absence, the officiating priest and the teacher [should do so]. 15.14.

The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) for one who is to be sacrificed for, and the teacher (*ācārya*) for his disciple—in their absence, that is, when the preceding relative is absent—[are to be included]. This separate mention is intended to indicate that there is no requirement for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the case of officiating priests and teachers when one performs a *śrāddha*. Thus, it should be understood that for the preceding relatives, expiation must necessarily be performed. Furthermore, for those performing a *śrāddha* for officiating priests and teachers, prosperity (*abhyudaya*) ensues by virtue of the force of the injunction. The inclusion of the phrase "in their absence" in the preceding rule—"maternal sapindas and disciples" (GDh 15.13)—is also intended to indicate their eligibility [for the *śrāddha*]. It should be understood that the *śrāddha* is to be offered only to those who are worthy. Why? Because of the force of another Smṛti text. As Prajāpati has said:
And for those killed by cows or Brahmins, by lightning or by a king,
as well as for those who commit suicide and likewise for the fallen (patitas).
For Brahmins killed by serpents, for those who wander about according to their own lusts,
and for those who have resorted to heretical sects, no funeral rites (pretakarma) are prescribed.
If that lowest of men should perform [the rite] out of affection, fear of consequences, or other such motives— even if he has been killed by a Caṇḍāla— I shall declare the expiation for him.
Whoever should carry or cremate any one of these deceased persons shall perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance; if it was done intentionally, he shall perform the Tapta-kṛcchra.
Having merely touched such a corpse, or likewise caused it to fall, one should not eat for one night;
however, if it was done intentionally, one should fast for three nights.
Having performed a *śrāddha*, one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance; if done intentionally, one should perform a *sāntapana*.
Likewise, for those who eat at a *śrāddha*, the penance is double that for celibate students (*brahmacārin*).
Thus [ends the verse]. 15.14.

One should not feed a thief, a eunuch, an outcast, an atheist, one who lives by such [atheistic] means, one who has killed a hero, one whose younger brother marries before him, one whose elder brother’s wife marries before her husband, one who officiates for women, a village priest, one who neglects his sacred fires, a drunkard, a rogue, a false witness, or a professional messenger. (15.15)

Since these individuals might otherwise be eligible for marriage through the possession of qualities such as being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), they are here prohibited. A "thief" (*stena*) refers to one who steals gold and the like; he is excluded because he is already considered fallen (*patita*). A "eunuch" (*klība*) is one whose virility is destroyed; thus the Blessed Vāsudeva said, "Do not yield to weakness, O son of Kuntī" (BhG 2.3), and so forth. This does not refer to a person of the third gender (*tṛtīyaprakṛti*), because such a person lacks the status of being learned in the Vedas and thus would not have been eligible in the first place. A "fallen man" (*patita*) is one who has killed a Brahmin and the like. An "atheist" (*nāstika*) is one whose intellect is fixed on the non-existence of the next world and so forth; he too is one whose mind is corrupted, whereas one whose actions are corrupted is taught to be fallen due to the habitual performance of censurable acts. One who "lives by that" means one who subsists by means of atheism itself, specifically through the gateway of the Lokāyata (materialist) treatises. A "slayer of a hero" (*vīrahā*) is a killer of any human being, since the word "hero" (*vīra*) is applied to a man in such passages as "and of a woman who has no hero [husband]" (MDh 4.213). Alternatively, it may mean one who performs the Soma-pressing in vain, based on the Vedic revelation: "He who presses the Soma is indeed a slayer of the heroes of the gods. An "agredidhiṣū" and a "didhiṣūpati": the word "husband" (*pati*) is connected to each term. An *agredidhiṣū* is an elder sister who is married before her younger sister; that same elder sister is then called a *didhiṣū*. Thus says Manu: [Manu 3.173] "The husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried is called a *didhiṣūpati*; the elder sister is called an *agredidhiṣū*. And: [Manu 3.174] "The husband of an *agredidhiṣū* is a *didhiṣūpati*; both of them, having committed this sin, fall from their caste after a year. And: [Manu 3.175] "A younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried is called a *didhiṣū*; the elder sister is called an *agredidhiṣū*. And: [Manu 3.176] "One who marries a *didhiṣū* is a *didhiṣūpati*, and one who marries an *agredidhiṣū* is a *didhiṣūpati*; both of them, having committed this sin, fall from their caste after a year. And: [Manu 3.177] "An elder sister who gives herself away while her younger sister is still unmarried is an *agredidhiṣū*; she, along with the one who marries her, is fallen. And: [Manu 3.178] "If a younger sister is given in marriage before the elder sister, both of them—the giver and the taker—are called *agredidhiṣū* and *didhiṣūpati* respectively. And: [Manu 3.179] "The elder sister who gives herself away while her younger sister is unmarried is an *agredidhiṣū*; she, along with the one who marries her, is fallen. And: [Manu 3.180] "If a younger sister is given in marriage before the elder sister, both of them—the giver and the taker—are called *agredidhiṣū* and *didhiṣūpati* respectively. And: [Manu 3.181] "The elder sister who gives herself away while her younger sister is unmarried is an *agredidhiṣū*; she, along with the one who marries her, is fallen. And: [Manu 3.182] "If a younger sister is given in marriage before the elder sister, both of them—the giver and the taker—are called *agredidhiṣū* and *didhiṣūpati* respectively. And: [Manu 3.183] "The elder sister who gives herself away while her younger sister is unmarried is an *agredidhiṣū*; she, along with the one who marries her, is fallen. And: [Manu 3.184] "If a younger sister is given in marriage before the elder sister, both of them—the giver and the taker—are called *agredidhiṣū* and *didhiṣūpati* respectively. And: [Manu 3.185] "The elder sister who gives herself away while her younger sister is unmarried is an *agredidhiṣū*; she, along with the one who marries her, is fallen. And: [Manu 3.186] "If a younger sister is given in marriage before the elder sister, both of them—the giver and the taker—are called *agredidhiṣū* and *didhiṣūpati* respectively. And: [Manu 3.187] "The elder sister who gives herself away while her younger sister is unmarried is an *agredidhiṣū*; she, along with the one who marries her, is fallen. And: [Manu 3.188] "If a younger sister is given in marriage before the elder sister, both of them—the giver and the taker—are called *agredidhiṣū* and *didhiṣūpati* respectively. And: [Manu 3.189] "The elder sister who gives herself away while her younger sister is unmarried is an *agredidhiṣū*; she, along with the one who marries her, is fallen. And: [Manu 3.190] "If a younger sister is given in marriage before the elder sister, both of them—the giver and the taker—are called *agredidhiṣū* and *didhiṣūpati* respectively. And: [Manu 3.191] "The elder sister who gives herself away while her younger sister is unmarried is an *agredidhiṣū*; she, along with the one who marries her, is fallen. And: [Manu 3.192] "If a younger sister is given in marriage before the elder sister, both of them—the giver and the taker—are called *agredidhiṣū* and *didhiṣūpati* respectively. And: [Manu 3.193] "The elder sister who gives herself away while her younger sister is unmarried is an *agredidhiṣū*; she, along with the one who marries her, is fallen. And: [Manu 3.194] "If a younger sister is given in marriage before the elder sister, both of them—the giver and the taker—are called *agredidhiṣū* and *didhiṣūpati* respectively. And: [Manu 3.195] "The elder sister who gives herself away while her younger sister is unmarried is an *agredidhiṣū*; she, along with the one who marries her, is fallen. And: [Manu 3.196] "If a younger sister is given in marriage before the elder sister, both of them—the giver and the taker—are called *agredidhiṣū* and *didhiṣūpati* respectively. And: [Manu 3.197] "The elder sister who gives herself away while her younger sister is unmarried is an *agredidhiṣū*; she, along with the one who marries her, is fallen. And: [Manu 3.198] "If a younger sister is given in marriage before the elder sister, both of them—the giver and the taker—are called *agredidhiṣū* and *didhiṣūpati* respectively. And: [Manu 3.199] "The elder sister who gives herself away while her younger sister is unmarried is an *agredidhiṣū*; she, along with the one who marries her, is fallen. And: [Manu
"If a younger sister is married while the elder sister remains unmarried, she is to be known as an *agredidhiṣū*, while the former [the elder sister] is recorded as a *didhiṣū*.
The husband of these two is [the *didhiṣūpati*]. Alternatively, he alone is designated by the term "husband" (*pati*), as Prajāpati has said:
He who, out of lust, becomes attached to the wife of his deceased brother—
even though she has been appointed [to bear a son] according to dharma— is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*.
"He is called an *agredidhiṣū* while his brother is still alive. Or, as stated by Vyāghra:
"The wise call the husband of a woman who previously had another husband an *agredidhiṣūpati*."
A Brahmin whose wife is a younger sister married before her elder sister is called an *agredidhiṣū*.

"One who officiates for women" (*strīyājaka*); the word "officiant" (*yājaka*) is connected with each [term]. He who performs sacrifices for women, such as those dedicated to Kāmadeva and others, is a "woman-officiant. A "village-officiant" (*grāmayājaka*) is one who officiates for many. An "ajapāla" is one who subsists by guarding goats. An "abandoned-fire man" (*utsṛṣṭāgni*) is one who, contrary to the scriptures, abandons either the *śrauta* or *smārta* sacred fire. A "liquor-drinker" (*madyapa*) is one who subsists by dealing in liquor such as that from coconuts, or one who consumes liquors other than *surā*. A "wicked person" (*kucara*) is one of reprehensible conduct; reprehensible conduct includes being a teacher of one's own son, or having a habit of worshipping and begging from deities and others. A "false witness" (*kūṭasākṣin*) is well known. A "juggler" (*prātihārika*) is one who subsists by means of magic. One should not feed these. Since the prohibition of feeding them is already established by the prohibition of touching those who have fallen (*patita*), this section is commenced for the purpose of prohibiting the feeding of those who have performed penance. (15.15)
And he whose [birth] was through a legitimate union. || 15.16 ||
An *upapati* is a paramour; and by the phrase "of whom he [is the paramour]," it is meant that she is an unchaste woman whose wife he is. One should not feed these two. (15.16)

One who drinks from a sacrificial pit, a seller of Soma, an arsonist, a poisoner, one who has violated his Guru’s bed, a servant of a multitude, one who approaches a woman who should not be approached,

a violent person, an elder brother whose younger brother marries first, a younger brother who marries before his elder, one who causes a marriage to be contracted for another, one who performs the marriage rites for another, one who abandons himself, one with bad nails, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, and one with three [defective] teeth— [these are those excluded].

[One should avoid] those who are intent on rebirth, gamblers, debtors, slaves, impostors, those who have a Śūdra as a husband, those who have rejected the Vedas, the lazy, the gluttonous, merchants, those who live by manual crafts, and those whose habits consist of gambling, instrumental music, clapping, dancing, singing, and so forth. 15.17.

The mention of the *kuṇḍa* is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *golaka*; he who eats the food of such a person is a *kuṇḍāśin*. By the prohibition against eating the food of a *kuṇḍāśin*, the prohibition of both the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka* is established by implication. Their specific natures are to be understood from another *smṛti*, as Manu says:
"Two types of sons, the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*, are born from the wives of others:
the *kuṇḍa* when the husband is alive, and the *golaka* when the husband is dead" (MDh 3.174).

A *soma*-seller is one who sells the *soma* creeper or sells the ritual acts accomplished by it. An incendiary is one who sets fire to a house. A poisoner is one who gives a poisonous substance. An *avakīrṇin* is a student (*brahmacārī*) who has intentionally violated his vow of celibacy. As Manu says:
"The knowers of Dharma and exponents of the Veda declare that for a twice-born man established in his vows, the intentional emission of semen constitutes a transgression of his vow" (MDh 11.120).

A servant of a *gaṇa* is one who carries out the errands of groups. One who approaches those who should not be approached (*agamyāgāmī*) is one who defiles a maiden; according to some, this refers to one who has sexual intercourse with a woman who shares his *pravara*. Because of the instruction regarding equality in the rule, "In the case of a female friend, a uterine sister, a woman of the same *gotra*, a pupil’s wife, a daughter-in-law, and a cow, it is equal to violating one's own bed" (GDh 23.12), such a person is included under the category of the "outcast" (*patita*). A violent person (*hiṃsra*) is one who delights in the killing of living beings. An elder brother whose marriage remains unperformed while a younger brother marries is the "one who marries before the elder" (*parivettā*), and consequently, that elder brother is the "one superseded" (*parivitti*). One for whom the consecration of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) was performed while the younger brother had not yet performed his is the "one whose fire was taken over" (*paryāhita*), and the younger brother is the "one who caused the fire to be taken over" (*paryādhātā*).
But surely the terms *parivitti* and *parivettṛ* also apply respectively to the *paryāhita* and the *paryādhātṛ*, since this is seen to be so in another Smṛti. As Manu says:
"He who enters into the union of wife and *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as a *parivettṛ*; the elder brother is the *parivitti*. [MDh 3.171]
And consequently, it would be useless to mention the *paryāhita* and the *paryādhātṛ* separately.
To this it is replied: both are mentioned for the purpose of including both the one who performs the sacrifice (*yājana*) and the one who gives the girl (*kanyā-dāna*). As Manu says:
"The *parivitti*, the *parivettṛ*, and she by whom the *parivitti* is performed... [64]
"All of them go to hell, including the donor and the officiating priest as the fifth. (Manu Dharma Śāstra 3.172). An exception to this rule should be observed, as Uśanas has said:
"The sons of a paternal uncle, the sons of a stepmother, and likewise the sons of another's wife..."
"There is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] when there is union with a wife and the *agnihotra* fire.
Thus also says Vasiṣṭha:
"One who is insane, a sinner, a leper, an outcast, or even a eunuch..."
"And one suffering from consumption (rājayakṣman) should not be waited for. Thus says Śātātapa:
"In the case of one who is impotent, one ruined by the country, one who has fallen [from caste], or likewise one who has renounced the world..."
"And there is no fault in marrying [a younger sister] when she has been appointed according to the Yogaśāstra.
Likewise, Kaṇva says:
"If one whose mind is addicted to vices, or if he should be an atheist..."
There is no fault in superseding a younger brother who has acted improperly.
And so forth.

One who has abandoned his own self is a reckless person. According to some, this refers to one who carries a weapon in his hand. One with coarse hair is *śipiviṣṭa*; according to some, this means one whose generative organ is deficient. One with deformed nails is one whose nails have been ruined without cause. One with black teeth is one whose teeth are dark, provided it is not due to disease. A son of a remarried woman is the son of an unchaste woman. A gambler is one who plays at dice. This is also an indication for those who trade in clay elephants, horses, and so forth. An *ajapa* is one who has merely been initiated but lacks Vedic learning (*aśrotriya*). A royal servant is one who performs errands for a king, such as a messenger and the like. A counterfeit-maker is one who deals in false weights and measures, or one who is a cheat by any means whatsoever. A husband of a Śūdra woman is one for whom she alone is the wife. A *nirākṛti* is one who does not abide in any stage of life (*āśrama*). A leper is one afflicted with skin disease, or one who seizes land. A usurer is a moneylender who operates by forbidden means. A merchant is one who lives by the occupation of a Vaiśya, provided that such an occupation is possible. One who lives by crafts is one who subsists on carpentry, painting, and so forth, as well as one who learns those arts from them; this is because of the use of the prefix *upa*. One addicted to the bow is one who subsists on the science of archery. One addicted to musical instruments is one who subsists on the flute, lute, and so forth. One addicted to rhythm is one who subsists on beating drums and the like. One addicted to dancing is one who subsists on dancing. One addicted to singing is one who subsists on singing. One should not feed these. From this very prohibition, it is established that they perform improper acts; therefore, theft and other such acts must not be committed. (15.17)
Those who have been divided against their father's will. || 15.18 ||
And those who have been divided from their father against his will—by the word "and," it is implied also by their mother—one should not feed them either. 15.18.
And some [teach] their disciples and those of the same lineage. 15.19.

By the word "and" (*ca*), the *yājyās* (those for whom one sacrifices) are included; by the second "and," those of the same *ṛṣi*-lineage (*samānārṣeya*) are included. Because of the use of the singular "some" (*eke*), Gautama maintains that only those worthy of being fed (*bhojanīya*) are intended. In this regard, it should be understood that if they possess good qualities, then one should feed them; if they are devoid of good qualities, then they are not to be fed. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "One should also feed disciples who possess good qualities" (VaDh 11.33). There, by the word "also" (*api*), those of the same *gotra* are likewise included. 15.19.
One should feed more than three [guests]. 15.20.

Since the rule “or odd-numbered [guests], according to one’s enthusiasm” (GDh 15.8) applies without distinction, this [present verse] is stated for the sake of specification: even in the absence of enthusiasm, one should feed an odd number [of guests] beyond three. 15.20.
One who possesses virtuous qualities. || 15.21 ||

"One should feed even one," because of the use of the singular number (*ekavacana*). Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Or else, one may feed a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, who is endowed with learning, conduct, and character, and who is free from inauspicious marks" (VaDh 11.29).

The non-inclusion of the word "or" (vā) is for the purpose of permitting both [alternatives]. Thus Manu says: "One should feed even a single learned man at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors; one obtains abundant fruit, but not even many who are ignorant of the mantras. (MDh 3.129)
Thus [ends the section]. 15.21.
One who performs a *śrāddha* immediately after [the period of impurity] and then approaches a Śūdra woman causes his ancestors to dwell in her excrement for a month.
By this, celibacy is prescribed for both the eater and the giver. And so Manu says:
"A twice-born man invited to a rite for the ancestors should always remain self-restrained;
he should not recite the Vedas while that śrāddha lasts. (MDh 3.188)

"Sadyas" (immediately) is an adverbial modifier meaning "he leads [her] away immediately. The mention of a Śūdra woman is for the purpose of defining the duration of time; for other women, the time is shorter. The mention of the "talpa" (bed) is intended to mean "wife. Consequently, the fault is more severe in the case of another [woman]. The meaning is that by dwelling near her for a month with the ancestors, he becomes connected with as much sin as there is in that offense. (15.22)
Therefore, on that day he should observe celibacy. || 15.23 ||
Since this fault exists, one should avoid sexual intercourse on that day even during the fertile period, because of the statement of the underlying reason. 15.23.
It is defiled by looking at a dog, a caṇḍāla, or one who has fallen from his caste. 15.24.

Food or a *śrāddha* rite that has been looked upon by dogs and other such creatures becomes defective. The meaning is that in the case of ordinary food, it is unfit to be eaten; in the case of a *śrāddha*, however, it becomes as if it were never performed at all. || 15.24 ||
Therefore, one should give [the gift] in an enclosed space. || 15.25 ||

Since this is so, one should give [the food] in a concealed place. The statement of the reason is that even other than at a *śrāddha*, one must eat only in a screened enclosure (*pariśrita*). || 15.25 ||
Or he may scatter sesame seeds.
It serves to pacify faults that have not been rectified. Furthermore, by the power of another Smṛti, the ancestors attain satisfaction. As Bhṛgu has said:
"Even water, when offered to a twice-born man mixed with sesame seeds for the ancestors, becomes a cow of plenty;
therefore, this is what the ancestors accept. (15.26)
Or one who purifies the assembly may pacify it. || 15.27 ||
The one who purifies the company, who will be described later, shall pacify the fault of not being surrounded [by others]. || 15.27 ||

Those who purify the company are: one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga), a senior Sāmaga, one who has thrice kindled the Nāciketa fire, one who knows the three Madhu verses, one who knows the Trisuparṇa, one who maintains the five fires, a Snātaka, one who knows both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas, one who knows the Dharma, and one who is the offspring of a woman married according to the Brahma rite. || 15.28 ||

And these, being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), are called "purifiers of the assembly" (*paṅktipāvana*) because they purify—that is, render faultless—the row [of diners] through their possession of superior qualities. One who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅgavid*) is one who understands the meaning of at least one of the six limbs. Likewise, it is said in the *Purāṇa*:
"Even he who has mastered one of the fourteen branches of knowledge, as well as those who know the absolute liberation of the Self (*ātmakaivalya*), all of them are purifiers of the assembly."

A *jyeṣṭhasāmaga* is one who studies the *jyeṣṭhasāman*, which is a specific *sāman* of the *chandogas*; thus, one who studies that is a *jyeṣṭhasāmaga*. The *triṇāciketa* is a specific *ṛk* of the *adhvaryus*. The *trimadhu* is a specific *sūkta* of the *bahvṛcas*. The *trisuparṇa* belongs to both the *bahvṛcas* and the *taittirīyas*. A *pañcāgni* is one who maintains five fires, including the *sabhyāvasathyas*. A *snātaka* is one who has completed his studies and vows. One who knows the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas* is so even without knowledge of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*). A knower of *dharma* is one who knows the meaning of the *dharmaśāstras*. One whose lineage is descended from a *brahmadeyā* (a woman married by the *brāhma* rite) is the progeny of a marriage performed according to the *brāhma* form. The particle *iti* indicates manner; as Vasiṣṭha says: "One who knows the *triṇāciketa*, the *pañcāgni*, the *trisuparṇa*, the *caturmedha*, the *vājasaneyin*, one who knows the six auxiliary sciences, a *chandoga*, a *jyeṣṭhasāmika*, one who knows the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*, one who studies his own duties, and he whose ten generations on both the maternal and paternal sides are known to be *śrotriyas*—these learned men and *snātakas* are purifiers of the row (*paṅktipāvanas*). [VaDh 3.19]. This is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those mentioned in other *smṛtis* as well. 15.28.
And likewise in the case of sacrificial oblations. 15.29.

Regarding the oblations in rites for prosperity (*abhyudayakarman*): the plural number indicates that this applies not only to the *daiva* rite which is an ancillary part of the ancestral rites, but rather to all rites for prosperity as well. Although the meaning is already established by the word "and" (*ca*), the word "only" (*eva*) is used for the purpose of excluding those who purify the row (*paṅktipāvana*). (15.29)
Some say that one should offer *durvā* grass and other items specifically at the *śrāddha* ceremony; some say specifically at the *śrāddha* ceremony. || 15.30 ||

Those who have been enumerated beginning with the Durvālas should be fed only at a *śrāddha* rite, and not at a *daiva* rite; this is because of the mention of "some" (*eke*). However, Gautama does not hold this view, for he maintains that the option is determined by the possibility or impossibility of the situation. (15.30)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the *Maskarīya-Gautama-bhāṣya*.
Regarding the sixteenth chapter,
since this dharma is common to the twice-born (*dvijāti*), he says [the following]:
Having performed the Upākarma ceremony on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Proṣṭhapada, one should study the Vedas for the duration of the rainy season.

The full moon day conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇā is called Śrāvaṇī; the formation of this derivative term should be understood as an optional one. Starting from that day, what occurs during the rainy season is "vārṣika"; this too is for the sake of technical designation, and thus the usage in the rule “abhito vārṣikam” (on both sides of the rainy season) is established. Alternatively, having begun with the full moon of Proṣṭhapadī, and having performed the *upākaraṇa* (the formal opening ceremony), he should study. Study consists of both the acquisition of what was not previously learned and the rehearsal of what has been mastered. The *chandāṃsi* are the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. This is what is meant: having performed the *upākaraṇa* on either the Śrāvaṇī or the Proṣṭhapadī full moon, he should carry out the study of the Vedas connected to the rainy season starting from that point. 16.1.
He states for how long one should study:
"For four and a half months, or for five [months] during the southern course of the sun. (16.2)
The option subsequent to the *upākaraṇa* is to be understood with reference to whether the purpose has been accomplished or not. 16.2.
While studying, a student who has shaved off his body hair shall not eat meat. 16.3.

A *brahmacārī* is one who avoids sexual intercourse; he has his body hair removed but does not have a beard grown. By the mention of "hair" (*loman*), nails and so forth are also included. He shall not eat meat, even that which remains after the worship of the gods. This is a rule for the householder, as there is no possibility of its application to a *brahmacārī*. Regarding the preservation of celibacy, he may approach his wife during her season. Why? Because of the traditional law (*smṛti*) stating: "They teach that for a householder, approaching [his wife] only during her season constitutes celibacy. If, by the term "having removed body hair," the state of having hair already trimmed were intended, then since this would already be established by the rule "he shall not suddenly have a grown beard" (GDh 9.7), the present rule would become redundant. Therefore, by the force of its being stated here, it is understood specifically as the state of not having [the hair] trimmed. 16.3.
Or the observance may last for two months. 16.4.

This rule of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) lasts for two months; there is an option depending on one's capacity. The inclusion of the term "rule" (*niyama*) is intended to indicate its mandatory nature. And thus, in the absence of this rule, the cessation of the tendency toward study should be understood [as the consequence]. 16.4.
Studying in this manner,
he should not study when the wind carries dust during the day.

One should not study as long as a wind that carries a rain of dust blows during the day. Although the phrase "one that carries dust during the day" would have sufficed, the inclusion of the word *vāyu* (wind) is for the purpose of indicating that one should not study even when there is merely a whirling gust (*vātyā*). Thus Uśanas says: "A whirlwind is a *piśācī*; therefore, one should not study during it. Because of the mention of "during the day," there is no fault at night; if [study] were intended for the night as well, it would have been established simply by not mentioning "day" at all. 16.5.
In the case of one who hears [the recitation] by ear at night. || 16.6 ||
Regarding "karṇaśrāviṇi": when the wind is audible at night—that is, when it fills the ear with sound—one should not study. Because of the mention of "night," there is no fault during the day. (16.6)
amidst the sounds of arrows, kettledrums, clay drums, and the cries of those in distress.

The *vāṇa* is a lute (*vīṇā*), as seen in the *Mahāvrata* [section] where it says, "the *vāṇa* has a hundred strings. The *bherī* and *mṛdaṅga* are well known [types of drums]. The word *garta* refers to the sound of a chariot, or an indistinct noise. The word *ārta* refers to the sound of wailing, or such things as shouting. The word *śabda* is connected with each of these; as long as their sounds persist, there is no study [of the Veda]. 16.7.
In the clamor of dogs, jackals, and donkeys. || 16.8 ||

The word *hrāda* is to be connected with each [term] individually: namely, to the sound (*śabda*) of dogs and so forth when they are combined—that is, in a "howling together" (*saṃhrāda*) of dogs, a "howling together" of jackals, and a "howling together" of donkeys. This is because the author of the Commentary has stated that the prefix *sam-* signifies "becoming one" (*ekībhāva*). By the logic of the "stick and cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikā*), this should be understood to apply even to the three combined. And thus, there is no fault in [the rule applying to] each one individually. (16.8)
In the red rainbows and mists. || 16.9 ||

One should not study when there is a red rainbow or when there is mist. "Lauhitya" refers to the red color of the sky; when that is seen, one should not study. Likewise with the "moonbow" (indradhanus), which is well known. "Mist" (nīhāra) means snow. As long as these are visible, one should not study. 16.9
And when clouds appear outside the rainy season. || 16.10 ||

When there is a cloud accompanied by water during the non-seasonal rains, there is no study for anyone; the word "and" (ca) implies that this also applies when lightning is seen. As long as the phenomenon is visible, there is a suspension of study. Thus Kaṇva says: "One should not study when lightning is seen. 16.10.
He has urinated and defecated. || 16.11 ||

As long as urine or feces have arisen, there is a suspension of study even if they have not been voided; however, once they have been voided, it is because it will be stated later that "one is impure even mentally" (GDh 16.47). || 16.11 ||
In the night, at the twilights, and in water. || 16.12 ||

By the word *niśā* (night), midnight is meant, not the night in general, because there is no commencement of specific exceptions such as those found in the rule "during lightning and at night" (GDh 16.25). Therefore, one should not study while standing in water at midnight or during the twilights. 16.13.
And it rains. || 16.13 ||
One should not study for as long as the ritual of rain-making lasts; and because of the word "ca" (and), also when it rains out of season, and for a day and night. 16.13.
Some [say] it is the continuity of the roof-thatch. || 16.14 ||

Some maintain that one should not study when it rains in an unbroken stream; Gautama, however, maintains that one may study. This option depends on whether the purpose has been achieved or not. 16.14.
[The rule] regarding the serving of food to the teacher. || 16.15 ||

The two teachers of the gods and the asuras are Śukra and Bṛhaspati; one should not study while they are serving food. Some say that "serving the teacher" refers to the taking away of the food of a sub-teacher (upādhyāya). 16.15.
And [the same applies] to two luminaries. 16.16.

He is equal to the sun and the moon because they are mentioned in the dual number; one should not study during an eclipse, and by the word "and" (ca), [it is implied] when the teacher has met with calamity. 16.16.
One who is frightened, one standing in a vehicle, one lying down, or one with legs crossed over [the seat]. || 16.17 ||

"Frightened" means one who is currently afraid; "mounted on a vehicle" means one who has ascended a horse or similar conveyance; "lying down" means one who is occupying a bed; "with feet raised" means one who has placed one foot upon another, or whose feet are set upon a stool or similar object. The compound is analyzed as a non-regular (visama) compound in order to include one who has climbed a tree as well. (16.17)
In cremation grounds, at the edge of a village, on great highways, and in places of impurity. || 16.18 ||

A *śmaśāna* is a place where corpses are burned; one should not study near it. A *grāmānta* is the boundary of a village; one should not study near it. A *mahāpatha* is a royal road, and *āśauca* is a place of impurity. One situated in these places should not study. Some say that *āśauca* is caused by birth or death. That is incorrect, because it has already been mentioned previously. Others say it is for the purpose of making known the absence of study even in the case of immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*); for even when there is immediate purification, only giving, receiving, and eating are to be performed, but not study. Others say it refers to the period before ten nights have passed. According to some, in the view that it applies to the mother, the father, or the mother’s mother, this is intended to make known the absence of study for the *sapiṇḍas*. Others maintain that the instruction is for the purpose of stating that one should not study in the vicinity of someone who is under *āśauca*, just like the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā. Furthermore, the mention of the *śmaśāna* is for the sake of a prohibition based on past precedent, since the case of the present-day site is already covered by the rule: "and also while studying in a cremation ground" (GDh 1.66). Therefore, one should not study in a place that is traditionally heard of as having been a cremation ground through a lineage of oral tradition. 16.18.
In the presence of a Śūdra, one should avoid foul odors, internal corpses, and those who are unfit to be spoken to.

"Fetid" means having a foul odor. "In a village containing a corpse" refers to one where a dead person has not yet been removed. "Divākīrti" refers to a barber, even if he is a Śūdra, but not a Caṇḍāla; for since the Caṇḍāla is already excluded by the general prohibition against Śūdras, his exclusion here would be established by implication. One should not study in his vicinity. Alternatively, by the mention of "divākīrti," his occupation is intended; thus, the meaning is that one should not study after shaving but before performing purification. Some, however, identify the word *divākīrti* specifically with the Caṇḍāla and explain it in connection with the word *anta* (within), saying: "in a village within which a Caṇḍāla is present. Thus says Āpastamba: "There is no study in a place where a corpse is inside, or where a Caṇḍāla is inside; but there is no study within the boundary of those who have not yet been removed" [ĀpDhS 1.9.14–16]. Why is there a prohibition regarding a deaf person in the presence of a Śūdra? Because this rule is commenced here again, even though the matter was already established by the rule: "Now, when he hears the Veda [being recited]" [ĀpDhS 1.5.20]. 16.19.
And [the same applies] when there is spitting or belching. 16.20.
One should not study when there is an acid eructation; by the use of the word "and" (ca), it is implied that one should also not study during other conditions such as fever and the like. 16.20.
And the word "Sāman" [is used] for as much of the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda as [it contains]. 16.21.

There is also a suspension of study for the *Ṛg* and *Yajus* as long as the sound of the *Sāman* is heard. The particle *ca* (and) serves to indicate that there is likewise a suspension of study for the *Sāman* itself according to other recensional traditions (*śākhā*). Thus, another *Smṛti* states: "And there is a suspension of study for the *Sāmans* in other recensions. Although the dual number should have been used, the plural form *ṛgyajuṣām* is employed to include the *Sūtras* and other such auxiliary texts belonging to them.
