The inclusion of the word *yāvat* (as long as) implies that one must not study even upon merely hearing the sound; otherwise, he would have simply said, "and for the *Ṛg* and *Yajus*, the word *Sāman* [is the cause of suspension]. (16.21)
Thunderbolts, earthquakes, the appearance of Rāhu, and meteors are not immediate [in their results]. || 16.22 ||

From the time these occur until the second [recurrence], they cause a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*); thus they are called *ākālika*. "Nirghāta" is a thunderclap; "bhūmikalpa" is an earthquake; "rāhudarśana" is an eclipse; "ulkā" is the fall of a meteor.

Regarding such passages as "One should not recite the Veda for three days during the impurity (*sūtaka*) of a king or of Rāhu," one should observe that there is an option (*vikalpa*) based on whether the purpose has been fulfilled or not, in accordance with other Smṛti texts that prescribe longer periods. (16.22)
And when thunder, rain, and lightning appear while fires have been kindled. 16.23.

"When the fires have been kindled" means at the time of the Agnihotra oblation, that is, during the twilight (saṃdhyā). These phenomena, beginning with thunder, being present, cause the impurity to last until the same time on the following day. The word "and" (ca) is used for the purpose of including all [the causes] together, so that it may not apply to each one individually or to any two of them alone.
In the rainy season, [he should eat] once a day. || 16.24 ||

During the rainy season, at the time of twilight, these [periods] do not constitute an interruption of study (*anākālika*). They cause a suspension of study for the duration of the day. By the word "day" (*ahaḥ*), the night is also implied, as seen in Vedic passages such as, "The day is black and the day is white. Therefore, when [the twilights] are observed at the morning twilight, it should be understood that there is no study during the day; when they are observed at the evening twilight, there is no study during the night. (16.24)
And in the case of lightning, [the impurity lasts] for the night until the end of the second watch.

When lightning is seen during twilight or during the rainy season, the night is a period of non-study for three parts [of its duration]. Because of the word "and" (ca), when it is perceived in the morning, the entire day is also a period of non-study—not just for three parts as in the case of the night—since the *Jābāli-gṛhya* states: "In the morning, when there is lightning, the day is a period of non-study. (16.25)
In the case of the commencement [of the vow] at one-third [of the night] and so forth, everything [applies]. 16.26.
If that [thunder] which is perceived at twilight has its occurrence beginning after the first part of the day has passed, then the entire night is a time unfit for study. 16.26.
According to some, meteors and lightning are included [in this category]. 16.27.

A meteor is equal to lightning; as there is no study during lightning, so it should be understood that there is none when a meteor falls—this is the opinion of some, but not that of Gautama. The option is based on whether the purpose has been accomplished or not. (16.27)
The thundering occurs in the afternoon.
When thunder occurs in the afternoon, it becomes equal to lightning; the meaning is that it causes a suspension of study (anadhyāya) until the end of the night. || 16.28 ||
Even at nightfall. || 16.29 ||
The meaning is that even during the first part of the night, one should observe a suspension of study as before, until the latter part of the night. 16.29.
Everything [is considered night] up until midnight. 16.30.
Beginning from the first part of the night until midnight, he makes the entire night a time for non-study. || 16.30 ||
Even by day, it is accompanied by light. 16.31.
If thunder occurs during the day before the afternoon, then there is a suspension of study as long as there is light; that is to say, for the entire day.
And when the king residing in his realm has died. || 16.32 ||

"Residing in the realm" means residing within one's own kingdom; [this refers to the period] when the king has passed away. The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of drawing in the rule regarding the suspension of study lasting until the same time [the next day]. Consequently, there is a suspension of study lasting until that same time. 16.32.
And having lived abroad, they shall reunite with one another. || 16.33 ||

When a teacher and pupil, or fellow students, travel abroad together and remain inseparable from one another, then there is a suspension of study for as long as they are away; by the use of the word "and" (ca), it is also [an interruption] when they meet [after being apart]. 16.33.
In the case of eating at a *śrāddha* for humans or at a *manuṣya-yajña*, where the completion of the Veda has been interrupted by a crowd, one must fast for a day and a night.

A "disturbance" (*saṃkula*) is a calamity such as a riot in a village caused by some reason; a "fire-panic" (*agnisaṃbhrama*) is an outbreak of fire or a conflagration; the "completion of a Veda" (*vedasamāpti*) refers to the completion of a section within the Veda, as in the expression "the village has been burnt," or it may refer to the completion of a recensional branch (*śākhā*). "Vomiting" (*chardiḥ*) is well known. A "śrāddha" is one performed for a single deceased person (*ekoddiṣṭa*) and so forth, [referring here] to the eater therein. At a "sacrifice to men" (*manuṣyayajña*), that is, at a gathering of friends; at a "meal" (*bhojana*), meaning a meal where many Brahmins are fed—in these cases, there is a suspension of study (*anādhyāya*) for a day and night. || 16.34 ||
And on the new moon day. 16.35.
There is a suspension of study for a full day and night; by the use of the word "and" (ca), it is also on the full moon day. 16.35.
Or for two days. 16.36.

On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), as well as for two days or the aforementioned day and night, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*). It should be understood that this applies to the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) in both cases. In this regard, a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*) should be observed: for the Veda, the suspension lasts for two days, while for the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and so forth, it lasts for only one day and night. Thus Uśanas says: "There is a suspension of study for all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) except for the Epics and Purāṇas on the days of the lunar phases. (16.36)
The full moon days of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Āṣāḍha. || 16.37 ||

Because of the word "ca" (and), since the preceding [rule] had already established the non-study period, the term "paurṇamāsī" here includes the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*). On these days there is no study. Thus, there is no fault on other *pratipads*. In this regard, the option should be understood as depending on whether the purpose has been fulfilled or not, according to the statement of Auśanasa: "On the *pratipads*, one should not reflect [on sacred matters]. (16.37)
The three Aṣṭakās last for three nights each.

There are three Aṣṭakā festivals during the dark fortnights following the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī; they cause a suspension of Vedic study for three nights. Therefore, on those [days]—namely the seventh, the eighth, and the ninth—there is a cessation of study for three nights. 16.38.
Some say [the last one]. 16.39.
They maintain that only the last *aṣṭakā* causes a suspension of study; as before, there is an option. 16.39.
On both sides of the rainy season. || 16.40 ||

The meaning is "at the beginning and at the end. *Vārṣika* means that which occurs during the rainy season; thus, the study connected with that period is being referred to. By the word *abhitaḥ*, both that which is performed before and after—that is, what is undertaken at the start and what is done at the conclusion—are included. The phrase "a three-night suspension of study" (*trirātram anadhyāyaḥ*) carries over [from the previous rule]. The meaning is that there is a three-night suspension of study both at the *upākarma* and at the *utsarga*. Thus Uśanas says: "At the *upākarma* and at the *utsarga*, there is a three-day suspension of study. (16.40)
All [these] occur when there is a conjunction of rain, lightning, and thunder.

All teachers maintain that when rain and the other phenomena occur together, there shall be a suspension of study for three nights. Gautama, however, states: "When thunder, rain, and lightning appear while the sacred fires have been kindled, the suspension lasts as long as those conditions persist" (GDh 16.23). In this case, there is an option as previously described. 16.41.
In that which is flowing. 16.42.

The phrase "for three nights" continues [from the previous rule]. On whichever day the god rains in scattered showers, if on that very same day there is also a conjunction of lightning and fire, they maintain that in that case too there is a period of three nights. 16.42.
After a meal during a festival. || 16.43 ||

On a festival or on any occasion of prosperity, there is a suspension of study for that day and night following the meal; the meaning is that on a festival such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), there is a suspension of study after one has eaten. (16.43)
And [the same applies] to that which has been studied. || 16.44 ||

Furthermore, for one who has already begun his studies—that is, one who has commenced learning—the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) occurs after a meal even when it is not a festival; by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), this suspension after a meal also applies to one who is studying the Vedānta. (16.44)
And for four muhūrtas during the night. || 16.45 ||

One should not study during the first four *muhūrtas* of the night, because of the force of another *smṛti* text regarding the thirteenth lunar day. As Uśanas says: "On the thirteenth [lunar day], one should not study during the first four *muhūrtas*. (16.45)
Some [say it is] always in the city. || 16.46 ||

Some maintain that there is always a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) in a city or a village; however, Gautama does not hold this view, because it would follow that those living in villages could never study at all. In this regard, it should be understood that where Śūdras and others predominate, there is a suspension of study, whereas where the twice-born (*dvijāti*) are numerous, one should study. (16.46)
Even the mental [act] is impure. 16.47.

One should not engage in study even mentally when one is unpurified. Thus, mental study is not prohibited during other occasions of non-study (*anadhyāya*). Alternatively, the mention of "mental" (*mānasa*) is for the sake of the obligatory (*nitya*) rite; that is, being impure, one should not recite even the obligatory prayers. And so it should be understood that there are no other occasions of non-study regarding the obligatory rite. As Manu says: "There is no non-study regarding the obligatory rite, nor indeed regarding the mantras for the *homa* offering. There is no non-study regarding the obligatory rite, for that is remembered as the 'Brahma-sacrifice' (*brahmasatra*). (MDh 2.105–06)
Thus [ends the verse]. 16.47.
For those who perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha), [the impurity lasts] until the same time the next day. || 16.48 ||

Regarding the givers and the eaters, however, because it has been stated [in GDh 16.34], "by those who have received a mixed [offering]," the plural number is used for the purpose of indicating all types of *śrāddha*, so that it might not apply only to the givers in the case of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. (16.48)
And also when there is contact with one who has performed a śrāddha with uncooked food. || 16.49 ||

When food that has not been prepared (*akṛtānna*) is given for the sake of the ancestors in the absence of a formal meal-offering, that is an *akṛtānna-śrāddha*. Because of the statement regarding the conjunction of both the giver and the recipient, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) lasting until the same time the next day. The word "and" (*ca*) implies that this applies elsewhere as well for the sake of the ancestors. As Manu says:

"Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever may constitute a śrāddha offering—even after accepting it, there is a suspension of study; for Brāhmaṇas are said to have their hands as their mouths. (MDh 4.117)
This very thing is the characteristic mark of the *āmaśrāddha*.
And whatever vehicles they remember, those very ones they remember for each realization. 16.50

One should not study those days of suspension from study (*anadhyāya*) which the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras* record for each Veda and each branch (*śākhā*), and by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), those mentioned in other legal treatises (*dharmaśāstra*) as well; this is how the connection [of the verse] is to be understood. (16.50)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Maskarīya-gautama-bhāṣya*.
The seventeenth chapter begins:

It has been stated that even the mind is impure; since that impurity is also produced by food, he speaks [the following] with the intention of distinguishing between what is fit to be eaten and what is not.
A Brāhmaṇa may eat at the houses of twice-born men who are praiseworthy in their own duties.

The meaning is: those who are highly praised for their own duties—not for the duties of Kṣatriyas and others—but who, having abandoned wealth and pleasure, are devoted to the performance of their primary duties; [this refers to] those twice-born men (*dvijāti*) who have been initiated (*upanīta*). Since eating is already established by implication, this statement is for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*). The mention of "Brāhmaṇas" is for the purpose of indicating the twice-born in general. Some say it is for the purpose of permitting Kṣatriyas and others when they are not being praised. "He should eat" means he should perform the act of eating. When it is said "of those who are praised," since people might be considered praised merely out of self-importance, the phrase "their own duties" is included. Although it would have been sufficient to say simply "of those who are praised, their own," the inclusion of the word "duty" (*karman*) is for the purpose of excluding optional rites (*kāmya*). The plural number in "in their own duties" (*svakarmasu*) is for the purpose of declaring the preeminence of those who practice the combination of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*). (17.1)
And he should accept it. 17.2.
This is their wealth; the particle "ca" (and) has this meaning: that one should teach them and cause them to perform sacrifices. || 17.2 ||
Likewise:

Fuel, water, fodder, roots, fruits, honey, *abhayā*, beds, seats, dwellings, vehicles, milk, curd, vessels, fish, *priyaṅgu* grain, garlands, paths, and vegetables are not to be refused by anyone. (17.3)

Fuel is wood; water, even when contained in jars and the like; fodder is grass; roots and fruits are well known; honey is that produced by bees; "abhaya" means protection; "abhyudyata-śayyāsana" (beds and seats offered) are well known; "āvasatha" refers to shelter and the like; vehicles and so forth are well known; "śapharī" is a specific kind of fish; "priyaṅgu" is a specific kind of grain; "srak" refers to strung flowers; "mārga" is the meat of deer; "śāka" is well known. Because of the inclusion of the term "apraṇodya" (not to be refused), these are not to be rejected. Since they are "unasked for" (*ayācita*), [they are acceptable]. In this Sūtra, by the word "abhyudyata," that which is brought into the presence of the recipient is meant. In that regard, there is no restriction regarding the species [of the gift]. Thus says Manu:
"Prājāpati has declared that alms which are being offered, brought forward, and not previously announced, may be eaten even from one who has performed evil deeds. (MDh 4.248).
This is the exception to the rule.

"One may eat the food of one who has faith, even if he is a thief, and especially so for one who performs many sacrifices; but never the food of one who initiates many pupils. Thus it is said, and likewise another [verse]:

“[Food] offered by a physician, a hunter, a surgeon, a fowler, a eunuch, and an unchaste woman, even if it is brought forward, is not to be accepted. (VaDh 14.19) In this context as well, it should be understood that only edible substances are intended, based on the indicative mark (liṅga) in the verse: “Prajāpati considered [such food] to be edible” (MDh 4.248). Thus, although such food may be brought forward, it is not to be accepted. Because of the rule regarding what is not to be rejected (*apraṇodya*), there is a fault in rejecting it. And so says Vasiṣṭha:

"The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years, nor does the fire carry his oblations, for him who treats her with contempt" (VaDh 14.18). In that case as well, one should accept only edible substances, because of the separate mention of "unworthy twice-born men"; yet, because of the use of the word "all," this includes even from a Śūdra. While one could have said "from all," the use of the form "of all" (*sarveṣām*) is intended to indicate those related to oneself. Thus, there is no fault in not accepting what someone gives after having stolen it from another.
And another [type of gift] is for the maintenance of one's ancestors, gods, teachers, and dependents. || 17.4 ||

The mention of "supporting" (bharaṇa) refers to necessary duties. Supporting one's father consists of performing the *ekoddiṣṭa* and other rites, as well as the uninterrupted performance of *śrāddha*. Supporting the gods consists of the morning and evening *agnihotra* oblations and so forth. The "elders" (*guru*) are the father and others. "Dependents" (*bhṛtya*) are sons, slaves, and so forth. Supporting these means providing them with food, clothing, and the like. On account of these occasions, even other things [such as fuel] are not to be refused; this is indicated by the word "and" (*ca*). Since it is stated that these are for the purpose of "supporting," one should not become nourished by taking from them for oneself. Some say the word "and" (*ca*) is for the sake of hospitality (*ātithya*). Thus says Vasiṣṭha:

“Desiring to abandon his wife for the sake of his guru, or wishing to honor the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from anyone; yet he should not satisfy himself with that. [VaDh 14.13] In times of distress, however, accepting what is requested is prescribed by the rule: “Sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts are permitted for all [twice-born classes]. [GDh 7.4]. Here, however, the point is that one should not reject what is being offered. Thus, it is demonstrated that even when not requested, if something is obtained during a time of distress, it is acceptable as a gift. Since this refers specifically to times of distress, it should be understood that it must not be accepted when there is no such distress. (17.4)
If there is no means of livelihood [otherwise], it may be obtained from a Śūdra. || 17.5 ||

The term "not to be rejected" (*apraṇodyam*) continues to apply here, but not the phrase "if there is no means of livelihood" (*vṛttiś cet*) from the preceding rule. If one's livelihood cannot be maintained without accepting gifts from a Śūdra, then one may accept from a Śūdra; however, one must not perform sacrifices for him, eat his food, or teach him. Thus says Manu:

"A wise man should not eat cooked food from a Śūdra, even if he is in a state of ritual impurity (*āśauca*). In the absence of other means of subsistence, he may take from such a person only raw grain sufficient for one night. (MDh 4.223)
And so on. Likewise, Vasiṣṭha says:
"He who engages in sexual intercourse while the food of a Śūdra remains in his stomach—his sons belong to the one whose food it was; for from food, semen is produced. [VaDh 6.27]

Regarding officiating at sacrifices, however, he will state: "One who performs sacrifices for a Śūdra, one who performs sacrifices for the sake of a Śūdra," and so forth [GDh 20.1]. Likewise, regarding teaching, he will state: "One who has a Śūdra as a pupil, and likewise a teacher," and so forth [MDh 3.156]. || 17.5 ||
The exception to this is as follows: cattle-herders, field-plowmen, family associates, those who cause work to be done, and personal attendants are those whose food may be eaten. 17.6.

A cattle-herder is one who protects livestock; he is entitled to eat the food of the owner of the animals. Likewise is the field-plougher. Thus says Uśanas: "One's own cowherd and the plougher of one's own field are to be fed," and so forth. A family associate is one who has come down through tradition in the form of a friend. A barber is a hair-cutter. An attendant is a servant. From these signs, the Śūdra status of the barber is determined. And thus says Manu: "The field-plougher, the family friend, the cowherd, the servant, and the barber..."

"These are those among Śūdras whose food may be eaten, as well as he who offers himself [as a servant]" (MDh 4.253), and so forth. From the context, if the maintenance of life were impossible without eating the food of a Śūdra, then the food of these [specific individuals] is to be eaten. Why? Because, although it would have been sufficient to say "the food of those who provide family connections, those who cause [one] to act, and female servants," the use of the term *bhojyānnāḥ* (those whose food is to be eaten) indicates that it should be understood as "that which is to be consumed. 17.6.
And a merchant who is not an artisan. 17.7.

The phrase "whose food may be eaten" (*bhojyānna*) is to be supplied [to each clause]. A Śūdra who subsists by trade is also one whose food may be eaten, provided he is not a craftsman such as a potter and so forth. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that even a non-Śūdra who is a craftsman is one whose food may not be eaten. (17.7)
In this very context, he states another thing that is unfit for consumption:
"That which is always unfit for consumption. (17.8)

That which is given day after day to one who has no protector must not be eaten as a regular practice; or rather, one must never eat in another's house at all times except in times of distress. As Manu says:
"Those foolish householders who subsist on the cooked food of others...
(MDh 3.104), and so forth. 17.8.
[Food] into which hair or insects have fallen. || 17.9 ||

The mention of "hair" (*keśa*) is intended to include the hair of all parts of the body. The mention of "insects" (*kīṭa*) is also for the purpose of indicating impure living beings. "Fallen in" (*avapanna*) means that it has become fit for consumption at the very time of cooking; such food is unfit to be eaten. By stating this, it is made known that food prepared after the time of cooking may be eaten once the appropriate expiation has been performed. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "But one may, at will, remove the hair and insects, wash it with water, sprinkle it with ashes, and then consume it as fit food, provided it is praised by word of mouth" (VaDh 14.23). In the case of a large quantity of food, the expiation should be understood to apply even when the contamination occurs at the time of cooking itself, as Manu has stated.

"Food that has been burnt by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, sneezed at, or defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth. [MDh 5.125] In this context, the mention of "birds" should be understood as referring to any bird other than a crow, because a different expiation is seen for the latter. As Parāśara says:
Food cooked in more than one *droṇa* that has been defiled by dogs or crows should not be discarded; for the sake of its purification, one should present it to Brāhmaṇas.

"Food that has been sprinkled with water purified by the Gāyatrī mantra recited eight thousand times, and over which fire has been carried (paryagnikṛta), may be eaten by the Brahmins. The plural number [of Brahmins] should also be understood as depending on the circumstances of place, time, and so forth. As Vyāghra says:
Having understood the place, the time, as well as the measure, the substance, the purpose of the substance, the justification, and the circumstance, one should determine the purification.
Thus [ends the section]. 17.9.
It was defiled by the footprints of a menstruating woman and a black bird.

The phrase "not to be eaten" applies throughout. The mention of a woman in her menses is intended to illustrate all types of impurity. The mention of a "part" (pada) is also intended to illustrate any part of the body that is impure. "Defiled by these" means touched by them. (17.10)
That which has been looked upon by a killer of an embryo, smelled by a cow, or corrupted in its essence.

A *bhrūṇahan* is a slayer of a Brahmin. And so Vasiṣṭha says: "Having killed a Brahmin, one becomes a *bhrūṇahan*" (VaDh 20.23). The mention of that term is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for dogs, Caṇḍālas, and outcasts, because they are taught together in the rule: "Looking at a dog, a Caṇḍāla, or an outcast is defiling" (VaDh 23.33).

But if this were so, there would be a comprehension of those things taught together; then, because of their being mentioned together in the sūtra "Caṇḍāla and the fallen" (VaDh 23.33), and because in the sūtra "Dog and Caṇḍāla" (VaDh 23.33) the mention of either one would establish the other through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), the inclusion of both would be redundant.

To this it is replied: the commencement [of the rule] is for the sake of restriction; the prohibition applies only to the three [specific categories] mentioned in the act of looking, and not to those included in the *patita-sūtra* such as women who have recently given birth (*sūtikā*) and so forth. Therefore, it is entirely logical that by the mention of the "destroyer of an embryo" (*bhrūṇahan*) here, dogs and the like are also included. This being the case, since there is no contradiction, in the sūtra "a menstruating woman, a black bird... (GDh 17.10), by the mention of the "menstruating woman," those included in the same sūtra such as the *patita* and others are also included. Consequently, it should be understood that what has merely been touched by a menstruating woman and the like is not [necessarily] unfit, whereas what has been looked at or touched by a destroyer of an embryo and the like is. Furthermore, [food is unfit if] it has been smelled by a cow due to proximity, if it is corrupted in its nature (*bhāvaduṣṭa*), if it is given by a giver with ill-will (*apadhyāna*), or if it causes dissatisfaction to the mind of the eater.
Sour gruel alone, without curd. 17.12.

That which becomes sour is *śukta*, but it is not sour by its very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), because of the observation of the exception "not curd" (*adadhi*). It is like *kāñjika* and other such substances when unmixed with another substance; that is unfit for consumption. Curd that is not curd—that is, even pure curd when mixed with another substance such as buttermilk—is fit for consumption. || 17.12 ||
Again, it is established. || 17.13 ||
That which attains a state equal to its previous cooking, and not [a state of] coldness or under-cooking, because it is taken up again. || 17.13 ||
One should avoid stale food, leafy vegetables, oil, meat, and honey.

"Stale" means that which has been kept overnight, with the exception of vegetables and the like. Vegetables and the like may be eaten even when stale. "Vegetables" refers to those not mixed with oil; "edibles" refers to flour-based foods and the like; and "oil" refers to ghee and the like—it should be understood that these may be eaten even when mixed with such substances, as seen in other *smṛtis*. As Manu says: "Whatever food or eatable, not being censured, is mixed with oil, that may be eaten even if it is stale, as well as the remains of sacrificial oblations (*haviḥ*). (MDh 5.24)

And meat, even when not combined with fat. Although honey is already included by the mention of "fat," its separate mention is for the purpose of prohibiting honey that has stood overnight, even for a woman. Thus, there is also an *upaniṣad* of the ritualists (*kalpakārāṇām*): "Therefore, women do not eat honey. (17.14)
Having spoken of that which is defiled by association and that which is defiled by time, he now states that which is defiled by its source:

"Of those who have abandoned their vows, of prostitutes, of those accused of crimes, of those whose occupation is unknown, of jailers, carpenters, misers, prison-keepers, physicians, hunters, usurers, those who eat the remnants of others' meals, and those who hate their own group. (17.15)

"Abandoned" means ownerless. A "prostitute" (*puṃścalī*) is an unchaste woman; by this very term, a courtesan is also included as a matter of course. And so says Vasiṣṭha: "The food of a *gaṇa* and the food of a prostitute" (VaDh 14.10). An "accused" (*abhiśasta*) is one made notorious for a fault. One who is "not to be designated" (*anapadeśya*) is one who cannot be specified as either female or male; the meaning is that he is a person of the third gender (*tṛtīyā prakṛtiḥ*). A "punisher" (*dāṇḍika*) is one appointed by the king to carry out suppression. A "carpenter" (*takṣa*) is a chariot-maker. A "miser" (*kadarya*) is one addicted to vulgar speech, according to the observation of the Brāhmaṇas: "One should not utter what is vulgar; if one utters what is vulgar, they call him a miser. A "jailer" (*bandhanika*) is a guard of the prison. A "physician" (*cikitsaka*) is a Brāhmaṇa doctor, according to the observation in the Brāhmaṇa of the Taittirīyas: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not practice medicine. And likewise says Vasiṣṭha:
"A Brahmin does not become crooked by being a merchant, nor by being an actor, nor by performing service for a Śūdra, nor by being a thief, nor by being a physician" (VaDh 3.3).
Some say [he becomes so] by living as a thief; others say by being a surgeon.

As it is seen in the statement: "The physician, the hunter, the surgeon, and the snarer" (VaDh 14.19). Here, the *mṛgayu* is a hunter; if he is one who does not shoot with arrows, he is a trapper. An *ucchiṣṭabhojī* is one who eats the food of another's leavings. A *gaṇa* is a multitude of people. A *vidviṣāṇa* is an enemy. The food of these persons is unfit to be eaten. Since there is an instruction regarding the non-eating of the food of both those who are praiseworthy and those who are blameworthy, their food must not be eaten even in times of distress. (17.15)
Those unworthy of the company [are mentioned] before Durvāla. 17.16.

The food of those previously mentioned as unfit for the company (*apāṅktya*), beginning with thieves and ending with those who have abandoned themselves, is not to be eaten so long as they have not performed penance; however, this applies even to those such as the slayers of Brahmins once they have performed penance, according to the statement of Āpastamba: "In this world, no restoration of status is found for him, but his taint is removed" (ĀpDh 1.24.25). || 17.16 ||
[Gifts] rendered void by [the recipient's] rinsing the mouth or rising [from his seat]. || 17.17 ||
"Vain food" is that which is cooked for one's own sake without intending it for guests and the like. Thus, there is a verse among the Bahvṛcas:
"The thoughtless man finds food in vain; I speak the truth: it is his destruction."
"He does not nourish the noble one, nor his friend;
he who eats alone becomes solely a sinner. (RV 10.170.6)

That which is interrupted by sipping water (*ācamana*) is when one has eaten half [the meal], sipped water, and then eats that same food again; that which is interrupted by rising (*utthāna*) is when one has risen immediately after eating half [the meal] and then eats again. All three of these types are unfit to be eaten. Although it should have been stated as "interrupted by sipping water and rising" (*ācamanotthānavyapeta*), the plural number is used to indicate that if either sipping water or rising is performed by one person at a single row (*ekapaṅkti*), then for the other person it becomes unfit to be eaten. Thus says Uśanas: "And that which is done with non-heavy persons regarding sipping water and rising. In this way, there is no fault if it is done by heavy persons. (17.17)
From worship [performed] with equal or unequal [means], there arise the unequal and the equal [results]. || 17.18 ||

Having performed an unequal honor—such as providing a seat or personal service—toward one who is equal in learning, family lineage, and so forth, and having performed an equal honor toward one who is unequal, one must not eat where food is given if there is such inequality or equality regarding the honor; that is, one should not eat in such circumstances. || 17.18 ||
And [the offering] that is not honored. 17.19.

Food that has not been honored with a mantra and a salutation; as Vasiṣṭha says: “One should honor the meals with the words ‘It is pleasing’ in the evening and in the morning” (VaDh 3.69). By the use of the word “and,” it is implied that one should call out, “Who will eat? And so Vasiṣṭha says: “And it is also called out, ‘Who will eat? (VaDh 14.9). || 17.19 ||
And the milk of a cow during the period of birth-impurity, before ten days have passed, [is forbidden]. (17.20)

The milk of a cow that has recently calved and whose ten-day period has not yet elapsed is unfit for consumption; by the use of the word "and," curds and other such products are also included. (17.20)
And [the same applies] to goats and buffaloes. 17.21.

The milk of goats and buffaloes that have not passed ten days since calving is unfit for drinking, as is their curd and other products. The word "and" (ca) is used to include goats within the scope of the rule. Their separate mention is intended to indicate that cow's milk may sometimes be consumed after seven nights have elapsed without fault. (17.21)
The milk of sheep, of camels, and of one-hoofed animals is always unfit for drinking. || 17.22 ||

The inclusion of the term "always" (nitya) indicates that this prohibition applies not only for ten days; because of the use of the suffix denoting a modification (*vikāra-pratyaya*), even urine and the like are not to be drunk by these [women]. In this way, it is understood that for those mentioned previously, urine and such may be drunk. "Single-hoofed" (*ekaśapha*) refers to those with one hoof, such as mares and the like. The others are well known. The compound *viṣamāsaḥ* is intended to include all wild animals, such as deer and so forth. And thus says Manu: "And of all wild animals, except for the buffalo... [MDh 5.9].

By the word "and" (ca), he includes the milk of human women as well. Although the term "unfit for drinking" (apeya) is already under discussion, it is repeated here for the sake of establishing a permanent rule. Consequently, this establishes that even in cases of extreme distress, the milk of goats and buffaloes is permitted, even if they have not passed ten days since giving birth. || 17.22 ||
And [the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied] after the words *syandinī*, *yamasū*, and *saṃdhinī*. || 17.23 ||

The phrase "milk is not to be drunk" is to be supplied [to each clause], such as "curd and so forth, even if constant. *Syandinī* is one whose udders are excessively swollen. *Yamasūḥ* is one who has twin offspring. *Sandhinī* is one who is milked after an interval of one period, or by means of another calf; according to some, she is called *sandhinī* when she is milked while pregnant. By the word "and" (*ca*), those that are diseased are also included. (17.23)
And [the same applies] to one who has no desire for offspring. 17.24.

That which comes from cows whose calves have departed, and those who are separated from their calves by loss or death—of these, the milk is not to be drunk. The separate mention [of "those whose calves have departed"] is for the purpose of avoiding a prohibition that would apply only to milk, so as not to exclude curds and other products; furthermore, the word "and" (ca) is intended to include the milk of goats and buffaloes as well. (17.24)
Now those which are inedible by their very nature are stated:
among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the hare, the jackal, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise [are edible]. (17.25)

He will state later on that these are "not to be eaten"; this [term] is drawn back here [to apply to the present context]. Those who have five claws on their hands and feet—namely, the five five-clawed animals such as jackals, monkeys, and so forth—are not to be eaten, with the exception of the porcupine and others. The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including milk, urine, and leavings. The *śalyaka* is the thorny boar. The hare (*śaśa*) is well known. The *śvāvit* is the bat. The *godhā* is well known. The *khaḍga* is the horned deer. The tortoise (*kacchapa*) is well known. Regarding those which are not to be eaten, their urine and other excretions should be understood as unfit for drinking.
The urine of animals whose meat is unfit for consumption, as well as their leavings, are declared to be inedible;
and their excrement is likewise so declared.

This is because of Vatsa’s statement. The use of the nominative case in the expression "pañcanakhāś ca" (and five-nailed animals) is intended so that all parts of the body may be included. If only the flesh were intended, then the use of the genitive case would have been appropriate. In this way, blood and other such substances are also indeed unfit for consumption. This principle should be understood to apply everywhere. (17.25)
Animals with teeth in both jaws, those with hair on their bodies, those without hair, those with solid hooves, and the kalaviṅka, plava, cakravāka, and haṃsa birds [are not to be eaten]. || 17.26 ||

"Those with two rows of teeth" refers to humans and the like. Since their consumption is already prohibited by the fact that they are five-toed animals (*pañcanakha*), they are mentioned again for the sake of emphasizing the gravity of the penance (*prāyaścitta*). This should be understood as the case in other specific injunctions as well. "Hairy ones" (*keśin*) refers to those possessing an excess of hair, such as the *camari* cow and others. "Hairless ones" (*aloman*) refers to snakes and the like. "Single-hoofed ones" (*ekaśapha*) refers to horses and the like. The *kalaviṅka* is the village sparrow. The *plava* is the *śakaṭabila* (the water-crow). The *cakravāka* and the swan (*haṃsa*) are well known. (17.26)
Crows, herons, vultures, hawks, water-birds with red feet and beaks, domestic cocks, and pigs; || 17.27 ||

Crows and other such birds are well known. All water-birds are included without distinction. "Red-footed" refers to pigeons and the like; "red-beaked" refers to chakoras and the like. The term "domestic" is connected with both the cock and the pig; thus, there is no prohibition against wild species. The lack of compound formation [in the original] is for the purpose of prohibiting others as well, such as carnivorous animals and so forth. (17.27)
And [the same applies] to the words *dhenu* and *anaḍuh*. || 17.28 ||

A *dhenu* is a milch cow; an *anaḍvān* is a bull. The mention of these two is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for calves and other such animals as well. If it is asked, "In that case, one should have said 'and the cow' (*gauś ca*)," it is replied here: the particle *ca* is for the purpose of including them among those fit to be eaten (*bhakṣya*). This instruction is intended so that, in the context of being edible, only those two are included and not the calves and others. And thus says Vasiṣṭha: "But the cow and the bull are to be eaten, for they are declared pure in the Vājasaneyaka" (VaDh 14.46). In this regard, it should be understood that when they have arrived in the form of guests, the cow and the bull are edible, whereas others are inedible, because of the indicative mark of Vasiṣṭha: "Even in the worship of ancestors, gods, and guests, one may likewise kill animals—this is the teaching of Manu" (VaDh 4.5); and, "Now, for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya who has arrived as a guest, one should cook a large bull or a large goat; in this very way they provide hospitality to him" (VaDh 4.8). || 17.28 ||
Meat from animals that have not been slaughtered for sacrifice, meat from those that have perished naturally, and meat not intended for consumption are forbidden. || 17.29 ||

"One whose teeth have not fallen out" means one whose milk-teeth have not yet been shed. "One who has collapsed" means one who is afflicted by disease; others say it refers to one who has died naturally. "Meat prepared in vain" (vṛthāmāṃsa) means meat cooked solely for one's own sake. Although the meaning is already established by the word "vain" (vṛthā) itself, this further instruction is intended to emphasize the gravity of the penance required. Furthermore, this should be understood as referring to meat that is otherwise edible, since there is no possibility of consuming meat that is inherently inedible. (17.29)
The red exudations from the shoots of the *kisa-layaka* and *śuna* trees were flowing.

*Kisalaya* refers to the first sprout of all plants. *Kyāku* is the *ahicchatra* or *chatrāka* (the mushroom). *Laśuna* is well known. If they are red exudations (*niryāsa*), then likewise Manu says: "Red exudations of trees" [MDh 5.6], and so forth. Thus, there is no prohibition regarding asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) and similar substances. || 17.30 ||
And [the word] *vraścana* [is also used]. 17.31.

"Produced from incisions" means those that grow from trees as secondary shoots; these, whether red or not red, are unfit for consumption. Thus, because camphor and similar substances are neither produced from incisions nor are they red, they are not prohibited. Some divide the sūtra into two parts, reading "red ones and those produced from incisions"; even in their view, camphor and the like remain unprohibited. Others explain the term as "resins of trees"; according to them, there is a prohibition of asafoetida and similar substances. By the word "and" (ca), onions, leeks, and so forth, which are taught in other Smṛtis, are included. (17.31)
The nicu, dāruvaka, balākā, śuka, madgu, ṭiṭṭibha, māndhāla, and nocturnal prowlers are not to be eaten. || 17.32 ||

The *nicudāru* is the woodpecker; the *madgu* is the water-diver, characterized by its habit of submerging in water; the *ṭiṭṭibha* is so called because of its habit of imitating the sound "ṭiṭṭibha"; the *mandhāla* is the *vāgguda*; the *naktaṃcaras* are the owls and others; the rest are well known. It has been stated that the verb "are not to be eaten" (*abhakṣyāḥ*) is to be connected with the term "five-toed animals" (*pañcanakhāḥ*) and those that follow. (17.32)
Those that peck with their beaks, those that scratch with their claws, and those that walk on webbed feet may be eaten. || 17.33 ||

Since one [category] is established by the teaching of the other, the teaching of both groups is for the purpose of favoring those cases for which there is neither a specific injunction nor a prohibition. "Piercers" (*pratudāḥ*) are those who eat by pecking repeatedly with their beaks, such as peacocks and the like. "Scatterers" (*viṣkirāḥ*) are those who eat by scattering [the food] about, such as quails and the like. "Non-web-footed" (*ajālapādāḥ*) are those that do not have webbed feet, such as gourds and the like. (17.33)
And fish that are not altered [by cooking]. 17.34.

"Deformed" refers to those whose form is different from that of the hands. The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of including those with scales. The meaning is that only those possessing both qualifications—being scaled *and* undeformed—are edible; not those possessing only one qualification. Since "those with webbed feet" were mentioned previously, here the prohibition of webbed-footed animals and of those possessing only one of the two qualifications should be understood. This should be understood similarly in the subsequent cases as well. (17.34)
And those who deserve execution may be spared for the sake of dharma. || 17.35 ||

Those animals previously killed on account of dharma, such as at the beginning of a sacrifice, though otherwise unfit to be eaten, are fit to be eaten; the word "and" (ca) implies also when there is danger to one's life. Thus Manu says: "One may eat meat that has been consecrated with sprinkling, or at the desire of Brāhmaṇas, or when one is engaged according to rule, or indeed when there is danger to one's life" (MDh 5.27).
But is it not the case that since this is already established by the scriptural injunctions regarding those killed in sacrifices and the like, the instruction here is purposeless?

To this it is replied: those [acts] which are performed specifically with reference to an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) entail no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) only when eating the remnants of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), but not when eating the remnants for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭaprayojana*). For this very reason, instead of saying "for the sake of sacrifice" (*yajñārtha*), it is said "for the sake of dharma" (*dharmārtha*). By this alone, the eating of the flesh of the *avakīrṇin* animal is also refuted, because that is intended as an expiation (*prāyaścittārtha*) and not for the sake of an unseen result. And thus, just as there is an entry into the Smṛti-prescribed expiation for eating meat for a visible purpose, it is understood that the same applies to the injury (*hiṃsā*) involved in that context. With this very intention, it was also stated by Manu:
"One may perform the sacrifice with clarified butter in times of distress; likewise, one may perform the sacrifice with a cake made of flour," and so forth.

One should consume food that has been killed by a predator or whose defects are unseen, after sprinkling it with water, provided it is praised by word; one should consume it, one should consume it. || 17.36 ||

One may eat the meat of an animal killed by predators such as lions after merely sprinkling water over it. The qualification "killed by a predator" applies specifically to cases where no visible defect is present, as well as when it is commended by word. The meat of an animal killed by a predator is fit for consumption provided that it is free from visible defects and is commended by word. "Free from visible defects" means it has not been taught among the list of forbidden foods, since its fitness for consumption is established precisely by this teaching. "Commended by word" means it is approved by others. Thus, what is neither taught among the permitted nor the forbidden, but is prescribed for times of distress, is here authorized for use even when not in distress. Furthermore, the plural number indicates that purity belongs only to that which possesses all three qualifications, and not to that which possesses only one. In the same way, regarding the rule "one may even consume the flesh of a boar" (GDh 3.31), the absence of visible defects and so forth should be understood. Although "he should eat" (*aśnīyāt*) would have sufficed, the use of "he may consume" (*upayuñjīta*) implies that abstaining from eating is better than eating. And so says Manu:
"There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse; this is the natural inclination of living beings, but abstention bears great fruit" (MDh 5.56). || 17.36 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Maskarīya-gautama-bhāṣya*.
The eighteenth chapter begins: The general and specific duties of the stages of life (*āśrama*) have been declared; now, the duties of women must be stated, so he says:

A woman is not independent with respect to dharma. (18.1) "Not independent" means dependent on another; regarding dharma pertaining to the next world, her entitlement to dharma is together with her husband, but not with independence as a man possesses. Thus Manu says:
"For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast."
"By that through which she serves her husband, by that she is glorified in heaven.

[MDh 5.155] Śaṅkha also stated: "Neither vows, fasts, restrictive observances, sacrifices, nor the duty of giving bestows favor upon women other than service to the husband; however, with the permission of her husband, the practice of vows, fasts, restrictive observances, and so forth, is the duty of women."

But surely, since the Vedic and Smṛti rites are prescribed with the man as the intended beneficiary, and because a woman has no independent entitlement to them, a prohibition against her would be untenable. If it is argued that the statement regarding her lack of independence is for the purpose of showing that the woman also shares in the fruit of performing religious duties together with her husband, that is incorrect; for this very point is already established by the fact that she is the "partner in dharma" (*sahadharmacāriṇī*). Furthermore, if she is called "not independent," it is not known to what she is dependent. If you say "dependent on the husband," no; for her dependence on the husband will be stated later in the passage, "She must not transgress her husband" (GDh 18.2). If you then argue that this [present verse] will state her non-deviation [from him], no; for deviation regarding dharma, artha, and kāma is already prohibited.

To this it is replied: This undertaking is intended for the sake of enabling a woman to perform religious means (*dharma-sādhana*) such as fasting and giving, provided she has her husband’s permission, because the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*) are obtained through the mediation of the husband. Thus, the statement of Śaṅkha was shown: “But at will, with the husband’s permission,” and so forth. Likewise, regarding the matter of giving, Nārada says: “They say that transactions performed by a woman are invalid in the absence of an emergency, especially the giving, mortgaging, or selling of a house or field. (NSm 1.22)
And so forth. This refers to the husband's property;
however, regarding the woman's own property, the woman herself shall be its owner, and the husband is fit to enjoy, protect, and maintain it with her permission, but not to waste or destroy it.
If it is argued that this is because of Kaṇva’s statement, we say no, because another Smṛti is observed to say otherwise. Thus Vyāghra says:
"Woman's property must never be given away or offered as a sacrifice by anyone;
however, if previously authorized by her husband, it must indeed be given by the woman."
And likewise Lokākṣi says:
"A woman is declared to be the sovereign over wealth, but not in matters of mortgage, gift, or sale;
therefore, a mortgage or the like executed by her never becomes valid."

In this way, even regarding the statement of Kaṇva, ownership should be understood as existing only after excluding giving, mortgaging, and selling. As for what was asked, "To whom should she be subject?", there too she must be dependent on her husband, her son, or her father at the appropriate times. Thus Manu says:
"In childhood she shall remain under the control of her father, under that of her husband in youth, and under that of her son in old age; a woman does not deserve independence. [MDh 5.148]
And likewise, another [verse] in that very same place states:
"Whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an elderly woman, a woman should not perform any action independently, even within her own home. (MDh 5.147)
Thus [ends the section]. 18.1.
And since such unrestricted conduct regarding anything other than dharma would thus follow, he says: "She shall not transgress against her husband. (18.2)

The meaning is that she should not engage in anything whatsoever without her husband’s permission, or even when it is forbidden by him. Although one could simply say "the master" (*pati*), the term "husband" (*bhartṛ*) is used to indicate that this applies to whoever provides her maintenance. (18.2)
Furthermore: "Restrained in speech, sight, and action. (18.3)

The word "syāt" (should be) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. One who speaks only as much as is necessary for the purpose is restrained in speech (*vāk-saṃyatā*). One who does not look at those who perform improper acts, such as spectators and the like, is restrained in sight (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyatā*). One who is engaged in household duties is restrained in action (*karma-saṃyatā*). || 18.3 ||
Childless and desiring offspring, he was Devarāta.

"Without a husband" (*apatih*) means one whose husband is absent, or one whose husband is unfit. And so says Bṛhaspati: "When the husband has disappeared, died, renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen from his caste—in these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women."

The meaning is that if a woman who is childless and desires offspring should wish for a child, she may procreate one through her husband’s brother (*devara*). The *devara* is either the elder or the younger brother of the husband. (18.4)
He states by what procedure one should produce [it]: "One should not let the time for the dance pass, having been impelled by the Guru. (18.5)

"Authorized by her elders" means she has been appointed by both her husband’s kin and her father’s kin. "She should not let the fertile season pass" means she should not refrain from union except during the period of fertility (*ṛtu*). Even there, if conception occurs on a single day, it happens on that very day; if not, it does not happen during that entire season. Thus says the *Brāhmaṇa* of the Talavakāras: "If the semen is emitted on the first day, it results in a conception; therefore, what is emitted thereafter is in vain and is cast away. In this case as well, it should be understood that she is anointed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). As Uśanas says: "Having anointed his entire body with clarified butter, he should approach her who has been appointed and whose entire body has been anointed with clarified butter. (18.5)
From the offerings of rice-balls, the lineage, and the ancestral sages. || 18.6 ||

In the subsequent sūtra, the particle *vā* (or) carries forward the sense of optionality (*vaikalpika*) as well as the sense of absence (*abhāva*). Consequently, by virtue of the governing context (*adhikāra*), in the absence of a husband’s brother (*devarā*), one who desires offspring may take [the seed] even from a mere *sapiṇḍa*; in his absence, from a mere *sagotra*. Here, by the word *sagotra*, one who shares the same water-ancestors (*samānodaka*) is to be understood, because of the observation in another Smṛti: "One should take [the seed] from the nearest [relative]. Those related to the seers (*ṛṣi-sambandha*) are one's own kinsmen (*svakulya*). 18.6.
Or, [the rule applies] from the mere presence of the womb. || 18.7 ||

In the absence of all [suitable candidates], she may be given to one who belongs merely to the Brāhmaṇa caste. The word *mātra* (merely) denotes the mere quality of caste; therefore, it should be understood that this refers to one who lacks qualities when those possessing qualities are unavailable. Her separate mention is for the purpose of prohibiting her being given away to another when a man of noble family is available. And so Vasiṣṭha says: "Indeed, while a man of that same family is available, she must not go to another" (VaDh 17.80). 18.7.
Some say that [the gift] should not be from one who is not a deity. 18.8.

Some maintain that one should not procreate offspring from a brother-in-law or other sapinda relative; however, the Teacher [Ācārya] holds that in the absence of a brother-in-law, one may do so even from another. 18.8.
An offspring does not belong to the progenitor beyond the second [generation]. 18.9.

Having passed over the second, one should not produce a third; thus, the second is permitted. If one produces a third, it belongs to the progenitor, such as the husband, and not to the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*). Consequently, that [third] becomes unfit; this much is intended here. (18.9)
[The rule applies] to another [word] than the *samaya* [technical term]. || 18.10 ||

If an agreement has been made in the form, "Your pleasure [is mine], my child [is yours]," then even a third [son] belongs to the other, the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*). Therefore, the intention is that this is not faulty. || 18.10 ||
And [the inheritance belongs] to the field [of one who is] living. 18.11.

The word "ca" (and) serves the purpose of drawing in [the phrase] "of another. The intention is that the offspring which is produced in the field—that is, by the wife—of a living husband who is incapable of procreation belongs to the owner of the field alone, even without an agreement, and this applies even if it exceeds one [offspring] from a second [man].
Of that [self], from another. || 18.12 ||

If offspring is produced even while the husband is alive through another man—that is, one other than the husband such as a brother-in-law—or through transgression, that child belongs to the biological father alone, even if he is the second, and not to the owner of the field (the husband). || 18.12 ||
Or [it arises] from two. (18.13)
In this way, the offspring thus produced belongs either to the progenitor or to the owner of the field; the meaning is that he becomes a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* (belonging to two lineages). || 18.13 ||
But it is for the sake of protecting the husband alone. 18.14.

When protection, maintenance, nourishment, and the performance of sacramental rites are carried out by the husband, the offspring born from another man through a lapse belongs to that husband alone; the word *tu* (but) is for the sake of specification. Even if he is unprotected—due to being an ascetic, lost, fallen, or the like—it still belongs to him; it belongs especially to whoever is capable of providing protection. || 18.14 ||
The rule has been stated regarding the death of the husband; now he speaks concerning his disappearance: "If the husband has disappeared, there is a period of six years of waiting. (18.15)

When the husband has departed for another country, a wife must not produce offspring for six years; after that period, if she so desires, she may produce offspring only after obtaining the authorization of her elders—this is the intended meaning. Why? Because of the observation of Vasiṣṭha’s Smṛti: “They say that a son born of a woman who is not authorized belongs to the progenitor” (VaDh 17.63). 18.15.
When it is being heard, one should approach. 18.16.

If, after six years have passed, the husband is heard from, she should go toward him alone while he is being heard from; the intention is that she should not procreate offspring by means of another man. (18.16)
But there is cessation [of the offense] when he has gone forth, because of the possibility [of such a case]. || 18.17 ||

If the husband has renounced the world (*pravrajita*), there is a cessation of approaching him due to that circumstance; the meaning is that she should not go to him. Alternatively, there is a cessation of procreating offspring due to that circumstance; she should not produce offspring. The word *tu* (but/then) is for the sake of distinction. Some explain that in the absence of desire, she should not procreate, but rather remain self-restrained (*saṃyatā*). [The rule] "she should not procreate offspring when he has renounced" implies, by virtue of the word *tu*, that she herself may also renounce, since it is impossible to know the intention of one who resides in another land.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the period for the acquisition of knowledge is twelve years.

It should be understood that the wife of a Brāhmaṇa who has gone abroad for the purpose of acquiring knowledge (*vidyā*) shall wait for twelve years; she may go to meet him once offspring has been born, but if he has renounced the world (*pravrajita*), she must cease [waiting]. Here, because of the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa," it is understood that previously this applied to Kṣatriyas and others. Alternatively, since "knowledge" is mentioned here, it refers specifically to a Brāhmaṇa who has gone for the sake of wealth. By the force of other Smṛtis, there is no waiting period in cases involving sexual desire. As Vasiṣṭha says: "The wife of one who has gone abroad shall wait for five years; after five years, she may go to her husband's presence. If he went away for the sake of dharma or wealth, then she should act as if he were dead, if he went for the sake of pleasure" (VaDh 17.75–77). And thus, even for a Kṣatriya or others who have gone for the sake of knowledge, half and half [of the period] should be assigned compared to a Brāhmaṇa. For one who has gone for the sake of wealth, the rule stated by Vasiṣṭha is to be observed. As Vasiṣṭha says: "In this manner, a Brāhmaṇa woman who has not borne children waits five years, and six if she has borne; a princess who has not borne waits four, and five if she has borne; a Vaiśya woman who has not borne waits three, and four if she has borne; a Śūdra woman who has not borne waits two, and three if she has borne" (VaDh 17.78). By this same logic, even in connection with the pursuit of knowledge, the status of "not having borne children" should be understood as being reduced by one year. (18.18)
And likewise, when there is an elder brother, the younger brother [may marry] in the matters of taking a maiden as a wife or establishing the sacred fire.

If the elder brother has not taken a wife, has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), or is away on a journey, the younger brother may act in exactly this same manner. From the use of the word "thus" (*evam*), a complete extension (*atideśa*) of the rules is heard; however, from that [extension], one should understand that approaching [the elder's wife] is permitted when he is merely absent, whereas it is prohibited when he has renounced the world (*pravrajita*). If it is argued that, in the case of one who has renounced the world, the requirement of self-restraint (*saṃyatatva*) would also apply, we say no, because of the observation of other *smṛtis*. As Uśanas says: "When the elder brother has renounced the world, there is no period of waiting (*kṣapaṇa*); he may marry immediately," and so forth. If it is further argued that for one who has gone abroad for the sake of wealth, a six-year period would apply, we say no, because of the force of another *smṛti* even in that case. As Vasiṣṭha says:
"But since he who is superior in dharma and artha has been gone for twelve years, it is right that he be awaited by his brother, even though he is heard from repeatedly. Thus [it is said].

By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), there is an inclusion of those [periods] mentioned in other Smṛtis. As Vasiṣṭha says: "If one does not wait for an elder brother who has not settled [in marriage] for eight, ten, or twelve years, he becomes liable to penance. In that context, when [the period] is heard of frequently, it is twelve years, because it is stated repeatedly; when it is heard of only slightly, it is ten years; and when it is not heard of at all, it should be understood as eight years. For a Kṣatriya and others, half and half [of these periods] should be calculated as before. This is the exception [to the general rule].
One who is insane, a sinner, a leper, one who has fallen from his caste, a eunuch,
and one afflicted with pulmonary consumption— it is not right to wait for such persons.

This should be understood as stated in other Smṛtis beginning with these words. Since the status of the younger brother is established by implication through the mention of the "elder" alone—given that the terms are relative—the use of the plural number is intended to indicate that the fault applies specifically to those born of the same mother, and to include even the fire-maintaining rites prescribed in the Smṛtis. (18.19)
Some say there are six. 18.20.

Some maintain that one should wait for exactly six years. In this regard, it should be understood that if the one who has gone abroad is extremely old, he should wait for six years; otherwise, he should wait for twelve years. (18.20)
Having spoken incidentally, he now states the duty regarding women:
"A maiden, having passed three menstrual periods, may unite herself with one who is blameless, having set aside her paternal ornaments. (18.21)

The meaning is that if, after three seasons have passed, the father or others do not give this maiden away, she may herself choose a husband who is blameless and endowed with noble lineage and other such qualities. She should do so having set aside the ornaments given by the father and others. The mention of the "father" is illustrative; thus Manu says: "A maiden choosing her own husband shall not take the ornaments belonging to her father, nor those of her mother, nor those given by her brothers; if she should take them, it would constitute theft" (MDh 9.92).
Thus [ends the section]. 18.21.
At what time should she be given away by her father and others? To this he says: "The giving [of the girl] should take place before puberty. (18.22)
One should give her away before the appearance of the menses. 18.22.
For it is said:
"One who does not give is at fault. (18.23)
Not only is there an absence of merit for one who does not give [a daughter in marriage], but what is more, for the couple there arises a sin equal to the killing of a Brahmin. As Vasiṣṭha has said:
"As many seasons as touch a maiden who is of equal status and being solicited with desire..."
"By those two, the mother and father, as many embryos as have been conceived are thereby slain"— this is the declaration of the Dharma.
[VaDh 17.71] Thus ends section 18.23.
Some say [the period begins] prior to the acquisition of the garment. 18.24.

Because the time [of menstruation] is difficult to discern, one should give [the garment] before the acceptance of the cloth; the meaning is that one should give it at the very moment she becomes bashful. Thus some hold this view. There is an option based on the availability of the groom. 18.24.
It has been stated that when the father or others give [the bride], they should give her clothed and adorned. To the question of how this should be done in the absence of wealth, he says:
"The taking of wealth is for the sake of accomplishing the marriage. (18.25)

The taking of another's property means the appropriation of what has not been permitted; the meaning is that for the sake of accomplishing a marriage, one should take whatever is necessary so that the marriage is consummated, and in the absence of one's own property, one should give after having stolen it. (18.25)
Moreover: "And in attachment to the system of Dharma. (18.26)

The interruption of an established ritual obligation (*dharma-tantra*), such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice and the like, constitutes "attachment" (*saṅga*). When such attachment occurs, one may take the property of another. The use of the term "tantra" (obligation) indicates that this applies only to what has already been commenced and is necessary to complete; it does not apply to taking for the purpose of initiating what has not yet begun. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to carry forward the phrase "for the sake of success" (*siddhy-artham*). One should take only as much as is required to complete the rite, and nothing more. Thus, if one takes more than that, it is indeed theft. (18.26)
From where is that to be taken? To this he says: "From a Śūdra. (18.27)
For wealth exists for the sake of sacrifice, and a Śūdra has no entitlement to Vedic rites; therefore, one should first take it from a Śūdra. (18.27)
In the absence of such [a person], it may be from anyone else other than a Śūdra. 18.28.

Although it could have been stated simply as "in other cases as well," the specific mention of the *śūdra* is for the purpose of including the *vaiśya* and the *kṣatriya*. That is to say: in the absence of that [the *brāhmaṇa*], from a *vaiśya*; in the absence of that, from a *kṣatriya*. (18.28)
In that case as well:
for one who has many cattle but performs inferior rites. || 18.29 ||
One of inferior action is he who performs unsuitable work, or he who does not do anything at all; from such a person one should receive [it]. (18.29)
[The same applies] to a hundred [cows] belonging to one who has not maintained the sacred fires. || 18.30 ||

Even for one who has performed other rites but has not established the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), [the fine is] "one hundred cows. The mention of "hundred" is intended as an indication of the quantity of the substance; the meaning is "worth one hundred *niṣkas*. This applies everywhere in this manner. (18.30)
And [the penance] for one who does not drink soma is that of a thousand cows.

One may also take from one who, though he maintains the sacred fires and possesses a thousand [cows], does not drink the Soma; the word "and" (ca) implies that it may be taken from others as well. One may also take from one who, despite possessing abundant wealth, does not perform the corresponding ritual acts. 18.31.
Not only are there these two causes for taking another's property, but furthermore: "And without having enjoyed the seventh [requisite], one does not store it up. (18.32)
Having gone seven times without eating due to the loss of his wealth, he may take the property of another. Thus says Manu:

"Likewise, when one has reached the seventh meal-time without having eaten the six previous meals, he may take from one of inferior conduct according to the rule of 'not providing for tomorrow' (aśvastana). [MDh 11.16]

The word "and" (ca) has the sense of indicating that this pertains to those whose capacity for action is inferior; likewise, the statement of Manu has been cited: "For the sake of non-accumulation, [one should eat] only enough to fill the belly.
Even from those whose actions have not declined. 18.33.
In this state, even for those who perform their prescribed duties—as indicated by the word "even" (api)—as well as for the maintainer of the sacred fires and the drinker of Soma. 18.33.
If, while taking [the goods], he is led before the king by a royal officer and is questioned on account of the theft, then, being questioned by the king, he should speak. 18.34.
He should declare it—that is, he should speak of it—when questioned, but he must not deny it out of fear; nor, however, should he go of his own accord to report it. 18.34.
For this reason:
"Therefore, he should indeed be supported, provided he is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct. (18.35)

The word *hi* has the sense of "because. Because it must be supported by him, according to the statement: "He shall support Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas" (GDh 10.9). This applies if he is endowed with learning and good character—that is, if he is fully equipped with learning, which is the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda, and with good character, which is the performance of the duties enjoined therein. If it is argued that the state of being endowed with learning and good character is already established by the very mention of "those who must be supported," since the instruction to support those learned in the Vedas is given in the passage, "He shall support Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas" (GDh 10.9), we reply: No, because there is also an instruction to support even those not learned in the Vedas, as stated in, "Brāhmaṇas who are indolent, as well as non-Brāhmaṇas" (GDh 10.10). Thus, it is demonstrated that in the case of seizing the property of others, a non-Brāhmaṇa is not to be supported. The use of the word "by him" indicates that his support is for the sake of dharma alone, and not for the sake of his livelihood. (18.35)
In the case of an affliction of the Dharma-tantra, there is no fault in performing it; there is no fault.

Because he must be supported, therefore, in the event of an affliction to his *dharma* or his *tantra*—whereby the word *dharma* refers to the *agnihotra* and other rites, the word *tantra* refers to marriage, and the word *pīḍā* (affliction) refers to self-affliction, as indicated by the phrase "without having enjoyed the seventh [year]"; the meaning is: in the case of the interruption of religious duties, for the sake of accomplishing a marriage, and in the case of self-affliction—there is no fault in committing theft for him. The meaning is that there is no punishment. The intention is that when an affliction to *dharma* or *tantra* occurs due to the king's negligence, and the theft has been committed such that the thief's own fault has arisen, it is not proper to inflict punishment upon the Brāhmaṇa.

Some explain it as follows: if one is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct, he should speak because he is to be supported; even one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) may speak. Therefore, even for one who is not learned in the Vedas, there is no punishment when there is an obstruction to the performance of dharma.

Others explain it thus: "He should support those learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriyān*) means that whoever is one who ought to be supported must indeed be supported even for such an offense. The word *hi* has the sense of *eva* (indeed). The corresponding meaning is that he should also be given [a share] appropriate to that [offense]. He should not punish even one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), because there is no punishment for him even for that offense. Why? Because this sūtra, beginning with the words "in the case of injury to the system of Dharma" (*dharmatantrapīḍāyām*), is intended for the sake of one who is not learned in the Vedas. || 18.36 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the *Maskarīya-Gautama-bhāṣya*.
The nineteenth chapter begins:

The fivefold dharma was introduced as that which is to be explained. Among those, four kinds have been stated; now the fifth kind of dharma, the occasional (*naimittika*), must be discussed. To introduce that, he provides a summary of what has been said.
The duty of the social classes and the duty of the stages of life have been explained. 19.1.

Furthermore, what is accomplished by this sūtra? If it is argued that this is a restatement of what has already been said for the purpose of introducing a topic not previously mentioned, that is incorrect; for the subsequent [topic] can be stated even without such a summary. If it is argued that the purpose is to satisfy the listeners' further curiosity, that too is incorrect, since that is already achieved simply by the commencement of the specific treatment (*naimittika*). Moreover, the mention of "castes and stages of life" (*varṇāśrama*) need not be made, because dharma is being expounded in connection with them anyway; the summary would be complete even by saying merely "dharma has been explained. For, in a complete summary, one must also include the exposition of both the duties pertaining to castes and stages (*varṇāśramadharma*) and the qualities of dharma (*guṇadharma*).
Because it serves no purpose, the two *ca*-particles are also redundant; therefore, this sūtra is inconsistent. To this we reply:

some first explain that they are for the sake of establishing the substratum (*ādhāra*). This is incorrect, because it is already known from the very commencement of the sūtra: "The castes and the stages of life" (GDh 11.31).

Others, however, explain this as being for the purpose of exempting the Śūdra from the penance for eating forbidden food (*abhakṣya*). That too is incorrect; for in the passage, "Of the twice-born who are praised in their own duties" (GDh 17.1), the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is stated for the purpose of illustrating the twice-born in general, not for the purpose of illustrating the Śūdra specifically. Why? Because of the observation of other Smṛtis. As Manu says:
"This has been declared in its entirety regarding the edible and non-edible foods of the twice-born" (MDh 5.26).

Thus, since a Śūdra lacks the qualification for the rules regarding what may and may not be eaten, his lack of liability for penance is established by implication. Others explain that this [text] is intended to grant him eligibility for certain duties of his class even prior to initiation (*upanayana*); but that too is incorrect, because it has already been stated in the very passage, "The classes and the stages of life... (GDh 11.31).

Others explain that this is for the purpose of ensuring that women also obtain the duties (*dharma*) of their caste (*varṇa*) and stage of life (*āśrama*). That too is incorrect; for since she is uninitiated prior to marriage, her status as a member of a caste is already established by the inclusion of the word "castes" (*varṇa*) in the rule, *varṇā āśramāś ca* (GDh 11.31). Furthermore, because she is initiated later, she is entitled to the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*) due to the inclusion of the word "stages of life" (*āśrama*). Regarding this, Manu says: "The rite of marriage is declared to be the initiation (*upanayana*) for women," and so forth. Since this is already established from that very source, what is the purpose of this present sūtra?

Others say: "This is a restatement for the sake of what follows; that which was stated regarding the duties according to the division of castes shall apply to those very same individuals even with respect to what is about to be said. And from this, they conclude that the accomplishment of penance (*prāyaścitta*) is established even for a *śūdra*. That too is incorrect, because there are only two causes for penances: the non-performance of what is enjoined and the practice of what is forbidden. Regarding the non-performance of what is enjoined, Manu says:
"In the case of neglecting the obligatory rites prescribed by the Veda, and in the case of violating the vows of a *snātaka*, fasting is the penance. (MDh 11.203)
And regarding the practice of what is forbidden, Bṛhaspati says:

"But he who performs a forbidden act, especially a Brāhmaṇa, shall undergo fasting for one night if no specific penance has been prescribed; but if a specific one has been prescribed, each [act] requires its own."
And therefore, since [the application of penance] is already established for a Śūdra as well, this [text] was not commenced for the purpose of attaining that [status].

To this it is replied: this is for the purpose of removing a doubt; for later on, Vedic rites such as the *punaḥstoma* and others will be cited, and those do not belong to a Śūdra. Therefore, the doubt—that by analogy with those [Vedic rites], there might be an exclusion of [penance] for the other [classes] as well—is removed. Alternatively, the mention of the social class (*varṇa*) is for the sake of favoring the penance in consideration of specific stages of life (*vayaḥ-avasthā*). As Bhṛgu said: "He who is eighty years of age, or a child less than sixteen..."
"Women and the sick deserve only half of the expiation.
Or [this may depend] on the specific degree of strength, as Bhṛgu says:
"Whatever has been prescribed for one who is weak is likewise declared for children and the elderly."
"Or even by one whose conduct is contracted, likewise during a reversal of time. Vyāsa also says:
"Place, time, age, power, knowledge, and likewise that which is produced by the intellect..."
"Having recognized that practice is devoid of intellect, one should speak of renunciation. Thus it is said.

The word *ca* (and) is intended to include intermediate [classes]; and their inclusion is for the purpose of obtaining half of the penance even for them. Consequently, they should be considered as belonging to the caste of their mother.
