The mention of the *āśrama*s (stages of life) is for the purpose of establishing the possibility of penances; just as the formulation of penances is made for the sake of destroying sin, so too is it done with respect to the *āśrama*s. And thus, there is a distinction among recitations (*japa*) and other acts based on what is possible: for instance, fire-offerings (*homa*) and giving (*dāna*) are not possible for a forest-dweller (*bhikṣuka*), because he possesses no sacred fires and has no property; likewise, giving is not possible for students (*brahmacārin*s). The second *ca* is for the purpose of drawing in the duties of women; since that is already established by the mention of *varṇa* and *āśrama*, this further restatement is for the purpose of formulating penances. An example of this is the statement of Bhṛgu: "He whose years are eighty," and so forth. And likewise Aṅgiras.
Even a woman who has approached [a man] unintentionally shall incur half the sin;
however, before twelve years have passed, even a man shall become a sharer of half [the guilt].
Thus [ends the section]. 19.1.
Now he states the cause for penance: "Furthermore, this person is defiled by a blameworthy action. (19.2)

But surely, the non-performance of what is prescribed and the practice of what is forbidden are causes for expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and since that will be established in the subsequent sūtra, this present sūtra is indeed redundant. To this it is replied: The connection with karma belongs only to one who performs action without knowing the Self, but not to the knower of the Self; for there is no connection with defilement (*lepa*) in the case of either the non-performance of what is enjoined or the practice of what is forbidden. This [sūtra] is intended to establish that only the non-knower of the Self has the qualification for expiation. Thus says the *Atharva-upaniṣad*:
"The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are severed,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
Therefore, this [teaching] is for the ignorant.

Now, following the performance of ritual action—*khalu* being used here for emphasis—the meaning is "this very person. By the word "this," he points to the embodied *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field) through direct perception; by the emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), he excludes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Thus says the Upaniṣad: "Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree.
Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1]

He is called *puruṣa* because he dwells within the city (*puri śayanāt*). Thus says the Upaniṣad: "He who knows Him hidden in the secret cave, in the highest heaven" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1). He is defiled—that is, connected—by reprehensible action (*yāpyena karmaṇā*). Even though he is also connected by righteous action (*dharmeṇa*), nevertheless, because there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) regarding a connection with dharma, only adharma is mentioned here. If it is argued that the word *atha* is redundant because it has already been stated that "this person is indeed defiled by reprehensible action," implying an inevitable connection with whatever action has been performed, we say no. It serves the purpose of enjoining the performance of recitations (*japa*) and other rites even when the occasion for expiation (*prāyaścitta-nimitta*) has not been specifically observed. And so says Manu:

"A twice-born man of the highest rank should perform even a single *kṛcchra* penance during the course of a year for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly; but for that which is known, it is especially so. (Manu Dharma Śāstra 5.21).
Thus, it is made known that there is indeed an expiation even in the case of what is done unintentionally. And likewise, Manu says:
"The wise know that expiation is required for a sin committed unintentionally;

some say it is also required for one committed intentionally, based on the evidence of the revealed scriptures" (MDh 11.46). Therefore, it should be understood that the penance is more severe for an intentional act and lighter for an unintentional one. And so he will state: "For sexual intercourse with a woman of the lowest caste, a year-long *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed if done unintentionally, but twelve nights if done intentionally," and so forth. The inclusion of the word "action" (*karman*) is intended to indicate a connection even with actions performed in a previous birth. And thus Manu says:
"In this world, certain evil-minded men undergo a transformation of their appearance due to their current misconduct, as well as by what was done in the past. [MDh 11.48]

In that very same place, he says: "The killer of a Brahmin suffers from consumption" (MDh 11.49), and so forth. Thus, when symptoms such as consumption are observed, the purpose of this teaching is that an injunction for expiation must be performed even for deeds committed in a previous birth; this is the meaning. While it could have been stated simply that "one is defiled by sinful action," the inclusion of the term *yāpya* (curable/contemptible) is for the purpose of making known that even a [so-called] *dharma*, if it is censured by the world, becomes *adharma*. And so Manu says: "One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of dharma."

"And also a dharma that results in unhappiness and is censured by the world. (MDh 4.176) The term *yāpyena* is a compound with an irregular formation (*visamāsa*). It is intended to make known that even if one has not committed the act oneself, one nevertheless becomes liable for penance through mere accusation, because the act is condemned by others. And so Vasiṣṭha says:

"Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a crime causing loss of caste (*patanīya*) or a minor offense (*upapātaka*), one should subsist on water for a month and repeat the *Śuddhavatī* verses; he is purified—so it is understood. By this, the case of one who is falsely accused is explained. (VaDh 23.37–39)
Thus [ends the section]. 19.2.
If it is asked how one is tainted by a blameworthy action, it is through the practice of its means. If it is asked what those means are, he says:

namely, officiating at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, eating what is not to be eaten, speaking what is censurable, neglecting what is prescribed for the disciplined, and practicing what is forbidden. (19.3)

The phrase "such as this" (*yathaitat*) is for the purpose of providing an illustration. Sacrificing for those unfit to sacrifice (*ayājyayājanam*) means officiating at sacrifices for those who are fallen (*patita*). Consuming what is not to be eaten (*abhakṣyabhakṣaṇam*) means eating garlic and the like. Speaking what is blameworthy (*avadyavadanam*) means speaking falsehoods and so forth. The non-performance (*akriyā*) of prescribed duties (*śiṣṭasya*), such as the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*), means their failure to be carried out. The practice (*sevanam*) of prohibited acts (*pratiṣiddhasya*), such as violence (*hiṃsā*), means their performance. The particle *iti* serves to indicate completion, signifying that "this much constitutes the means of unrighteousness (*adharma*). Now, one might object: since the mention of "prohibited acts" (*pratiṣiddha*) already includes sacrificing for those unfit to sacrifice and the rest, their separate enumeration is redundant.

It is said: these are mentioned by their own names in order to make it known that they are not to be performed even though they have been permitted. Consequently, it is established that even for one who is ignorant (*avidvān*), there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) when these are practiced in times of distress (*āpad*); for in that regard, it has been permitted that "for all [the twice-born], officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts [are permissible]. Likewise, the eating of forbidden foods (*abhakṣya*)—even those not included in the category of permitted foods—is permitted in times of distress. Similarly, even untruth is permitted in another Smṛti in times of distress, as Vyāghra says:
If speaking to someone always causes suffering to their speech and mind,
then one should speak untruth there, just as was the word of the tiger.

Thus, by the force of this permission, there is a lighter penance; that too consists of one-fourth of what was first prescribed. As Uśanas says: "Having crossed over a calamity by means of actions ordained for times of distress, one should again perform one-fourth of the penance for those [actions]. (19.3)
In this regard, they deliberate whether one should perform an expiation or not.
Regarding that connection with a curable act, the exponents of the Veda deliberate and investigate whether an expiation must be performed for its removal or whether it need not be performed. 19.4.
"One should not do so," they say. 19.5.
First, some say that one should not perform [the rite] by the power of rebirth alone. || 19.5 ||

In the case of the rules for times of distress (*āpadkalpa*), there is no fault, as they are prescribed for such occasions. But even in the absence of distress, if one fails to perform what is enjoined or engages in what is prohibited, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) would be useless. Why?
Because "karma is not exhausted" (by mere expiation). 19.6.

The word *hi* has the sense of "because. Because an action performed does not perish without yielding its fruit—nor is it destroyed by expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*)—therefore, an action residing within the self yields its fruit until its destruction. Thus says Śaṅkha:
"Just as seeds remain in the earth and jewels in the ocean, so do actions reside in the self and come forth [to bear fruit]."

After yielding its fruit, it perishes of its own accord, just as the potency of a seed does upon the emergence of the sprout. Thus says the Śruti: "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action, and sinful by sinful action. Furthermore, no one is observed here to experience mere pleasure (without any trace of suffering) from which one could infer that his inauspiciousness (*aśubha*) is destroyed by expiation (*prāyaścitta*). As for those Vedic expiations such as "one offers an oblation when [the vessel] is broken" or "one offers an oblation when [the rice] is spilled," these are subsidiary parts of the ritual (*karmāṅga*) contingent upon specific circumstances, not intended for the removal of defects. Even in the world, when a hole in a jar is plugged with lac or similar substances, only the capacity for functional efficiency is restored; there is no return to the original state. Nor can the inauspiciousness, which persists by pervading the self, be removed, just as salt dissolved in water cannot be extracted. By means of merit (*dharma*) produced through expiation, unrighteousness (*adharma*) is merely suppressed, not destroyed, just as the coldness of water is suppressed by heat, since coldness is seen to return once again. (19.6)
"One should act"—this is another [instruction]. 19.7.

"One should perform penance"—this is another view. "There is nothing superior to this"—this is another established conclusion (*siddhānta*); such is the meaning. Regarding the performance of duties according to the rules for times of distress (*āpatkalpa*), although penance is shown by one statement as being enjoined by that very statement, penance is indeed meaningful even when there is no distress. How so? It is exhausted precisely through the experience of suffering caused by recitation (*japa*) and other such acts; because the experience of suffering caused by recitation and the like has that [penance] as its cause, even that which lasts for a long time is exhausted by what lasts for a short time. Just as in the world, a chronic disease is exhausted by the drinking of medicine that causes only brief pain.

But how is it understood that unrighteousness (*adharma*), which yields abundant results of suffering, is exhausted by the experience of even a small amount of suffering? It is understood from scripture (*āgama*). And he demonstrates this: "It is known that 'having sacrificed with the *Punarstoma*, they return to the *Savana*'; 'having sacrificed with the *Vrātyastoma*; he who sacrifices with the *Aśvamedha* crosses over all evil, he crosses over the murder of a Brahmin'; and 'one should cause one who is being falsely accused to sacrifice with the *Agniṣṭut*'" [GDh 19.8–11].

This is his intention: that this matter—namely, "this is a means for accomplishing Dharma" and "this is a means for accomplishing Adharma," and "when this is performed, Adharma is destroyed"—is accessible only through scripture (*āgama*), and not accessible through logical reasoning (*upapatti*), because it is not an object of other means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, all the arguments stated regarding the non-performance of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) are refuted precisely on account of their contradiction with scripture.
As for what was said—that there is no restoration of a jar once it has been pierced by filling it with lacquer and the like—[that too is refuted].

To this it is replied: In that context, what is intended is simply the production of fitness (*yogyatā*), for there is no contradiction in saying that the production of a jar is not meant; likewise, even by means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), it is only the fitness of the person that is produced through the destruction of demerit (*adharma*). As for the objection that the removal of qualities pervading the self is impossible—like salt pervading water—that is not contradictory, for it is like the removal of a dye from cloth by means of alkaline substances and the like. Furthermore, as for the "overpowering" (*abhibhava*) mentioned, that too is refuted by the very scriptural statement: "He overcomes all evil. If only overpowering were effected, then the verbal expression "he overcomes" (*tarati*) would be untenable. As for the claim that expiations are auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of ritual acts, that is not universal; for where there is a specific occasion (*nimitta*), such as the non-performance of an enjoined act or the performance of a prohibited one, they serve to destroy that fault, as in: "He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice overcomes the murder of a Brahmin" (GDh 19.10). Where neither of those two exists, it should be understood that the expiation is an auxiliary part of the rite with respect to that occasion.
But surely, if this point is established by scripture, then a single example alone would be appropriate; one must state the purpose for providing so many examples.

It is said that the presentation of multiple examples is for the purpose of demonstrating the diversity of the objects [of purification]. Furthermore, by means of the example of the *punaḥstoma*, he demonstrates this first: that the fault incurred from accepting what should not be accepted is destroyed. This is because of the Vedic revelation: “Having accepted much from one from whom it should not be accepted, one should sacrifice with the *punaḥstoma*. The mention of accepting what should not be accepted is intended to illustrate eating what should not be eaten and speaking what is blameworthy as well, since another Vedic text is seen stating: “One overcomes the eating of what should not be eaten and the speaking of what is blameworthy by means of the *punaḥstoma*. (19.7)
And when they have thus become disqualified from all ritual acts, it is known from scripture: "Having sacrificed with the *punarstoma*, they return again to the *savana*.

By the word *savana*, ritual action (*karman*) is meant. "Re-attainment" means that he once again becomes fit for the performance of rites prescribed by the Vedas (*śrauta*) and the Smṛtis. The plural form "they come" (*āyanti*) is intended to illustrate other instances such as eating forbidden food or speaking what should not be spoken. The phrase "it is known" (*vijñāyate*) is intended to indicate that this is based on Vedic revelation (*śruti*). (19.8)
And having performed the Vrātyastoma sacrifices.

The particle *ca* serves to draw forward the phrase "coming for the third time" (*savanam āyanti*). The plural number in *vrātyastomaiḥ* indicates that there are four *vrātyastoma* sacrifices well-known from the Śruti. Those who have passed the time for initiation are called *vrātyas*; because these sacrifices are to be performed by them, they are called *vrātyastomas*. And so Vasiṣṭha says:

"One whose *sāvitrī* has been lost shall perform the *uddālaka-vrata*: he should subsist for two months on barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), for one month on milk, for half a month on curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*), for eight nights on clarified butter (*ghṛta*), for six nights on unhusked grain, eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) for three nights, subsist on water for three nights, and fast for one day and night. Alternatively, he may go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), or he may perform the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice. [VaDh 11.76–79]

The mention of the *vrātya* is also an illustration for minor offenses (*upapātaka*), because the *vrātya* is listed among the minor offenses in the rule: "Minor offenses consist of those excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅktya*) prior to Durvāsas, the killer of a cow, the murderer of a Brahmin, the composer of mantras, the *avakīrṇin*, and one who has lost the *Sāvitrī*" (GDh 21.11), and because another Smṛti text states: "The *vrātyastoma* sacrifice destroys the minor offense" (GDh 19.3). Thus, it is demonstrated by this that the defects of minor offenses are destroyed. 19.9.
"He who performs the horse sacrifice overcomes all evil and overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin. (19.10)

By the phrase "all evil," he demonstrates the destruction of that sin which arises from the non-performance of what is enjoined and the practice of what is prohibited. The separate mention of "even the killing of a Brahmin" (brahmahatyā) is for the purpose of making known that the killing of a Brahmin is the gravest of all unrighteous acts; otherwise, since it would already be included under the category of practicing what is prohibited, it need not have been stated separately. Thus says Vyāsa:
"There is nothing greater than the killing of a Brahmin among sins, nor than the horse-sacrifice among merits."
Thus [ends the section]. 19.10.
And one should cause him who is being falsely accused to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut. 19.11.

By citing the Agniṣṭut sacrifice, [the author] demonstrates the destruction of defects caused by the demerits of other bodies; for indeed, false accusation does not occur without human transgression. The word *ca* (and) serves to draw back the phrase “it is known” (*vijñāyate*). The particle *iti* is used to indicate that each [example] refers to a separate scriptural passage (*śruti*). For thus, since such [scriptural] evidence is seen everywhere regarding this subject, expiation must certainly be performed.

But surely, regarding a matter that is to be understood through scriptural injunction, what is this deliberation concerning the performance or non-performance of the penance? That [deliberation] is not tenable. If it were performed, then—starting from the point where it is said, "The initiation of a Brāhmaṇa"—it would have to be performed from that time onward.

It is said: this discussion is intended to make known that there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the repetition or the combination of great sins (*mahāpātaka*). For it is seen in the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) that "karma is not exhausted," and therefore [the expiation] should not be performed; rather, each [sin] must be dealt with separately. Thus, there is expiation for the repetition or the combination of other [sins], such as minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and so forth. Some say: this discussion is for the purpose of praising expiation.
Others say: "Expiation applies only to what is done unintentionally, not to what is done intentionally.

That is incorrect, because it would result in contradiction with such statements as: "For approaching a woman of the lowest caste (antāvasāyinī), there is a *kṛcchra* penance for one year if done unintentionally, but twelve nights if unintentionally [for other offenses]" [GDh 23.33]; "If it was preceded by knowledge, then three nights" [GDh 20.9]; and "And in the case of a blameworthy act performed with prior intent" [GDh 25.10].
Others say: "This discussion is intended to demonstrate the gravity of an intentional act."
That is incorrect, because it has already been made known in this very passage: "Now, moreover, this person... [GDh 19.2]. || 19.11 ||
The means of expiation for that are recitation, austerity, burnt offerings, fasting, and giving gifts.

The "expiations" (*niṣkrayaṇāni*) for that act which requires atonement are the means of purification; just as in the world there are ashes and other such things for the purification of bronze and similar materials, so too are these [recitations] for unrighteous acts. Regarding the word "of that" (*tasya*), there might otherwise be doubt as to whether these refer to the *punarstoma* and other sacrifices, or to recitations (*japa*) and the like. "Recitation" (*japa*) refers to the repeated practice of the Upanishads and other texts to be mentioned hereafter, characterized by being spoken aloud, whispered, or mental. As Manu says: "A sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) is ten times superior to a ritual sacrifice (*vidhiyajña*); a whispered one is a hundred times superior, and a mental one is recorded as being a thousand times superior. (MDh 2.85)

Austerity (*tapas*) refers to that which will be described, such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth. Fire-offering (*homa*) is the casting of substances such as clarified butter (*ājya*) into the fire, preceded by mantras such as the *vyāhṛtis*. Fasting (*upavāsa*) is the restraint of all the sense organs. And thus say the authors of the Purāṇas:
"In this world, turning away from faults and dwelling together with virtues—that is to be known as fasting, not the mere emaciation of the body."

As for the fact that they recite "fasting" (*anāśaka*) among the types of austerity, that refers to the complete renunciation of food; it is so called because it is taught together with [other] difficult practices and because it is designated as "fasting. Giving (*dāna*) is the bestowing of substances such as gold upon a worthy recipient (*pātra*). The use of the distributive compound (*visamāsa*) is intended to indicate that each individual act constitutes a means of expiation. (19.12)
In that regard, he first states the nature of recitation (*japa*):

"The Upaniṣads, the Vedāntas, the *Saṃhitās* among all the Vedic meters, the *Madhu* hymns, the *Aghamarṣaṇa*, the *Atharvaśiras*, the *Rudras*, the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Rājan* and *Rauhiṇa* Sāmans, the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*, the *Puruṣagati*, the *Mahānāmnīs*, the *Mahāvairāja*, the *Mahādivākīrtya*, any one of the *Jyeṣṭhasāmans*, the *Bahiṣpavamāna*, the *Kūṣmāṇḍas*, the *Pāvamānīs*, and the *Sāvitrī*—these are the purifiers. (19.13)

The *Upaniṣads* are the secret *Brāhmaṇas*. The *Vedāntas* are the *Āraṇyakas*. Among all the meters (*chandas*), the *Saṃhitā* is intended, not the individual words (*pada*) or the *Krama* arrangement. The qualification "among all the meters" is for the purpose of making it known that this applies not only to one's own recension (*śākhā*). The *Madhus* are those verses containing the word "honey," such as "The winds blow honey for the righteous one" (*madhu vātā ṛtāyate*, RV 1.90.6). The *Aghamarṣaṇa* begins with "Righteousness and Truth" (*ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca*). The *Atharvaśiras* is well-known in the *Atharvaveda*. The *Rudras* are those containing the word "Rudra," such as "Obeisance to your wrath, O Rudra" (*namas te rudra manyave*, VS 16.1). The *Puruṣasūkta* begins with "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads" (*sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ*, RV 10.90). The *Rājarauhiṇe* are the two *Sāmans* sung upon this verse: "Men call upon Indra at the distribution of spoils" (*indraṃ naro nemadhitā havante*, RV 7.27.1). Although they are *Yajus* formulas, they are called by these names; hence the mention of *Sāman*. The *Bṛhat* is sung upon the verse "Verily we invoke you" (*tvām iddhi havāmahe*, RV 6.46.1). The *Rathantara* is sung upon the verse "We cry out to you, O Hero" (*abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ*, RV 7.32.22). The *Puruṣagati* is sung upon the verse "I am the first-born of Righteousness" (*aham asmi prathamajā ṛtasya*, RV 7.27.1). The *Bṛhat* is based on the two verses beginning with "Verily we invoke you" (*tvām iddhi havāmahe*, RV 6.46.1). The *Rathantara* is on the verse "We cry out to you, O Hero" (*abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ*, RV 7.32.22). It is also sung upon the verse "I am the first-born of Righteousness" (*aham asmi prathamajā ṛtasya*, TaitBr 2.8.8.1). The *Mahānāmnīs* are the *Sāman* on the verse "Know, O Maghavan" (*vidā maghavan*, AitĀ 4.15). The *Mahāvairāja* is sung upon the verse "Drink the Soma" (*pibā somam*, RV 6.17.1). The *Mahādivākīrtya* is the *Sāman* on the verse "Radiant, great, drink" (*vibhrāḍ bṛhat pibat*, RV 10.170.1). Any one of the *Jyeṣṭhasāmans* is intended, which is a single *Sāman* among the three-verse groups (*tṛca*) of "Be gracious to us, O Goddesses" (*śaṃ no devīḥ*, RV 10.9.4) and "The bright face of the gods" (*citraṃ devānām*, RV 1.115.1). The *Bahiṣpavamāna* consists of the verses beginning with "Sing to him, O men" (*upāsmai gāyatā naraḥ*, RV 9.11.1). The *Kūśmāṇḍas* are the *Yajus* formulas beginning with "Whatever offense against the gods, O gods" (*yad devā devahelanam*, VS 20.14). The *Pāvamānyas* are those characterized by the theme of purification (*pavamāna*), such as "With the sweetest, most intoxicating [draught]" (*svādiṣṭhayā madiṣṭhayā*, RV 9.1.1). The *Sāvitrī* is well-known. The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including what has not been mentioned; therefore, other *Sāmans* and so forth mentioned in other *Smṛtis* should be understood. The word "iti" (thus) indicates the manner: "of this very kind. Thus, only those recited in other *Smṛtis* such as the *Śivasaṃkalpa* are to be included, and not those not recited there such as the *Śrīsūkta*. The irregular compound (*visamāsa*) is for the purpose of indicating that each individual item is purifying.

But surely, since recitation has been stated to be the means of expiation, and since these [elements] are the instruments for that, their purifying nature is already established; thus, the mention of "purifying" (*pāvana*) is redundant.
It is replied: the mention of "purifying" is intended to make known that these possess a purifying quality even on occasions other than those of formal expiation. (19.13)
Now he states the rules for food for one engaged in recitation and other such practices:
"The vow of milk, eating vegetables, eating fruits, *prasṛta-yāvaka*, consuming gold, consuming clarified butter, and drinking Soma—these are pure. (19.14)

*Payovratatā* means subsisting on milk. From the mention of a *vrata* (vow), the rule regarding fasting (*upavāsa*) is to be understood. *Śāka* is well-known [as vegetables]. *Phala* refers to mangoes and the like. Regarding *prasṛtayāvaka*: although it should have been stated as "eating a handful of barley-gruel" (*prasṛtayāvakāśana*) based on the context, this specific expression is used for the purpose of including the rules mentioned in other *smṛtis*. Thus Uśanas says:

Having bathed and become pure while the stars are still visible, one should cook a handful of barley in a copper vessel until it becomes gruel (*yavāgū*). At the time of cooking, one should perform a protection rite with this mantra: “Homage to Rudra, lord of beings, lord of mountains; do you protect this. Then, having poured [the water] out with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), purified it with the mantra beginning “Of the god Savitṛ,” and offered an oblation over it with the *Sāvitrī*, one should then consecrate it:
“You are barley; you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are joined with honey.”
It is remembered by the sages as the purifier that washes away all sins.
Whatever deed has been done by speech, whatever deed has been done by action, and whatever has been ill-conceived by the mind—
may the barley grains purify all of that misfortune and the dark-throated goddess of ill-fortune for me.
O barley grains, purify for me everything— my terrible royal offense joined with great sins, as well as my conduct toward women and children and all my duties.
The theft of gold, the violation of vows, officiating at the sacrifice of one for whom it is forbidden,
and the reviling of Brahmins— may all these be purified for me by the barley grains.
May the barley grains purify for me all [the sins] of having been cast off by a dog or a pig, of being the leavings of crows and the like, and of failing to serve my mother and father.

May the barley grains purify for me all this: the food of a group, the food of a courtesan, the food of a Śūdra, food from a corpse or during a birth-impurity, the food of a thief, and likewise all that is unfit to be eaten.

With these six [verses], and then having tasted [the water] with the verse, "Brahmā among the gods," and then with the verses beginning "For breath thee" (*prāṇāya tvā*), he may thereafter eat everything according to his desire. Having drunk it for six nights, he is liberated from all sin arising from the transgression of observances, from the practice of what is forbidden, from eating what should not be eaten, and from minor offenses (*upapātaka*). Having drunk it for seven nights, he purifies the killing of an embryo, violating the Guru’s bed, stealing gold, drinking liquor, and so forth. Having drunk it for eleven nights, he drives away sins committed in the past. Having drunk it for twenty-one nights, he beholds the *gaṇas*, he beholds the Lord of the *gaṇas*, he beholds the sciences (*vidyās*), and he beholds the Lord of the sciences. Thus, day after day, without overeating, he should consume barley-gruel (*yavāgū*).
Thus [it is said].

Gold and the other items are well known. By the use of the particle *iti*, which expresses a manner, the consumption of others such as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth is also to be understood. The repetition of the verb "he consumes" (*prāśayet*) is for the purpose of making known that each individual item is purifying (*medhya*). (19.14)
Now he states the locations for recitation and other rites:
"All mountain peaks, all rivers, holy lakes, sacred bathing places (tīrthas), dwellings of sages, cow-pens, and sacrificial enclosures—these are the [proper] regions. (19.15)

"All mountain peaks" refers to all mountains; the inclusion of the word "all" is for the purpose of including even those that are not meritorious (*apuṇya*), since [the text] specifies "meritorious" (*puṇya*) above. Meritorious [mountains] are Kailāsa and others; non-meritorious ones are those not intended [to be mentioned]. Meritorious rivers are the Gaṅgā and others; non-meritorious ones are small streams. Meritorious lakes are the unfailing ones such as Śrī-Puṣkara. Holy places (*tīrtha*) include Kanyā-tīrtha and others. Abodes of sages (*ṛṣi-nivāsa*) are the hermitages of Vasiṣṭha and others. A cow-pen (*goṣṭha*) is well known. A sanctuary (*pariṣkanda*) is a temple; [as stated in the verse]: "And the sanctuary of the gods, a Brahmin, and a lordly tree."
One should constantly perform circumambulation of Vārāha as well as Vāmana.

Thus, because of the traditional recollection (*smaraṇa*) of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). The particle *iti* serves as an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other sacred groves (*puṇyāraṇya*) and the like; in this way, Naimiṣa forest and others are to be understood. The irregular compound (*visamāsa*) has the purpose already stated. (19.15)
Now he describes the nature of austerity (tapas):
"Celibacy, truthful speech, touching water at the [three] libations, wearing wet clothes, sleeping on the ground, and fasting—these are the austerities. (19.16)

"Celibacy" (*brahmacarya*) and so forth are well known. By the word "pressings" (*savana*), the forenoon, midday, and afternoon are meant, because of the use of the plural number. The particle "iti" is for the purpose of including breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other such practices. Thus says Kavaṣa:

One should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) every day, both evening and morning, for sins committed through the anus, genitals, mind, speech, ears, skin, nose, eyes, or tongue. For eating the food of a Śūdra, having sexual intercourse with his women, or accepting gifts from him—when these are all combined—one should perform seven breath-restraints for seven days; if they are separate, three days each. For consuming forbidden foods, whether chewed, eaten, drunk, or licked; and for selling impure things—with the exception of honey, meat, ghee, oil, lac, salt, curd, alkaline substances, and milk—one should perform twelve breath-restraints for twelve days, twelve for each day. For minor offenses (upapātakas), one should perform twelve breath-restraints for half a month, twelve for each day. For those equal to mortal sins (pātaka-samānas), one should perform twelve breath-restraints for four months, twelve for each day. Furthermore, for acts causing loss of caste (patanīyas), one should perform twelve breath-restraints for six months, twelve for each day. For acts equal to violating the Guru’s bed (gurutalpa-samānas), one should perform twelve breath-restraints for one year, twelve for each day. Moreover, they cite this:
"Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava,
performed day after day, purify even the slayer of a Brahmin within a month.
Thus, the specific timing for other daily recitations and such acts is to be understood accordingly.
And so say the authors of the Purāṇas:
"Breath-control, celibacy, silence, and fasting—
these are the forms of austerity, as is meditation upon the Supreme Lord."
The *homās* (fire-oblations), such as the *kūśmāṇḍagaṇahoma* and others, are well known from other *smṛtis*. As Uśanas says:

"In the case of approaching a woman who should not be approached, stealing gold, misappropriating a deposit, eating forbidden food and the like, consuming what should not be eaten, sexual intercourse on sacred festival days (*parvan*), approaching a woman during her courses, or officiating at a sacrifice for one for whom it should not be performed—one should, having had one's hair, nails, and beard shorn, bathe, and from that time forward offer clarified butter once with each of the four *kūśmāṇḍa* verses for seven days, twelve days, half a month, or a month.
As Vyāghra says:

One should perform the Gaṇahoma for all sins—whether they be minor offenses (upapātaka), major offenses (mahāpātaka), or others—even those committed in the past. By performing it even once, one overcomes everything; how much more so by repeated practice! Furthermore, they cite this: "By performing the Vaiśvānarī, the Vrātapatī, and likewise the Pavitreṣṭi at every season, one purifies ten generations."
Thus it is known, it is known. Because it is already well-established, it is not mentioned here; the same applies to the fast as well. 19.16.
Now he shows the means for practicing generosity:
gold, a cow, clothing, a horse, land, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and food—these are the things to be given. (19.17)
Gold and the other items are well known. The particle *iti* is for the purpose of including gems and so forth. (19.17)
He now states the [appropriate] times:
“The year, six months, four, three, two, or one; twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, and a day and night—these are the times. (19.18)
By the use of the particle *iti*, only the night and the day are understood. || 19.18 ||

Now, since it is impossible to teach an expiation for every single sin because of their infinite number, he says: "In the absence of a specific instruction, these very [penances] may be performed optionally; they are heavy for heavy sins and light for light sins. (19.19)

These very [acts], such as recitation (*japa*) and the rest. The word *eva* (only/very) serves the purpose of restriction. For if it were merely stated, “these [apply] when there is no specific instruction,” then the application of recitation and the rest would only occur in cases where penances have not been taught by their own specific names. Because of the particle *eva*, even when a penance has been specifically taught, the fulfillment [of the requirement] is achieved through repetition. “When there is no instruction” (*anādeśe*) means where another penance has not been taught. This being the case, even when a penance is taught, it occurs together with these [recitations and so forth]. “By way of option” (*vikalpena*) means by various combinations; in some cases only recitation, in others only austerity (*tapas*), and so on, should be performed. In the absence of this [rule], there would be no possibility of combining two or three of the taught recitations and other acts. But when it exists, the establishment of combinations—such as recitation in one case, austerity and giving (*dāna*) in another—is achieved. Where, then, is the application of these? To this he says: “In sin” (*enasī*) means in evil; “heavy” (*gurūṇi*) means great penances; “light” (*laghūni*) means small penances. If it is asked how the heaviness or lightness of an unrighteous act (*adharma*) is to be known, it is said: by intention (*abhisaṃdhi*), lack of intention, repetition, and so forth. As Āpastamba says: “He who kills while negligent incurs the fruit of the offense; it is greater when done intentionally. The same applies to other blameworthy acts, as well as to those with meritorious fruits, according to the repetition of the act” [ĀpDh 1.29.2–5, 18]. However, where there is only a prohibition, the heaviness and so forth should be understood in relation to royal punishment, or by the description of censures, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and the ripening of results in another Smṛti, or by the degree of suffering and the like. (19.19)
The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa constitute the universal penance; this is the universal penance. 19.20.

He will explain the nature of the *kṛcchra* and other penances. The meaning is that the "universal expiation" (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) applies not only when no specific rule has been prescribed; rather, depending on the capacity [of the offender] and other factors, it may be either heavy or light, and either public or secret. The separate mention of the *cāndrāyaṇa* is for the purpose of prescribing the *cāndrāyaṇa* alone in place of the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra*. And thus, its prescription in place of those two is also established. The particle *iti* is used for the purpose of prescribing them even individually. Consequently, the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* together constitute a universal expiation, as does the *cāndrāyaṇa* alone. The singular number is used for the purpose of prescribing all of them collectively. Some explain that the particle *iti* is intended to include the manner [of performance] as well. As Manu said:

"Abstaining from food for twelve days by one who is self-controlled and vigilant—this is the penance called *parāka*, which destroys all sins. (MDh 11.215) In place of the *prājāpatya* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, the *parāka* should be understood [as the substitute]. Why? Because of the observation of an equivalent penalty. As Lokākṣi has said:
One should cause thirty-three paṇas to be paid for a Prājāpatya penance;
likewise, one hundred and twenty-five paṇas should be caused to be paid for a Sāntapana penance.
For the *atikṛcchra*, however, it is likewise four hundred and sixty-seven;
and for the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*, it is five hundred *paṇas*.

"And one should cause [the offender] to pay five hundred paṇas as parāka, along with a fine of thirty-three [paṇas]; so say the exponents of the Veda. Here, *prāyaścitta* means "expiation" (*niṣkrayaṇa*). If it is argued that, this being the case, it should be stated as "expiation for all," it is replied: this is for the purpose of making known that whatever is performed for the sake of expiation receives the designation *prāyaścitta*. A technical term (*saṃjñā*) is established to convey its literal meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*). Thus says Vyāghra:
"Prāya" is said to mean austerity (tapas), and "citta" is called restraint (saṃyama).
The wise know that *prāyaścitta* is austerity joined with restraint.
Thus [ends the verse]. 10.20.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the *Maskarīya-gautama-bhāṣya*.
The twentieth chapter:

Regarding the rules for penance (*prāyaścitta*) in connection with curable offenses (*yāpyakarman*), it has been stated. In that context, if the father is involved in a curable offense, what should the son do? To this, he says:

One should abandon a father who is a regicide, a priest for a Śūdra, one who performs sacrifices for the sake of a Śūdra, a corrupter of the Vedas, a killer of an embryo, or one who associates with outcastes or with the wife of an outcaste. 20.1.

One should abandon [him] according to the procedure to be described. By the statement "the father," the abandonment of the son and others is established by implication (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*), as it follows from the father's own words. One who kills a king—that is, one who harms a king who conducts himself according to justice through malevolent magic (*abhicāra*)—is to be abandoned. Thus, there is no abandonment for one who causes the death of a king who acts unjustly through malevolent magic. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Purāṇa*: "He who harms a king by whom a member of the fourfold assembly has been killed is an evildoer; he must be excluded by everyone and not [treated] according to the sacred formulas."

As for what he will say, “There is never a lack of subsistence for one's mother and father” (GDh 21.15), that should be understood as referring to other cases. Regarding the "sacrificer for a Śūdra" (*śūdrayājaka*), this refers to one who causes a Śūdra to perform the *Niṣādasthapati* sacrifice, because that specific sacrifice is prescribed for him. If that is so, then in the case of killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*), it should be understood as applying to everyone, just like the injunctions. A "sacrificer for the sake of a Śūdra" (*śūdrārthayājaka*) is one who performs a sacrifice after having obtained wealth from a Śūdra. Thus says Manu: "Those who, having obtained wealth from a Śūdra... (MDh 11.42). A "corrupter of the Vedas" (*vedaviplāvaka*) is a teacher who teaches those who should not be taught. A "killer of an embryo" (*bhrūṇahā*) is a killer of a Brahmin; the mention of that term is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*). As Manu has said: [he lists various types of fallen persons].

"The sapinda relatives and kinsmen shall perform the water-libation for one who has fallen from his caste outside the village on an inauspicious day in the evening, in the presence of agnates, officiating priests, and gurus" (MDh 11.182).
"And he who lives together with outcastes (*antāvasāyin*). Outcastes (*antāvasāyin*) are Cāṇḍālas and others; as Aṅgiras says:
"The Caṇḍāla, the Śvapaca, the Kṣattṛ, the Sūta, the Vaidehaka, as well as the Māgadha and the Āyogava—these seven are the Antāvasāyins.
He dwells together with them in one place; by the use of the word "and" (ca), this includes the Cakrika and others, as Kaṇva has stated:
"The wheelwright, the Pulkasa, the Jambha, the one who lives by donkeys, and the lamp-maker—these, born of Śūdras, are proclaimed to be untouchable.

The connection [of the verse] is "he shall live with an Antāvasāyinī," meaning he practices sexual intercourse with her. Now, there arises a doubt: when these causes such as being a regicide and so forth exist, does the state of being fallen (patitatva) occur, or not?

What follows from this? If he is indeed an outcast (*patita*), then having included them in the very same list as "the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of spirituous liquor" (GDh 21.1), one need only say, "one should abandon a fallen father"; thus, the term "slayer of an embryo" (*bhrūṇahan*) would not need to be mentioned here. If, however, he is not an outcast, then abandonment is not appropriate. In another Smṛti as well, the rule for abandonment is stated specifically in connection with being an outcast; and so the verse of Manu is shown: "The water-libation for the fallen should be performed," and so forth (MDh 11.182).

To this it is replied: first of all, the state of being an outcast (*patitatva*) does indeed occur in these cases. Nevertheless, they are not listed among the major sinners (*pātakin*) for the sake of lightening the penance. The mention of the "slayer of an embryo" (*bhrūṇahan*) is intended to indicate that the penance for these cases is equal to that [of the slayer], by establishing an equivalence with him. Where there is an equation, a degree of inferiority is also understood, as in the expression "the minister is equal to the king. Among these, the penance for some is heard in the texts, such as "for killing a Kṣatriya, a six-year penance" (GDh 22.13), and likewise "for sexual intercourse with an Antāvasāyinī woman, a year-long *Kṛcchra* penance" (GDh 23.33). For those for whom no penance is found, a universal penance (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) must be prescribed. Thus, in every case involving such equivalence, a universal penance alone should be observed. If it is argued that, in that case, because the penances are equal, the enumeration of false witness (*kauṭasākṣya*) and the like here would be redundant, we reply: this separate treatment is begun so that one understands that among these very outcasts, a father must be abandoned, but not in other cases. In this context, the status of being an outcast should be understood to apply even to the killing of a king and so forth when done unintentionally. Why? Because among those taught together, the state of being an outcast is seen to apply even in the case of one who acts unintentionally. As Manu says: [Manu 11.89] "Even if he has killed a Brahmin unintentionally, he becomes pure by performing the penance for twelve years... etc.

"By approaching women of the Caṇḍāla or lowest castes, by eating their food, or by accepting gifts from them, a Brahmin falls through ignorance; through knowledge, however, he becomes equal to them. [MDh 11.175] Thus ends section 20.1.
Now, the procedure for his renunciation is stated:
having assembled his teachers of knowledge and those related by birth, they should perform all the funeral rites, beginning with the water libations. 20.2.

Of that person who is to be abandoned—not one’s own self—the *vidyā-gurus* (teachers of sacred knowledge), namely the *ācārya*, the *guru*, and the *upādhyāya* (the plural being used to include all three); the *yonisaṃbandhas* (blood relations), such as maternal uncles, maternal grandfathers, and so forth (here too the plural serves the same purpose as mentioned before); and by the use of "and" (*ca*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), those for whom one performs sacrifices (*yājya*), and others—having assembled them together and made it public by saying, "This man has committed such an act; I shall abandon him"—his sons and other kinsmen shall perform all the funeral rites, such as the offering of water and the *śrāddha*, while he is still alive. 20.2.
And they would overturn his bowl. || 20.3 ||

And those very same relatives who are to overturn the vessels for this [deceased] person who is to be abandoned—“overturning” here means not pouring water [on them]. The word “and” (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction with the offering of water. It should be understood that so as not to let the *śrāddha* rite follow immediately after [the overturning], one should perform the *śrāddha* after first performing the offering of water and then overturning the vessels. (20.3)
To explain how they should be overturned, he says:

A slave or a laborer, having brought a vessel of impurity from a heap of refuse and filled it from the jar of a female slave, should, facing south, overturn it with his foot while pronouncing the name [of the deceased], saying, "I make so-and-so waterless. (20.4)
A slave (*dāsa*) includes those who carry the banner (*dhvajābhṛt*) and others. As Manu says:

"The one who carries the banner, the slave for food (*bhaktadāsa*), the one born in the house, the one bought, the one given, the one inherited from a father, and the slave by punishment—these seven are the origins of slavery" (MDh 8.415).

A laborer is a hired servant; there is an option between these two depending on the circumstances. Having taken some impurity from a refuse heap—that is, from a latrine—into an impure vessel, the female slave or attendant fills it from her own jar. By this very [statement], the impurity of the slave's jar elsewhere is to be understood. Facing south, he should overturn it with his foot—that is, he should cast it away in an anti-clockwise direction—having uttered the mantra: "I render so-and-so, Devadatta, waterless. Since the mention of the name is already established by the word *amum* ("this one"), the phrase *nāmagrāham* ("mentioning the name") is for the sake of clarity, and does not mean that he should mutter it in a whisper. 20.4.
All of them, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder and with their topknots loosened, should touch it.

All the *sapiṇḍa* relatives—not only the son—should touch that slave or laborer; the meaning is that they should come into physical contact with him. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*), that is, wearing the sacrificial cord in the reverse manner; with their topknots loosened, having let down their hair-tufts. By this very indicative mark, one should understand that for other auspicious rites such as sipping water (*ācamana*), a person with a loosened topknot is unfit. (20.5)
The teachers of sacred knowledge and those related by blood shall look on. || 20.6 ||
But the meaning is that they should not touch [it]; and by the word "and" (ca), the officiating priests and others are also included. 20.6.
Having touched water, they enter the village. || 20.7 ||

Having performed this rite in this manner, they then bathe and go home. All the funeral offerings (*śrāddha*) and so forth are completed on that very same day. And because of the instruction regarding entry into the village, it follows that this [rite] must be performed outside. 20.7.
After that, having conversed with him, he should remain for one night reciting the Sāvitrī, provided it was done unintentionally.

After that renunciation, having conversed—that is, having engaged in speech—with the one by whom [the food] was renounced; this expiation is to be understood as applying when done through ignorance. From the use of the singular "he shall stand," it follows that even someone other than a relative may be involved; however, by virtue of the context, it refers specifically to relatives. "For one night" means for a full day and night, he shall not eat. While muttering the *Sāvitrī* mantra. 20.8.
If it was done intentionally, [the penance lasts] for three nights. 20.9.

But he who intentionally converses with such a person shall observe for three nights the rule prescribed for one of this kind; and this applies as long as that person has not performed penance. This refers to conversation concerning other business, not to inquiries on the road and the like; in those cases, the rule stated by Parāśara should be observed: "Upon sneezing, upon spitting, when touched by the teeth, likewise upon speaking an untruth, and upon conversing with outcasts, one should touch the right ear. (PārSm 12.19)
Thus [ends the section]. 20.9.

But he who would be purified by penance—once he is purified—they should fill a vessel made of gold with water from a most sacred pool or from flowing rivers, and then cause him to touch those waters. 20.10.

The word *tu* (but) has the sense of restriction. One who is purified by penance (*prāyaścitta*) is not [purified] by royal punishment. By stating this, it is implied that in other cases, even royal punishment may be a cause of purification. Consequently, it should be understood that in those other cases, purification occurs even for one who has been punished by the king. When he is purified, the meaning is that he has performed his penance in the presence of the public. Having filled a vessel made of gold—a golden vessel—from an exceptionally meritorious lake that is mostly unfathomable, or from flowing rivers with constant currents; because of the plural number, [it refers to] many [streams]. There is an option according to what is possible. Then, they should bathe him—who has performed the penance—with the mantras to be mentioned hereafter, using that vessel. By implication, [this applies to] those who previously abandoned him. (20.10)

Then they should give him that vessel; having accepted it, he should recite these sacrificial formulas: "Peaceful is heaven, peaceful is earth, peaceful and auspicious is the intermediate space; I take here that which is luminous," as well as the *pāvamānī* verses and the *taratsamandī* verses. (20.11)

Then, immediately after, they should give that full vessel to him who has bathed. Having accepted it, he should mutter this mantra. With which mantras? It will say, "Peaceful. With these very *yajus* verses already mentioned beginning with "Peaceful is the sky," with the eight *pavamānī* verses beginning with "Pavamāna, the winner of light," and with the four *taratsamandī* verses. || 20.11 ||
And one should offer clarified butter with the Kūśmāṇḍa verses.

Because of the use of the singular number in the word "juhuyāt" (one should offer), only one person should offer, not all the kinsmen and others. Among them, this should be understood as applying to the one who is qualified. One should offer clarified butter with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* verses beginning with "yad devā devaheḍanam," and by the force of the word "ca" (and), also with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*. 20.12.
One should give gold to a Brāhmaṇa, and a cow to the teacher.

At the conclusion of the *homa*, one should give gold to a Brāhmaṇa endowed with exceptional qualities; for although the right to receive gifts belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone, the specific mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" here [is used] for that purpose. This applies to the one who has performed the penance (*prāyaścitta*), not to the performer of the *homa*. Or, he may give a cow to the *ācārya*. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include gold as well. He should give either a cow or gold to the *ācārya*, who is the performer of the *homa*. Both of these are primary options; it should be understood that both the cow and the gold are alternatives, since they are presented as equal options. (20.13)
But for one whose penance ends only with death, he becomes pure upon dying.

But for one to whom a penance ending in life—that is, ending in death—is prescribed, if he dies while striving [to perform it], he is purified by that very death. This is stated even though it is already known: it is for the purpose of prohibiting *sapiṇḍa* relationship even when there is a recovery [from illness]. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the sake of specification. If, having resolved upon a penance ending in life, he should die in the midst of the penance, then he is purified; specifically, because he died after having performed the penance. Thus says Vyāsa: "If one who is always striving in dharma should die in the middle [of his efforts]..."
For one certainly attains all of that; regarding this, I have no doubt.
Thus [ends the verse]. 20.14.
They should perform all the funeral rites for him, beginning with the offering of water.

All the rites for the consecration of the deceased, beginning with the water-śrāddha and so forth, as many as there may be—all these are to be performed for him who has been purified by the penance ending at death, for him who has been rescued [from suicide], and for him who dies in the interval. By implication, they are not to be performed for anyone other than these. From the use of the word "all," the sapindas should also observe the period of impurity (āśauca). (20.15)
This very same water for pacification [is prescribed] for all minor offenses (upapātaka).

This very thing which was mentioned as "water for pacification" (*śāntyudaka*)—that water which was prescribed for bathing after being consecrated with the mantras beginning with "The sky is peaceful" (*śāntā dyauḥ*) and so forth—is to be used in all cases; that is to say, in all instances, including even those minor offenses (*upapātaka*) equal to the great sins (*mahāpātaka*) which will be described hereafter, this [rite] must also be performed at the commencement of their penance and so on. (20.16)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Maskarīya-Gautama-bhāṣya.
The twenty-first chapter:
The rule for the abandonment of those who have fallen [from their status] has been stated. To address the question of who these people are, he says:

Those who have killed a Brahmin, those who have drunk liquor, those who have violated the bed of their guru, those related by birth to their mother or father, thieves, atheists, those who habitually perform censured acts, those who abandon those who are not outcasts, and those who abandon outcasts—these are outcasts (patita). || 21.1 ||
A "brahmahā" is one who has committed the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. A "surāpa" is one who has drunk *surā* of whichever of the three types is prohibited for him. As Manu says:
"Gauḍī, Mādhvī, and Paiṣṭī—*surā* should be known to be of these three kinds.
Just as even one of them must not be drunk, so all must be avoided by the best of the twice-born. (MDh 11.94)

*Gurutalpagaḥ*: one who approaches the bed (*talpa*) of a guru; by the word *talpa*, which denotes a bed, the wife is indicated—that man who approaches her for sexual intercourse. *Mātṛsaṃbandhagaḥ*: one who marries a girl on the mother’s side within five generations. *Pitṛsaṃbandhagaḥ*: likewise on the father’s side within seven generations. *Yonisaṃbandhagaḥ*: the husband of a sister. *Stenaḥ*: a thief of gold. *Nāstikaḥ*: one who denies the existence of the next world and so forth. *Ninditakarmābhyāsī*: one who habitually and intentionally practices what is censured or forbidden. Because of the mention of "action" (*karman*), this refers only to physical acts, not to transgressions of speech or mind. *Patitātyāgī*: one who does not perform the renunciation of those who have fallen (*patita*), such as the slayers of Brahmins and others. *Apatitatyāgī*: one who, out of hatred or other motives, abandons those who have not fallen. These, beginning with the slayer of a Brahmin, are the fallen ones. (21.1)
And those who cause others to commit mortal sins. || 21.2 ||
Those who employ others in sinful acts; and by the word "ca" (and), the one who consents is also included. 21.2.
And practicing with them for one year. || 21.3 ||
By associating with them for a year through the sharing of vehicles, seats, and beds, one likewise falls; as Kaṇva says: "By associating with an outcaste for a year, one falls;
those who discourse on Brahman say this applies constantly through the use of vehicles, seats, and beds."
By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is also implied that one falls immediately through officiating at sacrifices and so forth. Thus says Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya:
"By officiating for [a fallen person], by forming a matrimonial alliance, by studying [their Veda], or by eating together with them—one falls immediately by associating with a fallen person."
Since there is no distinction made between intentional and unintentional acts, the penance should be understood as lighter in the case of what is unintentional. As Vasiṣṭha says:

"Regarding association with outcasts—whether through Vedic study or through marriage—if any property was received from them, one must renounce it; one must not dwell with them. It is known that by going toward the northern direction, fasting, and studying the Saṃhitā, one becomes purified. [VaDh 20.45–46]

In this context, the second occurrence of the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "by means of [reciting] the *Brāhmaṇa* or the *Saṃhitā*" is intended to include [the recitation of] the *Yajus*, *Sāman*, and *Āraṇyaka* as well. Since the study of a *Saṃhitā* is only possible for one who has already studied the Veda, the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* should be understood to last for as long as it takes an unlearned person to complete the study of the *Saṃhitā* of their own *Śākhā*. This is seen in another *Smṛti*: "One should study the *Saṃhitā* and recite the *Sāvitrī* for that same length of time. Likewise, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the *Svādhyāyabrāhmaṇa* of the Taittirīyas: "Without eating, one should study the Veda, the *Svādhyāya*, three times; or else, one should recite the *Gāyatrī* [Sāvitrī] for three nights," and so forth. Because such indicative marks from the *Brāhmaṇas* are observed, even though the *Vasiṣṭhasmṛti* does not specify it, the study of the *Saṃhitā* should be understood to be performed three times. One *Prājāpatya* penance should be understood to correspond to each single recitation. As Kaṇva says:
"One should perform one recitation of the Veda, or else a *prājāpatya* penance;
or the wise man should give ten thousand cows as a gift. Regarding intentional acts, however, that which was stated by Manu should be observed.
"Whichever of these a man associates with after that person has fallen, he must perform the very same vow as that person for the sake of purification from that association. (MDh 11.181).
This should be understood to apply to cases occurring within one year, as stated by Vyāghra.
"But if one enters into association with an outcaste without knowing [their status],
having performed the renunciation of what was received, he should perform the *sāntapana* penance. However, in the case of intentional action, that which was stated by Kaṇva should be observed.
"But if association with one who has fallen [from his caste] has been intentionally entered into,
then after performing the renunciation of what was received, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Regarding eating together, Lokākṣi says:
Having eaten food with those who have fallen [from their caste], one is purified by the Parāka penance;
however, having learned of it, one should perform that specific vow—so the knowers of Dharma understand.
Thus [ends the section]. 21.3.
What constitutes their state of being fallen? He says: "Falling is the loss of the duties of the twice-born. (21.4)

"Loss from the duties of the twice-born" means loss of eligibility for those rites prescribed by the Vedas, such as the Agnihotra, and those prescribed by the Smṛtis, such as the Aṣṭakā. Although one should have said "loss from duties," the inclusion of the term "twice-born" indicates that their status is like that of a Śūdra; for even a Śūdra is considered fallen and exists in the same condition as one of the inverse castes. 21.4.
Not only is there a fall [from one's position], but furthermore: "And there is no establishment in the other world" (21.5).

Furthermore, there is non-establishment [of the result] in the next world because there is no connection with the fruit of whatever merit he has performed even prior to serving those who cause a fall from caste; by the word "and" (ca), it is implied that there is infamy in this world as well. This determination of the essential nature of the category of sin is for the purpose of establishing his lack of entitlement to the duties of the twice-born and for the purpose of encouraging the performance of penance. (21.5)
Some call that hell. 21.6

They consider hell to be a state where one lacks the capacity for action and where there is no enjoyment of the auspicious in the next world; for hell is characterized by the arising of extreme suffering for one who is abandoned by friends and kinsmen, since it is a cause of misery. As the author of the *Niruktabhāṣya* says: "Hell (*naraka*) is a state of humiliation, a going downwards; no delight (*ramaṇa*) is found in it. Gautama, however, considers it to be a portion of hell (*narakabhāga*). 21.6.
The first three [of these] are not to be designated as such, according to Manu. (21.7)

Among these sins, the first three—killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), drinking liquor (*surāpāna*), and violating the bed of one’s guru (*gurutalpagamana*)—are "unspeakable" (*anirdeśya*), because there is no prescribed expiation for them. Manu says:
"For the intentional killing of a Brahmin, no atonement is ordained" (MDh 11.89).
The same applies to the drinking of liquor.
"Intentional [killing], which cannot be specified [as a particular penance], is remembered as resulting in the end of life" (MDh 11.145);

such passages are to be understood here. Or, it is stated that they "cannot be specified" because there is no possibility of restoration (pratyāpatti). As Āpastamba says: "In this world, there is no restoration for him, but his taint is destroyed" (ĀpDh 1.24.25). The mention of Manu is intended to show that Manu is the one who remembers (smarta) the entire meaning of the Smṛti. Regarding this, the authors of the Purāṇas say: "The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, and those mantras belonging to the Atharvans..."
And that which was proclaimed by the Seven Sages as Smṛti, Manu declared that.
Thus [ends the section]. 21.7.
Some say that one who violates the bed of his guru does not fall [into hell] if it concerns women. 21.8.

Regarding one who engages with women, some maintain that he does not fall from his caste by approaching other women, provided he avoids the bed of his guru (*agurutalpa*). Gautama, however, holds that he falls in all such cases. This distinction should be understood as being based on the difference between intentional and unintentional acts. Although the term *agurutalpa* alone would have sufficed, the explicit mention of "women" (*strī*) is for the purpose of including women of all four castes, so that the status of being fallen may apply even in the case of women born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*). Thus Manu says: "Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or lowest castes, having eaten [their food], and having accepted [gifts from them]..."
"A Brahmin falls through ignorance; through knowledge, however, he attains equality. [MDh 11.175]

If it is argued that one falls [from caste] only after committing these three acts and not by mere sexual intercourse, that is incorrect; for expiation is prescribed for the mere act of intercourse itself. As Vasiṣṭha says: “Now, furthermore, in the case of killing an embryo, one should subsist on water for twelve nights, fast for twelve nights, or go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; by this very [rule], intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman is explained. This should be understood to apply to a single instance of unintentional intercourse. In the case of repetition therein, the expiation for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*) should be observed. As Manu says:

"One should perform the vow for violating the Guru's bed after having emitted semen into one's own female relatives, into the wives of a friend or a son, into virgins, and into women of the lowest castes" (MDh 11.170).

Therefore, because the penance for an outcast is extended to both repeated practice and a single act, one certainly falls even by the mere act of sexual intercourse. The plural number in the word "women" (*strīṣu*) is for the sake of honorific emphasis. One falls even upon women who are not themselves outcasts; as Kavaṣa has said:

"A twice-born man who approaches a fallen woman unintentionally falls [from his caste]; in the case of repeated practice, he must perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa-vrata*). If it is done intentionally, he should perform that same vow. Here, because the rule for the *gurutalpa* vow is extended to cases of intentional repetition, one should look to the rule stated by Vasiṣṭha regarding a single instance of approaching her: "Having approached the female friend of a Guru, the female friend of a Guru, an outcaste woman (*apapātrā*), or a fallen woman, one should perform a quarter of the year-long *kṛcchra* penance" (VaDh 20.16). It should be understood that even in the case of a single intentional approach, one must perform that same vow. 21.8.
A woman falls [from her caste] by causing an abortion or by serving a man of a lower varṇa. 21.9.

Whatever has been taught regarding the killing of a Brahmin and so forth, this should be understood to apply to women as well as men. That which is additional for her is now stated: "By having sexual intercourse with a *bhrūṇahan*, she falls. The term *bhrūṇahan* is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for one who is fallen (*patita*). A man of lower caste is a Śūdra. Some say that because of the use of the prefix (*upa-*), it refers to the reverse order (*pratiloma*). As Vasiṣṭha says: "But four [wives] are to be abandoned: one who goes to a pupil, one who goes to a teacher, one who especially kills her husband, and one who has gone to a *juṅgita*. [VaDh 21.10]

Because of this instruction on renunciation, for if one does not renounce an outcaste, one would incur the state of being an outcaste oneself. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include [these acts] together with the killing of a Brahmin and so forth. Some say it refers to causing an abortion; as Vasiṣṭha says:
"Those who know the Dharma recognize three sins of a woman in this world:
the murder of her husband, the killing of an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*), and the destruction of her own fetus. [VaDh 28.7]

In that regard, regarding association with those who have fallen (patita) or those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), the penance should be understood to be the same as for men, according to the statement of Manu:

"One should know this very rule to apply even to women who have fallen. Although a woman who serves a Śūdra—that is, one who maintains association with a Śūdra—falls, nevertheless, the penance should be observed until the birth of a child. As Vasiṣṭha has said:
"The wives of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who have had intercourse with a Śūdra are purified by penance if they have not conceived; others are not. Thus it is said.
Likewise, the penance for that very case is also stated in that same work:
"According to the respective caste, they shall perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa. [VaDh 21.13]

“*Cāndrāyaṇottaram*, *cāndrāyaṇe uttare*, and *cāndrāyaṇāny uttarāṇi*—these should be applied respectively to a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, and a Vaiśyā. Since it has been stated, ‘Those who have had intercourse with a Śūdra are purified if they have not conceived’ (VaDh 21.12), it should be understood that those who have had intercourse with a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya are also purified even if they have conceived. In this regard, for one who has had intercourse with a Kṣatriya, the penance is *cāndrāyaṇottara*; for one who has had intercourse with a Vaiśya, the penances are *cāndrāyaṇe uttare*. Similarly, for a Kṣatriyā who has had intercourse with a Vaiśya, the penance is to be determined as *cāndrāyaṇottara*. As for men, in the case of approaching women in the reverse order (*pratiloma*), one should look to what was stated by Vasiṣṭha: ‘A Śūdra [approaching] a Brāhmaṇī... (VaDh 21.1) and so forth. However, in the case of approaching women in the natural order (*anuloma*), he will state later: ‘Two [years] for another’s wife’ (GDh 22.31) and so forth. Here, among those who have fallen (*patitāḥ*), only the four [wives] are to be abandoned. Why? Because by the word *tu* (‘but’) in the restrictive phrase ‘But the four’ (VaDh 21.10), Vasiṣṭha establishes that abandonment applies only to these four. For the others, however, one should look to what was stated by Manu.”

"One should apply this very same rule even to women who have fallen [from virtue]; they should be given clothing and food and should dwell near the house. [MDh 11.188] He will also state this later: "And a woman who is unfaithful," [GDh 22.37], and so forth. 21.9.
Giving false testimony, slandering the king, and making a false accusation against one's guru are equal to mortal sins (pātaka).

Giving false testimony means speaking untruthfully when one is called upon as a witness, despite the exception stated in the rule: "There is no fault in speaking untruth in certain cases" (GDh 13.24). Backbiting directed at the king (*rājagāmi paiśunam*) is the reporting of another's faults to the royal court. By using the word *gāmī* ("that which goes to") instead of *rājan* ("the king"), it is understood that this includes even those reports that reach the king indirectly through others. Speaking directly of some false accusation against one's teacher (*guru*), meaning the preceptor (*ācārya*), constitutes defamation. These acts should be regarded as equal to mortal sins (*pātaka*), that is, equal to the great mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*).
"Insisting on falsehood toward a guru is equal to the killing of a Brahmin" (MDh 11.55);

since this is seen in another Smṛti, these acts are equal to a mortal sin only when committed intentionally (*buddhipūrva*), and not through negligence, delusion, and so forth—this is the purpose of the compound formation. And thus, there is no fault when [the act is done] through negligence and the like. (21.10)

Among those unfit for the company at a meal, from the time of Durvāsas onwards, the killing of a cow, the abandonment of the Veda, the composition of mantras against it, the violation of a vow of chastity, and the loss of the Sāvitrī—these constitute secondary sins (upapātaka).

Those previously mentioned as persons whose food should not be eaten—excluding those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*) and those who give false testimony—are distinct from atheists (*nāstika*), for the latter are enumerated separately among those whose food is forbidden. Why is this? Because there are three types of atheists. Thus say the authors of the Purāṇas:
"Atheists are declared to be of three kinds by those who know the Dharma and perceive the truth:
the one corrupted in action, the one corrupted in mind, and likewise the one corrupted in speech."
"But one who is corrupt in speech incurs a minor offense (upapātaka), while one who is corrupt in mind incurs a major offense (pātaka);
however, through repetition, one who is corrupt in action is said to incur a mortal sin (mahāpātaka). Thus it is said.

In this context, one who is corrupt in speech (*vāg-duṣṭa*) is listed among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*); one who is corrupt in mind (*manas-duṣṭa*) is listed among the major sins (*pātaka*); and one who is corrupt in action (*kriyā-duṣṭa*) is described by the very rule: “one who habitually performs censurable acts” [GDh 21.1]. Regarding him who is listed among the minor offenses, the penance prescribed by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: “An atheist (*nāstika*), having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, shall desist from atheism” [VaDh 21.29]. As for him who is listed among the major sins, that which was stated by Āpastamba should be observed: “This same [penance applies] to others who have fallen [from their status] as well” [ĀpDh 1.28.14]. However, regarding a person guilty of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), before its repetition, the general penance (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) should be observed. But in the case of repetition, the penance for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) as stated by Vasiṣṭha—beginning with “Now, furthermore, regarding the killing of an embryo” [VaDh 23.38] and so forth—should be observed. Enough of this digression; we shall now explain the subject at hand.

A "cow-slayer" (*gohantṛ*) is a cow-killer. A "neglector of the Veda" (*brahmojjha*) is one who, having studied the Veda, forgets it through negligence; however, one who intentionally abandons it is an atheist (*nāstika*), and his fault is even more severe. Thus, in this case, for one who forgets it through negligence, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "The neglector of the Veda, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, should again receive the Veda from a teacher" (VaDh 20.12). For the other [the intentional abandoner], that which was stated by Manu should be observed.
"Denying the Vedas, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend, and eating forbidden food or drink—these six are equal to the drinking of liquor. [MDh 11.56]

One who performs sacrifices and other rites for a cow-killer or for one who has killed a Brahmin is a *tanmantrakṛt*. An *avakīrṇin* is a student (*brahmacārī*) whose celibacy has been violated. He is mentioned again here because he is included among those excluded from the company at meals (*apaṅktya*); the point is that even if such a student has performed an expiation, he must still be avoided as an offender of a secondary sin (*upapātakin*) until he has performed the specific penance for that secondary sin. Some explain this repetition as being intended to distinguish between heavy and light penances based on whether the student is a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*) or not; that is, the penance is light for the temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*) and heavy for the lifelong one. However, that view is incorrect, because the punishment for a lifelong celibate is double, as seen in the law-code of Kavaṣa: "The penalty for an *avakīrṇin* is double. A *vrātya* is one who has lost his right to the *Sāvitrī* initiation. On these grounds, there is a secondary sin (*upapātaka*). The assignment of these names is for the purpose of prescribing the appropriate expiations. (21.11)
An officiating priest and a teacher who teach out of ignorance, as well as those who serve those whose conduct leads to a fall from caste, are to be abandoned.

Due to ignorance, one may abandon an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*); due to failure in teaching, one may abandon a teacher (*ācārya*). There is no fault in abandoning these two for such reasons. Since it is impossible for one who is ignorant to perform the duties of an officiating priest, there is no sin for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) who abandons him. Likewise, if a teacher does not teach properly due to laziness or other such causes, there is no fault for the student who abandons him. Furthermore, regarding "service to those whose conduct leads to loss of caste" (*patanīyasevā*), this refers to the performance of acts that cause loss of caste, such as traveling or sitting together with an outcaste. Why is this so? Because, although it would have been sufficient to say "the two outcastes are to be abandoned," the specific mention of "service to those whose conduct leads to loss of caste" implies that this explanation is intended to justify abandonment even before the completion of the full year [of penance], as the case of abandoning an outcaste who has not yet become an outcaste is already established by the previous rule. If it is argued that in this case too the fault of abandoning one who is not an outcaste would still apply, it is replied: No, what is intended here is not the abandonment of sitting together and so forth. What then? It is the engagement of another officiating priest and the approach of another teacher.
