The fault attaches to one who abandons sitting together and so forth, but not to one who engages another officiating priest or teacher. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), those whose conduct leads to minor offenses (*upapātakin*) are also included. (21.12)
Elsewhere, one falls away from what has been abandoned. || 21.13 ||

Except for the previously mentioned causes of ignorance or teaching [the dharma to the unqualified], one falls from [the path] by abandoning or relinquishing them; therefore, one must not abandon or relinquish those two. || 21.13 ||
And some say that he who accepts it [is the one who becomes impure]. 21.14.

And for one who abandons his officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) or teacher (*ācārya*), the meaning is that he who is the recipient [of their gifts], or the priest or teacher who performs the officiating or teaching for him, falls; by the word "and" (*ca*), some hold that even his fellow student falls. Gautama maintains that one falls through knowledge [of the transgression], but not through ignorance. (21.14)
There is never any lack of livelihood for one's mother and father. 21.15

"In no state whatsoever" means even in a state of having fallen [from virtue]. "Non-service" means lack of attendance; that must not be done. The meaning is that they are to be served even in that state. Service consists of salutation and so forth. (21.15)
But they shall not divide the inheritance. 21.16.

The meaning is that they shall not divide—that is, they shall not take—his inheritance, which refers to his wealth. "A mother’s inheritance" refers to her *strīdhana* (woman's property). The use of the word "but" (*tu*) implies that in the absence of such inheritance, food and clothing must be provided even from one's own property. Since there is an injunction for providing food and clothing even in the case of those who are destitute or in a state of fallenness (*patita*), it follows by implication that this applies even to those who have not fallen. In this regard, it should be understood that there is no abandonment even of a mother who has fallen. Why? Because of the observation of other *smṛtis*. As Vasiṣṭha says: "But a mother does not fall toward her son," and so forth. That was stated with the intention that even in a state of fallenness, a mother must not be abandoned by her son. (21.16)
The fault in falsely accusing a Brāhmaṇa is as great as that [in killing him]. 21.17.

If one accuses a Brāhmaṇa of a fault, saying, "This sin has been committed by you," then whatever demerit (adharma) accrues to that person who makes the accusation, the same amount accrues to the accuser as well. For example, if one accuses another of being an outcast (patita), he himself becomes an outcast. Just as he is to be shunned by the world, so too must the accuser be shunned; yet, even through the penance performed by the accused, the accuser is also restored to his status. || 21.17 ||
Twice [he is] sinless. || 21.18 ||

But he who makes a false accusation incurs double the guilt of the accuser, both because of speaking untruth and because of the accusation itself. Here, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate any member of the twice-born classes. Accordingly, another Smṛti text has been recited without distinction: "By saying 'he is an outcast' regarding an outcast, or again 'he is a thief' regarding a thief, one incurs equal guilt by such speech; if it is false, one incurs double the guilt. [VaDh 20.30]

In this context as well, the mention of "one who has fallen" (*patita*) is an elliptical expression that includes even those guilty of minor offenses (*upapātaka*). This is indicated by the evidence from another *Smṛti*: "It is known that one who has falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a sin causing loss of caste (*patanīya*) or a minor sin (*upapatanīya*) becomes pure after subsisting on water for a month while reciting the *Śuddhavatī* verses; by this, the case of one who is falsely accused is explained" (VaDh 23.39, 41). Thus, it should be understood here as well that the fault lies only in the false accusation of a major or minor sin, and not in every instance. Furthermore, this fault belongs only to the previous speaker, not to everyone who subsequently deals with the person. As Āpastamba says: "Having recognized the fault, the former person should not be one who publicly declares another to be fallen" (ĀpDh 1.21.20). || 21.18 ||
And likewise when there is violence toward the weak, if one is capable of preventing it. || 21.19 ||

Where there is injury or destruction of a weak person, if one is capable of liberating or rescuing them, then by not liberating them, this person incurs as much fault as the killer. By the word "and" (ca), it is implied that if one is capable of providing food, medicine, clothing, and so forth to one afflicted by hunger, disease, and the like, then by killing such a person, this person incurs exactly as much fault as [the killer]. Now, one might object: "Does not the fault also accrue to one who deprives another of their means of sustenance?"

It is said: because the cutting off of food and the cutting off of life are unequal. When food is cut off, the cessation of hunger can still be achieved even by means of roots and the like; however, when life is cut off, there is no remedy whatsoever. || 21.19 ||
For threatening an angry Brāhmaṇa, one shall not go to heaven for a hundred years.

When a Brahmin who is innocent is threatened with a raised weapon by one who is enraged—and not out of jest or the like—he incurs a sin resulting in a hundred-year fall into hell, which excludes him from heaven. This rule applies specifically to the case of a Brahmin of the same caste. However, if the offense is committed by those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes against a Brahmin, the penalty is doubled, tripled, or even quadrupled, respectively, for the killing of a Brahmin by those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes. Regarding the question of whether there is no fault when the victim is guilty—such as in the case of being an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor)—[the answer is that] there is still a fault. The phrase "falling into hell" implies a duration of a hundred years. This refers to a case involving a person of the same caste. When the act is performed by Kṣatriyas and others, the punishment increases accordingly. Thus, if a Brahmin is killed by a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, the penance is doubled, tripled, or even fourfold.

This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in the *Smṛti* of Prajāpati. For the years [of penance] as well, a doubling or tripling should be postulated. By this very logic, when a Brāhmaṇa commits [the offense], it should be understood that for those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, the penalty is three-quarters, half, and one-quarter [respectively]. Just as it is for a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, so it should be postulated for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya; likewise, just as for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, so it should be postulated for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra. In this manner, it should be understood for every higher caste when a killing is committed by a lower and lower caste. (21.20)
In the case of a blow, the fine is one thousand. || 21.21 ||
If one strikes with a weapon or with the hand, it results in the loss of heaven for a thousand years, because of the specific qualification [of the rule]. 21.21.
Upon seeing blood, as much of it as he might scoop up from the dust after it has flowed out—so much he should collect. 21.22.

When blood is caused to flow from a Brāhmaṇa, that blood shall flow out from him; for as many particles of dust as it collects or forms into clods, for that many thousands of years there is a fall into hell—meaning for an immeasurable period of time. This statement regarding the specific gravity of the offense is for the purpose of making known the specific nature of the expiation. As Kaṇva says:
"One should perform the Kṛcchra penance after threatening [to strike], and the Atikṛcchra upon striking;
one should perform both the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra upon causing blood to flow from a Brāhmaṇa."
A specific punishment should be understood from the specific nature of the expiation. 21.22.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the *Maskarīya-gautama-bhāṣya*.
The twenty-second chapter begins:
The causes for penance have been stated; now, therefore, the penances must be declared for each specific sin. Regarding that, he first states the penance for the very first [offense].
Expiation: For a slayer of a Brahmin who has been thrice shorn, there is immersion in fire. 22.1.

The term *prāyaścitta* is used for the purpose of indicating the subject matter; that is, this is indeed an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and not for the sake of some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). "In fire" means attachment or clinging, which is to say, falling. The word "three times" is a qualification of the falling. Furthermore, in the act of falling, one should understand that the head is turned downward. As Manu says:
"Or he should throw himself three times into a kindled fire with his head hanging down. (MDh 11.73)

For whom is this expiation intended? For the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, that is, for one who has killed a Brāhmaṇa. "Emaciated" means one whose body has been withered by the renunciation of food; as the Kāṭhaka Śruti states: "Emaciated by fasting, he should ascend the fire. 22.1.
Or he might become a target for those who bear arms in battle. || 22.2 ||

The "target" (lakṣya) is that which is to be pierced by arrows; it may be located either in a battle (*janya*) or in the midst of an army. The phrase "of those bearing weapons" refers primarily to a battle consisting mostly of archery, and not one consisting mostly of other types of weapons. (22.2)
Or, carrying a skull-topped staff and a skull-bowl in his hands, he may enter a village for alms for twelve years as a celibate student, proclaiming his deed.

The *khaṭvāṅga* is well known. The *kapāla* is the head of a corpse. As Manu says: "Having made the head of a corpse his banner" (MDh 11.72). Its wearing is for the sake of a sign. He should practice in this manner for twelve years. He is a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), avoiding sexual intercourse. He should enter the village solely for the purpose of begging; that alone shall be his food. Even the act of wandering for alms is to be done with an earthen vessel. As Śaṅkha says: "An earthen vessel. At other times, he should remain in the forest alone. Because of the instruction regarding celibacy and begging, it should also be understood as a religious observance (*vrata*). As Kaṇva says:

"With the sacred grass in hand, carrying a staff, with teeth stained by mud, covered in dust, dwelling at a sacred ford, clad in *kuśa* grass, and wearing matted hair—one becomes a slayer of a Brahmin.
Thus [it is said]. "Proclaiming his deed" means always saying, "I am a slayer of a Brahmin. (22.3)
He should step aside from the path so as not to be seen by the noble one. 22.4.

One should not deviate from the path upon seeing a noble twice-born man; by this same principle, it should be understood that one should avoid him from behind, from the side, and from afar. In that regard, when he is within the distance of a cow-tail whisk (*govālavyajana*), a bath with one's clothes on (*sacelasnāna*) should be performed. As Vyāghra has said:
"One should avoid a Caṇḍāla and an outcaste from afar;
within the distance of a cow-tail whisk, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on."

It should be understood that one must avoid even a Śūdra by avoiding physical contact with him. As Lokākṣi said: "In the case of contact with those who have committed a mortal sin (mahāpātakin), bathing is prescribed for all social classes; if one eats without having bathed after such contact, one should perform the Taptakṛcchra penance."
One should drink water for three nights infused with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* and milk;
this is likewise prescribed for contact with menstrual blood, a *caṇḍāla*, or a corpse.
Thus [ends the section]. 22.4.
By subsisting on standing and sitting postures and bathing in water at the three times of the day, he shall become pure.

Except at times when there is a conflict, such as during the periods for ritual sipping (ācamana) and so forth, he should remain standing for the entire day; likewise, he should pass the night in a seated posture. By performing the three daily ablutions (triṣavaṇasnāna), he is released from the sin caused by the killing of a Brahmin. The word "becomes pure" (śudhyet) serves as a concluding summary.
Or, for a Brahmin, [it is permissible] when life is at stake or on account of that [life]. 22.6.

Or, he may be purified if, on account of that [act], a Brāhmaṇa recovers his life—meaning, having rescued one who was being killed by thieves, tigers, or the like. Since the life-force of one person has been severed and restored to another, by this same principle, it should be understood that purification results from saving all [beings] from slaughter, through the restoration of the life-force of those belonging to that same species. 22.6.
Or, when there is a deficiency of material, he should perform at least three [offerings] in succession.

By virtue of the context, this refers to the wealth of a Brāhmaṇa, such as gold and so forth, which is sufficient for his livelihood—wealth (*draviṇa*) being of the nature of life itself, according to the scriptural insight: "For these [external objects] are the external vital breaths" (*prāṇā hy ete bahiścarāḥ*). One would be purified by rescuing that wealth when it is being carried off or has already been carried off by bandits; or, in the event of its loss, by restoring it. "Three times attempted" means that human effort (*puruṣakāra*) has been exerted three times. As Manu says: "Or having attempted at least three times, or having recovered all his property..."
"Or by recovering his life for the sake of that [brahmin], he is liberated. (MDh 11.80).

From this very indicative mark, it should be understood that purification occurs even through the gift of wealth sufficient for a poor man's livelihood, provided it is given without causing him distress.
Or at the final purificatory bath of the horse sacrifice.

The mention of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is for the purpose of excluding other intervening rites. By the force of the statement itself, they should cause him to touch water; the word "he becomes pure" (*śudhyet*) is understood to carry over. Because of the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) and because these are mentioned as a summary, these penances are indeed independent. Some say this refers to one who has already commenced the twelve-year penance. And so Śaṅkha, having stated that "one attains purity after twelve years," says: "Or, in the interim, by releasing a Brāhmaṇa or by rescuing twelve cows. In that case, in the event of repetition, it should be understood as a specific qualification for the completion of the commenced twelve-year penance; however, in the absence of repetition, they are indeed independent penances. (22.8)
Even in another sacrifice, if it ends with the Agniṣṭut [stotra], [the same applies]. 22.9.

That sacrifice which is other than this is an "other-sacrifice" (anyayajña); its purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) is that sacrifice which ends with the Agniṣṭut, meaning it has the Agniṣṭut in the middle. That [sacrifice] is either the Sarvamedha or a Sattra; having bathed there as well, one would become pure. 22.9.
A slayer of a Brahmin does not become so merely by the taking of life; what then?
If he is incited to the killing of a Brahmin, he becomes one even without having killed him. 22.10.

"Created" means determined or resolved; that is the sense. One who has formed the resolution, "A Brāhmaṇa must be killed," with respect to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, becomes a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa even without having actually killed him. The intention is that this very same penance applies to him as well, because such a resolve is seen [as constituting the offense]. By this same principle, in the case of the killing of any living being whatsoever, that specific penance [prescribed for that species] should be understood to apply, since the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" here is intended merely as an illustration. (22.10)
And likewise in the case of an Ātreyī woman. 22.11.

An *ātreyī* is a Brāhmaṇī woman who has reached puberty; as Vasiṣṭha says: “They call her an *ātreyī* when she is menstruating and has bathed after her period, for it is in her that future offspring may arise” [VaDh 20.35–36]. When she is killed, one becomes a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahā*). The particle *ca* (and) is intended to include Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well when they have arrived at a Soma sacrifice, as Manu says: “Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very same vow;
likewise for killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who knows [the Veda], and also a woman who is an *ātreyī*” [MDh 11.87].

The word "thus" (evam) is for the purpose of indicating that this applies to all penances (*prāyaścitta*). Others, however, say that an *ātreyī* is one belonging to the Atri lineage; from the specific mention of the *ātreyī*, it should be understood that one does not become a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*) if she is not of the Atri lineage. (22.11)
And [the impurity lasts] for a Brāhmaṇa until the pregnancy is known. 22.12.

If a Brāhmaṇa is killed by means of medicine or other methods while still in the womb and his gender—as male, female, or neuter—is not yet known, he becomes a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahā*), provided that [the fetus] was conceived in a Brāhmaṇa woman. However, if the gender is known, it should be understood that the status applies according to the specific gender. The particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of extending the rules regarding penance. Thus, this penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa, which is of many kinds, is to be applied in consideration of the intention or lack of intention of both the killer and the one being killed.

On this point, some say: first, it is appropriate to consider whether one should kill or not kill, because the gravity or lightness of the act has been stated in relation to performing it intentionally or unintentionally; and because by the rule "one who habitually performs censurable acts" (GDh 21.1), the gravity of the fault is heard to apply even in the case of repetition. However, that which concerns the calculation of gravity or lightness with respect to the victim being killed is improper, as there is no indicative evidence for it. Furthermore, in the injunction "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," a prohibition against killing is prescribed with reference to a Brāhmaṇa. And a qualification of the subject under reference is not intended to be significant—whether he be virtuous or devoid of qualities—just as in the case of "He cleanses the cup with the *daśāpavitra*," where singularity is not intended to be significant. Therefore, the prohibition is based solely on the genus of Brāhmaṇahood, and any accepted quality is not a factor.
This is incorrect, because there exists a rule that proclaims the gravity of the offense with respect to the quality of the person being killed. As Manu says:
"One may indeed kill, without hesitation, an assailant who approaches, even if he be a teacher, a child, an elderly person, or a Brahmin of great learning. [MDh 8.350]

Since the killing of even those who are highly learned (*bahuśruta*) and so forth is already established by the very permission granted for the killing of an *atatāyin* (one who seeks to kill), their specific mention is intended to make known that there is a particularly grave fault in killing those who are highly learned and the like. Just as greater gravity is understood in relation to praiseworthy actions—by which the expiation for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā-prāyaścitta*) is prescribed even for the killing of a *rājanya* or a *vaiśya* engaged in a *savana* sacrifice, according to the rule: "And if a *rājanya* or a *vaiśya* who know [the Veda]... (MDh 11.87)—so too: "The best of the twice-born should perform this very same expiation for one year... (MDh 11.126).

Since it has been stated separately regarding the killing of a Vaiśya established in his duty, "Having killed a Vaiśya established in his duty, one should give one hundred cows" (MDh 11.129), whereas for another [Vaiśya], the penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) applies by the rule, "The killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya" (MDh 11.66).

As for the claim that "the qualification of that which is being designated is not intended to be significant," that too is incorrect. By the very injunction regarding penance (*prāyaścitta*), the prohibition of killing a Brāhmaṇa is inferred; for there is no explicit statement prohibiting the killing of a Brāhmaṇa in which one could say that the qualification is not intended to be significant. Even if such a statement did exist, the qualification could nevertheless be intended to be significant precisely by the force of the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*). Furthermore, just as the qualification would be unintended, so too would the number be unintended; consequently, the same penance would apply equally whether one were killed or two were killed, which is not desired. Therefore, even in the case of the rule "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," it is indeed possible to know that the fault is more severe when killing one who possesses [excellent] qualities; thus, everything stated is entirely logical.
For killing a Kṣatriya, the standard vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) shall be observed for six years.

When the killing of a Kṣatriya has been committed, the *ṣaḍvārṣika* celibacy—that which lasts for six years—is also *prākṛta*, meaning natural or ordinary, in the sense that it is devoid of the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and other such ascetic accoutrements. Consequently, the meaning is that the very penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa must be performed for six years. This refers to a case of intentional (*buddhipūrva*) killing of one who follows the prescribed conduct (*vṛttavat*). Regarding the killing of one who does not follow such conduct (*avṛttavat*), [the text states]: "The killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya, as well as atheism (*nāstikya*), are minor sins (*upapātaka*). [MDh 11.66]

Thus should the expiation for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) be understood; the same applies hereafter as well. In that regard, for a killing committed intentionally, one should look to what will be stated: “The same applies to those who extinguish the sacred fires, those who are excluded from the community, and for minor offenses” (GDh 22.34). However, for an unintentional act, that which was stated by Manu should be observed:

“Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses should perform this very vow for the sake of purification; likewise, one who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*) may perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance” (MDh 11.117).

Because of the governing context of "of a Brāhmaṇa," this refers specifically to a Brāhmaṇa. However, for one of Kṣatriya birth, it should be understood as twelve years; for a Vaiśya, eighteen years; and for a Śūdra, twenty-four years. In this manner, it should be inferred in subsequent cases as well. (22.13)
And he should give cows numbering one thousand and one bulls.
Regarding those who have maintained their conduct: as before, this should be understood as referring to cases where the act was unintentional. As Manu says:
"A fourth part of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa is prescribed for the killing of a Kṣatriya;
an eighth part for a Vaiśya who maintains his conduct; but for a Śūdra, it should be known as a sixteenth part. (MDh 11.126)
Having said this, he spoke again:
"But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born should give one thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh for the sake of his own purification."
Or, restrained and with matted hair, he shall perform the vow for a Brahmin-slayer for three years,
dwelling at a great distance from a village and making his abode at the foot of a tree.

Thus it should be understood. In this same way, in all cases, one should understand that the ordinary vow of celibacy (*prākṛtabrahmacarya*) lasting for six years, accompanied by the giving of gifts, is also required. As Uśanas says: "For the killing of a Kṣatriya, there is the vow of a Brahmin-slayer (*brahmahavrata*) for six years, and at its conclusion, the gift of one thousand cows with a bull. This applies to the intentional killing of one endowed with the qualities of an anointed king (*abhiṣeka*). But for unintentional killing, he himself says: "Or he should observe it for eight years. (22.14)
In the case of a Vaiśya, it is for three years. || 22.15 ||
The common [rule] regarding celibacy is to be understood as applying to the Kṣatriya case. 22.15.
And he should give one hundred and one cows, including a bull.

As before, this refers to an intentional act. And so it has been stated by Manu and cited here: "One should perform this very [penance] for one year," and so forth. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), the entire preceding [rule] is included. That too applies to the intentional killing of one who possesses extreme virtues. However, in the case of unintentional killing, this very rule—"They should perform this very vow" (MDh 11.117)—is to be understood. For it would be improper if the same penance were applied to a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya; thus, it would not apply to those who have not practiced [the required virtues]. If it is argued that, in that case, equality would result for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya who have not practiced [virtues] under the rule, "The same applies to those who extinguish the sacred fires, those who are excluded from the community, and those guilty of minor offenses" (GDh 22.34), it is replied here: the deficiency must be compensated for through austerity (*tapas*). And so says Manu.
"In whatever action he has performed that causes unease of mind, he should perform penance for it until it becomes a source of satisfaction. (Manu Dharma Śāstra 11.233)

In this manner, [the rule] is to be applied everywhere. This being established, in the case of an intentional killing of a Vaiśya who possesses virtuous qualities, that which is stated in another Smṛti should be observed. As Uśanas says: "Having killed a Vaiśya, one should perform the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa for seven months. In all cases, when there is an excess of qualities or when the act is habitual, an increase in the recitation of prayers (*japa*) and so forth must also be prescribed. Since the obligation to "give" is already established by the general context, the explicit mention of "should give" again is for the purpose of including other types of property in the absence of cows. And thus Vyāghra says:
In the absence of cows, one should give a niṣka, or half a niṣka, or even a quarter;
or rather, whatever he might accept, that one should give to a śrotriya.
In the case of a Śūdra, [the penance lasts] for one year. || 22.17 ||
This [penance applies] to the intentional killing of a twice-born slave. || 22.17 ||
Regarding that very same [act] when unintentional, he says:
"He should give cows with a bull as the eleventh. (22.18)
Since cows are already the subject under discussion, the mention of "cows" (*go*) once again is for the purpose of specifying that the gift of cows must be of the white color. And so says Manu:
"Having killed a Śūdra, one should perform this very same vow for six months;
furthermore, one should give to a Brahmin eleven bulls and white cows. (MDh 11.130)

By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), that which was previously prescribed for one who has already committed an offense should also be understood to apply here in the case of intentional killing; however, in the case of unintentional killing, the rule beginning with "one who extinguishes the fire" (*agnyutsādi*, GDh 22.34) applies. Regarding the intentional killing of a wifeless woman, they should perform this very same vow (*vrata*); but in the case of unintentional killing, a *taptakṛcchra* penance is to be observed. As Uśanas says: "Having killed a Śūdra, one should perform a *taptakṛcchra*. In this regard, the rules stated in other Smṛtis concerning the *anuloma* and *pratiloma* castes should be consulted. As Vyāghra says: "For all those born in the direct order (*anuloma*), as well as for the killing of their mothers..."
The wise man should point out that very same thing regarding half of women as well.
"In the case of killing an Ātreyī woman, one should declare that which is prescribed for [killing] a mother;
likewise for an unknown fetus, according to the statement of Vyāghra.
This same principle is to be understood as applying to women born of inverse unions (pratiloma). Regarding men in such cases, however, Aṅgiras says:
"But for those of the lowest castes, in the case of approaching [for intercourse], eating [their food], or killing them, purification occurs through the Parāka penance; so said the venerable Aṅgiras.
This refers to intentional acts involving those born of Śūdras; however, in the case of unintentional acts, a Cāndrāyaṇa penance should be understood as required. As Lokākṣi has stated:

"In the case of the killing of those born of Śūdras who are *pratiloma*, how should it be? If done intentionally, it shall be a *parāka*; if unintentional, likewise an *aindava* (cāndrāyaṇa). Regarding those originating from Śūdras, since they possess equal qualities according to the rule, "But from a Śūdra, one of fallen conduct is born in a woman of unequal status" [GDh 4.27], equality of penance is indeed appropriate. He states the same for others as well in that very place.
"For others, a fourth part [of the penance] is prescribed by the wise for the killing of those of one's own caste; the same rule that is declared for a Śūdra is stated [to apply here].

The meaning therein is that whatever penance has been prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra—whether in the case of *anuloma* (mixed-caste) or *pratiloma* (inverse-caste) unions—that very same penance should be understood to apply even to the killing of one's own caste. Regarding the Śūdra, however, it is stated in that very same context: [text follows].
The vow may consist of a whole, a half, three-quarters, or even a quarter,
regarding the abandonment of [unlawful] sexual intercourse and eating within the [prescribed] caste and measure.
Thus [ends the verse]. 22.18.
And likewise with the daughter of an Anātreyī. || 22.19 ||

Since the extension (*atideśa*) [of the penance] is already established by the word "and" (*ca*) alone, the inclusion of the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) is for the purpose of extending the penance prescribed for killing a *rājanya*; it is so that what was mentioned immediately before [the penance for killing a *brahmin*] should not apply. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "In the case of injuring a non-*Ātreyī* *rājanya*, [one should perform the penance for] injuring a *rājanya*; in the case of injuring a *vaiśya*, [one should perform the penance for] injuring a *vaiśya*" [VaDh 20.37–38], and so forth. If it is argued that it should have been stated right there, we reply: its mention at the end is for the purpose of indicating that even after the penance has been performed, one should not live together [with such persons]. And so says Manu: "Those who kill a *brahmin* and those who are ungrateful, even if purified according to the law... [MDh 11.189].
"And one should not dwell with those who kill those who have sought refuge, nor with those who kill women.
And [the penance for killing] a cow is like that for a Vaiśya. || 22.20 ||

Having killed a cow, one should perform the penance as prescribed for a Vaiśya. In this context, the killing refers to one who possesses the means (to perform the rite), and intentional action (*buddhipūrvatva*) is understood from the context. Therefore, in the case of intentionally killing a cow endowed with the quality of yielding much milk, the three-year period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) mentioned for a Vaiśya should be observed. Furthermore, for one possessing wealth, there is the gift of one thousand cows along with a bull. Why? Because, in the case of killing a king, the observance of celibacy for three years and the gift of a thousand cows are seen to serve as substitutes (*pratinidhi*). Likewise, the statement of Manu has been cited: “One thousand cows and a bull,” and so forth.
If it is asked how it is known that there is a heavier penalty for [killing] a cow yielding much milk, it is said:
"For the killing of small animals, however, the fine is two hundred [paṇas]" (MDh 8.297).
In this context, by the term "small animals" (*kṣudrapaśu*), cows of little utility are meant, not goats or sheep.
But for donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five māṣakas. [MDh 8.298]

Thus, because distinct punishments are seen for these cases, it is understood from the observation of lighter punishments in those specific instances that a more serious fault attaches to acts involving many purposes. In the case of killing her unintentionally, it should be understood that one must give one hundred cows with a bull as the hundred-first; or, if that is impossible, one-year-long celibacy (*brahmacarya*). That which was prescribed for a Vaiśya regarding the combination of giving gifts and performing austerities should also be understood to apply here. Its scope is the intentional killing of this very cow when she has been taken into the care of a Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, there is greater gravity in the case of a cow taken into the care of a Brāhmaṇa.

This is because of the indicative mark (liṅga) in the verse: "In the case of cows belonging to Brāhmaṇas, and in the breaking of a tethering post" (NSm 19.40). Here, it should be understood that if one is unable to give a cow as a gift, one should give a *niṣka*, half a *niṣka*, or even a quarter (*pāda*). Thus, the statement of Vyāghra has been cited:
"In the absence of cows, one may give a *niṣka*, or half a *niṣka*, or even a quarter."

And so forth. In that regard, the gift of a thousand cows or a thousand pieces of gold belongs to the king; for one of equal status, half a *niṣka*—this is one position. However, for an ordinary person, it is a quarter. Why? Because of the statement of Jātukarṇi regarding this matter of making a gift: "A thousand cows or a thousand [pieces] of gold are prescribed for a king;
half of that is said for one of middle rank, while a quarter should belong to an ordinary person."
And likewise, Manu also says in a certain context:
"Where an ordinary person would be fined one kārṣāpaṇa, there the king should be fined one thousand; such is the settled rule. [MDh 8.336]

By this [rule], it is understood that the king’s penance is greater than that of an ordinary person (*prākṛtajana*). When all [the prescribed options] are impossible, one should observe the maintenance of ordinary celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for four years. This applies everywhere. In the case of killing her unintentionally, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed. As Vasiṣṭha said: “If a cow should be killed, he should remain for six months performing the *kṛcchra* or *taptakṛcchra* penance, wrapped in her wet hide,” and so forth. The understanding that this refers to an unintentional case is due to the governing term “unintentionally” (*aprekṣāpūrva*) in the rule: “If a Brāhmaṇa woman [is killed] unintentionally” (VaDh 21.16). In that context, because of the dual number in “they two should give a bull and a cow” (VaDh 21.22), two killers are understood. Therein, in the case of killing a bull, a bull should be given; in the case of killing a cow, a cow, etc., should be given. Or else, that which was stated by Vyāghra [should be followed].

"If a man should kill a cow through ignorance, he should then give seven hundred *paṇas* to a poor *śrotriya* for the sake of his own purification. Regarding the word "cow" (*gām*), by the force of the particle "and" (*ca*), that which was stated for a *śūdra* should also be understood here. In that case, for the intentional killing of a cow of little utility, one should understand the gift of eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh, accompanied by a year-long penance. For the unintentional killing of that same cow, the rule stated by Jātukarṇya should be understood. As he said:
"If one should kill a cow unintentionally with the permission of Brāhmaṇas, then, having performed three Prājāpatya penances, he should present a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
This [rule] should be understood as referring to the intentional killing of that very same cow which has been accepted by Brāhmaṇas, as stated by Manu: As he says:
One who has killed a cow, being afflicted by a minor offense (upapātaka), shall drink barley gruel for a month;
wearing a garment made of cow-hair, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with a wet hide.
For two months, with his senses restrained, he should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent salt, at every fourth mealtime, and perform his bath using cow urine.
He should follow those cows during the day, and while standing, he should inhale the dust rising from them;
having served and paid homage to them, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night.
While they stand, he should stand; while they walk, he should follow;
likewise, while they sit, he should sit, self-restrained and free from longing.
Whether she is afflicted by illness or consecrated for sacrifice, or threatened by fears such as thieves and tigers,
or fallen or mired in the mud, one should rescue her with all one's life-force.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first doing so for the cow to the best of one's ability.
Whether it be one's own or another's, whether in a field, a house, or a threshing floor,
one should not speak of a cow that is eating, nor of a calf that is drinking.
Whoever, following this rule, attends upon cows,
removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months.
"One who has properly observed the vow should give ten cows and one bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas" (MDh 11.108–109).

However, in the case of unintentional [killing], the standard period of *brahmacarya* for one year should be observed. If the death of a calf occurs unintentionally, then the gift of ten cows and one bull should be observed. Furthermore, regarding the calf, there is also a reduction in the severity [of the penance].
For calves, the fine shall be half; for milch cows, the fine is equal [to the value of the crop].
For bulls and breeding oxen, the same has been declared by the wise.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Prajāpati:
"But if a man intentionally kills a calf,
he should then perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for the sake of his own purification, or he should give five hundred paṇas."

Thus, that which is stated in the *Kavaṣasmṛti* is to be observed. He must be made to pay its value to the owner, based on the indicative mark [of the text]: "And he shall be made to pay that wealth to him" (MDh 8.176). In this case of killing, the punishment for Śūdras is half; this is according to the statement of Lokākṣi:
"But for all the twice-born, the full punishment is ordained;
those who know the Dharma know that for Śūdras it shall be half-punishment."
Thus [ends the section]. 22.20.
And [the same penance applies] for the killing of frogs, mongooses, crows, crabs, rats, mice, and dogs. || 22.21 ||

In this context, the mention of the "crow" (kāka) by Manu is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those animals listed in the verse on "flesh-eaters" (*kravyāda*), those listed in the verse on "village-pigs" (*viḍvarāha*), and those listed in the verses on the "cat" (*biḍāla*) and the "wild cat" (*mārjāra*).
[Manu Smṛti 11.154: "Having consumed the urine or excrement of a village-pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
For eating the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, and cocks,
as well as that of hell-beings, crows, and cranes, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.
Having consumed the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mouse, a dog, or a mongoose, one must likewise perform this penance.
"One should drink *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā* if [food] has fallen into it containing hair or insects.
Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay, a frog, a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra. (MDh 11.159; MDh 11.131) Thus [it is said].

It should be understood that for the killing of these [animals] collectively, one should perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra. The particle *ca* (and) serves to include the expiation for the killing of a Śūdra. This remains the same whether the act was intentional or unintentional. However, in the case of killing them individually and unintentionally, specific rules are prescribed in another Smṛti among certain animals such as the village-pig and others: "Having killed a boar, one should give a jar of ghee; a partridge, a droṇa of sesame; a parrot, a two-year-old calf; and a crane, a three-year-old calf."

"Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, or even a peacock, as well as a monkey, a hawk, and a vulture, one should give a cow to a Brāhmaṇa. (MDh 11.134–35). This [penance] applies to the killing of large animals; however, for the killing of each individual [smaller animal], only a *kārṣāpaṇa* should be given. Thus says Vyāghra:
For the killing of swans, peacocks, aquatic birds,
monkeys, hawks, or vultures, a twice-born man shall pay one paṇa as a fine.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for killing an elephant, five dark-colored bulls; and for killing a goat, a sheep, an ox, or a donkey, a one-year-old calf.
"Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
for non-carnivorous animals, a heifer; but having killed a camel, a *kṛṣṇala* [of gold].
In cases of intentional acts, a punishment proportionate to the offense should be determined, as stated in the section on assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*).
In the case of killing a human being, one quickly incurs guilt equal to that of a thief;
for large living beings such as cows, jackals, camels, horses, and so forth, the guilt is half.
For the killing of small animals, the fine is two hundred;
for the slaying of living beings [of larger size], the punishment has been determined accordingly.
For auspicious deer and birds, the fine shall be fifty [māṣakas];
for donkeys, goats, and sheep, however, the fine shall be five māṣakas.
"But the fine for killing a dog or a pig shall be one *māṣika*. [MDh 8.296–98].
For those who have committed these acts intentionally, it is said: "One should either drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one *yojana* on foot."
Or he should touch the water in a flowing river, or mutter a hymn addressed to the waters.

This is how it should be understood. In that regard, drinking milk or traveling on a journey should be seen as intentional; however, if unintentional, bathing, the recitation of a *sūkta*, and the chanting of prayers (*japa*) are prescribed. This is similar to the injunction regarding sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Even in the case of killing calves, a gradation of severity should be observed. For humans, the distinctions have been stated according to caste (*varṇa*) and other factors. Regarding boars as well, he will state: "For a boar, a jar of ghee" (GDh 22.26). Here also this should be understood: as for the statement that the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance applies to the consumption of urine or feces, there too all these [animals] are included, and the *Cāndrāyaṇa* should be seen as applying when the act is intentional. In that context, the *Taptakṛcchra* has been prescribed for eating [the meat]. Furthermore, where the drinking of *brahmasuvarcalā* is prescribed for eating the leavings of food, here too all these [animals] are included. And in this matter, since the *Cāndrāyaṇa* has been mentioned separately for the consumption of human urine and feces, it should be understood to apply to those [animals] excluding them. Even there, by the mention of "urine," semen is also included, because its instruction is identical to the instruction for the penance for consuming human urine and feces.
"Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one should fast for three days;
but having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance.

[MDh 4.222] He will also state later: "And in the case of consuming urine, feces, or semen" [MDh 11.156]. In the case of intentional consumption, the Cāndrāyaṇa is to be understood as the penance; however, in the case of unintentional consumption, the Sāntapana is prescribed, as Lokākṣi has said:
"Having consumed the urine or excrement of boars, donkeys, camels, or likewise of monkeys, a twice-born man shall perform the Sāntapana penance. Thus it is said.

In this case as well, all of these are to be included. Furthermore, the prescription for the *taptakṛcchra* penance applies only when the act is intentional; in that instance, a re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) must also be observed. Thus, he will state later, with reference to the *taptakṛcchra* accompanied by re-consecration: "And [the penance for eating] the flesh of carnivorous beasts, camels, and donkeys" (GDh 23.5). However, in the case of unintentional consumption, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha is to be observed: "Upon eating the flesh of dogs, cocks, village pigs, herons, vultures, *bhāsa* birds, crows, pigeons, humans, and owls, there shall be fasting for seven nights, purification until the excrement is gone, and re-consecration" (VaDh 23.30). In this way, the inclusion of those mentioned here within those [other rules] is to be understood. Moreover, even where the drinking of *brahmasuvarcalā* is prescribed, that too excludes what has been left over by a human. As Uśanas says:

If one intentionally eats the remnants of a Brāhmaṇa’s meal, one should perform a hundred *prāṇāyāmas*; for the remnants of a Kṣatriya, a thousand; for the remnants of a Vaiśya, ten thousand. If intentional, [the penance is] a *Prājāpatya*, an *Atikṛcchra*, and a *Kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. For eating the remnants of a Śūdra, one should drink barley-gruel (*yavāgū*) for seven nights; if intentional, it is a *Parāka*. Likewise, when a twice-born person eats the remnants of another twice-born person, or when Śūdras drink water that has been the remnants of a Brāhmaṇa’s meal, they should perform sixteen *prāṇāyāmas*; for Kṣatriyas, thirty; for Vaiśyas, forty; and for Śūdras, drinking *kuśa* water for three days. If intentional, then for three, four, five, and seven days respectively, they should drink the *pañcagavya* in those same respective orders. For intentionally eating the remnants of an outcaste (*antyaja*), the penance is a *Mahāsāntapana*; if unintentional, it is a *Cāndrāyaṇa*. Thus it is said.
Manu has also stated something:
"Having drunk water that is the leavings of a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days;
likewise, having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or even the leavings of a woman or a Śūdra. [MDh 11.148]

"Having eaten forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights" (MDh 11.152). Thus, even the drinking of *suvarcalā* [leaves], if unintentional, lasts for only one night as there is no distinction made; however, if intentional, it is the *sāntapana* penance. As Jātūkarṇi has said:
"Of the jackal, the crow, the cat, the dog, the iguana, and also of cows..."
"Having eaten the leavings of food from a *māta* (mother), a twice-born man shall perform the *sāntapana-kṛcchra* penance.
In this regard, that which was stated by Kavaṣa should also be observed:
"The [penance] for a *kṣatriya* shall be half that of a *vipra*, and for *vaiśyas* it shall be half of that."
"The wise know that for Śūdras, the penance is exactly half of that.

This is to be understood as applying everywhere. The mention of "violence" (*hiṃsā*), although its status as a governing factor is already established, is stated here to show that [the rule] applies only in cases of violence and not even when one has merely touched [an impure thing]. (22.21)
Having killed a thousand of those possessing bones. || 22.22 ||
For the killing of a thousand other beings possessing bones, the penance for killing a Śūdra applies. || 22.22 ||
And [the same applies] to boneless animals and to the carrying of a load by an ox. Pāṇini 2.23.22.

When creatures without bones, such as worms and the like, are killed in a quantity equal to the load of an ox, this penance for killing a Śūdra applies. It should be understood that here the penance for killing a Śūdra applies when the act is intentional, and not otherwise; thus it should be understood in all cases of extended application (atideśa). || 22.23 ||
Or alternatively, he may give something small in each case for those [deceased ancestors] who possess bones.

Now, if neither the completion of a thousand nor the completion of a hundred loads of grain is required, then one should give something small—perhaps merely the value of a *kākaṇī*—to each individual immediately thereafter. From the word "or" (*vā*), it follows that one may perform recitation (*japa*) and so forth; from the word "also" (*api*), it follows that this applies even to boneless creatures. Thus Manu says:
"But for the killing of those with bones, one should give some small gift to a Brahmin;
for in the case of injuring those without bones, one is purified by *prāṇāyāma*. [MDh 11.141]

In that regard, for the intentional killing of beings possessing bones, one should give at least a *kākaṇikā*; however, if it was unintentional, six *prāṇāyāmas* are required. For beings without bones, three *prāṇāyāmas* are prescribed for intentional killing, but only a single *prāṇāyāma* should be understood as necessary for unintentional killing. Thus says Kaṇva:
"For the intentional killing of beings with bones, a man should give a *kākaṇikā*;
but if it was done unintentionally, he should perform six *prāṇāyāmas* for them."
Those who know the Dharma understand that if one intends to kill boneless creatures, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas); if done unintentionally, one should then perform one.
Thus [ends the section]. 22.24.
In a thicket, [the fine is] a load of straw and a māṣa of lead. || 22.25 ||

The term *ṣaṇḍa* refers to one of the third gender (*tṛtīyā-prakṛti*), but not to a eunuch (*klība*); for the latter, since he may attain the status of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), he is prohibited from participating in a *śrāddha*, and furthermore, because he is connected with the performance of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*). When such a person is killed, there is no specific distinction of caste [for the offense]: "A load of straw for a cow, and a māṣa of lead for a Brāhmaṇa. Because it is mentioned without a compound, the terms are separate; and by the word "and" (*ca*), equality is also implied. In that regard, when done unintentionally, the penalty is separate; when done intentionally, it is combined. (22.25)
In the case of a boar, there is a jar of ghee. || 22.26 ||
When a pig has been killed, a jar filled with clarified butter should be given to a Brāhmaṇa; however, the specific scope for this has already been stated. 22.26.
An iron staff against a snake. || 22.27 ||
By the word *loha*, black iron (*kārṣṇāyasa*) is meant. As Manu says:

"Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give a black-iron adze" (MDh 11.133). This applies when the act is intentional; however, if it is unintentional, only a *māṣa* weight [of iron] should be given, according to the statement of Auśanas: "Having killed a snake, one should give a *māṣa* weight. || 22.27 ||
The suffix *jīla* occurs after the word *brahmabandhū* when it denotes movement. 22.28.
"Calanā" means unchaste. Regarding Kṣatriyas and the other castes, that which was stated by Manu should be observed, as he said:
"Having killed women who are not restrained, one belonging to any of the four castes shall give separately a Jīla, a bow, a goat, and a sheep for purification. [MDh 11.138]
"Jīla" means a leather bag. "Movement" also implies being frequented by many men in secret. As Prajāpati has said:
"A woman who approaches many men in private should be known as an unchaste woman and, manifestly, a courtesan."

Thus, due to association with three men, it should be understood that the previously mentioned penance for killing applies prior to that point, while this [present penance] applies thereafter. Even prior to association with three men, half of the previously mentioned [penance] should be assigned for each successive man. As Kaṇva has said:
"For a woman established in virtuous conduct, the full penance is prescribed; however, for one who has been active with each man, that penance shall be reduced by half."
This refers to an intentional act; however, in the case of an unintentional act, that which was stated by Vyāghra should be observed:
"For approaching unchaste women, the penalty for courtesans shall be half of a *pāpa*;
likewise for killing a woman of any of the four castes who is not faithful."
And for the purification of these, one should respectively give a conch shell, mother-of-pearl, and a goat.
Thus [ends the verse]. 22.28.
In the case of a courtesan, there is nothing [to be done]. || 22.29 ||

If a Vaiśya woman who lives by her own work is killed, nothing at all need be done; this refers to an unintentional act. But in the case of an intentional act, half of what has been prescribed for an unchaste woman should be understood to apply:
"Half the sin of an unchaste woman shall be incurred in approaching courtesans.
This is the eternal law for all four castes.

This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of Prajāpati’s dharma. Alternatively—the term *vaiśika* means "that which is done with courtesans"; thus, when sexual intercourse is practiced openly with a woman who is a nominal Brahmin (*brahmabandhū*), the meaning is that no penance for approaching another's wife need be performed. And by this, it is understood that there is some penance for intercourse practiced in secret with such a woman. That [penance] should be determined analogously to [the penance for] violence (*hiṃsā*). Here, since the penance for approaching another's wife is prohibited, it is understood that there is indeed something else [required]. Thus says Śaṅkha:
"A twice-born man shall perform a Prājāpatya penance for approaching a female animal or a prostitute.
This [rule] applies to a single instance of such an act; however, in the case of repeated practice, that which was stated by Saṃvarta should be observed. As he said:
"In approaching a female animal or a prostitute, one should perform a Prājāpatya penance."
"But for stealing a cow, a man should perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Regarding the excessive repetition of that act, the penance for minor offenses (upapātaka) mentioned by Manu should be observed. As he says:
"Stealing grain, base metals, or cattle; associating with women who drink liquor... [MDh 11.66]
Regarding one born of her, that which was stated by Kaṇva should be observed. As he said:
"But he who is born of a courtesan, subsisting on alms and with his senses restrained, attains purity after reciting the Sāvitrī a hundred thousand times."

Whatever has been stated regarding the practice of courtesan-like behavior with a *brahmabandhu* (a nominal Brahmin) should be understood to apply equally when such behavior is practiced with a *kṣatrabandhu* (a nominal Kṣatriya) and others as well. Thus said Kavaṣa:

"When a courtesan-like act has been committed with kinsmen of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, a learned man should perform a *prājāpatya* penance; however, in the case of repetition, he must perform a *kṛcchra*."
For the Kṣatriyas and others, half and half [of the penance] should be prescribed.

On this point, some explain as follows: "In the case of a Brāhmaṇī woman, falling from caste (*pātitya*) is declared upon contact with a Śūdra: 'A woman falls [from her status] by causing an abortion or by serving a man of inferior caste' (GDh 21.9). Therefore, they argue that for those who enter into a relationship with others while she—being a Brāhmaṇī—is connected to a Śūdra caste, the very penance for approaching a fallen woman (*patitāgamana*) must be performed.
That is incorrect.

Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or lowest castes, having eaten their food, or having accepted gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his caste] through ignorance; through knowledge, he becomes their equal. [MDh 11.175]

This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Consequently, it is understood from this that even when there is contact with a Śūdra or others through intentional (*matyā*) action, Brāhmaṇīs and the like attain equality with the Śūdra and others, whereas through unintentional (*amatyā*) action, they remain subordinate to them. If it is argued that, even so, the same penance prescribed for having sexual intercourse with an unfaithful Śūdra woman would also apply to a Brāhmaṇī who has had a connection with a Śūdra—here it is replied: it does not apply because of the statement regarding their equality. Therefore, the penance is exactly as previously stated.

Others explain it thus: for one who has sexual intercourse with a Śūdra or similar person through unintentional contact with them, there is the penance for a mortal sin (pātaka); however, if it is done intentionally, there is the penance for approaching a Śūdra woman, based on the statement: "But through knowledge, she attains equality" (MDh 11.175).

That too is incorrect. For here also, if unintentional contact were held to be more serious than intentional contact, that would contradict such statements as, "more so by intention" (ĀpDh 1.29.3). This being the case, the meaning of the verse, "Having approached a Caṇḍāla woman or a woman of the lowest caste... (MDh 11.175), should be understood as follows: through unintentional contact with Caṇḍālas and others, one becomes fallen (*patita*) and is no longer entitled to the duties of the twice-born; it does not mean that the sin of killing a Brahmin or similar crimes has occurred. Thus it is said: "The loss of the twice-born from their duties is falling" (GDh 21.4). This refers to the loss of entitlement to rites, not the loss of caste (*jāti*); therefore, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). However, in the case of intentional contact, there is also a loss of caste, and therefore there is no expiation. By the phrase "one falls through ignorance" (MDh 11.175), it is stated that one is disqualified from the duties of the twice-born, not that the sin of killing a Brahmin or similar crimes has occurred. Furthermore, because of the statement regarding equality—namely, that one attains equality with whomever one intentionally associates and is not entitled to rites through expiation—it follows that there is no expiation by way of this attainment of equality. In the case of women of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes having intentional contact with a Śūdra, this equality should be understood to apply only when she has given birth; for it is taught that purification occurs for her if she has not yet given birth.

"The women of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes who have had sexual union with a Śūdra are purified by penance if they have not conceived; others are not. Since this establishes the purification for one who has had union with a Śūdra but has not conceived, it should be understood that one who has had union with a man of a lower caste remains impure. Because the text specifies "of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya," it follows that even a Śūdra woman who has conceived is purified. Furthermore—
"In the case of one who has given birth, that [penance] shall be reduced by half for each successive person.

Regarding this, it should be understood as follows: in the case of contact with a Kṣatriya woman [by a Brāhmaṇa], it is half; in connection with a Vaiśya woman, half of that; and in connection with a Śūdra woman, half of that again. Concerning the rule "having sexual intercourse with a woman who drinks liquor" (MDh 11.66), an objection is raised: when one approaches a Brāhmaṇa woman who drinks liquor, the penance for approaching an outcaste (*patita*) ought to apply, rather than the penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*), because she becomes an outcaste through the act of drinking liquor.

To this it is replied: the state of being fallen (*pātitya*) consists in being equal to a *śūdra*, not in being equal to the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), as Manu has said: "He whose Veda residing in his body is once inundated by liquor—his Veda departs and he attains the status of a *śūdra*" (MDh 11.97).

Therefore, because of his equality with a Śūdra, the very penance already mentioned applies, and not the penance for approaching an outcast (patita). Likewise, it has been stated here as well: “In the case of the interchange of actions between an Ārya and a non-Ārya, there is equality” (GDh 10.66). This "interchange," however, refers to the fact that drinking liquor is not prohibited for a Śūdra but is prohibited for Brāhmaṇas and the others. In that regard, when a Śūdra—who is exempt from the prohibition on liquor—engages in it, while a Brāhmaṇa or another who is subject to the prohibition does so, there is equality on account of that act. Thus, it should be understood that a Brāhmaṇa or other who drinks liquor is equal to a Śūdra who is exempt from that [prohibition]. Even though he is equal to a Śūdra, he must nevertheless be understood as untouchable, because he is included under the term "outcast" (patita) in the rule: “An outcast, a Caṇḍāla... (GDh 14.29). If it is argued that this refers only to those [others] exempt from the prohibition, we say no, because of the force of other Smṛti texts. Thus Kaṇva says:

The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—these indeed are outcasts (patita) and untouchable; and one who associates with them is equal to them.
For the loss of a bed, a wife, or wealth, there are separate years [of penance]. (22.30)

The word *lābhavadha* (obstruction of gain) is connected with each term individually: "obstruction of the bed," "obstruction of the gain of wealth," and so forth. By the word *talpa*, which denotes a bed, the wife is meant; however, because she is the cause [of the act], the maiden is included here by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). "Food" refers to that which is prepared or unprepared. "Wealth" refers to gold, cattle, and the like. "Gain" means acquisition. "Obstruction" means creating an impediment. This is what is intended: when a maiden, food, or wealth is being obtained, one must perform a year-long period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) separately for each instance after having created an obstruction or prohibition. This rule applies to intentional acts. In the case of unintentional acts, however, that which was stated by Uśanas should be observed: "In the case of obstructing a maiden, food, or wealth, [one should perform] a Prājāpatya penance. This refers specifically to the obstruction of a Brāhmaṇa’s gain; for Kṣatriyas and others, the rule should be determined according to whether the act is unrighteous or righteous. (22.30)
There are two [types of] adultery. || 22.31 ||

For approaching the wife of another, the penance is two years of ordinary celibacy (*prākṛtabrahmacarya*). This should be understood to apply when conception occurs from approaching a Brahmin woman; prior to conception, the penances are the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*. As Vyāghra has said:
"If a Brahmin should intentionally approach a Brahmin woman who is unwilling, he should perform the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*; if it was through negligence, he should perform only half."
If he has approached her once while she was desirous, the penance is half of a *taptakṛcchra*;
for approaching the wives of kings and others, a Brahmin shall perform half of that [half] for each.
"One should observe this vow together with the wife of a *śrotriya*;
if she is not a *śrotriya*, the penance is double; and if she is protected [by another], it is only half.

Regarding the birth of a child in the wife of a *kṣatriya*, one should understand that half of the rule "two [years] for the wives of others" (*GDh* 22.31) applies, based on the indicative mark: "Half and half for kings and the others. Regarding the wife of a *vaiśya*, the penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) prescribed by Manu should be understood, starting from: "They should perform this very vow" (*MDh* 11.117). For the wife of a *śūdra*, the *atikṛcchra* penance applies, according to the statement of Kaṇva.
"A Brahmin who has approached the wife of a Śūdra should perform the *atikṛcchra* penance;
for a Vaiśya [approaching a Śūdra wife], the *cāndrāyaṇa*; and for a Kṣatriya, the vow is the same as that for a Brāhmaṇa.

If a Brāhmaṇa has, in due order, married wives born of all four castes, then when he approaches a Brāhmaṇī wife, whatever [penance] has been prescribed, that very same [penance] should be understood to be reduced by one quarter when approaching a Kṣatriyā wife and so forth, according to the statement of Vyāghra:
"Those born from the four castes by a Brahmin alone shall practice the vow in their respective order, diminished by one quarter for each successive caste. Thus it is said.

This same principle should be understood to apply to Kṣatriyas and others as well. If a Brāhmaṇa approaches a Śūdra woman who is the wife of another Brāhmaṇa, he should perform a *prājāpatya* penance, according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha: “If a Brāhmaṇa should intentionally approach the wife of a Brāhmaṇa, for one whose religious duties have not ceased, it is a *kṛcchra*; for one whose religious duties have ceased, it is an *atikṛcchra*” [VaDh 21.16]. This refers to a single instance of approaching her unintentionally. However, if it is intentional, the penance is doubled, based on the indicative mark: “only half [is required] in the case of negligence. In the case of repeated practice, the principle of reducing by a quarter (*pādahīna*) should be observed. Whatever has been stated regarding a Brāhmaṇa’s approach to the wives of Kṣatriyas and others, that very same rule should be understood to apply to Kṣatriyas and others when they approach their own caste wives. Why?
Whatever a Brahmin commits in sexual union with the wife of a king,
a Kṣatriya likewise commits when engaged in union with her for that same purpose.
Thus, because of the characteristic marks of Prajāpati’s dharma. 22.31.
Three [days] for one learned in the Vedas (śrotriya). 22.32.
This applies specifically to the occasion of conception during sexual union. It has also been stated prior to conception:
"One should observe this vow together with the wife of a Vedic scholar" (Vyāghra under 22.31).

After conception, this very same rule is to be understood as applying until the birth of offspring. If it is argued that it is improper for the penance to be identical when there is frequent repetition [of the offense], it is said in response: even in the case of women, identity of penance is observed despite frequent repetition prior to conception.

Regarding the statement, "The women of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes who have had intercourse with a Śūdra... (VaDh 21.12), there is likewise no fault in this case either. Similarly, there is also the statement of Kavaṣa: "Whatever has been prescribed regarding the conception of a fetus, that very same penance one should perform until death."

"A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and likewise a Śūdra. Alternatively, the deficiency may be remedied through recitation (*japa*) and other such means. As it is stated in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "In whatever rite has been performed, if there should be a lack of lightness in one's mind... [MDh 11.233].

And so forth. In that regard, if one who has committed an offense and performed the penance becomes guilty of the same offense again after a year has passed, he must perform double the previous penance. Why? Because:
"For a guilty person accused after a year has elapsed, the fine is double. [MDh 8.373]

This is because of the observation regarding the penalty (*daṇḍa*). It should be understood that this applies for a period starting from one year and lasting for that same duration. Regarding the period prior to one year, the Commentator (Bhāruci) has explained that in the first month, the portion of twelvefold [penance] is to be calculated month by month. Thus, a three-monthly fulfillment should be arranged for each month. This refers specifically to one who has performed the penance, as indicated by the use of the two terms "of the accused" and "of the wicked. For one who has not performed the penance, however, fulfillment is achieved through recitations (*japa*) and other such means. In this regard, the loss of caste (*pātitya*) should be understood to occur before the fourth act of approaching [the wife] when one forcibly seizes the wife of an extremely learned (*atyanta-śrotriya*) Brāhmaṇa who has children and is devoted to her husband, according to the statement of Āpastamba: "They teach that in the case of a single union with a woman of the same caste who has had another husband previously, one quarter falls away. Likewise, for repetition, a quarter falls away for each instance; at the fourth, everything [falls away]. (ĀpDh 2.27.11–13). 22.32.
And in the case of obtaining property, there shall be its relinquishment. 22.33.

And if property has been obtained from another's wife, its relinquishment must be performed; "relinquishment" (tyāga) means abandonment without the formal rite of acceptance (pratigraha). By the word "and" (ca), one should also restore whatever food and other items have been consumed. 22.33.
Or he should cause it to go to its proper place. || 22.34 ||
The meaning is that one should offer food and other such things to the master himself under some pretext. || 22.34 ||
If one employs a mantra that is prohibited, even if it is a "thousandfold speech" (sahasravāka). 22.35.

The "application of mantras" (*mantrayoga*) refers to the acts of officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) or teaching (*adhyāpana*) for one who is prohibited and of an unworthy *dvija* caste. If this is done, one must observe the standard period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) for one year. This [penance] applies when the act is committed unintentionally; otherwise, the status of being an outcaste (*patita*) would result. Furthermore, if that "application of mantras" consists of a "thousand recitations" (*sahasravāka*), the word *vāka* denotes a "metrical foot" (*pada*), and the word *sahasra* expresses a large number. Therefore, the meaning is: if he studies a large work. In this way, for a small amount, the study of the aforementioned *saṃhitā* should be understood [as the measure]. This concerns the case of an outcaste; however, regarding the case of one who has committed a minor offense (*upapātakin*), that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed.

"In the case of hearing of an outcast, a Caṇḍāla, or a corpse, they shall remain for three nights with speech restrained and fasting; it is known that by practicing this up to a thousand times, they become purified. By this same rule, those who teach what is censured and those who sacrifice for such persons are explained. And it is known that they become purified by the renunciation of their sacrificial fees. [VaDh 23.34–36]

In this case as well, due to ignorance, those who have recited less than one thousand [verses] must remain restrained in speech and fasting for three nights. However, for those who have recited more than that, the recitation of the entire studied portion—up to a maximum of one thousand times—is to be observed while consuming sacrificial food (*haviṣya*). Regarding cases of intentional knowledge, however, if one exceeds one thousand recitations, one should be regarded as having committed a minor offense (*upapātaka*), as it is said: "one who has composed a mantra for that [purpose]. Therefore, for cases below that, a recitation of three thousand is to be observed, according to the statement of Auśanasa: "One should practice the recitation of three thousand repetitions of the section [of the Veda] performed in violation."

Others, however, explain "mantra-yoga" as studying together or performing sacrifices together; thus, having studied or sacrificed together with one who is prohibited, it is considered ordinary *brahmacarya*.

In this case as well, that same penance previously mentioned should be understood to apply according to the distinction of the subject matter, because studying and sacrificing together are equivalent. (22.35)
And the same applies to those who extinguish the sacred fire, those who have been excluded from society, and those who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka). || 22.36 ||

One whose Vedic fires (*śrautāgni*) remain separated for a long period due to the ruin of his country or other such causes is an *agnyutsādī* (one who has extinguished the fires). He is described as a *nirākṛti* (one who has been excluded); he is not classified as a minor offender (*upapātakin*), because he is mentioned after Durvāla. However, the *utsṛṣṭāgni* (one who has abandoned the fires) is explained as being quite different: one who has abandoned the Vedic fires out of atheism (*nāstikya*). In this regard, the distinction between the cases should be understood as follows: for one who abandons the rites out of atheism, or for whom a long time passes due to the ruin of his country and so forth, there is a year of ordinary celibacy (*prākṛta-brahmacarya*); but if the time is short, it is the *prājāpatya* penance. As Vasiṣṭha says: "He who casts away the fires, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, should have them re-consecrated" (VaDh 1.23). For one who abandons them out of laziness and the like—even in the absence of atheism or the ruin of his country—the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance is to be observed, as Manu says.
"A Brāhmaṇa who, out of desire, neglects the sacred fires for a month should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, for that is equal to the killing of a hero. (MDh 11.41).
This refers to one who has neglected them for a month; therefore, it should be understood that the subsequent penance is more severe than the Kṛcchra.
If an Agnihotrin intentionally neglects the sacred fires for more than a month,
he must perform both the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa penances without hesitation.

Because of this statement, even within a month [of the transgression], it is indeed the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance; for the author of the *Bhāṣya* has stated, "Or the mention of 'month' is for the sake of clarity. Furthermore, in all such cases, the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādhāna*) and the expiation for the lapse of time (*atītakālahoma*) are to be understood. And so says Jātukarṇi:
"He should offer oblations into the fire or bestow wealth upon a Brahmin for the lapse of time.
When the fire is lost, the twice-born man, having performed the re-establishment according to rule, should give [the gift] as prescribed."

This statement is to be understood as applying both to the *śrauta* (Vedic) and the *smārta* (traditional) rites. Thus, when a long period of time has elapsed, the gravity of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) increases; therefore, there is no need here to perform a supplement of recitations (*japa*) and the like. For the *smārta* fire, however, there is only the re-establishment of the fires (*punar-ādhāna*) and the performance of the *atītakāla-homa*; there is no other expiation. In the case of atheism (*nāstikya*), however, a *prājāpatya* penance is to be observed. Thus Vyāghra says: "The twice-born who abandons the fires out of atheism should perform a *prājāpatya* penance; otherwise, there is simply the re-establishment of the fires and likewise the giving of gifts."

Regarding those others who have been declared *apāṅktya* (unfit for the company at a meal) but are excluded from the category of *upapātaka* (minor offenses), one should also observe what was stated by Manu:

"Eating only at every sixth mealtime for a month, the constant recitation of the *Saṃhitā*, and daily burnt offerings (*homa*) with *śāla-ka* wood—these are the means of purification for those who are *apāṅktya*. [MDh 11.200]
The plural number in the term "upapātakas" (minor offenses) is intended as an indication of those mentioned in other Smṛtis. As Manu says:

"Killing a cow, sacrificing for those unworthy to sacrifice or sacrificing for oneself, adultery, selling oneself, abandoning one's teacher, mother, father, or son, and neglecting one's Vedic study or the sacred fires;"
Being superseded by a younger brother, as well as the superseding of a younger brother;
giving away one's daughter to either of them, and officiating at a sacrifice for either of them.
Violating a maiden, usury, the breaking of a vow,
and the sale of a tank, a garden, a wife, or a child.
The state of being a *vrātya*, abandoning a wife who bears children, teaching for a fee,
receiving instruction for a fee, and the sale of goods that ought not to be sold.
Authority over all types [of crafts], the operation of great machines,
the harming of medicinal plants, living off women, malevolent magic, and root-rites.
Felling trees that are not yet dry for the sake of fuel,
undertaking actions for one's own sake, and likewise eating censured food.
Not maintaining the sacred fires, theft, non-payment of debts,
studying improper scriptures, and engaging in the arts of the stage.
"Stealing grain, base metals, or cattle; associating with women who drink liquor; killing a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; and atheism—these are minor offenses (upapātaka). [MDh 11.59–65].
Regarding these, the specific expiation for some is heard in another Smṛti. As Vasiṣṭha says:

A younger brother who has married before his elder brother (parivitta) shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, then enter the household life, and marry that very same woman. Now, the elder brother who has married after his younger brother (parivividāna) shall perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penances, give her to that younger brother, and then enter the household life again and marry that very same woman. The husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried (agredidhiṣūpati) shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, then enter the household life, and marry that very same woman. The husband of an elder sister whose younger sister has already been married (didhiṣūpati) shall perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penances and give her to that younger brother. [VaDh 20.7–10]

And so forth. Regarding the killing of a cow, this has also been stated; likewise regarding officiating at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, regarding adultery, and regarding the abandonment of one's Vedic study and sacred fires.
