And concerning the defilement of a maiden, Vasiṣṭha says: "Having approached the wife of a teacher, the friend of a teacher, a woman who is outcasted, or one who is fallen, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for one-fourth of a year" (VaDh 20.16). This should be understood as applying when the act is committed unintentionally. But if done intentionally, [Manu says]: "Having discharged semen in women of one's own lineage, or in the wives of a friend or a son, or in virgins, or in women of the lowest castes, one should perform the vow prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed" (MDh 11.170).

Thus, the penance for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa-vrata*) mentioned by Manu is to be understood. Although it was stated in general terms, nevertheless, specific penances must be observed according to the particular caste (*jāti*): “For a Brāhmaṇa girl, the full [penance]; for a Kṣatriya girl, half,” and so forth. Regarding the state of being a *vrātya*, that which was spoken by Vasiṣṭha has been cited: “One whose *Sāvitrī* initiation has lapsed shall perform the *Uddālaka-vrata*,” and so on. Manu also says:
“Those twice-born men for whom the *Sāvitrī* has not been recited according to the rule...”
"Having made them perform three *kṛcchra* penances according to the rule, one should initiate them.

[MDh 11.191] In this regard, it should be understood that if a long period has elapsed, the *uddālakavrata* applies; for a middling period, the three *kṛcchras*; and for a very short period of delay, the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice. Regarding teaching for wages, it is stated that "one who corrupts the Veda" [GDh 20.1] is meant. If this is done repeatedly, loss of caste (*pātitya*) occurs, and in such cases, abandonment is prescribed by the words "one should abandon the father," [GDh 20.1], and so forth. Elsewhere, Manu says: "Having abandoned one who has come for refuge, and having corrupted the Veda, a twice-born man..."
"By subsisting on barley for one year, he casts off that sin.
[MDh 11.198] Manu has also spoken regarding the practice of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*):
"Having performed sacrifices for those who have lost their caste (*vrātya*), or having performed the funeral rites for others..."

“One removes the sin of *abhicāra* (malevolent magic) and *ahīna* (an incomplete sacrifice) by means of three *kṛcchra* penances. [MDh 11.197] This refers to the killing of a twice-born (*dvijāti*). However, for the killing of a *śūdra* and others, one should follow the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: “Having performed *abhicāra* against a *śūdra*, one should perform a *prājāpatya* penance. Regarding the eating of forbidden food, however, he will state later: “In the case of eating what should not be eaten, there is the state of being free from excrement (*niṣpurīṣībhāva*)” [GDh 23.23], and so forth. In that regard, if this is done intentionally and repeatedly, it is equal to the drinking of liquor (*surāpāna*). As Manu says: “Eating forbidden food and things censured—these six are equal to the drinking of liquor. [MDh 11.56]

And thus, when the practice is unintentional, it should be understood as a minor offense (*upapātaka*). For those minor offenses for which no specific rule is prescribed, this one-year period of ordinary student-life (*prākṛta-brahmacarya*) should be observed. This refers to cases of habitual practice; in other instances, that which was stated by Manu applies:

"Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses shall perform this very same vow for the sake of purification, with the exception of the *avakīrṇin*, or else they may perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*. (MDh 11.117)

In that case as well, if the act was unintentional, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed; otherwise, the expiation for killing a cow (govadha-prāyaścitta) should be understood to apply. Since the extension [of the rule] is already established by the word "and" (ca), the use of the particle "eva" is intended to indicate a complete extension of the rule. Consequently, [other provisions] such as "upon obtaining the object, there is its relinquishment" (GDh 22.33) should also be understood to apply. 22.36.
And a woman who has been unfaithful, even if she is guarded, shall receive only alms-food. || 22.37 ||

A woman should perform this same penance. This applies to one who has committed adultery—that is, one who has been unfaithful. Since adultery with a Śūdra has already been mentioned, this refers to adultery with a twice-born man. If the act was intentional and occurred only once, this applies to adultery with a man of the same caste, as the penance for a man’s adultery with another’s wife is stated elsewhere: “That which [is prescribed] for a man regarding the wives of others” (MDh 11.176). However, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa woman’s adultery with a Kṣatriya, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: “In the event of sexual intercourse, she should wear a garment smeared with ghee for one year; she should sleep on a bed of Kuśa grass in a pit filled with cow-dung. After one year, having submerged herself in water, she should offer oblations with her head eight thousand times while reciting the Sāvitrī; she then becomes purified” (VaDh 21.8). In the case of adultery with a Vaiśya, that which was stated by Auśanasa should be observed: “An unfaithful woman shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year. Furthermore, in the case of approaching a woman of higher status, half of the penance should be assigned for each successive lower class. Likewise, it is heard in the scriptures regarding mere conversation: [the following should be applied].

"In the case of a transgression against her husband committed through the mind, she should eat barley-gruel or milk-rice for three nights and sleep on the ground; after the three nights, while submerged in water, she should offer oblations with one hundred and eight repetitions of the *Sāvitrī* verse for each head [of rice]; it is declared that she thus becomes purified. In the case of verbal connection, having performed this same penance for a month, after the month she should, while submerged in water, offer oblations with four times one hundred and eight repetitions of the *Sāvitrī* for each head.

[VaDh 21.6–7]. This also applies to a single instance of speaking; however, in the case of repetition, that which was stated by Manu applies, because of the hearing of the word "again" (*punaḥ*). As he said:

"Furthermore, if she should become thoroughly defiled after being approached by a man of equal status, the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are prescribed for her purification. (MDh 11.177) In the case of conversation with a man of lower status, it should be understood that the penance is double; in the case of conversation with a man of higher status, it is half. Thus, a woman who has committed adultery and is not purified shall, while remaining guarded and protected, receive only enough food to sustain life for her maintenance; from the use of the word "but" (tu), it is implied that she shall also receive clothing for the purpose of covering her private parts. (22.37)
For intercourse with non-human females, excluding cows, there shall be an oblation of ghee with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras; [this applies] for the sake of a woman. (22.38)

If one engages in sexual intercourse for the sake of a woman with non-human females such as mares and the like—excluding cows—one must perform an oblation of clarified butter with the *Kūśmāṇḍa* verses beginning with "yad devā devaheḍanam. It should be understood that due to repetition [of the act], there should be a repetition of the oblations. || 22.38 ||
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Maskarīya-gautama-bhāṣya*.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter, which states the penance for drinking liquor as it follows in the sequence.
In the case of a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk liquor, they should pour hot liquor into his mouth; he becomes pure when he dies. 23.1.
By the word *surā* here, all three types of liquor are intended, because of the mention of the Brāhmaṇa, and because all three types are prohibited for him. As Manu says:
"Liquor made from molasses, from honey, and from flour—these should be known as the three kinds of *surā*.
Just as one [type] is not to be drunk, so are all [three] by the best of the twice-born. (MDh 11.94)

Since it will be stated later, “*amatyā pāne* [GDh 23.2],” it is understood that this [penance] applies to intentional drinking. This same expiation should be understood to apply to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya as well for drinking *paiṣṭī* liquor, because that alone is prohibited for them. As Manu says:
“Liquor is indeed the impurity of foods, and sin is called impurity;
therefore, the Brāhmaṇa, the Rājanya, and the Vaiśya shall not drink liquor. (MDh 11.93)
Likewise:
"A twice-born man who has drunk liquor through delusion shall drink liquor that is fire-colored;
when his body has been consumed by it, he is then released from that sin. (MDh 11.90)

Because the term "twice-born" (*dvija*) is used in the rules for penance (*prāyaścitta*), it is understood that for whichever person a particular substance is forbidden, if they drink it intentionally, the penance for drinking that very substance when it is fire-colored is precisely that. This should also be understood to apply here to the intentional repeated consumption of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* liquors by a Brāhmaṇa, and to the intentional single instance of drinking *paiṣṭī* liquor by any of the three twice-born classes. Why? Because another penance is seen prescribed for the intentional single instance of drinking *gauḍī* and *mādhvī*. As Vasiṣṭha says: "In the case of drinking intoxicants (*madya*), however, if one has drunk *asurā* or *surā* unintentionally, the penance is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*, the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and a second initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*)" (VaDh 20.19). Since it is stated here, "if one has drunk *surā* unintentionally," it follows that the drinking of other intoxicants (*madya*) was done intentionally. Furthermore, the *atikṛcchra* mentioned here is the *taptakṛcchra*, because of the observation of another Smṛti text: "Having drunk intoxicant (*madya*), one should perform the *kṛcchra* or the *taptakṛcchra*" (Paithinasi). It should be understood that "hot" means "fire-colored," because the passage begins with the words, "he is purified when dead. "They should pour [it on him]" (*āsiñceyuḥ*) means they should sprinkle it upon him from all sides. This is a designation of the causal agent rather than the direct agent; the one who drinks does so himself. As Āpastamba says: "The drinker of *surā* shall drink *surā* that is fire-colored" (ĀpDh 1.25.3). The plural number in "they should pour" is intended to indicate the plurality of those who instruct [the penance]. Thus says Manu.

"Whatever expiation for sins those three who know the Vedas may prescribe, that shall serve for their purification, for the word of the learned is indeed purifying. Thus [says Manu, MDh 11.85]. Śaṅkha also says:
"Having been approved by the assembly and having properly confessed his offense according to the truth, whatever those who know the rules prescribe shall be the supreme means of purification for him.

[The word] *āsye* means "in the mouth"; one who has died [from drinking liquor] is purified—that is, he becomes pure—by death alone. In the phrase "having drunk *surā* in the mouth," the word *surā* is intended to include cow urine and other such substances as well. As Manu says:

"Or one should drink cow urine the color of fire, or water, or milk, or ghee, or even the juice of cow dung until death" (MDh 11.91). Since the word *brāhmaṇa* denotes the caste (*jāti*), this same penance applies to a Brāhmaṇī woman as well for drinking *surā*. As Śaṅkha says, referring specifically to women: "She should avoid *surā*, garlic, onions, leeks, meat, and so forth, which are unfit to be eaten; for this body consists of food, and thus it is declared to be of the same nature [as that food]," and so on. Likewise, Vasiṣṭha also says:

“Half of the body of that man falls [with him] whose wife drinks liquor; for one whose half-body has fallen, no expiation is prescribed. (VaDh 21.15). Likewise, in that same work: “The gods do not lead that Brāhmaṇī who drinks liquor to the world of her husband; indeed, she wanders here [in this world] with her merit exhausted, becoming a leech in water or a pearl-oyster shell. (VaDh 21.11).
Others, however, based on observing the customs of other regions, say:
"In former times, women were enjoyed by the gods—Soma, Gandharva, and Agni;
they go to men afterwards, and therefore women are free from blemish."

Furthermore, because of the observation in the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti*: "Soma gave them purity, Gandharva taught them speech, and Agni granted them the state of being edible by all; therefore, women are free from blemish" (VaDh 28.5–6), they do not accept this penance for a Brāhmaṇa woman.
In that regard, the conceptual differentiation established by the arrangement of place is to be understood. 23.1.
If one drinks milk, ghee, water, or air for three days each, that is the *taptakṛcchra* penance. (23.2)

The ministers [argue that the prohibition applies] to the Gauḍī and Mādhvī liquors through ignorance, because the word "drinking" is mentioned again in the context of the rule regarding drinking. And so Manu says:

"Having drunk Vāruṇī through ignorance, one is purified by the purificatory rite alone; but having done so intentionally, there is no other instruction [than death]; this is the settled rule. (MDh 11.146)

Regarding this as well, the Commentator [Bhāruci] has explained: "by means of the purificatory rite accompanied by the *taptakṛcchra*. And thus, this should be understood to apply to a Brāhmaṇa who has unintentionally drunk *paiṣṭī* liquor once. As Manu says:
"Or he may eat grains or oil-cake once at night for a year, wearing clothes of hair, with matted locks and carrying a flag, in order to remove the sin of drinking *surā*. (MDh 11.92)

Regarding the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, however, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed, beginning with: “And in the case of ignorance regarding *surā*,” [VaDh 20.19]. Even in the case of intentional and habitual practice of that [drinking], the penance ending in death (*maraṇāntika*) alone should be observed for all three [castes]. As Vasiṣṭha says:
“But in the case of habitual practice of *surā*, the twice-born man should drink it when it is fire-colored. [VaDh 20.22]

In this context, however, the word *tu* (but) expresses a distinction. For the twice-born, in the case of the repeated unintentional consumption of *paiṣṭī* liquor, that [liquor] must be drunk when it has reached the color of fire; and for a Brāhmaṇa, in the case of the repeated unintentional consumption of *gauḍī* or *mādhvī* liquors, purification occurs only through death from drinking that [liquor] when it has reached the color of fire. Thus Vyāghra says: "Having intentionally or unintentionally drunk liquor again, the best of the twice-born, having then drunk that [liquor] when it has reached the color of fire, shall be purified from that sin upon dying."
However, for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, there is no prohibition against [consuming] *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* liquors. Thus Vyāsa said:
"I have seen Keśava and Arjuna both intoxicated by honey-wine (*madhvāsava*), both anointed with sandalwood paste, and both reclining upon the same couch."

Consequently, for a Brāhmaṇa who has unintentionally drunk Gauḍī or Mādhvī liquor even once, he must perform the penance of milk and the other substances for three days each. The separate mention of milk and the rest is intended to preclude their being taken in a sequential order. Thus Vasiṣṭha says:
"For three days he should drink hot water; for three days he should drink hot milk;
having drunk hot ghee for three days, he should subsist on air for the final three days."

"Thus is the *taptakṛcchra*. [VaDh 21.21] Here, "hotness" applies only to water, ghee, and milk, because it is possible for them to be so; it does not apply to air. The phrase "that is the *kṛcchra*" is intended to include the general injunction regarding the *kṛcchra*. This refers to such rules as: "He should stand during the day and sit during the night," and so forth. [GDh 26.6] 23.2.
Then, for him, there is volitional formation (saṃskāra). || 23.3 ||

The word "then" (*tataḥ*) means immediately after the period of penance. The inclusion of the word "his" (*asya*) is for the sake of clarity, meaning "of him who has drunk [it]. Furthermore, even in the case of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, this provision serves to extend the rite of purification (*saṃskāra*) to them when they intentionally drink *paiṣṭī* (liquor made from flour) even once; it is so that their exclusion—which follows from the fact that the qualification [for the penance] belongs specifically to Brāhmaṇas—does not occur. Alternatively, it is for the sake of what follows: that in the case of consuming urine and other such substances, the rite of purification is for the Brāhmaṇa alone. The "rite of purification" (*saṃskāra*) here refers merely to the initiation (*upanayana*), and not to the observance of Vedic vows and the like. The nature of this "re-initiation" (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) is to be understood from other Smṛti texts. As Manu says:
"Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
these are indeed discontinued at the rite of re-consecration.
And [the same applies] upon consuming urine, feces, or semen. || 23.4 ||

This same expiation applies to the consumption of urine and the like. The word "ca" (and) serves to include the rite of re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). This refers to intentional acts; why? Because of the statement of Manu: "Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one should fast for three days;
but having eaten it intentionally, as well as semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance. [MDh 4.222]

Since the author of the *Bhāṣya* (Bhāruci) has stated that the word *kṛcchra* here refers to the *taptakṛcchra*, and because other penances for eating forbidden foods are taught later on, it should be understood that this refers to the drinking of human urine and so forth. Furthermore, in the case of unintentional consumption, the three-day period is to be understood from the rule itself: "Having eaten the food of any one of these, however, unintentionally, one should fast for three days" (MDh 4.222); for a different penance is seen for intentional acts. As Kaṇva says:
"Upon intentionally consuming meat, urine, or feces, a twice-born man shall not eat for three days; however, if he did so intentionally, he must perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
Even in cases where it was unintentional, a re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) is to be observed, as Manu has stated:

"Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or that which is mixed with *surā* liquor, the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the rite of re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) again. (MDh 11.150).

Some maintain that this very penance applies here; however, that should be understood to apply to a single instance of swallowing. And thus, where a penance for swallowing urine or feces has been prescribed—as in the passage beginning "and of crows, donkeys, and camels"—it should be understood to apply to all except humans. 23.4.
And [the same applies] to the limbs of beasts of prey, camels, and donkeys. 23.5.

The term *prāśane* (in the case of eating) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. *Śvāpadāḥ* refers to those whose feet are like those of a dog (*śveva padāḥ*); that is, jackals and other animals with feet resembling a dog’s. *Uṣṭra* (camel) and *khara* (donkey) are well known. For the consumption of their limbs—such as flesh, skin, and so forth—the penance is this very same one. Since they are prescribed as having feet like a dog’s, the same applies by implication to the dog itself; and because of the word *ca* (and), it also applies to humans. (23.5)
And [the same applies] to the village cock and the pig. 23.6.

In the case of divination by means of the limbs of the body, this same expiation applies. The separate formulation [of this rule] is for the purpose of excluding these two cases from the rule "and of one bitten by the aforementioned [creatures]" (GDh 23.8). Regarding this [act], such as when done intentionally, that which was stated previously applies. The word "ca" (and) is intended to carry over the requirement of a renewed consecration (punassaṃskāra). || 23.6 ||
If one who has drunk liquor smells a fragrance [of it], he must perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and consume clarified butter.

Since the term *surāpaḥ* (one who drinks *surā*) is not further specified, it refers to every such person. Regarding "smelling the odor" (*gandhāghrāṇe*), it means smelling the odor of *surā*, but not the odor of the body. Even there, it does not refer to smelling the odor of *surā* that resides in something else; for if the intention were merely to say "smelling the odor of *surā*," the specific designation *surāpasya* (of one who drinks *surā*) would have been unnecessary. Therefore, one should understand that causing loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakarattva*) occurs when one smells the odor of *surā* residing in something else. As Manu says: "Causing injury to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling what should not be smelled or drinking intoxicants, dishonesty, and sexual intercourse with a male—these are recorded as causing loss of caste. [MDh 11.67]
Likewise, regarding expiation:

"Having intentionally committed any one of the acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the *sāntapana* penance; if done unintentionally, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance. (MDh 11.124)

Whatever is prohibited for someone, that [prohibition] should be understood to apply to the smelling of its odor as well, since no distinction is made. For the twice-born, the penance for causing loss of caste (jātibhraṃśakara) should be regarded as common to all; there is no application here of the rule "half for a Brāhmaṇa, a quarter for a Kṣatriya," because of the observation of other Smṛtis. As Kaṇva says:
"Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or likewise a Vaiśya, having smelled the odor of *surā*, shall perform the Sāntapana vow."

Three *prāṇāyāmas* are to be understood [for the Brāhmaṇa], since the plural number is fulfilled by that many alone. The consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*) is merely a rinsing of the body; having performed that, one may eat, because there is no rule prescribing a full fast (*upavāsa*). The use of the non-compound form and the particle *ca* is for the purpose of allowing both individual and collective interpretations. Therefore, for the Brāhmaṇa it is the collective [set of three], but for the Kṣatriya it is the *prāṇāyāmas*, and for the Vaiśya it is the consumption of clarified butter. Even in that regard—a specific distinction must be observed for the Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). As Manu says: "But a Brāhmaṇa who drinks Soma, having smelled the odor of one who drinks liquor..."
"Having restrained his breaths three times in water and having consumed clarified butter, he becomes purified. (MDh 11.149).
There is no distinction for the Kṣatriya and others, as there is no specific scriptural statement to that effect. 23.7.
And for one bitten by previous [snakes]. || 23.8 ||

This same penance applies to one bitten by carnivorous animals and the like, as well as by humans; the word "and" (*ca*) implies that it also applies to domestic carnivores and the like. Thus Manu says:
"Bitten by dogs, jackals, or donkeys, or indeed by domestic carnivores, or by humans, horses, camels, and pigs, one is purified by *prāṇāyāma*. (MDh 11.199)
In this case as well, the subject matter should be understood in the same way. For a Brāhmaṇa bitten by these [dogs], that which was declared by Vasiṣṭha should be observed:
"A Brāhmaṇa who has been bitten by a dog goes to a river flowing to the ocean, performs one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and becomes pure after consuming clarified butter. [VaDh 23.31]

Since the mention of the dog (*śva*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for these [other animals] as well, this triad of breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) should be understood to apply to a Kṣatriya. For a Vaiśya, one breath-restraint is to be understood as prescribed by Manu, because of the use of the singular number in the phrase "by means of a breath-restraint" (*prāṇāyāmena*). However, there is no fault in the case of a Śūdra. And for a woman, bathing with her clothes on (*sacelasnāna*) is to be understood. Thus said Jātukarṇi: "A Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, or a Vaiśyā who has been bitten by a dog or even by wild beasts, become pure after bathing with their clothes on; of this there is no doubt."
Thus [ends the section]. 23.8.
One who has violated the teacher’s bed shall lie upon a heated iron bed.
One who has sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru shall lie down upon a red-hot iron bed glowing like fire.
Or he would embrace a blazing iron image.
A *sūrmi* is a hollow iron image in the form of a woman; others say it is a piece of wood with a hollow interior. One should embrace—that is, hug—it while it is blazing. 23.10.

Or, having cut off his penis together with the testicles and holding them in his cupped hands, he should walk straight toward the southwest until his body collapses; dead, he shall be purified. 23.11.

Having cut off the *liṅga*—the male organ together with its seed and its root—and having placed it in both hands, he should go straight toward the southwest (*nairṛṭī-diś*) without avoiding wells and such. Until the fall of the body—that is, until death—he shall be purified once dead. And this applies as a general rule for all [offenses], because it ends only with death. Thus, since these options are established, the mention of "either" (*vā*) is for the purpose of restriction. Consequently, in the case of a union between those two by mutual desire, the first [penance] applies; in the case of one incited by her, the second; and in the case of a woman incited by the man himself, the third. This also refers to a Brāhmaṇa’s intentional, single instance of intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman. However, for an unintentional, single instance of intercourse, that which was stated by Manu should be observed.
"Carrying a skull-topped staff or clad in rags, with a beard, in a solitary forest, he shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year with a concentrated mind. [MDh 11.105]

That also applies when there is a union by mutual consent; it should be understood as the rule of Uśanas for one who has been incited by her [the woman] when she herself was incited by him: "One who violates the bed of his guru shall perform the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa for one year, or the *taptakṛcchra* penance for six months. Thus, in the case of approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman, if it is intentional and occurs once, or if it is unintentional but repeated, the penance ends only in death. In the case of approaching a Kṣatriya woman, that which was stated by Vyāghra should be observed: "The *kṛcchra*, the *atikṛcchra*, and likewise the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*."

"A Brahmin [incurs] a three-month penance for approaching the wife of his guru who is of Kṣatriya birth. Regarding this, if the act is intentional and occurs once, and both parties have acted out of mutual desire, the penance is an *atikṛcchra*. If he was incited by her, it is a *kṛcchra*; if she was incited by him, it is a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. Even in those cases, if it is intentional and repeated, the penance is indeed one ending in death. As Kavaṣa said:
"A twice-born man who intentionally approaches the wife of his guru who is a daughter of a Kṣatriya..."
"Having cut off the penis along with the testicles, he becomes pure upon death.
This [penance] prescribed by Kaṇva should be understood to apply to a single instance of unintentional sexual intercourse:
"The Cāndrāyaṇa, the Taptakṛcchra, and likewise the Atikṛcchra."

"A twice-born man who, out of ignorance, goes once to the wife of his guru who is a Kṣatriya woman... In that case as well, if the act proceeds from the desire of both, it is a *taptakṛcchra*; if he was incited by her, it is an *atikṛcchra*; and if she was incited by him, it is a *cāndrāyaṇa*. But in the case of repetition—having gone again to the wife of his guru, the daughter of a Kṣatriya, unintentionally...
Having cut off only the testicles, he shall be purified whether he lives or dies.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Jātūkarṇya. Regarding intentional intercourse with a Vaiśya woman once, Kavaṣa says:
"Having intentionally approached his teacher’s wife who is a Vaiśya once, a twice-born man should perform the Taptakṛcchra, the Parāka, and likewise the Sāntapana penances for one month."

In that case as well, if the act proceeds from the desire of both, it is a *taptakṛcchra*; for one who is incited by her, it is a *sāntapana*; and for one who incites her himself, it is a *parāka*. In the case of repetition, the tip of the penis must be cut off. As Lokākṣi says: "Having gone again and again to the wife of a Guru, even repeatedly, he shall be purified from that sin only after having the tip of his penis cut off."

By this very indicative authority (*jñāpaka*), it should be understood that the penance prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*) applies even when the act is repeated many times. Regarding a single unintentional approach to a Vaiśya woman who is the wife of one's Guru, Prajāpati has said: "A twice-born man who, through ignorance, has once approached the wife of his Guru who is a Vaiśya, shall not eat for five nights, or likewise seven or eight."

In that case as well, if the engagement occurs through mutual desire, the penance lasts seven nights; if he was incited by her, five nights; if she was incited by him, eight nights. However, in the case of repetition, there must be the observance of celibacy until death. Thus says Hārīta:
"A Brahmin who, deluded by ignorance, repeatedly has intercourse with a Vaiśya woman, shall practice celibacy along with its six ancillaries for as long as he lives."
Regarding intentional sexual intercourse with a Śūdra woman, Jābāli said:
"Having intentionally approached his teacher’s Śūdra wife even once, a Brāhmaṇa should then perform an Atikṛcchra, a Taptakṛcchra, and likewise a Parāka."

In this case as well, it should be understood that if the act proceeds from the desire of both parties, it is a *taptakṛcchra*; if she was incited by him, it is an *atikṛcchra*; and if she incited herself, it is a *parāka*. However, in the case of repetition, one must observe celibacy for twelve years. As Upamanyu said: "If a Brahmin, being composed and of uncorrupted soul, intentionally approaches the Guru’s Śūdra wife, he should practice celibacy for twelve years."
Regarding ignorance, Dīrghatapas said: "Having approached the Śūdra wife of his guru even once, a Brahmin, being composed, shall perform the Prājāpatya, the Sāntapana, and a fast for seven nights."

In this case as well, if the act proceeds from the desire of both parties, the *sāntapana* penance is prescribed; if he was incited by her, the *prājāpatya*; and if she was incited by him, a fast for seven nights. However, in the case of repetition, that which was stated by Manu should be observed:

"Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the *cāndrāyaṇa* for three months, subsisting on sacrificial food or barley-gruel, for the removal of the sin of violating the Guru’s bed" (MDh 11.106).
Common women do not incur the sin of violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*), according to the statement of Vyāghra:
"The offense of approaching another’s wife as defined by caste, the defilement of a maiden, and likewise the violation of the Guru’s bed— these do not apply in the case of a common woman."

Gurus other than the teacher (ācārya) are the father and so forth; for Vasiṣṭha states that this same rule applies to the wives of the teacher and others, based on the extended application (*atideśa*) in the rule: "And likewise toward the son, pupil, and wife of the teacher" (VaDh 20.15). 23.11.

In the case of a female friend, a woman born of the same womb, a woman of the same lineage, the wife of a pupil, a daughter-in-law, or a cow, the penance is equal to that for violating one's own bed. || 23.12 ||

A *sakhī* is a female friend; a *sayoni* is a sister; a *sagotrā* is one who shares the same ancestral lineage (*ekārṣeya*). When sexual intercourse is practiced with these women—along with the wife of a pupil and the wife of a son—the atonement is equal to that for violating the Guru’s bed. The mention of various categories is intended to include the wives of friends and others. Thus says Manu:
"One should perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed after having spilled semen upon women who are sisters, the wives of a friend or a son, virgins, and women of the lowest castes. (MDh 11.170)
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of including wives who are dependent and so forth. Thus Vyāghra said:

"The wife of one who is dependent, even if he is learned; of one who has maintained the sacred fires; of a yogin; of a teacher; and likewise of a king—even if she has renounced the world [is protected by the king]."
Having approached a nurse, a daughter, a granddaughter, a maternal friend, or likewise a paternal friend, one must practice the penance prescribed for violating the Guru's bed.
Thus [ends the section]. 23.12.
"Scattered [ashes]," say some. 23.13.

Some, however, maintain that the vow of the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken the vow of chastity) must be performed, but not the vow for violating the Guru’s bed. The particle *iti* is intended to exclude doubt. If it were stated simply as "one [vow] is that of the *avakīrṇin*," there might arise the apprehension that even for one who has violated the Guru’s bed, the fault is equal to that of an *avakīrṇin*. This alternative view is to be understood with reference to intention (*abhisaṃdhi*). When there is intention, it is equal to violating the Guru’s bed; when there is no intention, however, it is the vow of the *avakīrṇin*. Thus, in this case, it should be understood that after performing the *kṛcchra* penance caused by adultery, one must further perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin*. So says Jātūkarṇi.

"But regarding the wives of the teacher and others, one should perform the vow for violating the Guru's bed (*gurutalpa-vrata*); with a concentrated mind, one should likewise perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin*. Even in the case of what is equal to violating the Guru's bed, it should be determined as being more than adultery (*pāradārya*) but less than violating the Guru's bed. That too should be regarded simply as the penance for another's wife, but as being greater than the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. And for the *Cāndrāyaṇa*, a reduction by a quarter should be made according to the order of the social classes (*varṇa*). Thus says Prajāpati:"

"But regarding the wives of a teacher, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow; it is decreed that for the [other] castes, it is reduced by a quarter in successive order. Thus it is established. Furthermore, the penance for an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) spoken of in secret will be stated [by the author] beginning with: "Regarding this they ask: 'How many kinds of *avakīrṇins* are there? [GDh 25.1]. And likewise, Prajāpati says:

But in the case of approaching the wives of a teacher (*ācārya*) and others, having completed the act of adultery, one who has spilled his seed (*avakīrṇin*) should offer clarified butter into the fire for a month, a fortnight, ten days, seven days, or five days, respectively according to the order of the castes, with the two [mantras]: “I am spilt by desire, O Desire; to Desire, svāhā! I am afflicted by desire, I am afflicted, O Desire; to Desire, svāhā! They teach that one should perform this oblation twice over if the wife of a *śrotriya* is approached, and half [that amount] if she approached him of her own accord. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the statement that "in all matters concerning equalization, the universal expiation alone is to be observed," this is to be understood as applying when no other specific expiation is available. 23.13.

In this context, the loss of caste (*pātitya*) for a woman who has intercourse with one of inferior varna has been stated. Since the general penance for those who have fallen from their caste would otherwise apply to her, he says:
The king shall cause a woman who has had intercourse with a man of lower caste to be devoured by dogs in public.

A woman of low caste (*nihīnavarṇā*) has been explained in the passage: "In the case of killing an embryo and in serving a man of low caste" (GDh 21.9). If she has sexual intercourse with such a man, the king shall have her devoured by dogs in public, in the presence of the people. Thus says Manu: "But that woman of high birth who, arrogant because of her caste and her virtues, transgresses against her husband—the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a place where many people are assembled" (MDh 8.371).
This royal punishment applies when the act was unintentional; if it was intentional, that which was spoken by Vasiṣṭha should be observed.

If a Śūdra approaches a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Śūdra in *vīraṇa* grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be shaved and having anointed her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a black donkey and cause her to be paraded along the high road; thus she becomes purified—so it is known. If a Vaiśya approaches a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Vaiśya in red *darbha* grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be shaved and having anointed her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a white donkey and cause her to be paraded along the high road; thus she becomes purified—so it is known. If a Kṣatriya approaches a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Kṣatriya in reed-leaves (*śarapatra*) and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s head to be shaved and having anointed her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a white donkey and cause her to be paraded along the high road; thus she becomes purified—so it is known. In the same manner, a Vaiśya [is treated] for approaching a Kṣatriya woman, and a Śūdra for approaching a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman. [VaDh 21.1–5]

Since it has been stated that "going to one of inferior caste" is the offense, this penalty for a Brāhmaṇī woman must be inferred when she intentionally approaches a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya. As Manu says:
"But a restrained woman who serves a man of lower caste should be kept confined in her home;
however, a man of lower caste who serves a woman of higher caste deserves death. [MDh 8.366]

This same [penalty] should be understood to apply even in the case of approaching a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya woman, because it has been stated in general terms. And likewise, this penalty for one of lower caste is common to women of the twice-born castes, precisely because it was stated in general terms. However, regarding sexual contact with those born in the natural order (anuloma), Vyāghra says: "When there is mutual union among those of the casters born in the natural order, but in the reverse order, the king should then have that woman devoured by monkeys."
"If a man intentionally kills jackals, he deserves death;
this same rule applies even to those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) when they deviate from their own species.
This statement by Manu is to be understood as applying both to intentional and unintentional sexual union with women of the inverse order (*pratiloma*).
"In the case of an inverse union, there shall be execution for the man and the cutting off of the nose and other features for the women.
But is it not said:
"One should apply this very same rule even to women who have fallen from their status"? [MDh 11.188]
Thus,

since it is already established by the rules "whatever [penance] for a man regarding another's wife" and "and whatever vow one should cause her to perform," this rule concerning punishment is redundant.

To this it is replied: for her who approaches the king of her own accord, there is only punishment; for her who is brought by force, there is both punishment and penance (*prāyaścitta*); and for her who neither approaches of her own accord nor is brought by force, there is only penance. This same principle is to be observed everywhere regarding punishment and penance. In this context, regarding those of inverse castes (*pratiloma*) who deviate from their own caste—since, according to the rule "But one of inverse birth is devoid of dharma" (GDh 4.25), there is an absence of prescribed penance—a punishment must be devised for others in order to avoid the fault of the mixture of castes (*saṃkara*). And thus:

"In the case of the reverse order, there shall be execution for men and the cutting off of the nose and other [limbs] for women"—this should also be understood to apply to them. Likewise, regarding the major and minor sins (*pātaka* and *upapātaka*), that punishment which has been declared for a Brāhmaṇī’s son born of a man of the next lower caste (*anantara*) should be understood to apply to him; and similarly for those born of one or two intervening castes. Why? Because it is said:
"One must never study in the vicinity of a Caṇḍāla."
Likewise, even for a Pāraśava, he is traditionally considered to be half as [sinful] as a Caṇḍāla.
Thus, because of the characteristic mark of the tiger's nature. 23.14.
One should cause a man to be executed. || 23.15 ||

The word "publicly" (*prakāśam*) carries over [from the previous verse]. Furthermore, the method of execution should be understood as that described by Vasiṣṭha, and it has been cited specifically. Since there are no other specific statements regarding intentional or unintentional intercourse, whether occurring once or repeatedly, in all such cases, execution alone is to be understood. Likewise, in the case of the castes—whether in the direct order (*anuloma*) or the inverse order (*pratiloma*)—when there is a transgression within one's own class or a transgression with another, execution alone is to be understood. To this effect, the statements of other Smṛtis have also been cited. And thus, it should be understood that for women as well, in the case of intercourse occurring once or repeatedly, the punishment is exactly as previously stated. (23.15)
Or as it has been stated: || 23.16 ||

The passage beginning with "liṅgoddhāra" (the removal of gender) and so forth should be understood as applying to a Śūdra as previously stated; therein, it should be understood that what was previously stated applies to a virtuous Śūdra, while this [present rule] applies to another. 23.16.
One who has committed the *avakīrṇa* offense should sacrifice a donkey to Nirṛti at a crossroads.

An *avakīrṇin* is a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) whose celibacy has been violated. As Jātukarṇi said: "The wise call him an *avakīrṇin* who, while observing the vow of a student, emits semen through intentional emission because of lust."

However, where no other expiation exists—as in the case of taking a woman as a *putrikā* (appointed daughter) and so forth—this expiation should be observed. Thus, in other cases, there is the establishment of two expiations together with the expiation for sexual intercourse with a maiden and the like. With a donkey (*gardabha*), that is, a *khara*, which is one-eyed, dedicated to the deity Nirṛti, the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) shall sacrifice at a crossroads in the forest itself, not everywhere, in a common (*laukika*) fire. As Vasiṣṭha says: “If a student (*brahmacārī*) should approach a woman, he should sacrifice a donkey animal dedicated to the Rakṣases at a crossroads in the forest in a common fire, or he should offer a *caru* oblation dedicated to Nirṛti” [VaDh 23.1–2]. In this regard, it should be understood that the donkey is for one who is not a *śrotriya* (learned in the Vedas), while the *caru* is for one who is a *śrotriya*. He should sacrifice and offer oblations according to the procedure for a *sthālīpāka*. This must be done only at night, not by day, as Manu says: *“He shall sacrifice a donkey to Nirṛti at night in a common fire at a crossroads in the forest.”* [MDh 11.118] [The remainder of the passage follows: ...having sacrificed, he shall touch the fire while reciting the verse beginning with “O Agni, you are the healer of diseases. Then, having bathed, he shall enter the village. This applies to one who has intentionally committed the act; for one who did so unintentionally, the penance is half. For one who has approached his mother, a sister, or a female relative, the penance is the same as for a *gurutalpaga* (one who violates the teacher’s bed). For one who has approached the wife of a paternal uncle, a maternal uncle, or a brother, the penance is the same as for violating a maiden. For one who has approached the wife of a friend, a *sakhā*, or a *sabrahmacārin*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī* (the wife of a king). For one who has approached the wife of a *śrotriya*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a *vaiśyā*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a *śūdrā*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a *caṇḍālī*, a *pulkasī*, or a *śvapākī*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a cow, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman during her courses, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is forbidden, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by law, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by another man, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by both men and gods, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by both men and ancestors, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by both men and *ṛṣis*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by both men and *brahman*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by all beings, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman* and *kṣatra*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, and *viś*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, and *śūdra*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, and *śūdra*, and all beings, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, and who is also protected by *brahman*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, and who is also protected by *brahman* and *kṣatra*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, and who is also protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, and *viś*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, and who is also protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, and *śūdra*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, and who is also protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, and who is also protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, and who is also protected by *brahman*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, and who is also protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, and who is also protected by *brahman* and *kṣatra*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, and who is also protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, and who is also protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, and *viś*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñī*. For one who has approached a woman who is protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, and who is also protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, *viś*, *śūdra*, and all beings, and who is also protected by *brahman*, *kṣatra*, and *viś*, and *śūdra*, the penance is the same as for violating a *rājñ
"But one who has spilled his seed shall, at night, sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads with a one-eyed donkey, according to the procedure for a *sthālīpāka*. [MDh 11.118]

In this regard, the following procedure for the *homa* sacrifice should be understood: having performed the *homa* according to the rules for the *sthālīpāka* up until the principal offering (*pradhānayāga*), one should offer the animal meat with the mantras prescribed by Vasiṣṭha, because it is stated there: "One should sacrifice of that" (VaDh 23.3). The oblations therein are four: "To Desire, svāhā! To the one who desires desire, svāhā! To Nirṛti, svāhā! To the deities of the Rākṣasas, svāhā! (VaDh 23.3). Since this is an offering of the omentum (*vapā*), there is no *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, as it is established in the Jaimini-Gṛhya-Sūtra: "The *sviṣṭakṛt* occurs elsewhere than at the offering of the omentum and the offering of clarified butter. Having thus sacrificed with the sacrificial food (*havis*), one should again sacrifice with clarified butter for Vāyu and the others with the mantra beginning "May they sprinkle me" (*saṃ mā siñcantu*). As Manu has said:

"Having performed the oblations in the fire according to rule, and finally with the verse beginning 'sam' (RV 8.48.3), one should offer oblations of clarified butter to Vāyu, Indra, the Guru (Bṛhaspati), and Agni. [MDh 11.119] Having thus offered, one should again pour out the remainder of the oblation according to the procedure for the *sthālīpāka*. The repetition of the oblation should be understood as resulting from this specific practice, as Kaṇva has said:

"On the first day, at night, one who has committed an emission [of semen] should sacrifice with a donkey; thus, according to the repetition [of the offense], he becomes pure in one year. Thus, in the case of repetition, there is only a repetition of the oblation (*homa*), not a repetition of the time period. (23.17)
Having put on its skin with the hair turned upwards, carrying a red vessel, he should go for alms to seven houses while proclaiming his deed.

The hide (*ajina*) is the skin of that donkey. Although this is already established by the context, the explicit mention of "his" is for the purpose of restriction: it means that the hide must belong to the very donkey with which the sacrifice was performed, and not to any other. That too must have its hair pointing upward and its fur on the outside; having put that on, he should carry a red vessel—either one made of copper or one of a red color. Every day, he should go for alms to exactly seven houses while proclaiming his deed, saying, "Give alms to an *avakīrṇin*," thus announcing, "I am an *avakīrṇin*. Furthermore, the wearing of the hide occurs only at the time of wandering for alms, and not at the time of the fire-oblation (*homa*). And so Manu will also state [this] only after the oblation.
"When this offense has been committed, having worn the skin of a donkey,
he shall go for alms at seven houses, proclaiming his own deed" (MDh 11.122).
Even the eating of food is to be done only once a day, as Manu says:
"Subsisting on alms obtained from them, eating only once a day, and performing ablutions at the three periods of the day, he becomes pure in one year. [MDh 11.123] Thus [ends the section]. 23.18.
He shall be purified after one year. || 23.19 ||

By practicing in this manner for one year, he becomes purified. This should be understood as applying to all twice-born (*dvija*) castes without distinction; likewise, Manu has employed the term "twice-born" [in the following verse]:
"The knowers of Dharma who expound the Veda declare that the intentional emission of semen by a twice-born man observing a vow constitutes a transgression of that vow" (MDh 11.120).
And thus, this principle—that half [the penance] applies to a Brāhmaṇa and half to a Kṣatriya—does not apply here. As Śāṇḍilya also said:

"A twice-born man who has broken his vow of chastity, as well as a king and a Vaiśya, having performed the sacrifice with a donkey and subsisting constantly on alms, becomes purified after one year, being composed in mind."

In this case, even when there is an intentional emission without a woman, only the *homa* (oblation) is to be understood as required. As Vasiṣṭha says: "This very same [penance applies] even upon the intentional emission of semen" [VaDh 23.4]. The same applies to sexual intercourse with a man. Thus says Kāśyapa:

"Having indulged in sexual intercourse with a man, and likewise having performed an intentional emission, a student (*brahmacārī*) shall bathe after repeated practice and then perform a sacrifice with clarified butter."

For forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and others as well, this very same penance should be understood as being more severe than a *kṛcchra*. As Vasiṣṭha says: "A forest-dweller, upon breaking his initiation (*dīkṣā*), should perform a *kṛcchra* for twelve nights and then increase the great thicket (*mahākakṣa*); a mendicant (*bhikṣu*) should act like a forest-dweller, with the exception of the increase of the *soma*. Here, the mention of "twelve nights" is intended to include the three *parāka* penances. As Śāṇḍilya says: "If a forest-dweller or an ascetic (*yati*) should intentionally break [their vow], they shall perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin*, conjoined with the three *parākas*."
Even for those who have performed their penance, social contact must not be maintained; as Kauśika has said:
"For lifelong celibates, forest-dwellers, and ascetics who have broken their vows—even if they are purified in this world, no restoration [to full status] is recognized."
Regarding the intentional discharge [of semen] by ascetics (*yatis*) and forest-dwellers (*vanasthas*), that which was spoken by Kaṇva should be observed:
"Having intentionally discharged [semen], a householder should perform ablutions with the *Vāruṇī* verses;
both a forest-dweller and an ascetic, however, should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* vow."
"One should sip water three times with the *gṛhya* mantras, namely the three: *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*.
A renunciant (*yati*) and a forest-dweller (*vanastha*) should further recite the sixteen [verses] beginning with 'punar mām'.
This also applies except in the case of dreaming. Regarding even dreaming, Kāśyapa said:
"Having performed three prostrations to the Sun in a dream, a householder should perform [the penance];
likewise, an ascetic and a forest-dweller should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite three times.
Regarding sexual intercourse with a human being for a householder, that which was stated by Manu is to be observed.
"Having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man or again with a woman, or on a bullock-cart, or in water, or during the day, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.

And thus, the penance for acts causing loss of caste (jātibhraṃśakara) should be understood from this [text] as applying elsewhere. [This applies] when the woman is indeed one's own wife, and specifically regarding intercourse during her fertile period (ṛtu). Thus said Aṅgiras:

"However, during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), bathing is prescribed for the couple due to the suspicion of conception; but when one approaches [the wife] outside the fertile period (*anṛtu*), purification is like that for voiding urine or feces. Regarding sexual intercourse during the day, a wiping with the *vāruṇī* verses must be performed. As Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
Having engaged in sexual intercourse on the eighth, the fourteenth, or on a festival day,
one should bathe with one's clothes on during the day and purify oneself with water-libations dedicated to Varuṇa.
"In the case of impurity due to death, as well as during a *śrāddha*, one should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* vow;
at a solar or lunar transit (*saṃkrānti*) and during an eclipse, one should perform the *Taptakṛcchra*.
Regarding sexual intercourse with a man, that which was spoken by Kaṇva should be observed for both forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*).
Having engaged in sexual intercourse with a male, a forest-dweller or an ascetic shall become pure from that sin by performing both the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
Thus [ends the section]. 23.19.
Enough with this digression; now the subject at hand is commenced.

If semen is emitted without fear, without disease, and without dreaming, one must, for seven nights, refrain from kindling the fire, begging for alms, and [other such duties], and perform an oblation of clarified butter or two fuel-sticks with the *retasyā* verses. (23.20)

This refers to an unintentional case, since the previous rule was stated regarding intentional acts. "Upon the emission of semen" means when semen is discharged; "in a state free from fear and disease" means while not suffering from illness; "without performing the kindling of the fire, gathering fuel, or wandering for alms for seven nights" means failing to do so while not being ill. And thus says Manu: "Without having performed the wandering for alms" (MDh 2.187), and so forth. Alternatively, there is an oblation of clarified butter and fuel-sticks with the two *retasyā* verses, namely, "May my [seed] return to me" and "May my mind return. There is an option between the fuel-sticks and the clarified butter depending on what is available. However, in the case of emission during sleep, that which was stated by Manu should be observed.
"A twice-born student who has unintentionally emitted semen in a dream shall bathe, worship the sun, and recite three times the verse beginning with 'punar mām'. (MDh 2.181).
This same rule should be understood to apply even when emission occurs due to fear or disease.
If one unintentionally emits semen during fear, illness, or in a dream,
one should worship the sun and then recite the verse beginning with "punar mām."

This is because of the characteristic marks of Prajāpati’s dharma. And likewise, that which has been stated regarding the emission of semen in a dream for forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) should be understood to apply equally to fear and disease. As for what was stated for the lifelong celibate student (*naiṣṭhika*), that very same penance should be understood to be doubled. As Hārīta says:

"Whatever a student under training (*upakurvāṇa*) might do, whether intentionally or unintentionally, a lifelong celibate student (*brahmacārī naiṣṭhikaḥ*) shall perform that very same penance doubled."

Others, however, explain it as: "except in the case of seminal emission during sleep, provided that fear or disease are excluded"; for them, an equivalent option should be understood as stated by Manu. Even other than in the case of sleep, an expiation must be sought. (23.20)
A student who has fallen asleep after sunrise shall remain standing for the day without eating, and one who has fallen asleep after sunset shall remain sitting for the night, reciting the Sāvitrī.

“Upon whom the sun has risen” means that the sun rises while he is still lying down. Although the mention of the *brahmacārin* (celibate student) is already implied by the context, it is stated here so that a different penance might not apply to householders and others; for them too, there is the possibility of the rule “and this applies to the subsequent ones, provided it does not conflict” (GDh 3.10). Regarding the householder, one should consult the opinion of certain authorities as stated by Āpastamba: “Some say he should restrain his breath until sunset” (ĀpDh 2.12.15). For the ascetic (*yati*) and the forest-dweller (*vanastha*), however, the penance is fasting accompanied by the *brahmakūrca* rite. As Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says:
"If a forest-dweller (vanastha) and an ascetic (yati) are both overtaken by the rising sun,
they should subsist on the *brahmakūrca* and recite the *praṇava* for a day.
The procedure for the *brahmakūrca* is also to be understood from another Smṛti, as Prajāpati has said:
Having taken and placed either a leaf of the *pālāśa* tree, a lotus leaf, copper, or even one made of gold, one should then commence the ritual action.
Taking cow’s urine with the Gāyatrī mantra, cow dung with "gandhadvārā," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhikrāvṇo."

Reciting "śukram asi" and "tejo 'si," he should take clarified butter; reciting "devasya tvā," he should take water with *kuśa* grass. Having fasted on the fourteenth day, he should then perform the rite on the full moon day.
One should provide twice as much urine as cow dung, four times as much clarified butter,
eight times as much milk, and likewise five times as much curd.
Then, having placed [the food] upon *darbha* grass with *pālāśa* leaves,
one should lift it up and offer it to the deities in the proper sequence.
Having likewise offered oblations to Agni, Soma, and Savitṛ with the Praṇava, he should likewise perform the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
Having offered thus, one who is composed should then contemplate the remaining evil; having stirred it with the *praṇava* alone, one should churn it out with the *praṇava*.
Having extracted it with the *praṇava* alone, he should drink it with the *praṇava* as well;
performing this *brahmakūrca* rite month after month, the twice-born man [attains purification].
"His soul liberated from all evil, he goes to the heavenly world.
Even if the evil of embodied beings remains in their bodies, residing within the bones, the Brahmakūrca burns it all away, like a blazing fire consumes fuel. Thus it is said.

One should stand day after day without eating; one should remain standing during the day, but at night one must eat. For one who has practiced this—standing while performing the *saṃdhyā* worship—if the sun sets upon him, he too shall not eat during that night. This practice is to be understood from the indicative mark: "He should stand during the day and sit during the night" (GDh 26.6). In both cases, he should recite the *Sāvitrī*. Thus says Manu:
"If the sun should rise while he is lying down out of intentional negligence..."
"Or if he sets [the sun] while reciting [the mantra] out of ignorance, he should fast for a day. [MDh 2.220]

This applies both when done intentionally and unintentionally, based on the indicative mark (liṅga) in the text: “Or he may go to sleep [if it happens] through lack of awareness. In this case, bathing with one's clothes on is to be understood, according to the statement of Śaṅkha: “One who has been overtaken by the sunrise or sunset of the sun shall bathe with his clothes on and mutter the Sāvitrī verse as it follows the [three] libations. Here too, the phrase “provided there is no danger and no disease” is understood, for the purpose of declaring that there is no fault in those cases. Thus says Jābāli: “One who is overtaken by the sunrise of the sun while free from danger and disease becomes liable for penance. In this regard, it should be understood that half [of the penance] applies to a Brāhmaṇa and [the other] half to a Kṣatriya. 23.21.
Having seen something impure, one should look at the sun after performing breath control (prāṇāyāma).

An impure person refers to a *caṇḍāla* or similar individual; upon seeing such a person, one should perform a single *prāṇāyāma* and look at the sun. Because of the context, this applies to a religious student (*brahmacārin*) during his period of observances. For lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*) and others, that which was stated by Manu should be observed:
"Having sipped water and being pure, he should always mutter, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to his enthusiasm and *pāvamānī* verses according to his ability" (MDh 5.86).

For a householder, the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) is to be used [as a substitute], because the *Jābāli-gṛhya-sūtra* states: "Upon seeing something impure, a twice-born man should mutter the *praṇava*. For all [castes], except during times of formal observance (*niyamakāla*), there is merely the requirement to look at the sun, according to the statement of Auśanas: "Upon seeing something impure, one should look at the sun, or at a Brāhmaṇa, or at cows, or at fire. Furthermore, because the term "twice-born" (*dvija*) is employed in the *Jābāli-gṛhya*, this rule applies generally to the twice-born; for a Śūdra, there is neither an injunction nor a prohibition. (23.22)
In the case of eating what is unfit to be eaten, there is the state of being devoid of excrement.
In the case of eating forbidden foods such as garlic and the like, one must achieve the state of being free from fecal matter through emesis or purgation. Thus says Manu:
"One who desires his own purity must not eat food that is unfit for consumption;
what has been eaten unknowingly should be vomited up, or else quickly purified by means of cleansing agents. (MDh 11.160)
If, due to the passage of time, the food has become stale and it is impossible to perform emesis or purgation, one should observe what is stated in another Smṛti. As Prajāpati says:
"Having consumed food that should not be eaten, one should give away the value of that food to a Brāhmaṇa;
one should remain for a day dressed in wet clothes, or else provide a cow's daily ration."

Regarding food defiled by improper ownership (*parigraha-dūṣita-bhojana*), one should give its value to a Brahmin according to what was consumed; in the absence of that, one should give a day’s fodder for a cow; and in the absence of even that, having eaten sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) once, one should remain dressed in wet clothes for as many days and nights as the number of days it was consumed—this is the sequence there. For those things defiled by time, location, or inherent nature, the rule stated by Vyāghra is to be observed.
Having consumed food that should not be eaten, one should practice eating only at night, or one should eat food free from pungent condiments and salt day after day.
"One should drink the milk of a tawny cow, warm from the milking;
this *kṛcchra* penance, performed by Vyāghra, purifies even a dog-eater. Thus it is said.

In this case as well, for eating food corrupted by time (*kāla-duṣṭa*), one should observe the *naktabhojana* (eating only at night) penance; for eating food corrupted by its source (*āśraya-duṣṭa*), one should eat food free from alkaline salt (*akṣāra-lavaṇa*); and for eating food corrupted by its nature (*svabhāva-duṣṭa*), one should drink the milk of a tawny cow (*kapilā*). The phrase "day after day" applies to all [the following]. The meaning is: for as many days as the forbidden food was eaten, for that many days [the penance is to be observed]. Furthermore, regarding eating once [per day], among the [penances] mentioned in the preceding verse—such as the giving of wealth (*vyaya-dāna*) and so forth—it should be understood that only that specific amount [of the prescribed gift] is to be given. Even for wearing wet clothes, it lasts for only a single day. In the verse concerning *naktabhojana*, when eating once [per day], the meal is complete; when eating twice [per day], the meal consists of only half the usual amount. Regarding the consumption of forbidden food by Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, the principle stated by Kavaṣa applies: namely, half and half of that [half] respectively. This being the case, half and half of the [gifts] mentioned in the verse on the giving of wealth should be calculated. In the verse on *naktabhojana*, it should be understood that for a Brāhmaṇa, the meal is devoid of flavorful substances (*rasa-dravya*); for a Kṣatriya, it contains some flavorful substances; and for a Vaiśya, it contains a greater quantity of them. In the verse on drinking milk, it should be understood that for a Kṣatriya there is drinking twice [per day], and for a Vaiśya, drinking thrice [per day]. Thus, when one has unknowingly eaten any of the four types of forbidden food, one should perform emetics and purgatives, provide the gifts of wealth, and then observe the penance to be described later, beginning with "fasting for at least three nights" (GDh 23.24). When the act is intentional, the penance should be performed after providing the gifts of wealth and so forth, because there is no distinction made in the verse concerning the giving of wealth. And regarding emetics and purgatives, it is because it has been stated that "what is known [to be forbidden] is burnt [by these]."
Now he states the expiation:
fasting for at least three nights. (23.24)

Since the rule *“prior to the five-clawed animals”* (GDh 23.27) will describe those things that are defiled by their source, their time of acquisition, or their manner of preparation, this present rule should be understood as referring to those things that are defiled by their very nature (*svabhāva*). Among these, since garlic and the like, as well as certain animals, will be treated in the two subsequent sūtras—“*for seven nights, or those that have withered of their own accord*” (GDh 23.25–26)—it should be understood that this present rule applies to others besides those. Furthermore, regarding intentional eating even once, this [present rule] applies; however, for unintentional eating once, one should look to what was stated by Manu: *“In the case of the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day”* (MDh 5.20). Even here, regarding the intentional eating once of birds such as the *baka* crane and others, one should look to what is stated in another Smṛti. As Śaṅkha says: “Upon eating the flesh of the *baka*, *balākā*, *cakravāka*, *haṃsa*, *plava*, *khañjarīṭa*, *kāraṇḍava*, *vaṭahāra*, *caṭaka*, domestic pigeon, parrot, *śārika*, *kiraka*, *sārasa*, *ṭiṭṭibha*, owl, pigeon, red-footed bird, web-footed bird, *cāṣa*, *bhāsa*, *madgu*, *bhañji*, porpoise, crocodile, *makara*, *timi*, *timimigila*, ant-hill lizard, or *labhi*, one should abstain from food for twelve nights, or drink barley-gruel mixed with cow’s urine. Regarding unintentional eating, Uśanas says: “Upon eating the flesh of the *balākā*, *plava*, *haṃsa*, *kāraṇḍava*, *cakravāka*, *khañjarīṭa*, domestic pigeon, *vaṭahāra*, *vīṭaka*, red-footed bird, owl, parrot, *sārasa*, *ṭiṭṭibha*, *bhāsa*, *madgu*, great *ṭiṭṭibha*, *cāṣa*, *bhāsa*, web-footed bird, crocodile, *kulika*, or carnivorous fish and the like, one should drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for three nights. Since the act of threatening (*avagūraṇa*) is the least among all [offenses], the periods of three or five nights should be understood here according to the capacity [of the offender]. (23.24)
Or for seven nights. || 23.25 ||
This refers to the subject of garlic and similar items. As Manu has said:
"Having intentionally eaten a mushroom, a village pig, garlic, a village cock, an onion, or a leek, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste]."
"Having unknowingly eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra.
Thus, there should be seen no option regarding the Sāntapana; for unintentional consumption, both the Sāntapana and a seven-night fast apply.
He himself consumed only fruits that had fallen of their own accord, never overreaching for more.

The word *vā* (or) is supplied [from the previous context]. The term *śudhyet* (he is purified) is to be supplied here as well. "Fruits" refers to those that have fallen of their own accord and have not been split by crows or other such creatures. The inclusion of the phrase "fallen of their own accord" is for the purpose of prohibiting injury to stationary beings (*sthāvara-hiṃsā*). The intention is that one who consumes them does so without overstepping the limits, meaning without performing an investigation into their qualities or defects. This refers to the removal of hunger. The meaning is that he is purified in the amount of time required for this state to be accomplished. Regarding the unintentional consumption of animals such as single-hoofed ones that are otherwise unfit to be eaten, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance mentioned by Manu should be understood to apply.
"Having eaten dried meat and mushrooms growing from the earth, as well as anything unknown that has been situated in a slaughterhouse, one should perform this very same vow.
[MDh 11.155] In the case of intentional consumption, it should be understood that a Cāndrāyaṇa penance accompanied by a Taptakṛcchra is required. Thus says Śāṇḍilya:
If a Brahmin intentionally eats food that is forbidden to eat,
he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow together with the Taptakṛcchra penance.
Thus [ends the section]. 23.26.
Prior to the five-clawed animals, there shall be emesis and the consumption of clarified butter.

Regarding that which was previously declared unfit to be eaten from among five-nailed animals, the penance for consuming it is emesis and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*); there is no other separate penance as in the previous cases. Although the state of being "devoid of feces" (*niṣpurīṣībhāva*) alone would suffice, by the force of the initial statement and the word "and" (*ca*), in some instances fasting (*upavāsa*) is also required. The lack of a compound indicates that the actions may be performed either individually or collectively, depending on the gravity of the offense. In that regard, prior to the list beginning with those "accused" (*abhiśasta*), there is only the consumption of clarified butter; during the consumption of clarified butter, the intake of other food is prohibited, and that consumption should continue until the body is saturated. Prior to the list beginning with those "excluded from the row" (*apāṅktya*), there is emesis and the consumption of clarified butter; prior to the list beginning with cow's milk and so forth, there is one night of fasting; and prior to the five-nailed animals, there is only emesis—thus it should be understood. However, regarding non-five-nailed animals, it has been stated: "Of the limbs of beasts of prey, camels, and donkeys" (GDh 23.5). This applies to eating once unintentionally; if done intentionally, the *taptakṛcchra* penance mentioned by Manu should be observed.

"Having eaten the food of any one of these others unintentionally, one should fast for three days; but having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance. [MDh 4.222] In this regard, when the act is not preceded by conscious intent and vomiting is impossible, a three-day fast is to be observed. Regarding the repeated intentional consumption of these four types of food mentioned above—excluding the meat of animals such as dogs and the like, and excluding the food of those of inverse caste (pratiloma), the fallen (patita), those in birth-impurity (sūtaka), and those in death-impurity (śāva)—that which was stated by Manu is to be observed. As he said:

"Having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or the leavings of women and Śūdras, or having consumed forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights. [MDh 11.152] Or else, that which was stated by Aṅgiras:
If one consumes that which is unfit to be eaten, drunk, or licked,
as well as semen, urine, or feces, what shall be the expiation?
Having drunk water from these— lotus, udumbara, bilva, kuśa, aśvattha, and palāśa— one becomes pure after seven nights.

Thus concludes the penance for eating forbidden food (*abhakṣyabhakṣaṇa*). For one who is capable, a *kṛcchra* is to be observed. As Vasiṣṭha says: "In the case of eating what has been licked by a dog or a crow, or the leavings of a Śūdra, an *atikṛcchra* is prescribed; in other cases, a *kṛcchra*" [VaDh 14.33]. Regarding the repeated consumption of garlic and similar items, the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* mentioned by Manu should be observed: "Or else, in the case of the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day" [MDh 5.20]. And in the case of repeated consumption of meat, three *cāndrāyaṇas* are to be observed. As Prajāpati says:
"One should perform three *cāndrāyaṇa* penances for eating forbidden food or meat;
however, having done so even once, one should perform only one—so says Prajāpati.
There are two types of outcasts (*patita*): the outcast and the great outcast (*mahāpatita*). The great outcast is one who commits a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*). As Manu has said:
"Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher's wife, and associating with those who commit such acts—these they call the great sins (mahāpātaka). [MDh 11.53]

One who is other than these is a *patita* (outcast); his state of being an outcast consists in the loss of the duties of the twice-born (*dvijāti*). In that context, the *patita* is enumerated among those whose food is not to be eaten (*abhojyānna*), since for others [the status of] untouchability (*aspṛśyatva*) is already established. And thus, the *patita* is not merely untouchable. As Uśanas says: "The *patita* and the one who has committed a minor offense (*upapātaka*) have food that is not to be eaten; the one who has committed a great sin (*mahāpātaka*) is also untouchable. And so, because the perpetrator of a great sin is enumerated among those whose food is not to be eaten, another penance (*prāyaścitta*) must be observed. In that regard, if one unintentionally eats the food of a *pratiloma* or a perpetrator of a great sin even once, an *atikṛcchra* penance is to be observed. As Hārīta says:
The food of one born of a Śūdra from a woman of higher caste who has transgressed the natural order,
the food of a perpetrator of a mortal sin (mahāpātakin), and the food of a woman and an ungrateful person;
Likewise for one who has fallen after having ascended [the funeral pyre], for the husband of a woman of the same lineage,
