for those who have resorted to heretical sects, and for an ascetic as well.
If a Brahmin eats [forbidden food] once through negligence, he should perform the *atikṛcchra* penance;
if he does so intentionally, he should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*; and if it is raw food, he should perform half of that.
"In the case of eating [forbidden food], it is half [the penance]; in eating together [with such a person], threefold;
in eating his leavings, fourfold; and in drinking his water, half of that again.
Thus, in every case, it should be understood that if it is raw grain (*āma*), it is only half, and so forth. The same is heard regarding repeated unintentional practice as well.
"In the case of eating the leavings of food unknowingly through repeated practice, one should perform a quarter of a *kṛcchra* penance for a year;

likewise, in the case of intentional repeated practice, the best of the twice-born should perform thirty *kṛcchras*. In that regard, for the intentional repeated practice involving *caṇḍālas* and others, one should observe the very same [penance]. As Manu says: "Having approached women who are *caṇḍālas* or outcastes," and so forth. Even concerning the subject of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), that which was stated by Āpastamba should be observed:

"Covering the area from below the navel to above the knees, bathing at the three times of day, eating food that is neither pungent nor salty, he shall not enter a house for twelve years; then there will be success, then union with the Noble Ones. This same rule applies to others who have committed acts causing loss of caste (*patanīya*). [ĀpDh 1.28.11–14] In all matters concerning those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) and the direct order (*anuloma*), an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be prescribed. For those born in the inverse order from Śūdras, and for those born in the direct order from Śūdra women by twice-born men, it should be understood as being like the case of eating the food of a Śūdra. As Śāṇḍilya said:
"Food was ordained as equal for the twice-born when it is produced by a Śūdra born of a Śūdra woman through transgression of the order, even from the wives of those [higher castes].
Regarding the eating of a Śūdra's food, Prajāpati says:
The food of a Śūdra is declared to be unfit to be eaten by a Brāhmaṇa;
if he eats it once through ignorance, he should drink the Brahmakūrca mixture once.
"But in the case of repeated practice, one should consume that blameless raw food;
however, if it is done intentionally, one should perform a three-night penance, and for habitual practice, one should perform the Kṛcchra.
Regarding the eating of food from a house where there is birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*śāva*), that which is stated in another Smṛti should also be observed. As Garga says:
If one eats intentionally during a period of impurity caused by death or birth, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
if there is intentional repetition, one should then perform a Kṛcchra followed by a Cāndrāyaṇa.
"But for three days one should perform [the penance] unintentionally, and in the case of repetition, indeed the *kṛcchra*.
This also refers to the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa when another Brāhmaṇa is impure. Regarding the impurity of Kṣatriyas and others, it is stated therein:
"Twofold, threefold, and even fourfold."
"Thus it is proclaimed regarding the period of impurity for those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes.

In that regard, whatever penance has been prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa during the impurity caused by another Brāhmaṇa should be understood to apply to the Kṣatriyas and others as well. However, among lower castes, it should be seen as increased in the sequence of double and triple; among higher castes, it should be decreased according to that same sequence. Likewise, it is stated in that very same source: "For all [castes] among those of the same caste, the ransom (niṣkraya) is recorded as being like that of a Brāhmaṇa."
"Increasing gradually and decreasing gradually, even among those of lower and higher castes.
Thus, it should be understood that in all cases, the penance is to be performed only after the period of impurity has elapsed:
"He who eats their food becomes pure after ten days" (MDh 5.102).
This is because of the indicative mark [in the scriptures]. In that regard, for one who has eaten [at a funeral] due to a formal injunction (*niyoga*), the rule stated by Vasiṣṭha is to be observed:
"He who eats during the impurity (*āśauca*) of a Śūdra, or even during a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), becomes a worm at the end of his own body and subsists upon that very excrement."
"And if a twice-born man eats by appointment when a corpse has not yet passed ten days, he shall go to a terrible hell and be born among the wombs of animals. [VaDh 4.31–32]

“It is known from tradition that one who studies the *Saṃhitā* while fasting for twelve months or twelve half-months becomes purified” (VaDh 4.33). In this regard, it should be understood as follows: for food eaten during the period of impurity (*aśauca*) of a Śūdra, the penance lasts twelve months; for a Vaiśya, ten months; for a Kṣatriya, eight; and for a Brāhmaṇa, twelve half-months. Likewise, since garlic and similar items are mentioned separately, the drinking of barley-gruel (*yavāgū*) for seven nights prescribed by Manu should be understood to apply only to those who have avoided such things. Furthermore, its inclusion among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*) is likewise intended to indicate that one should not associate with such a person, rather than to include it within the category of penances (*prāyaścitta*), or to include it in the ritual of purificatory water (*śāntyudaka*) like the case of the student who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*). In the case of intentional and repeated practice, the penance should be regarded as equal to that for drinking liquor (*surāpāna*).
"Consuming forbidden food or drink constitutes six acts equal to the drinking of liquor," according to the statement of Manu (MDh 11.56). That [penance] is also two *cāndrāyaṇas*. As Garga said:
"When the intentional consumption of things that should not be eaten or drunk has been performed..."
"One should perform two *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, for that [act] is equal to drinking liquor.
In this case, it should be understood that the penalty for the one who feeds [the sinner] is double, because Kātyāyana stated: "The punishment for the one who feeds is double.
Enough with excessive talkativeness; we shall now explain the subject at hand: "In cases of verbal abuse, falsehood, and violence, penance lasts for a maximum of three nights. (23.28)

Regarding verbal abuse (*ākrośa*), this applies except in cases involving extreme sins (*atyantapātaka*) or secondary sins (*upapātaka*). Regarding falsehood (*anṛta*), it refers to lying after having promised to bear witness or in matters such as the non-payment of debts. Regarding injury (*hiṃsā*), it concerns stationary beings (*sthāvara*), since injury to mobile beings has already been addressed. "Three nights at most" means for all [other] multi-night durations; thus, one should calculate it as one night, two nights, or three nights. "Austerity" (*tapas*) refers to what has been prescribed, such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*); that constitutes the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). In that regard: for abusing a Brāhmaṇa, three nights; for abusing a Kṣatriya, two nights; for abusing a Vaiśya, one night; for abusing a Śūdra, one day. This is how it should be understood regarding verbal abuse. Regarding falsehood as well, the sequence should be understood according to the object, starting with a Brāhmaṇa. And regarding injury: for a fruit-bearing tree, two nights; for a shade-tree used for livelihood, one night; for such [other trees], it is merely one day. This also applies to an act performed without the owner's permission and for some other purpose.

Others explain as follows: when one is falsely accused by someone else through mere abusive sound (*ākrośa*), [the penance is as stated]. But in the case of being falsely accused face-to-face (*saṃmukhābhiśasta*), that which was spoken by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa," and so forth. In that context, for a sound denoting a mortal sin (*pātaka*), the penance lasts three nights; for what is equal to a mortal sin, two nights; for a minor offense (*upapātaka*), one night; and in other cases, merely a day. And by the word "violence" (*hiṃsā*), those who have made a firm resolve to commit violence are meant. Thus says Vasiṣṭha:

One who voluntarily abandons his life while still living shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and fast for three nights; constantly wearing an oily garment, restraining his vital breaths within himself, he should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times. Furthermore, according to this same procedure, he may recite the Gāyatrī, or else, having kindled the fire, he should offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras.
Thus [VaDh 23.19–21].

In that regard, for a Brāhmaṇa and others, having caused a wound or similar injury with a weapon or the like while the victim remains alive: if [the act was committed] intentionally, there is a *kṛcchra* penance; if only by thought (*buddhi-mātre*), there is a three-night fast. For a Kṣatriya, having caused a wound or similar injury while the victim remains alive: wearing wet clothes, there is a three-night recitation of the *Aghamarṣaṇa* or the chanting of the *Gāyatrī*; if intentional, this is merely a three-night austerity (*tapas*). For a Vaiśya, having caused a wound or similar injury while the victim remains alive: wearing wet clothes and eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), one must daily perform oblations (*homa*) with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras three times each; if intentional, this is merely a three-night austerity. For a Śūdra, having caused a wound or similar injury while the victim remains alive: for one day and night; if intentional, it is merely a single day’s penance. This should be applied accordingly. The meaning of the word "falsehood" (*anṛta*) applies to these cases as well.
Others explain that by the word "insult" (ākrośa), physical violence (daṇḍapāruṣya) is meant.

That is incorrect. First of all, regarding a Brāhmaṇa, an expiation for verbal assault against a Brāhmaṇa has been stated: "Threatening while enraged," and so forth (GDh 21.20). By that very rule, it is possible to determine the penalty for all castes through the principle that "for a Kṣatriya, it is half [of what is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa]," and so on. Therefore, this [present rule] pertains specifically to the subject of verbal assault. Even therein, this applies to the case of a learned Śrotriya reviling one who is not a Śrotriya. However, when one who is not a Śrotriya reviles a Śrotriya, a penalty corresponding to the offense must be determined according to the rule: "A Kṣatriya [should pay] a hundred [paṇas] for reviling a Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 12.8), and so forth. For Kṣatriyas and others as well, when reviling their own respective caste, a penalty corresponding to the offense must be determined. As for the specific fines, they have been stated by Manu.
"For the twice-born, when committing an offense against one of a different caste, the fine is twelve [paṇas]; for unutterable offenses, that same fine shall be doubled. [MDh 8.269]

In this manner, a punishment corresponding to the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must also be determined for a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*). Where an expiation alone is prescribed and no punishment is mentioned, there a punishment must be devised; however, where a punishment alone is mentioned and no expiation, there an expiation must be devised. Thus, expiation is established even in cases of "unmentionable" offenses (*avacanīyapada*). An "unmentionable" offense refers to false accusation regarding many types of diseases such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), and does not concern mortal sins (*pātaka*) or minor sins (*upapātaka*), because a greater severity of expiation is observed in those cases. Furthermore, the expiation for the fault of lying applies here specifically to the case of a consecrated fire-sacrificer (*āhitāgni*) concerning property matters. Thus says Prajāpati:

"If one who drinks Soma should speak untruth, he should perform the supreme penance for three nights, or he should offer seven full oblations of clarified butter with the mantra 'svāhā'. Regarding matters concerning what is not beneficial (*anartha*), one should observe what will be stated later: "In the case of a transgression of speech or mind, there are the five *vyāhṛtis*" (GDh 25.12). If it is argued that this refers to secret (*rahasya*) offenses, we say no; for since it has been stated, "The penance is the same because there is no distinction" (GDh 25.9), it does not mean that the rule does not apply to public (*prakāśa*) offenses. In the case of what is harmful (*anartha*), there is the touching of the right ear. As Vyāghra says:
"One should touch the right ear upon speaking a falsehood, spitting, touching the teeth, sneezing, or conversing with outcasts" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.30).

However, in the case of being a witness, speaking falsely constitutes a sin equal to that of the major offenses (pātaka) for those who maintain the sacred fires and others; as it is said: "False testimony," and so forth (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 21.10). Regarding the false statement made after having given one's word, Hārīta says:

"Having made a promise, if one should speak falsely, whether it be a lie or even a truth, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow accompanied by the Taptakṛcchra penance. Thus it is said; furthermore, a specific rule for the religious student (brahmacārin) should be observed, as Garga has stated:
"One should observe celibacy for three nights or one night for speaking untruth;
likewise, for eating honey or meat, or for carrying out a corpse, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance.

In this regard, the period is three nights for matters concerning wealth, and one night for other matters. However, for the consumption of forbidden meat, this [penance] preceded by the *taptakṛcchra* must be performed. If it concerns an unintentional act, it is like the penance for an *avakīrṇin*; but if it concerns an intentional act, there must be a renewal of the sacraments (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). Thus says Prajāpati.
Having eaten meat, a celibate student (brahmacārī) must undergo the rite of re-initiation (punaḥsaṃskāra);
in the case of repetition, he must perform the lunar penance (aindava), and one who is a lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) must perform double that.

"One dwelling in the forest should perform it threefold, and an ascetic (yati) should perform it fourfold; likewise in the case of eating meat, speaking untruth, and carrying out a corpse. As for the carrying out of a corpse, this refers to those other than a student (brahmacārī) who are not [related to] a teacher (upādhyāya) and so forth. As Manu says:
"Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own *ācārya*, *upādhyāya*, father, mother, or guru, the one observing a vow (*vratin*) is not deprived of his vow.

[MDh 5.91] In this regard, it has been stated that the word "own" (*sva*) is connected with each term individually; therefore, it refers to one's own *ācārya* alone, and not to the *ācārya* of one's *ācārya*, and so on in all cases.
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, one's conduct toward him is required to be the same as toward the teacher himself. [MDh 2.205]

Thinking, "Let it not be thus," it follows that there is indeed a lapse of the vow (*vrata-viyoga*) upon the removal of those [impurities]. In that case, it should be understood that after performing the *kṛcchra* penance, one undergoes re-consecration (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*). Since there is no lapse of the vow in the case of the teacher (*ācārya*) and others, the absence of impurity (*aśauca*) is also established; for it has been stated: "The ten-night impurity due to death (*śāvam āśauca*) applies to the *sapiṇḍas*, except for the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the initiated (*dīkṣita*), and the student (*brahmacārin*)" [GDh 14.1]. Even before the ten days have passed, one becomes impure at the time of offering the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa-nirvāpaṇa*). Thus says Śāṇḍilya: "When a student performs the removal of the funeral cakes for his father..."
"One should remain impure for that much time; thereafter, having bathed, one becomes pure.
Thus it is said. Regarding eating without having bathed, the penance prescribed by Prajāpati should be observed:
"When a practitioner of a vow eats without even bathing after having offered the funeral ball (piṇḍa) to his father..."
Having touched a corpse, a woman in her courses, a Caṇḍāla, or likewise a woman who has recently given birth;
"If unintentional, it shall last for three nights; if done intentionally, one should perform the Sāntapana penance.

Furthermore, regarding householders and others touching or eating [food] from those who have recently given birth (sūtaka), the rules stated in other Smṛtis should be observed. As Vyāghra says: "When a householder eats after having touched an untouchable (aspṛśya)..."
If it was unintentional, it should last for three nights; if intentional, one should observe it for six nights.
"A renunciant (yati) and one dwelling in the forest (vanastha) should perform that very same [rite].
Where, however, there is no specific distinction for the student (brahmacārin) and others, it should be understood that the rule is the same for all. As Uśanas says:
"Having touched a Caṇḍāla or a Śvapaca, or even [the remains of] excrement, urine, or food-leavings..."
"Purity shall be attained after three nights; having eaten what is left over [from such a person], one should perform the six-fold penance. Likewise, Vyāghra also says:
"One who has been touched by a Caṇḍāla or a menstruating woman (udakyā) should simply perform a bath."
"Being touched by what has been left over [from such a person], one should perform the penance for three nights.
Likewise, Yama also says:
"He who, being thirsty, drinks water from the water-vessels of a Caṇḍāla..."
But he who casts it out at that very moment should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
"If one does not discharge water [from the penis] while the food in the body is still undigested, the Prājāpatya penance should not be given; rather, he should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra.
Thus also says Vyāsa.
If one unintentionally drinks water that has come into contact with the vessel of a Caṇḍāla,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night, bathing, and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
"Therefore, having bathed, one should act accordingly; out of desire, one should perform the *sāntapana* penance.
Regarding those [impurities] in a pond or a well, the same has been stated by the wise. Thus also says Vyāghra:

"Having consumed water from a well containing feces, urine, or food remnants, the twice-born are purified in three nights; for a jar [of such water], the Sāntapana penance is prescribed. Thus also says Śātātapa.

"Having passed urine or excrement, a twice-born man who eats while failing to perform his purification out of delusion must observe a three-night fast; however, if he does so intentionally, he should perform the Sāntapana penance. Thus also says Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha.
"If one eats in a single row, provided he does not touch another and a boundary has been established with ashes, his row is not defiled. Thus [it is said].

Likewise, Śaṅkha states: “In the event of voiding urine or excrement within water, one must bathe with one’s clothes on and perform an oblation with the Mahāvyāhṛtis. Similarly, in that same work, another rule is given: “Having discharged semen, urine, or excrement into water, one should fast for three nights and mutter the mantra ‘idam āpaḥ pravahata. In that very same text: “Upon seeing a bad dream or an ill omen, one should give ghee and gold. Other Smṛti texts should also be consulted in this manner. (23.28)
If he is truthful in speech, there is an oblation with the Vāruṇī and Mānavī verses. || 23.29 ||

But if he has been provoked by a truthful statement, or reviles him with truth—by implication, it is understood that previously he was provoked by untruth—then an oblation (*homa*) must be performed with clarified butter (*ājya*) using the *vāruṇī*, *mānavī*, and those addressed to Prajāpati deities; or else the previously mentioned three-night rite should be performed. Since there is no specific distinction, the oblation is performed only once. This applies to the three *vāruṇī* verses and likewise the *mānavī* verses. Due to the use of the plural number, they may be used either optionally or collectively. In this regard, it should be understood that if one who is not learned in the Vedas reviles a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), the verses are used collectively; in the opposite case, they are used optionally. (23.29)
Some maintain that there is no fault in speaking untruth in the context of marriage, sexual intercourse, jesting, or when one's life is at stake.

The intention is that at the time of marriage, when inauspicious signs appear among those present on the side of the bride or the groom, there is no fault in speaking falsely for the sake of pronouncing auspicious words; likewise in sexual intercourse, such as when one's lineage (gotra) is mistakenly mentioned, and in jest—that is, in ridicule—and in a situation involving one who is afflicted or suffering, where something is said for the purpose of alleviating that suffering: some hold the view that in these circumstances, there is no penance for speaking untruth because there is no fault. Gautama, however, maintains that even in these cases there is a fault. In this regard, Gautama’s opinion should be understood to apply to one who is bound by religious observances (niyamastha), while the opinion of the others applies to anyone else. (23.30)
But indeed not for the sake of one's teachers. 23.31.

One should not speak untruth even for the sake of one's gurus, such as in matters concerning marriage and the like. The particle *khalu* is used here for emphasis, meaning "never," even according to a single person's opinion. The word *tu* (but/rather) serves to specify a distinction: one should not speak untruth even for the sake of gurus such as maternal uncles, and especially so for the sake of the teacher (*ācārya*). (23.31)
What, then, is the reason for this? It is this very one:
"Even by speaking a falsehood to a teacher regarding matters of little consequence, even if only in thought, one slays seven generations of ancestors before and after oneself. (23.32)

It destroys and afflicts—joining them with sin—the seven who come after, such as sons, and those who have passed away before, such as parents; this applies even when one considers a falsehood in one's mind for the sake of a teacher, let alone when one speaks it. This holds true even for minor purposes, much more so for great ones. (23.32)
For sexual intercourse with an outcaste woman (antāvasāyinī), there shall be a year-long Kṛcchra penance.

The woman of the lowest caste (*antāvasāyinī*) has been explained in the context of the rule: "And he who would lie with women of the lowest caste" (GDh 20.1). If sexual intercourse is committed with her, for a single act of going, there is a year-long *kṛcchra* penance; that is to say, one must remain for a year according to the procedure of the *prājāpatya*. || 23.33 ||
For ministers, it is twelve nights. || 23.34 ||

And thus it is understood that this was previously [stated] as being intentional (*buddhipūrva*). Although it should have been called simply "kṛcchra," the specific mention of "twelve nights" (*dvādaśarātra*) is for the purpose of including the *parāka* penance. As Aṅgiras has said:
"In the case of approaching, eating with, or killing those of the lowest castes (*antyaja*), purification shall be by means of the *parāka*; so the venerable Aṅgiras declared."

This [penance] also applies to one who has desisted even before the emission of semen. Why? Because of the traditional rule (smṛti) regarding an action performed at a prior time: "Having emitted semen into his own kind... (MDh 11.170). Therefore, it is understood that there is a lightness of penance. And in this way, in cases such as approaching a maiden (*kumārīgamanādi*), a half-penalty and half-penance should likewise be observed. But when the act of intercourse is completed, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "For twelve nights he should subsist on water; for twelve nights he should fast; or he may go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. By this very [rule], intercourse with a Caṇḍālī woman is explained" (VaDh 23.38, 40–41). In the case of intentional repetition, the penance for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*) should be observed. Even there, because of the employment of the word "equal" (*sama*) and because of the prescription of a fine of one thousand [paṇas]—namely, "But [the fine for] a woman of the lowest caste is one thousand" (MDh 8.385)—three *Cāndrāyaṇa* penances should be observed, since they are equal to the fine of one thousand. In that regard, in the case of unintentional repetition, the penance should be observed as long as no pregnancy has occurred; there is no assumption of a greater [penance]. Why?
"Double the fine is for a wicked man who has been accused for a year,
as well as for cohabiting with a *vrātyā* woman or a *caṇḍālī* woman"—
this is the indication from the text. Alternatively, the *kūśmāṇḍa* oblation should be understood [as the penance], as Prajāpati has stated:

"O best of the twice-born, if one is not satisfied with the penance for sexual union with all women, he should offer clarified butter with the *kūśmāṇḍa* mantras. Thus it is said; however, when a conception has occurred, there is no penance. As Śāṇḍilya says:
"Even for a twice-born man who has fathered a child upon women of the lowest caste, whether intentionally or unintentionally, no expiation is prescribed; by his very birth, he is a Caṇḍāla.
Thus, there is an absence of expiation when the act is committed intentionally and repeatedly.

"By approaching, eating the food of, or accepting gifts from Caṇḍālas or women of the lowest castes, a Brāhmaṇa falls [from his status] through ignorance; through knowledge, however, he becomes their equal. (Manu Smṛti 11.175). According to this statement of Manu, the expiation prescribed here for eating food should be understood as half [the amount] even in the case of accepting a gift. Why?
Of the cooked, the uncooked shall be half; whatever else has come for consumption, this other substance is declared to be half of that.
Thus, from the words of Vyāghra. 23.34.
For approaching a woman in her courses, there is a three-night penance; for approaching a woman in her courses, there is a three-night penance. (23.35)

In the case of approaching a woman during her menses, there shall be fasting for three nights. Although the context already concerns sexual intercourse (*gamana*), the repetition of the word "approaching" is intended to include entry [into her presence] beyond that which is permitted for one's own wife, as well as to restrict it to entry only with one's own wife. In this regard, it should be understood as follows: if the act occurs once unintentionally, the rule stated by Śātātapa should be observed: "Upon handling urine or feces without water, upon touching a dog or a crow, and upon approaching a woman in her menses, one must bathe with one's clothes on and perform the *mahāvyāhṛti* oblation. For repeated unintentional acts, the rule stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "Upon approaching a woman in her menses, one should give a white bull with black genitalia. However, this present rule applies to intentional intercourse occurring once; for repeated intentional acts, the rule stated by Manu should be observed.

"Having discharged semen among non-human females—with the exception of cows—into a woman in her courses, into those who are not the proper womb, or into water, one shall perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.

[MDh 11.173] In this regard, it should be understood that for a Kṣatriya woman the penance is double, and for a Vaiśya woman it is triple. Likewise, it should be known that for a Brāhmaṇa the penance is half [of what is prescribed], and for a Kṣatriya it is [half of that], and so forth. Regarding sexual intercourse, the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* oblation should also be observed. The repetition [of the concluding verse] is intended to mark the completion of the chapter. 23.35.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the *Maskarīya-gautama-bhāṣya*.
Regarding the twenty-fourth chapter:
the expiation for those who have confessed their sins has been stated; however, since the expiation for those whose sins have not been confessed must now be declared, he says the following.
Secret expiation is for a fault that has not been made public. 24.1.

The secret [atonement] must be kept undisclosed so that it is not known by others. The undertaking of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is for the purpose that even by a small [act], there may be the removal (*niṣkṛti*) of a great sin. "Of one whose fault is unmanifest" means of one whose transgression is unknown to the world. By the word "antara," it is meant that which cannot be performed otherwise; thus, the meaning is "of one whose transgression is unknown to others. In cases such as adultery or association with outcasts, it is not possible for the knowledge to belong to the perpetrator alone, because [otherwise] it would be impossible [to conceal]. But how is it that a non-public sin is considered a minor offense, rather than being of a uniform nature like the consumption of poison? No logical justification need be sought here, as it is to be understood from the scriptural statement itself, just as in the distinction between intentional and unintentional acts. Alternatively, this is stated because [the public act] is necessarily to be performed. For he who commits a public sin proceeds regardless of either world [this or the next]; his intention (*saṃkalpa*) becomes greater, and consequently, the gravity of the fault increases, and he becomes a cause for the engagement of others, since people generally follow what others have done. Therefore, in the case of a public act, both the cessation of public censure and the expiation must be performed; whereas in the other case, there is merely the destruction of the sin.
If one desires to accept something that should not be accepted, or has already accepted it, one should recite over water the four-verse hymn beginning with "taratsamandī" (VS 16.1–4). 24.2.

One should mutter these four verses beginning with “tarat sa mandī dhāvati” in the waters in the form of the *aghamarṣaṇa* mantra; otherwise, one would be recognized by others. This recitation should be understood as lasting for three nights. Thus says Manu:
“Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that is censured, a man is purified in three days by reciting the *taratsamandī*. [MDh 11.253]

And this should also be understood regarding the consumption of *haviṣya* (sacrificial food): when one desires to accept—that is, wishes to take—property belonging to someone who is unfit to be accepted due to defects of birth or conduct; by speaking thus, he shows that there is a secret penance even for a sin committed intentionally, and that there is a fault even in the mere desire to accept what is unfit to be accepted. This is to be seen as distinct from what he will state later: “Or [for] the transgression of speech and mind, [there is penance] for what is forbidden” (GDh 25.12). Or, having accepted it, one should perform this very rite; because of the word “or,” it also applies to having eaten what is unfit to be eaten. In that case, when one did not previously know that "this person is unfit to be accepted," then one should recite the mantra after having accepted it; otherwise, it should be understood that it was known beforehand. Here, regarding the eating of what is unfit to be eaten, it should be understood as referring to things other than semen, urine, and excrement, because Śaṅkha has stated: “Upon consuming semen, urine, or excrement, one should drink water consecrated with the syllable *Oṃ*. Where no specific mantra for recitation is mentioned, the eleven [syllables of the Gāyatrī] should be understood as the minimum. In this regard, the distinction between intentional and unintentional acts is as follows: it should be performed after forming a resolve such as, “I have committed this transgression intentionally; let this be the expiation for it”; by that much, the penance becomes more severe. Thus says Āpastamba: “He who kills while intoxicated [by passion] incurs the full fruit of the offense along with the intention” (ĀpDh 1.29.2–3). But in the case of an unintentional act, the mere expiation should be performed without a formal resolve. Likewise, Vasiṣṭha also shows the severity of the expiation based on the mental contemplation of the sin: “Having mentally contemplated a sin, one should recite three times the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *Oṃ*, or the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn” (VaDh 23.23). Therefore, the determination of the expiation depends on the distinction between intentional and unintentional acts. In the case of repetition as well, one should repeat that same penance.
The best of the twice-born, whose fault is well known, should perform the fulfillment of his recitation (japa) and other rites;
likewise, for a sin committed in secret, he should practice that very same penance.
Thus, from the words of Prajāpati. 24.2.
Desiring to eat what is unfit for consumption, one should scatter [seeds] over the earth. || 24.3 ||

The four kinds of food that are unfit to be eaten have been mentioned previously. One who "desires to eat" (bubhukṣamāṇaḥ) means one who wishes to consume it. The mention of "desiring to eat" is for the purpose of indicating an emergency; therefore, it should be understood that if survival is not possible without consuming it, then one may do so. "One should sow in the earth" means one should cast it into the ground.
Others, however, read "āvaped" as "pṛthivyām āvapet," and they explain it as "one should cast it upon the earth.
That is incorrect, because if that were the case, it would be understood by others [as a different act]. (24.3)
Some say that for one who has sexual intercourse during another season [than the prescribed period], purification occurs by touching water.

The second case ending has the sense of connection with the word *eka* (one). "In the midst of the season" means during sexual intercourse or approaching a woman for that purpose. Some say that purification comes from touching water—that is, from bathing with one's clothes on. Gautama, however, desires that after bathing with one's clothes on, one should also perform the ritual wiping (*apāmārjana*) with the *ābliṅga* and *vāruṇī* verses. And so he will state later: "Deceit, calumny," etc. (GDh 25.10). Since "sexual intercourse" (*āramaṇa*) has been mentioned, this refers to one's own wife. In the case of another's wife, this additional expiation for violating another's wife (*paradāra-prāyaścitta*) should be observed. That too he will state: "Regarding this they ask: 'How many ways does the *avakīrṇin* enter? (GDh 25.1), and so forth. 24.4.
Some [say it occurs] "among women. || 24.5 ||

Some maintain that for those who have engaged in sexual intercourse with female animals such as mares—with the exception of cows—this very same ritual bathing in water is prescribed. Gautama, however, will state this in the passage beginning with "anārjava" (GDh 25.10). Regarding the cow, one should look to what was stated by Manu: "But being self-controlled, he should fast for three days, entering the water three times a day;
having recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, he is released from all sins" (MDh 11.259).
Some describe it thus: "This very same penance applies to women who are unchaste.
That is incorrect;
for "A woman is not defiled by her paramour, nor a Brahmin by his Vedic ritual."

For it has been stated by Vasiṣṭha: "Water is not defiled by urine or feces, nor is fire by the act of burning. Likewise, in times of distress, it should be understood that there is no fault even for a Brahmin who is corrupted by Vedic ritual action. 24.5.
Regarding the secret penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa, he now says: "Or, one may observe a milk-vow for ten nights, a second period with ghee, and a third with water. (24.6)

One who observes the milk-vow subsists on milk; likewise for the first ten nights, the second with ghee, and the third with water. According to the word "or" (vā), he may instead eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) throughout these thirty nights. The option is to be understood according to one's capacity. 24.6.
He states the prescription of its qualities:
"In the [periods] beginning with the day, one should eat only one meal, with clothes moistened by water. (24.7)

“During the first parts of the day,” such as the forenoon, he is “one who eats but one meal,” meaning he does not eat in the evening. Because of the plural number, this refers to the milk-vow (*payovrata*) option during three ten-night periods; consequently, eating twice while consuming sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) is not contradictory. He should have his clothes wet with water, that is, he should wear damp clothing. This also should be understood not to apply to the rule beginning with “only during that vow” (GDh 24.12), so that he may not become visible. 24.7.
"Body hair, nails, skin, flesh, blood, sinews, bone, and marrow"—these are the oblations; "I offer them into the mouth of Death" is the end of all [the formulas]. (24.8)

The *mantras* beginning with "hair" (*loman*) and so forth [are to be used]. How is this understood? It is because this is not an instruction regarding substances; because the instruction ends with the particle *iti*; because the phrase "at the end of all" (*antaḥ sarveṣām*) is introduced as an addition (*anuṣaṅga*); and because of the mention of the *homa* offering. Therefore, one should perform the *ājya-homa* into the fire with these *mantras*. The phrase "in the mouth of oneself" (*ātmano mukhe*) is the addition for all [the *mantras*] beginning with "hair. The actual application is: "I offer my hair into the mouth of Death," and so forth. (24.8)
The expiation for the killing of a learned Brahmin. 24.9.

This is the expiation for killing an embryo as previously described. The repetition of the word "expiation" (*prāyaścitta*) in this section on expiations is for the sake of an unseen spiritual purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and not for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Although one could have used the masculine designation "the killer of an embryo" (*bhrūṇagha*), the use of the neuter term "sin" (*pāpa*) is intended to indicate that this [expiation] applies only when the act is committed once. In the case of repetition, however, a more severe penance must be devised, as stated by Manu: "One who desires to remove even gross and subtle sins should mutter for a year the verse beginning with *ava* and the verse beginning with *yat kiṃcedam*. (MDh 11.252) || 24.9 ||
Now, another [point]: the rule has been stated. 24.10.

Now another expiation will be stated. The previous one was optional; this is distinct from the previous expiation for killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*). The rule has been stated: "Or he may subsist on milk" (GDh 24.6), and so forth. Now, however, specific provisions are being enjoined. 24.10.
One should offer oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, beginning with "O Agni, do thou protect us," and with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras, using clarified butter.

One should offer clarified butter (ājya) daily, in sequence, once each day, with the mantra beginning “O Agni, do thou carry us across” (RV 1.189.2), with the Mahāvyāhṛtis beginning with Bhūr, with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras, and with those beginning “Whatever offense against the gods, O God” (GDh 27.7). The mention of *ājya* (clarified butter) is to be applied to the preceding [rule] as well, according to the maxim of the lion’s glance (*siṃhāvalokita*). Some hold that wherever there is no specific mention of a substance, it applies everywhere. By the use of the word “and” (*ca*), it is also to be offered with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om). 24.11.

Or, observing that same vow, one who is exhausted by breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) for the [sins of] killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, or violating the Guru’s bed should mutter the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn; this is equal to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice.

By that very statement beginning with "or one who observes the milk-vow" (GDh 24.6), one should perform penance for the four sins starting with the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. Here, "theft" refers specifically to the theft of gold, because it occurs in association with the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, the drinking of liquor, and violating the Guru’s bed. One who is exhausted and weary from breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) should mutter the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, beginning with "Righteousness and Truth" (*ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca*). This is equal to—that is, equivalent to—the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). By this, he shows that for the drinking of liquor and other such sins, bathing at the conclusion of the horse sacrifice is the cause of purification. By the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*), the horse sacrifice itself should also be understood [as a means of purification]. As Manu has said:
"Just as the Aśvamedha, the king of sacrifices, is the dispeller of all sins, so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the destroyer of all sins. [MDh 11.260] Thus [it is said]. 24.12.
Or he should repeat the Sāvitrī a thousand times; indeed, he purifies his own self.

By virtue of the context, it follows that by practicing the *Sāvitrī* many times for one month regarding these very same sins, one attains purification quickly. The particle *ha* is a *nipāta* used to indicate that this is a Vedic injunction. The word *eva* serves to emphasize restriction. The word *vā* indicates that the practice of the *Sāvitrī* is a cause of purification even for other sins as well. Thus says Vasiṣṭha:

"Desiring purification, even when situated amidst all sins, one should employ the Goddess [Sāvitrī] with a maximum of a thousand recitations, a middle of a hundred, and a minimum of ten" (VaDh 26.15).
The restrictive emphasis (avadhāraṇa) should be understood as intended to demonstrate its state of being the most purifying. As Vyāghra said:
"There is no recitation equal to the Sāvitrī; no oblation equal to the Vyāhṛtis;
no gift equal to food and water; and no austerity equal to non-violence."
Thus [ends the verse]. 24.13.
Or, by repeating the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times while submerged in water, one is released from all sins; one is released. 24.14.

Observing that very vow, by practicing the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times for thirty nights within the water, one is released from all evil committed knowingly or unknowingly; the meaning is that one becomes purified. || 24.14 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the *Maskarīya-Gautama-bhāṣya*. The twenty-fifth chapter [begins]:

The secret penances for the great sins (*mahāpātaka*) have been stated. Now, those for the minor sins (*upapātaka*) must be declared. Among them, the penance for one who has broken his vow of celibacy (*avakīrṇin*) is stated first; this is because he is guilty of a minor sin and because his penance is extended from elsewhere. In this regard, a Vedic text is cited to demonstrate the extreme gravity of the offense.
Regarding this, they say: "In how many ways does one who has broken his vow of chastity enter [into expiation]? || 25.1 ||

Seeing the gravity of this fault, the distinguished ones say: "In how many ways?"—for the word *avakīrṇin* denotes one who has broken his vow (*avipluta*), that is to say, one who is stained (*rakta*). By this, the intention is: "Where does his life-force and so forth go? (25.1)
Having thus raised a doubt, he himself says:
"The Maruts [conquered] by means of breath, Indra by means of strength, Bṛhaspati by means of sacred luster, and Agni by means of all the rest. (25.2)

One enters the Maruts—the winds—by means of the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*); Indra by means of strength, that is, the power of enthusiasm; Bṛhaspati by means of splendor (*tejas*) born from the study of the revealed scriptures (*śruti*) and so forth; and Agni by means of the other [breaths]. By the use of the restrictive particle *eva*, it is indicated that there is no entry into others such as the mind (*manas*). By the inclusion of the term "all," it includes the eyes, ears, and other senses. One becomes undisturbed, empty, short-lived, lacking enthusiasm, devoid of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and deficient in sight and other faculties. This scriptural passage has been cited for the purpose of generating a sense of urgency or, alternatively, in connection with the topic of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). (25.2)
Now he states the expiation:
On the night of the new moon, having established the fire, he offers the oblations of clarified butter for expiation. 25.3.

If it is argued that the word "he" (*sa*) is redundant because the subject "one who has broken his vow" (*avakīrṇī*) is already under discussion, [we reply: it is for the purpose of referring specifically to one who has committed the offense in secret; otherwise, since a Vedic passage is cited as an example, there might be the suspicion that this expiation applies to all celibate students (*brahmacārin*). On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), during the dark fortnight, "at night" should be understood as meaning "at midnight," for otherwise it would be too public. "Having established the fire" means having produced fire by friction from some piece of wood; otherwise, since the presence of fire is already established by the mention of the act of offering (*juhoti*), this instruction would be unnecessary. The mention of "expiation" (*prāyaścitta*) is for the purpose of making known that the performance of the rite must follow immediately after the transgression, or [to indicate] that which is stated in other Smṛtis.

[This is] for the purpose of establishing the general rule for expiation beginning with: "And one should daily recite the Sāvitrī and purificatory texts according to one's ability" (MDh 11.225). Furthermore, the mention of *ājya* (clarified butter) is for the sake of restriction. Thus says the Gṛhyasmṛti: "There are four sources of *ājya*: that from the udder, or that from outside, curds, or milk. The mention of the oblation (*āhuti*) is for the purpose of performing the *homa* with focused attention. 25.3.
"I am besprinkled by desire, I am besprinkled, O Desire; to Desire, svāhā! I am milked by desire, I am milked, O Desire; to Desire, svāhā! || 25.4 ||
The entire recitation of the mantra is [authoritative], because it is found to be so in the directly revealed scripture (pratyakṣa-śruti). || 25.4 ||
Having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, sprinkled water around it, and prepared the sacrificial site, he should rise and worship [the fire] three times with the verse, "May they sprinkle me. (25.5)

At the conclusion of the oblation of the two mantras, having offered one fuel-stick silently, he then sprinkles water around [the fire] with the formulas beginning, “O Aditi, you have granted your consent. Then, having performed the rite for the sacrificial site as prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of the Chandogas, he should rise behind the fire and worship the established fire three times with the verse, “May they sprinkle me. (25.5)
For the purpose of praising the attendance upon the fires, he cites a Vedic explanatory passage (arthavāda):
"There are indeed these three worlds; [this is for] the conquest and the mastery of these worlds. (25.6)

These three worlds are known as Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar. Their *abhijitiḥ* is their non-falling away; their *abhikrāntiḥ* is birth right there [in those worlds]. By saying "by conquest" (*abhijityā*) and "by advancement" (*abhikrāntyā*), the text shows that for one who has spilled his seed (*avakīrṇin*) without performing expiation, there is no place at all even in the three worlds. The word *vai* is meaningless, according to the statement: "Vedic syllables may be meaningless. The direct designation "these worlds" is for the sake of emphasis. (25.6)
Regarding this very matter of ritual action, some say that he who might feel as if purified should sacrifice in this manner and recite the consecratory formulas in this manner. 25.7.

With reference to this very rite, the meaning is "having performed it. According to the opinion of some, he who might feel as if purified—even after performing the secret penance prescribed in the relevant section—should offer this very oblation and likewise worship the fire in this same manner. 25.7.
"The bridegroom is the sacrificial fee," [so it is said]. || 25.8 ||

It should be given before the performance of the rite; because it is to be performed by oneself, it must be given to another Brāhmaṇa. Due to its gravity, this should be understood as referring to the case of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*). According to Gautama, however, there is merely a repetition of that same expiation. 25.8.
The penance applies without distinction. 25.9.

The common expiation for all those who have committed minor offenses (*upapātakin*) has already been stated. Some explain this as a supplement to the following sutra: "The expiation to be described applies without distinction to both secret and public offenses. In that regard, it should be understood as supplementary to those [offenses] prescribed for public cases, whereas for secret cases it stands independently. The mention of "expiation" implies that one should not show disregard even when the offense is slight. (25.9)

Having emitted semen in a Śūdra woman, in a non-vaginal opening, or during a blameworthy act—even if done intentionally—after practicing crookedness, calumny, forbidden conduct, or consuming forbidden food, one should touch water while reciting the *abliṅga* verses and the *vāruṇī* verses.

Crookedness (*anārjavam*) is mental action consisting of lack of straightforwardness or deceit (*śāṭhyam*). Slander (*paiśunam*) is verbal action consisting of speaking ill of others. Violation of a rule (*niyamalopaḥ*) is physical action consisting of engaging in prohibited conduct. Consuming what is not food (*anādyasya prāśanam*) is the enjoyment of various kinds of non-food. And having discharged semen into a *śūdra* woman, that is, having engaged in sexual intercourse with her. The separate mention [of this case] even though she is a married woman is for this purpose. Although the penance for this is indeed the same as that for a minor offense (*upapātaka*), nevertheless, because of the specific instruction, it should be understood that this very one applies. Having thus considered the relationship between the general and the particular, the settled rule must be applied in all cases. The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including a menstruating woman. "And in a non-vagina" means in the mouth and so forth; from the word "and," it includes discharging [semen] through effort. "And in a defective act" means when an act has been performed that causes pain to another; from the word "and," it includes the non-performance of what is enjoined. Even if preceded by intention, the meaning is "even if prepared for that purpose. Although the consumption of non-food and so forth is already included under "the practice of what is prohibited," they are mentioned separately for the purpose of emphasizing their avoidance with great care, or for the sake of the severity of the penance. Consequently, purification should be seen as being performed many times. Some say "defective act" refers to theft. In that case, it should be understood as other than the theft of gold, because that is mentioned [under the category of mortal sins] in the passage beginning "killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor... (GDh 24.12). Others say it refers to injury (*hiṃsā*). In that case too, it should be understood as excluding mortal and minor sins, because those two have already been mentioned. Regarding the phrase "even if preceded by intention," some explain the word "even" (*api*) to mean "also in the case of repetition. That is incorrect, because it has already been stated that the penance is repeated for each instance of repetition. It is for the purpose of showing that even in the case of unintentional acts, there should be no lightness [of penance]. With verses addressed to Water (*abliṅgābhiḥ*), i.e., those whose deity is Water, such as "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and so forth. Because of the plural number, there should be at least three. With verses addressed to Varuṇa (*vāruṇībhiḥ*), i.e., those whose deity is Varuṇa, such as "imaṃ me varuṇa" and so forth. Having first bathed, he should pour water over his head. The irregular grammatical construction is for the purpose of indicating an option. Therefore, it should be understood as "either with the *abliṅga* verses or with the *vāruṇī* verses. (25.10)
Or with other purifying substances. || 25.11 ||

The mention of "purifiers" (pavitra) is intended so that the inclusion of only those [mantras] which are purifiers—such as the Aghamarṣaṇa and others—may be understood; there is an option between them according to what is possible. 25.11.
If there is a transgression of speech or mind that has been forbidden, the five vyāhṛtis [are to be recited].

In the case of transgressing what is forbidden, or in the case of transgression of speech and mind, the previously mentioned expiation applies. This is stated for the sake of specification: the five *vyāhṛtis*, beginning with *bhūḥ* and ending with *puruṣasatya*, should be recited eleven times in the form of an adoration of the Sun, following the sprinkling (*mārjana*) with water-mantras. 25.12.
In all cases, he should sip water with the formula: "May the day and the sun purify me," in the evening. 25.13.

"In all actions" means in actions such as dishonesty and the like. Some maintain that there should be a sipping of water (*ācamana*) for each of the *vyāhṛtis*; however, that is incorrect, because it would entail [the requirement] of "all" [of them]. The inclusion of the word "all" is so that it does not apply only to the three immediately preceding [syllables]. The mention of "water" is for the purpose of excluding alkaline substances and the like. Thus, having consecrated [the water] in the evening and morning, one should sip water for every sin. This is an optional alternative according to what is possible. (25.13)
Or he should offer eight fuel-sticks; having offered with the verse beginning "devakṛtasya," he is released from every sin—he is released. 25.14.

Or he should offer eight fuel-sticks with these mantras: “Thou art the expiation for sin committed against the gods, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for sin committed against men, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for sin committed against the ancestors, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for sin committed by oneself, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for sin committed by another, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for whatever sin we have committed by day or by night, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for every sin, svāhā! The meaning is that one should perform this very act after having offered [the oblations] with these mantras and without doing anything else. The particle *eva* (only) is used to indicate its preeminence. Consequently, when possible, this alone should be performed. One is liberated from all sin—not only from dishonesty and the like, but even from sins such as officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice. (25.14)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the *Maskarīya-Gautama-Bhāṣya*.

The twenty-sixth chapter begins: "The *kṛcchra*, the *atikṛcchra*, and the *cāndrāyaṇa* have been described; these constitute the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). Regarding this, he speaks the following for the purpose of defining the nature of the *kṛcchra*:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the penances (kṛcchra). 26.1.

The word *atha* (now/then) serves the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) and the purpose of demarcating the preceding mention of inauspicious things. Furthermore, these [words] also serve the purposes of religious merit (*dharma*) and worldly prosperity (*artha*). Thus says Śaṅkha: "One should purify the body according to one's ability through restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), mantras, vows (*vrata*), and so forth. By the word *vrata* here, the *kṛcchra* penances are intended. The word *ataḥ* (therefore) expresses the reason: because these [penances] also serve the purpose of auspiciousness, we shall therefore explain them. The mention of the term *kṛcchra* is for the sake of providing a technical name (*saṃjñā*). This is an etymological name (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), for it means that which liberates (*mocayati*) one from suffering (*kṛcchra*) or sin (*pāpa*). (26.1)
Having eaten sacrificial food for breakfast, he shall not eat for three nights. || 26.2 ||

He should consume for three days morning meals consisting of pure sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) prepared from rice and other grains, mixed with ghee and the like, and free from alkaline substances and salt. By using the term "meals" (*āśān*), he indicates that one should not eat to complete satiety. Having consumed [this] for three days, he should likewise not eat for three nights.

Now, one might object: since eating in the evening and morning is already established as the norm, the prohibition of eating at night is already accomplished simply by the mention of the "morning meal."

It is said: because of the specific mention of "sacrificial foods" (*haviṣyān*), there might arise the suspicion that one should eat sacrificial food in the morning but eat whatever is available in the evening; therefore, this statement is made to prohibit even the eating of whatever is available at night. (26.2)
Then, for another three days, he should eat only at night.

Immediately thereafter, there is another three-day period; by the inclusion of the word "another," it is established that the previous [three days] are also accomplished. One should eat only at night the ordinary sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), as before. 26.3.
Then, for another three days, he should not beg from anyone at all. || 26.4 ||

The word *atha* (now) serves to indicate a new topic. There is no specific restriction regarding the time for eating once [a meal] obtained without asking; however, the mention of "another" (*apara*) is intended to establish its similarity to the preceding three-day period. Consequently, the requirement that the food be fit for sacrifice (*haviṣya*) and that one should not eat to satiety (*atisauhitya*) should also be understood to apply here. One should not request anything from even a kinsman. In this way, there is no prohibition against what is obtained without being asked.

Some say: if, when food is being offered, one should say, "I will not eat non-sacrificial food (ahaviṣya)," then by implication a request for sacrificial food (haviṣya) has been made; therefore, in this case, there is no restrictive rule regarding the eating of sacrificial food.

But others say: "By this, receiving gifts is prohibited; since the prohibition against eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) pertains to the acceptance of what has not been offered by way of a request, it is not a prohibition of such food. Thus, there is no prohibition regarding one's own [food]. Since the rule 'one should not beg' would already be established, the specific formulation 'not anyone at all'—by the force of its introduction—indicates that even begging for the sake of attendants and the like must not be performed. (26.4)
Then, furthermore, he should fast for three days.

The word *atha* has the meaning already stated. Immediately thereafter, one should remain without food for three days. Here, the inclusion of the word "another" (*apara*) is for the purpose of establishing the performance of the three-day rite even by way of another method. As Vasiṣṭha says:
"One day in the morning, one day at night, one day with unasked food, and one day as a *parāka*—in that very manner, two further four-day periods."
"For the sake of favoring the Brahmins, Manu, the best among the upholders of dharma, has indeed declared the *śiśukṛcchra* for children, the elderly, and the sick. (VaDh 23.43).
For one who is unable to perform a fast, the rule stated by Bhāradvāja should be observed.
If a Brahmin performing the Prājāpatya penance is unable [to do so] day by day,
he should properly feed five pure Brahmins at a minimum, having honored them well.
Thus [ends the section]. 26.5.
Now he states the rule regarding the qualities [of the posture]:
"One who desires speed should stand during the day and sit during the night. (26.6)

During times not incompatible with eating and other such activities, he should remain standing during the day and sit during the night. In this way, since sleep is inevitable, it should be understood that he should resort to sleep only while remaining seated. By day and by night, he should be desirous of quickness; "kāma" here means intent. The meaning is that he should destroy even any experience that has arisen in every respect. Alternatively, he should constantly maintain the thought: "By every effort, may I quickly become pure."

Some explain: for one who desires purification quickly, he should stand during the day and sit at night; however, there is no fixed rule for one whose intention is, "I shall perform purification gradually according to my capacity. Thus, due to the abundance of auxiliary qualities (*guṇa*), the severity of the penance is inferred. Accordingly, this [penance] prescribed by Gautama should be understood as a *prājāpatya* accompanied by the full procedure (*itikartavyatā*) when it occupies the place of two *prājāpatyas*. When it occupies the place of a single *prājāpatya* alone, it is without the procedure. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Eating in the morning for three days, likewise in the evening, eating what is unasked for, and the *parāka*—this is the *kṛcchra*. [VaDh 24.2]

Others say: for those such as women and *śūdras* who do not have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to mantras, they should perform [the penance] without mantras according to the method taught by Vasiṣṭha and others; whereas for those who do have that entitlement, this [present rule applies]. Others read "one desiring speed" (*akṣiprakāmaḥ*) and explain it thus: one desiring speed should perform the *prājāpatya* [penance], but one desiring speed should instead perform what was taught by Vasiṣṭha. And so it has been said: "Now, if he wishes to act quickly, he should subsist on air for a day."
Standing in water throughout the night until dawn is equal to the Prājāpatya penance.
Having performed the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra eight thousand times when the sun has risen, one is released from all sins, provided that one is not a killer of an embryo. (VaDh 27.17–18) 26.6.
One should speak the truth. 26.7.

One should speak the truth as it actually is. The intention is that even in matters such as marriage and the like, one must not speak untruth by adopting the side of some [parties]. And thus, it is understood that even through truthful speech, the destruction of evil occurs. (26.7)
One should not converse with those who are ignoble. || 26.8 ||

The non-noble ones (anārya) are those castes other than the twice-born, as well as those who are outcasts from the castes; this is because of the use of the plural number, which includes [all] females, males, and neuters. 26.8.
One should constantly employ [the mantra] in Raurava and Yodhājaya. || 26.9 ||

The *raurava* and *yodhājaya* *sāmans* are sung upon this *ṛc*: “O Soma, being purified, flow in a stream. It should be understood that the word “constantly” (*nityam*) applies everywhere, as in the rule “he should stand during the day” (GDh 26.6) and so forth; for although one might have expected the verb “he should recite” (*japet*), the use of the term “he should employ” (*prayuñjīta*) indicates this. Some maintain that because of the word “constantly,” it should be connected with the form of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). Others hold that it means “repeatedly” or “many times. (26.9)

At each pressing, he should perform the ritual touching of water and purify himself with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, which contain the word *pavitra*, and with the eight verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ*. 26.10.

At each *anusavana*—that is, in the forenoon, midday, and afternoon—the bathing consists of touching water (*udakopasparśana*), because of the use of the prefix *upa*. One should perform the purification (*mārjana*) with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, which contain the word "purifier" (*pavitravatī*), and with exactly four verses beginning with *pavitraṃ te vitataṃ*; for since no specific number is mentioned, the plural number would remain unfulfilled without the number three. And one should sprinkle the water on the head after consecrating it with the eight verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ*. Others explain that the bathing is performed with these very verses because they are indicated by the instrumental case; furthermore, because the word *mārjana* is taught in the middle [of the sequence], the bathing is also performed with other purifiers. (26.10)
Now follows the libation of water (udakatarpaṇa). || 26.11 ||

Immediately thereafter, its inclusion [in the ritual] is for the purpose of ensuring the performance of the libations at each of the three daily sessions (*anusavana*). Thus, it is understood that water-libations (*udakatarpaṇa*) are also required for occasional (*naimittika*) ablutions. So says Bhṛgu:
"Ablution is said to be of three kinds: obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*).
For all three of these, this same procedure for libation always applies."

Regarding the phrase "touching water" (*udakopasparśanam*): where there is already a context concerning water, the mention of "water" again is for the purpose of ensuring that the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is performed even while standing in water. Thus, after stating a contradiction in another *smṛti*, it is further justified as follows: "That water which is not offered upon the ground is not accepted [by the ancestors], whether it is in [other] waters, in vessels, when one is angry, or when offered with only one hand."
Likewise: "One should never offer water to the ancestors while standing in water;
rather, having emerged from the water, one should perform the libation of water in a clean place."
Having said this, it was stated:
"All the hosts of gods are water; the hosts of ancestors are remembered as water.
Therefore, water should be given in the waters; what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible."
Likewise:
One should offer handfuls of water for the deities and the ancestors in the water;
one should offer handfuls of water for those who have died without the funeral rites on dry land.
Thus [ends the section]. 26.11.
Furthermore, as to from whom and how that [arises], he says:

Homage to Hamāya, Mohamāya, Maṃhamāya, to Dhūnvan, the ascetic, to Punarvasu; homage! Homage to Mauñjyāya, Ūrmyāya, Vasuvinda, Sarvavinda; homage! Homage to Pāra, Supāra, Mahāpāra, Pāradā, Pārayiṣṇu; homage! Homage to Rudra, Paśupati, the Great God, Tryambaka, the Solitary One, the Overlord, Hara, Śarva, Īśāna, Ugra, the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, the Compassionate One, Karpardin; homage! Homage to Sūrya, Āditya; homage! Homage to Nīlagrīva, Śitikaṇṭha; homage! Homage to Kṛṣṇa, Piṅgala; homage! Homage to Jyeṣṭha, Śreṣṭha, Vṛddha, Indra, Harikeśa, Ūrdhvaretas; homage! Homage to Satya, Pāvaka, Pāvakavarṇa, Kāma, Kāmarūpin; homage! Homage to Dīpta, Dīptarūpin; homage! Homage to Tīkṣṇa, Tīkṣṇarūpin; homage! Homage to Saumya, Supuruṣa, Mahāpuruṣa, Madhyamapuruṣa, Uttamapuruṣa, Brahmacārin; homage! Homage to Candralalāṭa, Kṛttivāsas; thus [be it]. 26.12.

This is not a single mantra, because of the use of the plural number in the expression "these very oblations of clarified butter" (*etā evājyāhutayaḥ*). What then? These thirteen mantras, beginning with the salutation (*namaskāra*) and ending with the salutation, are to be understood as such, since that is how they are seen to be recited in the Śruti. Consequently, the libation of water (*udakatarpaṇa*) should be performed with these mantras ending in salutations.

Others, however, say: "These mantras are fifty-six in number, ending in the dative case of the recipient. Still others say: "They begin with the salutation but do not end with it, because that is how they are seen to be recited."
This indeed is the worship of the Sun. 26.13.
This very *yajus* is the worship (*upasthāna*) of the Sun.

Now, since the word "worship" denotes an action, its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "*yajus*"—which denotes a mantra—is untenable; therefore, it must be stated that "the worship of the Sun is performed by means of these [mantras]."

This is not a fault. Since *upasthāna* means "that by which one stands near" (*upatiṣṭhate ’nena*), it is the *yajus* itself that is designated as such; thus there is no fault. Consequently, "the standing near of the Sun" (*ādityopasthāna*) implies, by its very meaning, an injunction for an action. The word *eva* (only/this very) is intended to indicate that this same mantra is to be used even for the water-libation (*udakatarpaṇa*). Otherwise, if it were merely stated "this is the standing near of the Sun," it might follow that the water-libation should be performed with the mantra prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. Furthermore, this should be understood as being in addition to the obligatory rites, or for the purpose of performing them according to the specific recensional tradition (*samāmnāya*). From this, it is understood that the water-libation and other such acts are to be done differently. If it is argued that praising the Sun with a mantra dedicated to Rudra is inappropriate, this is not a fault. For there is no such thing as an excessive burden for a scriptural injunction, and because the Sun is a partial manifestation (*aṃśa*) of Rudra. Thus it is said in the Purāṇa: "The eight forms of the Lord Śarva are named Earth, Water, Wind, Fire, Sacrificer, Ether, Moon, and Sun. If it is argued that this is contradictory because the Sun is seen there as Viṣṇu, there is no fault, because the two are non-different. And so it is said in the *Bhagavad-gītā*: "Among the Rudras, I am Śaṅkara" (BhG 10.23). Since the instruction regarding the standing near of the Sun follows immediately after the water-libation, it should be understood that the standing near of the Sun is to be performed three times at each of the three daily libations (*anusavana*).

Others explain: "Since it would have been sufficient to say, 'Now, the water libation and the worship of the Sun,' the fact that a separate rule is formulated implies that the worship of the Sun is to be performed only once every day.

Others maintain that the separate formulation is for the purpose of including this practice even in cases other than those requiring expiation (*prāyaścitta*). There is no contradiction, as there is with the word *vacana*, because the singular number is used despite the plurality already stated. || 26.13 ||
These indeed are the oblations of clarified butter. || 26.14 ||

Although it could have been stated simply as "and the oblations of clarified butter (*ājyāhutayaḥ*)," the specific expression "these very ones" (*etā eva*) is intended to exclude the possibility of a plurality of oblations. Therefore, these thirteen oblations of clarified butter are to be understood. The particle *eva* (only/very) serves the same purpose as in the previous case, namely to restrict the application according to the traditional recension (*samāmnāya*). Consequently, the mantras beginning with the salutation (*namaskāra*) and ending with the exclamation *svāhā* are to be understood [as the offerings]. Why? Because of the force of the term "oblation" (*āhuti*). Although the mantras are masculine in gender, the feminine designation "these" (*etāḥ*) is used because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "oblation."

Some explain: "These [offerings] are fifty-six oblations of clarified butter (ājya) with the dative case endings; the use of the feminine gender is for the purpose of referring to the dative case endings. This too should be understood as occurring at each pressing (anusavana), like the single-time worship of the Sun, because there is no mention of immediate succession. In this manner, he should proceed for twelve nights. 26.14.
At the end of twelve nights, having cooked a sacrificial oblation (caru), he should offer it to these deities.

At the end of twelve nights, not every day; or on the thirteenth day, because of the use of the sixth case-ending [to indicate time]. Since the injunction "he should offer with the *caru*" would have been sufficient, the inclusion of the words "having cooked" (*śrapayitvā*) is for the purpose of indicating the sequence: having purified [the grain], having cooked it, having sprinkled clarified butter over it, and having removed it from the fire. The word "he should offer" (*juhuyāt*) is intended to enjoin the act of oblation. In this matter, one should follow the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* as prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. If it is argued that the phrase "to these deities" need not be stated because it is already established by what is about to be said later, we reply that there is no fault, as the instruction is given for the sake of ensuring that the ritual is preceded by meditation (*dhyāna*). 26.15.
She said: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! To Agni and Soma, to Indra and Agni, to Indra, to the All-gods, to Brahmā, to Prajāpati, to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt! || 26.16 ||

The twofold recitation of the word *svāhā* is for the purpose of its application (*anuṣaṅga*) everywhere. The particle *iti* is used to indicate the inclusion of the specific form [of the mantra]. Therefore, in cases such as "to Indra," one should not append "to Puruhūta" and so forth; rather, only that [specific name] should be used. || 26.16 ||
Then follows the gratification of the Brahmins. || 26.17 ||

After the fire sacrifice (homa), on the following day, one should perform the satiation of Brahmins according to one's ability; it should be understood that even in that case, one should feed at least three. 26.17.
By this very [rule], the Atikṛcchra is explained.

By this very same procedure for the *prājāpatya*, the *atikṛcchra*—which produces even greater suffering—is also explained. If it is argued that this is already established by the plural number in the word *kṛcchrān*, we reply: the mention is intended to indicate that, like the *agniṣṭoma*, the first [penance] serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*). Consequently, even in the case of the *sāntapana* and other such penances, one must formulate an interpretation that does not contradict [the rule] beginning with "he should stand during the day" (GDh 26.6). The specific nature of these, however, is to be understood from other *smṛtis*. Thus says Baudhāyana: "For one who is self-controlled and vigilant, fasting for twelve days..."
This penance called Parāka is the destroyer of all sins.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass,
followed by a one-night fast, is known as the *sāntapana* penance.
Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise ghee—
one whose food consists of these for five nights is purified by the *pañcagavya*.
Those who expound the Veda declare that the Mahāsāntapana penance consists of practicing each of the [five] substances, beginning with cow urine, three times for seven days each.
Consuming grain-particles, oil-cakes, and buttermilk, or likewise subsisting on raw grain and air for one, three, five, or seven days— this Tulāpuruṣa rite is the destroyer of sin.
Barley-gruel for seven nights destroys the sins of embodied beings;
or fasting for seven nights achieves the same—this has been observed by the wise.

A twice-born man who observes the three bright fortnights of the months of Pauṣa, Bhādrapada, and Jyeṣṭha— dedicating himself to the constellations Ārdrā, the sky (the full moon), and the sun— is liberated from sin, with the exception of those sins that cause loss of caste.
By fasting on the new moon day and eating only sesame seeds on the full moon day,
one is liberated from the sins committed during the bright and dark fortnights throughout the year by means of these sacred festivals.
One who subsists on almsfood is purified from [the contact of] those who maintain the *agnihotra* fire in one month;
from those who dwell in the forest according to the *yāyāvara* mode, in ten or seven days.
A twice-born man who subsists on food given by the wealthy is purified in one day;
however, for one who adheres to the "pigeon-livelihood" (kāpotavṛtti), he is purified merely by drinking water after a single day has passed.
By reciting the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, *Sāmaveda*, or any other Veda three times through to completion while fasting, one is liberated from sin.
He who gives food, speaks the truth, and is non-violent toward all beings surpasses all those previously mentioned as purified by mantras.
The *trimadhu*, the *chandasa*, the *rudra*, the *gāyatrī* accompanied by the *praṇava*,
and the seven *vyāhṛtis*— the recitation (*japa*) of these is the destroyer of sin.
The Mṛgāreṣṭi, the Pavitreṣṭi, and also the Pāvamānī sacrifices—
these, when combined with the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice, are indeed destroyers of sin.
And listen now to this other secret being told:
one is liberated from all sins, with the exception of the great mortal transgressions.
Performing the sprinkling with purificatory blades (pavitra), reciting the Rudraikādaśinī,
offering oblations of clarified butter with the Vyāhṛtis, and bestowing gold, cows, and sesame seeds;
One should eat cooked barley-gruel with cow urine and the liquid from cow dung, along with curd, milk, and ghee; such a person is instantly liberated from sin.
He who has fathered a son on a Śūdra woman, and he by whom an unapproachable woman has been violated—
both of them are liberated from that sin after seven nights by this rite.

For consuming semen, urine, or feces; for eating forbidden food; for performing the *paryādhāna* rite; for sacrificing as a younger brother whose elder brother is unmarried (*parivitti*); and for being such an elder brother (*parivitta*)—this is the remedy.
"Even after committing many deeds here that are not sins,
one is released from all evils"— this is the teaching of the virtuous.
The authoritative scripture of the Mantra-path and its ritual procedure have been proclaimed,
by means of which Bharadvāja and others attained identity with Brahman.
With a clear heart, the brahmin, through the act of consuming milk and curd,
attains those various desires that reside within his heart.
O Brahmins, for one who has turned away from all sins and is engaged in meritorious deeds,
his ritual actions succeed even without effort.
