Therefore, those brahmins who are upright, being purified and acting with rectitude, quickly attain whatever they desire in their hearts.
Thus, these yogic exercises (yantras) should be performed by the wise man for as long as it takes for the impurity of the body to depart from the self.
Purified by these diagrams, having fasted for three nights and being pure, one whose self is cleansed should undertake that rite by which they desire to attain supernatural power.
The *kṣāpavitra*, the *sahasrākṣa*, the *mṛgāra*, the two *aṃhomuc* hymns,
the *pāvamānī* verses, the *kūśmāṇḍa* verses, and those verses addressed to Vaiśvānara.
Offering oblations of rice cooked with ghee three times a day for seven days,
observing silence, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), and restraining the activities of the senses;
If one gazes upon a lion in a water-pot filled with water at a crossroads,
saying "ma," one is released from all sins, even from a great transgression.
One is liberated even from that accumulation of evil deeds committed in old age, youth, or childhood, or those produced in previous births.

"Having fed the twice-born with milk-rice mixed with ghee, one should cause cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold to be given to those who have eaten. [cf. BDh 4.5.15–7.9], and so forth. Enough of this digression; that which is relevant is now being stated. 26.18.
But its specific distinction is stated:
he should eat only as much as he would take up [in one mouthful] at once. 26.19.

One should eat only as much of the sacrificial food (haviṣya) as can be taken up by a single hand in one motion during those very days. This is an injunction regarding the size of a mouthful (grāsa). Thus says Manu: "One should eat one mouthful each for three three-day periods as before;
then one should fast for the final three days. That is called the Atikṛcchra. [MDh 11.213]

The third is the water-eater (*abbhakṣa*); that is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. At the very same time for eating that was previously mentioned, one should drink only water. Such is the nature of this third *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. The mention of "third" is intended to indicate that sequence even when only the third is mentioned, as in "the second, the third," etc. And so he will say later: "Having performed the first," [GDh 26.20], and so forth. Although it would have been sufficient to say "the third by means of water" (*adbhis tṛtīya*), the inclusion of the word *bhakṣa* (eating) is for the purpose of showing that water also performs the function of food. Consequently, there is an absence of drinking water outside of the prescribed time. The creation of a technical name is for the sake of conventional usage. 26.19.
Now he states the fruit of these:
"Having first practiced them, one becomes pure, cleansed, and fit for action. (26.20)

Having first performed the Prājāpatya penance, being pure and free from the defect caused by the non-performance of prescribed duties, purified, and having exhausted the demerit produced by the practice of forbidden acts, he becomes and attains *karmaṇya*—that is, fit for the performance of optional and obligatory rites.

But is this not redundant? For its purpose is already established by the very injunction regarding expiation (*prāyaścitta*), since in the rule "one should perform [it]," its nature as a cause for the destruction of sin has been demonstrated. Furthermore, since that is also established by the word "from the first" alone, the inclusion of the phrase "having performed [the penance]" is likewise redundant. Likewise, the mention of the distinction between types of unrighteousness (*adharma*) through the words "pure" (*śuci*) and "purified" (*pūta*) yields little fruit, since both are established by the word "purified" alone. The same applies to the term "fit for action" (*karmaṇya*). If the intention is that one becomes eligible for ritual action simply by being free from unrighteousness, then it need not be stated, as it is already implied. If, on the other hand, the intention is the attainment of a more distinguished result, that too is incorrect; for whatever the specific fruit of a particular action may be, that alone it shall be, and no additional excellence of fruit arises.

To this it is replied: This undertaking is for the purpose of making known that these two types of dharma performed in another body are the means for their exhaustion. The inclusion of the term *caritvā* (having performed) is for the purpose of making known that [the purification] occurs through a single performance, because of the subsequent statement, "whatever else other than the great sins" [GDh 26.21], and because the prescription of penance generally applies only to the practice of what is prohibited. Furthermore, the word *pūta* (purified) might give rise to the suspicion that it refers only to prohibited matters; therefore, the word *śuci* (pure) is used. And it should be understood that this refers to [dharma] that is known, since it was previously stated that [the purification applies to] those [sins] declared in the Veda that are unknown.

[Objection: But surely this too is established by the mention of the "universal expiation" (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), because that applies generally to acts committed both intentionally and unintentionally. [Reply: It is said: this [expiation] has a specified scope, whereas that [universal expiation] has an unspecified scope. The same should be understood regarding prohibited matters as well. Furthermore, the phrase "in a rite" (*karmaṇye*) is for the purpose of making known the fact that when there is a connection with unrighteousness (*adharma*), there occurs an obstruction to the fruit of the rite. (26.20)
Having performed the second [twelve-year vow], he is liberated from whatever other sin he commits that is other than the great mortal sins (mahāpātaka). || 26.21 ||

"By performing the *atikṛcchra* penance, one becomes liberated from sins other than the *mahāpātaka*s (great crimes). Thus, while the destruction of the sin resulting from the transgression of *yama* and *niyama* is effected by the former [penance], this [penance] effects the exhaustion of the sin committed as a minor offense (*upapātaka*). Furthermore, because it is stated that this is a universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) when combined with the preceding [practices], it should be understood that it also exhausts even a *mahāpātaka* committed unintentionally. || 26.21 ||
By performing it for a third time, one removes all sin. || 26.22 ||

By performing the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penance, one destroys even a *mahāpātaka* (grave sin) committed unintentionally. Why? Because this [penance] is equal to the two preceding ones, and because the *sarvaprāyaścitta* (universal expiation) accompanied by the *cāndrāyaṇa* is the cause for destroying a *mahāpātaka* committed intentionally. Thus, this [penance] should also be performed in the place of the two preceding ones. The statement beginning with "the second," etc., should also be understood as referring to that same subject. This instruction is given so that there may not be a total combination of all [penances] in the case of the *sarvaprāyaścitta*. 26.22.
Now, having performed these three *kṛcchra* penances, one becomes bathed in all the Vedas and known by all the gods—both he who knows thus and he who knows thus. 26.23.

Now, immediately after this, one should perform these very three [penances] without interval, and not the *taptakṛcchra* and others. The term "kṛcchras" (difficulties) is used for the purpose of performing them with great intensity. In this same way, the *ārdravastra* and other penances are also to be understood; likewise, the recitations (*japa*), oblations (*homa*), and so forth. The phrase beginning with "in all" is stated with the intention that one becomes connected with a fruit equal to that which belongs to one who has bathed after studying all the Vedas. "He is known by all the gods" means he is capable of going to their world. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate [the following] with what precedes: he who knows thus, and he who understands the nature, procedure, and fruit of the *kṛcchra*. By the word "and," it is meant that the previously mentioned fruit belongs to one who performs [the rite] after knowing it, and not merely through the act itself or through knowledge alone. Thus, the fruit should be understood as corresponding to each individual case.

Some maintain that [the destruction of evil] occurs even through each [action] individually; that is incorrect, because the destruction of sin results from the performance [of the rite] itself, and not from knowledge alone. And so Manu says:
"Even though the fruit of the *kataka* tree is a purifier of water,"
The water does not become clear merely by uttering his name. [MDh 6.67] || 26.23 ||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the *Maskarīya-gautama-bhāṣya*.
The twenty-seventh chapter begins:

It has been stated that there are the *kṛcchra*, the *atikṛcchra*, and the *cāndrāyaṇa* penances. Among these, the rule for the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* has been explained. Now, with the intention of explaining the rule for the *cāndrāyaṇa*, he says:
Now, therefore, follows the Cāndrāyaṇa. 27.1.

The word "we shall explain" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The word *atha* (now/then) indicates the commencement of a new topic (*adhikāra*). Because its fruit is equal to that of the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, it does not follow immediately after them. Alternatively, the word *atha* signifies a reason (*hetu*), because this [penance] is connected with such a fruit. *Cāndrāyaṇa* is the name [of the rite]. It is so called because it conforms to the movement of the moon (*anvarthatvāt*). The singular number is used because it refers to the genus (*jāti*). Furthermore, this indicates that the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* and other such rites mentioned in other *smṛtis* constitute a universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). Thus says Manu: "When midday has arrived, one should eat eight mouthfuls..."
With self-restraint, one should perform the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa using sacrificial food.
A twice-born man, having performed his daily rites, should eat four morsels in the morning;
he should eat four when the sun has set—thus he should perform the Śiśu-Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If one who is composed eats eighty-three morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in any manner whatsoever for a month, he attains the same world as the Moon.
And so forth. 27.1.
The rule for that has been stated in the section on the Kṛcchra penance.

Of that [penance] in all its forms, because of the inclusion of the word "that" (tat), the rule—that is, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—has been stated, beginning with "In the first *kṛcchra*, he should stand during the day" [GDh 26.6]. || 27.2 ||
But whatever distinction there is here is now stated: shaving and the observance of vows. (27.3)

If it is a *vrata*, then shaving—the removal of hair and so forth—must be performed. If this is for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), then it constitutes such a rite; for by the word *vrata*, expiation is intended in another Smṛti. As Manu says:
"By these vows, the twice-born who have manifested their sin are to be purified" (MDh 11.226).
And thus, it is made known that if it is for the sake of the unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*), then that [vow] occurs even without shaving.

Others, however, say that this refers to the vow of a student (*brahmacāri*), because it is seen so stated in such passages as, “there are four types of those who observe the vow” (MDh 11.121). On this view, it applies to a householder even in the absence of that [student’s] status. This same principle should be understood to apply to the *kṛcchra* penance and others as well.
To state its own nature, he says:
"One should fast on the day before the full moon. (27.4)
Fasting (upavāsa) is the renunciation of food; the meaning is that one should perform it on the fourteenth day. || 27.4 ||

The satiation is performed with these [verses]: "Swell up" (*āpyāyasva*), "May your milks" (*saṃ te payāṃsi*), and "New, new" (*navo nava*); as well as the oblation of clarified butter and the consecration of the sacrificial food. || 27.5 ||

With these three verses—“Swell up! Let [the waters] come together for you; let your milks come together, let your strengths come together; new, ever-new he becomes as he is born”—one should perform the water-libation (*udakatarpaṇa*), the oblation of ghee, and the consecration (*anumantraṇa*) of the sacrificial food (*havis*) that is about to be described.

Regarding this, some say: because it is accepted that an increase in the constituent parts results in an increase in the fruit, and because there is an extension of the rule for the *kṛcchra* penance, those acts such as the water-libation and so forth which are prescribed for the *raudra* *kṛcchra* by means of the *yajus* formula are to be combined (*samuccīyante*) with these.

That is incorrect; for according to the principle that "that which is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) is set aside by what is directly heard in scripture (*pratyakṣa-śruta*)," its cessation alone is logical. Now, should each [rite] be performed individually according to the respective order of these [mantras], or should everything be performed with them combined?

Others say: because of the singular number in the expression "ājya-homa" (ghee-oblation), one should perform each [rite] individually; for if they were combined, there would be a multiplicity of rites due to the multiplicity of mantras, and consequently, the plural number would result from the distinctness of the oblations. (27.5)
And the attendance upon the moon. || 27.6 ||

By the force of the word "and" (ca), these [rites] themselves must be performed. If that [deity] is not seen, then the rite for the Sun is to be performed, because of the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra: "Suṣumna, the ray of the Sun. Here, because the meanings are different, the worship of the Sun—which would have been obtained through the extension (*atideśa*) of the rule for the *kṛcchra* penance—is set aside. || 27.6 ||
And he should offer oblations with the four verses beginning, "O gods, whatever offense against the gods... (RV 10.2.4–7). || 27.7 ||

With the *ṛc* verses beginning, "Whatever offense against the gods... one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) when no other instruction is given. The mention of the feminine gender and number refers to the meaning of the *ṛc* verses; this is stated to exclude the *yajus* formulas, which are also recited in the Yajurveda in similar forms. Thus, including the preceding [formula], there are five or seven oblations of clarified butter.
And at the end, with the words "devakṛtasya," [he offers] with fuel-sticks. || 27.8 ||

The [mantras] beginning with "devakṛtasya" have been stated [GDh 25.14]. With those mantras, one should perform eight oblations of fuel-sticks (samidh-homa). At the end—that is, at the conclusion of the Cāndrāyaṇa—and by virtue of the word "ca" (and), also at the beginning. 27.8.
"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, tapas, satyam, yaśas, śrīs, ūrj, iḍ, ojas, tejas, puruṣa, dharma, śiva"—with these [words] there is the consecration of the morsels. 27.9.

These fifteen mantras begin with the *praṇava*. With each one of them, in their proper sequence, the consecration (*anumantraṇa*) of the morsels should be performed. The consecration of the sacrificial food (*havis*) was previously mentioned; however, when the final *piṇḍa* is set aside, then the final mantra [is also used]—thus the end of the mantras is to be understood. || 27.9 ||
Or he may offer all of them with the mental recitation of "namaḥ" or "svāhā" for each mantra.

Having performed a salutation or the utterance of *svāhā* for each individual mantra at the end, one should mentally consecrate all morsels of food. There is an option according to one's preference; because of the word "all," the consecration applies to food that has been divided, but not to food that is undivided. Furthermore, these are mantras for consecration (*anumantraṇa*), not mantras for eating (*bhakṣaṇa*). Therefore, having thus consecrated the food, one should eat it. 27.10.
The measure of a mouthful is that which fits without distorting the mouth. || 27.11 ||
The measure [of food] should be just that much by which the mouth is not distorted—that is to say, it should not be opened too wide. || 27.11 ||

Cooked rice, alms-food, barley-meal, grains, barley-gruel, vegetables, milk, curd, ghee, roots, fruits, and water—these sacrificial offerings are increasingly praised in the sequence listed. || 27.12 ||

These are the twelve substances. Among these sacrificial substances (*havirdravya*), each subsequent one is more excellent than the preceding one, because it causes less physical distress. *Caru* is a sacrificial food that must be cooked by oneself; *bhaikṣa* (alms) is that which is obtained by a religious student (*brahmacārin*) or brought for him. The remaining items are well known. The mention of "sacrificial" (*havis*) is for the purpose of indicating that they are to be prepared like a sacrificial offering. From this, the exclusion of salt, molasses, and similar items is established. In that regard, the morsels of the substances are to be formed using a leaf-cup (*puṭikā*), and the distribution should be made according to the principle stated in GDh 19.19: "For heavy persons, heavy [morsels]. 27.12.
Having eaten fifteen morsels on the full moon day, one should eat during the dark fortnight by decreasing the amount by one morsel each day.

Having observed a fast on the fourteenth day and having eaten fifteen morsels of one of these sacrificial foods on the fifteenth day, he should then eat [only] one morsel each day starting from the first day of the dark fortnight until the end of the dark fortnight. The mention of the "latter half" (aparapakṣa) is for the sake of completeness; he should complete the entire fortnight in this manner, rather than filling the required number of days irregularly. Or, it is stated again for the purpose of indicating that this applies even to one who is traveling and eating only once a day. 27.13.
Having fasted on the new moon day, he should pass the fortnight of the waxing moon by increasing [the number of morsels] by one each day.

Then, having observed a fast on the new moon day, one should eat during the bright fortnight by increasing the intake by one morsel starting from the first day of the lunar phase. Thus, on the full moon day, there are fifteen morsels. Because it is thin in the middle, this is called the "ant-middled" (*pipīlikāmadhya*) fast.
For some, it is the opposite. || 27.15 ||

According to the opinion of some teachers, this very [practice] is reversed: having observed a fast on the fourteenth day, one should eat a single morsel on the new moon day (amāvāsyā). Then, beginning from the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), one should eat during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) by increasing the intake by one morsel each day; thus, on the fourteenth day, there are fifteen morsels. Then, there is a fast on the full moon day (paurṇamāsī). On the first day of the next fortnight, there are fifteen morsels; thereafter, one should eat during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) by decreasing the intake by one morsel each day.

Others, however, explain it differently and erroneously: having fasted on the full moon day, one should eat during the dark fortnight beginning from the first day (pratipad) by decreasing the amount by one morsel each day; then, starting from the new moon day, one should eat during the bright fortnight by increasing the amount by one morsel each day. Because it is narrow in the middle, this is called "barley-shaped" (yavamadhya). Therefore, the previously mentioned [method] and this one are respectively "ant-shaped" (pipīlikāmadhya) and "barley-shaped. || 27.15 ||
And this is the Cāndrāyaṇa month.
That by which the moon is followed through its waning and waxing is the *cāndrāyaṇa*; the month associated with that is also called *cāndrāyaṇa*. (27.16)
Having attained this, one who is free from evil and free from sin destroys all transgression. || 27.17 ||

Having performed such a Cāndrāyaṇa, one becomes free from sin (*vipāpa*) through the destruction of the transgression caused by the non-performance of prescribed duties; one becomes free from impurity (*vipāpman*) through the eradication of the defilement caused by the performance of prohibited acts. It destroys all other kinds of sin as well, even that which has entered another body. Thus, it is indicated that the Cāndrāyaṇa must be performed when there is the non-performance of what is prescribed or when one is afflicted by leprosy and similar ailments.
Having attained the second [birth], he purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first, as well as his lineage. || 27.18 ||
The sūtra is explained by its very utterance. || 27.18 ||
But having reached a year [of practice], he attains the same world as the moon; he attains it. 27.19.
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of immediate succession. He goes to *salokatām*, that is, to *sālokya* (the state of being in the same world). || 27.19 ||
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the *Maskarīya-Gautama-bhāṣya*.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.

Regarding the division of inheritance, which was indicated by the sūtras, "The owner [is he who is entitled to] the inheritance, purchase, etc. (GDh 10.38) and "The debt belongs to the heirs" (GDh 12.37), he now explains it.
After the father's death, the sons shall divide the inheritance. 28.1.
Now, why is there no mention [of this] prior to the penance (*prāyaścitta*), as in other cases?

Regarding this, some say: "If sons forcibly urge their father toward partition, or if a father, despite his sons being entitled to perform the rites, does not effect the partition as it has occurred, then for these two there is no penance"—it is for this purpose [that it is mentioned].

However, this is not to be deliberated upon such that an absence of penance would be intended in no case of transgression whatsoever. Therefore, this statement is made solely for the sake of emphasizing the gravity of the penance.

The Sūtra is now explained: "after the father's death" means when he has passed away. And a *ekaśeṣa* (elliptical compound) should be understood, as in the rule "the father with the mother. Thus Manu says:
"After the father and the mother have passed away, the brothers, having come together, shall divide the paternal inheritance; for they have no authority while the two are living. [MDh 9.104]

Because the word *pitṛ* (father) is a relative term, the inclusion of the son (*putra*) is made even though it is already implied; this is for the purpose of specifying that the partition applies only to males. Thus, regarding women, it is heard in the Taittirīyaka Śruti: "Therefore, women are without power and without inheritance" [TaitS 6.5.8.10]. Likewise, regarding eunuchs, Vasiṣṭha says: "But those who have entered another stage of life, as well as the impotent, the insane, and the outcasts, are entitled to no share" [VaDh 17.52]. Although the phrase "after [the father] has lived or desires [to give]" is already understood from the statement [of Gautama], "or while he lives, if he so desires" [GDh 28.2], it is explicitly stated here to demonstrate that it occurs after the performance of the *ekoddiṣṭa* and other funeral rites. *Riktha* refers to paternal property acquired through agriculture and other means, according to conventional usage.
"They should divide. On this point it is deliberated: does ownership exist prior to division, or does ownership arise upon division?
On this matter, some say that it is upon division [that ownership arises].

That is incorrect, because it would follow that all [sons] must divide [the estate]. If it is argued that by virtue of the scriptural statement, the rule applies only to sons, [we reply that this is not so], based on the indicative mark (liṅga) in the verse: “They have no power over the two while they live” (MDh 9.104). Why? Because since the absence of division prior to [the death of] the father and mother is already established by the very rule stating “after the father and the mother,” the fact that the text merely prohibits their power (*īśatva*) indicates the continued existence of ownership (*svatva*). Otherwise, the prohibition would be purposeless, as there would be no possibility for such power to arise. Therefore, division occurs only when ownership exists. If it is then argued that, in the case of one who has already fathered a son, the taking of another’s property would follow because the status of being a son has been transferred, we reply that there is no fault, as it functions in both cases just like birth. Furthermore, due to the prohibition of power, the impossibility of giving away the sons is established as a matter of course. 28.1.
When the mother's menstrual flow has ceased, or when she is living and desires it. || 28.2 ||

Or, even while the father is living, there may be a partition with the mother’s permission once she has ceased her menstrual flow; however, the father’s will prevails, not that of the sons, because of the grammatical coordination [of the word] “while he lives” (*jīvati*) with the subject. This partition should be understood as pertaining to the sons’ eligibility for performing ritual acts.
Or the eldest may maintain all the others like a father. (28.3)

Or rather, the eldest alone, having taken all the wealth, should maintain and support his younger brothers; the meaning is that he should not effect a partition. He should act like a father, just as a father maintains them. This rule is to be understood as applying when the younger brothers lack the capacity to perform religious rites, provided the eldest brother adopts the conduct of an elder brother. 28.4.
But in the case of partition, there is an increase in merit. || 28.4 ||

The word *tu* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Since the increase of merit (*dharma*) occurs through the performance of acts such as giving to guests by each individual, therefore partition alone is more appropriate. This instruction is for the purpose of showing that partition must be made even during childhood, provided there is a difference in intellect. Furthermore, by the mention of "increase," it makes known that merit indeed accrues even to the one who provides the shares. (28.4)
Now, as to how he is to be divided, he says:
"A twentieth part belongs to the eldest; [he receives] a pair [of animals], a chariot yoked on both sides, and a bull. (28.5)

From the entire paternal estate, the twentieth part belongs to the eldest son. A "pair" refers to a well-known pair of cattle. "Animals with two rows of teeth" refers to horses, mules, and donkeys; a chariot yoked with any one of these as available. A "bull" is well known. This preferential share (uddhāra) belongs to the eldest son when it is possible [to provide it]. 28.5.
The one-eyed, the lame, the fraudulent, and the servant—these are the many [subdivisions] of the middle [class]. 28.6.

*Kāṇaḥ* is well known [as one-eyed]. *Khoraḥ* means old; however, if the reading is *khoṭaḥ*, it means one who is deficient in his feet. *Kūṭaḥ* means one who is deficient in horns. *Vaṇṭaḥ* means one whose tail has been cut off. Since no specific distinction is made, this should be understood as applying to all [animals], such as cows, horses, and so forth, according to their respective possibilities. This is the share for the middlemost [son], provided that they are many; the meaning is that there are shares for the others as well. || 28.6 ||
A ram, an iron vessel, a house with a draft-ox, and one of each kind of quadruped for the youngest brother. || 28.7 ||

*Aviḥ* (sheep) is well known. Because of the singular number, there is one; *dhānya* (grain) refers to rice and so forth; *ayaḥ* (iron) is metal. The dual number for grain and iron is used for the purpose of allotting them in proportion. And thus, one should not take everything. One house equipped with a cart, and one each of the quadrupeds such as cows and so forth, separately and in proportion, the younger ones—the youngest—should take. This is the special portion for the youngest (*kaniṣṭhoddhāra*). 28.7.
Everything other than that is concentration (samādhi). 28.8.
Thus, what remains after the preferential shares have been set aside is to be divided equally.

Now, an objection may be raised: since equal division applies to everything by default, once the preferential share has been mentioned in the rule, it follows that the remainder must also be divided equally; therefore, this sūtra is unnecessary.
This is not a fault, for if the father himself performs the partition, this [sūtra] is intended to prohibit the preferential share.

Others, however, say that this [rule] is for the purpose of prohibiting the father’s preferential share (*uddhāra*). And this method is to be understood as applying when both the eldest and the youngest sons are virtuous. (28.8)
Or the first-born may receive two shares. || 28.9 ||
"Two parts" means two shares; that which belongs to him is "two-share-possessing" (dvyaṃśī); the meaning is that two portions constitute the preferential share for the eldest son. || 28.9 ||
Each one [is the cause] of the others. || 28.10 ||
This distinction is to be understood as applicable only if the eldest alone is virtuous while the others are devoid of virtue. || 28.10 ||
Or, each desirable object of wealth shall be obtained by each person in order, starting from the first.

Each person should take one intended category of property in order of seniority; in that case, the taking of a specific desired object itself constitutes the preferential share (*uddhāra*). This rule should also be understood to apply if all [the heirs] are virtuous. (28.11)
Moreover: ten animals. 28.12.

By the phrase "in the form of wealth," since there would otherwise be the possibility of taking only a single animal for the sake of a desired object, this statement—"ten animals are to be taken"—is intended to establish a restriction on the number. (28.12)
In that case as well:
[the rule does not apply] to single-hoofed animals or bipeds. 28.13.

The meaning is that ten each of horses and so forth, as well as ten each of women and so forth, are not to be taken [as a preferential share]. If all are devoid of special qualities (*nirguṇa*), then the division must be made equally; for no distinction is mentioned here, and because another Smṛti text repeats [the rule], that is its purpose. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Now follows the division of inheritance among brothers" (VaDh 17.40). When some are endowed with qualities and others are devoid of them, then the eldest, having taken a tenth part as a preferential share (*uddhāra*), shall divide the remainder equally. As Uśanas says: "A tenth part is the preferential share for the eldest; the intended portion is for the youngest. In this region, this very division is to be observed, according to established custom. 28.13.

The division of those belonging to the same caste who have the same mother has been stated; now, he speaks in order to explain the case of those who, though of the same caste, have different mothers: "The bull is the additional share for the eldest. (28.14)
The eldest son of the youngest wife receives an additional share (*uddhāra*) consisting of a bull; the remainder is to be divided equally. 28.14.
The sixteen-year-old bull belongs to the eldest son of the daughter.
One born of the eldest wife is called *jyaiṣṭhineya*. His special share (*uddhāra*) consists of fifteen cows and one bull; the remainder is divided equally.
He lived in harmony with his younger brother, the son of Vājī and Aikṣvī. || 28.16 ||

This division is indeed equal. Between the eldest son born of the youngest wife by a *jyaiṣṭhineya* (the son of an appointed elder brother) and the younger son born of the eldest wife, the seniority of one is based on the mother and that of the other on birth. This [rule], too, should be understood as applying to those who possess virtuous qualities. 28.16.
Or there may be a specific distribution of shares according to each mother within one's own group. 28.17.

But when there are many wives of the same caste who have children by different husbands, then, because a division based on the sons is difficult to carry out, the inheritance is divided according to the mothers alone. Furthermore, the specific share for each within their own group should be observed; that has been stated in the passage beginning with, "The eldest receives one-twentieth," and so forth. (28.17)
This applies as long as he has sons;

however, for one who has no sons, the father, being childless, should offer oblations to Agni and Prajāpati and, having made an agreement, saying, "This offspring is for my sake," he may designate a daughter as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*).

The father, however, and not even the mother, may relinquish or hand over [the child], but not give him away by legal authority because of his status as a son; for the mantras recited at the taking of the hand are established as applying only to maidens. [MDh 8.226]

And because it has been stated thus: "A *putrikā* is a daughter. "Childless" means one who has no son. Having performed the sacrifice to Agni and Prajāpati—if he is one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*)—it should be understood that he offers two oblations according to the procedure for the *sthālīpāka*. Then, at the time of the gift, having made an agreement with the bridegroom in this manner: "The offspring who shall be born from her is for our sake," when she is thus bestowed, the son who is born belongs to the maternal grandfather and not to the biological progenitor; such is the intended meaning. (28.18)
According to some, she is called "Putrikā" merely by virtue of the [father's] intention. 28.19.

But when it is impossible to carry out the previous injunction, one makes the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) even before the gift—by means of choosing [the bride] and so forth—thinking: "Whatever offspring shall be born of her, that shall be mine. Some maintain that by this alone the status of being a son is established. This alternative should be understood as depending on the possibility [of the circumstances]. (28.19)
Therefore, out of doubt regarding that, one should not marry a woman who has no brothers. || 28.20 ||

Out of apprehension for that [consequence], one should not take all the daughters of anyone who is childless. Why? Because, although "her" (*tām*) should have been said, the text begins with the phrase "one who has no brother" (*abhrātṛkām*). (29.20)
But for him who has not even a daughter appointed as a son (putrikā), his kinsmen related by funeral offerings (piṇḍa), family name (gotra), and ancestral sages (ṛṣi) shall divide the inheritance.

Those connected by the *piṇḍa* (ancestral offering) are the *sapiṇḍas*; in their absence, those connected by the *gotra* (lineage) are the *sagotras*; in their absence, those connected by the *ṛṣi* (progenitor) are the *samānārṣeyas*. Thus, in the absence of one who is proximate, a more distant relative shall be the partaker of that property. || 28.21 ||
And [the inheritance] of a childless woman. 28.22.

This [rule] applies even in the absence of a son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*). Why? Because, under the heading concerning those "without offspring" (*anapatya*)—in the rule "the appointed daughter [is the heir] for one without offspring" (GDh 28.18)—the term "without offspring" is mentioned again. When they, being connected by the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and other rites, should divide the inheritance, then the woman also shall receive a share. From the word "and" (*ca*), the teacher (*ācārya*) and the pupil (*śiṣya*) are included; this is by implication when there is a total absence [of other heirs]. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "In their absence, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*). (28.22)
Or he may seek to obtain seed. || 28.23 ||
Or rather—the meaning is that one should desire seed from a sapinda or other relative, that is, one should procreate offspring; this may be by choice or by obligation. || 28.23 ||
In Devaravatī, he took another-born [son] as one who has no share. || 28.24 ||
When a husband is present, offspring produced by another is not entitled to a share, because it is born of lust; this is an exception to the rule concerning the *kṣetraja* son.
The property of a woman belongs to her daughters who are unmarried and not established in life.

Woman’s property (*strīdhana*) is of six kinds, as Manu has stated: "That which is received at the nuptial fire, that which is received upon being brought home, that which is given as a token of affection, and that which is obtained from her mother, brothers, and father— this is declared to be the sixfold woman’s property" (MDh 9.194).
Furthermore, whatever other property she has acquired through her own labor becomes, upon her death, the property of her unmarried daughters who have no offspring;
others say it belongs to sons who are not established [in life] and have not been married;
still others say it belongs to those who are destitute.

And by the word "ca" (and), [it is implied] "and of the husband. Here, the sequence should be understood as follows: in the absence of unmarried daughters, the sons who are without property shall take [the estate]; in their absence, those who are unmarried; in their absence, childless women; and in the absence of all these, the husband. || 28.25 ||
The sister's dowry belongs to the uterine brothers after the mother's death. 28.26.

The property obtained on account of giving away a sister in the *ārṣa* and *āsura* forms of marriage belongs to the uterine brothers after the mother; that is to say, when she has died. And thus, it is stated that in the absence of the father, the mother alone is intended as the heir.
And some [hold] that it was previously [so]. 28.27.

Some maintain that even before the mother's death, the sister’s fee (śulka) belongs to the uterine brothers. An option regarding this should be understood in view of her conduct. Alternatively, some maintain that as for what was stated previously—"the woman’s property belongs to the daughters" [GDh 28.25]—that applies only after the mother's death, not while she is living. The scope has been explained. 28.27.
The division of the inheritance among the hungry ghosts belongs to the eldest son.

When brothers who are ununited and divided carry on separate affairs, if one among them dies childless, from what source [does his share come]? Because the section concerns those who are childless: that share belongs only to his own respective eldest brother, not to all; he is equal to a father. As for those born of two mothers—whether of the same caste or of different castes—and those who have not been separated by their mother, that share belongs only to the eldest of each respective group. 28.28.
When a *saṃsṛṣṭin* has died, the *saṃsṛṣṭin* is the heir to the inheritance.

But he who, even though partitioned, is reunited again due to necessity, becomes a sharer in that [reunited] portion. The repetition of the word "again" (punaḥ) is for the sake of including uterine brothers; for others, it remains as previously established. || 28.29 ||
That which is born of a divided estate belongs to the father alone.

By the rule, “When the mother’s menses have ceased,” [GDh 28.2], if a son is later born after the sons have already divided the inheritance and performed the marriage rites, he shall receive only the paternal share. Thus, in the case of partition while the father is still living, it follows as a matter of course that the father also possesses a share. Even then, according to another Smṛti text stating, “Two shares for the father,” two shares for the father are to be understood. (28.30)
A physician may, at his own discretion, not give what he has earned himself to those who are unlearned in the medical science.

However, that which is acquired by oneself without depleting the father’s property—whether through medical practice or by means of receiving gifts and the like—one need not give to the others at will, according to one's desire. As Manu says:
"That which one acquires by one's own labor without depleting the father’s property, being obtained through one's own efforts, one is not obliged to give if one does not wish to do so."
"But whatever constitutes the wealth of knowledge belongs to that person alone as their own wealth," and so forth. [MDh 9.206, 208] 28.31.
Those who are unlearned shall divide [the estate] equally. 28.32.
However, whatever the foolish sons might earn through agriculture and other such means, they should divide that equally. Thus it has been said:
"But if wealth should accrue from exertion to all those who are unlearned, the division therein shall be equal; for that is not the paternal estate—such is the settled rule" (MDh 9.205).

And although this is established by the sense of the matter, it is stated for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*); consequently, one does not give even an unequal amount to a non-physician, and even if it is taken from a non-physician, the physician gives only an equal amount. // 28.32 //

Since it is stated that "sons shall divide the inheritance" (GDh 28.1), one might think that this traditional rule applies only to legitimate sons born of the wife (*aurasa*). To prevent this, he says: "Sons—the legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*), the son begotten on the wife (*kṣetraja*), the adopted son (*dattaka*), the made son (*kṛtrima*), the son secretly born (*gūḍhotpanna*), and the cast-off son (*apaviddha*)—are the sharers of the inheritance. (28.33)
The *aurasa* son is one who is procreated by oneself upon one's own wife. Thus Manu says:
"That son whom one procreates oneself in one’s own consecrated field (wife), one should know him as the *aurasa*, the first-enumerated son" (MDh 9.166).
The *kṣetraja* (field-born) son is he who is procreated through the means of *niyoga*. As Manu says:
"He who is born on the wife of one deceased, impotent, or diseased, by one duly appointed according to the sacred law, is known as the *kṣetraja* son" (MDh 9.167).
That which is given by another through formal acceptance; as Manu says:
"The son whom the mother or the father may give with water in times of distress—one who is similar [in status] and given with affection—he is to be known as the *dattrima* (given) son. [MDh 9.168]
The *kṛtrima* (artificial son) is one who is made [your son], as in: "You are my son. As Manu says:
"But he whom one may make similar, devoid of [the father's] virtues and defects, yet endowed with the qualities of a son—he is to be known as the *kṛtrima*. [MDh 9.169]

"Born in secret" (*gūḍhotpanna*) means one who has been produced in concealment. Where the progenitor (*bījī*) is not known, he belongs to the caste of the mother because the progenitor is unknown. The same applies to the son born of a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*) and the son of an appointed daughter (*kānīna*). As it is said: "He whose birth in the house is not known to belong to anyone—he is one born in secret in the house; he shall belong to him whose wife gave birth to him" (MDh 9.170).
One who has been abandoned—that is, cast off by another—is taken up by someone else with full awareness. As it is said:
"A son whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by both his parents or by either of them is called an *apaviddha* (abandoned son). [MDh 9.171]
These are the heirs to the inheritance. 28.33.

The son of an unmarried woman, the son received with a pregnant bride, the son of a remarried woman, the son of an appointed daughter, the son given himself, and the son bought are entitled to share the family lineage. 28.34.
The *kānīna* is one born of an unmarried girl (*kanyā*); he belongs to him who marries her. Thus it is said:
"A son whom an unmarried girl may bear in secret in her father’s house, one should call by the name *kānīna*; he originates from the maiden and belongs to the husband" (MDh 9.172).
The *sahoḍha* is born when the woman is married while already pregnant. As Manu says:
"If a woman who is pregnant, whether her condition be known or unknown, is married, that child belongs to the one who marries her; he is called *sahoḍha* in this world" (MDh 9.173).
The *paunarbhava* is the son of an unchaste woman. He belongs to that man who, having remarried her, begets a son upon her. As Manu says:
"She who has been abandoned by her husband, or who is a widow, or even one who acts of her own accord—having become a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman), the son she bears is called *paunarbhava*."
"If she be one whose virginity is intact, or even one who has returned after having gone away, she deserves to undergo the marriage rite again with a husband born of remarriage.
[MDh 9.175–76] The son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) has been mentioned previously. The "self-given" (*svayandatta*) is he who offers himself of his own accord. Thus it is said:

"One who is deprived of his mother and father, or has been abandoned without cause, and who offers himself to someone—that is known as *svayaṃdatta* (self-given). [MDh 9.177] "Bought" means one who has been acquired through wealth. As Manu said:

"He who may purchase from his mother or father for the sake of offspring—whether he be similar or dissimilar to him—that son is his 'purchased' (krītaka) son. (MDh 9.174). The meaning is that these [other sons] partake of the lineage (*gotra*) and perform the offering of water and other rites for the sake of the status of a son. And thus, these do not partake of the inheritance; however, the preceding ones partake both of the inheritance and of the lineage. Why is this so? Because they are mentioned together with the legitimate (*aurasa*) son, and because of other Smṛti texts.

"The legitimate son (aurasa), the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), the adopted son (datta), the made son (kṛtrima), the son secretly born (gūḍhotpanna), and the cast-off son (apaviddha)—these six are heirs and kinsmen. [MDh 9.159] "Kinsmen" means those who share the lineage (gotra). Since the right to share the lineage follows directly from being a son, that statement here is intended to exclude their right to inherit property. Furthermore, since their right to inherit is excluded when the legitimate son and the others exist, these other sons—by virtue of being sons—are entitled only to food and clothing when the legitimate son and the rest are present. As it has been said:
"However, it is just for a wise man to give to all of them according to his ability food and clothing for life; for he who does not give becomes an outcast. (MDh 9.202).
In the absence of such [means], however, he indeed becomes an heir to the estate, because he serves as a substitute for a son. As it has been said:

"Wise men declare these eleven sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja*, as described above, to be substitutes for a son (*putrapratinidhi*) to prevent the omission of religious rites" (MDh 9.180). Furthermore, a substitute yields the full fruit when the primary substance is absent, just as the *pūtīka* plant does in the absence of *soma*. The mention of the daughter’s son (*putrikāputra*) here is for the purpose of establishing his right to the family lineage (*gotra*). However, his right to the inheritance (*rikthabhāktva*) indeed exists even when a legitimate son (*aurasa*) is present, as Manu has stated: [Manu 9.136] "The son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), who is equal to a legitimate son, shall take the paternal estate; he shall offer the funeral cakes to his own father and to his mother's father. [Manu 9.142] "But if a legitimate son is born after that, he shall take four shares; the other [the daughter’s son], having obtained the status of a son through the agreement, shall take a single share. [Manu 9.173] "The son of an appointed daughter, being equal to a legitimate son, shall receive the paternal wealth; he shall offer the funeral cakes to his own father and to his mother's father. [

"But if a son is born after a daughter has been appointed, the division there shall be equal, for there is no seniority for a woman. [MDh 9.134] The reason the son of a Śūdra wife is not mentioned here is either because he is not a legitimate (aurasa) son or because he is not an heir to the estate. Thus it is said:
The son of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya is not an heir to the estate;
whatever his father may give him, that alone shall be his wealth. [MDh 9.155] || 28.34 ||
In the absence of a legitimate son and the others, the one entitled to a fourth part [receives it]. 28.35.

In the absence of the six [sons] beginning with the legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*), the son born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*) and the others are entitled to a fourth share, or they may take the entire inheritance; this is indicated by the word "or" (*vā*). Thus says Śaṅkha: "The acquired property goes to the eldest; in his absence, to the *kṣetraja* and the son of the appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*); in their absence, to the other three; and in their absence, to the six [remaining sons]. Others, however, say that the phrase "in the absence of the legitimate son of the body and the rest" refers to the meaning of the subsequent sūtra. Consequently, the *kānīna* and the others are entitled to a fourth part, or they are merely entitled to subsistence. (28.35)
The division of property for sons born of wives of the same caste has been stated. Now he declares the specific rule regarding sons born of wives of different castes:
"The eldest son of a Brāhmaṇa born of a Kṣatriya wife, if endowed with good qualities, shares equally [with his brothers]. (28.36)
The son of a Brāhmaṇa born of a Kṣatriya woman, if he is the eldest and endowed with good qualities, shares an equal portion with the younger son born of a Brāhmaṇa wife.
The other [shares] are diminished by the eldest's share. 28.37.

The "extra portion" (*uddhāra*) for the eldest, previously mentioned in the passage beginning with "the twentieth part belongs to the eldest" (GDh 28.5), is excluded; he shall receive the other property equally. The meaning is that there is no preferential share. Although the reference is primarily to the property itself, nevertheless, by the force of the initial statement, only the prohibition of the eldest's special share is intended here. Otherwise, it would have been necessary to say, "one endowed with virtues receives the eldest's share"; thus, one devoid of virtues does not receive an equal share. In this regard, the statement of Manu should be consulted.
"A Brahmin son shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share. [MDh 9.153]

If it is argued that a prohibition has been stated regarding the son of a Śūdra woman, it is replied: the prohibition applies to one born of a woman whose virginity (*akṣatayoni*) has been violated. One born of a woman whose virginity is intact is entitled to a share. Since [the status of] being born of a woman whose virginity has been violated can indeed occur through means such as being the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the phrase "for those who lack an *aurasa* son and so forth" is the implied remainder. Those [authorities] explain that in the absence of an *aurasa* son and the others, this [son of a Śūdra woman] shares equally. When those [other sons] exist, the rule stated in another *Smṛti* should be observed. Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "The son of a Brāhmaṇī wife shall take three shares; the son of a Rājanyā wife, two shares; the others shall divide the remainder equally" (VaDh 17.48–50). An alternative application depending on conduct (*vṛtta*) should be understood here. (28.37)
In a case where there is a gathering of sons born of a Kṣatriya woman and a Vaiśya woman, it is the same as with the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman.

When the son of the Vaiśya woman is endowed with excellent qualities and is the eldest, while the son of the Kṣatriya woman is younger and there is no son of the Brāhmaṇī at all, then just as that son of the Kṣatriya woman shares equally with the son of the Brāhmaṇī, so too the son of the Vaiśya woman shares equally with the son of the Kṣatriya woman, being deprived of the additional share due to seniority. And thus, in this case, it is made known that the additional share for seniority belongs to the eldest son of the Kṣatriya woman. (28.38)
If [the woman] is a Kṣatriya. 28.39.

"The son of a Vaiśya woman who is the eldest and endowed with good qualities shall have an equal share"—so it is stated. This means that even from a Kṣatriya father, if the son of the Vaiśya woman is the eldest, he receives an equal share with the younger son of the Kṣatriya woman. Some say that the same should be understood regarding the son of a Śūdra woman from a Vaiśya father; however, that is incorrect, because it has been so stated by Manu. (28.39)
Even the son of a Śūdra woman shall, if he is obedient, receive a means of subsistence from one who has no other offspring, according to the rule for a pupil.

Even for a Brāhmaṇa who has no son of the twice-born caste, one born from a Śūdra womb shall receive only so much as is necessary for him to be capable of performing tasks such as agriculture, provided he is intent on service like a pupil; the meaning is that he should follow his brother and his brother’s wife as he would a teacher, because the rule for a *antevāsī* (resident pupil) is characterized by specific service. Regarding the statement "a fourth part [of the estate] for his offspring" and so forth—why? If it is argued that this is because of the mention of one born from a "defiled womb" (*kṣatayoni*), [the answer is: because of the word *api* (even), which implies reproach, he is entitled to a share in this case as well. (28.40)
Even the son of a woman of all castes (sarvarṇā), if he behaves unrighteously, would not receive [the inheritance], according to some.

Even the son of a woman of the same caste—even by the force of the word "even," it follows that an eldest son who is ill-behaved also falls; some maintain that he would not receive a share. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "But those who have entered another stage of life, as well as the impotent, the insane, and the outcaste, are entitled to no share" (VaDh 17.52–53). The Teacher [Baudhāyana] maintains that he *would* receive a share. This alternative depends on whether or not he can be reformed. (28.41)
The Vedic scholars shall divide the inheritance of a childless Brāhmaṇa.

"Learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriyāḥ*) means those who are advanced in the knowledge of the three Vedas, not merely those who study the *Chāndogya* alone. Thus Manu says: "Those learned in the three Vedas, pure and self-controlled," and so forth (*MDh* 9.188). "Heirs of one without offspring" means heirs of one for whom no son exists. They shall divide the inheritance with the permission of the king, as the mention of the "king" occurs later in the text. (28.42)
For others than kings, [the rule is] as follows. || 28.43 ||
In the absence of all these, the king alone shall take [the property] from the Kṣatriyas and the other castes.
The dull-witted and the impotent should be maintained. || 28.44 ||

The *jaḍa* is one whose mind is impaired; the *klība* is one of the third gender. These two must be maintained by providing food and clothing. This is also an elliptical designation for those who are mute and so forth. Thus Manu says:

"Those who are impotent (*klība*) or outcastes (*patita*), as well as those born blind or deaf, the insane, the *jaḍa*, the mute, and whoever are devoid of sense organs, do not receive a share. (MDh 9.201) || 28.44 ||
The offspring of a fool is entitled to a share. || 28.45 ||

The offspring of one who is mentally deficient (*jaḍa*) is entitled to a share. By the inclusion of the term "entitled" (*arha*), it is meant that he receives a share if he is capable, and not merely by virtue of being the offspring of a deficient person. Although one might have expected the expression "the offspring of a deficient person" (*jaḍāpatyam*) to be used, the use of an irregular compound (*visamāsa*) is intended to include the offspring born of the wives of eunuchs and others. Thus Manu says:
"If, however, there should somehow be a desire for wives on the part of eunuchs and the like, their offspring, having continued the lineage, is entitled to a share. (MDh 9.203)

From this very indicative mark (*liṅga*), one may infer their sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) as far as possible. Otherwise, since they have fallen from the *Sāvitrī*, their offspring would indeed be utterly unworthy. Or rather, it should be understood as referring to one who has performed the penance (*prāyaścitta*). And thus, that which was previously permitted even for one who had fallen [from caste] should also be understood as referring to one who has performed the penance. By speaking in this way, he makes known this: that even after the time of partition, a share must be given to that [offspring]. (28.45)
As in the case of the son of a Śūdra woman, so it is with those born from women in the reverse order of castes.

The meaning is that even for those born of women in the inverse order (pratiloma) who are intent on service, the means of subsistence should be given just as it is for the son of a Śūdra. In that regard, since service is possible for Caṇḍālas and others, it should be understood that they are to be given an even lower [means of subsistence]. Thus, it should be understood that this same rule applies to those born in the inverse order as well. || 28.46 ||
There is no division regarding food prepared for the sake of water and security. 28.47.
Water refers to wells and the like. *Yoga* is what is desired (*iṣṭa*), while *kṣema* is what is performed for public welfare (*pūrta*). Thus says Lokākṣi:
"Those who perceive reality declare that *kṣema* is *pūrta* and *yoga* is *iṣṭa*; moreover, these two are said to be indivisible, as are beds and food."

When cooked food has been prepared for the sake of a festival, there is no fault [in giving it] because of the mention of "prepared" [food], as this applies to rice and other such items; in these cases, there is no division. Regarding that, some hold that like the bed, the rice and other items should be given to one person alone; others desire them to be given to either the eldest or the youngest. It should be understood that other items are to be kept for the group as a whole. (28.47)
And [the same applies] when women are united [with others]. || 28.48 ||

And as for those women who have been taken by fathers—who are free from fear of the next world—for the purpose of sexual enjoyment, one might ask: "Why is their lack of fault not accepted? If this is asked, it is because an expiation is heard in the rule: "For men, there is death in the case of [intercourse with] a woman of lower caste" (GDh 28.46). Furthermore, there is no partition of property among them with the sons. The intention is that food and clothing must be given to them when they are old, and [the husband] should go to other [wives]. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), other things are also included which, due to their singular nature, cannot be divided. As Manu has said:
"Garments, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women,
security of possession (yogakṣema), and pasture land— they declare these to be indivisible.
When a matter is not already known, it should be performed as recommended by at least ten learned men who possess the capacity for reasoning and are free from greed. 28.49.

"Known" (*ājñāta*) means understood; its opposite is "unknown" (*anājñāta*). Regarding that which has not been correctly understood or is subject to doubt, [the decision must be made] by at least ten people—meaning, by no fewer than ten—who are "learned" (*śiṣṭa*), that is, those who have understood the meaning of the Vedas. As Manu says:

"But those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements (*paribṛṃhaṇa*), has been mastered in accordance with the Dharma—they are to be known as learned *brāhmaṇas*, the direct authorities for the revealed scripture (*śruti*). (MDh 12.109)

"By those possessing reasoning" (ūhavadbhiḥ) means by those capable of inclusion and exclusion (ūhāpoha), that is, by those whose intellects have been refined through the study of the Mīmāṃsā and other sciences. "By the ungreedy" (alubdhaiḥ) means by those free from craving. "Praised" (praśastam) means commended, as in "this is appropriate here. "That should be done" (tat kāryam) means it is to be performed; the intention is that it must be carried out in their presence. || 28.49 ||
Four who have mastered the four Vedas, three of whom are the foremost; and three ascetics who each know the Dharma separately—these ten at minimum they call an assembly (pariṣad). || 28.50 ||

Only Brāhmaṇas, because they alone have the authority (*adhikāra*) for the proclamation of Dharma. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "A Brāhmaṇa should proclaim the Dharmas" (VaDh 1.40). There must be four, not just one, even if he is a knower of the four Vedas (*caturveda*). They are those who have mastered the four Vedas along with their secret portions (*sarahasya*), that is, those who have studied the Vedas together with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*). The "highest" refers to the first three stages of life (*āśrama*), as described in the third chapter. The mention of "stages of life" is made so that the term "Brāhmaṇas" alone might not be understood [to exclude others]. These too are accepted only if they know the meaning of the Vedas, for those who lack such knowledge have no authority. However, this was stated with reference to the performance of their own specific duties (*svadharma*). The "three who know the separate treatises on Dharma" (*pṛthag-dharmaśāstra-jña*) means three, not just one, even if he knows all Dharmas. And these are mentioned separately by taking into account their status as knowers of the Vedas and their belonging to the stages of life. The learned call an assembly (*pariṣad*) consisting of at least these ten members. This is also for the sake of providing consistency with other Smṛtis. Furthermore, it is intended to include groups of three or more in the absence of these [ten]. And so says Manu:

"Whatever dharma an assembly of at least ten members may determine, or even one of at least three who are established in virtuous conduct—that dharma one should not unsettle. Thus [says Manu, MDh 12.110]. Likewise, Vasiṣṭha also says:
"Whatever four or even three who have mastered the Vedas may declare, that should be known as Dharma, and not the opinion of thousands of others. (VaDh 3.7).
In this regard, it should be understood that when a large number is impossible, a small number may be accepted. 28.50.
But in the absence of these, whatever a learned man who knows the Veda and is disciplined says when there is a conflict of opinions. || 28.51 ||

"That" is to be supplied as "that [assembly] is to be performed. The word *tu* (but/however) serves for emphasis. It means that these [qualities] must be present without exception; it does not mean that even a few of them may be absent as long as some are possible. Although the word *vā* (or) already establishes the alternative of absence—as in the phrase "or one who is not learned in the Vedas"—this specific instruction is given to indicate that [the assembly is valid] when all those previously mentioned qualities are impossible, and not merely when there is an impossibility of having a group of ten or more. A *śrotriya* is one who has mastered the entirety of the Vedas, not merely one who studies the mantras and brāhmaṇas mentioned in other Smṛtis, because extensive recitation is what is intended here. In this context, a "knower of the Veda" (*vedavit*) is one who knows its meaning. The term *śrotriya* is used because one is seen to know the meaning even without excellence in the textual recitation. A *śiṣṭa* is one who abides by his own duty (*svadharma*). Even if there is a disagreement—that is, a difference of opinion—even a single such person is an authority.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because Yama and Prabhava are the causes of living beings. (28.52)

Because from the Veda arise both [the cessation and the engagement of worldly existence]—whereby the word *yama* denotes the cessation of *saṃsāra* and the word *prabhava* denotes its very commencement—and because the means for both are understood through the Veda, the Veda is the authority in cases of conflicting opinions. As Manu said:
"The four castes, the three worlds, and the four stages of life separately;
the past, the present, and the future—all these have attained their established proof from the Veda" (MDh 12.97).
And the mention of "Yama" at the beginning is for the purpose of making it known that the cessation of saṃsāra is the supreme goal of human life.
Furthermore: "In matters of harming or favoring others... (28.53).

"The Veda alone is the authority"—this is the completion of the sentence. Regarding the connection with violence—namely, in the case of "these animals and so forth are to be killed in sacrifice"—and regarding the application of favor—namely, in the case of "all [classes], beginning with Brāhmaṇas, are to be favored"—the Veda alone is the authority. And by means of that, the intended meaning is "one who knows the Veda. (28.54)
Now he states the fruit of the knowledge of Dharma: "The knower of Dharma, by virtue of his specific qualities, attains the heavenly world through both knowledge and resolute application. (28.54)

The *dharmin* is one who possesses only dharma; the intention is that he remains so specifically until the dissolution of the world (*pralaya*). A *dharmavit* is one who, having known [the dharma], puts it into practice. Why? Because of the mention of "knowledge" (*jñāna*). "Adherence" (*abhiniveśa*) refers to its performance. And thus Vasiṣṭha says: "One who is righteous" (*dhārmika*), and so forth. (28.54)
Thus, this is the Dharma, the Dharma. || 28.55 ||
"Beginning with 'The Veda is the root of Dharma' (GDh 1.1) and ending with this [verse], the remainder of the sentence is that the designation 'Dharma' belongs to Gautama. || 28.55 ||
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the Purāṇa-Maskarīya-Gautama-Bhāṣya;
and this composition of Gautama, the Maskarīya-Bhāṣya, is complete.
